# Feedzai Pulse

Feedzai Pulse is a cutting-edge enterprise data science platform that integrates big data analytics and machine learning techniques with a native runtime production environment to fight financial crime in real time. Feedzai combines in a single enterprise platform all the critical tools needed to manage data science projects across their entire life cycle. Pulse is designed with an open and flexible data architecture. This makes it a powerful platform to solve any number of different business use cases across financial institutions and merchants.

On this page

# About Pulse

Was this page helpful?Â 

The Feedzai Platform processes events to detect and remediate financial crime. In the life cycle of the events, Pulse performs two main roles:

  * At its core, Pulse comprises a **Real-Time Risk Engine** that processes and scores events for the different use cases, makes an automated decision about them and triggers alerts if necessary.
  * Pulse also functions as a **Data Science Studio** for the Feedzai Platform, providing a user interface for data scientists to create rules and models that will be used by the Risk Engine to detect financial crime and suspicious activities.



Pulse in the Feedzai Platform context

## Main functionalitiesâ

The following sections describe Pulse's main components and their functionalities.

### Source Data Modelingâ

With **Source Data Modeling** capabilities, Pulse supports a schema-agnostic architecture, making it easy to customize the schemas of master data streams for each business use case. Data scientists and engineers can use the built-in data analysis tools to validate data schemas, clean data and analyze datasets quickly.

Pulse automatically analyzes imported datasets, creating field mappings and histograms that identify patterns and provide insights into the data. These insights can be used to identify parameters which can be used to enhance the projects. Data scientists and engineers can create stratified samples and natively design new features that are semantically equivalent both at model training and at runtime.

### Segment-of-One Profile Engineâ

One of the most powerful concepts within the platform, **Segment-of-One Profiles** allow Pulse to create hundreds of granular profiles, for different attributes in an event, rather than just estimating behavioral correlations.

This means that events can be scored using each Segment-of-One attribute within the data stream, making the results become significantly more precise.

For example, instead of evaluating a single debit transaction against a cohort of other similar debit cards (e.g. Visa Debit cards from ABC Bank), Segment-of-One will allow Pulse to, in just a few minutes, build a profile for every single debit card. Finally, Pulse evaluates the incoming event against these profiles, which can number in hundreds or even thousands.

### Data Science Studioâ

Pulseâs **Data Science Studio** is the ultimate unified toolset for any data science team. It simplifies many aspects of traditional data science work, effectively making it accessible to other user profiles including fraud and business analysts.

Data scientists now have a powerful, yet easy to use, design studio to build data science projects and train [machine learning models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models). Teams can collaborate together on projects, share insights and improve outcomes, focusing on the real data science and not on the tooling and infrastructure.

**Data transformations** can be developed to create new [data sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) and [metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric) that can be used in models and runtime workflows.

[**Plans**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) allow data science teams to quickly and easily transform data, combine data sources, and natively deploy these transformations to the runtime environment.

### Machine Learning Modelsâ

Pulse is designed to support all stages and iterations of the data science loop. The main end goals of this data science work are to efficiently iterate and train **machine learning models** , visually evaluating and easily comparing them.

As the data scientist uncover patterns, understand and transform data, Pulse lets them go even further by easily enriching events with simple features, metrics and any other advanced derived features.

Models are continuously retrained with new data as events are processed and alerts are decisioned. This native retraining of models allow financial institutions and merchants to evolve models and adapt to changing consumer behavior rapidly.

### Rule Engineâ

A simplified **Rule Engine** and its respective management UI allow data science teams to develop any detection and decision rules needed to optimize the performance of their projects. This adds an extra layer of depth to machine learning models.

Similarly to models in the data science loop, Pulse extends the same iterative approach to the development and evaluation of rules.

The performance of rules can be evaluated in real time, making it possible to iterate over them and achieve optimal outcomes. The engine is able to execute any rule in real time, regardless of its complexity, including access to Segment-of-One Profiles, or sequence in the execution workflow.

### Workflow Orchestratorâ

Pulse **Workflows** define the step-by-step process that the Real-Time Risk Engine follows when processing events. Workflows deploy the data science work seamlessly by combining data, plans, models and rules to drive real-time outcomes.

In Pulse, deploying a model into production takes hours instead of months. Users are able to leverage Segment-of-One Profiles in models and rules, and execute all data science work on a single platform without the need for creating new custom code. Pulse's integrated runtime environment ensures that the result of the data science loop is ready to go into production and yield the same decisions as observed at design time.

Pulse's execution engine consists of a series of high performance enterprise services that operate symbiotically in real time to process and score events with sub-millisecond latency.

## Feedzai IQâ

In addition to the advanced data science capabilities, Pulse also offers the option to leverage **Feedzai IQ** , a suite of ready-to-adopt risk assessment solutions providing AI-powered insights based on aggregated intelligence from across the Feedzai global network.

**Feedzai IQ** can be used out of the box without requiring any [data preparation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data), [model training](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/), or [historical data collection](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data), thus enabling rapid deployment and immediate value realization without extensive data science work, and saving potentially months of lead time.

Specifically, Feedzai IQ provides **TrustScore** , a federated risk score that encompasses the insights and patterns from Feedzaiâs global footprint to enable real-time scoring of fraud and financial crime risk.

### TrustScoreâ

Feedzai **TrustScore** is a federated machine learning model that provides a real-time risk score for every event processed by Pulse, with high accuracy and lower false positive rates than traditional rules, based on global risk patterns aggregated through the Feedzai community.

TrustScore models are continuously updated and fine-tuned, reacting quickly to changes in the fraud landscape.

#### Federated learningâ

The training of the TrustScore models is done by Feedzai within its machine learning infrastructure, gathering insights from the diverse range of financial risk patterns across its entire client base, by means of federated learning techniques. These techniques allow financial inteligence sharing while keeping the data segregated and confidential within each customerâs environment.

The federated learning approach works by using [aggregations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#aggregation) from across the Feedzai network to train models which are kept isolated from each other. These models are later deployed to process real-time data streams in production environments. When a new transaction or event occurs in a client's production environment, it is simultaneously analyzed by all these specialized expert models. The resulting federated scores are aggregated via quality-aware weighting algorithms, producing a single, accurate and privacy-preserving TrustScore for each event.

#### Risk Strategy integrationâ

**TrustScore** is available for deployment as a ready-to-use risk score, either standalone or as part of a broader risk strategy. It can be seamlessly plugged into [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) or [combined](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/outcome-combinator) with other signals for a more comprehensive risk assessment.

It can also be used as a starting point for developing custom [models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), or as an additional input to influence an existing risk scoring model.

## Administrationâ

Pulse includes an **Administration** module for system administrators to easily configure and maintain the platform. System administrators are able to set up environments quickly, configure clusters, and deploy Pulse in high availability configurations.

Pulse's security framework supports granular security configuration and access control. Access management and permissions can be configured within Feedzai.

## Getting started with Feedzai Pulseâ

Feedzai Pulse is a state-of-the-art and very complex platform. It is designed to fully support tasks for different user profiles while abstracting away most of this complexity and making sure that users do not become overwhelmed with the amount of possibilities.

Now that you have a glimpse of what Feedzai Pulse is, you can read more about the [core concepts](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts) to further understand how Pulse works and what you can accomplish with this platform.

# Security Entities

This section gives you a high-level overview of the main security components or entities that exist in Pulse.

Security in Pulse has four core entities, each with its purpose:

  * Permissions
  * Roles
  * Groups
  * Users



Together they provide a flexible and comprehensive security model.

## Permissionsâ

In Pulse, permissions are used for controlling access to resources. For example, the permission `application:apps:create` allows the creation of a new application.

Pulse already comes with a list of predefined internal permissions. They can be used when creating roles.

A full list with all the permissions in Pulse can be found on the [List of Permissions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/permissions) page.

### Permission contextsâ

Permissions have the following structure: `<context>:[<resource>]:[<right>]`.

For example, to allow a user to create a sandbox evaluations within the application context, the user must have the `application:sandbox_evaluations:create` permission.

The permission contexts are the following:

  * **admin** \- All things related to administration (e.g. configuration, deployment, etc). This context is intended only for system administrators.
  * **application** \- This is the context of all resources (e.g. data science models, rules, schemas, etc).
  * **pulseviews** \- This is the context for UI-related actions (e.g. login, tab management, etc).
  * **security** \- Security-related actions belong to this context (e.g. creating users, groups, etc).



Warning

To log in, users must have the `pulseviews:login` permission.

## Rolesâ

A role is a set of permissions. Each user or group can have many roles. If a user belongs to a group, it has all the roles of that group.

Roles are typically created to ease the management of permissions. For instance, the update permissions of different resources can belong to a single role called _updater-role_. From now on, we can use the _updater-role_ to refer to all update permissions, instead of using individual permissions.

### Default rolesâ

Pulse already has some roles created by default. These roles can be selected when creating a new user from the Administration view:

  * **admin** \- The administration role. It has permissions to do everything.
  * **pulseviews** \- This role can view, update and delete all resources, but it only has view rights over security.
  * **pulseviews-reader** \- This role can only read resources, nothing more.
  * **developer** \- The user with this role has permissions to do everything except system administration.



The following table shows the permissions for each default role.

Permission name| Permission| pulseviews| pulseviews-reader| developer| admin  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
Group hierarchy read| security:ownership:read| | | |   
Role read| security:roles:read| | | |   
Permissions read| security:permissions:read| | | |   
Tenant read| security:tenants:read| | | |   
Tenant domain read| security:tenantdomains:read| | | |   
Pulseviews all| pulseviews:*| | | |   
Pulseviews login| pulseviews:login| | | |   
Application all CRUD| application:*| | | |   
Application all read| application:*:read| | | |   
Management tabs all| pulseviews:management:tabs:*| | | |   
History read (single resource)| application:history:resource:read| | | |   
History read (application-wide)| application:history:global:read| | | |   
Everything| *| | | |   
  
## Groupsâ

A group is a security component that can have multiple roles. Not only that, they also provide a hierarchical way to control access to resources.

The hierarchical structure of groups is what makes them a powerful authorization abstraction, because **a group can do, at least, everything that its descendants do**.

Roles are not propagated

If User A belongs to a child group that can update a given hierarchy, User B, belonging to a parent group, will also be able to do it. The only exception to this rule is if User B does not have the static permission to update hierarchies. Groups entitle static permissions via roles but these are not propagated in any way through the group hierarchy.

### Theoretical use caseâ

An easy way to understand how groups behave is to map them to an hypothetical company organizational positions. Each group is a position occupied by some employees. An employee in a management position can see the work items of its subordinates, but the reverse is not true.

Consider the following positions of an hypothetical company.

And consider some of that company employees connected to their respective positions. The connections between users and groups can be read as: Lisa _**is a**_ Managing Director.

Now imagining Lisa has some reports she wants to share with specific positions, lets see how she can accomplish that using groups.

  * **Human Resources Report** \- Peter, Kate and any future HR worker should be able to see it, so this report should be visible to the group '_HR Worker_ '. Notice that both Carl and Lisa will be able to see this report. Also notice that besides being respectively '_HR Salaries Worker_ ' and '_Hiring Worker_ ', both Peter and Kate must also be '_HR Worker_ '.
  * **Salaries Report** \- This report should be visible for all workers responsible by salaries, so it should be visible to the groups '_Finance Salaries Worker_ ' and '_HR Salaries Worker_ '. This report will be visible to Arthur, Mary, Peter and their superiors, John, Carl and Lisa.
  * **Arthur Performance Report** \- This report should only be visible to Arthur and his bosses. This is not a good use-case for groups because in order to solve it, a new child group of '_Finance Manager_ ' called '_Arthur (Finance)_ ' has to be created and linked to Arthur. If the report is then made visible to this group, both Arthur and his superiors will be able to see it.



### Example use caseâ

Consider the following scenario, a card brand company provides different data to issuers and acquirers, in their turn, each acquirer will only have access to a subset of that data, and so on. A possible groups hierarchy to map this scenario could be as follows.

Considering the structure above, deploying Pulse in this company to **provide services to other companies** is just a matter of assigning users to each position and sharing them with other companies. Each application resource must then be given the correct visibility so that only users of those particular groups can see it.

## Usersâ

A user is usually associated with "someone" using Pulse. It is used to prove the entity is who it says it is, through **authentication** , and to make sure it has the rights to do what it is trying to do, through **authorization**.

Users can have both **roles** and **groups**. Roles are usually associated with a user to define its **static permissions**. That is, permissions that **always** apply to a user, and that cannot be controlled for each application or resource instance. On the other hand, groups can be used to specify **per-instance permissions** , and are used to control the visibility a user will have over each resource instance, see [Securing Metadata](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/securing-metadata).

warning

A user can be authenticated through external authentication. In this case, the password field is not required.

### Managing users and credentialsâ

Pulse has several features designed to help manage users and their credentials. These features need to be explicitly configured if you want to use them.

There are several features designed to prevent access by unauthorized users. These features block a user thus preventing him from signing in and use his account. The user is informed that his account is blocked when he tries to log in. Users can be blocked by:

  * Explicitly blocking them in the user page in the administration section of the user interface.
  * Users that do not login for a given period of time can be blocked automatically.
  * Block the user after multiple failed login attempts.



After being blocked, users need to be enabled by an administrator in the web user interface administration section.

There are also several features designed to enforce that users have secure credentials:

  * Password strength verification. Passwords are checked to contain three or more of the following types of characters:
    * 1 upper case letter
    * 1 lower case letter
    * a number (0-9)
    * a special character (!@#$%^&*)
  * Password uniqueness verification. It is not possible for a user to re-use one of their previous passwords.
  * Administrators can mark the password of a user as expired. This will prompt the user to insert a new password before he can log in. Alternatively, the user password can also be changed in the administration user page.
  * Password age verification. If the user did not change the password in a given period of time, the password is automatically marked as expired.



Other features include:

  * Invalidate user session after a period of inactivity.
  * Log authentication related events to the audit log:
    * login
    * logout
    * session expiration
    * account disable
    * password expire
    * password change
    * user creation



### Default usersâ

Users in Pulse can be disabled due to a variety of reasons, including too many failed login attempts, password expiration or inactivity. However, Pulse relies on making internal calls for communicating between the Pulse Servers and its App Engines to function properly, and those calls require authentication.

In order to handle internal and external authentication and ensure PCI-DSS compliance, Pulse creates the following two users on startup:

  * `pulse`: User with full permissions for external authentication, e.g. in Pulse APIs.
  * `system`: User with full permissions that cannot be used for external authentication, i.e. it is impossible to log in to Pulse. This user is exclusive to internal Pulse usage, so you should not try to use it.

# App Collaboration Loop

Was this page helpful?Â 

To build a Fraud Prevention solution, [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) and Data Science resources such as [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) and [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) have to be developed, tested, and then deployed into Production to score transactions in real-time. These stages are often performed in different environments to ensure that the work in Development does not affect the work in Production. The stages are also performed by different teams at Feedzai and from Customers, including Data Scientists, Engineering Teams, and Fraud Analysts. The concept of collaborating on a Fraud Prevention solution using Pulse Applications (**Pulse apps**) is known as [**App Collaboration**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications#app-collaboration).

Similarly to the [Data Science Loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop), **App Collaboration** is not a one-time process. It requires a constant integration between the work developed in offline environments with the work in Production. This concept is described in this guide as **App Collaboration Loop**.

This guide covers the following two key ideas:

  * How to structure an application in different environments.
  * Workflow between environments.



## Introduction to App Collaboration Loopâ

**App Collaboration Loop** sets a working methodology so that different teams can collaborate together by developing various resources simultaneously and then bring the latest improvements faster and reliably to Production. **App Collaboration Loop** is recommended whenever you want to update Pulse resources (e.g. **Models** , **Plans** , [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules), [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists)).

This working methodology is performed by different teams and requires different environments as follows:

  * Offline environments:

    * **Data Science environment (DS):** Used by Data Science teams to develop tasks included in the **Data Science Loop** (e.g. improve **Models**).
    * **Development environment (DEV):** Used by Engineering teams to test more complex **Rules** , add schema fields, as well as to integrate Pulse resources developed in DS and in Production with the resources evolved in DEV.
  * Runtime environment:

    * **Production environment (PROD):** Used by Analysts to process transactions in real-time, and to write [Self-service Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules#self-service-rules). PROD is set up and then continuously updated by the Engineering team (e.g. update **Pulse app** or software versions).



### Block ownershipâ

If you are getting started with the App Collaboration approach, this section will help you understand how to set up your environment using **Block ownership** to develop Pulse resources.

App Collaboration approach

If you are already familiarized the **Block ownership** concept, you can skip this section and visit the section Workflow between environments to learn how to evolve a **Pulse app** from DEV/DS to PROD.

To evolve an application in a collaborative way, App Collaboration uses the concept of Block ownership. With this concept, each Pulse resource is evolved as a block by a single team within a single environment. As an example, a machine learning Model is evolved only by Data Scientists within the DS environment. The image below illustrates a typical example of three environments (DEV, DS and PROD) using Block ownership:

caution

The block ownership illustrated above assumes the following:

  1. Between each deployment, each block evolves in a single environment (i.e. in DEV, DS, or PROD).
  2. For each environment, all the resources are evolved using a single Pulse cluster.



Some resources are often developed by various teams (i.e. owners), for example, [Rules Projects](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules#rules-projects). Using the concept of resource ownership, each Rules Project should be owned by one team and should be only modified (e.g. adding/removing/editing Rules) by the team that owns each Rules Project. One possible solution is to divide the Rules Projects as follows:

  * _**Eng. Rules:**_ Represents Rules Projects with higher complexity, which are only evolved by Engineering teams in the DEV.
  * _**DS Rules:**_ Represents Rules Projects that are closely related to Data Science, which are only evolved by Data Scientists in DS.
  * **Self-service Rules:** represents Rules Projects containing simple Rules which are only written by Analysts in PROD, using Case Manager.



See the page **[How to organize your work with blocks](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/how-to-organize-your)** to learn to set a **Pulse app** with this structure.

## Workflow between environmentsâ

The figure below illustrates the procedure to bring new improvements to PROD after the initial deployment:

When to use this approach

You should follow the procedure below to deploy any resource type (e.g. Models, Plans, **Rules** , **Lists**). This procedure allows Fraud Analysts to use PROD to score transactions and evolve SSR, while Data Scientists and Engineers evolve resources in DS and DEV.

App Collaboration approach

The workflow explained in this section is specially designed to be adopted after the initial deployment, i.e. when you have already a live solution, to continuously improve the project with subsequent deployments.

The numbers shown in the diagram represent the following steps:

  * **Step 1:** Export the resources that are being developed in DS and import them in DEV. See the Section Migrating Data Science work to DEV for more information about this step.

  * **Step 2:** Export SSRs from PROD to DEV. This is required because SSRs might have changed while you evolved your applications in DEV and DS. Therefore, you need to ensure that the SSRs being written in PROD are migrated to DEV to test the full solution before the new deployment. See the Section Migrating SSRs from PROD to DEV for more information about this step.




After having your work fully developed and tested, you can bring the latest version of your application to PROD. One option is to perform a blue-green deployment.

The steps above are broken down into key topics in the next subsections.

### Step 1: Migrating Data Science work to DEVâ

Migrating the resources to DEV requires loading them in the Data Science tab and applying them in the runtime Workflow. Check the page [How to organize your work with blocks](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/how-to-organize-your) to understand how to map resources between Data Science tab and runtime Workflow.

The following pages will help you to accomplish this stage:

  * [**Exporting**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources#lists) and [**Importing Lists**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources)  
Allows you to migrate Lists to DEV. By default, when you run the export and import wizards, all the Lists are migrated automatically (i.e. this only include List metadata). All the other resources (i.e. Plans, Models and Rules Projects) can be optionally migrated using the selection options provided on the wizards.

  * [**Exporting**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources#plans) and [**Importing Plans**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources)  
Allows you to migrate the work related to the [Feature Engineering](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop#feature-engineering) stage of the Data Science loop. This includes the configurations that add fields to your dataset schema once the Plan is executed in the new environment (e.g. to add derived features, historical profiles). Optionally, you can choose to migrate Plan executions. Note that, every time that Data Scientists works on a Plan that has impact on the Data Source, the Model has to be re-trained. In this case, you also need to export and import the Model.

  * [**Exporting**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources#models-projects) and [**Importing Models**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources)  
Allows you to migrate the Model configurations, and optionally, you can include the binary of the Model.

  * [**Exporting**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources#rules-projects) and [**Importing Rules Projects**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources)  
Allows you to migrate the block of Rules developed by the Data Scientists in DS. By exporting and importing Rules Projects you are migrating the entire Rules Project with its Rules, and optionally, you can include a list of Rules Snapshots.

Block ownership - Rules Projects

Feedzai strongly recommends to evolve Rules Project using the concept of Block ownership to get the most out of the App Collaboration Loop with multiple teams working on the project. If multiple teams make changes simultaneously in the same Rules Projects using different environments (i.e. not adopting the resource ownership), you will have to merge changes manually by opening and editing the JSON file obtained by the Export Resource tool.




In addition to the links above, consider the following typical scenario:

  * An engineer is working on a Plan to add derived features to a data schema in the DEV environment. At the same time, a Data Scientist is working on a Rules Project that is using the old schema. The Import resource option allows you to choose the new schema when importing the Rules Project from DS to DEV, assuming that the new schema is already configured in that Rules Project in the DEV environment.

tip

Check the section [Schema Conflicts](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources#stage-3-schema-conflicts) in the page [Importing resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) to learn how to perform this operation.




### Step 2: Migrating SSRs from PROD to DEVâ

During the DS and DEV work, Fraud Analysts might evolve the blocks of SSRs in PROD. Completing this stage ensures that you integrate the most recent changes in PROD with the new improvements in DEV. This stage should be done before bringing the new app version to PROD to test the full solution before the new deployment. The easiest way to accomplish this stage is by exporting and importing SSRs from PROD to DEV, respectively.

The following pages will help you to accomplish this stage:

  * [**Exporting**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources#rules-projects) and [**Importing SSR**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources)  
In PROD, you can use the Export Resources wizard to select the Rules Projects related to SSRs and export as a zip file. This file can be then imported in DEV using the Import Resources wizard.



## Learn Moreâ

The following pages allow you to complete different tasks related to the App Collaboration Loop:

  * [How to organize your work with blocks](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/how-to-organize-your)
  * [How to version and store](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/how-to-version-and)

  * [Exporting Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources)

# Managing Users

Was this page helpful?Â 

The following sections describe how to create and manage users in Pulse.

caution

Only users with the `usermanager` role can manage other users. Users tagged with the `admin` or `developer` roles **can not** be edited or deleted.

The **User Management** dashboard can be accessed by selecting the  icon in the navigation bar.

info

Users tagged with the `admin` role will have access to additional administration features, and must therefore access the **User Management** tab by first selecting the  icon in the navigation bar, and then selecting the  icon in the sidebar.

## Create a userâ

  1. In the navigation bar, select the  icon to access the **User Management** page.

  2. Select the  button to open the prompt to create a new user.

  3. Enter all necessary details.

     * **Full Name** (mandatory)
     * **Username** (mandatory)
     * **Email** (mandatory)

info

The email input will be used to set and recover the user's password.

     * **Roles** (mandatory)
     * **Tenants** (optional)
  4. Select the **Create** button.




The newly created user will receive an email in the assigned email address to set a password. They may also need to activate 2FA, if Pulse is configured to make it mandatory. After the password and 2FA are set, the new user will be able sign in to their account and use it normally.

## Edit a userâ

To edit a user, do the following steps:

  1. In the navigation bar, select the  icon to access the **User Management** page.

  2. In the list of users, select the  icon next to the username of the user you want to update.

  3. Edit the fields in the dialog to make the intended changes. **Mandatory** fields cannot be left empty.

  4. Select the **Save Changes** button.




## Unlock a userâ

A user can be locked out of the system if one of the following scenarios occur:

  * If the user tries to sign into the account unsuccessfully too many times.
  * For inactivity, i.e. if the user doesn't sign in for a prolonged period of time.



If a user gets blocked as described above, a **User Manager** can change their status. To do this, do the following steps:

  1. In the navigation bar, select the  icon to access the **User Management** page.

  2. Select the **Unblock User** button in the **Status** section of the blocked user.




The user is now unblocked and can sign into the account.

## Disable a userâ

Users can be disabled permanently, for example when a person no longer is associated with the company through which they had access to Pulse.

A **User Manager** can disable another user by performing the following steps:

  1. In the navigation bar, select the  icon to access the **User Management** page.

  2. Select the  icon in the **Status** column of the intended user.

  3. Select the **Confirm** button in the confirmation prompt.




The user will no longer be able to login into the platform with their credentials.

## Export usersâ

A User Manager can export a list of users, alongside some of their attributes, by performing the following steps:

  1. In the navigation bar, select the  icon to access the **User Management** page.

  2. Select the  button in the table header.




This will trigger the download of a CSV (comma-separated value) file with the following attributes: name, email, full name, roles, groups, tenant groups, enabled/blocked state, and External Auth.

info

Users stored in an external Identity Provider (such as Okta, Microsoft Active Directory, etc.) will only be exported after the user logs in for the first time in the Feedzai system. These users can be identified by having the External Auth attribute set to true.

## Next stepsâ

For user management in a multi-tenancy context, see [Tenant User Management](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/manage-users/tenant-user-management).

# Reviewing List Changes - Four Eyes Check

Was this page helpful?Â 

[Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) provide a way to amplify the power of [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) by allowing repetitive patterns to be defined as a single rule that then gets applied to a large number of values. Given the high level of automation that lists enable, ensuring every change is reviewed by a second pair of eyes helps prevent unwanted or unplanned changes from being published.

If the **Four-Eyes Check for Lists** functionality is enabled in your Pulse environment, changes to lists will not be published right away; instead, they will be queued for review. Such pending list changes only go live after a reviewer approves them.

Reviews of changes made to lists can be requested and performed directly in the Pulse interface. This page describes both sides of the review process: how to request a review for changes to lists, and how to perform such a review.

## Prerequisitesâ

To allow reviews of list changes, an administrator must set the `pulse.global.managedListsRevision.enabled` property to `true` in the Administration > Configuration view. The default value of this property is `false`.

Optionally, for the notification emails to work as designed, the following settings can be configured as well. However, if you don't intend to use the notification emails, these can be skipped:

  * The SMTP properties must be configured, so that the notification emails are properly sent.
  * The `pulse.global.managedListsRevision.notifications.email.from` property: sets the email address from which Pulse sends the notification email to the reviewers. By default, it's `[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)`.
  * The `pulse.global.ui.host` property is used to configure the URL where Pulse runs, and by default it's set to `http://localhost:8080/`. The notification email contains a link to the list changes that need to be reviewed, and the link starts with the URL set in this property. If the default value is not set to the actual value, the link in the email won't work.



Get in touch with Feedzai to set up four eyes check for lists in your Pulse environment.

### Set up a static e-mail to receive all Four Eyes Check notificationsâ

In addition to direct notifications sent to the author and reviewer in four eyes checks, Pulse allows setting up a static e-mail address which will receive all four eyes check notifications. This allows Pulse users to review the open revisions more thoroughly, and thus catch errors that might otherwise be missed. Note that the recipient of these emails will not be addressed directly, as they will be merely copies of the notifications sent to the author and reviewer of the corresponding four eyes check.

Notifying multiple users

This e-mail address can be set to that of a mailing list, which allows multiple users to receive every four eyes notifications.

To enable notifications for Pulse managed lists, provide the e-mail address via the following Pulse property: `pulse.global.managedListsRevision.notifications.email.staticreviewer`.

## Request a review for list changesâ

info

Users need to have the `application:managedlistitems:revision:create` [permission](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application#permissions) to request reviews of list changes from others.

To request a review of a change made to a list, perform the following steps:

  1. In the sidebar, select the  icon to open the **Lists** view.
  2. Select the list you want to make changes to.
  3. Make the desired changes to the list. For example, adding a new item, editing or deleting an existing item, or importing a batch of items from a CSV file.

caution

You won't be able to make changes to list items for which there are already pending changes. Attempting to do so will show an error message indicating the ID of the pending review.

  4. Optionally fill the **Notify users** field to indicate specific users you wish to inform of your review request. If the notification settings are properly configured, and the users have an email address associated with their Pulse account, they will receive an email message notifying them of the pending changes.
  5. Select the  button to add the changes to the review queue.  
A floating success message will be displayed, confirming that the changes have been submitted for review.



## Review pending changes to listsâ

info

Users need to have the `application:managedlistitems:revision:read` and `application:managedlistitems:revision:update` [permissions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application#permissions) to view pending changes to lists and review them.

  1. In the sidebar, select the  icon to open the **Lists** view.  
Lists with pending changes will be marked with an **Unreviewed** label.

  2. Open the list with pending changes that you wish to review. Each item with changes will be marked with a label indicating the type of change (e.g. "Edited", "Added", "Deleted", etc.)

  3. Select the  button at the top right of the table of lists.  
The number in parenthesis is the count of unreviewed changes.

  4. Review the overall changes to the list. Change details will at first be collapsed, as indicated by the  symbol to their left.

  5. Expand the details of each change using the  button. This will display a side-by-side comparison of the old and new data associated with the change. Created items will have no content on the left side; deleted items will have no content on the right side. The image below shows an example with two changes â one adding a new item, and the other editing an existing item:

caution

Changes that consist of batch imports of list items will have no preview (as those can typically include thousands of items). In such cases, the only details that are shown are the number of imported items (in the "Name" column), the import mode (append without overwriting existing items, append with overwriting existing items, and complete rewrite), the change author, and the change timestamp.

  6. Select "accept" (âï¸ icon) or "decline" (â icon). For either action, a confirmation dialog is shown. It's possible to disable the display of this dialog in the future, but it's strongly recommended to keep it.  
A floating success message will be displayed, confirming that the changes have been reviewed and (if approved) will be applied to the list.

Source: https://cam.feedzai.com/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary
Title: Concepts Glossary | Feedzai Pulse
============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)
  * Concepts Glossary



On this page

# Concepts Glossary

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Acquirerâ

An acquirer represents the bank or the financial institution that acquires money from the client on behalf of the merchant as a payment for products or services.

In an every day scenario the acquirer is responsible for handling the merchant's transactions and collect payments from the clients issuers.

## Actionâ

Actions are asynchronous flags that are raised on events when some predefined condition is met.

For example the **Blocked** action is raised when a fraudulent transaction is found.

## Administratorâ

Pulse user that has admin role.

This user can:

  * **Monitor and Control** Pulse services.
  * **Manage** security configuration.
  * **Manage** Pulse's configuration attributes,
  * **View** Pulse's log and general information.



## Aggregationâ

An aggregation is the calculation of a metric for a combination of dimensions â i.e. one or more fields that are used to [group](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#group-by) the data into sets, each of which gets its own aggregation value.

For example, if the dimensions are State and Bank, the aggregation will be calculated for all the possible combinations of the available states and banks. If there are 50 states and 10 banks in the dataset, the aggregation needs to be calculated 500 times.

## AppEngineâ

An AppEngine is a conceptual group of services that run on their own process.

Services that run on an AppEngine are said to run on an **AppEngine Context**.

## Batchâ

The amount of events to be processed at the same time.

By default the events are processed one by one. However, most use-cases donât need a sub-second real-time resolution (where resolution is the max timeframe in which to report notifications). Itâs very common that a resolution of one second, or even more, is sufficient. Given that the current latency to process an event is low (sub-millisecond), multiple events can be processed at the same time, in **batches**. Batch option for stream definition, for example, serves for this purpose.

## Chargebackâ

A chargeback happens when a transaction made previously between an customer and a merchant is returned to the customer.

While this can happen in many different use cases, such a case would be making a return after purchasing an item in a store. Here the merchant will make a chargeback of the transaction made previously. It's basically a reversal mechanism for transactions.

## Clockâ

An important Pulse property that defines how a timestamp is generated for each event injected to stream.

If you are already using Feedzai Pulse interface you might already be familiar with choosing option for clock.

In this context three types of clock mean the following:

  1. **Event-based** -means that each event itself contains the timestamp
  2. **System clock** \- means that when the event arrives, the server marks it with the current time of the machine
  3. **Stream clock** \- means that when an event arrives its time is set according to the clock of the corresponding stream



## Clusterâ

All the Pulse software components that are connected to Zookeeper, these include Pulse Servers, Application Engines and external Batch Jobs. Each cluster lives in a single Data Center, and when referring to a Pulse deployment spanned across multiple Data Centers the used term is usually Global Cluster, but it will nonetheless be made clear.

## CNPâ

_Card Not Present_ transaction represents a payment card transaction that was made without the customer being physically present with the card.

Payments made over Internet are one example of CNP transactions since both the customer and the card wasn't physically present in the POS when the transaction was made. These types of transactions have a much higher rate of credit card fraud than their CP counterpart, mainly for the easiness of using counterfeit or stolen credit card data.

CP

Inversely, _Card Present_ transactions represent payment card transactions where the card was physically available when the purschase was made.

## Control Flowâ

Control flow is a mechanism by which it is possible for a computer program to make choices.

In the context of a Workflow, Control Flow are the mechanisms that allow to control how an event progresses through the Workflow Elements, namely if it should skip none, some or all of the Workflow Elements that follow.

## CPâ

_Card Present_ transactions represent payment card transactions where the card was physically available when the purchase was made.

CNP

Inversely, _Card Not Present_ transaction represents a payment card transaction that was made without the customer being physically present with the card.

## Data Centerâ

A logical and physical relation of nodes. Each Data Center has its own cluster and must have all the components of the system to work by itself. This means that it follows a shared-nothing approach in order to support scenarios of disaster recovery where a single Data Center must be able to fully operate without need of a system that belongs to another.

## Dead Letterâ

Built-in Action that is raised when an event reaches the end of its path in the Workflow.

This Action is used by the Event Storage Service to store the event in persistent storage.

## Dictionaryâ

Is a data-type which is similar to a map or a hash table in a typical programming language. It also maps keys to values. In PulseQL the keys would be the groups and the values are the aggregator results.

So, for example, for the transactions stream example, if we create a dictionary grouped by bank, the keys are names of banks and the values can be the average amounts. A snapshot of this dictionary could look like this;

bank| avg_amount  
---|---  
Bank A| $ 50  
Bank B| $ 30  
Bank C| $ 65.5  
  
Dictionaries support lots of operations. You can, for example, filter them, project their entries, aggregate them or lookup the value of a single entry.

## Dimensionâ

A dimension is an analysis axis that contains a limited set of values from which some can be selected, thus drilling in into that sub set. Along with Dimension Mappings they can transform machine codes into human readable information: `"0"`s and `"1"`s into `"United States of America"` and `"Portugal"`.

For example the total USA transactions could be at a given time 150K, drilling in in this case could be choosing to view the transactions only for the state of New York (which could be 10K). We could drill even further, if we had, for example, a bank dimension. In this case we would only see the transactions for a given bank in New York (which could be 2K).

## Eventâ

A single _packet_ of data within a stream; also called a "tuple". An event consists of fields with associated values, conforming to the stream's data schema.

The following is an example of a tuple for a stream of transactions:
    
    
    {  
     timestamp:      1,  
     state:          'Alaska',  
     bank:           'Bank of America',  
     rejected:       1000,  
     duration:       15.5,  
     amount:         1000,  
     operation_type: 'Withdrawals',  
     card_type:      'Visa',  
     client_type:    'ATM'  
    }  
    

## Event Processingâ

A set of technologies designed to process high-volumes of continuously arriving data in real-time.

In this context, continuously means that data may arrive at any moment over the course of arbitrarily long periods of time. For example, an application designed to monitor traffic in a highway system may be required to execute without interruptions for months or even years. During all this time, the application is continuously receiving notifications such as "car entered the highway", analyzing them and producing meaningful results like "there are currently 1000 vehicles inside the highway" or "the vehicle with license plate 11-22-AA drove through the highway at an average speed of 150 km/h". This information could then be displayed in a dashboard where a human operator could look at it and use it to make informed decisions. The important point to retain is that, in this kind of applications, one can't wait for all data to arrive before it is processed. Moreover, in most scenarios, it is desirable to process incoming data as soon as possible so that the resulting analysis is still up-to-date and relevant when it is acted upon.

## Explanationâ

An Explanation details why a given transaction reached a certain outcome and got a given score. It contains a list of reasons that help explain the outcome and gives the user further hindsight about the final decision.

Please refer to [this section](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/explanations) to learn more about Explanations.

## Featureâ

A feature is an attribute of an instance. It represents information necessary for a Machine Learning algorithm to identify a pattern.

Please refer to [this section](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#features) in order to obtain more details.

## Feedzai IQâ

Feedzai IQ is a suite of ready-to-adopt risk assessment solutions providing AI-powered insights based on aggregated intelligence from across the Feedzai global network.

For more information about Feedzai IQ, please refer to [this section](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/about-pulse#feedzai-iq).

## Fieldâ

A Field is a component of a data source's schema. In CSV file or other tabular data formats, a field corresponds to a column.

To learn more about fields, refer to the [Data fields](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#data-fields) section in the documentation about Data Sources.

## Groupâ

A virtual subset of members of the cluster that have similar functionality, i.e. all the Pulse Servers belong to a group of pulse servers but the Application Engines belong to another group.

Note that this is a distinct concept from the [Group By](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#group-by) operator used in plans.

## Instanceâ

Instance is an event that is enriched with the Features from the [Fraud Model Definition](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows).

The instance does not travel the Workflow, it is computed using the event data and then sent to FOS either for training or scoring.

Instance may also be used to refer to an incarnation of a Service like the [Fraud Rules Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#rules-service).

## Issuerâ

An issuer represents the bank or the financial institution that legally emitted the payment card to the cardholder.

In an every day financial transaction between a client and a merchant, the issuer is responsible for issuing the money to the acquirer bank. He does this on behalf of the client, usually assuming the liability for the client's capacity to pay off the debts.

## MCCâ

_Merchant Category Code_ is a four-digits number assigned to a merchant that represents the type of goods or services it performs.

This code is used to categorize the merchants by business area and activity in order to improve the transaction context. It's easy to understand why, the average transaction amount between a Bus Line merchant (MCC 4131) and a Car Dealership (MCC 5511) will be vastly different.

There are some merchants that have special MCC numbers assigned, the most known case being Airlines.

## Memberâ

A software component that is part of a cluster. Core members include Pulse Server and Application Engines.

## Merchantâ

A merchant represents a business person who trades in commodities produced by others with the public, also known as clients. It is usually represented by an acquirer in a financial transaction.

## Metricâ

A metric (also known as **profile** or **historical profile**) adds new fields to a data source, based on an aggregation of events over a period of time, to track entity behavior patterns.

At its core, a metric performs calculations, called aggregations âsuch as sums, counts, maximums, averages, etc.â on a specific data field (e.g. transaction amount), grouped by one or more fields (e.g. a credit card), and over a defined time window (e.g. the last 24 hours). This allows quantifying and monitoring behavioral patterns, making it easier to detect changes that may signal suspicious activity.

For more information about metrics, refer to the [Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#metrics) section in the documentation about Plans in Workflows.

## Nodeâ

An instance of an operating system. It doesn't relate to physical machines _per se_ since several operating system instances can reside in the same physical machine for example by the means of virtualization.

## Operationâ

Term used in the context of [Resource Versioning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/resource-versioning) to represent a modification made to a Resource.

## POSâ

_Point of Sale_ is the equipment used by a merchant to handle a customer payment inside a store.

Can also be called checkout and it calculates the amount owed by the customer in exchange for goods or services acquired. Typically issues a receipt after the payment was made.

## Planâ

A plan is a recipe of how to augment a data source via data transformations, essentially transforming one data source into another. Plans are typically used to prepare the data to be used to train machine learning models, or to transform the data in the runtime environment for processing via rules or models.

To learn more about plans, refer to the [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) page.

## Profile Update Job (PUJ)â

A batch process that reads transactions from the database, computes the metrics using the event processing engine and stores them to a data store.

## Reasonâ

A Reason represents a fact that was considered by Pulse when scoring a transaction that went through an workflow. It can detail both fraudulent and non-fraudulent behavior and is usually part of an Explanation.

## Replication Factorâ

Replication factor is the number of nodes which are running the same component in distinct physical machines. For example, a replication factor of two means that the Pulse Server is replicated across two physical machines as well as the Application Engines.

## Resourceâ

Represents any entity inside Pulse. Examples of resources include KPIs, Baselines, Lists, Rules, etc.

## Schemaâ

A data schema is a set of metadata that describes the attributes available in an event, and in particular their [data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types).

Refer to [Data schemas](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#data-schemas) for a detailed explanation.

## Scoreâ

Score is the value that represents the probability of an event being fraudulent. The higher the score the more likely is that the event is fraudulent.

The score is an integer value between 0 and 1000.

The process of calculating the score is named **scoring**. Please refer to [this section](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) to learn about models and training mechanisms.

## Serviceâ

Service is an isolated piece of software that provides some kind of functionality as a service to other services.

## Settlementâ

Usually the third and final step in a transaction, the settlement occurs between the issuers and the acquirer about two days after the original transactions were made.

It is in this step that the money is really transferred from the client (issuer) into the merchant (acquirer).

The reasoning behind this is that if a business receives 100 daily payments from bank A, it does not makes sense to make each individual transaction right in that moment. The transaction fees would be too high. What happens instead is that these 100 payments will summed in a single transaction that occurs X time later.

## Slackâ

The amount of time the events can "wait" for each other when they are coming from different sources.

Sometimes you can be interested in receiving events from multiple sources where clocks are almost (but not quite) synchronized. In this case you can defined a time slack where the events are re-ordered and processed in-order.

## Snapshotâ

A picture of the current state of data contained in the object requested at a pre-defined interval in time. It contains all the data of that object at that exact moment. It applies to all objects except streams.

## Streamâ

A stream represents a source of real-time data. It's like a connection port between the world and Pulse.

Similar to a table of a database, it is the data structure inside Pulse that defines the schema of the data that will be injected into Pulse.

## Tenantâ

Tenants are the individual entities to which Multi-Tenancy is applied to. They represent separate entities to whom data and certain resources (Rules, Environments and Templates) should be isolated. In order to allow this separation they are associated to users which inherit their isolation.

## Tenant Domainâ

Tenant domains are used to group multiple tenants based on a common domain, they work much like a normal group. It is through them that we specify which Tenants can have resources on a given [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) element.

## Timestampâ

The time the event occurs.

## Transactionâ

A transaction is an exchange of goods between two parties.

## TrustScoreâ

TrustScore is an aggregated risk score that combines the outputs from multiple models trained on relevant patterns from Feedzai's global client base. It uses federated learning techniques to allow financial intelligence sharing without relying on consortium-based data sharing or aggregation, thus ensuring data segregation and confidentiality.

For more information about TrustScore, please refer to [this section](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/about-pulse#trustscore).

## Tupleâ

A synonym for **event**.

## Windowâ

Time interval which defines which real-time events from the data stream should be used for calculating aggregations in a metric. For details on the syntax used to define windows, please refer to the [Time window](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#time-window) section of the documentation on Plans in Workflows.

There are two major types of windows:

### Sliding Windowâ

A [sliding window](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#sliding-windows) contains the events received within a fixed-size interval. This interval could be temporal or tuple-based. For example, a sliding window with interval equal to 5 minutes will contain only the events received during the past 5 minutes. As soon as the event becomes older than this threshold, it is expired from the window. The window in the example above is a time-based sliding window.

### Tumbling Windowsâ

Unlike sliding windows, tumbling windows expire all events at once, once they reach their predetermined size. Afterwards, they refill again and the cycle repeats itself.

#### Landmark Windowsâ

[Landmark windows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#landmark-windows) are similar to time-based tumbling windows except you may control the exact time the window expires.

### Non-Windowed Metricsâ

Non-windowed metrics are a type of metric that is not bound by a time window. They are limited only by the available historical data at the time of the metric's creation or update, which is determined by the data retention policy. For more information on this type of metrics, refer to the [Non-windowed Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#non-windowed-metrics) section.

## Workflowâ

A workflow defines how a transaction event is routed between processing steps in a fraud detection pipeline.

Each processing step of a workflow is performed by a service (e.g. rules service, scoring service). Thus, a workflow is defined by a list of services that process the transactions and the connections between them.

Please refer to [this section](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) to learn what are workflows and how they work.

On this page

# Core Concepts of Pulse

Was this page helpful?Â 

All tasks you perform with Pulse rely on a set of concepts that support the core of Pulse's functionality.

This page gives you the basics about the most important concepts of Pulse. For more details or for other concepts read the pages later in this chapter.

## Data science loopâ

The [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) is the process of creating and testing rules and models.

## Data sourcesâ

[Data sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) are historical datasets imported to a data science environment. You can use them for data exploration, feature engineering, model training, rule testing, etc.

## Plansâ

[Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) define a transformation flow of one data source into another data source. They are useful to systematize data cleaning, data processing, and feature engineering, both in a data science pipeline and in runtime.

## Modelsâ

Pulse enables you to quickly train [machine learning models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and evaluate the results over several iterations. It provides tools for you to extract relevant performance metrics and track your progress along each iteration of the data science loop.

## Rulesâ

[Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) define a pattern based on the fields of a data source that produces a binary result for each record that matches a condition. Pulse lets you define and evaluate the performance of blocks of rules using a data science approach.

## Workflowsâ

[Workflows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) represent the life cycle of a real-time event through the system. A workflow maps other concepts, such as data science concepts, into runtime components and ensures they are properly translated and orchestrated.

## Listsâ

A [list](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) represents a set of values and aims at improving the efficiency of rules when the same pattern needs to be checked against a large number of entries. For example, a list of credit card numbers, a list of merchants, etc.

## User-Defined functionsâ

[User-defined functions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions) (UDFs) enable you to extend Pulse beyond its off-the-shelf capabilities. They are especially useful when you need custom logic to process data, such as transforming data source fields with Plans or configuring conditions for rules.

# Getting Started

The following pages are a step-by-step tutorial on how to develop a simple application using Pulse. They will guide you through Pulse concepts and tasks described in the User Guide by presenting concrete examples.

These examples focus on detecting fraud in payments, in a transaction monitoring scenario. However, Pulse can tackle other use cases such as anti-money laundering.

This tutorial is just an overview of Pulse's fraud prevention applications to help you get started. You should explore each feature with greater attention to get a better understanding of all the concepts, resorting to the more detailed documentation whenever necessary.

## Objectivesâ

With this tutorial, you will learn how to execute a typical iteration of the [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop), which includes the following stages:

  1. Loading data.
  2. Processing data.
  3. Building and evaluating models.
  4. Building and evaluating rules.
  5. Creating a workflow that can be deployed in the production environment to process events.

  * [input.csv](/pulse/latest/input.csv)



Download them to the `PULSE_SERVER_HOME/var/datasources/` path on the Pulse server where you will be working.

In addition, for the last steps you will need to have an input adapter set up on your server where you will be working.

To get help with the data files or with the input adapter, get in touch with your contact person at Feedzai.

## Next stepsâ

Now that you have everything set up, go ahead and read the following pages to create your first data science resources and compose an event-processing workflow with them.

# Deploying a project into Production

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse delivers a full Data Science platform aimed at helping data scientists do their jobs, with increased performance. Additionally, Pulse makes Data Science much more accessible to other user profiles, such as risk analysts, without requiring them to acquire the same set of skills a data scientist must have.

Similarly, Pulse is also a platform that makes life easier for engineers whose task is to take the work of a Data Science team to Production. In reality, since Pulse is focused on removing barriers for every user profile, deploying a project to Production and managing its lifecycle can even be performed by data scientists themselves with minimal assistance from engineers.

It is quite common for engineers to struggle when translating offline Data Science and Machine Learning work into executable software that runs properly in a real-time Production environment. It may take a lot of iterations to finally deploy the Data Science work into Production and keep the same semantics and results that Data Scientists have designed and achieved previously.

Therefore, Pulse projects are designed to work in a way that abstracts away a lot of the complexity that engineers usually have to deal with. With a fully integrated Data Science modeling and run-time environment, Pulse enables a direct and seamless deployment, without any major effort.

How Pulse projects work

To learn more about how Pulse fully integrates Data Science with deployment and run-time, make sure to learn more about [how Pulse projects work](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/how-pulse-projects-work).

Once you have sign-off to deploy a Data Science project into Production, you must execute the following tasks:

  * [Creating a schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/creating-a-schema)


  * [Designing a workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow)

  * [Managing the project life cycle](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/managing-the-project-life-cycle)




Configuring components directly in Production

Since in Production, data comes into Pulse in real-time, there are some activities in Production that are not mandatory to be started in the Data Science stage. For example:

  * It is very simple to generate a **Schema** from a [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources). However, in Production you only need the data structure, not data itself, so you can [define a data Schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/creating-a-schema) manually,
  * Pulse provides a way to treat and evaluate the performance of **Rules** much alike a Data Science approach to evaluate, compare and iterate over **Models**. However, you can [deploy a Rules Snapshot](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules) with only the definition of a block of **Rules** into Production, without evaluating it against test data.



Additionally, it is recommended that you fully acquire all the necessary context and understand what concepts you are manipulating in your project. To learn more about how Data Science works in Pulse, and Pulse's core concepts, check the following pages:

  * [Data Science Loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop)
  * [Channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels)

  * [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models)
  * [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules)
  * [Sandbox Evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/sandbox-evaluations)
  * [Workflows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows)
  * [Outcome Combinator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/outcome-combinator)
  * [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists)
  * [Jobs and Job Profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/jobs-and-job-profiles)

# Feature Engineering

Was this page helpful?Â 

This section shows how to transform your raw and cleaned data into information that correlates with fraud or any other target variable, and select only information that is useful as input to your models.

Pulse supports the design of features and the selection of the relevant fields for your model with the following tasks.

  1. [Selecting important fields directly from your dataset](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/selecting-important-data-for-your-model)

If you want to create features to use them in models, it's useful to have initial statistics about which input fields are correlated with the target variable. In Pulse, you can generate statistics over your dataset to uncover correlations between data fields and the target variable you want to predict.

  2. [Creating a plan for the features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-a-plan-for-features)

In Pulse, a plan entity is a recipe of how to transform one data source into another. A plan contains map and metric operators that represent the new features. If you already have a plan for features, skip this step.

  3. [Adding lists to the plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-lists-in-features)

If you want to access list items of complex lists, you need to add them to the plan. For example, if you have a list with the information about the risk level each country has, you can add that list to the plan, and use it in your features and rules.

  4. [Using string fields in models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-string-indexing)

If your string fields have indexers, you can use the indexer in the model to score events.

  5. [Creating derived features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-derived-features)

Apply complex expressions over your dataset's existing fields to extract new features.

  6. [Creating metrics (historical profiles)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics)

Generate a large number of profiles and include time-based features.

  7. [Using PQL in features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features)

Learn how to use the Pulse Query Language (PQL) in map and metrics operators to define the "formula" of the new features.

  8. [Following best practices for plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/best-practices-for-plans)

Use best practices to organize map and metrics operators within a plan in a meaningful way.

  9. [Creating a data source with the features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/generating-instance-features-dataset)

Run the plan to create the data source that contains the new fields.




The pages in this chapter walk you through these tasks.

Title: How Pulse projects work | Feedzai Pulse
