On this page

# How Pulse projects work

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse projects integrate the work performed during the Data Science loop with runtime to accomplish a defined objective, e.g. detect fraud.

Data Scientists, Software Engineers and Fraud Analysts play a key role in the field of fraud prevention to transform raw data into valuable insights. However, this work has a number of complex challenges to address:

  * With traditional tool sets, Data Scientists often need to dig into different tools and techniques to execute their tasks. For each problem, Data Scientists need to adapt their approach and write customized code, e.g. scripts to import data, database queries, data visualization techniques.
  * Developing and iterating Machine Learning [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) require Data Scientists with special skills who are difficult to find in the market.
  * Organizations struggle when they need to deploy efficiently and accurately Data Science work in runtime. Usually, it takes several months for engineering teams to deploy a trained Model and ensure that is working as designed and tested during the Data Science stage.



Pulse projects are designed to address these challenges. The ultimate goal of Data Science work is to configure Pulse to run as a real time [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) to accomplish a target objective, e.g. detect fraud. Pulse projects provide the following:

  * Pulse delivers a full Data Science suite to help Data Scientists while handling most of the heavy work by running all the technological complexity behind the scenes.
  * Pulse makes it easy to perform Data Science work, allowing personas with different profiles to use the platform.
  * Pulse focuses on bridging Data Science and runtime together under the same platform. When you are developing your activities along the [Data Science Loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop), you are also performing some configurations that allow easy and quick deployments.
  * Pulse also allows access to [Feedzai IQ](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/about-pulse#feedzai-iq), a suite of risk assessment solutions that provide out-of-the-box AI-powered risk insights based on aggregated financial risk intelligence from Feedzai's global network.



## Environmentsâ

A key idea in Pulse is the possibility of working in different environments to develop and test your work before deploying it into production. In fact, regardless of the project, developing and testing Pulse resources is recommended to be performed in offline environments, i.e. it should never be done in the same environment that contains the runtime stage evaluating real-time transactions (i.e. production environment).

## Applicationsâ

Each project in Pulse is built as a Pulse application (**Pulse App**).

A Pulse App consists of a user defined session in which resources such as **Plans** , **Models** and **Rules** are developed.

Each application typically handles a specific use case (for example, Transaction Fraud or AML), and a set of channels (see [Channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels) for more details).

With this architecture, users can develop work in different applications using offline environments which can be then moved to production environment. This concept is referred to as **App Collaboration**.

Check the page [Working with Applications](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications) to learn more about App Collaboration in Pulse.

## Project stages: Data Science and Runtimeâ

Pulse projects are based on two main stages:

  * **Data Science:** Fully supports all the steps in the **Data Science Loop**.
  * **Runtime:** Executes the work that was developed in the Data Science phase in a runtime **Workflow**.



Similarly to configuring settings on a device, for example a smartphone, in which the general settings are used by various apps that might be installed; the Data Science phase can be considered as the initial configuration stages of your Workflow.

While running the **Data Science** phase in Pulse, you are:

  * Configuring and validating all the [concepts](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts) that your project needs to make good decisions in real-time. For example, configuring [Data Sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) and use them to train Models, transform incoming data into new features for your Model input with Plans.
  * Use of Pulse as a unified set of Data Science tools that fully supports your Data Science Loop, while keeping your focus on the ultimate goal of using this work to perform live decisions in runtime. Manipulate huge volumes of data, explore it efficiently and evaluate all your work using different tools (e.g. [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance)). This allows you to be confident that when you bring your Data Science work into a live Workflow.



While running the **Runtime** phase in Pulse, you are:

  * Applying the resources developed in the Data Science phase to a real-time scenario.
  * Using a native resource in Pulse referred to as **Workflow** with a final goal of performing decisions in real-time.
  * Defining a sequence of steps in the Workflow that will process events as the input and produce a final decision as the output.



info

There are some scenarios where you don't necessarily need to go through the Data Science phase. For example, deploying [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules). In this case, you would only need to define the Rules and the input schema for your Workflow. In such scenarios, Pulse lets you jump straight into configuring these concepts in a runtime Workflow so that it doesn't cause limitations to your work.

## Mapping between Data Science and Runtimeâ

To combine the Data Science and Runtime phases, Pulse maps the resources that are developed in the Data Science stage to an element in the Workflow referred to as **Service**.

The following diagram illustrates how [concepts in Pulse](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts) translate from Data Science to [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) elements:

In general, to deploy your work in a Workflow, you will be required to:

  * Generate the Workflow input Schema by exporting a Data Source and copying its structure and format.
  * Add runtime elements (i.e. services) to the Workflow:
    * **Plan Services:** Configure your deployable Plans and directly deploy them.
    * **Scoring Services:** Configure your Machine Learning Models and directly deploy them.
    * **Rules Services:** Configure your Rules in a Rules Project and directly deploy them.
    * **Custom Workflow Services:** To consume data, according to the input Schema from an external system, or to implement custom logic.
  * Configure your Scoring Services and Rules Services to contribute to the Workflow's decisions, i.e. [Outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes).



## Learn Moreâ

Now that you have an overall picture of how Pulse brings **Data Science** and **Runtime** together on the same platform, you can start working on your project as explained in the following sections:

  * [Creating a Data Science project](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project)
  * [Deploying a project into Production](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production)
  * [Working with Applications](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications)
  * [Channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels)

# Investigating Changes and User Actions

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse provides audit logs of changes that were made via user interface or via REST API calls. This can be useful for example when investigating a change in the behavior of the system, or during a security audit.

This topic describes how to view the audit logs.

Audit capabilities

Pulse audit can track what a certain user did or edited at a certain time.

Note that more complex investigations may require the assistance of Feedzai experts. In those cases, turn to your Feedzai contact person.

## Introductionâ

**Audit entries** are records of user actions and resource changes. Each audit entry contains different data, depending on the type of action or the change that was made.

Since the data contained in the audit entries covers a wide range of event types, Pulse adds **labels** to some specific data fields to make it easier to search the entries. For example, Pulse puts a label on the application name, so that users can filter entries by application name.

You can read more about how audit works and stores data in the [Audit](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/audit) topic.

## How toâ

Select the **Audit** option in the top right corner of the menu bar to view the list of changes made in the Pulse environment.

Each line in the displayed list is an audit entry, representing a specific user action or change.

### Viewing an audit entry's detailsâ

Select the audit entry line to expand its details. The details contain two sections: **Context** and **Labels**.

The Context section shows the data that was included in the request of the Pulse UI or REST API that initiated the change.

The Labels section shows the data fields of the audit entry to which Pulse added a label.

### Viewing differences for update actionsâ

For update actions, the Context section shows a comparison between the previous and updated version:

### Searching by label valueâ

Select any label value (highlighted in blue), to filter for all audit entries containing that label.

Upon selecting a label value, the label value is shown in the search box, and the list is filtered to only show audit entries that have the same label value.

### Filtering the listed audit entriesâ

**Use the built-in filters** to filter the audit entries by time **Period** , by the type of **Action** , or by **User** .

info

Remember that changes made to resources may not always be automatically taken into consideration by other parts of the application.

For example, if you change a rule, it is not automatically updated in a workflow. Workflows use a snapshot of the rules project, which include a certain version of the rule. Also, the application needs to be published after the changes, for the changes to be active.

## Examplesâ

### Identifying changes made to an application on a specific dayâ

To find all the changes made on a specific day of the last two months, perform the following steps:

  1. In Pulse, navigate to the **Audit** page.
  2. In the **Period** filter, select _Last 2 months_.
  3. Type the name of the application in the search box, and select **Search**.
  4. Use the web browser's search to find the entries of the day you are looking for. Use the format YYYY-MM-DD.



### Identifying actions taken by a specific userâ

To find all the changes made by a specific user in the last two months, perform the following steps:

  1. In Pulse, navigate to the **Audit** page.
  2. In the **Period** filter, select _Last 2 months_.
  3. Use the **User** filter to find changes and actions performed by the specific user in the last two months.



## Learn moreâ

Read [how to compare rules in two different snapshots](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/reviewing-rule-changes-in-a-snapshot).

# Building and evaluating your model

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse supports your Data Science loop by enabling you to quickly train your models and evaluate the results over several iterations.

A model project aggregates several iterations of a model and provides tools for you to assess whether the features you designed are useful, well constructed, etc. At each iteration, you are able to understand how close you are to reaching your projects goals and what actions you took to reach those results.

Building and evaluating your models with Pulse involves:

  * Training a model
  * Evaluating a model
  * Tuning model parameters
  * Comparing models



## Edit model evaluation pageâ

The **Edit Model Evaluation** page allows you to configure how you look at the results of your model and how you can evaluate them against models in your project.

The following image displays the **Edit Model Evaluation** page:

The **Edit Model Evaluation** page contains the following areas:

  1. **Evaluation target and comparison**



Defines the target value and model comparisons for your model evaluation. Select the **Target Value** you want to analyze in your model evaluation. This allows for the evaluation of any value of your model's target variable. For example, both **Fraud** and **Not Fraud**. Select the models you want to **Compare With** to have their evaluations plotted on the ROC Curve area and displayed in the Metrics table.

  2. **ROC curve**



Graphically displays the typical evaluation metrics of Machine Learning models, such as Recall and FPR.

Adjust the **X-Axis Range** and **Y-Axis Range** sliders to zoom in and out of your model's results. Select the **X-Axis** and **Y-Axis** metrics to generate a custom chart in the **X/Y Plot**. Any count and cost-based metrics are available.

  3. **Metrics table**



Displays the results plotted in the **ROC Curve** area in a tabular manner. Includes all metrics for all possible combinations of the configured breakdowns for the evaluation.

Adjust the **Threshold** slider to define the confidence you have in the model. This means that for example, all Data Source instances above the threshold are evaluated as Fraud. Select the  **View ROC** option in a row to display the graphical evaluation in the **ROC Curve** area for the selected breakdown.

### Evaluation Metricsâ

Select  from the  options menu to define custom metrics. For example, calculating your profit in using your model to automatically detect fraud vs. what you would have spent doing a manual revision. You can then display these custom metrics in the **ROC Curve** and **Metrics** table.

### Comparison Detailsâ

It is common that several models are trained and configured mostly identically. Select the  option to quickly examine the difference between models you are comparing. Changes are highlighted in a different color.

## Exploration pageâ

The **Exploration** page is designed to assist you in fine tuning your [model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models). It lets you:

  * Check the performance of your models at the defined thresholds.
  * Assess how close is the model to your success/acceptance criteria, without breaking client SLAs.
  * Detect possible cost-efficiencies when you make very small adjustments.



Select the  option from the **Model Project** page.

The following image displays the **Exploration** page:

The **Exploration** page contains the following areas:

  1. **Targets**



Displays comparative analyses of your evaluations under different criteria. For example, determines, for each evaluation, which one performs the best, i.e. captures the most fraud money, when you set the FPR at approximately 1%.

Displays the threshold and selected metrics for which the configured criteria reach their best performance.

Use the  option to configure the criteria you will use to explore a new target.

  2. **Evaluations**



Lists all existing evaluations in your model project, both resulting from single model evaluations and hyperparameter tuning. Use the search filter to navigate through these two evaluation types and use  checkboxes to select which **Evaluations** should be displayed for each item in the **Targets** area.

## Getting Startedâ

To start working on your models, learn how you can train a Model and/or perform a Hyperparameter Tuning.

### Application-level optionsâ

Let's see each of these options in more details.

#### Editing the applicationâ

You can **Edit** the name and the description of the application.

In addition to the name and description, the following options are also available:

  * **Auto-Healing** : When toggled, it monitors the state of the cluster and decides whether it needs to be repaired. If the application is in an invalid state, Pulse automatically triggers repair actions on the respective components.
  * **Lock Simple Rules Projects** : When toggled, Pulse stops all modifications to the Simple Rules Projects, depriving fraud analysts in Case Manager from adding any new rules to Simple Rules Projects.

With the **Export Resources** and **Import Resources** options, you can download/upload resources (features, rules, models, etc.) to transfer them from one Pulse environment to another.

# Rule Guide

This guide helps you write and maintain rules in Pulse. It also gives a short overview of how rules are deployed from the data science environment to production.

The following topics are not in the scope of this guide:

  * Self-service rules
  * Stateful rules



## Prerequisitesâ

This guide presumes the following:

  * The rules will be created in a data science environment by a data scientist or analyst who is familiarized with the [basic concepts of Pulse](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/glossary).

  * The data science environment has [cleaned historical data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data) that represents well the real-time data.

  * The data science environment has job profiles set up for resource-intensive plan executions. Contact Feedzai if you need help with this.

  * In the case of writing rules for an existing production environment, the data science environment is in the same state as the production environment.

This means that rules, models, plans and lists are identical in the two environments.




## The objective of rulesâ

Pulse rules can be used to control what happens with the transactions that have been previously scored by machine learning models. They can also be used to directly score and act upon events, a common case for starting projects with no available data yet to train models. Here business and compliance rules can be put in place to fight fraud.

In summary, with Pulse rules you can:

  * control what happens with a transaction that falls into a score threshold;
  * reflect business restrictions;
  * implement compliance rules;
  * react on newly found fraud patterns by implementing and testing a rule, without training a new model right ahead. This can be advantageous when a new fraud pattern is found and there is not enough historical data with that pattern to train a model.



### Rule life cycleâ

When setting up Pulse to process events, rules are put in place to reflect business rules, compliance rules, and other preventive measurements.

Besides creating the rules when setting up Pulse for the first time, you may need to add new rules to your environment later on as well.

This happens when you detect new financial crime trends, or when there is a new compliance or business rule in your organization.

The following image shows the life cycle of rules that are created in Pulse. Note that self-service rules created in Case Manager are not included in this life cycle, as they follow a completely different creation process.

The rule life cycle has the following stages:

  1. [Creating necessary lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-lists-and-adding-list-items): if the rules you want to create use lists, those need to be created before writing the rules.
  2. [Creating necessary features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features): analyze whether the fields that the rule needs are available in the data schema. If not, create the necessary features in a plan of Pulse, and run the plan to create the new fields in a new data source.
  3. [Creating or updating the rules project](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-or-updating-the-rules-project): when creating the first rules of a new Pulse setup, you first create a rules project that will group them. Rules projects are bound to the data schema. Hence, when adding rules to an existing set of rules, you have to update the data schema of the rules project if you have added new features as well. This will ensure that the new fields are available in the rules.
  4. [Creating or editing the rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules).
  5. [Creating a rule snapshot](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-a-rule-snapshot), and [evaluating rule performance using the snapshot](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/evaluating-rules-using-a-snapshot). A rule snapshot is a "photo" of the current rule configurations. It can be deployed and used later on in production. In addition, it can contain an evaluation of the included rules, which lets you assess the rule performance. The evaluation shows metrics like FPR and Recall for the rules. You can also export individual rule contribution during the evaluation, for further analysis.
  6. [Creating a sandbox evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-a-sandbox-evaluation), and [evaluating rule performance in sandbox](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/evaluating-your-rules-with-sandbox-evaluation). To evaluate decisions on transaction level, create a sandbox evaluation. Sandbox evaluations allow you to see the outcome of the rules project for each transaction.
  7. [Rule review](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/reviewing-rule-changes-in-a-snapshot). To ensure that you made the right changes and created the right rules, you can request a review from a peer.
  8. [Deploying the rules to the production environment](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/deploying-rules-to-the-production-environment): when the new set of rules matches your expectations, you export the created entities from the data science environment. Engineers of the production environment then import the exported entities to the production environment.
  9. [Monitoring rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/monitoring-rules): Feedzai Insights provides customizable dashboards to monitor the performance of rules.



To understand the basic concepts (rules, rule snapshots, plans, workflows, outcomes, etc.), check the [glossary](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/glossary).

# About Signing in to Pulse

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse provides a default sign in form in which you can enter your Username and Password to start a Pulse session. This Username and Password are associated with a Pulse User account that can be configured with a number of settings such as Pulse Groups, Pulse Roles, Tenants, among others.

There are two key functionalities in Pulse that impact the sign in process namely:

  * **Two-Factor Authentication** (2FA): Users are requested to sign in with two pieces of information to verify user identity. In this case, the user is prompted with a sign in form to enter its credentials (i.e. user account and password), followed by a second separate step in which the user has to provide a security code.
  * **Single Sign-On** (**SSO**): Users are created in Pulse by the concept of user provisioning and the sign in process include two different scenarios: Sign in initiated via an Identity Provider and Sign in initiated via a Service Provider.



## Learn Moreâ

Learn more about User sign in with **2FA** :

  * [Signing in with Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor)



Learn more about User sign in with **SSO** :

  * [Signing in with Single Sign-On](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on)

# Working with Applications

Was this page helpful?Â 

A Pulse application (**Pulse app**) is an interface that hosts resources developed by various end-users. With **Pulse apps** , Data Scientists, Software Engineers, and Fraud Analysts are able to collaborate on developing a Fraud Prevention solution. This concept is referred to as **App Collaboration**.

Pulse supports easy-to-use tools that allow users to develop resources in separate offline environments, and then combine the work in a production environment (see App Collaboration tools).

## Pulse Applicationsâ

Similarly to software apps which are interactive programs that allow users to perform tasks, a **Pulse app** is an interface that hosts resources developed by various end-users to perform certain tasks.

The ultimate goal of a **Pulse app** is to support the configuration of resources that work together to solve a well defined objective, e.g. detect fraud. To achieve this, **Pulse apps** are used to configure [Data Sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources), and develop [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans), [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules), among other functionalities. These resources are then configured on [Workflows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows), also hosted by **Pulse apps** , to process transactions in real-time.

Pulse resources are not bound to the host application. This allows multiple teams to develop resources in parallel using different environments. This concept is referred to as **App Collaboration** and is explained in more detail in the next subsection.

## App Collaborationâ

Developing a fraud-prevention application requires multiple teams to work together:

  * **Data Scientists:** Develop [Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop#feature-engineering) and **Models** using Data Science environments.
  * **Delivery teams** : Configure **Schema** and **Workflows** using Development environments.
  * **Engineering teams** : Write advanced **Rules** and populate [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) using Development environments.
  * **Fraud Analysts** : Write Self-service Rules (**SSR**) and populate **Lists** directly in Production.



Using the **App Collaboration** concept, each team evolves resources in parallel using **Pulse apps** configured on various offline environments. The changes are then transferred and combined in a trustful way with the resources that are Production. The image below illustrates the idea of **App Collaboration** :

The flow illustrated in the diagram above is not a one-time process. As fraud patterns evolve, and you gain new knowledge on your data, there is a need to re-engineer new features, retrain **Models** and write new **Rules**. These needs require a constant integration between work developed in offline environments with work that is in Production. Therefore, Feedzai recommends a working methodology that is explained in the page [App Collaboration Loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop) under the Operations Guide. This working methodology covers the following key points:

  * How to structure an application in different environments.
  * Workflow between environments.



## App Collaboration toolsâ

To make **App Collaboration** easy-to-use, Pulse provides a set of tools that allows you to migrate selected resources or the full **Pulse app** (i.e. PAPP file) between environments. The export/import tools foster the following:

  * **Merge resources:** Multiple teams working simultaneously on different resources can merge resources using Pulse UI.
  * **Standard working method:** You can easily manage a standard procedure to transfer resources to Production using **App Collaboration Loop**.
  * **Frequent updates:** Pulse services configured in runtime can be frequently updated in production because deployments are fast and easy to track.



### Migrating Resources and Pulse appsâ

Pulse allows migrating selected resources or entire **Pulse apps**. The decision to use one or the other depends on the type of changes that you want to migrate or the procedure that is in place for each project. Check the page [App Collaboration Loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop) for more information about the recommended procedure.

#### Export and import Resourcesâ

Pulse allows exporting and importing the following resources:

  * **Rules Projects** with or without snapshots.
  * **Lists** metadata.
  * **Models** with or without the binary.
  * **Plans** with or without executions.



Check the pages [Exporting Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources) and [Importing Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) to learn how to perform these operations.

#### Export and Import Pulse appsâ

Pulse allows exporting and importing the entire **Pulse app** through the UI. When updating a **Pulse app** in a live production environment, you should adopt the blue-green method to perform the update with zero downtime.

Check the page [Exporting and Importing Applications](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-and-importing-applications) to learn how to perform these operations.

## Application changes in runtimeâ

In Pulse, you can make changes on your **Workflow** , even when is processing transactions. These changes, however, are not immediately applied to the running application. Instead, they are only applied when you explicitly **Publish** the application.

Check the page [Publishing Application changes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/publishing-application-changes) to learn how to make your changes effective in the runtime **workflow**.

## Learn moreâ

The following pages allow a better understanding of how a **Pulse App** works:

  * [The Application Life Cycle](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/the-application-life-cycle)
  * [Publishing Application Changes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/publishing-application-changes)
  * [Exporting Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources)
  * [Importing Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources)

# Creating and Assigning Roles

A [role](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application#roles) is a set of [permissions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application#permissions) on Pulse resources (such as applications, models, rules, etc.). You can reuse roles across multiple users or groups for a centralized control and consistency.

The following sections describe how to create and use a role in Pulse.

## Creating a roleâ

To create a new role, complete the following steps:

  1. Select the  button in the menu bar to navigate to the **Administration** page.

  2. Open the **Security** tab.

  3. In the **Roles** section, add  a new role.

  4. Enter a **Name** for the role.

  5. You can add **Users** to the role now, or return to this form later to add users.

  6. In the **Permissions** field, select the [permissions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/permissions) that this role will grant to users.

  7. Use the **Save** button to create the role. If you want to create another role, you can use the  button next to the **Save** button and select **Save and New**.




You can find examples of typical roles in the [Typical permission setups](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/typical-permission-setups).

## Assigning a role to a userâ

To assign a role to a user directly, edit the role (see below) and add the user in the **Users** field.

Alternatively, [edit the user](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/manage-users#edit-a-user) and add the new role in the **Roles** field.

## Editing a roleâ

To edit a role, complete the following steps:

  1. Select the  button in the menu bar to navigate to the **Administration** page.
  2. Open the **Security** tab.
  3. In the **Roles** section, select the role that you want to edit.
  4. You can edit the list of **Users** that have this role, or the **[Permissions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/permissions)** that the role grants to users.
  5. Use the **Save** button to save the role.

# Creating and Using Groups

When Pulse users create a resource (rules project, plan, model project, data source, etc.) they can decide to make it visible only to certain groups.

For example, if a rules project is restricted to be visible only to a group, users of that group can view and edit that rules project if they have a role that allows them to view and edit rules projects.

The following sections explain how to create a group, how to add members to it, and how to set the visibility of a resource.

## Creating groupsâ

To create a new group, complete the following steps:

  1. Select the  button in the menu bar to navigate to the **Administration** page.
  2. Open the **Security** tab.
  3. In the **Groups** section, select _Hierarchical Groups_.
  4. In the group tree, select the  button to add a child group to an existing group.
  5. Enter a **Name** for the group.
  6. In the **Group Properties** field, you can add properties to the group in the form of key-value pairs.



## Adding users to a groupâ

To add a user to a group, complete the following steps:

  1. Select the  button in the menu bar to navigate to the **Administration** page.
  2. Open the **Security** tab.
  3. In the **Users** section, select the user.
  4. In the **Groups** field, add the group.
  5. **Save** the user.



## Using groups to limit visibilityâ

To limit the visibility of a resource, complete the following steps:

  1. Open the resource and use the  button to edit the visibility options.

  2. In the Visibility area, select the **Specific Groups** option.

  3. Select the groups to which the resource should be visible.

  4. For each group, select the actions (_Read_ , _Update_ , _Delete_) that can be performed on the resource.

Note that users will be able to perform the selected actions only if an administrator assigned them a role that allows performing that action.




### Exampleâ

Consider the following scenario.

  * Kate and John belong to the _data-scientist_ group.
  * John has a role that grants him Read permissions on model projects, but doesn't have any role with the _Update_ permission.
  * Kate creates a model project and sets it visible to the _data-scientists_ group, allowing group members to use their _Read_ and _Update_ permissions.



In this case, John can see the model project, but he cannot update or delete it.

# Securing Metadata

Pulse is designed to be used by multiple users. However, not all users need to have full rights over all metadata. As such, the metadata in Pulse can be secured to prevent undesired accesses.

Since controlling the permissions for each individual user in an application would not be manageable, Pulse allows resource instances to be shared with other [groups](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application#groups), instead of users. For instance, you can have a group _BankA_ where all users that are from Bank A will be on. Instead of allowing each user from this bank to have a certain right, you give these rights to the _BankA_ group. Because groups are hierarchical, you can have a sub-group of _BankA_ that has even less permissions (e.g. _BankA-Cashiers_).

## Setting the visibility of resourcesâ

Resources in Pulse are all configurable elements in an application â schemas, models, rules, data sources and so on. Given the multi-user nature of Pulse, it is common some resources not to be available for some users.

To secure resources, Pulse provides a way of setting the **visibility** of each resource instance.

That is, it is possible to allow a group to access KPI _A_ but not KPI _B_. It is also flexible to the point where you can define which of three different rights a group has over the instance â _read_ , _update_ and _delete_.

There is a fourth right, _info_ , that is activated whenever none of the previous rights are selected. When resources have _info_ right they will appear on the listing views but without any link to edit them. This serves the purpose of making the user aware of their existence without giving any further details about its properties.

Other rights

Read, update and delete rights are orthogonal to all types of resources. But some resources might have other specific rights. Applications, for instance, have a specific _manage_ right that controls the access to Publish/Stop the application.

The visibility of a resource can be configured on its view, under Advanced Options.

### Making a resource publicâ

The **default** security for a resource instance is basically no security. We call this **public visibility**. Essentially it means that everyone is able to view, update and delete it (as long as that user has the static permissions to do so).

Therefore, public resources should be used with care, given their non-existing security.

warning

Since resources are public by default, it is recommended that you configure their visibility upon creation, to avoid non-desired accesses.

### Making a resource privateâ

The higher security level for a resource instance is to make it private. If configured this way, an instance will only be visible to the user who created it. No other user will be able to view it or modify it. Not even users that belong to the same group as the creator.

### Sharing a resource with specific groupsâ

Besides making a resource public or hiding it from all users, it is also possible to share it with some groups. Not only that, you can also decide what actions a group can perform on that instance.

Groups are hierarchical. This is very useful when sharing a resource with a group. If you give _delete_ permissions to _Group A_ , **all ancestors** of _Group A_ will be able to delete the instance. The same applies to other rights.

## Configuring default visibility settingsâ

It is possible to define the default ownership settings with which new resources are created with. The common scenario of default ownership usage is the following: the need for some user's resources to have the same visibility settings (for example, being private resources or being resources that belong to some group). Such behavior would require applying the same visibility settings to each resource created by user. To facilitate this procedure, Pulse provides the mechanism that allow assigning the default settings for visibility per user. These settings will then be applied automatically to each created resource.

# Security Best Practices

This section covers some of the best practices for securing Pulse applications. It shows a sample security scenario and explains how each security entity helps keeping the application secure and maintainable. The page covers some generic security best practices you should pay attention to, even if your project organization differs from the sample scenario presented here.

## Local data source permissionsâ

By default, a Pulse user who has permissions to create data sources can access any file in the local filesystem of the Pulse server.

This means that by specifying `file://<path-to-file>` in the URL path, the user might be able to have the contents of sensitive files displayed in the data source preview. Examples include:

  * _/etc/passwd_
  * _/etc/shadow_
  * Credentials to other machines such as databases that are present in config files under Pulse directory: _conf/_



For this reason, Pulse has a property that limits the allowed paths. Note that this property only applies locally, and thus, remote locations such as HDFS should restrict file accesses using the remote system's permissions, using the property `allowedLocalDatasourcePaths`.

Below is an example on how to restrict the allowed local paths of source file locations for data sources, assuming that Pulse is installed in the path _/opt/pulse_ :

`pulse.global.allowedLocalDatasourcePaths=/opt/pulse/var/datasources`

info

The restriction on allowed local paths can also be specified per **Pulse app**.

## Sample security scenarioâ

The following diagram depicts a hypothetical scenario of an acquiring company deploying Pulse to provide its merchants with fraud detection and prevention capabilities. All merchants will benefit from the acquirer defined fraud detection rules and each merchant's own fraud analysts can create customized rules tailored to their specific cases.

## Security entities and their relationshipsâ

We will now look at each security entity, explain why it is needed and how it interacts with the other security entities. We will also analyze the role of each security entity on building our sample security scenario.

### Usersâ

Users are the most well known security entity. They are present in almost every system with authentication. Every subject that authenticates in Pulse must have a unique user. The authentication of the user can be managed by Pulse itself or by an external authentication system such as Active Directory. Users are only responsible for the authentication part. Authorization is handled by permissions and resource rights. Users belong to groups which are the easiest and more maintainable way of managing authorization.

note

When creating new users, it is a good security practice to always set the default ownership. In practice, this will ensure that resources created by that user will, by default, be created with those chosen groups and rights for each group.

### Groupsâ

Groups represent organization positions that users of the system will belong to. In our sample scenario, **user** _Merchant B Employee 1_ **belongs to the groups** _Merchant B Employees_ and _Merchant Employees_. We can say this user is an employee of Merchant B and also a generic Merchant employee.

info

It is useful to have the user belong to a generic group of merchant employees because some of the system resources might have to be shared to all merchant employees regardless of the merchant. This greatly simplifies the maintenance of the system.

In our sample scenario, an example of a resource that should be shared to the _Merchants Employees_ group is the _Generic Merchant Rules_ resource. In this case, the sharing would be **read-only** , we will see how to do that later.

Each group might have zero or more associated roles. Having roles associated to groups is useful in several ways. It helps managing what each user can do by just assigning them to their groups, instead of having to give roles to each user. It also helps when you need to revoke some role from all users in a group, in this case you just have to edit the group, instead of editing all the users. Learn everything about groups in the [Security Entities](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application) page.

### Roles and permissionsâ

A [permission](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application#permissions) is a right to do a very specific action. Pulse has many built-in permissions for managing the resources; for instance, the permission to _read fraud rules_ , or the permission to _create new fraud rules_.

info

A permission is just a right to do some action on a resource (e.g. _read fraud rules_). It says nothing about the right to do that action on a particular resource instance (e.g. _read fraud rule X_). Resource rights are the topic of the next section.

A [role](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application#roles) is just a set of permissions.

Permissions are the most fine-grained security entity. After creating suitable roles, you will not have to use permissions directly. They will be enforced through the association of users to specific roles and groups. As we said earlier when discussing groups, roles can be associated to groups, making the group indirectly associated with the permissions in those roles. Groups are the highest level security entity and you should use them to create secure and maintainable deployments.

In our example scenario, both _Merchants Managers_ and _Merchants Employees_ groups are associated with roles. The roles depicted here do not exist in Pulse and have to be created with the relevant permissions. The _rules-management_ role might give users of the _Merchants Managers_ group permissions to create, read, update and delete fraud rules. While a user of the _Merchants Employees_ group might only have permissions to manage templated fraud rules and read fraud rules.

Learn everything about roles and permissions in the [Security Entities](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application) page.

### Resource rightsâ

Resource rights dictate what users of a group can do to a resource instance.

Resource rights are granted when the resource instance is created or updated. To understand this section you should be familiar with the concepts covered in the [Securing Metadata](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/securing-metadata) page.

info

Resource rights never override the user's permissions. If a user does not have the permission to read fraud rules, a fraud rule shared with that user's group will still be invisible to the user.

Considering our sample scenario, _Merchant A Rules_ and _Merchant B Rules_ must be visible only to users of _Merchant A Employees_ and _Merchant B Employees_ groups respectively. To achieve this, the user creating the rule must share it with the group and grant that group the desired rights. In this case it could be the rights to do everything with the rule, since this would apply only to users of that group. The _Generic Merchant Rules_ should be shared with the _Merchants Employees_ group but only having _Read_ right. Remember that users belonging to groups higher on the groups hierarchy will have the same rights, if not more.

Read the [Typical permission setups](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/typical-permission-setups) for guidance on specific cases related to rights management.

## Use casesâ

This section covers some of the best practices related to common security use cases. Some are related to the sample scenario presented before while others are more generally applicable.

### Restricting the manage right on applicationsâ

When creating an application remember to configure the application ownership to Groups and grant the _manage_ right only to a restricted group of application administrators. This will prevent any user with access to the application from inadvertently or maliciously publishing or stopping the application.

### Creating a new userâ

When creating new users, there are no default assignments regarding groups, roles, etc. The administrator must know beforehand how to configure the new user for it to reach its goals. Usually adding users is not time consuming, since it's quite common to already have some roles completely configured, hence it's only a matter of connecting the new user to the designated groups and it's done.

So let's say you need to create a user that manages all the merchants - let's call it _Merchant Manager 1_. If you assign this user to the _Merchants Managers_ group, it will have access to all the groups that are below in the group hierarchy - that is _Merchant A_ *,** Merchant B* and _Merchants Employees_ \- besides all resources and roles assigned to the original assignment group (_Merchants Manager_). All the resources and roles bound to these groups will be available as well to this new user.

tip

The higher a user is in the groups hierarchy, the more rights will accumulate and therefore more power over the application resources.

# Typical Permission Setups

This page describes several scenarios that administrators often need to configure in Pulse.

Resource dependencies

Resources sometimes have dependencies between them, hence to access one, you might need to have access to another. These dependencies are not always obvious. If you are having difficulties with resource permissions, contact Feedzai's technical support.

## Basic read-only accessâ

A good reference of the permissions necessary for a user to be able to sign in to Pulse is the `pulseviews-reader` role. With the permissions of this role, a user can log in and view all the resources.

The permissions assigned to `pulseviews-reader` are as follows:

Name| Description  
---|---  
`application:*:read`| Allows the user to get the list and read metadata resource instances (e.g., applications, KPIs).  
`pulseviews:login`| Allows the user to log in.  
`pulseviews:management:tabs:*`| Allows the user to see all the tabs available in Pulse.  
`security:ownership:read`| Allows the user to read ownership information (necessary to check if he can see specific resource instances).  
`security:users:read`| Allows the user to read its metadata.  
  
## Restrict tenant permissions with rolesâ

In the context of multi-tenancy, Pulse allows large companies to manage multiple clients by configuring a tenant for each client. Multiple users can be associated with a tenant to allow access and management of each account in Pulse. The level of access and permissions given to each tenant is controlled by adding roles to the user with defined permissions. The following is the list of permissions for tenant users:

  * `pulseviews:login`
  * `security:ownership:read`
  * `security:permissions:read`
  * `security:roles:read`
  * `security:users:update`
  * `security:users:read`



These are the minimum permissions for a user to be able to log in. A user with this role will be able to log in to Pulse, but will not be able to do anything else (e.g. to open Pulse applications). The same applies to Case Manager; the user will need to have other roles with Case Manager permissions (`cm:...`), according to the work that user needs to do (e.g. CM admin, CM analyst, etc.).

## Pulse permissionsâ

A full list with all the permissions in Pulse can be found in the [List of Permissions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/permissions) page.

# Component Encryption

Was this page helpful?Â 

**Component encryption** provides secure communication between Pulse components.

Protecting sensitive data including credit card numbers, names and addresses is a big concern in the field of risk management. To address this concern, component encryption creates a trustful environment by securing in-transit data that is communicated across Pulse components. The goal of component encryption is to ensure data privacy and integrity.

In Pulse, component encryption is implemented using SSL/TLS.

## Introduction to component encryptionâ

Component encryption aims to protect the communication between components in Pulse. This includes securing the communication between the following components:

  * Internal Pulse components (e.g. between Pulse server and application engine).
  * Internal and external components (e.g. between Pulse server and storage).
  * External components (e.g. between various nodes of external components such as Cassandra nodes).



### How does encryption work?â

Pulse implements component encryption using SSL/TLS. With these protocols, the data communicated between components is encrypted using a shared secret referred to as encryption key.

The following steps summarize the process of generating and using an encryption key:

  1. Server sends its public key to the client. This key is included in a digital certificate chain that contains additional information about the server.
  2. Client generates the encryption key.
  3. Client sends the encryption key to the server. In this step, the encryption key is encrypted with the server public key.
  4. Server decrypts the encrypted key sent by the client using the server private key.
  5. At this point the server and the client share the encryption key. All the communications between the server and the client during an active session can be encrypted with this key.



### Authenticationâ

In addition to encryption, SSL/TLS typically requires an authentication step to establish a connection between two components. In a typical case, the authentication is performed by the client (i.e. client authenticates the server) which is referred to as server authentication. However, authentication can be also extended to enable mutual authentication, i.e. client authenticates the server and the server authenticates the client. This latter option is commonly referred to as client authentication.

To perform server authentication, the client is required to trust a certificate presented by the server. More specifically, the component acting as a client checks:

  * If the server certificate is valid.
  * If the server certificate is signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). There are different approaches to have signed certificates which are explained in the section SSL/TLS certificates.



### Component encryption with server authenticationâ

Component encryption with server authentication requires information that must be configured on both the server and the client side to establish a secure connection:

  * **Server side** : a private key and a signed certificate which certifies the information contained in the certificate.
  * **Client side** : one or more certificates that the client trusts.



Typically, the keys and the certificates can be stored in various formats. In Pulse, this information is stored in Java KeyStore (JKS) format. Pulse follows a conventional nomenclature:

  * **keystore:** A file that contains private keys and certificates.

A keystore file is protected with two passwords: one for the whole store and one for accessing the private key. Note that a keystore can contain more than one private key as long as each private key has a different password.

  * **trustore** : A file that contains only certificates.

A certificate contains a public key and a digital signature generated with the private key of the certificate authority that issued it.

The access to a truststore file can be optionally secured with a password named truststore password. Technically, a truststore file is just keystore with no private keys; we make this distinction only to make it clear the purpose of the store.




Component encryption with server authentication only requires configuration of a keystore on the server side and a truststore on the client side.

The next section presents a diagram of the Pulse architecture for a better visualization of the components that require configuration of component encryption.

## Pulse architecture with component encryptionâ

The following diagram shows a basic Pulse architecture comprising internal Pulse components (e.g. Pulse server, application engine) and external components (e.g. Cassandra, Spark):

The numbers represent communication encryption between components. As shown in figure, the protocol SSL/TLS for component encryption is combined with additional communication protocols depending on the component.

## Configuring component encryption in Pulseâ

To configure component encryption, Pulse requires a keystore when acting as a server and a truststore when acting as a client. The truststore has to contain a valid certificate signed by a trusted CA.

The default configuration of component encryption is done using `pulse.global` properties as described in the page [Configuration Overview](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/configuration-overview) page.

In addition to setting default Pulse properties, there are components that cannot be configured with the default approach (e.g. relational databases) or that need custom configurations. This is described in the [Configuring Encryption for External Components](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/configuring-external-components) page.

### SSL/TLS Certificatesâ

SSL/TLS certificates are stored inside keystores and truststores which are used in the authentication process.

There are different options to configure certificates for authentication including:

  * Using self-signed certificates and configuring all components to trust them.
  * Using certificates signed by an internal CA and configuring all components to trust this CA.
  * Using certificates signed by a commercial external CA. This is technically identical to the previous one but has an higher administrative overhead; however, well known CAs are typically trusted without requiring a truststore to be setup.



The second approach is the recommended in a production environment in Pulse, whereas the first approach is typically used in a testing environment. To help the configuration process, Pulse includes scripts to help creating keystores and truststores files with all the required certificates. Visit the [Creating Certificates](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/creating-certificates) page for more information on how to configure these scripts.

# Security Configuration

Similar to other services the configuration for this module is performed in the main configuration file `PULSE_HOME/conf/pulse.properties`. Properties can be configured with name space pulse.manager or pulse.global.

## Complete example configurationâ

The following is a complete example configuration.
    
    
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.createDefaults=true  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.hash=SHA-256  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.database.schemapolicy=none  
      
    # LDAP example:  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample1.enable=false  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample1.systemusername=cn=admin,ou=people,dc=example,dc=com  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample1.systempassword=superduperpassword  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample1.connection=ldap://example.com  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample1.template=cn={0},ou=people,dc=example,dc=com  
      
    # LDAPS example:  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample2.enable=false  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample2.systemusername=cn=admin,ou=people,dc=example,dc=com  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample2.systempassword=superduperpassword  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample2.connection=ldaps://example.com  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.ldap.sample2.template=cn={0},ou=people,dc=example,dc=com  
      
    # AD example:  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample1.enable=true  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample1.url=ldap://test-ad.zai  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample1.searchfilter=(&(objectClass=user)(userPrincipalName=${login}))  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample1.searchbase=DC=feedzai,DC=com  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample1.searchscope=2  
      
    # Another AD example with Default Domain and system's account:  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample2.enable=true  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample2.url=ldap://test-ad.zai  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample2.searchfilter=(&(objectClass=user)(userPrincipalName=${login}))  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample2.searchbase=DC=feedzai,DC=com  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample2.searchscope=2  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample2.defaultdomain=feedzai.com  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample2.systemaccountusername=pulse-ad-username  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.activedirectory.sample2.systemaccountpassword=7a724f8fe49eb0dc241d27e6b71e000a  
      
    # Another Example for configuration with PAM:  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.pam.sample3.enable=true  
    <target_namespace>.services.core.security.realm.pam.sample3.service=common-auth

## Configuring the security realmâ

You can also configure the security realm that you are going to use in this service's properties. `<name>` can be any user-defined string in case there are multiple realms configured. One name per realm.

info

If you are using LDAP or PAM, note that you will need to first create the users in the Pulse database, and mark them as external. Only afterwards you can authenticate using these services.

Parameter name| Type| Description| Mandatory| Default value  
---|---|---|---|---  
`realm.ldap.<name>.systemusername`| String| The system username (use only if the LDAP server needs system authentication).| No| N/A  
`realm.ldap.<name>.systempassword`| String| The system password (use only if the LDAP server needs system authentication). This field has configuration encryption support.| No| N/A  
`realm.ldap.<name>.connection`| String| The LDAP / LDAPS connection. When using LDAPS, add the certificate to the truststore of Pulse, using the [keytool](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/tools/windows/keytool.html).| Yes| N/A  
`realm.ldap.<name>.template`| String| The template to use for authentication. When performing authentication, {0} will be replaced by the username.| Yes| N/A  
  
### Configuring the security realm's active directoryâ

An active directory can be also be configured for the security realm.

Parameter name| Type| Description| Mandatory| Default value  
---|---|---|---|---  
`realm.activeDirectory.<name>.url`| String| The Active Directory LDAP enpoint (e.g. ldap://test-ad.zai). To use a SSL connection (e.g. ldaps://test-ad.zai), the Active Directory server certificate must be installed into the JVM key store.| Yes| N/A  
`realm.activeDirectory.<name>.searchBase`| String| The base tree node to start a search (e.g. DC=feedzai,DC=com).| Yes| N/A  
`realm.activeDirectory.<name>.searchScope`| Integer| The type of search scope to use: 0 (Base), 1 (One level) and2 (Subtree)| No| 0 (Base)  
`realm.activeDirectory.<name>.searchFilter`| String| The filter to use for authentication. When performing authentication `${login}` will be replaced by the username (e.g. `(&(objectClass=user)(userPrincipalName=${login}))`).| Yes| N/A  
`realm.activeDirectory.<name>.defaultDomain`| String| A default domain that will be appended to the username if no domain is already provided with the username (e.g. feedzai.com).| No| N/A  
`realm.activeDirectory.<name>.systemAccountUsername`| String| System's account username to be used on searching across the directory for the authorized users, instead of the end-users account. When provided, this should be specified in conjunction with the systemAccountPassword. If not provided, the end-user's account will be used.| No| N/A  
`realm.activeDirectory.<name>.systemAccountPassword`| String| System's account password to be used on searching across the directory for the authorized users. Check further information on systemAccountUsername.| No| N/A  
  
caution

LDAP protocol searches can have results with continuation references (<https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4511#section-4.5.3>).

In Pulse's context, this can impact the system at 2 situations:

  1. The allowed user set is spread across multiple servers (forest setup);
  2. A valid user credentials are provided, outside of the search parameters scope (user not authorized to access Pulse).



When either of these situations occurs, connectivity is required towards all possible endpoints which includes IP connectivity and SSL configurations (e.g. server's certificate validation).

Not doing so could lead to:

  1. Prevent login for authorized users;
  2. Long lasting requests waiting for connect timeouts.



### Configuring the Security Realm's PAMâ

PAM can be also be configured for the security realm.

Parameter name| Type| Description| Mandatory| Default value  
---|---|---|---|---  
`realm.pam.<name>.service`| String| The PAM service name. The name of the PAM service Pulse should use for authentication (must be in the /etc/pam.d directory).| Yes| N/A  
  
## Default security credentialsâ

By default, the module is configured to clean all security tables and create a default user with access to everything when you start the Pulse Server. If you don't want this to happen, you **must** set the `policy` to create (or simply remove the tag) and set `createDefaults` to `false`.

The default credentials use the username `pulse` and password `pulse`.

## HTTP adapter security configurationâ

The security configuration for the HTTP adapter is in the file `PULSE_HOME/conf/engine/web/http-adapter.ini`. There you can find the filters and the URL patterns being filtered. By default it looks like the following.
    
    
    [main]  
    authc.loginUrl = /login.jsp  
    ssl.port = 8443  
      
    [urls]  
    /login.jsp = ssl, authc  
    /streams/** = ssl, authc  
    /baselines/** = ssl, authc  
    /kpis/** = ssl, authc  
    

The **main** section is used to configure the filters. In this case, we are stating that the login page is "login.jsp" and that the SSL port is "8443".

The **urls** section is used to define the paths that will be filtered. In this case, everything beyond "streams", "baselines" and "kpis" will be secured using both defined filters.

If you want to learn more about Shiro filters, please refer to [Shiro Web Configuration](http://shiro.apache.org/web.html).

info

Pulse overrides the default Shiro behavior. For example, if you declare a new Shiro instance, rules or permissions will not apply.

## Using SSL in Pulseâ

Must change the default certificate

Pulse bundles a self-signed certificate which allows users to connect to it through HTTPS. This can be found in the conf/engine/jetty/ directory, comprising a keystore and a jetty.xml file. This certificate **must not be used in production** environments, as it is insecure. Learn how to set up a certificate in [Configuring an SSL Certificate for Pulse](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/security-configuration/configuring-an-ssl-certificate).

Title: Single Sign-On | Feedzai Pulse

# Single Sign-On

Was this page helpful?Â 

Single Sign-On (**SSO**) is a functionality that allows users to access various applications (_i.e._ to start a session) by signing in to only one of the applications. This eliminates the need for users to set different passwords as well as to sign in to each application individually.

Another component associated with this functionality is allowing users to sign out from all the applications at once (_i.e._ without having to sign out individually from all the applications). This component is commonly referred to as Single Logout (**SLO**).

**SSO** in Pulse is done using Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) as the protocol to authenticate and optionally authorize users that are provisioned by an external Identity Provider.

## Introduction to SAMLâ

SAML is an XML-based open standard for exchanging user authentication and authorization information between security domains. The primary use case of SAML is to enable **SSO** , which increases security, allows practical access to multiple applications and decreases administrative time and costs relative to the traditional option of signing in to each application individually.

SAML uses security tokens that contain assertions to communicate user information between a SAML authority, referred to as Identity Provider (IdP), and a SAML consumer, referred to as Service Provider (SP). At a high level, the IdP is the asserting party which is responsible for managing the identity information of users and to provide the information in form of tokens to the SPs. The SP corresponds to an application that requires user authentication to start an active session. The SP constitutes the relying party because it allows the user to sign in based on the information provided by the IdP. Note that the SP is not responsible for managing user credentials and does not even have access to the user password.

## SSO in Pulse using SAML 2.0â

SAML 2.0 is the current version supported by Pulse. In the context of **SSO** integration through SAML, Pulse acts as the SP, and the IdP is the server in which the user has an account and the user credentials are stored. There is a number of ways in which the IdP can be configured to manage user information, one of which is by a self-hosted Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) server.

AD FS is a service provided by Microsoft as a standard role for Windows Server that provides web sign in using existing Active Directory (AD) credentials. In the case of **SSO** implemented in Pulse, the IdP of choice is AD FS; however, any other standard-compliant IdP service may be used instead (Pulse is agnostic to the implementation). Since the implementation of SAML is not dedicated to Pulse, FeedzaiÂ´s Clients may have already a SAML architecture implemented before acquiring any of the FeedzaiÂ´s products.

Regarding SSO, Pulse has two different types of users:

  * **Non-SSO Users:** These users are created and their information is managed inside Pulse. They also [sign in using a Pulse form](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse).
  * **SSO Users:** External users that are able to [sign in into Pulse by using an external page](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on) which is managed by the IdP. Depending on how the user **authorization** is configured in Pulse, **SSO Users** can be handled in two distinct ways:
    * If authorization is configured to be managed by the IdP (default behaviour), users can be created only by the **automatic user provisioning**. When a new user signs in for the first time, it does not exist as a **Pulse User** (_i.e._ is not yet manually configured in Pulse). This Pulse user is created on-the-fly after being authorized by the IdP. The user credentials and additional user information are managed by the IdP which communicates with Pulse to provide user authentication and authorization.
    * If authorization is explicitly configured to be managed by Pulse, SSO users can login only after they are created in Pulse. In this case, user authorization (roles, groups, etc) is entirely managed in Pulse, and the IdP manages only the authentication.



Learn more about user provisioning in Pulse.

## Scenarios of SSO in Pulseâ

There is currently one supported scenario of **SSO** using SAML, namely the **SP-initiated** configuration.

In this case, when a user opens a Pulse URL, and is not already signed in, they are redirected to a URL that is managed by the IdP. In this IdP URL, the user is prompted with a sign-in form, and after being authenticated, they are automatically redirected back to the Feedzai URL. The user is then signed in to the application that they were accessing in the first place (_i.e._ Pulse URL) as well as to all the other applications that are configured as SPs.

### More on SP-initiated configurationâ

Consider the scenario in which the user browses to a Pulse URL that they have saved as a bookmark, or was sent by email. E.g.:
    
    
    http://pulseviews/management/#apps/datasciencedemo/datascience  
    

The following steps explain sign in via SP-initiated:

  1. User opens the Pulse URL.
  2. The user is redirected to the URL of the IdP, which is configured in Pulse, by sending a SAML authentication request.
  3. If the user does not have an active session, the user is prompted with a sign in form that is configured by the IdP and requires authentication (_e.g._ username and password).
  4. The IdP builds the SAML authentication response in the form of XML containing the userâs username and/or email address as well as other optional provisioning data, signs it using an X.509 certificate, and sends the information to Pulse. Pulse retrieves the authentication response and validates it using the certificate fingerprint. The user is now signed in to Pulse.



Note that, if the user is already signed in when opening the Pulse URL (_i.e._ Step 1), Steps 2 and 4 still apply; however, the user is not prompted with the sign in form mentioned in Step 3. The user might notice the address bar flicking as a result of Steps 2 and 4, but no further interaction is required.

Learn more about [sign in via SP-initiated in Pulse](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on/signing-in-via-sp-initiated).

## User Provisioningâ

Depending on how Pulse is configured, user authorization settings can be managed by the IdP (default behavior) or by Pulse.

### External authorization (using IdP)â

Automatic user provisioning is a mandatory component of Pulse SSO for external authentication. It is the concept of creating users on-the-fly at the first time that they sign in without being previously created as Pulse Users. In the case of SSO Users, provisioning is the only option to create users, since they cannot be manually created using the Pulse UI first, and after configured as SSO Users. When an SSO User signs, Pulse updates its information regarding the referred user. User provisioning is done through a SAML assertion that is sent by the IdP to the SP. This assertion contains attributes that can be configured in IdP service of choice. The assertion can be used to send additional information beyond the user identity (_i.e._ username) which Pulse will map to the correspondent configurations in the User Settings. This includes **Full Name** , **Language** , **Groups** , **Roles** , and **Tenants**.

### Internal authorizationâ

If Pulse is set up to use internal authorization, then SSO users need to be created both in the IdP and in Pulse. That means that an IdP user is authorized to access Pulse only if a user with the same identifier is created in Pulse. The authorization properties of that user (roles, groups) are managed in Pulse, as with normal users. In this case, there is no need to configure authorization settings in IdP since it will be ignored by Pulse.

## Sign outâ

Sign out is performed by the **SLO** component. Similarly to the sign in requests, the sign out comprises a LogoutRequest and a LogoutResponse.

Pulse supports sign out via **SP-initiated** \- a user signs out from one of the SPs.

There are different ways to implement the SP-initiated sign-out; for example, the application can initiate the LogoutRequest to the IdP. The IdP communicates with all the SPs to sign out all the active sessions without requiring further user interaction. The SPs reply back with a LogoutResponse.

## Session Managementâ

According to the SAML 2.0 specification, there is an attribute that may be included in the assertion named `SessionNotOnOrAfter`. This attribute corresponds to the time instant, encoded in UTC, at which the IdP and the SP sessions must be considered ended.

This is an optional attribute that can be added to the SAML assertion. If the attribute is not included, the time for the session to end is set by the same logic Pulse uses for Non-SSO user sessions. When the session is expired, the user can sign in via SP-initiated and continue the work at the point that was left when the session was expired.

## Learn Moreâ

To expand your knowledge on the SSO functionality, visit the following pages:

  * [Sign in via SP-initiated in Pulse](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on/signing-in-via-sp-initiated)
  * [Signing in as Pulse Administrator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on/signing-in-as-pulse-administrator)


  * [Configuring AD FS](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/single-sign-on/configuring-ad-fs)
