# Errors in App Collaboration

Was this page helpful?Â 

This page provides a list of errors that might occur when performing tasks associated to App Collaboration.

## List of errorsâ

See a list of error codes, descriptions and additional information in the following table:

Error Code| Error description| Additional information  
---|---|---  
APP_COLLAB_001| There is an existing **List** with the same name but it is not compatible with the **List** contained in the zip file generated by the partial export (i.e. [resource bundle](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/bundle-structure)).| With **App collaboration,** all the **Lists** are exported when using the partial export option and imported in the target environment using the partial import option. A **List** that does not exist it the target environment is created during the import. This error may occur when a **List** that is in the resource bundle already exists in the target with the same name and both **Lists** are not compatible to each other.  
APP_COLLAB_002| A partial request configuration was not found with the given id.| This error should not occur under normal operation. The browser issues the export in separate requests, one to prepare the export and another to actual perform the export. This error means that the actual export request is not able to find the previous export preparation data.  
APP_COLLAB_003| Partial import file not found or not readable.| This error should not occur under normal operation. It means that the uploaded zip file that was stored in disk can no longer be used in subsequent operations.  
APP_COLLAB_004| Non-deployable **Plans** cannot be partial exported.| This error occurs because only deployable **Plans** can be exported.  
APP_COLLAB_005| The Simple **Rules Project** must be exported with at least one snapshot.|   
APP_COLLAB_006| The Simple **Rules Project** must be imported with at least one snapshot.|   
APP_COLLAB_007| Binary **Model** requested but not found in the training folder.| This error occurs when the user selects to export the binary of the **Model;** however, this binary cannot be found.  
APP_COLLAB_008| Configuration for importing a **Model** must specify the destination **Model** Project id.| **Model** Projects are not created automatically when importing a **Model** , and thus a target **Model** Project must be specified in the import configuration.  
APP_COLLAB_009| **Workflow** validation error.| When trying to change the Workflow element to reference an imported resource (**Rules** snapshot, **Plan** execution or **Model**) the **Workflow** became invalid. The work-around may be to import without specifying new mappings in the Workflow.  
APP_COLLAB_010| The imported **Plan** becomes invalid using the local schema.| The **Plan** was valid with its source schema, but the user decides to import the **Plan** using the schema in the target environment, and the **Plan** becomes no longer valid. This might occur because some field referenced by the **Plan** does not exist in the target schema or the field type is not compatible.  
APP_COLLAB_011| Cannot override a **Plan** of a different type.| This error occurs because only deployable **Plans** can be imported.  
APP_COLLAB_012| Some of the resources selected for importing are missing in the zip file.| The import configuration is referencing resources that are not included in the zip file.

# How to Code Review

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

Code review is an essential step to ensure that you deploy resources that meet the quality standards required in the field of Fraud Prevention. This guide provides you recommendations on how to accomplish this action.

## How toâ

As an example, consider that you want to migrate a resource from **DS environment** to **DEV environment**. The recommended approach for sharing changes and perform code review comprises the following steps:

  1. Perform a [partial export](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources) of the relevant resources, for example, a deployable [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) in the **DS environment** (i.e. imagine that this step is executed on day 1).

  2. Import the resources in the **DEV environment** (e.g. the deployable **Plan**).

note

The resources will keep evolving in the **DS environment**.

  3. Perform a **partial export** of the same resource (i.e. the deployable **Plan**) in the **DS environment** (i.e. imagine that this step is executed on day 2).

  4. Compare the partial exports of the resource between day 1 and day 2. To do so, there are two options:

     * Version the day 1 export in git and replace it with the day 2 export, and then send the changes to review using the code review tools supported by your project (e.g. [Differential](https://phacility.com/phabricator/differential/)).
     * Export the resource from the DEV environment and perform a diff against the resource exported in day 2. See the page [Comparing resource versions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/comparing-resource-versions) for examples on how to perform this step.
  5. If you agree with the changes, import the resource obtained in Step 3 in the **DEV environment**.




## Next Stepsâ

Now that you know the code review process, check the page [How to merge](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/how-to-merge) to learn how to migrate your work to the target environment.

On this page

# How to Merge

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

The options [Export Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources) and [Import Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) allow you to migrate Pulse resources from one environment to another. Sometimes you might need to merge the work developed by various teams in a single environment.

This guide applies when you want to merge more than one bundle containing changes that are in different folders among all the bundles (see page [Bundle structure](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/bundle-structure) to learn how files are organized in a bundle). More specifically, this applies to the following situations:

  * Merge changes of different bundles containing different Pulse resources. For example, one bundle file contains **Rules Projects** and another bundle file contains **Models.**
  * Merge changes in different bundles containing the same type of resource but with different resource projects. For example, two bundles with **Rules Projects:** one of them contains a **Rules Project** named _Card Transactions_ and the other contains a **Rules Project** named _Country transactions_.



Merge the same resource

If you have more than one bundle containing the same JSON file that has evolved simultaneously in different environments (e.g. two files contain different **Rules** inside a **Rules Project** named _Card Transactions_), you might have to open the two JSON files to combine the changes. This operation is **not recommended** because it is extremely error prone.

## How toâ

You have two methods to merge your work in a new environment:

  * **Recommended approach:** Merging using Pulse UI.
  * **Alternative approach:** Merging manually by copying and paste the folders in the bundle file.



### Merging using Pulse UIâ

Recommended approach

Merging using Pulse UI is the recommended approach to minimize risks

If you are importing multiple bundles using the Import option, execute the following actions for each file you want to import:

  1. Select the **Pulse app** that will host the new resources

  2. Select the button  to open the application options:

  3. Select the option  to open the import wizard.

  4. Follow the instructions in the page [Importing Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) to complete the steps required by the import wizard.

  5. After importing, repeat Steps 2-4 to import the other bundle files.




### Merging manuallyâ

If you choose to manually merge the file before importing the bundle, execute the following actions:

  1. Copy and paste the JSON files of each bundle folder to a single folder on your operating system, following the [bundle structure](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/bundle-structure).

  2. Zip the folder of the resources to a final folder to be imported by the UI.

Zip the folders of the resources

You need to zip directly the folders of the resources rather than their parent folder. This is shown in the figure below:

  3. Select the option  to open the import wizard.

  4. Follow the instructions in the page [Importing Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) to complete the steps required by the import wizard.




#### Merging between JSON filesâ

Approach not supported

Merging between JSON files has to be done manually and is not supported by the product.

When you have JSON files with different versions of the same resource resulting from evolving the same block in different environments, you cannot use the options described above to merge the changes. In this case, you need to open the JSON files and combine the changes manually.

The page [Comparing resource versions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/comparing-resource-versions) provides typical examples of comparisons between changes within **Rules Projects** , **Models** and **Plans**. This examples give you an idea of what needs to be combine when merging JSON files.

However, you should keep in mind that merging changes in JSON files might require extra effort and planning. For example, if you merge a **Rule** into a **Rules Project** ,there are a number of implications including:

  * Define the **Rule** order.
  * Create a new snapshot to include the new **Rule**.
  * Add the snapshot to the runtime **Workflow**.



## Next Stepsâ

Now that you understand how to merge files, take a look at the page [Errors in App Collaboration](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/errors-in-app-collaboration).

# How to Organize Your Work with Blocks

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

While developing new profiles with Plans, re-training Models with new data, and testing new Rules, using offline environments, your Pulse Application (Pulse app) will keep evolving in Production. By structuring your work with the concept of [Block ownership](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop#block-ownership) you are allowing:

  * Multiple teams to work in parallel using different environments.
  * Easy and quick migration of resources between environments.



This page provides recommendations on how to set Pulse resources in the Data Science tab, and map them into the runtime Workflow using the concept of **Block ownership**.

## How toâ

This section guides you on how to combine resources developed in different environments into a single environment using a DEV environment as an example. Typically, a DEV environment contains the resources that are evolved by engineers, as well as the resources that are being evolved in PROD and in DS, which are recurrently [imported](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) to DEV.

### Use-case exampleâ

Imagine that you have three environments with the following resources:

| DS Environment| DEV Environment| PROD Environment  
---|---|---|---  
**Model**| **Evolving** : Model Project named _Card Transactions Detection_.| Contains the Model evolved in DS| Contains the Model evolved in DS  
**Plan**| **Evolving** : Plan named _Features Plan_.| Contains the Plan evolved in DS| Contains the Plan evolved in DS  
**Rules**| **Evolving** : Two Rules Projects named _DS Rules Project 1_ , _DS Rules Project 2_.| **Evolving** : One Rules Project named _Eng Rules Project 1_.| **Evolving** : One Rules Project named _Self-service Rules 1._  
  
Nomenclature

The names used in this scenario are given as examples to illustrate ownership. For example, in a real project, you will not have all the engineer Rules in the same Rules Project. In fact, you will most likely have the Rules grouped by logic in multiple Rules Projects. Therefore, the key point is to define which team will be the owner of each Rules Project (i.e. each block).

### Mapping resources in DEVâ

To start working on resources and use them in runtime, you have to create the resources in Data Science tab and configure them in the Workflows tab.

#### Data Science tabâ

The figure below shows the example of a DEV environment with the following resources highlighted:

  * The **Plan** _Features Plan_ imported from DS (see Block 1).
  * The **Model Project** _Card Transactions Detection_ imported from DS (see Block 2).
  * Four **Rules Projects** :
    * _DS Rules Project 1_ imported from DS (see Block 3).
    * _DS Rules Project 2_ imported from DS (see Block 4).
    * **_Eng. Rules Project 1_ evolved in DEV (see Block 5)**.
    * _Self-service Rules 1_ imported from PROD (see Block 6).



#### Workflows tabâ

The figure below shows the configuration of the runtime Workflow using the resources configured on the Data Science tab.

The key idea is to show you that each Project imported from a different environment and the Project that is being evolved in the current environment need to be mapped to a Workflow service (e.g. in this case four Rules Projects were mapped to four Rules services).

You can see the following Workflow services highlighted:

  * One Plan service: Corresponds to the Plan _Features_ (see Block 1).
  * One Scoring service: Corresponds to the Model Project _Card Transaction Detection_ (see Block 2).
  * Four Rules services: Correspond to the Rules Projects:
    * _DS Rules Project 1_ (see Block 3).
    * _DS Rules Project 2_ (see Block 4).
    * **_Eng. Rules Project 1_ (see Block 5).**
    * _Self-service Rules 1_ (see Block 6).



Check the page [Designing a Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow) under the User Guide to learn how to configure a workflow.

## Next Stepsâ

Now that you know how to organize your Pulse App, learn [how to version and store](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/how-to-version-and) your exported files.

# How to Version and Store

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

The main goals for versioning your work in a distributed version control system such as git are:

  * To have a bundle of the application ready for deployment (stable versions that are promoted to Production environments may be tagged).
  * To track the evolution of a Pulse application (**Pulse app**).



## How toâ

The method of versioning you work depends on the project specifications; however, the recommended approach is to version the **Pulse app** as a whole. This is done by:

  1. Generating the .papp file, for example by:

a. Using the option [Export Application](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-and-importing-applications).

b. Using the REST API; 

  2. Storing the file in git.




Limitations of this recommendation

There are a few aspects to have in mind associated to this recommendation as described below:

  * The binaries of the data science **Models** are not exported with the .papp file, and thus, they binaries have to be versioned separately.
  * The .papp file containing managed **Lists** with many items might become to large, and in this case, it might be preferable to store the .papp without **List** items.

# Tenant User Management

Was this page helpful?Â 

For use cases that support multi-tenancy, it is possible for system administrators to delegate [user management](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/manage-users/) capabilities to specific users from their tenants.

Such users need to have the `usermanager` role associated to them, and are referred to as **Tenant User Managers**.

Tenant User Managers have the following capabilities:

  * They are **only able to see and manage users that are associated with the same tenant** or a subset of their tenants. This ensures that the Tenant User Manager canât create, see or change users from a tenant they donât belong to.
    * If a user is associated to a tenant that the Tenant User Manager is not associated with, then this user wonât be visible to the latter. For example, if John is the User Manager for the tenants A, B and C, and Philip is a Fraud Analyst associated with tenants C and D; then, John canât see or manage Philip in the User Management feature. Only a User Manager not associated with any specific tenant (typically a Landord user) can manage Philip.
  * They are able to update any field from the users listed on the previous point, with the following limitations:
    * **Tenants** : The values for this field must be among the tenants that the Tenant User Manager is associated with.
    * **Roles** : These must be selected from a list of tenant roles configured globally by the Feedzai Customer Success (CS) team for all tenants.
    * **Groups** : These must be selected from among the groups that the Tenant User Manager is associated with, or any of their sub-groups.
  * They can create users. Such users must have a role and tenant, but assigning them to groups is optional.



caution

Prior to the introduction of the Tenant User Management feature, it was possible for a User Manager in a multi-tenant setup to be assigned to a tenant while remaining able to manage users from all tenants. This is no longer the case. For User Managers to be able to manage users from all tenants, they must not be assigned to any tenant themselves.

# Cluster Monitoring

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse allows monitoring the cluster through its UI. This topic explains how to set up notifications reporting status changes, how to analyse the cluster status, and how to change the leadership.

## Examining the Clusterâ

The Pulse cluster is organized in data centers. The image below shows the **Cluster** tab . At the top of this panel there is a list of data centers (two data centers in this example).

Each line of this list includes the data center name and the the data center overall status, which in this case is _Healthy_ , meaning that all nodes are running as expected.

However, the data center status may also be _Issue_ , _Critical, Unreachable_ or _Disabled. Issue_ means that although there are some faults the data center is able to work properly. The _Critical_ status is reported whenever there are faults and the data center cannot work properly. A data center is _Unreachable_ when it cannot be reached usually due to communication problems. The _Disabled_ status means that the data center was disabled manually.

The following table shows all data center statuses.

Status| Description  
---|---  
| All nodes are running as expected  
| Although, not all nodes are running, the data center will work as expected  
| There are faults and the data center cannot work as expected  
| Cannot communicate with the data center  
| Manually disabled for failover or maintenance  
  
Select the data center name to show its details.

The image above shows the data center panel. At the top, we can see the data center information including the total number of nodes, the number of nodes down and the overall status. At the bottom it shows a list of cluster components. These components may be the pulse server or applications engines. Each line includes the component type, the number of nodes running, the number of nodes expected to be running (replication factor), a link to view the nodes (View Hosts), and the component status.

After clicking in a View Hosts link, it presents the list of nodes and its status as the image below illustrates.

In the example illustrated by the image above, there are three pulse server nodes and all of them are up (running). If by any chance a node fails. The cluster monitor will report it by changing the node icon. The image below shows the data center panel when a pulse server node is down.

Moreover, the Pulse Server component also changes from healthy to Issue, the data center nodes down counter is increased and the data center status icon changes to a warning sign meaning that, although there is a node down, the system will work as expected. Nonetheless, we should investigate the reason of this fault an then fixing and restarting the node if possible.

The node details may be consulted by clicking on the node IP/Port link. As an example, the image below shows the down node details.

The node details include: the node type, a pulse server in this case; the uptime/downtime, here we can see, as the node status is down, that the _downtime_ is 13 minutes; the node status; the replication factor (the number of nodes expected to be running); the node leadership (whether if is the leader or not) and its location given by its IP address and port.

Status

Although, nodes only have two possible status (up and down), data center and cluster components may be:

  * **Healthy** , meaning that all nodes are up;
  * **Warning** (Issue), meaning that at least a node is up;
  * **Critical,** meaning that at least one of the cluster component has all its nodes down.



The image below illustrates a critical status. In this case, application _rta1_ is not running as all its nodes are down.

## Setting Up Status Changes Notificationsâ

Pulse allows sending email notifications reporting cluster status changes. These messages include reporting node status changes from UP to DOWN or DOWN to UP in both pulse server and application engine cluster nodes. To use this feature is important to have the SMTP settings properly configured. For example, for a Google SMTP account we would need to add the following configuration in **PULSE_HOME/conf/pulse.properties:**

SMTP Configuration Example  
---  
`pulse.global.smtp.host=smtp.gmail.com pulse.global.smtp.port=465 pulse.global.smtp.encryptiontype=SMTPS pulse.global.smtp.user=<USERNAME> pulse.global.smtp.password=<PASSWORD> pulse.global.smtp.from=<SENDER_EMAIL> `  
  
In this example, `<USERNAME>` and `<PASSWORD>`stand for the user credentials and `<SENDER_EMAIL>` stands for the email one should see in the from field when a notification is received.

The cluster status changes notification recipients are configured in the UI by selecting the cluster tab in the Administration view illustrated by the first image in the previous section.

By clicking in the add button (represented by a plus sign), a new recipient may be included to receive status changes notifications.

## Leadership changeâ

You can request to change the leadership to another node in the node group (of Pulse, or of the application) by selecting the  button next to the node that is the current leader.

Optionally, you can change the leadership status in the command line tool or via the Application Management REST API.

# JMX and Notifications

Was this page helpful?Â 

Feedzai Pulse provides a way of notifying monitoring teams when some indicators reach a specified threshold. Moreover, it exposes JMX Beans to extract JVM-related metrics meaning that it can be integrated with third-party monitoring tools such as Nagios.

## Notificationsâ

Monitoring teams can configure the system to send notifications when certain thresholds are surpassed. The configuration can be global to all applications running in the server or specific per application and both must be done in **PULSE_HOME/conf/pulse.properties**.

### Global configurationâ
    
    
    pulse.global.appengine.sendemailonfailure=true  
    pulse.global.appengine.monitoringemailaddress=[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)  
    pulse.global.appengine.heapthreshold=<MEMORY-IN-MB>  
    pulse.global.appengine.permgenthreshold=<MEMORY-IN-MB>  
    

In order to accomplish the same per application one must change `global` to `app.<APP-NAME>`.

### Per-application configurationâ
    
    
    pulse.app.<APP-NAME>.appengine.sendemailonfailure=true  
    pulse.app.<APP-NAME>.appengine.monitoringemailaddress=[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)  
    pulse.app.<APP-NAME>.appengine.heapthreshold=<MEMORY-IN-MB>  
    pulse.app.<APP-NAME>.appengine.permgenthreshold=<MEMORY-IN-MB>`  
    

The property names are quite self-explanatory so we won't get into much detail with them.

When the amount of memory used reaches the specified threshold, an e-mail is sent to the specified e-mail address informing about the occurrence. If you don't want a particular metric to be monitored, you can delete the entry or assign to it a negative value.

This configuration also notifies when applications crash. That kind of notification cannot be turned off once "sendemailonfailure" is set to "true".

note

Note that e-mail notifications will only be sent if the application crashes while running. If a crash occurs during a publish, or while the application is stopping, a crash notification e-mail is not guaranteed to be sent.

## JMXâ

Feedzai Pulse exposes JMX interfaces so that monitoring information can be retrieved and some operations can be performed. The JMX interface is only available when in the same host (localhost). It can be accessed both programmatically or using tools like [IBM Tivoli](http://www-01.ibm.com/software/tivoli/), [Nagios](http://www.nagios.org/).

If a quick and dirty option is needed, even [JConsole](http://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/management/jconsole.html) can be used to access the JMX endpoints available on Pulse. The following figure shows some of the information available when connected to the Pulse server running a Fraud Prevention application:

### Programmatic accessâ

It is possible to access Pulse's JMX endpoints using Java by getting a reference to the `MBean`. In order to accomplish that one must do the following:
    
    
    JMXServiceURL url = new JMXServiceURL("service:jmx:rmi://localhost:9010/jndi/rmi://localhost:9010/jmxrmi");  
    JMXConnector jmxc = JMXConnectorFactory.connect(url, null);  
    MBeanServerConnection mbsc = jmxc.getMBeanServerConnection();  
    ObjectName mbeanName = new ObjectName(StatusConsole.MBEAN_OBJECT_NAME);  
    StatusConsoleImplMBean console = JMX.newMBeanProxy(mbsc, mbeanName, StatusConsoleImplMBean.class, true);  
    

Having the reference, calls to the MBean can be made just by calling the desired methods. The following methods are available:

Method| Return| Description  
---|---|---  
`getName()`| String| The console name: StatusConsole  
`getUptime()`| String| A string representation of the uptime  
`getStartDate()`| Date| The start date  
`getJavaVMVendor()`| String| The VM vendor  
`getJavaVMVersion()`| String| The VM version  
`getOSName()`| String| The name of the Operating System  
`getOSArch()`| String| The architecture of the host  
`getOSVersion()`| String| The version of the operating system  
`getClusterNodes()`| List<String>| The list of cluster nodes that compose that Pulse instance. Contains information such as the host, port and whether the instance is hot (the running instance) or not  
`startShutdown()`| Void| Orders Pulse Server to gracefully shutdown itself  
  
The JMX endpoint described above is related to Pulse Server. It's also possible to access information about the running applications. For that, a lookup to the specific AppEngine must be made. This can be done by specifying the data center ID, the application slug (name), the instance IP address and RMI Port as in the following example:
    
    
    JMXServiceURL url = new JMXServiceURL("service:jmx:rmi:///jndi/rmi://localhost:6990/jmxrmi");  
    JMXConnector jmxc = JMXConnectorFactory.connect(url, null);  
    MBeanServerConnection mbsc = jmxc.getMBeanServerConnection();  
    ObjectName mbeanName = new ObjectName(AppStatusConsoleImplMBean.BASE_MBEAN_OBJECT_NAME + "<DATA_CENTER_ID>,nodeType=Apps,app=<APP-SLUG>,node=<HOST>-<PORT>"");  
    AppStatusConsoleImplMBean console = JMX.newMBeanProxy(mbsc, mbeanName, AppStatusConsoleImplMBean.class, true);  
    

After getting the reference, the following methods will become available:

Method| Return| Description  
---|---|---  
`getName()`| String| The name of the console: AppStatusConsole  
`getUptime()`| String| The uptime of the application  
`getStartDate()`| Date| The start date of the application  
`getAllocatedHeap()`| double| The total amount of memory in the JVM (Mb)  
`getUsedHeap()`| double| The amount of used memory in the JVM (Mb)  
`getInitialHeap()`| double| The amount of memory that the JVM initially requests from the OS for memory management (Mb)  
`getMaxHeap()`| double| The maximum amount of memory that can be used for memory management (Mb)  
`getInitialPermGen()`| double| The amount of PermGen that the JVM initially requests from the OS for memory management (Mb)  
`getMaxPermGen()`| double| The maximum amount of PermGen that can be used for memory management (Mb)  
`getUsedPermGen()`| double| The amount of PermGen used (Mb)  
`getTotalCPU()`| double| The CPU usage of all running processes, as a percentage of all processors.  
`getProcessLoad()`| double| The CPU usage of the process running this App Engine, as a percentage of all processors.  
`getActiveServices()`| List<String>| The list of service names running in the application  
  
For a reference with the difference between "allocated", "used", "initial" and "max" Heap and PermGen memory spaces, refer to the following [StackOverflow answer](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3571203/what-is-the-exact-meaning-of-runtime-getruntime-totalmemory-and-freememory/18375641#18375641).

### Configuring the JMX Serverâ

It's sometimes required to configure Pulse's JMX server due to firewall restrictions.

By default Pulse uses port 9010 for JMX access, this can be configured in Pulse's properties:
    
    
    pulse.manager.jmxport=9010  
    

After configuring the port you can use the following JMX URL to connect to:
    
    
    service:jmx:rmi://<listenAddress>:<jmxport>/jndi/rmi://<listenAddress>:<jmxport>/jmxrmi  
    

As for Application Engines, the default port used to establish the connection is the same as the RMI port. However, a random port will be automatically generated for the actual JMX connection. If you want to use a fixed port you must configure it:
    
    
    #Global setting for all applications  
    pulse.global.appengine.jmxport=9011  
      
    #Configuration for a specific application  
    pulse.app.<app_slug>.appengine.jmxport=9013  
    

In this case the JMX URL will be:
    
    
    service:jmx:rmi://<listenAddress>:<jmxport>/jndi/rmi://<listenAddress>:<jmxport>/jmxrmi

# Logging

Was this page helpful?Â 

All operations executed internally by Pulse are logged according to several levels of detail in log files located in the `PULSE_HOME/log` directory.

Pulse uses [SLF4J](http://www.slf4j.org/) logging facade making all the log calls agnostic to the actual logging framework in place. This allows changing the logging framework at deployment time if necessary. Nevertheless, Pulse is distributing [Logback](https://logback.qos.ch/) logging framework by default and this page discusses how to configure it.

## Configuringâ

The logging configuration file is located in `PULSE_HOME/conf/logger.xml`. This file includes different configuration parts from files present in `PULSE_HOME/conf/logger/* `.

For a more advanced configuration not covered in this article please consult the [Logback official documentation](https://logback.qos.ch/manual/configuration.html).

warning

Changing the logging configuration is on one's own responsibility. Changes might result in the loss of valuable information for investigating problems. If the default configuration is changed, support teams might not be able to help so one should be extremely careful when editing this file.

### Logging configuration filesâ

As mentioned above, the main logging configuration file is located in **PULSE_HOME/conf/logger.xml**. This file shouldn't be changed by clients as it does the inclusion of other logging configuration files present in **PULSE_HOME/conf/logger/** *:

  * **jmxconfigurator.xml** : Enables exporting logger configurations via JMX.
  * **filters.xml** : Defines filters to be applied to log messages.
  * **conversion-rules.xml** : Formatting rules for log messages.
  * **default-appenders.xml** : Defines the default appenders enabled in Pulse. **Clients in production should change this file** to disable BUFFER and STDOUT appenders.
  * **logger-jupyterlab.xml** : Logger and appender configuration to send all JupyterLab logs to its own file - _log/jupyterlab.log_
  * **logger-confidential.xml** : Logger and appender configuration to send all confidential logs to its own file - _log/CONFIDENTIAL-*.log_
  * **logger-metrics.xml** : Logger and appender configuration to log probes to disk.
  * **logger-legacy-audit.xml** : Logger and appender configuration to log legacy audit messages to disk.
  * **logger-audit.xml** : Logger and appender configuration to log new audit entries to disk.
  * **logger-events.xml** : Logger and appender configuration to log events to disk.
  * **logger-rules.xml** : Logger and appender configuration to log rules to disk.
  * **logger-default.xml** : Default logger configurations that are shipped with Pulse.
  * **logger-project.xml** : File that needs to be created by clients if they need to override logger definitions that are shipped with Pulse or if they need to add new logging configurations such as appenders or loggers.



### Log Filesâ

In order to easily pin point possible issues when running Pulse, Pulse Server and Applications write their messages to different log files.

Whatever the configuration in place might be, Pulse will always generate the following:

  * **pulse.log** : Logs all operations performed inside Pulse server
  * **app- <APP NAME>.log**: Logs all operations performed in an application engine



For additional GC (Garbage Collection) logs, the following flags were added by default to the JVM_OPTS of the Pulse and the applications:

  * **-Xloggc :log/pulse-%pid.gc -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps -XX:+PrintGCApplicationStoppedTime**



They will appear in a format similar to **< pulse|APP_SLUG>_GC_pid<PID>_<DATE>_.log.0.current** inside the logging folder.

tip

If the JVM is already running and it did not happen to be started with the necessary JVM_OPTS, it is still possible to enable some of them dynamically using the jinfo tool, e.g.:

  * **jinfo -flag +PrintGCDateStamps <pid>**
  * **jinfo -flag +PrintGC <pid>**



### DEV Markerâ

The development marker provides a much refined logging useful when developing Pulse Services and web applications. To turn it **on** or **off** just set the **OnMatch** tag to **ACCEPT** or **DENY** accordingly.

### Appenders Sectionâ

The appenders section define where the logging messages will end up. By default, Pulse is configured with three appenders: **STDOUT** , **FILE** and **BUFFER**.

  * **STDOUT** : Defines how messages are presented in the standard output (console);
  * **FILE** : Defines how messages are presented in the log file (for both server and applications). By default these files are rolled every week (each week will be in a zipped file) and a maximum of 8 week worth of history is kept;
  * **BUFFER** : Defines how messages are presented in the UI.



Do not use stdout append in PROD

It is _not_ recommended to have the STDOUT appended in production scenarios as it may cause the app-engines to block in some extreme error scenarios (for example [REQ-2666](https://issues.feedzai.com/browse/REQ-2666)).

An appender is defined in the configuration file with the `<appender>` XML tag. Inside each appender tag, there are several options mainly the **filter** and the **encoder**.

  * **FILTER** : Defines the minimum logging necessary (inclusively) in order for the encoder to be used;
  * **ENCODER** : Defines tags and colors for the logging messages given the package of the logger in use.



Under **filter** all available logging levels can be used (**ERROR** , **WARN** , **INFO** , **DEBUG** and **TRACE**). When you define a logging level, that level and the above ones (more critical than the one defined) will always satisfy the filter. For instance if you define **INFO** , then the **WARN** and **ERROR** messages are also logged.

With the encoder it's possible to define the timestamp format of the logging events and tag them with colors and labels. The following is an example of tagging the all the messages that have to do with the rules engine.
    
    
    <encoder class="ch.qos.logback.core.encoder.LayoutWrappingEncoder">  
        <layout class="com.feedzai.pulse.server.manager.logging.LoggerLayout">  
            <colored>true</colored>  
            <!-- Abbreviate the package -->  
            <abbrevLevel>true</abbrevLevel>  
            <!-- Show stacktrace -->  
            <showTraces>false</showTraces>  
            <!-- Color of the levels -->  
            <debugColor>1;30</debugColor>  
            <infoColor>0</infoColor>  
            <stdioColor>0;35</stdioColor>  
            <tagColor>1;30</tagColor>  
            <!-- Timestamp format -->  
            <timestampFormat>dd-MMM HH:mm:ss</timestampFormat>  
      
            <!-- Tag the events the match the package with text -->  
            <tagEvents>  
                <from>com.feedzai.pulse.service.rules</from>  
                <with>RULES</with>  
                <color>1|1;33</color>  
            </tagEvents>  
        </layout>  
    </encoder>  
    

### Logger Sectionâ

The logger section is where the main level filtering is made. Here levels are assigned to packages or even to their classes using the **name** property. This configuration can be overridden ultimately in the final appenders. For instance if you define here that a logger is enabled at the **DEBUG** level, but an appender is specified to only allow above **INFO** , the messages won't appear in that appender.

It's also possible to assign a logger some configuration. For instance you might want for all the logging messages of your application to go inside a specific file. For that you could create an appender and forward all the messages to go there.
    
    
    <appender name="MY_SERVICE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">  
        <file>log/my_service.log</file>  
    </appender>  
      
    <logger name="com.company.my.service" additivity="false">  
        <appender-ref ref="MY_SERVICE" />  
    </logger>  
    

The **additivity** parameter tells the logger that it mustn't be used in other loggers and therefore appenders. In this case, logging calls to that logger will not reach the **CONSOLE** , **BUFFER** or **FILE** appenders but only the **MY_SERVICE** one.

### Root Loggerâ

The root logger is the default logger where all the messages will wind up by default. The only case where that doesn't happen is when a logger is defined with the **additivity** parameter as **false**. Here are usually defined the destination appenders of the messages.

caution

We strongly advise not to change the appenders already under the root logger section.

## Lnav Supportâ

[Lnav](http://lnav.org/) is a log viewer that can help read and analyze logs. Among other features, it offers highlighting and a unified view over multiple log files.

For Lnav to support Pulse's log format you need to install the [Pulse log lnav configuration](/pulse/latest/feedzai-pulse-log-format.json):

`lnav -i feedzai-pulse-log-format.json`

This log format is valid for Pulse 15.1.5 and above. For previous 15.1 versions you should use [this configuration file](https://fdz.atlassian.net/wiki/download/attachments/92199278/feedzai-pulse-log-format-pre-15.1.5.json?version=1&modificationDate=1454855378000&cacheVersion=1&api=v2).

To launch lnav, do:

`lnav <pulse-path>/log/`

# Pulse Probes

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse probes provide a means to expose Pulse internal instrumentation data, allowing it to be stored in a central location for subsequent analysis.

## Probing Componentsâ

The Pulse probing architecture is composed of two components:

  * **Probes** that periodically measure some relevant metrics (for example, processing latency) and broadcast their values to a **metric server** that may be listening to them. Probing is performed either as a response to a pulse internal event (e.g. a fraud event passing by a fraud rules service workflow element) or on a periodic basis (e.g. get sample of X every Y seconds). Each probe has an associated **metric schema** , that contains the fields that correspond to the metric. Probes are normally tightly coupled to Pulse components.
  * **Metric Server** , that are subscribers of the metric information published by the probes and that store received metric information in CSV files. Metric servers may register/unregister themselves on the existing probes.



Note that the term "metric" in this context refers only to whatever is measured by probes, and should not be confused with PQL metrics.

Metric servers communicate with probes for registering/unregistering themselves and for probe discovery using a topic named `metrics_control_topic`; metric events are broadcast to metric servers through direct TCP connections.

This architecture is extensible, allowing you to create your own probes for any pulse component you develop (e.g., custom workflow services).

## Running a Metrics Serverâ

A metrics server deployment is composed of a single standalone jar file (**metrics-server- <version>.jar**) and a properties file with its configuration, named **metrics.properties** by default. A sample configuration file is included. In order to launch a metric server just run:

`java -jar metrics-server-<version>;.jar [properties_file]`

Metrics servers can run in two modes:

  * **Interactive (REPL enabled)** , where a shell is provided for registering/unregistering the server on probes in an interactive way.
  * **Non-interactive (REPL disabled)** , where the server will only handle auto-started probes (see _metrics.autostartprobes_ below). When used this way, the metric server must be started before the Pulse server (or, more exactly, before the probes that are to be listened for start).



The server run mode is specified in the _metrics.replenabled_ property of the configuration file (see below).

The _properties_file_ argument can be used in case you need multiple configurations on the same host. If not specified, the default _metrics.replenabled_ properties will be used.

## Interactive Commandsâ

The commands available in interactive mode are the following:

  * `l[ist] [pattern1[,pattern2]]` \- shows the available probes and their status. Absence of a pattern means all probes.
  * `r[eport] pattern1[,pattern2]` \- start listening on the probes specified in pattern.
  * `s[ilence] pattern1[,pattern2]` \- stop listening on the probes specified in pattern.



Probe pattern names support the wildcard characters `*` and `?`. The `*` wildcard matches a sequence of zero or more characters and the `?`matches exactly one character.

The list of existing commands can be displayed on the shell just by entering an empty line.

< 15.1.10

Make sure that you silence your patterns before exiting the server! If you report for a given pattern, shutting down the server and leaving interactive mode does not stop the pattern from being reported.

Since 15.1.11 metrics server will silence all probes when sucessfully shutdown.

### Exampleâ

Start by running the interactive mode and list all the available patterns.
    
    
    $ l  
    (...)  
    [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection) not reporting, schema: (uuid:STRING,timestamp:LONG,msg_type:STRING,rule_process_latency:LONG,rule_total_latency:LONG)  
    [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection) not reporting, schema: (uuid:STRING,timestamp:LONG,message_type:STRING,null_instance:BOOLEAN,scoring_fetchinstance_latency:LONG,scoring_fos_latency:LONG,scoring_total_latency:LONG)  
    [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection) not reporting, schema: (uuid:STRING,timestamp:LONG,msg_type:STRING,rule_process_latency:LONG,rule_total_latency:LONG)  
    (...)  
    

Select one of the available patterns, say `[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)`, to check its current status and schema.
    
    
    $ r [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)  
    $ l [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)  
    [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection) reporting, schema: (uuid:STRING,timestamp:LONG,message_type:STRING,null_instance:BOOLEAN,scoring_fetchinstance_latency:LONG,scoring_fos_latency:LONG,scoring_total_latency:LONG)  
    

Enable reporting for the above pattern.
    
    
    $ r [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)  
    $ l [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)  
    [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection) reporting, schema: (uuid:STRING,timestamp:LONG,message_type:STRING,null_instance:BOOLEAN,scoring_fetchinstance_latency:LONG,scoring_fos_latency:LONG,scoring_total_latency:LONG)  
    

Once instances pass through the defined fraud scoring service, some lines will be generated in the output file, define in the configuration file. Note that the time is represented in nanoseconds.
    
    
    mylocalhost,3538b328-134f-4d63-84cf-bd4c50db93e6,1465421548284,NORMAL,false,1967209,377659,2426728  
    mylocalhost,65b02454-11b1-42e9-b2ba-f0438c5933e0,1465421549518,NORMAL,false,795394,272169,1116582  
    mylocalhost,8bbed484-177e-4985-b835-7a4cb85c3950,1465421549676,NORMAL,false,844627,267752,1160902

## Metrics Server Propertiesâ

The `metrics.properties` has the following properties.

Property| Description| Default Value  
---|---|---  
**metrics.autostartprobes**|  The server will register on the probes that match these patterns and that start after the metrics server starts.  
  
Patterns support the wildcard characters `*` and `?`. The `*` wildcard matches a sequence of zero or more characters and the `?` matches exactly one character.|  None  
**metrics.host**|  The host of the metrics server. Probes will report connecting to this host.|  hostname reported by `InetAddress.getLocalHost().getHostName()` or `localhost` if that fails.  
**metrics.port**|  The port the metrics server is listening on. | 16161  
**metrics.replenabled**|  Whether the metrics server should run in interactive mode or not.| true  
**metrics.store.outputdir**|  Metrics will be stored to files in this folder. This folder will be created if does not exist.| Mandatory property.  
**metrics.messaging.***|  Messaging can be configured with the usual messaging configuration properties prefixed by `metrics.messaging.`.  
  
Must match the pulse-side messaging configuration.| Embedded ActiveMQ. Only works when probes and metrics server are on the same machine.

## Storing Metric Data Locallyâ

Probes can also be configured to write metric data directly to a local text file, using the logging framework. This setup doesn't require a metric server but allows only for metric data to be stored locally on (each) Pulse Server and doesn't allow individual probes to be "disabled", as when using the metric server.

The Pulse standard log configuration file (`PULSE_HOME/conf/logger/logger-metrics.xml`) includes a commented out section with an appender (`METRICS-ASYNC`, that in turn uses the `METRICS` appender) and a logger for that appender. In order to have the probes writing directly to files it is enough to uncomment this section.
    
    
    <!--  
        Start of metrics server local logging.  
        By default this logger is disabled. This means that probes will not be logged to disk,  
        only reported to the metrics server if enabled.  
      
        With this logger metrics server doesn't need to be enabled.  
      
        Use an AsyncAppender to avoid impacting the critical path of execution degrading processing latencies.  
    -->  
    <!-- METRICS SERVER LOGGING TAG  
    <appender name="METRICS" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">  
      <file>log/${pulse.logcontext}-metrics.log</file>  
      <encoder>  
        <pattern>%msg</pattern>  
      </encoder>  
      <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.TimeBasedRollingPolicy">  
        <fileNamePattern>log/${pulse.logcontext}-metrics.%d{yyyy-MM}-week-%d{WW}.log.gz</fileNamePattern>  
        <maxHistory>8</maxHistory>  
      </rollingPolicy>  
    </appender>  
      
    <appender name="METRICS-ASYNC" class="ch.qos.logback.classic.AsyncAppender">  
      <appender-ref ref="METRICS" />  
      <queueSize>2048</queueSize>  
      <discardingThreshold>0</discardingThreshold>  
      <includeCallerData>false</includeCallerData>  
    </appender>  
      
    <logger name="com.feedzai.metrics.probes.TextAbstractProbe" level="TRACE" additivity="false">  
      <appender-ref ref="METRICS-ASYNC" />  
    </logger>  
    METRICS SERVER LOGGING TAG -->  
    <!-- End of metrics server local logging. -->

# Web Monitoring

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse provides ways of managing and accessing information through the UI. This section describes what can be done and how it can be done regarding fine tuning your Pulse server via UI.

## What Can Be Controlled?â

Using the Pulse web interface it's possible to perform the following tasks:

  * **Monitor and control** Pulse services
  * **Manage** Pulse's configuration attributes
  * **View** Pulse's log and general information



## Manage Pulse Servicesâ

Pulse Server is organized in services that handle each task comprised in it separately. In this section you will learn how to check what services are started and how they can be controlled. Below is an image of the UI to monitor Pulse services as well as a small description about each component:

Beware

Do not stop or restart services if you don't understand the service dependencies of Pulse Server.

Switch between server node and application view

By default this tab shows the services information for the whole Pulse Server node. You can choose an application to manage its resources in the top right corner of the tab.

### Coreâ

The core services are the base components of the Pulse Server. You cannot restart them because they are required for the correct operation of other Pulse services. You can, however, view their state.

### Modulesâ

Modules are components that provide advanced features such as KPIs and Baselines. These services can be fully administered using the UI, just make sure you know the implications of restarting them.

### Adaptersâ

In the adapters section you can check the input and output adapters available in the system. This table will list all the adapters in action currently as well as their state.

### Standaloneâ

This section contains the services that were uploaded using the custom services interface.

### Webâ

Availability

Web services listing is only available for the whole server node view.

The web section shows all the applications running in Pulse Web Server. There are two types of applications:

  * **Core Service** \- these are the applications deployed with Pulse.
  * **Web App** \- applications deployed by the users.



## Infoâ

This tab provides us with an overview of the system running the Pulse Server along with a few other interesting details. It also shows how many services are running, applications deployed and statistics about Kpis, Baselines and PKernel objects. It is also possible to check the Cluster information where all the nodes are listed along with their types, status and IP addresses.

If your application is already running, you can choose it in the list of applications (Application Statistics sub-section) and pull charts that plot the CPU Usage and JVM Heap.

## Logâ

Feedzai Pulse logs all the operations being executed in the server in files. For ease of use the UI also allows you to access the last operations logged in your Pulse Server as well as download its log files.

To change the level of the logger being used in the web console go to your **PULSE_HOME/conf/logger.xml** file and search for the **BUFFER** appender section.

## Configurationâ

Internally Feedzai Pulse uses a _properties file_ to save its configuration, but connecting to the server and editing a file isn't always a feasible option.

This tab allows you to configure your Pulse Server using solely the UI.

Restart Pulse Server

All changes in configuration will need a restart of the service or even a full restart of Pulse Server.

## What's Next?â

Head over to [this section](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application/) and learn how to secure your application resources.

On this page

# Audit

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse keeps an audit log of changes made to the Pulse applications and resources, as well as user actions (e. g. login). Pulse logs these actions when they are initiated via user interface or via Pulse REST API endpoints.

## What is loggedâ

The audit log consists of the following:

  * **Audit entries** : the logs that capture a user action or a change. It contains data that was included in the request that initiated the action. Example: if you create a list item, Pulse includes in the audit entry the list name, the user session identifier, the values added, whether the list item is enabled, etc.
  * **Audit entry labels** : labels that are added to the data fields of the audit entries, to make them easy to browse in the Pulse UI. If a data field of the audit logs has a label, you can filter the audit entries by the value of that data field simply by clicking on the value.
  * **Audit entry search terms** : terms that you can search for in the audit entries, using the Pulse UI. Search terms don't appear on the UI, and they are not configurable. They can be used to search resources by identifier on advanced investigations.



Pulse creates an audit entry for the following:

  * Deletion, creation and update of data science entities (rules, models, lists, etc.)
  * Deletion, creation and update of security entities (users, tenants, permissions, groups etc.)
  * User actions (login, logout, change password, viewing or exporting list items, etc.)
  * Application import, export, publish, start, stop, etc.
  * Certain configuration changes (job profiles, autohealing, self service, etc.)



For a full list of logged actions, check the Action  drop-down on the Audit  screen in the Pulse UI. See the [Investigating changes and user actions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/investigating-changes-and-user) topic.

Pulse keeps all audit logs, but the Pulse UI shows only the last two months' audit data.

## Who can see the audit logsâ

Users with the `security:audit:read` permission have access to all audit entries.

Audit is enabled by default.

## Where are the logs storedâ

The audit log is stored in the Pulse database, in the following tables:

  * AuditEntry
  * AuditEntrySearchTerm



It's not recommended to access these tables directly. The recommended way to access audit logs is via the Pulse UI.

## Learn moreâ

Read how to [investigate changes and user actions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/investigating-changes-and-user) in the Pulse application.

On this page

# Channels

Was this page helpful?Â 

This page gives you a short overview of what channels are and how they can be used in an omnichannel detection scenario.

A **channel** is the means of communication through which data is received by the financial institution. Examples for different channels can be: ATM, bank branch, card, Internet banking, mobile banking, etc.

Typically, each channel has a different schema and different [data patterns](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types). Because of this, each channel may require a different strategy to prevent financial crime, as well as a different approach to alert management and reporting. For example, rules or machine learning model features based on payment terminal identifiers will be relevant for card transactions, but not relevant for internet banking transactions. Likewise, terminal identifiers are relevant to analysts looking at card alerts, but not to analysts looking at internet banking.

## Channels in Pulse and Case Managerâ

### Runtime channelsâ

In Pulse, each channel corresponds to the data of a specific runtime [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows). Workflows can be further organized into applications.

This setup helps teams working on different channels to manage the system effectively:

  * Users can configure each workflow with flexible logic that applies to a specific channel.
  * Updates to the detection strategy can be deployed independently for each channel. This is especially relevant when independent teams work on different channels.



Further, in Case Manager, users can connect each Pulse workflow to a different alert management configuration. For more details, see the Case Manager documentation.

### Channels in the data science environmentâ

In the data science environment, historical data from each channel is represented as a [data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources). These data sources can be used, for example, to build and train machine learning models.

## Cross-channel attacksâ

Treating each channel independently makes it easier to configure the system with the specifics of each channel in mind. However, itâs also important to look at the data from multiple channels holistically â for detection, alert management and reporting. This is because financial crime has evolved, and there are attacks that exploit gaps in systems where channels are disconnected. For example, if we just look at ATM data, all withdrawals look the same. But if we couple this with Internet banking data, we may notice that some withdrawals happen after a user logs into their account using a new device and raises the withdrawal limit. Such withdrawals are much more suspicious, because there is a risk that what preceded them was an account takeover.

Cross-channel attacks require an omnichannel approach to detection.

## Using data from multiple channelsâ

The main principle behind **omnichannel detection** in Pulse is to enable data scientists and analysts to build rules and models that use data from multiple channels, while still allowing teams to work on channels independently. This is achieved as follows:

  * Each channel has its own detection strategy, implemented in a workflow. Within that workflow, the channel is referred to as the **main channel**.
  * Data scientists and analysts working on the main channel can incorporate data from other channels, which are referred to as **secondary channels**.



In Pulse, data is analyzed with [plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans). A typical workflow will include one or more plans that compute features based on the data.

Pulse supports **[omnichannel plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#deployable-omnichannel-plans)**. Using these plans, data scientists and analysts can build profiles based on data from multiple channels.

  * In the data science environment, users can create and run omnichannel plans that consume data from multiple data sources â one data source for the main channel, and one for each secondary channel.
  * In the [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows), omnichannel plans are connected to other workflows â one workflow for each secondary channel.

# Data Science Loop

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse delivers a full data science platform that is focused on making your data science work much more efficiently than with your traditional toolset. Pulse is designed so that you can easily map your current paradigm to Pulse's concepts, while fully supporting the same data science loop.

Pulse supports the activities in the data science loop by enabling you to:

  * Extract deep knowledge over your data to obtain the most value out of it.
  * Iterate your work by performing continuous experiments and tuning to extract the best performance out of your model.
  * Focus on the real data science by iterating quickly to accelerate your experiments and ultimately obtain better results.



Feedzai IQ

With [Feedzai IQ](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/about-pulse#feedzai-iq), you can also use ready-to-adopt risk assessment solutions without extensive data science work, thanks to federated financial risk intelligence aggregated from the Feedzai global network.

The following diagram illustrates the sequence of stages in the data science loop.

## Data science stagesâ

The data science loop is composed of a sequence of stages with very specific goals and iteration cycles. The following sections explain each of these stages and cycles in more detail.

Additionally, you can learn more about the dedicated environment used in risk assessment strategies according to the data science loop in a dedicated page: [The Data Science Framework (DSF)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/the-data-science-framework).

### Clean and loadâ

The main goal of this initial stage is to improve the quality of your raw data so that you can extract meaningful insight from it and ultimately train your model with relevant data. The datasets you receive from your client often have quality issues and a different structure from the one you need to work with.

At this stage you will apply some preprocessing transformations on your data to:

  * [Import data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/importing-your-dataset-into-pulse)

Load your raw historical data, up to Terabyte size, to a system so that you can have access to it and start manipulating it with proper tools. For example, load a CSV file to a database or to a Hadoop cluster.

  * [Validate the data schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/validating-the-data-schema)

Map the raw data to your project's specifications. The raw data can be structured in an outdated or not representative way, so, for example, you may need to change the names of fields or convert the original classification labels into a binary set (e.g. several types of fraud to just _fraud/not fraud_).

  * [Clean up the data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/cleaning-up-the-data)

Fix inconsistencies in your raw data, remove irrelevant data/fields for data science (usually strings) or join datasets. For example, you may need to join a raw historical transactions dataset with the corresponding labels (e.g. _fraud_ or _not fraud_) and set all negative values in transaction amount fields to zero.




This stage is usually performed only once when you receive the historical data from your client.

### Analyze and sampleâ

During this stage, the goal is to understand your data and prepare it to be intensively transformed and experimented on during the Feature Engineering stage.

At this stage you start to uncover relations in your input data and transform it to be more representative of the problem you are solving to:

  * [Identify patterns](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/identifying-patterns)

Use data visualization tools and apply data visualization techniques over the data to understand it and to discover immediate patterns. For example, correlating the occurrence of fraud with its prevalence in a _Card Not Present_ situation.

  * [Create dataset sample](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/creating-a-stratified-sample)

Reduce the size of your dataset by generating another one that is better manageable and still representative of the specific problem you are solving. Extremely big datasets are not practical to iterate on because of their size. In addition, there isn't a clear advantage of training machine learning models over those big datasets. In fact, it may even be worse due to the curse of big data, where even noise can be considered a pattern when you have millions of data points. A solution is to balance the dataset by sampling 1%-10% of non-fraud transactions, making it better suited to a machine learning scenario. Reducing its size also reduces the requirements for distributed processing of large volumes of data while making it much easier/quicker to iterate on.




### Feature engineeringâ

Your model decisions are as good as the data that you feed to it during its training. Feature engineering represents the process of transforming the raw data (already cleaned and sampled) into selected and enriched data. The goal is to obtain the dataset that defines what features you will use as input to your machine learning model.

This is the most intelligence-intensive task in the entire cycle and the one where you will probably spend most of your time. Feature engineering is the most important contribution of the data scientist to the model. It includes the following tasks:

  * [Select important data for your model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/selecting-important-data-for-your-model)

Choose which of the fields in your intermediate dataset are significantly related to the problem you are solving and can be used directly as features. For example, a _card_present_ field is much more relevant for a fraud detection scenario than the first name of the customer.

  * [Design derived features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-derived-features)

Enrich your dataset by highlighting specific characteristics observable in the data. For example, add a boolean _isNational_ field based on the transaction country and add enrichment features such as _isDebit_ , _isCredit_ and _isTorNode_ to improve the data with insight from additional external sources.

  * [Design metrics (historical profiles)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics)

Characterize your data with time-based information that creates a unique profile for each individual data entity. For example, characterize spending habits of customer transactions by merchant type, country, or other field and aggregated over multiple time ranges such as 24 hours, 1 week, 1 month and 6 months.

  * [Generate instance/features dataset](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/generating-instance-features-dataset)

Bring all your feature engineering work together by transforming your intermediate data into a single dataset containing all the features you identified/designed. This final dataset is the input for your machine learning model and contains all the relevant data for the model to learn with the appropriate input to solve your target problem, for example, fraud detection.




### Build a modelâ

The goal of this stage is to take the transformed dataset, including all the computed features, and feed it to a machine learning algorithm in order to produce a model. The model is trained on a subset of the data to learn how to predict future behaviour based on features over historical data and evaluated on a different test dataset.

To create a machine learning model in Pulse, you can:

  * [Train a model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model)

Feed your features dataset to teach a machine learning algorithm how to predict future behaviour based on the knowledge you have generated in your dataset. The quality of your model's decisions is a direct consequence of the quality and relevance of the data in the training dataset. Additionally, when you test your model, you must not use any data contained in the training dataset. You should always have a separate dataset, for example, a small subset you extracted from your data before training, as you must always test the model over unknown data.

  * [Import a model that you created and trained externally](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model/importing-an-external-model)

Use the tools that you are familiar with to build and train your model, and then import it into Pulse.




#### Optimize model parametersâ

Within the process of building your model, one recommended step is to tune the model parameters so that you can optimize the performance of your model. There are no guidelines on which parameters to select for a given use case. As such, in order to select an optimum set of parameters, different combinations should be tested to find the one that makes your model operate at its maximum performance.

To adjust your model, you must:

  * [Tune the parameters of your model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters)

Iterate your models by configuring different sets of parameter values for each of your algorithm's parameters before training your final model. Try more than one algorithm simultaneously as well to get to the best set of parameters that produces the optimal model for your use case.




### Evaluate and compareâ

At the end of your data science process, you must assess the performance of your trained model. Evaluating a model is not about just generating a single "OK/not OK" metric. It must rather focus on analyzing the results for different metrics, under different perspectives, and for different data subsets. For example, you may want to understand if your model is performing better when catching _Card Present_ or _Card Not Present_ fraud.

Since this is an iterative process, you can compare the performance of your latest model against the performance of previous iterations and earlier models.

You can also evaluate the impact of each feature on your model with [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance).

To track how close you are to reaching your objectives you can:

  * [Evaluate your model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model)

Generate metrics and data visualization objects to let you analyze the performance of your model over an entire test dataset and over different segments and data subsets. Understand the impact of each feature on your model with feature importance. You can use this functionality to identify the subset of variables that contribute the most and the least to the model predictions. As a result, you can reduce model complexity and computation time. Understanding which features have higher impact on the model might also help you to identify new relevant features.

  * [Compare your models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models)

Understand how the current iteration of your model performs against previous versions and how close your current performance is to reaching your project's goals. You can compare metrics such as Precision, Recall and False Positive Rate (FPR), cost-based metrics such as fraud money Recall, ROC curves, etc. You can also compare the results of feature importance between two model evaluations.




In fact, while you are trying to reach your business objectives, evaluating, comparing and applying feature importance to your models does not end the data science process. It just closes the data science loop and starts a new iteration. Usually, lots of iterations are required to reach your final goal. You will often uncover new patterns, gain new insight, re-engineer your features and test different parameter combinations to maximize the performance of your model.

Iteration occurs at the following stages:

#### Model building and parameter optimizationâ

The most common iteration is to tune the parameters of your model with different parameter configurations and retrain it on the same dataset. A model has lots of parameters to configure and much more combinations that you can try out before you feel that the model is delivering top performance.

The approach that Feedzai uses to optimize parameters is to perform a grid search (parameter sweep) where Pulse creates a model for every combination of values.

#### Feature engineeringâ

You can reiterate your data science work from the Feature engineering stage. You can try to improve your model by extracting extra/different features from the original data that better correlate with the problem you are solving, for example, fraud detection, define more profiles and further enriching the data.

Getting average results is usually fairly straightforward when you already have some domain knowledge and compute a set of generic features. However, pushing a model to its optimal performance, and addressing the long tail of the problem is very hard and requires many Feature engineering iterations. You'll most likely end up designing much more features, that are very specific to your use case and data than you did for the initial iterations.

#### Data analysis and samplingâ

Reiterating your (almost) entire project is more common in the earlier stages when you are still unfamiliar with the available data. As you know the dataset better, your need to re-analyze the data will gradually decrease.

It is also common that you only uncover problems in your sampled data after you complete a full iteration and evaluate the results against external data, causing you to have to resample it and better balance it for your specific use case.

## Automate data science tasksâ

To accelerate the data science loop, you can automate some of the above tasks.

In Pulse, there are two possibilities for that:

  1. Automate steps 2-5 with AutoML

The [AutoML](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/automl) feature of Pulse automates almost the whole data science loop, from step 2 (Analyze & Sample) to step 5 (Evaluate & Compare). It helps at the kickoff of a new data science project, or when you want to augment the feature set of an existing model. [Start an AutoML run](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/creating-features-and-models-automatically) by defining the starting data source, the metric to optimize, and some other parameters. AutoML does the following for you:

     * Creates a feature [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) and executes it, resulting in a new dataset with the engineered features.
     * Creates a Hyperparameter Tuning to train models, and to evaluate them. AutoML prepares the best model for usage.
  2. Automate steps 4-5 with Hyperparameter Tuning

Use [Hyperparameter Tuning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/hyperparameter-tuning) to automate steps 4-5 of the data science loop: model building, parameter tuning, and model evaluation. To [start a Hyperparameter Tuning job](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters), select a set of ML algorithms and the parameter values you want to test them with. As a result, Pulse does the following for you in an automatized way:

     * Trains all the selected models with all the defined parameter values (parameter sweep).
     * Evaluates the trained models.



## Runtime activitiesâ

When your data science work is finished and the data science loop is closed, it's time to deploy it to Production. These deployment activities are usually reserved for engineers as the runtime environment is greatly different from the offline data science stage.

Integrating the results of the data science loop with the runtime environment is usually very challenging, time-consuming and requires advanced technical skills. It's also an iterative process of deploying, evaluating and benchmarking the results against the expected performance as designed during the data science stage. For every model that needs to be deployed, new engineering work is required.

It may take up to several months for engineers to be able to ensure that your data science work is correctly translated to runtime, maintaining the same semantics for data transformation, time-based profiles, enrichment and any feature, and that it yields the same results.

However, Pulse already integrates the data science and runtime environments making it much easier and quicker to deploy a project to Production. This makes runtime iterations much faster and safer as Pulse ensures that data science semantics are correctly translated to Production without requiring you to have a set of very sophisticated technical skills.

Learn more about [how Pulse projects work](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/how-pulse-projects-work) and how they integrate the data science loop and runtime tasks.
