On this page

# Data Sources

Was this page helpful?Â 

Data sources represent datasets that will be used for data science purposes within Pulse. An example of a source of data is a CSV file.

All data science concepts of the [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) depend on data or its schema:

  * [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) use data sources to perform decisions.
  * [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) receive a data source as input, and generate a transformed data source as output.



warning

When you create a new data source, you never load the actual data into the system. Pulse only maintains a pointer to the physical location of the data file, as loading the whole data set would be too memory-consuming. Pulse fetches the data from the file(s) from the physical location whenever a data science task requires it.

**Do not delete** the data file from your system, otherwise any subsequent data science tasks that depend on it will not work.

## Data fieldsâ

Data sources have **fields**. For example, in a CSV file, these correspond to the columns. Each field is characterized by a [data type](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types), which defines the possible values of the field.

A data source is comprised of records. For example, in a CSV file, each record is represented as a row. Typically, each record contains a value for each field. However, it is possible for a field in a record to have no value, i.e. _missing value_.

The following image shows how Pulse displays fields and values of a data source.

## Data schemasâ

When you create a data source and import information into Pulse, it also creates a **schema**. A schema describes the available data fields of a data source, as well as their [types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types).

Data might come from different sources and in different ways, and be manipulated at almost every stage of your project. Schemas, therefore, provide formatting and structure for data source manipulation/exploration during a data science stage and for real-time data coming into Pulse in Production.

info

All intermediate data manipulations in Pulse, whether during the Data Science stage or in Production, generate new schema instances. However, these schemas are internal and not accessible to characterize runtime data.

To translate the underlying (and implicitly created) data schema of a data source into a schema that you can configure for a runtime [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows), you must explicitly export the data source to a schema.

As an accelerator, the workflow allows you to directly copy the schema from an existing data source.

### Schema immutabilityâ

When you successfully create a data source and import data into Pulse, it automatically also defines the corresponding schema. Once you have a data source, you cannot edit or update its data schema.

Data schemas, and consequently, data sources are immutable due to the fact that most data science concepts and tasks fully rely on data sources. Therefore, to keep your project consistent, whenever you change the underlying structure of a data source, Pulse would have to propagate those changes further down your data science pipeline to [plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans), [models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), and [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules), where the data source has been used. Additionally, this would have potentially disastrous and hard-to-solve implications if you were already using plans, models, and rules in a runtime [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows).

However, changing a data schema after it has been involved, for example, in training a model, wouldn't even make sense, since model configurations and results are, by definition, also immutable.

On the other hand, changing a data source schema, with different field names and data types, and not propagating changes would, for example, break plans that were already configured to consume data in a specific way.

info

If you need to change the data schema of your data sources, you can do it by [duplicating the data source and then editing the data configuration](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/importing-your-dataset-into-pulse).

In reality, since the schema is immutable, this effectively generates a new data source with an updated schema.

In a data science process, whenever your data moves along a plan and suffers transformations, the data schema of the input data source remains unchanged. To reflect the result of data manipulation and transformations, since schemas are immutable, Pulse generates a new data source with a new schema. The subsequent stages in your data science pipeline should be configured accordingly to use the output data source.

info

Since everything relies on data, every time you use data and its schema definition during the data science stage, Pulse must ensure that everything is correctly translated into the runtime environment.

Every time you create/configure an entity that requires data and can be deployed directly into Production, Pulse uses a copy of the original schema to maintain the integrity of the original. For example, when specifying the input data schema for a [deployable plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) or when configuring a [rules snapshot](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules).

### Compatible data sourcesâ

In data science mode, operations are always done over the data source files that you import, such as CSV or Parquet files. After deployment, the data can come in different formats. For example, you can receive data over a socket reading ISO8583 messages or via a REST API. Production data must be compatible with your data sources to ensure the data processing operations will continue to work.

Moreover, if you want to, for example, run an evaluation on a trained model using different data, you also need to make sure it is compatible with the dataset originally used to train the model. Otherwise, the experiment will not be useful for your data science project.

In Pulse, two data sources are considered compatible according to the following table:

Concept| Compatibility strategy| Description  
---|---|---  
Plans| Equivalent| New schema must be equal to the one of the original data. Data must have the exact same format (type and possible values), order and names.  
Models| Superset| New schema can have any fields as long as it contains all fields of the original schema, with the exact same format (type and possible values) and names. The order is irrelevant in this case.  
Rules| Superset| New schema can have any fields as long as it contains all fields of the original schema, with the exact same format (type and possible values) and names. The order is irrelevant in this case.  
  
## Invalid instancesâ

**Invalid instances** are data rows (aka. instances, records, or events) that could not be read from the dataset for one of the following reasons:

  * The data row contains more or less data fields than the schema.
  * The data in one or more fields of the row is not in the format that the schema expects. This has three cases:
    * The type of the input data does not match the data type defined in the schema. Example: "10.0", when the field in the schema is an int, instead of a double.
    * The format of the input data does not match the format configurations of the data type defined in the schema. Example: "01-01-1990", when the field in the schema is a Date Time configured with the YYYY-MM-DD format.
    * The data field is a categorical, and the value of the input data is not in the list of the possible values defined in the schema. Example: "CAN", when the categorical type of the schema is configured to accept "CAD", "CNY", "EUR" and "USD".



note

Invalid instances are ignored in data science activities, for example when calculating metrics in a [data source analysis](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis), executing a [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans), [training a model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model), etc.

The Pulse UI shows information about invalid instances after you run a [data source analysis](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis).

To fix invalid instances, after investigating their cause in the UI, you can combine the following two approaches:

  * Change the data.  
Preprocess the dataset externally (e. g. using Python), to transform invalid values into valid ones.  
This approach helps when in the same data field, in different records there are different types or formats.
  * Change the schema.  
Duplicate the data source, and in the new data import, change the data type or the configuration of the data type.  
This can help if there is an issue with the field's data type in the schema, affecting all values of that field. For instance, in the case of a missing categorical value, or if you picked the wrong setting when defining a data type.



## Missing valuesâ

Some records in your dataset will most likely have empty fields (perhaps caused by faulty equipment). These, if untreated, would also lead to misleading results or failure during the training. Hence Pulse allows you to define how to represent missing values.

info

When you create a data source from a CSV file, you can define any of the following representations to be treated as missing values:

  * NULL
  * null
  * N/A
  * Empty string



When you run an [analysis on your data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis), it might indicate that the count of missing values is very high for an important field. In these cases, you may need to re-engineer your features or build a [data cleaning plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/cleaning-up-the-data) that detects and removes records that match the missing value representation you configured.

In case there are missing values for a target variable, those records are ignored in [model evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and [rule evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules).

# Jobs and Job Profiles

Was this page helpful?Â 

Jobs allow Pulse to execute computational tasks in a distributed way in a Spark cluster. Job profiles are useful to fine-tune how Jobs use available resources in a Spark node. The following sections describe in more details what they are and how they work.

## Jobs, Job Executionsâ

A job is a set of computational tasks for a certain goal. For example, to run a Model Evaluation the Pulse server needs to execute a set of calculations. Those calculations are the **tasks** of that model evaluation job.

To get the result of a job faster, Pulse distributes the tasks between the nodes of a Spark cluster. Hence jobs are often referred as **Spark jobs** or as **distributed jobs**.

A job execution is an instance of a job, which is created when the job is executed. Imagine a job as a list of instructions on how to execute a complex process or computation (e. g. a Hyperparameter Tuning or a Plan Execution). The job execution, on the other hand, is an instance of a job, created when a user or a program triggers Pulse to execute those instructions on a specific set of data.

Pulse creates a job execution for the following:

  * [Data Source Analysis](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis)
  * [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance)
  * [Model training](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training)
  * [Model Evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation)
  * [Plan Execution](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#plan-execution)
  * [Rules Evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/evaluating-rules-using-a-snapshot)
  * [Sandbox Evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/sandbox-evaluations)
  * [Hyperparameter Tuning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/hyperparameter-tuning)
  * [AutoML run](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/automl)
  * [Scheduled Metrics Jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/scheduled-metrics-jobs) (SMJs)



You can check job executions and their progress in the **Jobs** tab , under **Job Executions**.

## Job Profilesâ

A job profile is a set of Spark configurations that control how Spark jobs behave. For example, you can use them to ensure that Spark assigns enough memory to the node where the job is executed.

You can check Job Profiles in the **Jobs** tab , under **Job Profiles**.

The scope of Job Profiles can be the following:

  * **Default for the App** : applies to all jobs of the Pulse application. For each Pulse application, only one job profile can be [configured as default](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles#setting-a-profile-as-default-for-the-app).

  * **Default for a specific resource type** : each of these job profiles apply to one resource type of the following list:

    * Data Source Analysis
    * Feature Importance
    * Model Training
    * Model Evaluation
    * Plan Execution
    * Rule Snapshot
    * Sandbox Evaluation
    * Hyperparameter Tuning
    * SMJs

info

It's optional to have a default job profile for a resource type. If there is [a job profile configured as default for a resource type](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles#setting-a-profile-as-default-for-a-job-type), for that resource it overrides the default job profile of the application.

  * **Applied to a single job** : when creating a Data Science resource that can use job profiles, you can [select a job profile other than the default](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles#setting-a-profile-as-default-for-the-app), or you can [edit the properties on demand](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/editing-properties-on-demand), for that single job execution that you are creating.




To understand which properties were used in a job execution, open the Job Execution and select the  button.

Resources without default Job Profile

  * It's not possible to use job profiles with Registered Jobs and [Scheduled Metrics Jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/scheduled-metrics-jobs).
  * Although an AutoML run creates a job, you cannot assign a default Job Profile to AutoML jobs. This is because the AutoML job will start other jobs (Plan execution, Hyperparameter tuning, etc.) which can have their default job profile.



### Pulse Properties Profileâ

The Pulse Properties Profile (PPP) contains a read-only list of the Spark properties that are loaded from a preconfigured source.

info

By default that source is the **pulse.properties** file located in the **conf** folder. However, the PPP can be configured to read from other types of sources, such as RDBMS, NoSQL (Cassandra), etc.

You can check the PPP by accessing the **Jobs** tab  and opening the PPP in the **Job Configuration Profiles** table as shown in the following image:

When you [create a new job profile](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/creating-a-job-profile), the properties in the PPP are automatically inherited by this new profile. You can edit them, or add new Spark properties to the new job profile.

#### Updates in the PPPâ

When properties in the PPP are updated, those changes are also automatically propagated to the other job profiles. For example, if the PPP is updated with a new Spark property, it is also automatically included in all the existing job profiles.

Exception: updates that are not propagated

When in the PPP you update a property which already exists in a Job Profile with a different value, the change is not populated from the PPP to the Job Profile.

### Group Properties Profileâ

The Group Properties Profile allows specifying Spark properties at the level of Hierarchical Groups.

caution

Spark properties defined in the Group properties override those defined in the Job Profile, which in turn override those from the PPP. The order of precedence is therefore as follows: Group properties â Job Profile â PPP.

### Automatic profileâ

danger

This is an experimental feature that currently only works for Plan Execution jobs that employ a persistent PKernel via RocksDB.

In addition to static job profiles, we can also generate automatic configurations: this is an experimental feature that currently only works for Plan Execution jobs that employ a persistent PKernel via RocksDB.

The Spark configuration properties that are generated by the Job Profile Tuner are:

  * spark.memory.fraction
  * spark.memory.storageFraction
  * spark.task.cores
  * spark.executor.cores
  * Spark.executor.memory
  * spark.executor.memoryOverhead



For more information about these properties you may refer to <https://archive.apache.org/dist/spark/docs/3.3.2/configuration.html>. These properties override the ones in the default static profile.

When running a plan execution be aware that not all plans are eligible for auto-profiling. The conditions for eligibility are:

  * The plan must not be omnichannel
  * The plan must be a directed path graph (or linear graph); i.e., only a data source and a sink and each other operator in the plan must have at maximum one upstream operator as input and one downstream operator as output.



Under the hood, the job profile tuner (JPT), which is the component in Pulse that generates automatic profiles, uses heuristics that based on the job's input data and workload, as well as cluster availability state, attempt to generate a configuration that not only make a job viable (by executing it successfully) but also performant (minimizing latency while using resources efficiently). In a nutshell, the JPT attempts to predict the maximum memory that a Spark executor will require by assessing the artifacts that need to be maintained in memory during the job execution, such as the state of stateful operators (e.g., metrics), Pulse managed lists, and enrichers.

Since using a persistent PKernel all the times can incur a penalty in the job performance, we have a mechanism to automatically select the most appropriate state backend of the PKernel based on job characteristics, namely data distribution and window durations. To enable it, check the property `automaticStateBackend` in DataScience PKernel configurations.  The state backend selection will happen before the tuning of job profiles and, therefore, a profile can only be generated if the selector picks a persistent state backend for PKernel.

To help on debugging eventual problems with the JPT, which is still an experimental feature, users may also enable the automatic collection of job performance metrics: see the property `collectPerformanceMetrics` in Spark Job Service Configuration.

## Memory considerationsâ

When running Spark jobs, it's recommended to have a default profile for all jobs, and define job profiles for executing resource-intensive jobs.

Calculation tasks may fail if they have insufficient memory available. This might happen because each Spark node has fixed resources available, for instance a fixed number of cores and a fixed amount of memory. Some nodes may have larger resources than others, but by default it's not sure that the tasks that need large resources get assigned to those nodes. Typical examples of tasks needing larger memory are Model Trainings, Hyperparameter Tunings and Plan Executions.

If smaller jobs occupy the resources that have larger capacity, Pulse doesn't leverage the full potential of the Spark cluster. To ensure that the necessary resources are available for jobs that need them, you can use Spark properties to influence the number of cores and the amount of memory used by a job. Job profiles can regulate what kind of resources should be assigned to a job which is running with a specific job profile. For instance, you can have a default profile for all jobs, but define a job profile for executing Plans, and another one for Hyperparameter Tunings to make sure that these get the proper resources they require.

If these job profiles are created, you can use them when creating a job execution of a related Data Science resource.

Restrictive default settings

The default Spark settings are restrictive, for example, they allow 1GB of memory per node. It is recommended to create a Spark configuration strategy early on in a project, and keep adjusting the settings as you monitor the Job Executions.

## Learn moreâ

Learn how to do the following tasks related to Jobs and Job Profiles:

  * [Creating a job profile](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/creating-a-job-profile)
  * [Selecting a job profile](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles)
  * [Edit properties for a specific job execution on demand](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/editing-properties-on-demand)

# Limits

Within Pulse, **limits** (also referred to as **quotas**) are upper bounds on the number or size of resources that can be configured in an [application](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications).

Limits act as guardrails to guide users towards recommended usage patterns and best practices, with the goal of helping ensure optimal runtime performance, and preventing issues such as degraded stability in production environments.

Pulse limits are defined individually for each environment, allowing flexible setups while maintaining control over resource usage. Specifically, they are primarily targeted at runtime environments, where performance and stability are critical.

Limit adjustments

Pulse limits are performance safeguards, not rigid constraints.  
If your usage requires higher limits, reach out to the Feedzai Customer Service to request the necessary adjustments.

## Limits on Metrics operators in Plansâ

Pulse limits the number of [Metrics operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#metrics) that can be included in a [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans). By default, the limit is set to two Metrics operators per Plan, which allows common use cases such as cascading metrics.

The [Create/Edit Plan page](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/#createedit-plan-page) displays the usage of the Metrics operators quota above the plan data flow diagram. The indicator shows how many Metrics operators are currently used out of the allowed limit, e.g., "Metrics operators in use: 1 of 2":

When the limit is reached, the **Metrics** operator becomes disabled, so that no more operators can be dragged onto the plan diagram:

Additionally, dragging Metrics operators from the clipboard pop-up into the plan diagram is blocked if it would exceed the limit:

### Existing Plans exceeding the limitâ

If an existing Plan already had more than the allowed number of Metrics operators before this limit was introduced, it can still be opened and edited as usual. However, no new Metrics operators can be added until the total number is reduced below the limit.

Importing Plans exceeding the limit

Support for existing Plans exceeding the Metrics operators limit only applies to Plans currently in the application. [Importing resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) that include Plans with more than the allowed number of Metrics operators will fail with an error message indicating that the Metrics operators limit has been exceeded.

## Learn Moreâ

For more detailed information about organizing metrics across multiple operators, see [Best Practices for Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/best-practices-for-plans).

  * [Core Concepts](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts)

On this page

# Lists

Was this page helpful?Â 

A list stores a set of items. Lists are available for [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) to check the same pattern against a large number of values. E.g., a list of credit card numbers, a list of merchants, etc.

In the process of fraud detection is very common to define blacklists for blocking transactions from certain cards, or even define transactions with common parameters that should be up for review (triggering an alarm every time a transaction occurs). Lists allow you to group and manage these values so that you can use them efficiently with Rules.

When you define a list, the first thing you need to consider is which list type is best suited to your use case. Lists are essentially made of items, typically hundreds of them, where information will be stored. Depending on the items you must choose between one of the following:

  * **Simple list** : When only one piece of information is needed. Represents a list containing only numbers or strings (commonly used for blacklists/whitelists).

  * **Complex list** : When you need to store complex values, for example [tuples](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types). Each item is identified by a key and that key has a predefined set of fields. For example, the key of an item may be _country_ and its fields can be a set of _safe_merchants_ for that country.

Complex lists allow you to define rules that first check for the existence of the key and then verify conditions over the other fields. For example, when a transaction comes into the system, lookup if the country of the transaction is in the list of risky countries. If so, check if the transactions were done on "safe merchants" for that country.




## List Configurationâ

Imagine you want to create a list to store patterns used by potentially dangerous transactions. A [rule](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) can then verify if a transaction matches any dangerous pattern stored in the list and help reduce fraudulent transactions.

As an example, we will define the dangerous payments pattern as a country, a list of [MCCs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#mcc) and a list of terminal authentication methods. The next steps describe how such a list can be created.

When configuring a list, pay special attention to the following parameters:

  * **Name** : Choose a representative name as it will be used as the internal list name in RDL.  This internal name can't be changed and has some differences to the list name. For example, `"DangerousPayments"` will generate an internal name of `"dangerous_payments".`

  * **Tags** : Describe briefly the purpose of the list. Can be used in [API calls](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/data-types-in-rules#collections) to filter existing lists. For example, add the `suspicious` keyword to all the lists that contain dangerous patterns.

  * **Key Label** : Lists are implemented as a key-value store. The key can store multiple types of information ranging from card numbers, to MCCs or country names.

  * **Key Type** : Pulse supports two key types: **String** and **Number**. Consider the internal implementation  of the data structure and access capabilities of lists to understand why limits the available key types.

  * **Fields** : Defines the schema, or the internal structure, of items in a complex list.

High cardinality fields

Each list item will be stored in memory from the moment Feedzai Pulse starts.

This has a direct impact on the consumed memory, thus having the potential to cause problems with fields that have high value cardinality.




## List Itemsâ

After you have created a List you need to add items to it. In the case of a `DangerousPayments` list, the items are fraudulent patterns that represent suspicious transactions.

You can load entire lists, with a large number of entries, in bulk. Feedzai Pulse accepts a CSV file with the items' information and handles the addition process for each item transparently.

Upload Limit Recommendation

To ensure reliable processing and avoid straining system resources, it is recommended that each uploaded list file contains at most 40,000 items.

Note that this figure is a general guideline; the actual threshold for optimal performance can vary depending on the specific contracted resource sizing. If your list is larger than that, split it into multiple files before uploading.

Timespan support in items is an essential feature when creating watchlists. These lists allow you to, for example, add a card number that should be under watch during a given period of time after having suspicious activity. Lists support the following three timespan types:

Key uniqueness

The conjunction of the item `key` \+ `timespan` must be unique. In other words, Pulse will not add the card `0000-0000-0000-0000` to a List if it is already there with an overlapping timespan. For multi-tenant lists, the tenant unique id is also part of the unique key: `key + timespan + tenant.`

Note that the timespans are interpreted according to the workflow clock. See [Time, schedules and timezones](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/time-schedules-and-timezones) for more information.

## Multi-Tenancyâ

Lists in Pulse also support the multi-tenancy concept. A list can be of the type **Global** if the list is aimed to be used in a context that is not Multi-Tenanted or of the types **By Tenant** and **By Tenant Group** if the list is aimed to be used in a multi-tenancy project.

In a list of the type **By Tenant** , each Tenant will be able to see and manage a subset of all the items without impacting other Tenants.

To further detail how to create lists for multi-tenancy, visit [Creating Lists and Adding Items](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-lists-and-adding-list-items).

## Tokenized Listsâ

Once you have set up the Tokenizer, you will also be able tokenize lists. For example, black lists can be sometimes composed of Credit Card numbers, which in order to fulfil PCI DSS compliance, must be encrypted. Therefore, lists can be tokenized by specifying it during its [creation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-lists-and-adding-list-items). After defining the list as tokenized, you can see how the sensitive information has been encrypted.

For instance, when downloading the list of items, the CSV file no longer shows clear text PAN numbers, but tokens instead. All CSVs also show a column that indicates whether the key of the item is tokenized. In downloads, that column displays a **True** value if the list is encrypted, or **False** if it is not. When uploading, if set as **True** , it works as selecting the **Encrypted** checkbox in the item creation screen.

## Reviewing List Changesâ

Pulse supports a "4-eye check" review functionality for list changes, which places edits made to lists into a review queue, and only applies the changes if they are approved by a second person.

To learn more about this functionality, see [Reviewing List Changes - Four Eyes Check](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/reviewing-list-changes).

## Auditingâ

The purpose of auditing is to store the logs of changes (creation, edition and deletion) made to items in the lists. These audit logs display, among other data, when and who made changes to the items, as well as the corresponding new field values.

The audit entries are only accessible via Pulse REST API through a query by item key.

Pulse Database

Auditing is supported only by the relational Pulse Database (PDB).

Note that the audit entries are not visible in Pulse User Interface (UI); they are stored and available for other applications to fetch them.

# Models

Was this page helpful?Â 

A **model** represents knowledge collected about the behavior of a **target variable** in a data source. You collect this knowledge by running a machine learning algorithm against a historical dataset, to investigate the data patterns in it. This process is called [training a model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training). You create a model in order to use it later in a [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) to predict the value of the target variable in live data.

After training a model, you can evaluate its accuracy and compare it to other models. For this, Pulse generates statistics in a so-called [model evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation).

Models and model evaluations are organized into **model projects**.

## Model life cycleâ

Models give your application an intelligent edge by allowing you to configure, train, fine tune and deploy a binary classifier which will score each instance. The model lifecycle is fully aligned with Pulse's [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop).

Before using a model to score a system's incoming transactions for fraud detection, it must be properly trained using representative and verified data labeled for your target variable, for example, both fraud and non-fraud cases.

Model usage is separated into two distinct lifecycle phases:

  * **Training and evaluation** (in the data science environment)

Is an offline process that can be repeated with different settings and data until you are satisfied with the results. The performance of trained models is [evaluated](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model) using common performance metrics, such as F1-Measure, False Positive Rate, among others and by visualizing and comparing its ROC curve.

  * **Scoring** (in the production environment)

When model performance is good, meaning that it is achieving high detection and low false-positive rates, it is ready to be used in the fraud detection workflow of your application.




## Learn moreâ

To fully understand models, make sure you also go through the following concepts:

  * [Model training](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training)
  * [Model evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation)
  * [Feature importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance)
  * [White-box explanations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/white-box-explanations)
  * [Hyperparameter tuning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/hyperparameter-tuning)
  * [AutoML](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/automl)

# Outcome Combinator

Was this page helpful?Â 

The outcome combinator is a key concept in [workflows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) and [sandbox evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/sandbox-evaluations) that helps to create more stable Data Science projects and allows you to define the strategy on how to combine results into outcomes in workflows.

Outcomes

Outcomes represent the decisions produced as output based on the way a workflow has been modelled, e.g. Fraud/Not fraud. Pulse adds each outcome decision field (for instance, _fraud_) and outcome score field (for instance, _fraud_score)_ to the schema of events moving along the workflow.

## How Outcome Combinators Workâ

Scoring and rules services contribute to outcomes and respective scores with partial values. The message associated with every event that enters a workflow is complemented with further information on outcomes whenever the event is scored or processed by [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules).

The outcome combinator therefore takes all those partials results, retrieves any other relevant data from each of the steps (rules, [models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), etc) and combines all information. This expands the message and updates the decision information related to that given event.

Outcome combinators act every time that an event is processed by a workflow service, or resources in a sandbox evaluation, that contributes to a decision and adds results to the event. It is then when the combinator:

  1. Is executed in order to combine all the partial results generated up to that point, according to a combination strategy â typically a weighed average.
  2. Updates the fields associated to the outcomes. E.g. _fraud_ and _fraud_score_.



Outcome combinators guarantee that those fields always reflect the combined scores and decisions taken in the workflow up to that point, which can be used as input for the next service being processed. Outcome combinators define how to calculate the final score for an outcome, i.e. how to combine all partial scores produced by any resource.

## Learn Moreâ

Refer to the [Testing your work in a Sandbox environment](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/testing-your-work-in-a-sandbox-environment) page for more details on how Sandboxing works.

On this page

# Plans

Was this page helpful?Â 

Data science plans are functions that receive data and produce a transformation of that data (not necessarily with equal size).

Plans do much of the heavy processing required before you train your machine learning [models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) in the [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop). Plans are executed as distributed jobs in Spark which allows handling large datasets (e.g. hundreds or even thousands of TBs). In addition, they allow you to natively deploy a subset of these data transformations to a runtime [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) while keeping the same semantics as in the data science stage.

Check the [operators reference](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) to learn more about the possible elements you can include in your data science plans.

## What are plans used for?â

Plans define a transformation of one or more [data sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) into another data source. They are a vital concept in Pulse and they are a powerful contribution to the data science set of tools. Plans represent a way to boost the performance of:

  * **Data scientists:** Delivering a set of tools that make it easier to process data for the training of machine learning models.
  * **Engineers:** Abstracting a lot of the usual complexity involved in deploying data science work into production. With a fully integrated modeling and run-time environment, Pulse enables a seamless deployment of data transformations, without any major effort.



In a plan, it is possible to add, update and remove fields, calculate [metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric) on the data source, and even join data sources.

Plans are useful to systematize data cleaning, data processing, and feature engineering, both in a data science pipeline and in production. Typically, a data science project will have several plans that are executed in sequence and generate new data sources each as the output. These intermediate data sources are subsequently used as input for other plans.

## Types of plansâ

Pulse lets you design three main types of plans, each one aimed at different stages in your project:

  * **Deployable plans**  
It allows you to design and test, during the data science stage, the data transformations that you will use in a runtime workflow to process real-time events. For example, one or more plans that generate all features that your deployed machine learning [model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) needs to output a decision in runtime. Pulse ensures that all transformations in a deployable plan will work in runtime exactly as you designed them during the data science loop.
  * **Deployable omnichannel plans**  
In addition to the functionality offered by regular deployable plans, this type of plan allows to process data from multiple sources, to enable [channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels). Each input data source corresponds to a separate channel. At runtime, when omnichannel plans are deployed to the workflow, multiple workflows feed into the plan.
  * **Non-deployable plans**  
The purpose of these plans is to perform data transformations that are purely for offline data exploration purposes, during the data science loop, and that will not be directly deployed in a runtime workflow. For example, a plan that addresses quality issues in your raw data, a plan that samples your data into a more representative dataset, or a plan that joins the raw transaction data with the respective labels, e.g. _fraud/not fraud_.



### Deployable plansâ

A subset of the [transformations available](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) in plans can be deployed into production - typically the plan, or plans, that define the features to be used as input for your machine learning models - so that events can then be turned into instances and scored in real-time.

Using Plans in Production

This is extremely important since Pulse guarantees that such subset of the plans functionality will work properly in production for you to be able to score your instances in real-time.

That is very powerful, since in a deployable plan you devise a single piece of logic, and Pulse will apply the same semantics:

  * Offline during your data science iterations with great scalability.
  * In real-time, in production, with very low latency.



Workflow branching

Due to the fact that Pulse does not support parallel branches in runtime workflows, deployable plans only allow for a single data source to be configured as the input, and only one sink as the only output.

#### Integrated exploration and runtime stagesâ

A unique feature to Pulse is enabling you to deploy feature plans into runtime without effort. This tight integration of data science and engineering represents a huge boost in performance and productivity.

The way deployable plans work in Pulse removes the obstacles that commonly affect your project when it is ready to go into production. Pulse ensures the following:

  * Your data science work is seamlessly deployed into Production without any need for additional development.
  * Semantics do not change whether you are exploring your data and modeling your project, or your work is being executed in a production scenario. For example:
    * How Pulse partitions your data in a distributed environment.
    * How Pulse performs real-time and scheduled aggregations.
  * Off-the-shelf integration with Cassandra and batch processes to replicate aggregations with long time windows.
  * Execution in a high-performance streaming environment delivering sub-millisecond latencies.



The following image depicts a deployable plan â in this case, a plan that filters out internal transactions, unnecessary for the model, and generates metrics and features. Note that the plan's internal definition already includes a single [Source operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) and a single [Sink operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) (not editable) to ensure that the plan executes a linear path when deployed in runtime.

### Deployable omnichannel plansâ

In addition to the functionality offered by regular deployable plans, deployable omnichannel plans allow to process data from multiple sources, to enable [channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels).

These plans support working with two or more channels:

  * As explained in the [Channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels#using-data-from-multiple-channels) page, there is always a single main channel. When you place the plan in the Workflow, this is the channel processed and scored by that Workflow.
  * The remaining channels are secondary channels â they are only fed into the plan for additional information and to improve the detection on the main channel.



The main channel is equivalent to the input source in non-omnichannel plans. You can perform all the same transformations on the main channel that you would do in non-omnichannel plans.

The secondary channels can only be used in aggregations (in the [Metrics operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference)).

For example, let's say that you are processing ATM withdrawals (debit channel) and would like to check if the customer has recently logged into internet banking with a new device and increased the withdrawal limit (internet banking channel). In this case, _debit_ is the main channel (because you are scoring debit card events) and _internet banking_ is the secondary channel (because you are consulting it to improve the detection). See the [Creating metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics) page for more information on how to implement the relevant aggregation in Pulse.

At runtime, omnichannel plans are fed by workflows:

  * The workflow where the plan is deployed corresponds to the main channel, i.e. the data passing through this workflow will be sent to the input of the plan.
  * For each secondary channel, you will need to select a different workflow which is processing data for that channel. That data will be automatically fed into the plan.



### Non-deployable plansâ

A non-deployable plan is used only for data exploration purposes and any ETL task, for example in traditional data manipulation when joining and grouping data. When processing a data stream in real-time, in a Production environment, for example, to classify transactions as fraud or not, these activities are not repeatable nor applicable, such as joining data from separate sources.

These plans have no restrictions as to the [available operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) they can execute.

The following image depicts a non-deployable plan that joins data from different sources, in this case, historical transactions with the respective labels, and performs data cleaning operations such as removing unnecessary fields.

## Plan executionâ

A plan is just a definition, which means that there isn't actually any data bound to it, only an input [data schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources). To actually compute the output data source it is necessary to run it.

Running the plan creates a plan execution. A plan execution represents a snapshot of the plan at the moment it ran, the inputs used and the outputs created, during the data science stage. It allows you to deploy a (deployable) plan to runtime with the same exact configuration and semantics it had when you ran it initially.

For all [operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) that require you to define expressions (for example, adding and updating fields with the [Map operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#map)), you must do so with the [Pulse Query Language (PQL)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features). Thus, whenever Pulse runs data through a plan, whether it is during the data science stage or in real-time, Pulse is actually executing [PQL commands](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/operators-in-pql).

Distributed execution

The execution of plans runs distributed in Spark, so Pulse is able to transform data in parallel within a set of machines of a cluster.

This means that even for very large datasets, with several TB in size, Pulse is very fast and efficient when computing data transformations on your [data sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources).

### Immutabilityâ

Plan executions ensure that plans, like data sources and schemas, are immutable.

When you add a deployable plan to a runtime workflow, you must specify a plan execution. The plan execution contains the plan definition at the moment it ran during the data science loop, the inputs used and the outputs created.

This isolates the plan during data science from the same plan when deployed to production. This way you can safely change the plan definition itself without affecting your production workflow.

Correcting a plan

If you need to deploy corrections to your plan, you can simply run it to create a new plan execution and generate a new snapshot of the plan. Then configure the plan service in your workflow with the new plan execution.

### Data partitioningâ

A plan in Pulse is executed as a distributed job in Spark. This allows you to set up various plan operators to perform different data transformations and process large volumes of data.

Spark handles data that is organized into smaller logical chunks referred to as partitions to achieve high perfomance.

The way that data is re-organized into partitions is specific to the operators that you add to your plan. For example, to calculate metrics defined in the Metrics operator, Spark needs to re-organize the data by the _Group By_ fields configured in this operator.

Pulse has different options available to configure data partitioning so that the data re-organization is performed as homogeneous and well distributed as possible.

Check the [Data partitioning in Metrics operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/data-partitioning-for-the-metrics-operator) page to learn more about this functionality.

### Compressed file outputâ

Pulse implements a configuration that enables the output of plans to be directly compressed in storage.

This feature causes the underlying files to be stored as BZip2-compressed, and thus, taking up to 8 times less space on disk. As the trade-off, plans with compressed file output are slightly slower to read when used as input for other jobs such as model training, model evaluations, among others.

Check with your Feedzai contact person how to configure plan output file compression on the server.

On this page

# Rules

Was this page helpful?Â 

A rule defines a condition based on the fields of a [data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) that produces a binary result for each record that matches the condition. The condition to evaluate is defined by coding in [RDL (Rule Definition Language)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/operators-in-rules).

## Defining rulesâ

The following image shows how a rule is defined. This example depicts a rule for an account opening scenario to automatically accept the customers' application if their income is significantly above the average for the area where they live.

To fully understand rules in Pulse you must check all details regarding [how a rule is composed](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules/rules-components) and [how it works](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules/how-rules-work).

## Rules projectsâ

Similarly to [models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), rules are organized into rules projects. Rules projects define which data source field should be available for rules to target, for example, to set all transactions from a specific card automatically as fraud. In addition, rules projects act as logical containers that group rules related with the same context.

A rules project is associated with a data source. Since the rule concept is not directly related to machine learning, it does not involve a training stage. Thus, it is possible to deploy rules directly into Production without having them run over test data. So in fact, a rules project is bound to the schema of a data source and does not depend on the data itself.

info

You can evaluate your rules over any data source as long as it is [compatible](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#compatible-data-sources) with the data schema specified for the rules project.

## Target variableâ

When creating a rules project, you must define the data source on which the rules will operate. In addition, you must choose a **target variable** , which is the field whose value you are trying to detect with your rules. For example, _fraud_ /_not fraud_.

Pulse lets you target any categorical field in the data source schema. In practice, this means that rules can be useful both for binary and multi-class classification.

For each rule in the rules project, Pulse allows you to select which of the possible values should be set to the target variable if the rule is triggered. Thus, in the same rules project, you can configure some rules to set transactions as _fraud_ , and other rules that set transactions as _not fraud_.

When you evaluate rules in a rule snapshot, Pulse calculates the rule performance for each possible value of the target variable, letting you adjust the resulting visualization accordingly.

## Stateâ

Rules are usually stateless, but when you cannot use [plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) to calculate certain types of windows and add metrics as fields of a schema, Pulse lets you define these windows directly for a rules project.

Therefore, when you need to develop very robust rules that perform aggregations over time windows, you must configure how Pulse should manage their internal state.

info

It is recommended that whenever possible, you use [plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) to handle your time-aware operations in data science. The plan will generate data fields with these metrics, making them accessible to rules.

Activating state in your rules project is an advanced operation that must be carefully done and requires that the user understands the full implications of his actions:

  * By enabling state in a rules project, Pulse manages an isolated environment where all rules contained in the project will have access to [Pulse Query Language metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features) (i.e., aggregations) and [Rule Definition Language variables](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/operators-in-rules).
  * To activate state, the schema in your rules project must include a timestamp field. Otherwise, you cannot perform time-based aggregations.
  * When configuring partitioning fields, you must be extremely careful. They define how to distribute processing when generating a rule evaluation. Make sure data is correctly partitioned, otherwise the evaluation results may not make sense.



Learn more about state in rules by checking [how a rule is composed](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules/rules-components).

## Multi-tenancyâ

Multi-tenancy is the ability to support multiple tenants in the same environment offering a practical solution to apply rules to several tenants at the same time, as well as to customize rules for each tenant.

When creating a rules project, the user can select from the following options:

  * **Global** is used for rules that are not multi-tenanted.
  * With **Duplicated for Tenant** , the same rule applies to all tenants, but rule conditions can be computed using tenant-specific data.
  * With **By Tenant** , custom rules apply to individual tenants.



info

A **landlord** is a client who has a fraud prevention installation that he can offer to other clients, also known as tenants, acting as a reseller. A **tenant** is a client that uses a fraud prevention application provided by a landlord. Tenants have the possibility to create, manage and deploy their own rules and lists depending on the permissions the landlord has given to them.

### Duplicated for Tenantâ

When a rules project is set as **Duplicated for Tenant** it means that the set of rules applies to all the tenants in the same way. In terms of deployment, a rule snapshot is created and applied in runtime, the events are then grouped by each tenant and all rules defined in the rule snapshot are applied for each tenant individually, as illustrated in the following image.

### By Tenantâ

When a rules project is set as **By Tenant** , it means that a set of rules applies to specific tenants. In terms of deployment, a rule snapshot is created and applied in runtime, the events are then grouped by tenant and the corresponding set of rules are applied for each tenant, as illustrated in the following image.

## Advanced vs. simple rulesâ

Users can set the type to advanced or simple, the former being the default type.

This setting has the following meaning:

  * **Advanced rules projects** contain rules that can be written using a template and which may have an environment and state.
  * **Simple rules projects** contain rules that are not editable inside Pulse and may be used for self-service rules created in Case Manager.



When a rules project is set as _Simple_ , the _State_ input is hidden, the label for the _Actions_ becomes _Secondary Actions_ , and the multi-tenancy options are limited to _Global_ and _By Tenant_.

## Self-service rulesâ

With **self-service rules** (SSR), fraud analysts can write and deploy rules themselves very quickly.

The characteristics of self-service rules in a nutshell are as follows:

  * They are deployed directly to the Production environment, in real time.
  * They are created in Case Manager by analysts and/or their managers.
  * Governance can audit and support self-service rules.



This lets you implement completely new processes and achieve higher operational efficiencies while dynamically following changes in fraud patterns.

### Testing self-service rulesâ

Self-service rules can be tested in Case Manager, allowing production environments to execute Spark jobs processing the most recent events that have gone through a self-service rule block of a given workflow. These events will be tested against an updated version of that rule block and measure _Hit Rate_ , _Money Captured_ , etc.

In order for Pulse to process the data in the same way as when going through the live workflow, those events are stored in a custom data store used only for self-service rule testing.

This data store thus receives every event that goes through a self-service rule block in the workflow. Depending on the testing configuration in Case Manager, this data store keeps the data of the time interval that is necessary for rule testing.

### Auditing self-service rulesâ

Pulse can be configured to keep audit logs of the creation, edition, deletion, ordering, testing, and publishing operations made to rules. The raw logs are accessible via a REST API through a query that specifies a rule, a workflow element or an application. Get in touch with your contact person at Feedzai to get more information on the audit logs and the Self-Service Rules REST API.

# Sandbox Evaluations

Sandbox Evaluations allow you to test a sequence of [Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and [Rule projects](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) you have created in your Data Science application as if they were in production. By [creating](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/testing-your-work-in-a-sandbox-environment) and [analyzing the results](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/testing-your-work-in-a-sandbox-environment/evaluating-your-sandbox-results) of **Sandbox Evaluations** , you will be able to have a clear picture of how your Data Science project is performing before actually deploying it.

Sandboxing allows you to simulate and check the accuracy of your system before it is in production, so you can improve the performance of the metrics of your system in advance. For example, the fraud detection rate of the system is understood more precisely than by analyzing **Models** and **Rules** separately. This helps you have a broader understanding of your Data Science project and spot flaws that would be harder to detect just by analyzing resources in isolation.

Although Models can be trained in order to understand their performance in a specific field, this does not reflect the reality of a deployed system. Sandboxing enables the analysis of the performance of all these resources in a simulated [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows), being able to recognize those weaknesses that do not offer any added value to your system. For example, by testing **Models** and **Rules** together, you can see whether the configuration of your **Rules** does offer a better tool for detecting fraud.

Additionally, it allows you to see not only the performance by score, but also by decision, whilst testing rules only regard the decision itself.

## Improving the visibility over your projectâ

Sandboxing is also a way to validate [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) and [Outcome Combinators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/outcome-combinator). The following image depicts a Sandbox that analyzes a **Model** followed by a set of **Rules,** combining the results with a weighed average.

You can also get a clearer picture of how your system is doing by selecting partitioning fields: The Sandbox thus analyzes the different components of the workflow separately, the node only having visibility of that partition. Sandbox Evaluations also simulate the order in which events are processed.

You can also select **Models** and **Rules** to be segmented by particular values of breakdown fields, allowing you to analyze the performance of Models and Rules at once.

## Evaluating the Resultsâ

Once that the parameters of your **Sandbox Evaluation** have been specified, you can evaluate its results in order to find points to improve, creating a more robust Data Science project. You can visualize the results by Score and by Outcome separately in order to see how the system behaves independently of the outcome decision that was specified on the outcome decision field. You will be able to analyze various metrics that will allow you to grasp the functioning of your set.

The measured performance is therefore as accurate as when the system is deployed in production. With this, you can:

  * Identify problems with recall/catch rate, false positive rate or risk workflow optimization.
  * Use a system that runs past production traffic faster than a Production environment.
  * Reduce the time needed to validate system results previous to the production environment in order to test the performance of **Models** and **Rules** as a single system.
  * Simplify the testing of the entire system (**Model** , **Rules** and **Lists**).



Evaluating your Sandbox results against a test dataset is crucial in understanding how it is performing, and how close you are to reaching the objectives of your Data Science project. With a complete set of metrics, you will be able to have a complete understanding of how all the components of your Data science project work together and identify the points to improve for your project to be as precise as possible.

## Learn Moreâ

Discover more related to Outcome Combinators in the following pages:

  * [Outcome Combinator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/outcome-combinator): Learn more about what it is and how it works.
  * [Testing your work in a Sandbox environment](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/testing-your-work-in-a-sandbox-environment): Have a better grasp on how Sandboxing works.
  * [Evaluating your Sandbox Results](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/testing-your-work-in-a-sandbox-environment/evaluating-your-sandbox-results): Understand all the information that is shown after creating a Sandbox Evaluation.

# The Data Science Framework (DSF)

Was this page helpful?Â 

The Data Science Framework (DSF), also known as the Data Science Studio, is a dedicated environment used in risk assessment strategies for building, testing, and evaluating rules and models according to the [Data Science Loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop).

Its main capabilities include:

  * **Data preparation** : Read production data or ingest historical data, clean it, and analyze its quality and statistics to ensure it fits your schema. This is crucial to work with Rules, Models and/or ad-hoc analysis.
  * **Feature engineering and plan execution** : Create and test new features using Plans, which can then be deployed to production. Plans allow the application of generic data computations, typically to transform it or extend it to a new file output.
  * **Model and rule development** : Train Machine Learning (ML) models and create rule sets, and evaluate their performance against historical data to identify if further improvements are needed.
  * **Ad-hoc analysis** : Study and request ad-hoc reports or analysis via the DSF.
  * **Sandbox Evaluations** : Test a sequence of a Model and Rule project in the Data Science application.



## What are Data Science jobs?â

Data Science (DS) jobs are jobs initiated in the DSF environment, either via Pulse or JupyterLab, and processed through the Pulse application. While Pulse manages the job lifecycle, the heavy computational workload is shifted to the cluster, which allocates **executors** (i.e. processing units) throughout its **task nodes** (i.e. the actual machines that compose the cluster) to perform the computations as a Spark job.

Refer to [Spark's documentation](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/cluster-overview.html) to further understand its core functionality.

The resources allocated to each job are guided by the job configuration and workload, and bounded by the cluster configuration (i.e. size and number of task nodes, as well as the executors per node).

Pulse provides one default job profile that applies to all DS jobs, but _it is recommended that you adapt this default profile to better fit the jobs you'll be executing_. The default job profile is, essentially, a starting point to create other profiles.

## What are executors?â

Executors represent the **main processing unit** that do the actual work in your job (i.e. reading data, transforming it, caching it, and writing results).

When a job is launched/scheduled, the cluster allocates executors on the task nodes (i.e. machines). These executors borrow resources (i.e. cores and memory) from the task nodes to perform the computations and execute DS jobs.

When sizing the executors, _be mindful of this to avoid setting unrealistic bounds on the amount and/or size of your executors_.

Practical example

If you consider a task node with 16 cores and 128GB of memory, configuring executors to have nine cores and 50GB of memory would represent poor cluster resource usage, which would, ultimately, lead to poor performance. Here's why:

After allocating one executor (with nine cores), the cluster is left with seven available. As each executor borrows nine cores, the cluster is not able to allocate any more executors for that job.  
This way, it would only be possible to fit one executor, leaving seven cores unutilized.

Note that the remaining seven cores could still be used by other jobs, as long as the executors fit in the task nodes.

Dynamic executor allocation

Note that while you can explicitly define how many executors to run, the **general rule-of-thumb favors dynamic allocation of executors**. This lets the cluster decide how many executors to run depending on the workload.

Learn all about the importance and impact of tuning DS jobs in the [Using the Data Science Framework](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/using-the-dsf) page.

### `CollectionUDFs` classâ

Package: `com.feedzai.pulse.pkernel.runtime`

As the CollectionUDFs class is included in the runtime package of Pulse, you don't need to define an alias to use the functions of this class.

Lists vs Maps

The collection called Map of Pulse Query Language (PQL) and Rule Definition Language (RDL) is the equivalent of a Pulse list created under **Lists** . The following table refers to them as **Maps**.

Modifier and Type| Function| Description  
---|---|---  
Integer| count(Object collection)| Returns the number of entries in aÂ collectionFails with _UnsupportedOperationException_ Â if _collection_ is neither a Map nor a Collection.
    
    
    // Returns 2
    CollectionUDF.count(map("a": 1, "b": 2))  
  
Boolean| contains(ObjectÂ collection, Object element)| Checks if _element_ is present in _collection._ Fails with _UnsupportedOperationException_ if _collection_ is neither a Map nor a Collection**.**
    
    
     // Returns true
    CollectionUDF.contains(map("a": 1), 1)  
  
Integer| getInt(Object collection, Object? key)| Returns the integer valueÂ associated to _key._ If _collection_ is a List**,** negative keys start at the end of the list (0 is the first and -1 is the last element).Fails with _UnsupportedOperationException_ if _collection_ is neither a Map nor a List or if the value matching key is not null and not a number.Fails with _IllegalArgumentException_ if _collection_ is a List but _key_ is not a non-null Integer.
    
    
    // Returns 5
    CollectionUDF.getInt(list(1, 3, 5), -1)  
  
Long| getLong(Object collection, Object key)|  Returns the long valueÂ associated to _key._ If _collection_ is a List**,** negative keys start at the end of the list (0 is the first and -1 is the last element).Fails with _UnsupportedOperationException_ if _collection_ is neither a Map nor a List or if the value matching key is not null and not a number. Fails with _IllegalArgumentException_ if _collection_ is a List but _key_ is not a non-null Integer.
    
    
    // Returns 3
    CollectionUDF.getLong(map("a": 3), "a")  
  
Float| getFloat(Object collection, Object key)| Returns the float valueÂ associated to _key._ If _collection_ is a List**,** negative keys start at the end of the list (0 is the first and -1 is the last element).Fails with _UnsupportedOperationException_ if _collection_ is neither a Map nor a List or if the value matching key is not null and not a number.Fails with _IllegalArgumentException_ if _collection_ is a List but _key_ is not a non-null Integer.
    
    
    // Returns null
    CollectionUDF.getFloat(list(null), 0)  
  
Double| getDouble(Object collection, Object key)| Returns the double valueÂ associated to _key._ If _collection_ is a List**,** negative keys start at the end of the list (0 is the first and -1 is the last element).Fails with _UnsupportedOperationException_ if _collection_ is neither a Map nor a List or if the value matching key is not null and not a number.Fails with _IllegalArgumentException_ if _collection_ is a List but _key_ is not a non-null Integer.
    
    
    // Returns 2.5
    CollectionUDF.getDouble(list(3.14, 2.5), 1)

Fails with _IllegalArgumentException_ if _collection_ is a List but _key_ is not a non-null Integer.
