# Workflows

Was this page helpful?Â 

 _"A workflow consists of a sequence of connected steps where each step follows without delay or gap and ends just before the subsequent step may begin."_ (_in[Wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workflow)_)

Workflows represent what Pulse executes in runtime. As Pulse integrates the [data science concepts](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) with their runtime counterparts, a workflow is the result of deploying those concepts directly into a Production environment. A workflow is where you can compose these concepts into a sequence of processing steps that produce a decision in real time.

As an example scenario, fraud detection is a task comprised of several steps with the aim of blocking fraudulent transactions. Usually, transactions must go through one or more sets of [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules), one or more [models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) for scoring and [plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) that perform transformations on data, in order to determine if they are fraudulent.

Thus, we group these processing steps into a workflow. Workflows represent the life cycle of an event through the system. They define the path that information traverses between components that may filter and/or transform the event.

If there is one thing essential to workflows, it is data. Without it, there is no sense in having workflows and all the remaining application resources. So, workflows always operate over an expected input [data schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources).

The following image displays a runtime workflow in Pulse:

## Channelsâ

Each workflow typically corresponds to a particular channel through which the system receives information. For example, one workflow could be processing debit card transactions (debit channel), while another workflow would be dedicated to internet banking transfers (internet banking channel). Because different Channels typically have different Schemas (see below) and require a different set of rules and models, this approach ensures that each Workflow is optimized for the channel itâs processing. For more information on channels, see [Channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels).

## Outcomesâ

The ultimate goal of a runtime workflow is to produce a generic decision and insight on each event. Outcomes are flexible and use case-agnostic representations of those decisions. For example, _fraud/not fraud_ , or _suspicious/not suspicious_.

A workflow can be configured with several outcomes for finer-grained decisions. For example, adding the type of fraud to events, instead of just classifying them as _fraud/not fraud_.

Pulse adds each outcome decision field (e.g _fraud_) and outcome score field (e.g. _fraud_score_) to the schema of events moving along the workflow.

As you add elements such as scoring services and rules services, you must also configure how they affect these fields, i.e. how they contribute to each of the final decisions and scores of the workflow.

Another very important capability of outcomes is enabling you to manage feedback loops better, and to integrate with human validation. Whenever an event traverses a workflow, Pulse saves it in the [event storage](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/event-storage). Thus, it is possible to recover the Outcome of events at a later time to:

  * Generate reports on model accuracy and outcome distribution for a consistent evaluation of runtime performance.
  * Retrain models using the event storage as a source of data after receiving human input. This is especially important to close the loop on human feedback, for example, when Pulse classifies a transaction as fraud but a human analyst overrides the decision based on real-world evidence.



## Workflow schemasâ

Runtime workflows in Pulse must always be configured with an origin schema. This schema, configured at the workflow level, defines the structure and formatting of the events that Pulse consumes from an external source of data.

Workflow schema immutability

To ensure that the workflow is always capable of correctly consuming data, the [origin schema is immutable](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources).

However, as events flow through the different stages of the workflow, their schema can change. For example, new fields are added to the event when it is processed in a [plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) and enriched with features and profiles.

Additionally, if a workflow element only requires a subset of fields in the schema as input, only those are affected in the event once it receives the output of the element. The rest of schema fields remain unchanged and still available for subsequent workflow elements.

Mutable element schemas

Despite the fact that the schema you configure for input data in the workflow is immutable, the input and output schemas for each workflow element can be different.

This depends on the logic you implement for each workflow element, for example in a plan, by removing irrelevant fields, changing the names of fields to match project specifications, adding profiles, generating features and adding enrichment fields.

### Conflictsâ

Since workflow schemas are mutable, when an event reaches a Workflow Service its schema may have been transformed previously by another service.

When configuring a workflow service, if Pulse is unable to match fields from the workflow schema to the input or output schemas of the service, it will generate conflicts and invalidate the workflow configuration. Pulse generates a conflict for each field required by the service that is not present in the workflow schema with the same name and type. This can be due to:

  * Input fields with different names, for example _merchant_name_ and _mcn_.
  * When you remove fields with a [plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans).
  * When the service outputs a new field that already exists in the workflow schema.



In these cases, to fix your workflow, you must solve conflicts by manually mapping fields from the workflow schema to the input and output schemas expected in the service.

Removed fields

If a plan you configured for a plan service removes fields from the workflow schema, then you must ensure that subsequent services in the workflow do not require those fields. Otherwise, Pulse will generate schema conflicts, invalidate your workflow, and you will have no available fields to map from.

In these cases, you should redesign your plan, articulate it with the remaining data science work to be used in runtime, and redeploy it to your workflow.

### Extra fieldsâ

In runtime tasks, for example, when you [design a workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow), Pulse automatically adds the following fields to the event schema:

  * **timestamp** : The timestamp field is used to signal the date of a transaction in the UNIX Timestamp Format. See [Time, schedules and timezones](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/time-schedules-and-timezones) for more information.



Timestamp

The value for this field must always be greater than or equal to the previous value processed since it's not possible to go back in time.

Reserved words

The word _timestamp_ is reserved. Pulse does not allow you to use a [metrics plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics) to calculate metrics over a field named _timestamp_.

  * **UUID** : The unique id of the event. This field is used by several internal services and can also be used by external ones to uniquely identify an event, correlate results, access stored events, among others.

UUID

The system does not fill in this field automatically. The user building the application is responsible for setting it correctly when creating the events.

Reserved words

The word _uuid_ is reserved. Pulse does not allow you to name any field name as _uuid_.

  * **Outcome** : [Outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) represent decisions of your workflow, for example, _fraud/not fraud_. It is a categorical field used to mark an event as, for example, either fraudulent or not.

  * **Outcome score** : The transaction score that corresponds to the workflow decision represented by the outcome. Scoring services and rules services contribute to outcome scores.




## Workflow elementsâ

A workflow consists of processing steps (elements) and links between them. Each workflow element can process or transform the data as soon as the data arrives at it. Workflow elements can be seen as components that process data with the ability to apply operations such as filter and store.

Feedzai Pulse provides three main services:

  * **Rules service** : Is a Pulse service used to declare multiple [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) to detect and mark patterns, optionally contributing to an outcome.
  * **Scoring service** : Is a module that feeds events into a [model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and produces a score, optionally contributing to an outcome.
  * **Plan service** : Enables you to deploy data transformations you have defined and tested in [plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) at the data science stage, for example, to generate features before passing events onto the scoring service.



In addition to these core components provided off-the-shelf, Pulse also lets you include custom services in your workflows.

### Rules serviceâ

The **rules service** allows defining the [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) to be applied to a transaction event and the actions to be taken when the rule is matched. Additionally, a rules service can output a score and contribute to an outcome.

There are different mechanisms that can be applied when a given rule is matched:

  * The corresponding event contributes to an outcome, similarly to how the record is immediately marked as a target value during the data science stage.

  * Jump to the next workflow step, or even skip the remaining steps if the control flow of the rule is configured as _Stop Workflow_.

  * A specific action can be triggered and processed by custom services. They can then apply specific modifications to the corresponding transaction event when handling the action.

danger

The **rules service** **does not evaluate the rules** for every record that passes on Pulse. If the message respective to the record appeared due to a replica or recovery process and the rules project configuration is set to be [stateless](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules), then the rules will not be evaluated. This change is motivated by performance, since the calls to rules engine are expensive, avoiding some of the calls will reduce the execution time.




### Scoring serviceâ

A scoring service executes a [model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) that was previously trained during the [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop). The job of a scoring service consists in **producing a score for each event** that goes through the service. For example, a score that denotes the likelihood of the event representing a fraudulent transaction.

Additionally, and depending on how you configure the scoring service, it will also **contribute to one of the outcomes** in the workflow. In some cases, it may make sense for you to have a deployed model without influencing the final decisions of the workflow. For example, you may want to temporarily deploy a model just to test its live performance for a few days/weeks before phasing it in and start contributing to outcomes. In these cases, you can retrieve the scores, for example with a custom service, from the [event storage](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/event-storage) or using Pulse's API.

White-box explanations in the scoring service

You may need to edit the scoring services that are in production since a previous Pulse version and update explanations with the latest version of white-box explanations (WBE).

Note that you can still use the older version of WBE, but you will not be able to change the critical path.

Due to the complexity of this type of workflow element, you must first understand [models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) in Pulse in order to learn how scoring works.

### Plan serviceâ

The plan service reflects, in production, all the work done at a data science stage.

A unique feature to Pulse is precisely enabling you to deploy feature [plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) into runtime without effort. This tight integration of [data science](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project) and [engineering](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production) represents a huge boost in performance and productivity.

Thus, the plan service takes a set of data transformations, for example, to generate features out of raw data, that have been thoroughly tested as part of the data science stage in your project and marked as fit to be used on live data.

### Custom servicesâ

Custom workflow services are tailor-made programs that allow you to extend or modify Pulse's behavior to fit specific needs.

Their tasks can vary greatly in intent, but one common usage is to configure them as an [input adapter](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-input-adapters). These services are an essential tool to feed data to a workflow. They can be used to build tailor-made connectors that integrate your custom data sources (for example: CSV files, databases, sockets, etc.) with the workflow inside Feedzai Pulse.

Another usage is, generically, when you might also want to modify the events as they make their way through the workflow to match some specific condition.

## Designing a workflowâ

Workflows in Pulse offer a lot of flexibility in how you can combine elements and design a complex event processing pipeline in runtime.

However, most of the concepts you deploy to runtime in a workflow are originated during an offline data science stage. Thus, Pulse has to ensure the [consistency of these concepts in a Pulse project](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/how-pulse-projects-work), for example, [deployable plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans), and guarantee that they produce the same results both during the [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) and during runtime.

Parallel forks in workflows

Pulse does not support parallel forks in your workflows. Since Pulse is unable to enforce the consistency at design-time, it will always force a real-time event to follow a single linear path from input until the workflow terminates.

If you configure branches as mutually exclusive, you are explicitly guaranteeing that an event can only go through one path. If the branches are parallel, then Pulse will automatically route the event through the first branch that evaluates as _true_ and log a warning.

When joining branches into a single path at a workflow element, you must make sure that all incoming paths carry events with the exact same schema.

For more details on workflow design patterns and recommendations on how you can process events in runtime, check the [User Guide](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow).

### Exampleâ

Let's look at a simple use case and see what can happen to events while they're flowing through a workflow. The following diagram shows how different transactions are processed by the workflow:

### Designâ

Events have only two fields:

  * amount
  * country



The workflow is composed of the following elements:

  * One [input adapter](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-input-adapters). It connects to both rules services by forking the events flow through a filter: local and non-local transactions.
  * Two [rules services](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules), for both local and foreign transactions.
  * One [scoring service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models).



Consider that for each rules service you are using rules based on the amount field.

  * For the local transactions, the rules service executes a rule where the amount needs to be greater than 200
  * For foreign transactions, the second rules service executes a rule where the amount is greater than 1000.



For both cases, the rules are configured to stop the workflow.

### Executionâ

In this scenario, the events flow as follows:

  1. The input adapter consumes the events.
  2. The workflow forks the events whether they are local or not.
  3. The corresponding rules service runs the rule block for each type of events.
  4. Due to the **Stop Workflow** configuration, events that satisfy a rule condition will not be passed to other workflow elements.
  5. Only two events reach the end of the workflow.



## Workflow lifecycleâ

A workflow runs as a long-lived loop of reading and submitting events while managing the lifecycle of each workflow service as well. The workflow lifecycle is composed of three main moments as depicted in the following diagram:

  * **onCreate** : While you add elements to the workflow, configure and connect them, Pulse instantiates all services and performs internal actions such as validating the input and output schemas. This stage is executed at workflow design time. While the workflow execution is not started, all services should be ready to receive recovery events.
  * **onStart** : When you publish your Pulse application, the actual runtime begins, launching the workflow and starting to consume events through the input adapter. Additionally, Pulse assumes that all workflow and services configuration is valid. From this stage on, the workflow can only receive normal or replica events. For each service, depending on its type, Pulse executes specific logic to process events:
    * **Input adapter:** Run a single specific processing thread for the input adapter that consumes and submits events continuously while the workflow is running.
    * **Internal services:** Deliver messages to each service as a normal event traverses the workflow. After a service finishes processing the event it will reply indicating what the workflow should do with the event. For example, moving the event forward in the workflow and delivering a new message to the next workflow service, or dropping the event from the workflow and ending it.
  * **onStop** : When the Pulse application stops, the workflow also stops receiving and processing events.



Destroying a workflow

The full lifecycle of a runtime workflow does not work in a cycle. This means that when you stop an application and its runtime processing, Pulse will not reset the state of the workflow to the previous _onCreate_ stage.

In reality, when you stop an application, Pulse tears down the current internal representation of the workflow and creates a completely new one.

The workflow teardown includes the following tasks, in this order:

  1. Stop the partitioning router from receiving messages
  2. Stop the workflow synchronizer from receiving messages
  3. Stop the workflow services and deregister jobs
  4. Destroy workflow services
  5. Close the partitioning router
  6. Close the workflow connectors
  7. Close the workflow synchronizer
  8. Stop the workflow job manager
  9. Close the executors
  10. Close the connection to the event storage
  11. Stop collecting performance metrics about the workflow



## Workflow timeâ

Many workflow elements are tied to the notion of time, for example:

  * Enabling a list item at a given time.
  * Triggering a [Scheduled Metrics Job](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/scheduled-metrics-jobs) at a given time.



The way Pulse workflows deal with time might not be intuitive at first, so itâs crucial to understand the concepts of workflow clock and internal timezone. See [Time, schedules and timezones](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/time-schedules-and-timezones) for more information.

## Message processingâ

### Workflow recoveryâ

The recovery procedures for a workflow consists of replaying events which have already been processed and are present in the [event storage](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/event-storage). This is of the utmost importance since the underlying application may crash or fail for some reason, and upon its restart, all of its state is gone. For instance, you may have rules depending on windows, which will be empty and, thus, may be incorrectly evaluated.

Event Storage

Note that these events are obtained from the [event storage](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/event-storage), so the event storage must be enabled in order for the recovery to work.

Furthermore, in a high availability environment you may have more than one replica of a given application, and if one fails Pulse must restore its state in order to have a consistent event evaluation.

An application may have several workflows, and when starting/restarting the application all the workflows that have the recovery option enabled will be recovered synchronously. This means that Pulse will publish the events to the respective workflows on a timestamp basis so that scheduled jobs will run correctly.

Specific considerations

There are some caveats to the recovery procedures:

  * The event storage option must be enabled, otherwise, there is no event source;
  * If a workflow event storage database table is empty or simply does not exist, that workflow will be ignored;
  * In order for the recovery procedures to publish to the workflow, the workflow must contain an instance of a WorkflowInputService;
  * The Fraud Models are not updated in recovery;
  * The recovered events will not be stored in the event storage again.



Check how you can configure recovery for your workflows in the **Workflow recovery configuration** section of [this topic](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/advanced-workflow-configurations).

#### Checkpoint-based workflow recoveryâ

In a production environment, Pulse can be configured to store the necessary events for real-time metrics calculation on disk. In this case, Pulse creates **checkpoints** , i. e. regular snapshots about the events and the state of the metrics. After a server failure, Pulse can reload the last checkpoint and recover the metrics status starting from there. This saves time when the server needs to be restarted. However, it takes toll on the metrics calculation speed, as Pulse puts metrics calculation on hold while creating a checkpoint. Hence, this setting needs to be carefully tested.

Limitations

Note that this feature is in continuous development, and as of now it does not provide full feature parity to the previous, RAM-based version.

Additionally, if this feature is enabled, do not edit or remove existing metrics. Edited metrics are not recoverable after a server failure, meaning that those metrics will only take new events into consideration after any server restart.

### Workflow synchronizationâ

When in a distributed environment with more than one replica of an application, Pulse uses the underlying messaging platform to synchronize every message that reaches the workflow's [dead letter](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#dead-letter) to the other replicas.

Since it only sends the message in the dead letter, it has already been processed by the necessary workflow services, thus diminishing the work needed to be done in the other replicas, for instance not having to perform any scoring at a scoring service.

This behavior is similar to the workflow recovery procedures.

### Message processing summaryâ

| Normal| Workflow Recovery| Workflow Synchronization  
---|---|---|---  
**Actions**|  Yes| |   
**Dead Letter**|  Yes| Yes| Yes  
**Explanations**|  Yes| |   
**Event Storage**|  Yes| |   
**Profile Update Jobs**|  Yes (only if leader)| | Yes (only if leader)  
**Rule Evaluation**|  Yes| Yes| Yes  
**Scoring**|  Yes| |   
  
## Interaction between workflowsâ

In order to enable [Channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels), you might want to share certain information between workflows. For example, in the workflow processing ATM withdrawals, you might want to consult the number of recent devices used by the same customer in internet banking (assuming ATM and internet banking events are processed in different workflows). This can be achieved with [Omnichannel Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#deployable-omnichannel-plans). See [Plans in workflows - Omnichannel metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#omnichannel-metrics) for more information on how these Plans work in the Workflow.

## Learn moreâ

Title: Building a Model | Feedzai Pulse
============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)
  * Building a Model



On this page

# Building a Model

Was this page helpful?Â 

In this tutorial step, you will train and evaluate two models. They will be trained with the same parameters, and each will use a different training set:

  * The original dataset
  * The features dataset



info

In a real application, you would have to iterate further and try a greater number of models, varying not only the training data but also the model's parameters.

## Training a modelâ

To train a model in Pulse, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, add  a **Model Project** named _Models_.

  2. Add  a new model. On the New Model screen select **Train new model**. Name the model _RawData_ and set the data source and the features as follows*:*

     1. Use _RawTransactions_ as the training **Data Source**.

info

At a later stage, you will be using the enhanced data set, with the features you generated with the Features plan, to train a second model and compare it with this one.

     2. Use _Feedzai - Random Forest_ as Algorithm.

     3. Set _Fraud_ as the **Target Variable**. This is the field you are trying to predict on this project.

     4. Look for the _FraudStatusDate_ field in the **Fields to Select** table and remove it. This field indicates when a transaction has been marked as fraudulent. Like _Fraud,_ it would not be present in an input dataset. If you are predicting if fraud occurred, then you surely don't know when fraud has been detected. So, if you consider this field when training your model, results are completely useless.

You should remove any fields that you have found that don't contribute to a decision. In this case, any fields that don't help discriminate between fraud and not fraud. Also, note that the target variable "Fraud" was automatically removed. It wouldn't make sense to try to predict a field that is served as input to the model.

     5. Keep all other fields in the data source as input to train your model.

     6. Change the **Sampling Type** to _Under Sampling_ with 10%. You should do this since the proportion of interesting transactions, in this case, fraudulent ones, is very reduced. You can check the documentation to learn more about [sampling strategies at model training](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training).

     7. Use the default configurations for the **Provider** and Machine Learning **Algorithm**. Pulse uses the Feedzai Random Forest (FZRF) algorithm by default.

     8. Set the **Validation** to _Split Percentage_ with 80%. This means that only 80% of the dataset will be used for training the model. The remaining 20% are used to then test the performance of the model on unknown transactions and avoid [overfitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overfitting).

     9. Add an **Additional Cost Field** for _TransactionAmount_. This will allow you to measure the performance of the model in terms of cost, in this case, generating metrics such as _money FPR_ and _money Recall_.

     10. Configure your model to calculate **breakdowns** over all possible values for the _CardholderPresentCode_ field.

     11. Finally, **train** your model.

  3. Repeat the previous steps and create a second model with the same parameters as the previous one. Use _TransactionsFeatures_ as the input **Data Source** and name the model _FeaturesData._

Note that Pulse automatically generated a model evaluation for each of the trained models. This happens when you specify a **Validation Method** when you train your model.




## Evaluating and comparing your modelsâ

To evaluate and compare your two models in Pulse, execute the following actions:

  1. Select the _rawdata-trainEvaluation_ model evaluation and examine the information on the page.

     * **ROC and X/Y curves:** Plot the relationship between two metrics on a bidimensional chart. The ROC curve plots the Recall against the False Positive Rate.
     * **Recall:** Represents the percentage of _fraud_ instances that the model correctly identified, meaning that a recall of 50% tells you that if there are 10 fraudulent transactions, then the model identified 5 of them.
     * **False Positive Rate (FPR):** Represents the percentage of cases that are *not fraud *that the model wrongly identified as _fraud_.
     * **Threshold:** Feedzai score that represents fraudulent transactions. Try moving it to see how it affects the Recall, the FPR, and any other metrics. Basically, what you are doing by using the slider is traveling along the [ROC Curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic): the greater FPR you are willing to tolerate, the greater Recall you can achieve.
  2. Assess which of the two models is more suitable given your project's requirements. Set the **Compare With** field to _featuresdata-trainEvaluation_ so you can analyze metrics and performance for both models side by side.

Note that the _featuresdata-trainEvaluation_ is closer to the top-left corner of the chart (the ideal point), which is a strong indication that the Model usually performs better. For the same FPR (ideally low) it has higher Recall (as high as possible, since it identified a greater portion of _fraud_ cases). There are other metrics besides **Recall** and FPR and you can even [define your own metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/custom-evaluation-metrics).

Title: Building Rules | Feedzai Pulse

On this page

# Building Rules

Was this page helpful?Â 

[Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) are one way to contribute towards the score of a given decision, f _raud/not fraud_ in this case, while the other are rules.

Rules add an extra layer of security on top of machine learning models by letting you define conditions that, when met, help you classify your events.

This tutorial stage will help you define and evaluate simple rules. However, rules in Pulse are a very robust and complex feature that allows you to do much more. Don't forget to check the [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) page for further details.

## Defining rulesâ

To create rules in Pulse, execute the following actions:

  1. Create a [list](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) for suspicious merchants as follows:
     1. Name the list as _MerchantsAlert._ Leave all other fields with the default values.

     2. **Save and add items** with the following values: _Royal Fitness_ , _WALGREENS_ and _value_5._

  2. In the **Data Science** tab, under the Rules Projects section, add  a new rules project, and configure it as follows:
     1. Name it _Rules_.

     2. Copy the schema from _TransactionsFeatures._

     3. Set the **Target** to the _Fraud_ field.

     4. Add an **Action** named _MerchantsAlert_.

  3. Add  a new rule named _MerchantsAlert_ to the rules project and define its behavior as follows:
     1. In the **Variables** field, set an _isSuspicious_ variable that reflects if the _MerchantName_ of the transaction is contained in the _MerchantsAlert_ list.

     2. In the **Condition** field, set the rule to trigger if the merchant is suspicious and the _TransactionAmount_ is greater than 50.

     3. In the **Score Contribution** field, set the contribution to the _Fraud_ score as 200.

     4. In the **Actions** field, select the _MerchantsAlert_ action. This means that the rule will trigger this action if the Condition is met.

This rule is not very smart and serves as only as a demonstration of how you can configure a rule. This rule's behaviour defines that whenever a transaction with an amount above 50 was performed at a suspicious merchant, then Pulse should trigger an action and add 200 to the event's score. However, the rule does not mark the transaction as _Fraud_ since it this only a strong indication of fraud and not a certainty.

  4. Add  a new rule to the rules project. This rule is simpler than the first one, but it actually marks transactions as _Fraud_ based on the observation that fraud is more prevalent in transactions with a higher amount. Configure it as follows:
     1. Name it _TransactionAmount._

     2. In the **Condition** field, trigger the rule when the _TransactionAmount_ is greater than 600.

     3. Trigger the **Action** named _Block._

     4. Mark the transaction as _Fraud_.




## Exporting and evaluating rulesâ

Now that you have defined a block of rules, you must create a [snapshot](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/evaluating-rules-using-a-snapshot) so that you can use them in a workflow. While you are configuring the snapshot, you can also evaluate the rules performance over a specific data source as follows:

  1. Publish your application.
  2. In the _Rules_ rules project, add  a new snapshot called _Snapshot_.
     1. Include all your rules in the snapshot.

     2. **Evaluate** it using the _TransactionsFeatures_ data source.

  3. Once the evaluation finishes, open the snapshot and notice that there are 3 kinds of evaluations:
     1. **Block Evaluation** : shows the evaluation regarding the target field (_Fraud_) after all rules are executed.

     2. **Block Rule Evaluation** : similar to block evaluation, but instead of seeing all rules as a black box, you can drill down into the performance of each rule.

     3. **Individual Rule Evaluation** : similar to block rule evaluation, however the rules are not evaluated in sequence, but rather in isolation. This means that the result of a rule does have an impact on the evaluation of the next one.

In this scenario, you won't see any difference between individual rule evaluation and block rule evaluation because the first rule being applied does not mark events as _fraud_ or _not fraud_.

# Designing a Runtime Workflow

Was this page helpful?Â 

Now that all is set up, combine the previously created resources in a [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows). This workflow will be ready to be applied in the Production environment, to process events.

Before starting the following steps, get in touch with your contact person at Feedzai to make sure that you have an Input Adapter set up in the test environment where you are working. In the following steps, we will use an Input Adapter that is named _file-injector_. In addition, make sure that the sample data files mentioned at the beginning of this tutorial are downloaded to the Pulse server.

Then, go ahead and design your workflow as follows:

  1. In the **Workflows** tab, add a new workflow named _Workflow_.

  2. Set the **Origin Schema** to be the same as RawTransactions. In a real application, the schema would likely not contain the field you are trying to predict. In this case, it would have neither _Fraud_ nor _FraudStatusDate_.

  3. Represent the final decision of the workflow by adding an **Outcome** named _isFraud_ with a **Default Value** of _false_.

  4. Add an **Input Adapter** as follows:

     1. Name it _Input Adapter_.
     2. Under **Custom Service** , set it to use the _file-injector_ custom service.
     3. Select **Properties** to confirm that the _filepath_ is properly set. You can use a CSV with the same format as the workflow input schema. If you downloaded the sample data as suggested at the beginning of the tutorial, you can use the input.csv file under the `PULSE_SERVER_HOME/var/datasources/` path.
  5. Add a **Plan** service as follows:

     1. Name it _Features_.

     2. Configure it to run the _Features_ plan with the plan execution you generated when you first ran it.

     3. Connect it to the _Input Adapter_.

  6. Add a **Rules** service as follows:

     1. Name it _Rules_.

     2. Set it to contribute to the _isFraud_ outcome.

     3. Configure it to use the _Rules_ rules project and the _Rules Snapshot_ snapshot that you created of the rules.

     4. Connect it to the _Features_ plan service.

  7. Add a **Scoring** service as follows:

     1. Name it _FZRF Scoring_.
     2. Set it to contribute to the _isFraud_ outcome.
     3. Configure it to use the model project named _Models_ , and the _FeaturesData_ model.
     4. Connect it to the _Rules_.
  8. Finally, add a **Custom Workflow Element** to the end of the workflow that uses the _sink-logger_ custom service.

Connect it to the _FZRF Scoring_ service.

# Loading Data

Was this page helpful?Â 

The first step in your data science project is to load data into Pulse and begin your [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop).

Before starting the steps, ensure that the sample data file is downloaded to the `PULSE_SERVER_HOME/var/datasources/` path on the Pulse server where you are working. To get help with this, get in touch with your contact person at Feedzai.

To load a dataset into Pulse, execute the following actions:

  1. In a browser, navigate to your data science environment. Log in by using the credentials provided, which by default are **pulse** /**pulse**.

  2. Create a new application named _Fraud Training_.

  3. In the **Data Science** tab, add  a new [data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) named _RawTransactions_.

The URL depends on the operating system of your Pulse server and the path to the Pulse server home. For example: `file:///PULSE_SERVER_HOME/var/datasources/transactions.csv`.

  4. Examine the dataset by scrolling through the different columns and understanding what the dataset contains.

     1. Note that there are different ways this dataset represents missing values, such as using `-` in _AVSAddressNumber_ or `\N` in _AuthSequenceNumber._

     2. Add both `-` and `\N` to the **Missing Values** list.

     3. Proceed to the **Next** step.

  5. After Pulse has inferred the data type for each field, in the **Data Source Characterization** step, check if all the fields have suitable [data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) and correct those that don't.

     1. Change the type of some of the amount fields from _Categorical_ to _Numeric_ , such as _AdditionalAmount1_ and several others, whenever you think it may make sense.

Be careful not to change the data type of true categoricals such as _CashAdvanceAmount_ (does not contain numbers) or _AVSZipCode_ (even though it has numbers, it can be argued there is not an order in zip codes).

     2. Change the type of _ID_ fields (such as _AccountID_ or _RouterID_) to have a _String_ type rather than _Numeric_ or _Categorical_ , since it was not correctly inferred.

     3. Change the type of _RecurringBillingKey_ and _InternetAuthorizationIndicator_ to _Date Time_. Set the format of these fields to _Date Time,_ with _dd/MM/yyyy_ format.

     4. Use the  button to change the data type configuration of the _AdditionalAmount1_ field that you set up earlier. It is currently an _Integer_ field. Set it to be _Float_. This makes sense because _AdditionalAmount1_ has decimal places and you don't want to lose information.

  6. Scroll down to the bottom of the page and create your improved data source.

  7. Select your data source from the **Data Sources** list.

  8. Use the  button to analyze the data source. Select Fraud as a breakdown field. This way you can analyze correlations between fields of the data set, in particular, the _Fraud_ field, which is the domain goal in the scope of this application.

     1. Use the **View Statistics** option to better understand fields in your dataset, including arithmetic statistics of the field and its value distribution. It is also possible to click over the histogram to access the statistics view.

     2. View the statistics of the _TransactionAmount_ field by using the  button. Break the analysis down by _Fraud_ to observe that the mean value of _TransactionAmount_ is greater for fraudulent transactions.

# Processing Data

Was this page helpful?Â 

Now that you have loaded your data into Pulse, the next step is to transform your data and extract value from it. At this stage you will learn how to design [plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) so that you can design derived features or extract subsets of your original data set, before training a model.

## Designing derived featuresâ

It is often useful to enrich your dataset with derived features that can be useful to distinguish between the classes you wish your model to predict (in this case, _fraud_ and _not fraud_). Design a plan that calculates a feature as follows:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, add  a new plan named _Features_.
  2. Set the plan as **Deployable**. Generating derived features is useful both in data science and in production [workflows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows). Enabling this option allows you to take this work directly into the runtime environment without any extra effort.
  3. In the the **Schema** field, set the schema to be copied from the _RawTransactions_ data source (confirm the orange warning sign below) and **Save** it.
  4. Use a **Map** operator to calculate derived features. You can design a feature that represents the distance between the merchant and the customer's home location (since a greater distance has a higher correlation with fraud). Create a **Map** named _AddDistance_ to add a new _distance_ field to your data and configure it as follows:



## Designing historical profilesâ

Another kind of features that is also often useful are the ones based on [historical behaviour](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics). To calculate historical profiles (i.e. metrics), such as the daily count and sum of transactions, execute the following actions:

  1. In the _Features_ plan, use the  button to select other options, and select the **Plan Settings** option.

Under **Timestamp Field** , select the field called _Timestamp_. This is required so that Pulse knows which field from the dataset represents when events occurred so that it can build time-based features.

  2. Add a **Metrics** operator and connect it after the _AddDistance_ operator.

  3. Edit  the metrics operator to name it _Metrics_ and check the **Output Incomplete Instances** option.

Initial events will not have accurate metrics. For example, a metric with a window of 24 hours will only be correct after the first 24 hours of the data. Hence these events are called incomplete instances. By default, Pulse discards the initial events with incomplete metrics, to improve model training and evaluation. Select the **Output Incomplete Instances** option if you want to include them anyways.

  4. Add  a new metric, and define it as follows:

     1. In the **Group By** section, select the _AccountID_ field. This means that the metric will be calculated for each account.
     2. In the Window section, leave the default _1 hour_. This means that you want to calculate a metric based on the events of the last hour.
     3. In the **Aggregation** section, select the function _Count_. This means that the metric calculates the number of events in the respective window (last hour).
     4. Use the **Save** button to add the metric to the operator.
  5. Add  another metric following the same steps, but this time the window is _1 day_. This metric calculates the number of events in the last day.

  6. Add  a new metric, and define it as follows:

     1. In the **Group By** section, select the _AccountID_ field.
     2. In the **Window** section, leave the default _1 hour._
     3. In the **Aggregation** section, select the function _Sum_ , and the field _TransactionAmount_. This means that the metric calculates the total amount of the events in the respective window (last hour).
     4. Use the **Save** button to save the metrics.
  7. Add  another metric following the same steps, but this time the window is _1 day_. This metric calculates the total amount of the events in the last day.

  8. Use the  button next to the metrics' names to change them to _HourlyTrCount_ , _DailyTrCount_ , _HourlyTrSum_ , and _DailyTrSum_ , respectively.

  9. Use the **Save** button to save the metrics operator. Your feature plan will look like the following image:

  10. Use the  button to run the plan and create a new and enhanced data source including your features. Configure the execution as follows:

     1. In the **Data Source** section, select _RawTransactions_ as the input data source.

     2. In the **Data Sinks** tab, name the data sink as TransactionsFeatures, and leave the file type as the default (Parquet). In the **Directory Path** field, specify the output file URL. Set the path to the Pulse server home directory, ending with `/var/datasources/<filename>`.

Example: `file:///PULSE_SERVER_HOME/var/datasources/transactions-features.parquet`

The file path may vary according to the operating system of the Pulse server. You can not have a file with the same name in the datasources folder.

     3. Use the **Run** button to execute the plan.

  11. **Save** the plan and then press the **refresh** button on browser.

You can see in the **Data Science** tab that you now have a new data source. You can analyze it as you have done before with _RawTransactions_ , and assess the usefulness of the features you have designed.




## Sampling your dataâ

It is often useful, in the context of Data Science, to reduce the size of the dataset while generally maintaining the distributions of the random variables representing each feature. This is done via [stratified sampling](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/creating-a-stratified-sample).

Sampling improves the performance of your Data Science Loop since you will be able to iterate much faster on feature calculation and model training.

Create a stratified sample to reduce the number of _Accounts_ where there was no _Fraud_ to be 10% of its original size, as follows:

  1. Add  a new plan named _Stratify_.

Make sure that the **Deployable** checkbox is **not** selected. This means that this plan will be non-deployable. Non-deployable plans are useful for sampling data, which typically happens only in the data science environment, hence the plan won't need to be deployed to production.

  2. Add a new **Source** operator named _Transactions_ that copies the _RawTransactions_ schema.

  3. Calculate the number of _Fraud_ transactions per _Account_. First, add a **Map** operator, and connect it to the source**,** with the following configuration:

  4. Sum up the number of _Fraud Transactions_ by adding a **Group By** operator like the one below. This way, you will have the total of _Fraud_ transactions per account stored in a field named _nrFrauds_.

  5. Split the data set into two: accounts where there was fraud and accounts where there wasn't. Add a **Filter** operator as follows:

  6. Repeat the previous step, but this time with a _Fraudulent_ filter (use _nrFrauds > 0_ as the expression).

  7. Apply a **Sample** operator to the _Legitimate_ transactions to get only 10% of them.

  8. Join both sets from _Fraudulent_ and the reduced _Legitimate_ with a **Union** operator.

  9. Use a **Join** operator to join the result with the original _Transactions_ , so that you end up with the original data set minus 90% of the _Transactions_ belonging to an _Account_ where there was no Fraud.

  10. Finally, add a **Sink** operator.




You can run this plan as you have done with the _Features_ plan to generate a new data source (do not forget to select the RawTransactions as your base data source). You can then verify, by evaluating it and performing an exploratory data analysis, if this sample really is representative of the original data set. For most data sets, this is true. You will not be using this sample (or any other) during this tutorial since the original data set is fairly small already. This allows you to operate on it without resorting to sampling.

However, it is encouraged that you to use this technique on real projects with substantial data sets.

# AutoML Best Practices

Was this page helpful?Â 

Throughout the pages of this chapter, you will find some good practices for each stage of the AutoML process:

  1. Feature engineering
     1. Data source split
  2. Feature selection
  3. Training and evaluation
     1. Hyper-parameter tuning
     2. Model selection



As a general rule, a full AutoML usage (going through all three stages in one go) is preferable when you want to build your first model. In this case, AutoML serves as a kickstart to your data science loop.

When looking at AutoML as a whole, always try to run it first with a very aggressive sample of your data. The model results wonât be useful for any deployment, but you will be able to âbenchmarkâ how much time the tasks take. More importantly, you will be able to understand if your job profiles are configured correctly for this task: if using a random sample of 1% of your data only works with 1 GB of memory per executor to run, then the full data is expected to take at most 100 GB to run safely.

From the user perspective, most of the effort should be put into creating a good semantic file. Analyze your data, understand data skewness and relationships between variables. With that in mind you can avoid downstream issues in AutoML.

Title: Metrics Best Practices | Feedzai Pulse
============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)

On this page

# Metrics Best Practices

Was this page helpful?Â 

[Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#metrics) can be seen as the "basic unit" of Data Science work. Use cases like fraud prevention and anti-money laundering revolve around the concept of **change in behavior**. This is where metrics shine, by providing a straightforward way of aggregating data points through time efficiently. Metrics are also commonly referred to as **profiles** or **historical profiles**.

This chapter will cover topics such as the differences between Data Science Platform and Runtime, and a few optimizations that are helpful to bear in mind. In addition to the general best practices section below, the chapter includes subpages covering different aspects of best practices for working with metrics.

When thinking of a typology for [features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#feature), we can conceive the following categories:

  * **Atomic** : features that rely only on information present in their respective instance. Example: "Keyboard distance of the email address".
  * **Composite** : Features that combine two or more previously computed values. Example: "Ratio between transaction amount and account balance".
  * **Lookup** : Features that depend on a lookup table. This table can have the following behaviors:
    * **[Near-]static** : Never or rarely updated. Example: mapping country codes to coordinates, MCC to MCG.
    * **Dynamic** : Updated in batches at regular but sporadic intervals. Example: risky MCC, risky countries, etc.
  * **Metrics** : Temporal aggregations. These features require the definition of a time window, an aggregation field, and how the metric should update. Metrics can optionally include filters. Example: average money transferred by this customer in the last 24 hours.



Generally, you should only create features through the metrics operator if they fall into the "Metrics" category explained above.

info

Metrics are the most complex computations that the system will do both offline and in runtime. Expressions in metrics are written in Pulse Query Language (PQL). For details on semantics, symbols, and operators see the [official documentation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features).

As a rule of thumb, when defining the **Window update period** , it is recommended that short windows (1 day or less) be set to **real time** , i.e. events enter the window as they arrive; whereas longer windows (1 week, 1 month, ...) should be **scheduled** , i.e. events enter the window in batches. This aspect of how a window is updated is one of the major constraints when designing metrics. It will be explained more in depth in the [Constraints](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics/constraints) page.

## General Good Practicesâ

The following are some general good practices to consider when designing your metrics.

### Dosâ

  * Metrics in the same Metrics operator cannot depend on each other.
  * Best: 1 big metrics box with all the metrics in it (SMJs or not).
  * Second best: 1 box with SMJs and another with real-time metrics.
  * Make sure to **enable _Output incomplete instances_** in the metrics operators when running jobs in the Data Science Platform. Otherwise, the plan output will be missing data corresponding to the largest profile window (for example, if the dataset goes from Jan to Dec and the largest window is 3 months, the output dataset will start in April). This is especially important when there are metrics with very large windows (which could result in an empty output dataset) or multiple metrics operators (the effect will compound, and overall the sum of the largest window of each operator will be cut from the output).



### Don'tsâ

  * Avoid dependencies between metrics.
  * Avoid cascading [Scheduled Metrics Jobs (SMJs)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics/scheduled-metrics-jobs).
  * **Avoid redundant metrics**. While you may be tempted to compute the count of transactions for each customer over lots of different time windows (5 minutes, 15 minutes, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 3 hours, ...), it might cause a degradation in runtime performance (latency and memory) and sometimes even in DS metrics. It's a good idea to check for overly correlated features at least once during the modeling process, either directly by computing the pairwise correlations between features, or indirectly by trying different combinations of features and comparing the results of Feature Importance. For very large data sets you can compute the cross correlations in a sample of your data. Another source of excessive correlation is profiles with correlated group by fields: for example, card number and customer ID likely overlap a lot, while card number and merchant ID less so.



## Advanced techniquesâ

  * **Salting grouping entities with lots of missing values**. Suppose you want to compute profiles grouped by the field `ip_address`. However, in your dataset about half of the transactions don't have an IP address. You start by adding a filter to the metric window, something like `ip_address != null`; however this is not enough: when computing the profile, all the transactions will still be loaded and distributed to the executors before the filter is applied. Thus, there will be a very large partition with all the missing IPs, which will likely crash the Spark job. One way to circumvent that is to substitute that missing value by something else, such as the transaction ID. For that, create a new field `ip_address_salted` in a map operator before the metrics operator. Assign it a value similar to `ip_address ?? transaction_id`. Then, update the metric window filter to `ip_address_salted != transaction_id`. This will still yield the same end result, but without generating a massive partition in the Spark job.
  * It's seldom necessary to use cascading metrics (a metric that depends on a different metric from a previous metrics operator). However, if it is a deal-breaker for the project (such as in compliance cases) it is important to notify the team responsible for runtime deployments, as there is an important property that needs to be set to ensure correct computation of cascading metrics.



Advanced notes

Metrics in plans within the Data Science Platform will run the Feedzai stream processing engine on top of Apache Spark. This combination of technologies allows the processing of metrics in Data Science to be horizontally scalable, while maintaining the same feature definition that goes into runtime.

Despite Spark helping on the parallelization of metrics computation, you should bear in mind "the 4 Ss": **Spill** , **Skew** , **Shuffle** , **Small Files** â which are the most common sources of issues when running Spark. These topics will be covered throughout this documentation, when pertinent.

# Creating Features and Models Automatically

You can use [AutoML](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/automl) to create features and train models in an automated way. In addition, AutoML evaluates the models and recommends the most performant one. This saves you time to focus on more complex tasks.

The following sections explain how to create an AutoML run to reach those goals.

## How to create an AutoML runâ

To create an AutoML run that finds features and train models, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, expand the AutoML section if it is collapsed, using the  button on the top of the page.

  2. Select the  â or the  button to start a new AutoML run.

  3. Configure the training properties for your new models:

     1. Select the **Data Source** you will use to create features and train models.

     2. Upload the **Semantic File** , which contains the AutoML tags for the data fields. The tags link the fields to their meaning. To create the semantic file for your data source, you can download a template by using the **Download template file** option in the Semantic File field. Then simply add the tags to the fields. Learn more about [how to create a semantic file for a data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/automl/semantic-file#creating-the-semantic-file).

     3. Select the **Timestamp Field** from the list of available fields. Pulse uses the timestamp field to aggregate the data by time windows for the calculation of metrics.

     4. Select a categorical data field for the **Target Variable**. This is the variable that the models will predict.

     5. Select the Target Value, which is the value of the Target Variable that you want to detect.

For example, in the fraud detection scenario the Target Variable would be the _Fraud_ field, and the possible Target Values would be _True_ and _False_. Given that you want to detect fraud, select _True_ for the Target Value.

     6. Enable an **Additional Cost Field** to be available for the model evaluations. Select a field that represents the transaction amount, to have metrics such as the _Money Recall_ and _Money FPR_.

     7. Optionally, you can filter which events are taken into consideration when AutoML processes them to train the model.

        1. If you define a **profile filter** , AutoML will create metrics that consider events filtered by the defined expression. Example: you might want to filter for only transaction submissions and payment updates â `event_type = "transaction_submission" OR event_type = "transaction_payment_status_update"`

        2. If you define a **scorable filter** , AutoML will train the models based on events that satisfy the expression of this filter. Example: you might want to filter for only transaction submissions â `event_type = "transaction_submission"`

  4. Split the data source into smaller data sets for training, validation and evaluation. To do so, define the following:

     1. **Time range for training -** The training data set will be used for training models during the hyperparameter tuning phase of the AutoML run.

     2. **Time range for validation** \- The validation data set will be used for evaluating the models during the hyperparameter tuning phase, to find the best model.

     3. Use the **Enable test dataset** switch to define the time range for the dataset that will be used for the final evaluation of the best model found. If you don't define a test data set, Pulse will use the validation data set for this purpose.

In the time ranges the beginning timestamp is inclusive, while the ending timestamp is exclusive.

Planning the training, validation and test data sets

To avoid under- or overfitting, ensure that the selected time ranges don't result in empty data sets, or in data sets with too few data. A typical split ratio is 50% for training, 30% for validation and 20% for evaluation, as long as the data source size is sufficient for that.

  5. Select the **Metric to optimize** , and a fixed metric value that you want to achieve. For example, you want to optimize _Recall_ , while ensuring that the _FPR_ stays around 1%.

  6. You can configure **Advanced options** as follows:

     1. Set the **Number of Models** you want to train in this AutoML run. Note that this value heavily influences the run time of the AutoML job. We recommend that you test the run time with a few models first.

     2. Select the **Path to generated data source** , if you want to save the data in a specific path.

     3. Select the **Window sizes** for the [metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric). If the window size of a metric is 1 hour, it means that the metric calculated for a certain point in time is based on the data of the last hour before that given time. Each defined window size will generate another metric.

        * Metrics with **Real-time Updates** will be updated at every event.

        * Metrics with **Scheduled Updates** will be updated at the start of each day.




After setting up the AutoML process, you can follow up on its status on the top of the **Data Science** tab. When the AutoML job is finished, you can view the results in the same place:

  * The **Best Model** trained in the last AutoML run.
  * The **Features Plan** that created a data source with features based on Feedzai's experience in fraud detection.
  * **Details** about the job that executed the last AutoML run. In case of a failed AutoML run, you can start investigating here.



## Next stepsâ

  * Dive into the created model project, and use the [Exploration Mode view](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters/exploring-hyperparameter-tuning-results) to understand the best model.
  * Open the job details and go through the textual reporting that has details on the trained models.

# Interacting with Pulse via JupyterLab

JupyterLab is one of the most widespread tools used by data scientists to work with data. Pulse provides integration with JupyterLab, in the form of a service and an API that allows JupyerLab users to interact with Pulse data.

This topic contains information about how you can interact with Pulse using JupyterLab.

# Prerequisites

The following are the prerequisites to interact with Pulse using JupyterLab:

  * The JupyterLab Service of the Pulse server has to be enabled.
  * The client computer has to be set up  for the interaction.



# Using JupyterLab to interact with Pulse

When in Pulse, select the  button in the [toolbar](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/navigating-pulse) at the top of the page to use JupyterLab with Pulse. It opens a new tab in your browser with Jupyterlab, and shows a set of notebooks that demonstrate how to interact with Pulse.

The commands shown in the notebooks use the DS-API, an API provided by Pulse that allows you to explore the data and train models via JupyterLab, among other actions.

The possible actions are documented in the JupyterLab notebooks that are included with the JupyterLab integration on the client computer.

## JupyerLab notebooksâ

The following list gives you an overview of the notebooks that are available with the JupyterLab integration:

  * **Getting Started** notebook  
First steps of using the DS-API: loading data from/to Pulse and converting data to a format that you can use in JupyterLab.
  * **Datasources** , **Plans** , and **Models** notebooks  
How to interact with Pulse's data sources, plans and models using the DS-API.
  * **Data Loading** notebook  
How to use the DS-API to programmatically load data into Pulse.
  * **Data Exploration** notebook  
How to perform efficient data exploration, for instance, during the pre-modelling stage of a data science project. It shows how to compute descriptive statistics, perform semantic validation of features, and generate a report of the dataset. It also introduces the interaction with the exploration API to get more details of each feature, including distributions and plots.
  * **Data Sampling** notebook  
How to make use of Feedzai's sampling library to apply appropriate sampling strategies on large datasets.
  * **Join Data Labels Plan** notebook  
How to create and run a data science plan that joins two data sources.
  * **Bias Audit** notebook  
This notebook allows you to run a bias audit on your ML model for a given dataset.
  * **Rule Recommendation** notebook  
This notebook suggests which rules can be removed or reprioritized without affecting the system performance negatively, or sometimes even improving it. It's useful for reducing complexity in large rule sets.
  * **Indexers** notebook  
This notebook describes how to train and fit an indexer for a string field, how to customize indexer clipping, and how to fit multiple indexers in bulk.
  * **Feature Investigation** notebook This notebook allows you to uncover changes in data distribution in your feature space. This can be useful to understand and debug unexpected losses of performance in your models and rule systems.

# Processing your data

[Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) are Pulse's way of helping you become much more efficient with some of the most time consuming and technically demanding Data Science tasks.

**Plans** are a vital concept in Pulse, and one that makes it a very powerful Data Science tool. They represent a way to boost the performance of:

  * **Data scientists**  
Delivering a set of tools that make it easier to process data for the training of Machine Learning models. Data Scientists can now focus on real data science instead of solving engineering and tooling problems.
  * **Engineers**  
Abstracting a lot of the usual complexity involved in deploying Data Science work into Production. With a fully integrated modeling and run-time environment, Pulse enables a seamless deployment, without any major effort.



You can design **Plans** to assist you in the following activities:

  * Data cleaning, transformation, formatting, joining
  * Schema validation
  * Feature engineering



Typically, a data science project will have several plans that are executed in sequence and generate new data sources each as the output. These intermediate data sources are subsequently used as input for other plans.

## Create/Edit plan pageâ

The **Create/Edit plan page** lets you design a plan to transform your data from data sources. It enables you to visually compose a flow that takes your data input and outputs a new and transformed data source.

The following image displays the **Create/Edit plan page** :

The **Create/Edit plan page** contains the following areas:

  1. **Title and status**  
Name and type of the plan. Indicates whether the plan is [Deployable or Non-Deployable](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans).
  2. **Actions**  
Available operations over the plan. Use the  option to transform your data using the plan, and generate a new data source.
  3. **Operators**  
Available elements to compose the data flow of your plan. If the plan is deployable, you cannot use some of the operators. Check the [Operators Reference](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) for detailed information on all available elements.
  4. **Plan**  
Area where you design the data flow of your plan. Drag operators and drop them into the canvas to create the different stages in your plan. Drag the handles from an operator to another operator to connect and define the data path between them. Use the **Edit Operator** option to configure the behavior of each stage of your plan.

# Tuning Job executions with Job Profiles

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse enables you to optimize configurations that are used when handling large amounts of data.

Data scientists can use this functionality to tweak the properties used in various tasks within the [Data Science Loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) that are performed in a cluster-computing framework. For example, most of the Data Science tasks including running [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans), [Model Evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation), [Rules Evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules/rules-snapshots#evaluation-methods), are executed by Spark jobs.

Each type of Job may require different configuration settings to be performed efficiently. For example, depending on the size of your dataset you might have to adjust the Spark memory allocated to train a Model Evaluation.

Pulse allows you to configure Job Profiles with different sets of Spark properties. You can then select the Job Profile that best fulfils the needs of the target task that you want to execute.

## Memory considerationsâ

When running Spark jobs, it's recommended to have a default profile for all jobs, and define Job Profiles for executing resource-intensive jobs.

Calculation tasks may fail if they have insufficient memory available. This might happen because each Spark node has fixed resources available, for instance a fixed number of cores and a fixed amount of memory. Some nodes may have larger resources than others, but by default it's not sure that the tasks that need large resources get assigned to those nodes. Typical examples of tasks needing larger memory are Model Trainings, Hyperparameter Tunings and Plan Executions.

If smaller jobs occupy the resources that have larger capacity, Pulse doesn't leverage the full potential of the Spark cluster. To ensure that the necessary resources are available for jobs that need them, you can use Spark properties to influence the number of cores and the amount of memory used by a job. Job Profiles can regulate what kind of resources should be assigned to a job which is running with a specific Job Profile. For instance, you can have a default profile for all jobs, but define a Job Profile for executing Plans, and another one for Hyperparameter Tunings to make sure that these get the proper resources they require.

If these Job Profiles are created, you can use them when creating a job execution of a related Data Science resource.

Restrictive default settings

The default Spark settings are restrictive. For example, they allow 1GB of memory per node. It is recommended to create a Spark configuration strategy early on in a project, and keep adjusting the settings as you monitor the Job Executions.

## Learn Moreâ

Check the following pages to learn more about [Job Profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/jobs-and-job-profiles) in Pulse:

  * [Creating a Job Profile](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/creating-a-job-profile)
  * [Selecting profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles)
  * [Editing properties on demand](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/editing-properties-on-demand)
