# Using the Data Science Framework (DSF)

Was this page helpful?Â 

The Data Science Framework (DSF) is a dedicated environment used in risk assessment strategies for building, testing, and evaluating rules and models according to the Data Science Loop.

It allows for initiating Data Science (DS) jobs, either via Pulse or JupyterLab, that are then processed through the Pulse application. Before diving into the importance and impact of tuning jobs, learn more about the DSF and DS jobs [here](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/the-data-science-framework).

## Why tune DS jobs?â

Tuning DS jobs is the process of optimizing Spark configurations used by the cluster to handle specific workloads efficiently. This helps prevent:

  * Executions from hanging due to the lack of requested resources.
  * Executions crashing due to cheap job configurations.
  * Resource starvation caused by greedy job configurations.



tip

Choosing the appropriate configuration is **trade-off between whatâs available and whatâs needed**.

Note that there isnât a "one-size-fits-all" configuration. Heavier jobs will take advantage of more generous configurations, while lighter jobs will perform well with more sensible ones.

Additionally, clusters are shared by all team members, so guaranteeing that everyone is mindful of their job configurations is key to avoid concurrency issues and leverage the resources appropriately.

Jobs can be tuned either within Pulse (using Job Profiles) or in JupyterLab (by providing the Spark configuration when opening a session).

### Impact of tuning in the DS job life cycleâ

To better understand how job configurations affect the life cycle of a DS job, it is important to consider the scaling capacity and how resources are allocated and shared.

#### Scaling capacityâ

Scaling refers to the cluster's capacity to add and remove task nodes from the pool of resources at any time depending on workload. It occurs automatically based on demand given by the number of executors that are waiting to be allocated.

The scale-up strategy follows a tiered approach: the higher the demand (i.e. jobs pending/waiting for allocation), the more capacity is allocated. These tiers can be classified based on how fast more capacity is added (e.g., light, moderate, high, very high).

Capacity limits

There is an upper bound to the maximum capacity attributed to you based on your contract with Feedzai.

#### Resource allocation and sharingâ

Choosing adequate capacity for a job is important to allow for optimal execution times and sharing that capacity with other people in the team. To better understand how resources are allocated and shared within the cluster, it's important to know how jobs allocate capacity and what it means to have running Spark sessions.

##### How do jobs allocate capacity?â

When you submit a Pulse job or open a Spark session, the EMR (Elastic MapReduce) cluster registers the request and allocates resources dynamically depending on the workload. This means that if you request a job with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 8 executors, the job begins executing as soon as the cluster is able to allocate 1 executor. If during the job execution more cluster resources become available (e.g., because other jobs have finished or the cluster has scaled up), the cluster allocates additional executors, up to a maximum of 8.

info

Note that executors are main processing units for jobs and are indivisible. This means that while executors for the same job can potentially âliveâ in a different cluster node, each executor alone must fit entirely in a given cluster node.

Refer to the [What are executors?](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/the-data-science-framework/#what-are-executors) section for more details on these processing units.

On the other hand, if dynamic allocation is disabled, the job only begins executing when the cluster is able to allocate all the executors requested in the job configurations. For example, if you request a job with 8 executors (each with 12GB and 4 cores), the job will start once the cluster is able to fit those 8 executors within the pool of cluster resources available at that moment.

Refer to Applying configurations in JupyterLab and Applying configurations in Pulse for details on how to configure jobs/sessions, respectively.

warning

Disabling dynamic allocation is only recommended when debugging issues with the cluster.

Depending on the number of executors being requested by all the jobs registered in the cluster at a given moment (including jobs waiting for resources to begin execution, and dynamic allocation jobs already executing and requesting more executors), the cluster can scale up and add more nodes to its pool of resources.

In contrast, if the cluster resources are idle for a certain amount of time (e.g., because there are few jobs running) it can scale down and remove cluster nodes from the pool of resources.

What does this mean?

Both the cluster resource usage (i.e. all jobs from all users using the cluster at the same time) and the cluster total pool of resources (i.e. if the cluster is scaled up or scaled down) have an impact on the duration of your job. Therefore, _the exact same job might take a different amount of time to complete on separate occasions_.

When you submit your job, you can check its status (i.e. if it's running or waiting for resources) in the **YARN Web UI**. There, you can also find the total and available pool of cluster resources. These metrics can help you understand why your job hasnât started yet (e.g., if there isn't enough memory or cores to satisfy your job configurations).

You can also use the **YARN Web UI** to check the resource usage of your running jobs to make sure they aren't exhausting most of the cluster resources and adhere to fair cluster usage.

##### What does it mean to have running Spark sessions?â

Spark sessions are created in JupyterLab and represent the connection between your notebook and the cluster. Refer to the [Interacting with Pulse via JupyterLab](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/interacting-with-pulse-via-jupyterlab) page for additional information, including a list of available notebooks.

Note that once created, Spark sessions remain active until you either:

  * Close them using `spark_session.stop()`.  
OR  

  * Kill the notebook kernel.



warning

Be mindful of your active Spark sessions, and make sure you manually stop them if they're no longer needed. _Hanging (idle) sessions can occupy cluster resources and impact the other cluster users' experience_.

In some cases, Spark sessions that are idle for a long period are automatically closed, but this depends on the cluster's configuration.

### Common scenariosâ

Here are some scenarios where tuning Spark configurations is most commonly needed and what changes they require:

info

The following table provides guidance in terms of how different parameters could be configured, but choosing the appropriate configuration is **trade-off between whatâs available and whatâs needed**. Be mindful of job configurations to avoid concurrency issues and leverage the resources appropriately.

There isnât a "one-size-fits-all" configuration. Heavier jobs will take advantage of more generous configurations, while lighter jobs can be executed in an acceptable timeframe with less demanding configurations, and without compromising other user's jobs.

Scenario| Considerations  
---|---  
**Dataset analysis and rule evaluations**|  This scenario doesn't require you to limit the number of executors.  
**Model training**|  This is a _single-task/executor_ job, so:

  * The number of cores per executor equals the number of cores per task.
  * The rule-of-thumb for job memory and cores per executor is 1/4 of the task node size for both. This allows for running four models in parallel in just one task node, which complies with the default HPT notebooks (that launch four model training jobs simultaneously).

noteEven though model training jobs are single-task/executor jobs, you must **allocate more than one CPU per task using`spark.task.cpus`**. This is set by default to `1`. However, if you don't override this default, you're essentially running a job with X executors but only `1` will be used (which is a waste of resources). Since model training is a single-task/executor job, **make sure the task gets all the executor cores** by matching the `spark.task.cpus` to the `spark.executors.cores`.  
  
Essentially, this allows you to increase the number of cores per executor in order to leverage model training multi-threading (as long as that property remains aligned with the number of CPUs per task).  
**Plan executions**|  In this scenario:

  * Memory-heavy jobs benefit from parallelization.
  * Both the cores and memory per executor should be maximized.

  
**Data exploration/manipulation**|  In this scenario:

  * The necessary configurations vary depending on the data and type of exploration/manipulation that will be performed.
  * A _mixture of approaches_ is recommended.

  
  
## Applying configurations in JupyterLabâ

When creating Spark sessions via JupyterLab (e.g., when using notebooks), you need to provide the Spark configuration at the beginning:
    
    
    # Spark Session Parameters  
    SPARK_PARAMETERS = {  
        "spark.executor.cores": "7",  
        "spark.executor.memory": "8g",  
        "spark.executor.memoryOverhead": "5g",  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled": True,  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.initialExecutors": "2",  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors": "1",  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors": "6",  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout": "300s",  
    }  
      
    # Get SparkSession with default Pulse's configuration  
    spark = feedzai.get_spark_session(SPARK_PARAMETERS)  
    

The configuration examples below can be used to configure your Spark jobs:

note

Ensure you replace the values for each as needed.

Configuration aspect| Example| Cores per executor| 
    
    
    SPARK_PARAMETERS = {  
        "spark.executor.cores": "7",  
    }  
      
  
---|---  
Memory per executor| 
    
    
    SPARK_PARAMETERS = {  
        "spark.executor.memory": "8g",  
        "spark.executor.memoryOverhead": "5g",  
    }  
      
  
Dynamic allocation| 
    
    
    SPARK_PARAMETERS = {  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled": True,  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.initialExecutors": "2",  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors": "1",  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors": "6",  
        "spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout": "300s",  
    }  
      
  
### Validating Spark session configurationsâ

Once you've completed the configuration and before running a full job, verify jobs are behaving as expected. This helps spot issues early on, before committing to executing real jobs.

To do this, run the following test job:
    
    
    spark.range(100_000_000).count()  
    

Then, via the **YARN Web UI** :

  * Confirm the Spark session is in the list of **Applications**.
  * Monitor the Spark session **State** (running sessions should have `State = RUNNING`, while sessions that are waiting for resources should have `State = ACCEPTED`).



Additionally, check the **Spark History Server** to confirm that your Spark session configurations were correctly set. This can be accessed in the full list of configurations via the **Environment** tab.

## Applying configurations in Pulseâ

For DS jobs triggered in Pulse (e.g., plan executions, model training, rule evaluations, etc.), you can use [Job Profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/jobs-and-job-profiles/#job-profiles) to provide a Spark configuration.

Read all about [Tuning Job executions with Job Profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/) and learn how to:

  * [Create a Job Profile](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/creating-a-job-profile) to apply a set of property configurations when running jobs.
  * [Select the profile](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles) that is more suitable for the Spark job that you want to run.
  * [Edit Spark properties on demand](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/editing-properties-on-demand) to control the configuration of the Spark job that performs the calculations for a specific Data Science resource.



Jobs triggered via the DS-API

You can also trigger Pulse jobs from JupyterLab using the **DS-API**. In these cases, the job spark configurations are managed through a combination of:

  * Parameters sent through the DS-API method calls.
  * Pulse Job Profiles (**not** through `SPARK_PARAMETERS`).



As an example, refer to the [plan execution DS-API method documentation](https://documentation.feedzai.com/ds-studio-ds-api/25.0/reference/plan/#ds_api.plan.Plan.run) (see the `job_profile` and `job_properties` arguments).

# Creating a schema

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

The first stage involved in taking your Data Science project into Production, and designing a runtime [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows), is configuring how Pulse should expect to consume real data from an external source.

A **Schema** defines exactly how the real input data looks like. It defines the types of each field for transactions being processed in a runtime workflow.

## How toâ

To start configuring your data and add a schema to Pulse, execute the following steps:

  1. When you have completed your Data Science tasks and the project is ready to move to Production, in the **Data Science** tab, select a Data Source.

  2. the Data Source to a Schema. Pulse automatically generates a Schema with the same name as the Data Source. For example, Card Transactions.

  3. Navigate to the **Data Configuration** tab and select the newly created Schema.

Changing a Schema exported from a Data Source

You must take into account that adding or reordering fields in a **Schema** is not allowed since it is [immutable](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#schema-immutability).

  4. Examine the Schema fields and types to make sure it matches the incoming data to your fraud detection workflow.

Configuring the Workflow Schema

In alternative, Pulse allows you to automatically generate a Schema from a [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) when you configure the **Origin Schema** field of a [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows).




### Manually creating a schemaâ

In alternative cases when you don't have a dataset available, and thus go straight to deployment, you can manually specify a Schema. To do so, execute the following steps:

  1. In the **Data Configuration** tab, **Add** a new Schema.
  2. For each Field that your Schema should have, you must:
     1. Name the Field.
     2. Select the Field type.
  3. Optionally, select **Advanced options** to set the field as a [Dimension](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#dimension).
  4. if your Schema is still not complete. Repeat step 2.
  5. When you have added all Fields, save your work as a new Schema.



### Configuring Dimension Mappingsâ

**Dimension Mappings** allow you to define how dimension codes can be translated to human-readable descriptions.

After defining dimension mappings, their human-readable descriptions will be available throughout the whole product: dashboards, tooltips, labels, live-drill and so on.

Learn more about how dimension mappings help you [manage Dimensions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#dimension) in real-time applications.

When you create a [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) and export it, Pulse also accelerates your work by automatically generating a dimension mapping for each observed values in categorical fields.

To complete a configuration for a dimension mapping:

  1. In the **Data Configuration** tab, select a **Dimension Mapping** , or **Add** a new one.
  2. Finalize your configuration with any of the following operations.
     1. Adding  a new Item that maps a specific code to a description.
     2. Editing an existing Item to update the code-description mapping.
     3. Deleting an existing Item.



Dimension Mappings applicability

**Dimension Mappings** are only available for fields that have been defined as [Dimensions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#dimension).

## Next Stepsâ

Now Pulse knows how input data is formatted and what your fraud prevention workflow will consume. Proceed by configuring how you must [configure custom elements](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-custom-services) your workflow will use; for example, input adapters to consume data.

# Designing a workflow

Was this page helpful?Â 

Classifying real-time events comprises several stages. For example, fraud detection is a task comprised of several steps with the aim of deciding whether or not an event represents a fraudulent transaction. Thus, Pulse lets you group these processing steps into a workflow.

**Workflows** represent the life cycle of an event through the system. They define how information is passed on between components that may filter and/or transform the event.

A **Workflow** consists of processing steps (elements) and links between them. Each workflow element processes or transforms the data as soon it receives data. Workflow elements can be seen as components that process data with the ability to apply operations such as feature extraction, model scoring, decision/detection rules, etc.

The following image depicts a **Workflow** where input data is processed with a [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) to generate features, scored with a [Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), and evaluated by a block of [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules).

When designing a **Workflow** to process events in real time, the following activities are involved when adding and configuring elements:

  * [Configuring outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes)
  * [Adding input adapters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-input-adapters)
  * [Adding plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-plans)
  * [Adding models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models)
  * [Adding rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules)
  * [Adding custom services](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-custom-services)



## Workflow patternsâ

**Workflows** give you a lot of flexibility on how you can compose elements and define the path that events should follow. Check to following sections on some patterns you can use when designing a workflow.

### Branchingâ

Pulse allows you to configure your workflow path in a way that there are multiple branches that can process each event. A common scenario is to apply different operations based on the transaction's country.

This can be achieved by adding a filter to each of the branching service's links, as depicted in the following image. Note that the expression for the filter can make use of any **Workflow** schema field, and must be a stateless [PQL](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features) expression. Additionally, [UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions) are not supported.

Parallel branching

Pulse does not execute separate workflow branches in parallel. Thus, although branching is possible, a real-time event will always follow a single linear path from input until the workflow terminates.

You must always make sure that when you branch the workflow, all possible paths are mutually exclusive. This means that **an event must only be routed to exactly one of the possible paths**.

The following examples show how to branch a workflow into two paths without leading to unsupported behavior:

  * Link A filters by "amount > 2000" and Link B filters by "amount <= 2000"
  * Link A filters by "location == USA" and Link B filters by "location != USA"



If do not take these precautions there is more than one branch where the filter condition is _true_ , than Pulse will route the event to the first one that evaluates as _true_ , and write an exception to the log.

When joining branches into a single path you must make sure that all incoming paths carry events with the same **Schema** , as shown in the following diagram.

Since Pulse never executes both branches in parallel, once an event arrives at the [Plan Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-plans), it must have the same schema regardless of the original path it took.

Deployable Plans

[Deployable Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) only allow for a single [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) to be configured as input.

Therefore, you must ensure that if you perform data transformations in any of the branches when an event arrives at the join point it still has a data schema that is compatible with the expected input for the **Plan Service**.

#### Branching with Tenantsâ

Multi-Tenancy  allows managing multiple Tenants in the same installation. The resources that support **Multi-Tenancy** are **Rules** and **Lists**. You can, for example, apply the same **Rule** to all the Tenants, or different **Rules** to different Tenants with just a few [configuration steps](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-or-updating-the-rules-project).

However, imagine that you would like to have different **Plans** or different **Models** applied to different Tenants. This is still possible using **Branching with Tenants** as an alternative approach to the native **Multi-Tenancy** solution, as long as the different configured **Plans** and **Models** expect the same input and produce the same output [Schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#data-schemas), so that subsequent Workflow steps, such as **Rules** , can be then applied to these non Multi-Tenanted resources. This configuration can only be performed with special permissions, and thus, is at the level of the Landlord (_i.e._ the Tenants cannot use **Branching with Tenants**).

Branching with Tenants

Note that this alternative approach to the **Multi-Tenancy** solution is viable because normally the same **Plan** and **Model** is used with all the Tenants and only in exceptional cases, a few Models or Plans are segregated by tenant.

However, this is not the case for **Rules.** The normal scenario is to have many Rules applied to all the Tenants or many Rules segregated by Tenant. Thus, **Branching with Tenants** is not a practical solution to be used with **Rules Projects**.

Considering the scenario of two different **Plans** , this can be achieved with **Workflow** configuration by adding a filter to the branches that connect the **Input Adapter** to both **Plans** , as displayed in the following image.

Adapt Schema

Note that the Schema must have a field identifying the Tenant so that it can be used to configure the filter and allow a real-time event to follow the right path.

Considering the scenario of two different **Models** , this can be achieved with **Workflow** configuration by adding a filter to the branches that connect the **Plan** to both **Models** , as displayed in the following image.

Adapt Schema

Note that the Schema has to have a field identifying the Tenant so that it can be used to configure the filter and allow a real-time event to follow the right path.

### Applying different models to the same eventâ

Depending on the scenario you might need to get the contribution of several models before reaching a final decision, or just running events through different models to select the best result.

#### Contributing to an outcomeâ

To take into account the contribution of several models to the same [outcome](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) (for example _fraud_ and _fraud_score_), you must run events through different **Model Services** in sequence.

This pattern is very similar to a regular **Workflow** with a **Scoring Service** followed by a **Rules Service**. The contributions of the several models are simply reconciled using the configured weights for each **Scoring Service**.

The following image displays an example where events are scored by two models in sequence, contributing to the same decision. The final score takes the weights of each model into account.

#### Selecting the best modelâ

In scenarios where you want to run an event through several models and make your final decision based on the best absolute result, your **Workflow** should:

  * Include a **Scoring Service** for each model.
  * Configure separate [Outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) that represent the partial decisions of each model.
  * Include a [Custom Workflow Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#custom-services) that takes the outputs and outcomes of all **Scoring Services** and produces the final decision.



The following image displays a workflow where events are scored by two models in sequence, each one contributing to a different outcome, and a **Custom Service** to perform the final decision.

### Using detection and decision rulesâ

It is common to route transactions through different sets of [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) at different points in the **Workflow**. Typically, you may need to add the following types of **Rules** :

  * **Detection Rules** Used in conjunction with [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists), let you immediately identify events that match an entry in a list. For example, blacklisting and whitelisting.
  * **Decision Rules** Used in conjunction with [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), weigh in on the final [Outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) and scores for an event after it has been transformed and scored by a model.



The following image shows how such a workflow will look like.

## Edit Workflow pageâ

The **Edit Workflow page** provides a design area where you can model your [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) through which your application will process real-time events.

The following image displays the **Edit Workflow page:**

The Edit Workflow page contains the following areas:

  1. **Configurations**  
Depending on the active tab, **Workflow** or **Advanced** , contains the fields that you need to configure for your workflow. The most important fields are:
     * **Origin Schema**  
The [Schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/creating-a-schema) definition of the input data expected by the workflow. Select an existing Data Source to automatically [generate the respective Schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/creating-a-schema).
     * **Outcomes**  
[outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) to add decision and score fields to events, and effectively define to which decisions will workflow **Services** be contributing to. For example, fraud/not-fraud and the fraud score.
     * **Actions**  
The actions that workflow **Services** can generate. For example, a **Rules Service** may generate a **Block** action for transactions identified as fraud.
     * **Action Listeners**  
[Custom Services](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#custom-services) that execute custom logic to handle specific **Actions** whenever a **Workflow** element raises them.
  2. **Services**  
The available elements you can use to compose your workflow. The following elements are available:
     * **Input Adapter**  
Applies a [Custom Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#custom-services) to [consume external data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-input-adapters) and inject it into the workflow.
     * **Plan**  
Deploys [data transformations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-plans), exactly as modeled during the Data Science stage. Typically, to generate features out of raw input data before feeding it to a Machine Learning Model.
     * **Scoring**  
Runs the events through a Machine Learning [Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models), exactly as parameterized and trained during the Data Science stage. Contributes to an outcome and the corresponding score.
     * **Rules**  
Runs the events through a [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules) block, and similarly to the **Scoring Service** , also contributes to an outcome and the corresponding score.
     * **Custom Workflow Service**  
Deploys a [Custom Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#custom-services) to [perform specific operations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-custom-services) on events, that Pulse does not implement out-of-the-box.
  3. **Diagram**  
Canvas to where you must drag the **Services** and visually design your workflow.  
**Edit** services to define their main configurations such as Data Science snapshots, verify their input and output schemas and their mapping with the event schema, and properties.  
**Drag and drop** the handles to connect two services in the workflow. **Double-click** an edge connecting two services to edit a filter condition, for example, only allowing events from a specific country to advance through this edge. This can be used to route these events to a different model for scoring.

# Managing the project life cycle

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

When you finally deploy your project into Production, it marks the end of a cycle in your application. However, projects are not static and, most likely, require periodic maintenance and upgrading.

It is common that you receive recent and better data from your client, for example including human feedback with the final classification for transactions that Pulse original sent for review. Therefore, quickly closing the feedback loop is what allows your project to be up-to-date with how your business evolves, without falling behind due to cumbersome modeling, training, deployment and upgrading procedures.

You must be aware of the actions you need to undertake to upgrade your Pulse application, from Data Science stages to redeploying that work in your [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows), without breaking it or having to start from scratch.

How Pulse projects work

Make sure you fully understand [how Pulse projects work](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/how-pulse-projects-work) when you maintain and update your applications.

## How toâ

### Consuming new data and deploying new Modelsâ

When you need to take new data into account, you must repeat some of the Data Science tasks you have already completed before training your **Model** for the first time. Re-deploying the **Model** is also accomplished via the same procedure.

Consuming new data

The core of this task is to go through a new iteration of your [Data Science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) and retrain your Machine Learning **Model** before you configure it in a **Scoring Service** in your **Workflow**.

Retraining Models

Pulse lets you push your new data through the exact same analysis and transformation pipeline you used when first training the current **Model**.

So if you only need to retrain a **Model** , with the exact same configuration as the current one, you can directly reuse the Data Science **Plans** you used before.

Nevertheless, when analyzing the new data you may come to the conclusion that you need to reengineer your features or configure the **Model** with different parameters.

In this case, although it may be more complex as you need to create new **Plans** and evaluate new **Model** configurations, the process includes no additional/different tasks to the ones you first executed for the current **Model**.

To retrain your Machine Learning [Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) with improved/more recent data and deploy the new **Model** to Production, execute the following actions:

  1. Run your new data through the same Data Science pipeline you have used before. This includes configuring [Data Sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) and transformations with [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans).
     1. [Clean and load your new data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data) to create a new **Data Source** and obtain a high-quality dataset that adheres to your project's schema and requirements.
     2. [Understand and process your new data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data) to [analyze and sample it](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data), and [engineer your features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering) to generate a dataset that you can use to retrain your **Model**.
     3. Optionally, compute extra information and new features for your [features/instances dataset](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/generating-instance-features-dataset).
  2. [Build and evaluate a new Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model).
     1. [Train a new Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model) within your Model Project. In alternative, you can start a new **Model Project**.
     2. [Evaluate the new Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model).
     3. [Compare your new Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models) with the current one to assess your performance with the new data.
     4. [Adjust the Model parameters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters) and repeat the process until your reach your goal.
  3. Deploy the new **Model** in your **Workflow** . [Edit an existing or configure a new Scoring Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models) . Specify the new **Model** , and if applicable, specify a new **Model Project** .



### Deploying new Rules��â

Adding new **Rules** or editing existing ones and taking them to Production is accomplished by going through some of the same tasks you have already completed when building and deploying your **Rules** for the first time.

Rules Snapshot

The core of this task is to create a new **Rules Snapshot** and configure it in a **Rules Service** in your **Workflow**.

To add a new [Rule](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) to your project, or adjust an existing one, and redeploy it to Production, execute the following actions:

  1. [Build and evaluate your new Rule](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/getting-started/building-and-evaluating-a-rule).
     1. [Define/Edit a Rule.](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules) In alternative, you can start a new **Rules Project**.
     2. Create a new **Rule Snapshot** that includes the new **Rule** and new configurations you may have added, such as **Templates** and **Environment** code.
     3. Optionally, [evaluate the Rule](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/getting-started/building-and-evaluating-a-rule).
     4. Repeat the procedure if you need to further adjust and re-evaluate the **Rule** within the rule block.
  2. Deploy the new **Rule** in your **Workflow**.
     1. In your [runtime Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow), [configure a new Outcome](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) if the new **Rule** contributes to a different decision than the ones already configured.
     2. [Edit an existing or configure a new Rules Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules). Specify the new **Rule Snapshot** that includes your new **Rule** , and if applicable, specify a new **Rules Project**.



## Next Stepsâ

Your deployment is now complete. However, when you need to perform maintenance and update tasks to your Pulse applications revisit the relevant sections of this [User Guide](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide).

Title: Best Practices for Plans | Feedzai Pulse
============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)
  * [Feature Engineering](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/)

On this page

# Best Practices for Plans

Was this page helpful?Â 

Within a map or metric operator, you cannot refer to a field that has been added inside that same operator. In case of such dependencies, you have to use more than one operator to calculate the final field. Also, performance considerations need to be taken into consideration when organizing your maps and metrics into plans.

The following sections describe best practices regarding maps, metrics and plans.

## A simple planâ

Due to performance reasons, it is recommended to organize map and metrics operators in a single plan, containing all feature engineering logic.

In a simplified example, the plan could have the following operators:

  1. A map operator to calculate simple features.
  2. A metrics operator to calculate time-based aggregations.
  3. Typically another map operator to calculate features based on the metrics.



## Large number of metricsâ

It can happen that the plan has to calculate hundreds of metrics.

Due to limitations of Java, when a metrics operator contains around 200 metrics, the plan might crash. This number depends on the length of the metrics' PQL code. The solution for this is to separate the metrics into two or more operators.

When separating the metrics into two or more different metrics operators, it's a good practice to keep metrics in the same operator if they have the same field in the first place in the _Group By_ field. For example, if you have some metrics that group events by _Card_ , and some other metrics that group events by _Card_ and _ShippingAddress_ , then you can keep these metrics in the same operator to speed up the computation.

This way, Spark has to do only one shuffle for those metrics, which is usually the most time-consuming part of Spark computations. However, this technique has the cost of higher memory usage.

## Scheduled metricsâ

When you have scheduled metrics in a plan, Pulse has to recompute everything up to that point in the plan. If you have a lot of computations before the scheduled metrics operator, it might create a big overhead in computation time. This is usually a non-issue since scheduled metrics are normally computed during the night and are not subject to the real-time constraints. Nevertheless be aware of this in case you think your computations will be taking longer than a night in production.

As an exception to the one plan rule, having two plans in this situation can be a trade-off between storage space and computational times.

## Addressing errors in plan definitionâ

When defining the components of a **Plan** , you may encounter errors that would result in failures during the [plan execution](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#plan-execution).

Some of those errors are detectable when defining the Plan, and Pulse will show warnings to allow them to be fixed before deploying the plan to production.

One such error is defining [fields](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#field) based on a [PQL expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features) (e.g. within a [`Metrics` or `Map` operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference)). Operators that require null coalescing (i.e. [default fallback values](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#fallback-value)) will produce a warning in the UI if the coalescing operator (`??`) and value are missing:

To fix this situation, provide a fallback value in the PQL expression input field, e.g. `?? 0` or `?? ""`.

A similar warning will be shown if built-in functions are used in collections (like `List`s, `Set`s or `Map`s). For example, an expression like
    
    
    ["test", "test1", "test2"].contains("testing")  
    

will fail because the `contains` function is not supported in collections used in the PQL fields of Map Operators or Metric Operators.

Attempting to use such functions in that context will result in a warning in the UI:

The alternative is to use [UDFs (User Defined Functions)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions), e.g.:
    
    
    com.feedzai.pulse.pkernel.runtime.CollectionUDF.contains(["test", "test1", "test2"], "testing")  
    

Besides these preventive warnings, Pulse will also allow recovering from execution errors that are not detectable at design time. Refer to [Automatic Application Repair](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/automatic-application-repair) and [Workflow recovery](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#workflow-recovery) for more information on how to recover from execution errors.

Title: Creating a Plan for Features | Feedzai Pulse

# Creating a Plan for Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

In Pulse, a plan entity defines a transformation flow of one data source into another data source. In a plan it is possible to add, update and remove fields, or calculate metrics on the data.

To create a plan, execute the following steps.

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, add  a plan.

  2. Add a **Name** for the plan.

  3. Select the **Deployable** option. This option ensures that you can deploy your plan to another environment (e.g. QA or Production) later on.

  4. In the **Schema** field, specify the data schema that the plan is built on. You can select an existing schema, or an existing data source.

For example, if you select the* Data with Features for Models* data source, then the plan will be based on a copy of the current schema of that data source.

  5. Use the **Confirm** button to acknowledge that future changes in the origin schema won't change the schema of the plan.

  6. In the **Timestamp Field** , select the schema field that represents the timestamp of the events. When Pulse aggregates the data over a time period, it will consider this field as the timestamp of the event.

Only fields of [timestamp](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) type can be selected.

info

If you don't select a timestamp field for the plan, you won't be able to create metrics in the plan later on.

  7. If you want to use data from more than one channel, select the **Omnichannel** option, and configure the channels as follows:

     1. Add a **Name** for the **Main Channel**. This channel contains the events that you want to process, and uses the schema selected in step 4.

     2. **Secondary channels** provide additional information that you can use to process the events of the main channel. You can use the **Add Channel** button to add secondary channels.

For each secondary channel, add a **Name** , a **Schema** and the **Timestamp Field** that that channel will use.

There should be at least some fields that can be cross-referenced between the channels. For example, both schemas might include a customer identifier, even though it might be actually called differently in each schema.

  8. **Save** the plan settings.

# Creating Derived Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

This page describes how to edit and run an existing plan that creates a new data source with new features.

In the example shown, you can see how to add a new field that is calculated based on a single transaction. If you want to create a feature that is based on many aggregated transactions, you must use [metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric), i.e. historical profiles â refer to the page on [creating metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics).

## Adding the featuresâ

To add new features, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open the features plan.

  2. Drag a **Map** operator to the plan if there is none yet.

Clipboard

To save time, you can use the clipboard  to copy-paste operators in plans. This allows you to add operators without the need of specifying all their fields each time you create a new plan.

  3. Edit  the map as follows:

     1. Select the **Fields to Add** tab.

     2. In the **Output Field Name** column, specify the name of the new feature.

     3. In the **Expression** column, write the [Pulse Query Language expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features) that calculates the output value. For example, the following expression calculates whether the credit card was present at the transaction:
            
            if (POSEntryMode == 'Swiped' or POSEntryMode == 'Keyed' or POSEntryMode == 'Chip') then 'true' else 'false'  
            

     4. Define the **Type** of the output field. In the example of calculating whether the credit card was present at the transaction, the type of the output field is _Categorical_ , with two possible values: _true_ and _false_.

     5. Confirm that you want to add the field to the output schema, using the  button.

     6. Add all the features to the map operator by following the previous steps.

     7. **Save** the map operator.




## Creating the data source with the featuresâ

  1. To create a new data source which includes the new field(s), execute the following actions:
     1. With the plan still open, use the  button to execute the plan.
        1. In the **Data Source** tab, select the data source that will be the input for the plan. For example _Cleaned Transactions_ , or _Model Features v1_. If the plan has more than one channel, select the input data source for each channel.
        2. In the **Data Sinks** tab, configure the output of the plan:
           * **Name** for the output data source. For example, _Rule Features v1_. **Type** : _Parquet_ (default) or _CSV_ , depending on what type of output file you want to generate.

Parquet format is recommended

Using the Parquet file format for data files is highly recommended. Besides allowing a direct encoding of data types (which automates the mapping of field types when importing datasets), it also improves performance and disk usage: compared to CSV, Parquet files occupy less space and take less time to load.

           * **Directory Path** : the path and file name where Pulse will store the output file, containing the data of the new data source. Example: `file:///datasets/rule-features-v1.parquet`. Note that the format varies according to the operating system.
        3. Use the  button to execute the plan. It generates a new data source in Pulse, named _Rule Features v1_. Pulse also saves an output file with the transformed data to your filesystem.
     2. Check the new data source to confirm that its schema includes new fields.

# Creating Metrics

Was this page helpful?Â 

You can create new fields to augment a [data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) based on an aggregation of events over a period of time. These kind of features are called [**metrics**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric), or **historical profiles**.

Metrics describe typical behavior. For example: this customer typically uses two devices, and makes one transfer per month to pay the rent. Certain behavior patterns, or changes in the behavior, may help you detect financial crime.

Metrics operator limits

For performance reasons, there are limits to the number of Metrics operators that can be added to a Plan. For more information about this, see [Limits](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/limits).

To add new metrics, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open the features plan.

  2. Drag a **Metrics** operator to the plan if there is none yet.

Adding metrics operators

To save time, you can use the clipboard  to copy-paste operators in plans. This allows you to add operators without specifying all their fields each time you create a new plan.

  3. Edit  the metrics operator as follows:

     1. Add an **Operator Name** for the metrics operator.

     2. Add  a new metric to the operator. Later, when you run the plan, Pulse will add this metric to the output data source as a new field.

     3. Set the **Group By** fields over which to calculate aggregated metrics. For example:

        1. _AccountID_ , to aggregate metrics for each card number.
        2. _MerchantID_ , to aggregate metrics for each merchant.
        3. _AccountID_ , _MerchantID_ , to aggregate metrics for the profile of each card number in each merchant.
     4. If relevant, set the **Lookup By** fields (matching the count and types of the **Group By** fields) to define which group to retrieve.

tip

For more detailed information on setting up Lookup By metrics, refer to the [Using Lookup Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics/using-lookup-metrics) guide.

     5. In the **Window** section, configure the time window over which to calculate the metric.

        1. In the **Expression** field, add the time interval that you want to include. For example, _1 hour_ or _7 days_.

This means that you want to calculate a metric based on the events of the last hour, or of the last seven days.

For details on the syntax supported in window expressions, please refer to the [Time window](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#time-window) section of the documentation on Plans in Workflows.

        2. If you use the **Delay** field, recent events will not be immediately accounted for. For example, a 3-hour window with 1-hour delay means that out of the last 3+1=4 hours of events, the last 1 hour will not be considered. This is useful if you are computing a historical baseline profile and donât want it to be influenced by recent behavior.

        3. **Is tumbling** : tumbling windows expire all events at once, once they reach their predetermined size. Afterwards, they start filling again and the cycle repeats itself.

        4. You can define a **Filter** for the time window. Only events that fulfill the filter condition will be taken into account when calculating the metric. Use [Pulse Query Language (PQL) expressions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features) returning a boolean value to define the filter.

     6. In the **Edit Update Period** section, choose if the metric should be updated in real time, or periodically on a schedule.

        1. **Real Time** : ideal for metrics with a small window (e.g. less than one day), to ensure that rapid attacks are detected.

Under Real Time, select the _Update on every event_ option. The _Update every_ option is available for legacy reasons and should not be selected. This option is currently not accepted for omnichannel plans. It will be supported in future versions of Pulse.

        2. **Scheduled** : ideal for metrics with a large window (e.g. 1 month). Since there is less fluctuation in the long-term behavior, the metric can be updated less frequently. To specify when the metric should be updated, you can either set _Start of_ or _Scheduled_.

In the latter, you must type a [Cron expression](https://www.quartz-scheduler.net/documentation/quartz-2.x/tutorial/crontriggers.html), e.g. `0 0 12 * * ?` (i.e. _At noon every day_).

     7. In the **Aggregation** section, select the **Function** you want to use to calculate the metric. If the function needs a parameter, select the **Field** that provides that parameter.

Limitations when storing the state of real-time metrics on disk

Note that storing the state of metric on disk is in continuous development, and it does not provide full feature parity to the previous, RAM-based version.

Examples of functions:

        * To calculate the sum of the _TransactionAmount_ field over each time window, for each _group by_ field: the function is _Sum_ , and the parameter field is _TransactionAmount._
        * To calculate the number of the transactions over each time window, for each _group by_ field: the function is _Count_ , and it has no parameters.
     8. Optionally, in the **Advanced** tab of the Aggregation section, you can define a [Pulse Query Language (PQL) expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features). This tab allows you to compute more complex values. When calculating metrics in a plan that is based on more than one channel, the Advanced tab is not available.

     9. **If your plan has more than one channel** , do the following:

        1. Toggle off all secondary channels that are not relevant for the metric using the toggle next to the channel's name in the Group By section.
        2. You can decide not to include main channel data in the aggregation. To do so, select the **Do not include main channel data in the aggregation** option. Select this option when the main channel has no data relevant for the aggregation. For example, when processing debit card transactions, it might be useful to know how many devices the customer has used. This information can be aggregated from the online banking channel. But unlike online banking, the main channel (debit cards) will not contain any information about devices.
        3. After selecting the _group by_ field(s) for the main channel, select the matching field(s) for each active secondary channel. If there is more than one _group by_ field, the order of the fields **must** match across the different channels.
        4. If you selected an aggregation function that has parameters, select the parameter fields for each channel.
        5. Note that only scheduled metrics can use data from secondary channels. If you create a real-time metric with data from secondary channels, you will receive an error message when saving the metric.
     10. In the **Details** section, add a description for the metric.

  4. Use the **Save** button to add the metric to the operator.

  5. The metrics get a default name. You can hover over a metric and use the  button to rename it.

# Generating the Features Dataset

Was this page helpful?Â 

Typically, you want to train your machine learning model on a data source that contains derived fields and metrics. You can achieve this by building up your feature plan(s) and generating a feature data source.

This page gives you instructions on how to create such a data source.

## Preparing the planâ

To produce your feature dataset, compose a plan as described in the following pages:

  * [Designing derived features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-derived-features)

  * [Designing metrics (historical profiles)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics)

Target field

Real-time data, coming into Pulse in Production, will not include the target field you aim at predicting during the data science stage. In fact, in a workflow, you configure that target as an outcome that represents Pulse's decision for each instance.

Before deploying your feature plan to runtime, you may want to:

    1. Edit the map operator to remove the target field from the plan's output data source.
    2. Export the output data source to generate a schema without the target field.

Field dependencies

An [operator in a plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) that can add fields to the schema cannot have intra-operator dependencies. In map and metrics operators, you cannot refer to a field that has been added inside that same operator.




## Running the plan to generate the enhanced data sourceâ

  1. Use the  button to execute the plan.
     1. In the **Data Source** tab, select the data source that will be the input for the plan. For example _Cleaned Transactions_. If the plan has more than one channel, select the input data source for each channel.

     2. In the **Data Sinks** tab, configure the output of the plan:

        * **Name** for the output data source. For example, _Features v1_.
        * **Type** : the file format of the output data â _Parquet_ (default) or _CSV_.

Parquet format is recommended

Using the Parquet file format for data files is highly recommended. Besides allowing a direct encoding of data types (which automates the mapping of field types when importing datasets), it also improves performance and disk usage: compared to CSV, Parquet files occupy less space and take less time to load.

        * **Directory Path** : the path and file name where Pulse will store the output CSV file, containing the data of the new data source. Example: `<file:///datasets/rule-features-v1.parquet>`. Note that the format varies according to the operating system.
     3. Use the  button to execute the plan. It generates a new data source in Pulse, named _Features v1_. Pulse also saves an output file with the transformed data to your filesystem.

  2. Check the new data source to confirm that its schema includes new fields.



## Designing the final feature datasetâ

There are multiple approaches when using plans to obtain your final feature dataset. The one you choose comes down to how it best fits your requirements and work methodology.

### Single plan with one mapâ

The most straightforward approach is encapsulating all feature engineering logic into one map operator. This is the simplest approach and the one proposed in the current topic.

The following image depicts a simple features plan where all features are designed in the metrics operator and a single map operator.

#### Advantagesâ

  * Straightforward



#### Disadvantagesâ

  * Hard to maintain and reuse. With the number of features easily rising to hundreds, it is very hard to keep track of all features, group them by type, and generally keep them clean and organized in the same map.



### Sequential plansâ

A more segmented approach consists in using isolated plans to sequentially manipulate data, add features and metrics to datasets. In this case, you have to manually run each plan and manage how all intermediate data sources are consumed and produced.

For example, having separate plans to [design metrics (historical profiles)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics) and to [design derived features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-derived-features), that you manually run one after the other.

The following image depicts a composition of four separate plans. Each plan generates different features/historical profiles, taking as input the data source that the previous plan produced.

#### Advantagesâ

  * Feature engineering logic is isolated by plan, improving maintainability and reuse.



#### Disadvantagesâ

  * Hard and time-consuming to execute and reproduce the entire sequence. You have to manually execute each intermediate step, such as running each plan. You also must be extremely careful to ensure that you chain them together with the correct data sources to be consumed and produced.



### Single plan with several mapsâ

Another possibility, which Feedzai **recommends** , is using a single plan that contains all Feature Engineering logic split among several map operators. Each map adds different types of features to the dataset, effectively isolating logic while keeping complexity under control.

The following image displays an example of a features Plan where all features are grouped by type. Note that auxiliary fields are removed in the end and that all features that do not depend on historical profiles are designed before the metrics operator.

#### Advantagesâ

  * All feature engineering logic is contained in the same plan, simplifying the process. There is no need for manual, intermediate, actions and datasets.

  * Feature engineering logic is isolated by map, improving maintainability and reuse for each type of features. Even when the number of features becomes too large, they are still grouped by type. This allows you to:

    * Easily keep track of related features.
    * Know where each type of features is being generated.
    * Work on each type of features at a time and iteratively test and build up the plan.
    * Easily detect possible dependencies among features. For example, time-based features are derived from historical profiles.



#### Disadvantagesâ

  * The plan, although linear, becomes more complex with a lot more steps.

# Managing Metrics Backfills

The **Backfills** management area allows you to monitor, manually trigger, and manage [backfill jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/backfills) for your [metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#metrics). While backfills are automatically triggered when you publish changes to metrics, this area gives you more control over the process.

### 

Here, you can:

  * Manually start a backfill for specific metrics in a workflow.
  * Monitor the status and progress of all backfill jobs (both manual and automatic).
  * Cancel backfill jobs that are no longer needed.



## Triggering a new backfill jobâ

To manually trigger a backfill job, follow these steps:

  1. Navigate to the **Backfills** tab in your application.

  2. In the "Trigger Backfill" section, use the dropdown menus to select the metrics you want to backfill:

     * **Workflow** : Choose the [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) containing the metrics. You can only select one workflow at a time.
     * **Plan Services** : Select one or more [plan services](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#plan-service) within the chosen workflow.
     * **Metrics Operators** : Select one or more [metrics operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#metrics) from the selected plan services.
     * **Metrics** : Select the specific [metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#metrics) to be backfilled.

For Plan Services, Metrics Operators, and Metrics, you can use the "Select All..." option to include all items in the list. All fields are mandatory.

  3. Select the **Trigger Backfill** button.




A new backfill job will be created and added to the queue, visible in the "Triggered Jobs History" table underneath. Once it is picked for execution, the associated Pulse job(s) will be displayed in the **Jobs** tab:

### 

The jobs listed in this view can be matched to the corresponding backfill jobs in the **Backfills** tab via the **Name** column in both tables, which displays the full hash of the backfill job in the former, and a 6-character shortened version in the latter.

## Monitoring backfill jobsâ

The "Triggered Jobs History" table provides a detailed overview of all backfill jobs. For each backfill job, this table displays the following information:

Column| Description  
---|---  
**Name**|  The name of the job, composed of the name of the associated workflow and a 6-character shortened hash in parentheses â e.g., `workflow123 (az5LYD)`.  
**Type**|  The type of job, which is always `BACKFILL`.  
**Status**|  The current status of the job. See the list of possible statuses below.  
**Description**|  A brief description regarding the nature of the job (e.g., "Backfill triggered manually via Pulse UI" or "Backfill created automatically from publish").  
**TriggeredÂ by**|  The user who initiated the job. For automatic backfills, this will be "system".  
**Triggered at**|  The timestamp when the job was created.  
**Started at**|  The timestamp when the job execution began. This may differ from "Triggered at" if the job waited in the queue, and will show "No info available" if the job is still queued.  
**Finished at**|  The timestamp when the job was completed. It shows "No info available" for running jobs.  
**Updated at**|  The timestamp of the last status update for the job.  
  
This table is updated in real time, so it can be used to monitor the backfill jobs' details and progress. The most relevant columns to track the progress of a backfill job are:

  * **Status** : Indicates the current state of the job (e.g., `SCHEDULED`, `EXECUTING`, `FINISHED`). Refer to the full list of possible statuses below.
  * **Started at** and **Finished at** : Show when the job began and completed, helping to estimate duration.
  * **Updated at** : Reflects the last time the job's status changed, useful for tracking recent activity.



### Backfill job statusesâ

The possible statuses for a backfill job, and the corresponding meanings, are as follows:

  * `SCHEDULED`: The job is in the queue, waiting to be executed.
  * `SKIPPED`: The job was skipped due to [automatic optimization](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/backfills#backfill-optimization).
  * `STARTING`: The job has been picked up from the queue and is being prepared for execution.
  * `EXECUTING`: The job is currently running.
  * `FINISHED`: The job has completed successfully.
  * `STOPPING`: The job has been manually canceled and is in the process of a graceful shutdown.
  * `CANCELLED`: The job was successfully stopped after a manual cancellation.
  * `FAILED`: The job terminated due to an error.



## Viewing backfill job detailsâ

Besides monitoring the job's status, you can click on a backfill job's name in the "Triggered Jobs History" table (or the **Expand row** icon at the right edge of the row) to view more detailed information about that specific job, including its full ID (i.e. its unabbreviated hash), which metrics are being backfilled, which plan services and operators are involved, and what workflow they belong to.

### 

In this expanded view, the Workflow and Plan execution boxes contain links that you can use to navigate to them.

There is also a **Copy to clipboard** button next to each box, that allows copying the corresponding element name.

tip

In the metrics boxes, using the **Copy to clipboard** button will add a comma-separated list of metric names to the clipboard. This list can then be pasted in the metrics dropdown to schedule a new backfill, as a more convenient way to select multiple metrics.

## Canceling a backfill jobâ

You can manually cancel a backfill job if it is in the `SCHEDULED`, `STARTING`, or `EXECUTING` status. This is useful if you need to prioritize other jobs or if a backfill is no longer necessary. Refer to the [best practices for managing the queue of backfill jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics/railgun#managing-the-queue-of-backfill-jobs) for more information on when to manually cancel jobs.

To cancel a backfill job:

  1. Locate the job in the "Triggered Jobs History" table.
  2. Click the **Cancel Backfill** â¨ button in the **Actions** column for that job.



A confirmation message will appear, and the job's status will change to `STOPPING` while it cleans up. Once the process is complete, the status will update to `CANCELLED`.

# Selecting Important Data for Your Model

If you want to use models to score events, as part of your feature engineering work you need to find out which fields in your clean data source relate directly with fraud (or any other target variable). This will help you decide which fields to use in your models.

To examine your data source and discover which fields you can directly use as model features, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select your data source from the **Data Sources** list.
  2. Use the  option to generate statistics for the data source. Select which are the breakdown fields and values to slice the results into. For example, the _Fraud_ field.
  3. Use the **View Statistics** option for the field you want to inspect, to go in depth into the generated insight. For example, you can select the _TransactionAmount_ field. When looking into the analysis details to understand the data, you can do the following:
     1. Use the **Breakdown Fields** dropbox to break down the statistics by _Fraud_.
     2. Examine results for both **Breakdown Values**. Usually, fraud is correlated with higher transaction amounts. Thus, if when you look at statistics for fraudulent transactions you find that the _TransactionAmount_ is generally higher than for non-fraudulent ones, then it is likely that the _TransactionAmount_ field will make sense as a feature.



The following screenshot shows an analysis for events where Fraud=true:

The following screenshot shows an analysis for events where Fraud=false:

## Generated statisticsâ

Depending on the data types you defined for each field when [importing your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/importing-your-dataset-into-pulse), Pulse generates different metrics.

For numerical fields Pulse generates arithmetic metrics such as mean, minimum and maximum, while for categorical data Pulse only generates the total count and distinct values.

Breakdowns

When you run an analysis on a data source, you must always select for which breakdown fields and values you want Pulse to calculate statistics.

Skipping this action and simply calculating broken-down metrics for all possible combination of fields and values could rapidly cause Pulse to crash due to lack of computational resources.

Title: Using Lists in Features | Feedzai Pulse
============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)
  * [Feature Engineering](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/)
  * Using Lists in Features



On this page

# Using Lists in Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

To access a field of a list item in a plan, you need to add the field to the plan. This can be useful when you have reference data stored in lists, like risk levels, or country-related information. This topic describes how to add fields of lists to a plan, and how to access them in a feature.

Features cannot use multi-tenant lists

Multi-tenant lists are not supported in plans. More specifically, the user cannot select multi-tenant lists in a list operator.

If in a plan you want to use list values to compute features, you need to add the list field to the plan. This is the objective of the list operator. For each event that traverses the list operator, this field will be populated with the corresponding list item value from the list.

List items can have an **expiration date**. This expiration date applies to the list operator as well, meaning that if the corresponding list item is not valid at the time of the timestamp of the event, the field in the event will have a null value. You can set the timestamp field in the following places:

  * for a deployable plan under the Configure Plan Schema option.
  * in a non-deployable plan: for each operator, you can select the timestamp field individually, in the Timestamp Field option.



If there is no timestamp field defined, the list items that have expiration date are ignored.

## How toâ

To add a field of a list to a plan, perform the following steps:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open the plan you want to edit.
  2. Drag a **List** operator to the plan.
  3. Type a **Name** for the list operator.
  4. For each list field that you want to add to the plan, perform the following steps:
     1. In the **Output Field Name** column, type a name for the new field. This is the name by which you will be able to find the list value when using it in the plan.
     2. In the **List** column, select the list that you want to use in the plan.
     3. In the **Operation** column, select what you want to do with the list. The available operations are:
        1. **Get** : returns the value of the field specified in the List Field column, corresponding to the list item identified by the Item Value Expression. Applies only to complex lists.
        2. **Contains** : returns true if the list contains an item identified by the Item Value Expression.
     4. In the **Item Value Expression** column, type an expression that defines the key for which the list operator will retrieve the value. This expression is the connection between the event and the list. It is a [PQL expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features), meaning that you can use anything you can normally use in a map operator, for example:
        * event fields
        * constants
        * boolean and arithmetic operators
        * UDFs
        * coalesce operator
     5. In the **List Field** column, select the field of the list that you want to use in the plan. This field is available only if you selected a complex list in the List column.
     6. Use the  button to add the field to the list operator.
  5. **Save** the list operator.



As a result, in the features (map and metric operators) of the plan you can access the list value associated to the current event, by typing the name you gave in the _Output Field Name_ column. The value that this field contains is the value that belongs to the key you defined in the _Item Value Expression_.

## Exampleâ

You may have a positive/negative list about known merchants. A merchant may be risky, hence transactions with that certain merchant might need to be declined. Transactions with other merchants might need to be approved, or might need a review. A positive/negative list accumulates all this knowledge in one place.

In this case, the list is defined in the following way:

The list items have the _Merchant Id_ as key, and either 'decline', 'approve' or 'review' in the _Action_ field. Example:

Merchant Id| Action  
---|---  
898776| 'approve'  
556949| 'decline'  
132214| 'review'  
  
Now, you may want to use the knowledge accumulated in this list in the plan. For instance, when processing a transaction, you might want to calculate the number of transactions initiated by the same card with risky merchants.

To allow that, add the _Action_ field of the _Merchant PosNeg list_ to the plan. The key that will connect the event with the list is the _MerchantId_. The new field of the event will be called _MerchantAction_.

Now you can use the _MerchantAction_ field in the metric, as any other event field. It contains the action ('decline', 'approve' or 'review') according to the merchant of the event.

# Using PQL in Features

**Pulse Query Language** (**PQL**) is Pulse's query language that allows users to compute complex values based on input data fields.

This topic introduces the basic concepts of PQL.

To learn how to use PQL in some specific scenarios, read the following user guides:
