  * [Calling UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql#udf-calls)



## Usageâ

The following image shows an example of how PQL is used in a map operator to create a derived field in a plan.

This map operator adds a categorical field called _Card Present Flag_ , representing whether there was a bank card present in the transaction. The PQL expression is in the _Expression_ column.

## PQL expressionsâ

In the Pulse UI, users can combine the following building blocks (values, operators, functions, subclauses) into PQL expressions:

Building block / subclause| Purpose, observation| Example(s)  
---|---|---  
Constants of [primitive data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/pql-data-types-and-type-conversions)| Use a fixed value| 
    
    
    1.999
    'true'
    'Swiped'  
  
Input data fields| Use values of the input data.After typing the name of the data field, resolve the typed name to an existing data field name from the list that the UI offers.| 
    
    
    Amount  
  
`:` (i.e. the [cast operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/pql-data-types-and-type-conversions#cast-operator))| Convert data into another data type| 
    
    
    Amount:int  
  
[Arithmetic operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/operators-in-pql#arithmetic-operators)| Calculate a new value from two values of int, long, float or double type| 
    
    
    Balance - Amount  
  
[Boolean operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/operators-in-pql#boolean-operators)| Calculate a new true/false value| 
    
    
    and
    or
    !
    ==  
  
[Function calls](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql)| You can call two types of functions: built-in functions, and custom functions (aka. UDFs)| The following example calls the _between()_ built-in function:
    
    
    between(Amount, 0, 200)  
  
[Conditional expressions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/conditional-expressions-in-pql)| Return a value based on a condition|

Variable declarations| Declare auxiliary variables that help you calculating other values| The following example shows how you define two variables (first_timestamp and last_timestamp) in order to calculate a third value (last_timestamp - first_timestamp ) / 60*60*1000.0)
    
    
    ( let first_timestamp = first().Timstamp ?? 0 in
    let last_timestamp = last().Timestamp ?? 0 in
    ( last_timestamp - first_timestamp ) / 60 _60_ 1000.0 )  
  
Collections, tuples| Work on tuples, lists, sets, and maps of data instead of a single data field| In the following example, OrderItems is a list of orders. Each item of the list is a tuple with the following fields: ItemId, Quantity, Price
    
    
    OrderItems.get(0).Quantity  
  
[Aggregations, and functions over aggregated datasets](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics)| Aggregate data to calculate minimum, maximum, average, or alternatively to access specific records of the aggregated dataset|

`??`(i.e. the [coalesce operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/handling-null-values-with-pql))| Handle NULL values| 
    
    
    Amount ?? 0  
  
Reserved keywords

Some keywords and symbols cannot be used outside of their original purpose. See the list of [reserved keywords](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/reserved-keywords-in-pql) for more information.

# Using String Indexing

When scoring an event, models can take into consideration information stored in strings. For that, first you must generate a new numerical field (an index) from the string field, so that you can use the index as a feature in the model.

To index a string field, use the Data Science API (DS-API) of Pulse to create an indexer. An indexer allows to obtain the index value of the string field.

This page describes how to create new features based on a string field for which an indexer was already created.

## Prerequisiteâ

The steps described in this topic presume that a data scientist created an indexer for the string field that you want to use. The indexer is a list in Pulse, created with the frequency indexing algorithm. You can find the indexers in Pulse at the bottom of the list of lists, prefixed with `{StringIndexer}`.

Learn how to use the DS-API to create an indexer in the JupyterLab notebook provided with the Feedzai package.

## Using an indexed string field in a Pulse planâ

To use the indexed value of a string field, you must add it to the schema of the data source. For that, use a map operator that retrieves the index value from the indexer and adds it to the event. You can access the index in the map operator by using the user-defined function `FrequencyIndexerUDF(indexer_name, input_field_name)`. The following table shows the obligatory parameters you must provide when calling this UDF.

Parameter| Type| Description  
---|---|---  
indexer_name| String| The indexer_name to be used here is the one defined when the indexer is created. Request this information from the data scientist that created the indexer.  
input_field_name| Categorical| The data source field that you want to use.  
  
### Exampleâ

The following snippet returns the index value for the merchant_id field of the event:

`FrequencyIndexerUDF.transform("v1_merchant_indexer", merchant_id)`

## Advanced usage: clippingâ

Pulse's string indexer uses frequency indexing. The frequency index assigns a ranking to each value of the indexed field. The different values are called categories. The more times a string or category shows up in the training data set, the higher its ranking. Example:

If there is too much information stored in the indexer (i.e. too many categories), the new feature might cause overfit in the machine learning model. To limit that, you can use fewer categories through clipping.

You can use clipping in two different stages:

  * **When you create the indexer** , i.e. you don't include less frequent categories in the indexer at all.

The default clipping of DS-API uses 10000 categories as default for the maximum of categories stored in the indexer, and minimum of 100 samples per category. If there are more than 10000 categories, the less frequent ones are dropped. If any category has less than 100 observations, it is also dropped.

In the documentation of the DS-API included in the JupyterLab notebook, you can read how to clip the indexer when you create it.

  * **When you use the indexer in Pulse to retrieve the ranking for a string** , i.e. you ignore less frequent categories at lookup.




See the next section of this topic to learn how to influence the index clipping when you are retrieving the index values.

### Clipping indexers in Pulseâ

When you use the indexer to retrieve the ranking for a string, Pulse's default clipping ignores the less frequent categories of the indexer so that maximum 90% of the indexer's categories are taken into consideration, but minimum 10 categories.

The following table shows the two optional parameters that you can use to control index clipping for string fields in Pulse:

Parameter| Type| Description| Default value| Value range  
---|---|---|---|---  
clipping_max_categories_percentage| Float| Uses only the given percentage of categories from the indexer. For ignored categories and for other unknown input values, the indexer returns a default value, which is the number of categories in the clipped indexer.| 90.0| [0.0, 100.0]  
clipping_categories_limit| Int| Clips the least frequent categories until leaving only the defined number of categories, or until the clipping_max_categories_percentage criterion is met.| 10| >= 1  
  
With the clipping parameters, the full signature of the UDF is:
    
    
    FrequencyIndexerUDF.transform(indexer_name, input_field_name, clipping_max_categories_percentage, clipping_categories_limit)  
    

### Examples for clippingâ

The following examples show how to use the parameters of the FrequencyIndexerUDF:

  1. To use all the indexer categories, use the following expression in the map operator:


    
    
    FrequencyIndexerUDF.transform("v1_merchant_indexer", merchant_id, 100)  
    

  2. To eliminate the smaller categories in the indexer until only 16.5% of the indexer's categories remain, or only 20 categories remain:


    
    
    FrequencyIndexerUDF.transform("v1_merchant_indexer", merchant_id, 16.5, 20)

On this page

# Comparing models

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

At each iteration of your model, you will need to evaluate it. In reality, not only evaluate it but also assess how it performs in comparison with the previous iteration.

Pulse helps you in taking your conclusions on how your [feature engineering](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering) work, [model training](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model), and [parameter tuning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters) is evolving and progressing towards the goals of your Data Science project.

It may make sense to, for example, try out your model not only with adjusted parameters but also for different test datasets, different transaction time periods, etc.

## How toâ

While you evaluate your [models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), Pulse enables you to compare their performances:

  1. Directly by overlaying model evaluations.
  2. Using the exploration mode for business targets.



### Model Evaluationsâ

To compare two **Model Evaluations** , execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Data Science** tab, select a **Model Project** from the **Model Projects** list.
  2. Select an existing **Model Evaluation**.
  3. Select which is the evaluation you want the current one to be **Compared With**.



The information in **Model Evaluation** is divided into different panels that can be accessed for: Comparing **Performance Metrics** or Comparing **Feature importance**.

#### Comparing Performance Metricsâ

  1. To visualize comparison results:

     1. Analyze the **ROC Curve** and **X/Y Plot** , now with both the **Model Evaluation** and the **Comparison** evaluation visible.

     2. Analyze the Comparison results displayed at the top row of the **Metrics** table.

Comparison results

When you select a **Model Evaluation** for comparison, the **ROC Curve** , **X/Y Plot** and **Metrics** table display the evaluation results only for the main combination of breakdowns (All x All). This occurs even if the model evaluation has configured breakdowns.

  2. Select the  option to display evaluation parameters for both the selected and the comparison models. Differences are highlighted so that you can easily spot all [parameter adjustments](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters) you are testing.




#### Comparing Feature Importanceâ

This option is only available if the current Model Evaluation has Feature Importance computed (i.e. regardless of whether or not the model evaluation under comparison has it computed).

  1. Select  to visualize comparison results:



The following metrics are presented by default:

  * **#FPR** : Values of the count FPR for each feature for the current **Model Evaluation** (A) and for the evaluation under comparison (B).
  * **Absolute importance** : Bar chart comparing the **Absolute Importance** of both model evaluations.
  * **Rank** : The rank of the importance of each feature for each model evaluation.
  * **Delta** : The difference between Rank A and Rank B.



Feature Importance view

If you compare the current model evaluation with an evaluation that does not have feature importance computed, the **Feature Importance** view will only display data for the current model evaluation.

### Exploration Modeâ

To compare how different **Model Evaluations** perform for a Target, execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Data Science** tab, select a **Model Project** from the **Model Projects list**.
  2. Select the  option to explore evaluation results in your **Model Project**.
  3. [Configure Targets for evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model).
  4. Analyze the results for each **Target** and compare them among all selected **Evaluations**.



Comparing models

You can compare models using the [exploration mode within a hyperparameter tuning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters/exploring-hyperparameter-tuning-results) or using the [global exploration mode](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model#exploring-evaluation-results) in your model project, where you can combine results from model evaluations and hyperparameter tuning.

## Next Stepsâ

If your model produces the desired results, then your project is ready for [deployment into Production](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production). Check also [how Pulse projects work](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/how-pulse-projects-work) for some background to understand what is involved at this stage.

If your model needs further tuning, then start a new iteration in your Data Science project. For example, by [improving your model's features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering) and [adjusting parameters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters).

To add an extra layer of security on top of your Machine Learning model, you can also [build and evaluate rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide).

# Evaluating a model

Was this page helpful?Â 

Evaluating your [model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) against a test dataset is crucial in understanding its performance. This topic explains how to generate a [model evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation) over a trained model, and how to analyze the evaluation results.

## Generating a model evaluationâ

To generate an evaluation, execute the following actions:

  1. In the Data Science  tab, select a model project from the **Model Projects** list.

  2. Add  a new model evaluation.

  3. Add a Name for the model evaluation, select the **Model** , and the **Data Source**.

Training and testing datasets

Make sure that when explicitly evaluating a model you **do not** select a testing data source that intersects with the dataset you used for training.

  4. Select the **Target Variable**. It must match the format (data type and possible values) of the target variable of the model, if it has any.

  5. In the **Fields to Select** area, choose which fields in your test data source Pulse will feed to the model and press . Only _Numeric_ and _Categorical_ fields are available.

Testing data fields

Pulse feeds the test data to the model according to the data schema you provided at training time. This means that although different test field names are allowed, you must always specify your fields in the same order and with the same data types.

If the model training used a supervised ML algorithm, this rule applies to that field as well. If the model used an un supervised ML algorithm, then the target variable can be in any place within the schema of the evaluation data source.

  6. Enable  an **Additional Cost Field** to be available for the model evaluation. Typically, you can select a field that represents the transaction amount to have metrics such as the _fraud money recall_ and _fraud money FPR_.

  7. Enable  **Feature Importance** and configure the following input parameters. Check the page [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance#parameters) for more information about these parameters:

     1. **False Positive Rate**. The default value is 1.00%.
     2. **Sample Percentage**. The default value is 30%.
     3. **Random Seed**
  8. Select which are the **Breakdown** fields and values to slice the results into. For example, _Card Present_ vs _Card Not-Present._ Pulse will automatically display the number of possible breakdown combinations.

Breakdowns

The higher the number of possible breakdown combinations, the more computational resources will be consumed by training, and the longer will take to generate an evaluation for your model.

  9. In the **Output Result** area, select the **Score Instances** checkbox to generate a new data source and a CSV file in your filesystem, adding a Pulse risk assessment to each instance. The new data source includes extra fields with a Feedzai score, each one representing the likelihood of the transactions being classified as each of the possible values of the target variable. For example, in a fraud scenario, Pulse adds two fields, one with the score for fraud and the other representing the score for not fraud. To configure the output, add a **Name** for the data source and a **Directory Path** where it will be stored.

  10. **Evaluate** the Model using the  button, to create your model evaluation and compute feature importance.

Incompatible schema

If the data source selected in step 3 has a different schema than the data source used to train the model, an error message is displayed. In this case, you can select the  option to change the schema of the model evaluation.




### Analyzing the model evaluationâ

When you open an existing model evaluation, you have access to metrics to analyze the performance of your model. Additionally, if the model evaluation has feature importance computed, you have access to a tab to analyze the results of feature importance. However, if the model evaluation does not have feature importance computed yet, you can still perform this computation.

The following subsections will guide you through the following topics:

  * Analyzing performance metrics
  * Computing feature importance from an existing model evaluation. This is only needed if feature importance has not been yet calculated while generating the model evaluation.
  * Analyzing feature importance



#### Analyzing performance metricsâ

To analyze evaluation results, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select a model project from the **Model Projects** list.
  2. Select an existing model evaluation.
  3. Perform any of the following operations:
     1. Change the **Target Value** of your target variable for which you want to evaluate the results. For example, 0 representing _Not-Fraud_ and 1 representing _Fraud_.

When changing the Target Value

The following happens when you change the target value:

        * The specified target value will be interpreted as positive, while other values will be interpreted as negative. The ROC curve will reflect this reinterpretation.

        * The Score Distribution graph gets updated as well. The graph shows the distribution associated to the likelihood of the instance to be classified as the specified target value. In the case of two classes, the score distributions associated to them are mirror images with respect to the X axis.

If you make the non-usual choice of GENUINE as target value, then the score distribution will have high values for transactions that look legitimate, and low values for high risk of fraud. The FPR would be reinterpreted as the rate of fraudulent transactions mistakenly predicted as legitimate. Recall would be the "detection rate" of legitimate transactions, instead of the usual fraudulent transactions.

     2. Analyze the **ROC Curve** for the selected evaluation.

Exact values

Hover the mouse pointer over the plot line to inspect the exact values for the **Recall** and **FPR** metrics and the respective **Threshold**.

Cost-based Metrics

If you define a **Cost Field** , then the **ROC Curve** will also plot the values for **Cost Recall** vs **Cost FPR**.

     3. Configure the **X/Y Plot** to display a curve for any **X-Axis** and **Y-Axis**.

Exact values

Hover the mouse pointer over the plot line to inspect the exact values for the **X-Axis** and **Y-Axis** metrics and the respective **Threshold**.

     4. Analyze the **Metrics** table, displaying the selected metrics for all breakdown combinations you configured. Adjust the Feedzai score **Threshold** to visualize the respective results in the **Metrics** table.

Custom Evaluation Metrics

If you do not define a [Cost Field](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/cost-fields) for an evaluation, then Pulse will not be able to compute any custom evaluation metrics you may have configured and you will not have access to them.

     5. Use the  button to display a specific breakdown in the ROC Curve and X/Y Plot areas.

     6. Analyze the **Score Distribution** for the selected evaluation.

In a good model, the values of the target variable can be visually separated on the graph. In the following example, setting the threshold between 50 and 100 will separate _False_ from _True_.

  4. If you want to take your evaluation further at any point, you can enrich it by [comparing with other model evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models).



#### Computing feature importance from existing model evaluationâ

Compute Feature Importance in existing Model Evaluations

The option to compute feature importance from an existing model evaluation is available only if feature importance has not been computed yet for the selected model evaluation.

To compute feature importance from an existing model evaluation, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab , select a model project from the **Model Projects** list.
  2. In the **Model Project** window, select a model evaluation from the **Model Evaluations** list.
  3. Select the  button to configure the input parameters for Feature Importance:
  4. Set the following input parameters. Check the page [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance#parameters) for more information about these parameters:
     1. **False Positive Rate**. The default value is 1.00%.
     2. **Sample Percentage**. The default value is 30%.
     3. **Random Seed**
  5. Use the  button to compute feature importance for this model evaluation.



#### Analyzing feature importanceâ

To analyze the results of feature importance, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select a model project from the **Model Projects** list.

  2. Select an existing model evaluation.

  3. Select the  button to access the feature importance results:

Feature importance

If an error occurs during the computation of the feature importance, the  tab displays a warning. Check [Handling Feature Importance errors](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model/handling-feature-importance-errors) to learn how to re-compute feature importance.

By default, the list presents three columns: **Feature** , **Absolute Importance** and **Relative Importance**. Features are sorted by absolute importance. Absolute and relative importance are calculated based on the algorithm described in the [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance#how-pulse-calculates-feature-importance) topic.




You can perform any of the following operations:

  * **Sort and reverse order:** You can sort the list by any of the columns using the arrows on the right hand side of the column name (). You can reverse the sort by order by selecting the same column twice.
  * **Choose Metrics:** Use the  button to customize the columns that are listed in the feature importance results.
  * **Export Results to CSV:** Use the  button to export the results of feature importance to a CSV file with the following information: Feature, Target FPR, #Recall, #FPR, Absolute Importance, Relative Importance.



## Exploring Evaluation resultsâ

The **Exploration Mode** in your model project allows you to explore results both from single Model Evaluations and Hyperparameter Tuning.

To explore evaluation results and examine Model performance for business targets, for example, client SLAs, execute the following actions:

  1. In the Data Science  tab, select a model project from the **Model Projects** list.

  2. Select the  option to explore evaluation results in your model project.

  3. Select the  to view model evaluation metrics according to the target you configure. As an example, consider that your client SLA for project acceptance includes detecting fraud with 1% recall. Configure a target as follows:

     1. Define which is the metric that the target will reflect, in this case, _#Recall_.

     2. Define the **Configuration** for the new target by selecting which is the target metric and which is the preferred strategy to reach the target. In this case, _Under 1%._

     3. Choose which are the **Metrics to Show**. This means that Pulse displays the values for each selected metric when the model detects fraud with recall the closest (and inferior) to 1%.

Custom Evaluation Metrics

If you do not define a [Cost Field](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/cost-fields) for an evaluation, then Pulse will not be able to compute your [custom evaluation metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/custom-evaluation-metrics) and you will not have access to them.

  4. Use the search filters under **Evaluations** to select model evaluations and/or hyperparameter tuning results. Note that you can combine all results from one type of evaluations with all results from the other type.

  5. Analyze the results of the evaluations for each target.




## Using custom evaluation metricsâ

To configure a [custom evaluation metric](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/custom-evaluation-metrics) and make it available for model evaluations execute the following steps:

  1. In your Pulse application, use the **Options menu** and select .

  2. Add  a new evaluation metric.

  3. Name and add a textual **Description** to the evaluation metric.

  4. Configure an arithmetic **Expression** to calculate the value of the metric.

Available values

The available values you can use for your metric's expression are the ones of the confusion matrix metrics both for count and cost field sums. For example, `count_FalsePositives` and `cost_field_FalsePositives.`




## Next Stepsâ

More than generating model evaluations you must be able to track how the performance of your model is improving. As model training and evaluation is an iterative process, once you evaluate your current model you should [compare it with previous iterations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models).

# Training a Model

Was this page helpful?Â 

Once you have [designed features for your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering), the next stage is to assess whether they are useful for fraud detection, or for predicting any other variable.

At this point you need the [data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) that contains the features you have generated, to train a [model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and to validate it.

Importing a Model

Instead of training a model in Pulse, it is also possible to import a model that you created and trained externally. See [Importing an external model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model/importing-an-external-model).

## How toâ

To train a model, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab , select a model project from the model projects list.

  2. Add  a new model.

Duplicating an existing model

Instead of creating a model from scratch, you can duplicate an existing model that is similar to the one you want to create. For that, use the **Duplicate and Change** option. This option loads a copy of the model, with all the properties and values that were selected when the model was originally created.

This way you can fine-tune a model that needs only some adjustment.

  3. Select **Train model**.

  4. Configure the training properties for your new model as follows:

     1. Select the **Data Source** you will use to train the model. Typically one that has been the output of [running a features plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/generating-instance-features-dataset), or the result of splitting your dataset into training and testing subsets.

     2. Select the Algorithm. See the limitations that you need to consider.

At the end of the line in the Algorithm drop-down box, you can select the  button to get information about the algorithm.

     3. Set the **Target Variable** that the model will predict. For example, _Fraud_. This step is not required when using an unsupervised machine learning algorithm.

Target variables

Although the main goal of Pulse is to detect fraud, models can target any [categorical](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) variable.

     4. Choose which **Fields** in your Data Source the model will use in the prediction. Only _Numeric_ and _Categorical_ fields are available.

Removing fields from the model

If you suspect that some of the fields add only noise to the model, you can just remove them. Run an analysis on your Data Source, as you would do to [detect fraud patterns](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/identifying-patterns), and examine the statistics for each suspected field. For example, categorical fields with only one category, e.g. _empty value_ , should not be considered when training your model.

You can also compute the [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance) and remove the features that had a negative impact on the previous model iteration.

In the case of an **unsupervised machine learning algorithm** (e. g. Isolation Forest), remove the target variable. This avoids label leakage, since a realistic anomaly detection model does not have access to the label.




### Training parametersâ

When training a model, there are some typical configurations that control how Pulse will execute the training.

To configure the training, execute the following actions while you are adding a new model:

  1. Set a **Random Seed**. If you evaluate models with the same parameter configurations and the same seed, you should be able to replicate results for different models. If you execute several validations for the same model parameters configuration with different seeds, you should obtain statistically similar results.

  2. Select the **Sampling Type** and the Sample Percentage to define how to undersample or oversample your data.

  3. Configure the **Parameters** of the selected algorithm. For information on the parameters, select the Info button  at the end of each line.

  4. Configure the [White-box Explanations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/white-box-explanations) (WBE).

If WBE is set up for a trained model, Pulse calculates the features that led to a transaction's score in run time when the model is used. The output is available in Case Manager. You can select the following:

     * **Algorithm** : the algorithm that Pulse uses to calculate the contribution of the features.

     * **Number of Explanations** : the number of explanations that users want to obtain in Case Manager.

Only the most important features (i.e. the features that influence the transaction's score the most) will be shown in Case Manager.

     * **Target Value** : the value that the user wants to predict (e.g. false vs. true). This component is crucial, given that WBE are agnostic to any value.

  5. After selecting the above parameters, you have to edit the explanations. To do so, expand the White-box Explanations area using the  button.

There are 2 ways to edit the explanations:

     * Direct editing in the Pulse UI:

       1. Use the checkboxes under **Features** to select which features' explanations you want to take into consideration when analyzing a score in Case Manager.

       2. Optionally, add the features to an existing or new **Group**. If you group features, they will count as one in the list, leaving room for other important features to be on the list as well. For example, you can create a group called âamountâ, and use it to group several features that have the same property (e.g. amount).

       3. Add an **Explanation Message** to the features you selected. This message will be visible in the features that contributed most to the score.

The explanation can include the value of any feature or data field of the current event. To do so, start typing `/` followed by the name of the field, and select the desired field from the suggestions. You can use the `/current_value` shorthand to insert the value of the feature whose explanation you're currently editing.

     * Editing in an external editor:

       1. Select **Export Explanations** to save the current explanations as a CSV file, containing 4 columns: "Selected", "Feature", "Group" and "Explanation Message", and listing all the features with the current information.

       2. Edit the file in your preferred CSV editor (e.g. Excel).

The "Selected" column should have an 'X' for features you want to select, and be empty otherwise.

The "Explanation Message" column can contain `/`-prefixed references to a feature name that will be replaced by the actual value, as described above for editing via the Pulse UI.

       3. Select **Import Explanations** to upload the edited file back to Pulse and replace the explanations with the file's content.

caution

All the information in Pulse will be replaced by the file's content, which means you can lose explanations that may have been added in Pulse and are not present in the file.

If there are fewer features in the file than in the model, or if some features are not fully filled, a warning will be displayed to alert you to of the missing information.

tip

Export the files after filling all the fields, so that when editing the explanations on a similar model you just need to import the file you saved before. This can also be done by going to the edit page of a model and exporting the explanations it currently has.




While editing, you can search for features with a specific text, sort the order of the features by their name or their group, and hide the features that you have filled by clicking the "Show only incomplete features" button.

caution

After creating a model with WBE, it is possible to edit explanations again. In that case, do not forget to update the [**Scoring Service**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models) afterwards.

### Testing and validating your modelâ

When training a model, Pulse can automatically generate an initial Model Evaluation.

To configure how the initial Model Evaluation is performed, execute the following actions while you are adding a new model:

  1. Define the Validation Type to generate the initial evaluation. The following validation types are possible:

     * **Cross Validation** : Configure the number of folds in the dataset to generate the evaluation.

     * **Split Percentage** : Configure which percentage of the dataset you will use to train and which percentage you will use to test the model.

     * **No validation** : Pulse will not create an initial evaluation.

  2. Select the **Validation Data Source** that will provide the data for the initial model evaluation. It must have the same schema as the training data source.

  3. In the case of an unsupervised machine learning algorithm, select the **Target Variable** to be used for the evaluation. This is the field that the model aims to predict.

  4. Enable  an **Additional Cost Field** to be available for the model evaluation. Typically, you can select a field that represents the transaction amount to have metrics such as the _money recall_ and _money FPR_.

  5. Select which are the **Breakdown** fields and values to slice the results into. For example, _Card Present_ vs _Card Not-Present_. Pulse will automatically display the number of possible breakdown combinations.

Breakdowns

The higher the number of possible combinations, the more computational resources will be consumed during training time, and the longer will take to train your model.

  6. Configure the **Output Result** to generate a new Data Source and a CSV file in your filesystem, adding a Pulse risk assessment to each instance. The new Data Source includes extra fields containing the score distribution of the model among all possible target values of the Target Variable. For example, in a fraud scenario, Pulse adds two fields, one with the score for fraud, and the other representing the score for not fraud.




After Pulse finishes training your model, it automatically generates a Model Evaluation in your Model Project. For a model named _MyModelV1_ , Pulse generates a Model Evaluation named _mymodelv1-trainEvaluation_.

## Limitationsâ

When training models with DataRobot algorithms, consider the following limitations:

Provider| Limitation| Workaround  
---|---|---  
DataRobot| DataRobot converts binary categorical field values with the following content to "True/False":

  * 1/0
  * true/false
  * TRUE/FALSE

However, when using the model to score transactions in Pulse, the input data may contain values in the above listed format. In those cases, the scoring of the transaction fails with an error.| n/a  
DataRobot| Although string values can be used for features in DataRobot, they cannot be used for that purpose in Pulse.| Use a Categorical field instead.  
  
## Next Stepsâ

Now that your model is trained, you can [evaluate its performance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model), [tune parameters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters) and [compare it with other models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models).

On this page

# Tuning model parameters

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

To have the model with the best possible performance, you want to fine-tune parameters by doing multiple experimentations and combinations on them. The goal is to have a model that is better adjusted to a specific data pattern. To perform a hyperparameter Tuning is the fastest and easiest way to get to the model that yields the best results.

Pulse uses the **Parameter Sweep** , or in Machine Learning terms the **Grid Search** , to perform a hyperparameter tuning. This method is one of the standard methods used to retrieve meaningful results from a given search universe.

## How toâ

To perform an hyperparameter tuning, proceed as follows:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open a **Model Project** from the **Model Projects** list and start by adding  a **New Hyperparameter Tuning**.



  1. Select the **Data Source** you will use to execute your parameter tuning. Typically one that has been the output of [running a features Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/generating-instance-features-dataset) or the result of splitting your dataset into training and testing subsets.

  2. Set the **Target Variable** that you want to predict, like _Fraud,_ for instance.

  3. Choose the **Fields** the model will use to predict the **Target Variable**. Note that only _Numeric_ and _Categorical_ fields are available.

  4. Use the default **Random Seed** or set a new one in case you want to replicate past results.

  5. Set the **Sampling Type**. Note that if you select other than the **None** option, the **Sample Percentage** field is displayed for you to define how to undersample or oversample your data.

  6. Select the **Provider** for the machine learning algorithm and the **Algorithm** itself. Hyperparameter Tuning allows you to add more than one algorithm, which in practice means that various algorithms are trained and evaluated, each containing multiple parameters simultaneously.

Adding algorithms

You can add the same algorithm unlimited times. This can prove useful to evaluate different combinations of parameters.

  7. Configure the values you want to train both for **Common** and **Advanced** parameters. Each parameter field allows you to add multiple values. For information on the parameters, select the Info button .

  8. Configure how the evaluations will be performed by selecting the Validation Type from the available options:

     * **Validation Data Source** : To select the data source that will be used for testing the model performance.
     * **Cross Validation** : To configure the number of folds the dataset is split into.
     * **Split Percentage** : To configure which percentage of the dataset will be used for training and which percentage will be used for testing the models.
  9. Enable an [Additional Cost Field](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/cost-fields) to be available for the evaluations. Usually, you select a field that represents the transaction amount to have metrics such as the percentage of fraudulent amount caught (_money recall_).

  10. Select which are the **Breakdown** fields and values to slice the results into. For example, _Card Present_ vs _Card Not-Present_ Pulse will automatically display the number of possible breakdown combinations.




When the hyperparameter tuning is complete, Pulse will display the Finished status, meaning that you can open and start analyzing your hyperparameter tuning.

## Evaluating the results of hyperparameter tuningâ

After creating a hyperparameter tuning, you want to evaluate and explore its results to learn which are the evaluations that performed better in comparative terms. To evaluate the results:

  1. Open the hyperparameter tuning.
  2. Switch to the **Exploration mode** tab, which displays the results already filtered for that specific hyperparameter tuning.
  3. Create **Targets** and configure them. Add a set of metrics that you find more accurate for your purpose, such as finding fraud, for instance.
  4. Use the search box in Evaluations to filter the results, thus making it easier for you to visualize information.
  5. Analyze the results.



Learn more on the exploration mode and how to use it by reading the [Exploring hyperparameter tuning results](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters/exploring-hyperparameter-tuning-results) page.

Another way to evaluate and explore data is by opening the global exploration mode of models and hyperparameter tunings in the **Model Project**. Learn more about the global Exploration Mode by accessing the [Evaluating a model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model#exploring-evaluation-results) page. This exploration view enables you to compare single model evaluations with hyperparameter tuning evaluations.

## Exporting to a modelâ

Once you decide on the best set of parameters, the next step is to export the corresponding evaluation to a model. This is a necessary step to later be able to apply your model to a workflow.

Since the main goal of hyperparameter tuning is to allow you to iterate on a significant amount of different parameter sets, Pulse doesn't generate model binaries for each combination of parameters. For this reason, it is necessary to train the model with the best parameter combination during the export phase. However, Pulse keeps the metadata with the results of your hyperparameter tuning. So, when you export to a model, all fields will be already filled in with the optimized set of parameters you have previously chosen and you only need to go through the steps by selecting **Next**.

Exporting a hyperparameter tuning to a model

Even though the model is pre-filled with the parameters, you can still make changes to any field of the model.

Proceed as follows in order to train your model:

  1. Open the hyperparameter tuning from the corresponding list box in your **Model Project**.
  2. Open the **Evaluations** tab.
  3. Select the **Export to model** button of the corresponding hyperparameter tuning.
  4. Go through the different steps by selecting **Next**.
  5. Perform any other adjustment to a parameter, if needed. You may want to detail more on the evaluation of the model by defining breakdowns, for example.
  6. Finalize the creation of the **Model**.



## Next stepsâ

You may want to compare this model against other existing model evaluations, for that consult the [Comparing models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models) page.



================================================================================

# Creating a Rule Snapshot

Snapshots capture the current state of the components in a rules project, namely the rules and the execution order. Snapshots are deployable to other environments. You can use snapshots to test rule performance, as they can include an evaluation of the rules.

When working in a team, many colleagues may contribute to rules in Pulse, making various changes to rules at different times. When it's time to create a snapshot of the changes, it can be challenging to keep track of these changes. To ease this task, you can compare the current state of rules with an earlier snapshot's rules, and pick which versions you want to include in your new snapshot.

Also, in multi-tenant environments, the snapshot creation is slightly different. The following sections describe each of these cases.

## Creating a simple snapshotâ

To include the newest version of rules in your snapshot, perform the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select an existing rules project.

  2. In the **Snapshots** area, add  a snapshot.

  3. **Name** the rule snapshot.

  4. You can enable or disable rules in the snapshot using the checkbox next to the rule's name.

You can also choose the execution order by dragging rules into the right order.

  5. Select the **Create Snapshot** button to create the rule snapshot with the selected name and configuration.




## Combining rule versionsâ

When working in teams, you may want to compare the current state of rules with an earlier snapshot's rule version, and combine the versions you want to include in your new snapshot. This option is available only for:

  * Rules projects that are not stateful.
  * Snapshots that were created in Pulse version 20.0 or later.



To combine rule versions that you want to include in a new snapshot, perform the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select an existing rules project.

  2. In the **Snapshots** area, add  a snapshot.

  3. **Name** the rule snapshot.

  4. You can enable or disable rules in the snapshot by using the checkbox next to the rule's name. The rules you disable here won't be included in the snapshot. You can also choose the execution order by dragging rules into the right order. After selecting the rules and their order, select the **Compare** button to move forward.

  5. In the **With** field, select a snapshot with which you want to compare the current state of rules.

  6. In the **Snapshot Comparison** area, you can see the list of differences between the selected snapshot and the current status of the rules. The following statuses are possible:

     1. **Deleted** : a rule that existed in the selected snapshot was either deleted, or you deactivated it at the beginning of the new snapshot creation.
     2. **New** : a new rule that didn't exist in the selected snapshot.
     3. **Edited** : a rule that is present in the selected snapshot, but has been edited since then.
  7. Use the radio buttons in the **Rule Version** column to proceed with the new version or to roll back. Select **Accept** or **Reject** accordingly.

  8. For a side-by-side comparison of both versions of an edited rule, select the rule.

The pane below the Snapshot Comparison area displays both versions.

  9. After selecting the versions you want to include in the new snapshot, you can go ahead and **create** the snapshot. Optionally, you can **preview** the new snapshot and create an evaluation for it. [Read how to configure a snapshot evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/evaluating-rules-using-a-snapshot).




## Creating a multi-tenant snapshotâ

When rules of a certain rules project apply only to a certain tenant, the steps to create a snapshot are slightly different. For each tenant, you need to select which rules you want to set enabled in the snapshot. To do so, execute the following steps:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select the rules project.

  2. On the **Tenants** tab, choose a tenant.

  3. In the **Rules** area, use the  button to select which rules of the tenant will be active in the snapshot.

  4. Repeat the previous steps for each tenant.

  5. Go to the **Overall** menu and add  a snapshot.

  6. **Name** your snapshot. Verify the information about the number of tenants with and without active rules.

  7. **Create** the rule snapshot with the selected name and configuration.

# Creating a Sandbox Evaluation for Rules

By creating a sandbox evaluation, you will be able to test and evaluate your rules on a transaction level, i.e. the overall decision of the rules project for a particular transaction.

## How toâ

To create a sandbox evaluation, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, add  a sandbox evaluation.

  2. **Name** the sandbox evaluation.

  3. Specify the **Data Source** , i.e. the data on which rules will be tested.

  4. If you choose to use **Partitioning Fields** , transactions will be partitioned by the selected fields. That means that if you select _Card_ as a partition field, all transactions from that card will be processed together. Therefore, the node in charge of processing it will not have visibility of the transactions not associated to that card. This is typically what happens in production environments.

  5. Select the **Outcome Variable** , i.e. the value against which the evaluation will process its results.

  6. Choose the **Resources to Analyze**. You can add many rules, from different rules projects. For each rule you want to include, select the following:

     * **Resource Type** : Rules Project.

     * **Resource Parent** : the name of the rules project that includes rules you want to test.

     * **Resource to Evaluate** : the rule itself.

You can reorder the resources so that your sandbox evaluations simulate a production workflow as close as possible. The sandbox evaluation will apply rules to the events in the defined order.

  7. Choose your **Reporting** configuration. In this step, you will choose how the results of the evaluation will be presented.

     * By selecting no **Additional Cost** and no **Breakdowns** , you will see all metrics in general.

If you add an additional cost field, the system will collect all those metrics that are also weighed by a data source field (e.g. making events with higher values of the field impact the metrics more).

     * You can also choose **Breakdowns** to analyze metrics according to the possible values of a categorical field in the data source.

Breakdowns allow users to understand the impact of rules and models as segmented by the particular values of the breakdown fields that are selected, similarly to rule and model evaluations.

     * In the **Output Result** area, configure the new data source that will be created with the evaluation results.

  8. After running the sandbox evaluation, a new data source is created with the name you configured for the output result. Open the data source, and observe the new columns:

     1. In the first new column, you can find the outcome per transaction.

     2. In the second new column, you can find the score distribution per transaction. This will only be relevant if your rules contribute with a score for the final outcome.

# Creating a self-service rules project

## Whyâ

You must set up Self-Service **Rules** in Pulse so that users in Case Manager can write **Rules** themselves. These simple Rules are written in a language that is a subset of the RDL language used in Pulse. They differ from the regular **Rules** by not having windows (i.e. metrics), although they can use them if they are computed by a **Plan** and not by the **Rules** themselves.

The first step of Self-Service **Rules** configuration is to create a simple **Rules Project** that will store the custom **Rules** that analysts write in Case Manager.

## How Toâ

### Creating a Simple Rules Projectâ

In order to create a Simple **Rules Project** in Pulse, you have to follow the usual workflow. To create a Rules Project, execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Data Science** tab,  add a new a Rules Project.

  2. Set the Rules Project as **Simple**.

Self-Service Rules Projects

This kind of Rules Project is read-only in the UI after its creation and has an empty snapshot by default.




#### Managing Multi-Tenancy in simple rules projectsâ

Simple rules projects are associated to a workflow element that belongs to a workflow inside an application.

There are two kinds of Rules Projects that can be created: Global and ByTenant.

  * For non-tenanted solutions, the Rule Project must be configured as Global.

  * For tenanted solutions, landlords view Global rules separately from the Tenant ones so the project can be of two kinds:

Multi-Tenanted Scenarios

In a Multi-Tenant scenario you might need to have two projects:

    * One project set as **Global** : rules shared across tenants
    * One project set as **By-tenant** : with tenant-specific rules

    * Global: This kind of Rules Project contains the information (schema, decisions, etc) for the global rules.

    * ByTenant: This kind of Rules Project contains the information for the tenants rules. Tenant Groups are not supported.




## Next Stepsâ

Learn more about Self-Service Rules and how to enable them in the following pages:

  * [Adding rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules): Learn how to add the Rules projects you have created to the workflow.
  * [App Collaboration Loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop): Understand the constant integration between the work developed in offline environments and the work in Production.

# Creating Features

This section shows how to create new features that can be used in rules:

  1. [Creating a plan for the features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/creating-a-plan-for-features)

In Pulse, a plan entity is a recipe of how to transform one data source into another. A plan contains map and metric operators that represent the new features. If you already have a plan for features, skip this step.

  2. [Adding lists to the plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-lists-in-features)

If you want to access list items of complex lists, you need to add them to the plan. For example, if you have a list with the information about the risk level each country has, you can add that list to the plan, and use it in your features and rules.

  3. [Creating derived features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/creating-derived-features)

Apply complex expressions over your dataset's existing fields to extract new features.

  4. [Creating metrics (historical profiles)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/creating-metrics)

Generate a large number of profiles and include time-based features.

  5. [Using PQL in features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features)

Learn how to use the Pulse Query Language (PQL) in map and metrics operators to define the "formula" of the new features.

  6. [Following best practices for plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/best-practices-for-plans)

Use best practices to organize map and metrics operators within a plan in a meaningful way.

  7. [Creating the data source with the features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/creating-the-data-source)

Run the plan to create the data source that contains the new fields.

# Creating Lists and Adding List Items

A list stores items, for example blocked credit card numbers. A list can be used in rules to check if at your organization a field of a transaction is known for a specific characteristic. For example, the blocked credit card numbers are known for being correlated with fraud.

This page describes how to create a new list, and how to add list items to a list.

## Creating a listâ

To create a new list, complete the following steps:

  1. Go to the **Lists** tab and add  a new list.

The **New List** form is prompted, as shown in the following image: 

  2. **Name** your list.

  3. Select the **Value Type** , which determines what kind of list items the list will store.

     1. **Simple lists** consist of list items that contain data only in one field: the key. For example, a suspicious country list is a simple list if the only information that the list stores is the country code of suspicious countries.

     2. **Complex lists** consist of list items that have more than one field. The key field is still the identifier of the list item, but additionally there are other value fields. For example, a suspicious country list is a complex list if besides the country code (key), it stores a riskiness rate as well.

If you want to create a complex list, you need to specify the **Fields** that the list will store together with the key.

  4. Select the **Key Type** , which determines if the unique key for the list items is a _string_ or a _number_.

  5. Select a **Case Matching** option: _Sensitive_ or _Insensitive_. These options are only available for lists with the key type selected as string. After saving the form, the case matching cannot be edited.

Case-insensitive lists

In case-insensitive lists, the match between the list items and the value of the field of events processed by rules accessing this list is done by comparing case-insensitive strings. For example, consider a case-insensitive list of countries with the item _Portugal_ (i.e. upper case). Imagine that you are processing transactions with a country field and a given transaction has an entry with a string _portugal_ (i.e. lower case). In this case, a rule comparing these two values will be triggered.

  6. Enter a **Key Label**. This is the name of the field that is the list's key.

  7. Select a **Multi-Tenancy** option: _Global_ , _By Tenant_ , or _By Tenant Group_. This attribute controls who has access to the list items. In the case of options _By Tenant_ or _By Tenant Group_ , items added to a list of a tenant or tenant group are available only in that tenant or tenant group.

This attribute cannot be changed after saving the form.

  8. Use the  button to save your list preferences and start adding list items.




## Adding list itemsâ

To add items to a list, perform the following steps:

  1. Go to the **Lists** tab and select the list you want to edit.

  2. If you are adding items to a multi-tenant list, then use the **View as Tenant** or **View as Tenant Group** dropdown box to select the tenant or tenant group to which you want to add items.

  3. Add  items to the list.

By default, new list items are enabled and active, if no dates are set in the **Active from - To** fields.




### Importing list itemsâ

Instead of adding each list item individually, you can import list items in bulk from a CSV file.

To do so, complete the following steps:

  1. Go to the **Lists** tab and select the list you want to edit.

  2. If you are adding items to a multi-tenant list, then use the **View as Tenant** or **View as Tenant Group** dropdown box to select the tenant or tenant group to which you want to add items.

  3. Select .

  4. Upload or drag-and-drop the CSV file that contains the list items you want to import.

The fields and data type in the file must match the fields and data types of the list in Pulse. To see the CSV file format Pulse expects, add a couple of items manually to the list, and export them. Then examine the export file for the necessary info.

  5. Select if you want to **Add items** or **Replace all items**.

     1. The **Add items** option adds every item in the file, overriding any existing key.

If you select the **Do not overwrite duplicated items** checkbox, Pulse tries to add all items that are in the file. If any of the keys already exists, the import is cancelled with an error. Select this option if you want to avoid updating existing items.

     2. The **Replace all items** option deletes the whole list, and creates only the list items defined in the import file.

  6. **Save** the import settings to start the import and return to the list. Pulse will show a notification when the import is finished.




### Reviewing list changesâ

By default, changes to lists can only be reviewed after the fact. However, it is possible to set up 4-eye check functionality for lists, which places edits made to lists into a review queue, and only applies the changes if they are approved by a second person. To learn more, see [Reviewing List Changes - Four Eyes Check](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/reviewing-list-changes).

# Creating or Updating the Rules Project

Rules projects group rules that target the same variable of a specific data source, and can be executed in sequence.

This topic describes the following options for ensuring that your Pulse has a rules project for the rules:

  * Creating a new rules project
  * Updating an existing rules project in case you already had one before you added new features to the data source



## Creating a rules projectâ

If you don't have a rules project for the rules yet, create one by executing the following actions:

  1. In the Data Science  tab, add  a new rules project.

  2. Give a **Name** to your rules project.

  3. Select _Advanced_ for the **Type** of your rules project.

  4. Choose the **Origin Schema** on which the rules will be based.

  5. Choose a **Target Variable** which defines which field from the data source will be the target variable (e.g. Fraud/Not Fraud). You can target any categorical field of the data source.

  6. Create the list of **Actions** that will be possible to execute when the rules are triggered. For instance 'Block' and 'Accept'.

You can add parameters to pass information to the action you added. Use the  button next to it to do so.

  7. Select the **Multi-Tenancy** option that will be applied to the rules project:

     1. _Global_ : disables multi-tenancy for this rules project.

     2. _Duplicated for Tenant_ : applies all the rules to all the tenants included in the application.

     3. _By Tenant_ : allows selection of the tenants to which the rules will be applied.

Tenant alert

Tenant accounts should be created in the system, otherwise you can not manage multi-tenant rules projects.




## Updating an existing rules projectâ

If you already have a rules project for your rules, and you added new features in the previous step, the rules project needs to be updated to reflect the schema changes. Namely, the schema associated to the rules project has to be changed to the schema of the data source which contains the new feature.

You can do this as follows:

  1. Go to the **Data Science** tab.
  2. In the **Rules Project** section, select the configure  option next to the rules project.
  3. For the **Origin Schema** , select the Data Source that contains the features you want to include in the rules.
  4. Save the changes.

# Creating a Rule

A rule, when used in a workflow, evaluates if a certain condition is true for the current transaction. According to the result, the rule can trigger actions in the workflow like rejecting or accepting a transaction, and contribute to the score of the transaction.

The following sections describe how to create a new rule, or edit an existing one after adding new features.

## How toâ

To create a new rule from scratch, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select an existing rules project, and add  a new rule.

  2. Give your rule a **Name** , and describe it in a **Comment**.

  3. Write the [Rule Definition Language (RDL) expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/operators-in-rules) for the condition of the rule. If a transaction matches the condition, it triggers the rule.

For example, to check if the current transaction's card number is on the watch list, the condition is:
         
         CardWatchList.contains(TokenizedCardPAN)  
         

Best practice

Although it is possible to write complex expressions in the condition of a rule, it is recommended to [create a feature](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features) instead, using a map or metrics operator in a plan.

You have access to **Lists** in the drop-down menu as shown in the figure below. If the type of your rules project is _Global_ , you only have access to global lists. If the type of rules project is _Duplicated for Tenant_ or _By Tenant_ , you have access to all lists.

Rule Definition Language

Check the following pages to learn how to write expressions for rules:

     * [Operators in rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/operators-in-rules)
     * [Data types in rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/data-types-in-rules)
     * [Built-in UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/built-in-udfs)

  4. Optionally, write an **Explanation**. The explanation can be shown to users who review transactions when the rule is triggered. You can type the explanation text and use data field values, list items, and variable values to give details to the reader.

  5. The following four configuration options are available for you to control what consequences it has when the rule is triggered. They can be combined according to your business needs:

     1. Optionally, you can select which **Actions** of the rules project will the rule generate when triggered in a workflow.

Actions work like events, to which a custom workflow service can listen. For example, you can trigger the _Suspicious-transaction_ action in the current rule. If you have a custom workflow service listening to the _Suspicious-transaction_ action, the custom workflow service can send that transaction to an external review system for analysis. A typical example of this is the Alert Storage Service, which sends the suspicious transactions to Case Manager.

     2. Optionally, in the **Mark As** field you can select a value for the target variable field. This way you can mark an event as potentially fraudulent, or as a high risk transaction - depending on your use case and the target variable of your rules project.

If you don't select a value in the _Mark As_ field, the rule won't give any value to the target variable.

Note that the possible values of the _Mark As_ field come from the field that you set as target variable when [creating the rules project](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-or-updating-the-rules-project).

     3. Optionally, you can set how the triggering of a rule generates a **Score Contribution** to a workflow outcome.

The **Score** of the current rule will be combined with other scoring elements of the same workflow: models and other blocks of rules. The **Weight** you assign to the current rule can be taken into consideration when calculating the final score.

     4. In **Control Flow** , set how the workflow should proceed after triggering and processing the current rule. For example, you can choose to immediately stop the workflow when the current rule is triggered and processed.

This is especially useful when you want to ignore the evaluation of further rules, or even abort the rest of the workflow when a rule is triggered. Available options are as follows:

        * **Continue**

The execution continues with the next rule in the rule block. If there is no other rule in the rule block, then the workflow continues with the next workflow element.

        * **Stop Workflow**

The workflow execution stops. Actions resulting from the current rule will be triggered for the current event.

        * **Next Workflow Element**

No more rules are executed in this rule block. The execution continues with the next workflow element.

What happens to events after a workflow terminates?

The event is not lost. If the event storage is enabled in the workflow, once the event is out of the workflow it is stored in the database.




## Editing a rule after adding new featuresâ

If you added new features and want to include them in an existing rule, you just need to ensure that the origin schema of the rules project was updated. After that, the features will be available in the rules. You can edit the rule using the steps described in the previous section.

## Examples of rulesâ

This section gives generic examples of conditions used in rules.

### Countâ

The following rule uses a [feature](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features) called _Weekly_Count_per_Card_Pan_ , which is the number of transactions in the last week with the same PAN card as the current transaction. The rule is triggered if the same card has been used more than twenty times in the last week.
    
    
    Weekly_Count_per_Card_Pan >= 20  
    

### Mismatchâ

The following rule uses two [features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features) that calculate the city of the customer's address, and of the device of the transaction. The rule triggers if the two cities don't match.
    
    
    Customer_Addr_City != Device_IP_City  
    

### UDF callâ

To call a [User-Defined Function](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/built-in-udfs) (UDF) from RDL, the administrator has to define an alias for the UDF class in the Pulse properties.

The following rule calls a UDF that returns the keyboard distance of a string. The rule fires if the user's email address seems suspicious because the characters in it are very close to one another on a standard QWERTY keyboard.
    
    
    Strings.keyboardDistance(user_email_addr, 2) <= 5  
    

### Listâ

The following rule condition uses a list. The rule fires if the IP address of the device associated to the current transaction is on a watch list.
    
    
    IP_WatchList.contains(Device_IP ?? "")  // Tip: coalesce the argument to ensure it's not null.  
    

### Complex listâ

The following example shows the usage of a PosNeg list:
    
    
    PosNeg_List.contains(Email_addr) and PosNeg_List[Email_addr].status == "block"  
    

## Using rule templatesâ

Rule templates allow to create several rules with the same pattern, but with different values in custom variables. For example, you can define a rule template that checks if the transaction occurred in a certain currency, and the transaction amount is over a certain limit value. In this case, the currency and the limit value can be a parameter of the rule template. Then, you can instantiate this template with a different value for each country. This way you can have have several instances of the same logic but with different parameters. Using a template in these cases avoids errors and allows you to maintain all the rule instances centrally in the template.

### Example for rule templatesâ

Let's see an example for checking if the transaction occurred in a certain currency, and the transaction amount is over a certain limit value.

The rule template, with two input parameters:

A rule that creates an instance of this template with a specific currency and a specific transaction amount:

# Deploying Rules to the Production Environment

This topic gives a summary of how the rules are deployed to the development environment. Since the deployment is not performed by data scientists, the steps are not covered in detail in this document. The description gives only an overview of what happens next, as the planning process needs input from data scientists as well.

The deployment process of rules is different depending on whether this is the first deployment, or an iteration over an existing deployment. The following sections give a summary of both processes.

## First-time deploymentâ

The following sections describe the steps of deploying a project to production for the first time.

### Planning the workflow and the outcome combinatorsâ

A workflow defines the journey of the transaction through Pulse.

A typical workflow contains a combination of the following steps:

  1. Data input from the main data stream.
  2. Data input from enrichers (e. g. card-related information).
  3. Calculating new features based on the existing data fields.
  4. Applying blocks of rules.
  5. Running the scoring service with a model, i.e. applying a model on the data, thus contributing to the final score.
  6. Running custom services. A custom workflow service is custom Java code that performs a specific task.
  7. At the end of the workflow Pulse runs an outcome combinator that is configured for calculating the final outcome and score.



#### Outcome combinatorsâ

Outcome combinators define how to calculate the partial and final decisions and scores for an outcome in a workflow or sandbox evaluation. Outcome combinators take into account the triggered rules and applied models to provide a combination of all partial scores.

Pulse has a built-in outcome combinator, which calculates a weighted average of all the scores that the transaction got while traveling through the workflow. However, you can develop your own Java code to use it as a custom outcome combinator. This way, when a transaction travels through the workflow, the final outcome will be calculated by the custom outcome combinator according to your definition. Each of the triggered rules and applied models can be taken into consideration in a different way, and with a different weight.

### Transferring resources and creating the workflowâ

In the previous step, engineers planned the journey of an event through Pulse. In this step, this journey is implemented in the form of a workflow of Pulse.

To create the workflow, engineers first export the resources (schemas, plans, rules, models) from the data science environment, and import them to the production environment. Then they create the necessary services (input adapters, enrichment services, outcome combinators, etc.) and use them in the workflow, implementing the journey planned in the previous step.

## Updating an existing deploymentâ

To deploy the rule changes from the data science environment to production, engineers first have to export the resources that changed (schemas, plans, rules projects, etc.). Then they import these resources in the production environment.

In some cases, while data scientists are working in the data science environment on the rules, in the production environment changes may have occurred. For instance, adding a new self-service rule, or adding a new feature to a plan in production. In this case, before transferring the changes from the data science environment to production, the data science environment needs to be brought to the same state as the production environment. The best approach to perform this is to have a freeze period on the production environment, while no new changes are introduced until the resource transfer is done.

After the resource transfer, engineers update the production workflow to use the new version of the plans and rules you created, and they publish the new version of the application.
