# Evaluating Rules Using a Snapshot

You can evaluate your rules to assess their effectiveness, by analyzing a rule snapshot evaluation. This topic describes how to create an evaluation for a snapshot.

Multi-tenant rules projects

The snapshot evaluation is not available in multi-tenant rules projects.

## Prerequisiteâ

The following process presumes that you have a historical dataset where the feedback about the target variable's final value is saved in a separate field. This field is called the feedback field.

## How toâ

To run an evaluation of your rules over a historical dataset, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select the rules project that you want to evaluate.

  2. The following step is to clone your rules project.

The objective of this step is to ensure that changes that you do merely for the performance assessment do not affect the rules project that you want to deploy in production later on.

To clone the rules project, execute the following steps:

     1. If in your rules project you did not create a rule snapshot yet, [add a rule snapshot](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-a-rule-snapshot) now.

     2. Create a new rules project from the rule snapshot using the  button in the list of snapshots. This new rules project is where you create and test your rules.

     3. In the **Data Science** tab, in the Rules Projects area find the newly created rules project and use the  button to configure it.

     4. Change the **Target Variable** from the outcome field to the feedback field. For example, the outcome field can be the _Decision_ field, with the possible values _Approve_ , _Block_ , _Review_. Change it to the feedback field, which is the one that gives the information on whether the transaction is Fraud (e.g. received a fraud chargeback or was marked as Fraud by analysts), or Not Fraud. **Save** the changes.

     5. Open the rules project. Go to every enabled rule and edit the rule by updating the **Mark as** field. Change the field to mimic production. For example, if it is a block rule, select _Mark As_ , and select the value that the rule is supposed to act on, e. g. _Fraud_ , _Not Fraud_ , _Suspicious_ or _Legitimate_. This information is what allows the system to measure the performance of the rules.

     6. **Save** the rules project.

     7. [Create a new snapshot](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-a-rule-snapshot) for the cloned rules project. Enable and sort the rules for the snapshot according to the project preferences.

  3. Open the rule snapshot of the cloned rules project, and use the  button to start creating an evaluation for the snapshot.

Evaluation performance

Evaluations run distributed in a Spark cluster, thus being able to efficiently process very large volumes of data in consistently short amounts of time.

  4. Define the following configurations for the evaluation:

     * Select the **Data Source** on which you want to test your rules.
     * Define a **Filter**. During the evaluation, rules will be applied only to those instances that match the defined filter.
     * Define an **Additional** **Cost Field** , such as _Amount_ , if it makes sense in your scenario.
     * Define the **Breakdowns** of the charts that will show the evaluation: select **Fields** and **Values** for which you want Pulse to break down and explore the data. Pulse will calculate metrics for every combination of all selected values.
     * In the **Output Results** field you can use the **Export Evaluation** checkbox to export the output into a file. The output file will contain the individual rule contribution.
  5. Use the  button to start the job that calculates the metrics for the evaluation. The progress is shown next to the rule snapshot's name.

  6. When Pulse finished to calculate the evaluation metrics (Recall, FPR, Precision, and so on), analyze the results in the snapshot, on the following tabs:

     * **Block Evaluation** : shows the metrics calculated for the entire set of rules.
     * **Block Rule Evaluation** : shows the metrics per rule, but taking into account the Control Flow field set for each rule (Stop Workflow, Continue Workflow, Next Workflow Element). For example, if the first rule applied to the data is set to Stop Workflow, none of the remaining rules will be evaluated against transactions that triggered the first rule.
     * **Individual Rule Evaluation** : shows the metrics calculated for each rule individually, for each breakdown field combination (aka. series) of the evaluation. This tab presents evaluation results as if each rule runs individually, without taking into consideration the _Control Flow_ option and always assuming the _Continue Workflow_ option. By default, if more than one rule having the option _Mark As_ are triggered by the same transaction, then the first triggered rule's value prevails.
  7. You can show different evaluation metrics. To do so, use the drop-downs next to X-Axis and Y-Axis below the graph. To show different evaluation metrics in the Results table, use the **Choose Metrics** button.




## What to look for in the analysisâ

Each business is different, and each scenario requires a different type of analysis. Still, there are some simple things that you can always check when looking at the metrics included in the snapshot evaluation:

  * Does the current **block of rules** meet the expectations regarding metrics that are important to my business? The list of important metrics depends on the business scenario, but Recall, Precision, and FPR are good candidates to look at.

  * Check the **Alert Rate** metric for the rule block and for the individual rules. Does it look healthy? Does a rule trigger too many times, compared to your experience on the field?

  * If you exported the individual rule contribution into an output file (see Output Result field), you can check which rules triggered for each event.

This can help you to understand why a rule is performing differently from what you expected. It's also useful for validating whether or not the rules are catching the attacks they are designed to catch, by checking if they triggered for the corresponding events.

The output file is a .csv file stored in the path you defined in the Output Result option. For each event, the file contains a field called _Overall_ , which shows if the event triggered any rule.

In addition it contains one field for each rule, which shows if the event triggered that particular rule. A value of 1 indicates that the rule triggered, and a value of 0 indicates the contrary.

  * The **breakdown field** values can help you to identify when a threshold value needs to be fine-tuned. Does a certain value trigger too many alerts?




## Adding custom evaluation metricsâ

In addition to the metrics shown by default when assessing the rules performance, you can add your custom metrics. To do so, perform the following steps:

  1. Select the options menu  in your Pulse application.
  2. Select the **Evaluation Metrics** option.
  3. Add an evaluation metric to your project by defining a function that receives the following data:
     1. The number of True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP) and False Negatives (FN).
     2. The cost-TP, -TN, -FP and -FN. The cost field variants are based on a data field in the event that represents an amount, typically the transaction amount in a fraud detection scenario, rather than using a count-based approach.

# Evaluating Rules with Sandbox Evaluation

This topic describes how to analyze rule performance using sandbox evaluation results.

## How toâ

To analyze the sandbox evaluation results, go to the **Data Science** tab. From the **Sandbox Evaluations** list select the sandbox evaluation that you want to analyze.

## Result by Scoreâ

The **Result by Score** tab focuses on the field of the **Outcome Score** and the real final label. Based on that particular field, this allows you to understand the performance of your sandbox evaluation. Therefore, you can understand how the system behaves independently of the outcome decision that was specified on the outcome decision field. For example, it will help you decide whether to change the score threshold for the final decision.

In the **Result by Score** tab, you can perform the following actions:

  1. Analyze the **ROC Curve** for the selected evaluation.

Exact values

Hover the mouse pointer over the plot line to inspect the exact values for the **Recall** and **FPR** metrics and the respective **Threshold**.

Cost-based Metrics

If you define a **Cost Field** , then the **ROC Curve** will also plot the values for _Cost-Recall_ vs _Cost-FPR_.

  2. Configure the **X/Y Plot** to display a curve for any **X-Axis** and **Y-Axis**.

Exact values

Hover the mouse pointer over the plot line to inspect the exact values for the **X-Axis** and **Y-Axis** metrics and the respective **Threshold**.

  3. During the creation of a sandbox evaluation, you can select the breakdown for the metrics. Therefore, here you can see all the values for the metrics of the segmentation and its combinations. You can also change the threshold.

  4. Use the **View ROC curve** option to see which of the breakdown metrics can be seen in the ROC curve.

  5. You can also see the metrics per service for all the resources the sandbox evaluation has. This is useful for understanding the performance computation times of the resources analyzed in the sandbox. It helps you to grasp the performance gains or losses you will experience in your live workflow and evaluate the trade-offs.

For instance, you can identify whether a rules project takes too long (in the **Ind. Avg.**) whilst not adding much to the performance (by analyzing **Recall** and **FPR** metrics), therefore allowing you to consider whether to keep it.

  6. Export the results to a CSV file, if desired.




## Result by Outcomeâ

By analyzing the **Result by Outcome** , you can understand how the system behaves regarding the outcome decision that was specified on the outcome decision field. It works similarly to the **Result by Score** , but it does not provide a movable threshold. You can learn more about the performance of your Sandbox evaluation by analyzing these results:

  1. Select the outcome values to be shown either if _True_ or _False_.
  2. You can export the results to a CSV, both **Per Breakdown** and **Per Services**.

# Reviewing Rule Changes - Four Eyes Check

When creating or editing rules, you may want to ask other colleagues to review your work to ensure rule safety and high quality. If four eyes check is enabled in your Pulse environment, you can request a review directly in Pulse.

This page describes both sides of the review: how to request a rule review from a peer, and how to give feedback if you are requested to review rules.

## Prerequisitesâ

To allow reviews of rule changes, an administrator must configure the following:

  * The `fourEyeCheck.enabled` property must be set to `true`. After this property is set to _true_ , you need to refresh the Pulse page in your browser to be able to request reviews.



Optionally, for the notification emails to work as designed, the following settings can be configured as well. However, if you don't intend to use the notification emails, these can be skipped:

  * The SMTP properties must be configured, so that the notification emails are properly sent.
  * The `pulse.global.fourEyeCheck.notifications.email.from` property: sets the email address from which Pulse sends the notification email to the reviewers. By default, it's [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#f9898c958a9cb99f9c9c9d839890d79a9694).
  * The `pulse.global.ui.host` property is used to configure the URL where Pulse runs, and by default it's set to `http://localhost:8080/`. The notification email contains a link to the rule snapshot that needs to be reviewed, and the link starts with the URL set in this property. If the default value is not set to the actual value, the link in the email won't work.



Get in touch with Feedzai to set up four eye check in your Pulse environment.

### Set up a static e-mail to receive all Four Eyes Check notificationsâ

In addition to direct notifications sent to the author and reviewer in four eyes checks, Pulse allows setting up a static e-mail address which will receive all four eyes check notifications. This allows Pulse users to review the open revisions more thoroughly, and thus catch errors that might otherwise be missed. Note that the recipient of these emails will not be addressed directly, as they will be merely copies of the notifications sent to the author and reviewer of the corresponding four eyes check.

Notifying multiple users

This e-mail address can be set to that of a mailing list, which allows multiple users to receive every four eyes notifications.

To enable notifications for Pulse rules, provide the e-mail address via the following Pulse property: `pulse.global.fourEyeCheck.notifications.email.staticreviewer`.

## Purpose of peer reviewsâ

Ensuring every change is reviewed by a second pair of eyes helps prevent unwanted or unplanned changes from being published.

Snapshots that were not approved by a peer may still be published live, but the user importing the snapshot must explicitly confirm such a control bypass.

info

If the Four Eyes Check feature is enabled, changes by all users (even those with the approval role) are subject to a review from a peer. In other words, users cannot self-approve their own changes.

## Request a reviewâ

To request a review of a snapshot, execute the following steps:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, go to the rules project that contains the rule snapshot. Under **Snapshots** , select the snapshot that you created.

  2. Use the **Request Review** button to submit the snapshot for review.

  3. In the **Submit Snapshot for Review** window, fill in the following fields:

     1. **Change Description** : Describe the changes you made to rules, data fields and lists. Include the name of the snapshot that contains the rule's previous state for reference, if there is such a snapshot. This will let the reviewer know the name of the snapshot they should compare yours to. Usually it is the snapshot that was last published live.
     2. **Notify User(s)** : Type the name of the Pulse users that you want to invite to review the snapshot. In this field, you can select only users that have an email address configured in Pulse. If you don't find a user, contact your Pulse administrator.
  4. Use the **Submit** button to send the snapshot for review and request the selected users to review the changes included in the snapshot.

  5. As a result, the users you selected will receive an email with the following information:

     1. Review submitted on your behalf.
     2. The name of the rules project.
     3. The name of the snapshot.
     4. A link to the snapshot.
  6. You can follow up on the status of the review next to the snapshot's name:

  7. You will receive an email notification when the snapshot is accepted or rejected.




## Review rulesâ

If you are asked to review a rule snapshot, perform the following steps:

  1. Open the link from your email, or go to Pulse in the **Data Science** tab and look for the snapshot submitted for review.

  2. If there is a previous snapshot that you want to compare it with, use the **Compare with another Snapshot** button to see the differences.

  3. When you have decided whether the snapshot should be published or not, select the **Review Snapshot** button.

  4. Add your feedback in the **Explanation** field, and select the **Accept** or **Reject** button according to your decision about the snapshot.

  5. The user who requested this review will be notified of your decision via email.

# Rules Glossary

Here you can find a short definition for the most important concepts that this guide refers to.

### Listâ

A list stores items, for example blacklisted credit card numbers. It can be used in rules, to check if at your organization a field of a transaction is known for a specific characteristic. For example, in your organization the blacklisted credit card numbers are known for being correlated with fraud.

Lists can apply to the entire Pulse environment, or a single tenant, or a group of tenants.

You can set the expiration date of a list item, meaning that after a certain date the list item will be inactive. It doesnât get deleted from the list, but it gets disabled. Rules donât consider disabled list items.

### Outcome combinatorâ

Outcome combinators define how workflows and sandbox evaluations calculate the partial and final decisions and scores for an outcome. The default outcome combinator calculates a weighted average. However, you can develop your own outcome combinator service.

### Planâ

Plans define a transformation flow of one data source into another data source. In a plan it is possible to add, update and remove fields, calculate metrics on the data, and even join two data sources.

They are useful to systematize data cleaning, data processing and feature engineering, both in a data science pipeline and in production.

A plan doesn't have any data bound to it, only the data schema. To actually compute the output data source it is necessary to run the plan; see plan execution.

### Plan executionâ

When your plan is ready, you can test it by running it. Running the plan generates a plan execution and an output data source. A plan execution represents a snapshot of the plan at the moment it was executed. You can analyze the performance of a plan by looking at the statistics in the plan execution.

To deploy a plan to production, for example a features plan, you must run it in advance and create a plan execution. This means that you must always test and sign off on a plan for production before it can be deployed.

### Ruleâ

A rule is an elementary part of the real-time scoring system. A rule defines a set of consequences that happen if the current event of the workflow satisfies a certain condition. The consequences can be a combination of the following:

  * Making an outcome decision about the event, such as marking a transaction as fraud.
  * Contributing to the score of the event.
  * Calling actions, which are asynchronous notifications. Custom services catch the action calls, and as a result they perform a specific task. You have to implement custom services using Java.
  * Controlling the workflow, by determining what happens with it after the action is executed. You can continue with the next rule, or stop the workflow, or jump to the next workflow element.



### Rule snapshotâ

A rule snapshot represents a static picture of a set of rules. It contains an evaluation of the included rules, which lets you assess the rule performance.

To use a block of rules in a workflow, you must create a snapshot about the rules first. Running a rule evaluation for the snapshot ensures that you always test and sign off rule blocks for production before they can be used.

### Rule templateâ

Rule templates allow to reuse the rule definition in several rules. Sometimes it is useful to define the same rule with different parameters several times. For example, you may want to generate alerts if the total transaction amount for a card number in the last 4 hours is above a tenant-specific threshold. In this case, you don't have to copy and paste the rule's whole code for each tenant. You can create a rule template with the rule's code using a parameter for the threshold. Then you can instantiate that template in a rule, using the parameter to inject the right value.

### Rules projectâ

A rules project contains a group of rules that target the same variable of a specific data source, and can be executed in sequence.

Additionally, rules projects can contain the following components:

  * Rule templates, which make it easier to create many similar rules.
  * Rule snapshots, which serve to evaluate the performance of rules, and to sign them off for usage.



### Schemaâ

A schema describes the available data fields of a data source, as well as their types.

### Tenantâ

Tenants are useful for partners of Feedzai, to separate their customers' data. Each tenant can represent a customer, having access to that tenant's data exclusively.

### Tenant groupâ

Tenants are organized into tenant groups. They help partners of Feedzai to manage similar tenants in a centalized way. For example, they can apply the same configurations to all tenants in a group.

### Tokenizerâ

The Tokenizer is a component of Pulse that transforms sensitive information (e. g. customer name and credit card number) into tokens that can be shared without security risks. Data tokenization creates a more secure system that complies with PCI-DSS security standards.

### Workflowâ

Workflows represent the life cycle of an event through the system. They define the path that information traverses between components that may filter and/or transform the event, so that Pulse can calculate decisions and scores.

# Reviewing Rule Changes in a Snapshot

Rule snapshots capture the current state of the rules in a rules project. In addition, snapshots represent a unit of rules that is deployable to other environments.

If you edited existing rules, you may want to validate if you made the right changes, before using the new rule version. This topic describes how you can compare rules in two different snapshots of Pulse, to validate if you have made the changes you planned to.

The same procedure can be used for audit purposes, if you want to understand what changed in the rules compared to an earlier state.

## Prerequisitesâ

A rule snapshot is available for comparison if the following conditions are true:

  * The snapshot was created in Pulse version 20.0 or later.
  * The snapshot was created for a rule project that is not stateful.



## How toâ

To compare the rules in two snapshots, execute the following steps.

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, select the rules project that the snapshots were created from.
  2. In the **Snapshots** area, select the snapshot that you want to review.
  3. Select the **Compare with Snapshot** button, which takes you to the Compare Snapshots page.
  4. In the **With** field, select the other snapshot you want the first to be compared with. Typically, this second snapshot is an older version.
  5. In the **Snapshot Comparison** area, you can see the list of the rules included in the snapshots, and what changed from one to the other. The following statuses are possible:
     * **No change** : the rule is present in both snapshots, in an identical form.

     * **Deleted** : a rule that existed in the second snapshot isn't present anymore.

     * **New** : a new rule that didn't exist in the second snapshot.

     * **Edited** : a rule that is present in both snapshots, but with different content.

  6. To see a side-by-side comparison of the two versions of an edited rule in the two snapshots, select the rule. The pane below the Snapshot Comparison area displays the two versions.
  7. In addition, if the rule order is different in the two snapshots, you see this stated at the top of the Snapshot Comparison list.



## Learn moreâ

Learn more about [auditing in Pulse](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/audit), and how to [investigate changes and user actions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/investigating-changes-and-user) using the audit logs.

# Rules for Advanced Users

This page provides advanced examples of using Pulse to write [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules), via a selection of use cases.

The Examples are not Production Code

Note that the examples were simplified to better showcase the concepts and constructs of RDL. The code available in this page may not cover all the cases of each scenario and should not be used without review in Production environments.

## Access to Historical Dataâ

In this example we will see a use-case where we need to access historical data. Let us say we want to detect three consecutive transactions with an amount greater than $1000 that occurred in the last two hours.

The first thing to do is to write some auxiliary variables. These will contain the main logic that will be used in the condition block.

Variables
    
    
    // Collect all transactions in a two hours window  
    window2hours = event[every 3 tuples for 2 hours where amount &gt;= 1000];  
      
    maybeFraud = match  
      if (event.amount &lt; 1000) then // This breaks the consecutive &gt;= $1000 transactions.  
        window2hours.clear();  
        return false;  
      else if (window2hours.size () == 3) then // We got 3 transactions &gt;= $1000 within 2 hours.  
        return true;  // We got 3 transactions in our 2 hours window. Maybe that is fraud.  
      else  
        return false; // Still no fraud.  
    

We start by declaring a window where events will stay for 2 hours, since that is our time-span. Also, that will contain at most 3 events that specify the `amount >= 1000` predicate. Every other event will not be part of the window.

So, every time a new event arrives, it will either enter the window or not. Either way, we still have to decide what to do with this event. This leaves us with three possible scenarios:

  1. **The event has an amount of less that $1000** \- This breaks our requirement of three consecutive transactions of more than $1000. In this case, we must explicitly clear the window, because previous transactions of less than $1000 can no longer be taken into consideration for our fraud pattern.
  2. **The event has an amount greater or equal than $1000 and the window already has three events** \- This represents the fraud pattern we are trying to detect: three consecutive transactions over $1000 over a two hours window.
  3. **The event has an amount greater or equal then $1000 and the window still has less than three events** \- The current event contributes to our pattern, but it is still not the third consecutive transaction over $1000.



On each incoming event, after we have gone through all possible scenarios, the **`maybeFraud`** variable will be **true** if the pattern has been found or **false** otherwise. The condition will be a simple check on this variable:

Condition
    
    
    maybeFraud  
    

## Using Simple Lists to Group Dataâ

The most common case for using a simple [List](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) is to maintain lists of items and then check for the existence of a specific item. For example, to maintain a list of blacklisted card numbers:

Figure 1. Creating a New Simple List for Blacklisted Card Numbers Figure 2. Adding Items to the Card Blacklist

To check if a card is in a list write the condition as follows:

How to check if a card is in a List
    
    
    card_blacklist.contains(event.card_number)  
    

Explicitly iterating over Lists is not recommended

If you find yourself wanting to explicitly iterate over a List (e.g., using filter, all, etc) consider rewriting the rule, as this is highly inefficient as Lists are optimized for contains/lookup operations.

## Using Complex Lists to Efficiently Store Common Patternsâ

Imagine that it is necessary to block certain card numbers for certain countries. Suppose for example that we want to block 379867957393437 in USA and Canada and 340735948409065 in Spain and Italy. One possible approach would be to code this directly in RDL:
    
    
    // Variables  
    matchCard3437 = event.cardnumber == "379867957393437" and  
      (event.country == "USA" or event.country == "CANADA");  
    matchCard9065 = event.cardnumber == "340735948409065" and  
      (event.country == "SPAIN" or event.country == "ITALY");  
      
    // Condition  
    matchCard3437 or matchCard9065  
    

There are several problems with this approach:

  * It does not scale well as you need to add more card numbers and countries
  * It makes the process of maintaining the rule error prone
  * It does not allow to an Administrator to create a permission for a specific user to add or remove credit card numbers (and not change the rule logic)



The way to address these issues is to use the [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists), which allow us to create a list with the card number to blocked country list mapping.

First we want a complex list that has the card number as the key and has a blocked countries list as a field:

Figure 3. Creating a Complex List to Store Card Number to Blocked Countries List Pairs

Note that we choose the type of the key as string. This is a good idea for credit card numbers because it allows you to have hashed card numbers as keys.

Choosing the Correct List Type (Simple or Complex)

Complex lists are a good choice when it is necessary to perform lookups because they are internally implemented as a Map. Simple lists on the other hand are more suited for contains and exists operations because they are internally implemented as a Set.

Next we need to create some items:

Figure 4. Adding an Item to a Complex List Figure 5. Adding Another Item to a Complex List

Once we got the list setup, we can use it to rewrite our rule, resulting in a much more simple and maintainable code:
    
    
    // Variables  
    cardnum_entry = cardnumber__coutry[event.cardnumber];  
      
    // Condition  
    // We first need to check if there is any entry for the given card number  
    // and then we check if the blocked countries list contains the country   
    // where the current transaction originated from  
    cardnum_entry != null and cardnum_entry.blocked_countries.contains(event.country);  
    

## Correlating Multiple Transactions to Detect Known Fraud Patternsâ

To access past transactions a window can be used. In RDL, a window  is a time ordered set of transactions that has a range, which is either numerical or temporal.

Example 3: match transactions of 1$ followed by a transaction in a different location
    
    
    // Variables  
    // Get the last 2 transactions for the current card number  
    last2Events = event[2 tuples by card_number];  
    previous = last2Events.at(1); // Collections in RDL start in index 1  
      
    // Condition  
    // The count check is necessary because the window may have 0, 1 or 2 events  
    (last2Events.count() == 2) and (previous.amount &lt;= 1) and (previous.locations != event.location)   
    

When it is necessary to correlate multiple transactions, try to write the rule by looking at past transactions instead of future ones. Instead of "The next transaction will be in the same location", think "The previous transaction was on the same location".

Since windows are just lists, it is possible to use the collection methods:

Example 4: match transactions that surpass a $1000/hour limit
    
    
    // Variables  
    // Get the last 1 hour of transactions for the current card number  
    last1hEvents = event[1 hour by card_number];  
      
    // Condition  
    last1hEvents.sum(amount) &gt; 1000  
    

Methods of Collections in RDL

Collections in RDL have several methods, including `all`, `any`, `contains`, `filter`, `count`, etc.

It is also possible to use lambdas:

Example 5: match 5 sequential transactions of the same card that have a low amount (< $5)
    
    
    // Variables  
    last5Events = event[5 tuples by card_number];  
      
    // Condition  
    last5Events.count() == 5 and lastEvents.all(e =&gt; e.amount &lt; 5)  
    

Lambdas Can Impact Performance Severely

Try to only use lambdas for collections whose size is known to be small (<100 elements) and prefer filtering in the window (using the **where** operator) to the filter method.

## Using Templates to Reuse Codeâ

Rule Templates allow to parameterize rules and as such are useful when it is necessary to have several instances of the same logic but with different parameters.

One example would be writing a rule to trigger an alert if the sum of amount of the last N minutes of a specific card and terminal type is more than Y. If you needed to write only one or two rules with this logic it would be perfectly acceptable to write it like:
    
    
    // Variables  
    lastEvents = event[10 minutes where terminaltype == &quot;ATM&quot; by cardnumber];  
      
    // Condition  
    lastEvents.sum(amount) &gt; 1000  
    

However repeating this several times is error prone and cumbersome.

Using templates, we replace the literal values by template parameters:
    
    
    // Variables  
    lastEvents = event[$nMin minutes where terminaltype == $terminaltype by cardnumber];  
      
    // Condition  
    lastEvents.sum(amount) &gt; $yDolars  
    

Then to create rules we select the template and fill in the specific values:

Figure 6. Reusing RDL Code with Templates

## Detect Repeated Transaction Attempts With the Same Location and Amountâ

A common pattern for fraudulent transactions is to make several transaction attempts in the same location or change the location after several attempts. For example:

  * Transaction 1, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: accept
  * Transaction 2, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: accept
  * Transaction 3, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: accept
  * Transaction 4, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: accept
  * Transaction 5, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: block



Or:

  * Transaction 1, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: accept
  * Transaction 2, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: accept
  * Transaction 3, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: accept
  * Transaction 4, Location = Lisbon, amount = 50: accept
  * Transaction 5, Location = Coimbra, amount = 50: block



The following RDL code detects such patterns by first checking if either all or just the first 4 events have the same location (_ev.location == first.location_) and secondly by making sure that that _all_ lambda always evaluates to true for the last event (_ev.uuid == event.uuid_):
    
    
    // Variables  
    lastEvents = event[5 tuples by card];  
    first = lastEvents.at(1);  
      
    // Condition  
    lastEvents.count() == 5 and  
        lastEvents.all(ev.location == first.location or ev.uuid == event.uuid)  
    

## Detect Transactions With a Considerable Amount After a 1$ Transaction in the Same Locationâ

A common pattern for fraudulent transactions is to make an initial test transaction with a low amount and then make transaction with a large amount. For example:

  * Transaction 1, Location = Lisbon, Amount = 1: accept
  * Transaction 2, Location = Lisbon, Amount = 200: block



The following RDL detects such a pattern by picking the last two events (for the current event card number) and checking if the location is the same in the two and if the respective amounts are in the ranges described before:
    
    
    // Variables  
    lastEvents = event[2 tuples by card];  
    first = lastEvents.at(1);  
      
    // Condition  
    event.amount &gt; 100 and lastEvents.count() == 2 and  
      first.amount &lt;= 1 and  
      first.location == event.location  
    

## Detect Repeated Transaction Attempts With Decreasing Amountsâ

A common pattern for fraudulent transactions is to try to make a transaction with a large amount, decrease it if it fails (usually by dividing the amount by 2 or 3) and try again. For example:

  * Transaction 1, amount = 1000: accept
  * Transaction 2, amount = 500: accept
  * Transaction 3, amount = 250: block



The following RDL detects such a pattern for a multiple of 2 by asserting if the first 2 events of the last 3 events (if there are 3 events in the window) are multiples of the current amount.
    
    
    // Variables  
    lastEvents = event[3 tuples by card];  
      
    // Condition  
    lastEvents.count() == 3 and  
      lastEvents.at(1) == event.amount * 4 and  
      lastEvents.at(2) == event.amount * 2  
    

## Detect Bursts of Transaction Attempts and Alert When the Transaction Comes Throughâ

A common pattern for fraudulent transactions is to make attempts at performing a given operation (e.g., buying some goods) until the transaction is accepted (trying a different CCV at each attempt).

Suppose that code = 5 means that the transaction failed and code = 10 means that the transaction was accepted.

One example of this pattern could be:

  * Transaction 1, Location = Lisbon, code = 5: no alert
  * Transaction 2, Location = Lisbon, code = 5: no alert
  * Transaction 3, Location = Lisbon, code = 10: alert



The following RDL detects such a pattern by first checking if the location is the same in all the transactions (to determine that the origin is the same) and then by checking that all the transactions have code 5 (failed) but the last (the current) which was accepted:
    
    
    // Variables  
    lastEvents = event[3 tuples by card];  
    firstEvent = lastEvents.at(1);  
      
    // Condition  
    lastEvents.count() == 3 and  
      lastEvents.all(  
        ev =&gt; ev.location == firstEvent.location and  
        (ev.code == 5 or (ev.uuid == event.uuid and ev.code == 10))  
      )

# Password recovery

Was this page helpful?Â 

If a user needs a new password, there are two options to reset it:

  * By the administrator, on the user profile, under **Administration** \- **Security** \- **Users**.
  * By the user.



The following chapter describes how users reset their password without involving an administrator.

## Password reset by the userâ

To reset your own password, perform the following steps:

  1. Open Pulse.

  2. On the login window, select **Forgot password?**

  3. Provide your username. If the user profile has an email address configured, Pulse sends an email to that address with a token, which is a number. It is possible to request a new token, 30 seconds after the last one. Only the last token is valid, and it has a configurable validity time. By default, tokens are valid during 1 hour after they are generated.

  4. In the **Token** field, enter the token you received via email.

  5. Type the new password in the **New password** field, and repeat the same password in the **Confirm password** field.




Limited number of tries

The number of tries to save a new password with a certain token is limited. Consider the password policy before continuing to change the password. If you exceed the configured limit to change the password with a certain token, you can request a new token and try again.

  6. Save the change using the **Change password** button. Pulse saves the change and logs you in.

# Signing in with Single Sign-On

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse supports Single Sign-On (SSO) which allows you to access various applications (i.e. to start a session) by signing in to only one of the applications. You can learn more about Pulse SSO in the [Single Sign-On](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/single-sign-on) page under the Administrator's Guide.

## Sign in Scenariosâ

Pulse supports **SP-initiated** sign-in.

This scenario is initiated by the Service Provider (SP) and occurs when you access a Pulse URL, and you are not signed in. You are redirected to a URL that is managed by the Identity Provider (IdP). In this IdP URL, you are prompted with a sign in form and after authentication you are automatically redirected back to the Feedzai URL. Check [Sign in via SP-initiated](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on/signing-in-via-sp-initiated).

## User Provisioningâ

With Pulse SSO, users are created by the concept of user provisioning. If you are signing in for the first time and if your account does not exists as a Pulse User, your account is created on-the-fly after being authorized by the IdP.

## Sign in as Administratorâ

The recommended method to create users in Pulse is by User Provisioning. However, Administrators can still sign in to Pulse using a static URL and then add new user accounts. Note that this option should only be used under special situation as the recommended method to add user accounts is by User Provisioning.

Check [Signing in as Pulse Administrator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on/signing-in-as-pulse-administrator).

## Sign outâ

One component associated with SSO is allowing users to sign out from all the applications at once (i.e. without having to sign out individually from all the applications). This is component is commonly referred to as Single Logout.

## Learn moreâ

Now that you have an overall picture of Pulse SSO you can check user guide details presented in the following sections:

  * [Signing in via SP-initiated](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on/signing-in-via-sp-initiated)
  * [Signing in as Pulse Administrator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on/signing-in-as-pulse-administrator)

# About Signing in with Two-Factor Authentication

Was this page helpful?Â 

Two-Factor Authentication (**2FA**) is a functionality that requires you to sign in with two pieces of information to verify your identity. **2FA** creates a more secure authentication system while complying with PCI-DSS security standards.

## Sign in stepsâ

When you access any Pulse URL, and you are not signed in yet, you are redirected to the main Pulse sign in form.

  1. In this form, insert your Username and Password and use the  button to continue to the authentication step.

  2. You are prompted with another form that requests a second step validation to access Pulse. Enter the PIN Code generated by the code generator that you are using on your mobile device, such as Google Authenticator. Use the  button to access Pulse.




Authentication failure

If you either introduce wrong credentials (username or password) or a wrong PIN Code, your are redirected to the first Sign in form (i.e. step 1) to start the sign in process again from the beginning. This occurs because 2FA provides authentication only if username/password/code are correct without giving any clue to which step the user failed. This is a 2FA requirement to comply with PCI-DSS security standards.

## Configuring 2FA on your deviceâ

To sign in with 2FA, a code generator application has to be configured on your mobile device(s). Pulse is agnostic to the application used to generate the code. As an example, the instructions to configure 2FA on your device using Google Authenticator are provided in page [Configuring Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/configuring-two-factor-authentication).

## Resetting 2FA on your deviceâ

There are a number of scenarios in which you might want to reset the **2FA** configuration on your mobile device. Check the page [Resetting Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/resetting-two-factor-authentication).

## Learn Moreâ

Learn more about **2FA** configurations:

  * [Configuring Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/configuring-two-factor-authentication)
  * [Resetting Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/resetting-two-factor-authentication)

# Automatic Application Repair

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse has an **Auto-Repair** functionality that monitors the state of the cluster and decides whether it needs to be repaired or not. If the application is in an invalid state, Pulse will automatically trigger repair actions on the respective components. Fully repairing the cluster might involve executing several fix actions in sequence.

This functionality is not designed to fix the entire application all at once. It rather focuses on maintaining a small number of state validation rules, which when triggered and composed, allow the overall system to converge to a stable state.

It is possible that the **Auto-Repair** triggers a fix to a problem that will not return the system to a stable state. However, it guarantees that the system will be one step closer to a stable state. When each step is finished, it will allow for more fixes to be issued until the stable state is reached.

## Fixing issuesâ

Pulse **Auto-Repair** consists in actions that aim at fixing the following issues:

  * **Under replication** : Pulse will ensure that there are at least as many App Engines as the configured replication factor. If an AppEngine crashes, Pulse will automatically launch a new AppEngine node until reaching the replication factor.
  * **Over replication** : Pulse will ensure that the number of AppEngines for a provided application does not exceed the configured replication factor. If Pulse detects that there are more nodes running the application than the number defined in the replication factor, then Pulse will shut down the application in as many nodes as required to adhere to the replication factor. Selecting which nodes to shut down is not deterministic.
  * **Inconsistent versions** : When different nodes are running different versions of the application, or are not running the expected version, Pulse will automatically try to publish the expected version. In most cases this is the latest stable published version. If the application is in a _bootstrapped_ state, then Pulse ensures that all AppEngines are in that state.



## Configuring Auto-Repairâ

To enable or disable the **Auto-Repair** , execute the following actions:

  1. In your Pulse application, use the  **Options** menu and select the **Edit** option.

  2. Toggle the **Auto-Repair** configuration accordingly:




When the **Auto-Repair** feature is taking action, Pulse informs you that it is fixing your application.

In addition, Pulse also includes configuration properties that allow you to define the behavior of the **Auto-Repair** functionality individually by each faulty detection rule.

To configure the **Auto-Repair** functionality, execute the following actions in the Pulse advanced configuration:

  1. Activate or deactivate each type of issues to be detected and fixed. For example, if you set the `fixInconsistentVersions` property to `false`, whenever Pulse detects you are trying to publish an application and there are different versions running, you must synchronize them manually.
  2. Set the `checkPeriodMillis` property to, for example, 2 minutes.
  3. Set the `latencyActuationCycles` property to, for example, 3 checks. Pulse only resets the cycle count when the entire cluster is stable, and not when a fix action is triggered.



Recommended configuration

The recommended configuration is that you set:

  * `checkPeriodMillis` to a small interval.
  * `latencyActuationCycles` to approximately 3 cycles.



This ensures some balance as fixes are quickly issued, and Pulse still allows for some space when waiting for momentary problems (for example, network partition) to fix on their own. In this example, it would always take minimum 6 minutes to issue a fix.

# Exporting and Importing Applications

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse supports application import and export not only to augment interoperability between different installations but also to give the ability to save an application in an exact state.

Although that can be partially achieved using [versioning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/resource-versioning), exporting an application gives one the possibility to archive it.

## Exporting an Applicationâ

Applications are exported in a single `PAPP` file that contains all the application resources: KPIs, Baselines, Workflows and so on. In some situations there are security resources that are also exported with the applications; more on that later.

Exporting an application is actually quite simple: the user can do it through the `Export` option present in the application configuration menu. This is illustrated in Figure 1 and will prompt the download of the application `PAPP` file.

## Importing an Applicationâ

Importing and application is usually as simple as exporting it. The user only has to click on the _Import Application_ button present in the **Applications** tab and an informative wizard will guide the entire process.

The _Import Application_ wizard can have one to three steps depending on the complexity of the application being imported. If the application has neither security [Groups](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-application#groups) nor Multi-Tenant resources, only one step will be needed which allows the user to upload the application `PAPP` file.

### Applications With Groupsâ

Whenever an application has resources that have security Groups configured the Import Application wizard will require one additional step. In this step the user will match the Groups used by the application being imported and the groups that exist in the Pulse installation.

This matching operation is necessary to guarantee that security permissions remain unchanged.

The UI will automatically do a best-effort match of the groups by name and will also allow the user to remove the groups permissions from the resources being imported.

### Applications With Multi-Tenancy Enabledâ

Importing and Exporting Applications that contain Multi-Tenancy resources do not have any additional configuration step. However, there are a few considerations worth mentioning regarding the Application import with Multi-Tenancy. Tenants stored in the PAPP file are merged automatically by Pulse using the following algorithm:

  1. If the Tenant being imported has the same Unique Id (Key) of a Tenant in the current Pulse Installation, all resources of the Tenant being imported will be added/mapped to the Tenant in the current Pulse Installation.
  2. If there is no Tenant with the the same Unique Id in the current Pulse Installation, a new Tenant will be created verifying before hand that there is no naming collision.
     1. If there is a name collision, the Tenant Unique Id will be appended at the end of the name, _e.g._ "Tenant Name (Tenant Unique Id)".
  3. All the tenants stored in the PAPP file will be imported to the current Pulse Installation. Even if they are not being explicitly used in the Application being imported. Additional details:
     1. Even the Tenants without any explicit resource are used in runtime in case of a Rules of the type "Shared by All Tenants".
     2. When Exporting an Application, all the Tenants in the Pulse installation are stored in the PAPP file.

# Exporting Resources

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

Exporting resources allows you to build a bundle with resources developed in a Pulse application (**Pulse App**). You can use the option [Importing Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) to easily import the resources bundle in another **Pulse App** in the same environment or between different environments. You can export the following resources:

  * [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists)' metadata without List items.
  * [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) with or without the binary.
  * [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) with or without executions.
  * [Rules Projects](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules#rules-projects) with or without snapshots.



By default, the **Export Resource** option also adds automatically to the resource bundle the metadata related to all the **Tenants** and **Tenant Groups** of the Pulse instance in which your **Pulse App** is running. See the page [Bundle structure](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/bundle-structure) to learn how the files are organized.

## How toâ

### Exporting Pulse Resourcesâ

To **Export Resources** execute the following steps:

  1. Select the Options  button to open the application options menu:  

  2. Select the option â  â to open the export wizard. The image below shows the **Export Resources** wizard:
  3. Check the subsections below for more details about each resource type that you want to export.
  4. Once you have chosen all the resources that you want to export, select the button â 



#### Listsâ

List export

List metadata is automatically exported because **Rules** can have a dependency on any **List**. When importing the bundle, all the **Lists** are imported to the **Pulse app** , either by replacing or creating new ones.

To exclude the **List** metadata you have to edit the export bundle manually.

#### Models Projectsâ

While you are in the export wizard, to add **Model Projects** to your bundle execute the following steps:

  1. Select the tab â  **Model Projects** to access the exporting options of this resource.
  2. To add a **Model** to the list of exported resources:
     1. Search by the Name of your **Model Project** using the drop-down menu.
     2. Search by the Name of your **Model** using the drop-down menu.
     3. (Optional) Choose to â  Include the binary of the **Model**.
     4. Select the â  Add Resource button to add this resource to the exporting list.
  3. Repeat Step 2 to complete the list of **Model Projects** that you want to export.
  4. Check how to add another resource or return to the subsection Exporting Pulse Resources to save your bundle.



#### Plansâ

While you are in the export wizard, to add **Plans** to your bundle execute the following steps:

  1. Select the tab â  **Plans** to access the exporting options of this resource.
  2. To add a **Plan** to the list of exported resources:
     1. Search by the Name of your **Plan** using the drop-down menu.
     2. (Optional) Choose the Plan Execution that you want to add to this Plan using the Drop-down menu under Execution List.
     3. Select the â  Add Resource button to add this resource to the exporting list.
  3. Repeat Step 2 to complete the list of **Plans** that you want to export.
  4. Check how to add another resource or return to the subsection Exporting Pulse Resources to save your bundle.



#### Rules Projectsâ

While you are in the export wizard, to add **Rules Projects** to your bundle execute the following steps:

  1. Select the tab â  **Rules Projects** to access the exporting options of this resource.
  2. To add a **Rules Project** to the list of exported resources:
     1. Search by the **Name** of your **Rules Project** using the drop-down menu.
     2. (Optional) Choose the Snapshots that you want to add to this **Rules Project** using the Drop-down menu under **Snapshot List**.
     3. Select the â  **Add Resource** button to add this resource to the exporting list.
  3. Repeat Step 2 to complete the list of **Rules Projects** that you want to export.
  4. Check how to add another resource or return to the subsection Exporting Pulse Resources to save your bundle.



## Learn moreâ

To learn more about the resource bundle check the following pages:

  * [Bundle structure](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/bundle-structure)
  * [Comparing resource versions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/comparing-resource-versions)



Check the page [Importing Resources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/importing-resources) to learn how to import your resources.

# Importing Resources

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Introductionâ

After [exporting](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources) the resource bundle, you can import the zip file in another Pulse application (**Pulse App**). The following data and resources can be imported:

  * Resources imported by user selection: **Models** , **Plans** , and **Rules Projects.**
  * Metadata of resources automatically imported if the resources are included in the export bundle: **Lists** , **Tenant Groups** , and **Tenants.**



This guide explains you how to import resources in Pulse using the partial import option.

## How to import Pulse resourcesâ

To import resources execute the following steps:

First, select the Options  button to open the application options menu:  


Then, select the option â  to open the import wizard. The wizard guides you through several stages that are displayed in different tabs as described in the sections below.

### Stage 1: Upload Fileâ

  1. "Drag & Drop" the zip file containing the export bundle to the dashed box, or alternatively, use the option "browse for a file".  

  2. Use the button â  to proceed to Stage 2.



### Stage 2: Choose Resourcesâ

In the **Stage 2: Choose Resources** , you can select the resources that you want to import as described in the subsections below.

Lists

The resource **List** does not have a tab menu because the metadata of **Lists** is automatically imported as follows:

  * **Lists** that do not exist in the target environment are created with no items.
  * **Lists** that already exist in the target environment are updated with new metadata, however, their items are not affected by the import.



#### Model Projectsâ

warning

If models are imported via App Collaboration and imported to a clustered environment, the model binary is not propagated to all nodes and remains only in the leader node. It is recommended to set up the binary location for the Pulse folders in the same shared drive across all nodes.

To import a **Model** execute the following actions:

  1. Choose the tab â . The following image shows the import wizard:

  2. Use the  checkbox to choose the **Models** that you want to import. In Pulse, **Models** are imported individually by user selection rather than importing the full **Model Project** with several **Models** at once.

  3. For each **Model** , choose the local **Model Project** to which you want to store the **Model** in the target **Pulse App**.

Model Projects in the local Pulse app

You must have a **Model Project** in the target application to be able to import a new **Model**. If you don't select a _Local Model Project Name_ you will receive a warning message to add one.

  4. Optionally, choose the binary of each **Model** by selecting the â  checkbox.

  5. Once you have chosen all the resources that you want to import (i.e. **Models** , **Plans** and **Rules Projects**), select the button â  to proceed to the next stage.

Dummy Data Source

When you import a **Model** that does not have a compatible data source available in the target environment, Pulse automatically creates a new data source. This new data source contains only the schema, without data associated to it.




#### Plansâ

To import a **Plan** execute the following actions:

  1. Choose the tab â .

  2. Use the  checkbox to choose the **Plans** that you want to import.

  3. Choose the _Local Plan Name_ for the **Plan** in the target **Pulse app** :

     1. You can replace an existing **Plan** by choosing a target name.
     2. You can choose to save it as a new **Plan** by choosing the option _project_name_ â .
  4. Optionally, choose the **Plan Executions** that you want to import by  expanding the menu under the _Plan Executions_ column. By default, the **Plan Executions** are selected.

  5. Once you have chosen all the resources that you want to import (i.e. **Models** , **Plans** and **Rules Projects**), select the button â  to proceed to the next stage.

Dummy Data Source

When importing a **Plan** with **Executions** that do not have a compatible data source available in the target environment, Pulse automatically creates a new data source for each **Execution** that you choose to import. This new data sources contain only the schema, without data associated to them.




#### Rules Projectsâ

To import a **Rules Project** execute the following actions:

  1. Choose the tab â .
  2. Use the  checkbox to choose the **Rules Projects** that you want to import.
  3. Choose the _Local Rules Project Name_ for the **Rules Project** in the target Application:
     1. You can replace an existing **Rules Project** by choosing a target name.
     2. You can choose to save it as a new **Rules Project** by choosing the option _project_name_ â .
  4. Optionally, choose the **Rules Snapshots** that you want to import by â  expanding the menu under the _Snapshots_ column. By default, the **Snapshots** are selected.
  5. Once you have chosen all the resources that you want to import (i.e. **Models** , **Plans** and **Rules Projects**) select the button â  to proceed to the next stage.



### Stage 3: Schema Conflictsâ

Stage display

This stage is only displayed if you import a **Rules Project** or a **Plan** , and when both of these conditions are met:

  * You choose to override an existing resource in the target application.
  * The resource in the export bundle has a different schema compared to the same resource in the target application.



To complete the **Stage 3: Schema Conflicts** execute the following actions:

  1. For each resource, choose the schema that you want to keep:
     * **Keep Imported** : This allows you to keep the schema that is specified in the resource that is being imported.
     * **Keep Local** : This allows you to keep the schema that is currently in your target application.
  2. Select the button â  to proceed to the next stage.



### Stage 4: Workflowâ

This stage allows you to associate the resources that you chose to import in Stage 2 to **Workflow** services. See the page [How to organize your work with blocks](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/how-to-organize-your) to understand how to map resources in the Data Science tab to corresponding services in the Workflows tab in the context of **App Collaboration**.

Workflow configuration

To apply the new resources to the **Workflow** you need to have a **Workflow** already created with the service operators placed in the diagram. However, the services don't need to be fully preconfigured (e.g. the service Rules doesn't need to have either a **Rules Project** or a **Snapshot**) because the import wizard allows you to add the configuration to the **Workflow**.

To add or update new resources directly into the **Workflow** execute the following actions:

  1. Use the  checkbox to choose the _Resource Type_ that you want to map to a **Workflow** service.
  2. Select the name of the **Workflow** that you want to update with the new resource using the combobox under the column _Workflow_.
  3. Select the **Workflow** service to which you want to map the resource using the combobox under the column _Workflow service_.
  4. Repeat Steps 1-3 to map the desired resources to **Workflow** services.
  5. Complete the Wizard stages by selecting the button â .



## Learn moreâ

When you export and import resources it might be useful to have the following pages at hand:

  * [Bundle structure](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/exporting-resources/bundle-structure): to learn how the folders are organized in the zip file
  * [Errors in App Collaboration](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/errors-in-app-collaboration): To learn possible errors that might occur during export and import operations.

On this page

# Publishing Application Changes

Was this page helpful?Â 

In Pulse, you can make changes to the application even when it is running. However, these changes are not immediately applied to the running application. Instead, they are applied only when you explicitly re-publish the application.

To publish changes made to a Pulse application, complete the following steps:

  1. Select the âÂ  button in the top right corner.

  2. Review the changes that were made since the last publish.

  3. Select the **Rolling Publish** button to start publishing.

Workflow validations

The **Rolling Publish** button will be disabled while Pulse validates all workflows in the application, or if those validations fail. For more details on this integrity protection mechanism, refer to the Pre-publish workflow validations section.

Pulse publishes application changes on only one node/application replica at a time to avoid going offline entirely. Only minor delays in some events may occur.

**In very rare cases** , if you want to publish the changes on all nodes at the same time, select the arrow  next to **Rolling Publish** , and select the **Publish** option.

Publish option causes downtime

If you select the **Publish** option instead of **Rolling Publish** , Pulse will have a downtime. In production environments, the **Publish** option should be used only in exceptional cases by users that are very knowledgeable about the system.

Note that if you made changes to the schema that is in use in the workflow (and select the new version of the schema for the workflow), Rolling Publish cannot be used.

  4. Pulse shows the progress during the publish process:

  5. If you select the **Close** button during the publish process, Pulse still finishes publishing in the background. You can see that it was successful if the **Publish** button disappears from Pulse. This means that there are no changed waiting to be published.

  6. If you select the **Abort** button during the publish process, Pulse stops the process at that point. The state of the application after the abort is not predictable. You can roll back the application to the state at which it was before the publish. Read more about rollbacks in the Error handling section.

  7. If you keep the **Publish application** window open, it shows the result of the publish process. See the Error handling section if you encounter an issue.




## Advanced usageâ

### Live publishâ

If the update to the application can be done without the necessity to restart Pulse nodes, Pulse performs a **live publish**. Only minor delays in the processing of some events may occur.

You can see on the **Publish** button when a change is eligible for a live publish:

Live publish is restricted to changes in rules and lists.

More specifically, if any of the following have changed since the last publish, the application is not eligible for a live publish:

  * input schema
  * name and description
  * outcome configuration
  * outcome combinator
  * the connections between workflow elements
  * partition keys
  * advanced properties
  * action handlers
  * event storage enabled state
  * the set of workflow elements comprising the workflow
  * for workflow elements:
    * id
    * name
    * output and input mapping
    * outcome configuration



Even when everything in the previous list remains unchanged, if the workflow element configuration changes (e.g. referencing a different plan snapshot), the workflow will require a full publish. The only exception to this is that rule snapshots referenced in a rules workflow element may be updated while still allowing a live publish.

### Synchronizing inconsistent versionsâ

When Pulse is running different versions of an application in different cluster nodes, Pulse warns you to synchronize all nodes to use the same version before publishing.

To manually fix inconsistent versions, complete the following steps:

  1. Select the  button.
  2. Optionally, view unstable nodes to see which application versions are running on different nodes.
  3. Choose the application version to publish in all nodes. By default, Pulse synchronizes all nodes with the most recent stable version.



### Order of changes on each app replicaâ

When Pulse completes a **Rolling Publish** on a cluster with many app replicas, it proceeds in the following order:

  1. App replicas that are not published.
  2. App replicas that are published but not on the target version.
  3. App replicas that are published on the target version.
  4. Inside each category of the previous points, the leader app replica of each data center is the last one to be rolled out.



If you change the publish type to **Publish** instead of **Rolling Publish** , the rules are the following:

  * Pulse takes offline all nodes.
  * The "Stop", "Bootstrap", and "Publish" operations are executed on all data centers in parallel.
  * Other than the operations mentioned in the previous point, Pulse completes every operation on one data center at a time. The primary data center is always updated first. For all others, no order is guaranteed. If anything fails on one data center, it does not proceed to the next one.



### Error handlingâ

When an error occurs, you have the following options:

  * **Retry** : The application will be published again in all the replicas. Replicas that already applied the application changes will not do any work since they are already in the expected state.
  * **Rollback** : Every replica will recover its last stable version of the application, i.e., the last version successful published in all the replicas. The rollback preserves the operation configurations (e.g., restart, rolling vs parallel, etc...)
  * **Abort** : The application publish will be stopped. Notice that nothing else will be done. This means the state after the abort is not defined.



When publishing fails on a replica, the whole operation is considered as failed. Pulse will not publish the application in the remaining replicas. It shows the error and waits for the user to decide how to proceed.

### Schema changesâ

Rolling Publish does not apply when you change a schema that is used in a workflow, and select the new version of the schema for the workflow. Changing the schema makes messaging inconsistent and error prone since there could be replicas using an older version of the application. For example:

  * Trying to process rules that match removed schema fields.
  * Adding new fields to the schema. In this case, when persisting the events in the [Event Storage](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/event-storage), they will have more columns than expected.



### Multiple rollbacksâ

When there is an error during a publishing operation and the rollback also fails, you can use the **Rollback** button again.

Instead of restoring another previous version of the application, this will work as a retry to restore the last stable version of the application in all replicas.

### Multiple online versionsâ

When an update operation fails, there may be two or more application replicas with different versions of the same application.

If this occurs, then the application state will be set to _DEGRADED_. Whenever there are different versions of the same application in the data center, [workflow synchronization](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#workflow-synchronization) messages from replicas running a different version of an application will be discarded to keep consistency.

In addition, if the [Auto-Repair](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/automatic-application-repair) capabilities of Pulse are enabled, then Pulse will correct the inconsistent versions automatically, otherwise, it is the responsibility of the user to manually synchronize the applications as shown in this page.

## Pre-publish workflow validationsâ

Workflow validations occur when users open or modify a workflow. It is possible to save changes to a workflow before the validation phase is complete, or even if validation fails, to allow users to do incremental work on workflows without being blocked by validation errors. However, publishing an app with invalid workflows would result in an error and set the App into a degraded state (which in turn would create pressure on the remaining healthy apps). To prevent this, Pulse only allows publishing an application when all its workflows are successfully validated.

When an app's Publish button is selected, Pulse displays the Publish window, allowing the user to review the changes made since the last publish. At this point, Pulse automatically validates all the workflows in that app, and only enables the **Rolling Publish** button if all workflow validations succeed.

Title: Resource Versioning | Feedzai Pulse

  * [](/pulse/latest/)
