On this page

# Resource Versioning

Was this page helpful?Â 

Versioning is an orthogonal concept to Pulse. Whenever a user creates, updates or deletes any of the application resources, Streams, Dimensions, etc. or the applications themselves, these operations are logged to persistence storage. There are three types of revert operations possible:

  * Revert a specific resource to how it was before a given change occurred
  * Revert all latest changes made to an application up to some point in time
  * Revert the deletion of an application



We will look at how each of these revert types work, their restrictions and implications.

## Structure of the Operations Logâ

Each visible row in the log depicts a change. A change maps to one or more operations. Most of the changes will have only one operation but others will be a group of related operations. An example of a change comprising several operations is creating a Schema. Each schema field marked as dimension will also trigger the creation of a Dimension Mapping. So a new schema with two dimension fields will insert three entries in the operations log. One create entry for the schema and one create entry for each new dimension mapping. When a change is comprised of several operations it is possible to see the individual operations.

Change entries in operations log are always shown in descending time order, i.e. the newest change on top.

## Querying the Operations Logâ

The operations log is visible in several Pulseviews screens.

Depending on where in Pulseviews you are viewing the operations log, the information presented therein will vary. All application resources edit screens show the operations log for that particular resource. To view the application log for a particular resource the user must have the `applications:history:resource:read` permission.

A filterable in-application log is available in the History of the application. To view the global application log the user must have the `applications:history:global:read` permission.

A log of deleted applications is also available to administrators and allows the administrator to recreate the application as it was before being deleted.

## Reverting the Operationsâ

This section details how the reverting works and the requirements for each case.

### Reverting a specific resource operationâ

The main use-case for this revert strategy is to enable a user to revert a specific resource to the way it was somewhere in the past without changing the other resources in the application. If two users are editing different rules in the same application each user can revert his rule without impacting the other user's rule.

To revert a specific resource operation the user must have the `applications:history:resource:revert` permission.

Note that operations are grouped in changes, so when a revert operation is requested all the operations in that particular change will be reverted. This is necessary to ensure consistency when handling dependent resources.

This particular revert strategy is not always possible. If any resource that depends on this one or that this resource depends on has changed after the operation we want to revert, the revert will not be available. This limitation exists because it is not possible to guarantee that the resource would still have valid relationships with both the resources it depends on and the resources depending on them after the revert operation. In these cases, the only options left are reverting the changes by manually editing the resource or revert the application. See the next revert strategy.

The revert operation itself can also be reverted leaving the resource as it was if no revert operation has occurred in the first place.

#### Example of reverting a specific resourceâ

Assuming the user actions are:

  1. Create schema 1
  2. Create workflow 1
  3. Update workflow 1
  4. Create rule 1
  5. Update rule 1
  6. Update rule 1 (again)
  7. Create rule 2



For these operations, the operations log is as follows (oldest operations at the bottom):

Change| Resource| Operation  
---|---|---  
7| RULE 2| CREATE  
6| RULE 1| UPDATE  
5| RULE 1| UPDATE  
4| RULE 1| CREATE  
3| WORKFLOW 1| UPDATE  
2| WORKFLOW 1| CREATE  
1| SCHEMA 1| CREATE  
  
By reverting a single resource, it is possible to get the rule 1 as it was before change 5 (highlighted in red) without undoing the create of rule 2. This is achieved by reverting to the rule 1 as it was before change 5.

After this revert, the operations log would have a new entry, the opposite operation of the one we are reverting:

Change| Resource| Operation  
---|---|---  
8| RULE 1| UPDATE  
7| RULE 2| CREATE  
6| RULE 1| UPDATE  
5| RULE 1| UPDATE  
4| RULE 1| CREATE  
3| WORKFLOW 1| UPDATE  
2| WORKFLOW 1| CREATE  
1| SCHEMA 1| CREATE  
  
info

It is not possible to revert change 3 using this strategy because dependencies of that workflow (rules 1 and 2) have changed.

### Reverting an Application to a specific point in timeâ

This revert strategy is very simple and works by applying the contrary operation to each operation down to the chosen point. A

s long as the user has permissions to do so, it should always be possible to apply this strategy. One possible downside of this revert strategy is that all changes made from that point on will be reverted.

To revert an application the user must have the `applications:history:global:revert` permission.

Note that reverting multiple changes will be grouped together as one single revert changed, composed of multiple operations. In this revert strategy, the revert operation can also be reverted itself in one step.

#### Example of reverting an Applicationâ

Assuming the user actions are:

  1. Create schema 1
  2. Create workflow 1
  3. Update workflow 1
  4. Create rule 1



The operations log is:

Change| Resource| Operation  
---|---|---  
4| RULE 1| CREATE  
3| WORKFLOW 1| UPDATE  
2| WORKFLOW 1| CREATE  
1| SCHEMA 1| CREATE  
  
The user might want to revert the application state back to as it was _before_ change 3 (highlighted). This strategy would achieve this by reverting change by change down to change 3 (inclusive) so that in the end the operations log would be:

Change| Resource| Operation  
---|---|---  
5| WORKFLOW 1| UPDATE  
5| RULE 1| DELETE  
4| RULE 1| CREATE  
3| WORKFLOW 1| UPDATE  
2| WORKFLOW 1| CREATE  
1| SCHEMA 1| CREATE  
  
Notice that the change id is the same (5) in all the operations pertaining to this revert, so that this change can be undone in a single step, as the user expects.

### Reverting a deleted Applicationâ

The log of deleted applications shows all deleted applications that can be recovered to the state it was before being deleted. Applications that were deleted and then imported are excluded from the log since they currently exist. Only applications that don't currently exist are shown. To revert a deleted application the user must be an **administrator**. If the application was deleted multiple times, only the latest delete is shown. After reverting the delete, the application looks exactly as it was before being deleted.

# TCP ports used by Pulse

This page provides a list of TCP ports opened by the components of Pulse, when running it locally with default setup (embedded Zookeeper, ActiveMQ and H2 database).

## Pulse Serverâ

### Fixed portsâ

  * 2181: Zookeeper
  * 61615: ActiveMQ
  * 1099: Rmi Registry
  * 1100: Remote Pulse Server object
  * 9010: Jmx
  * 8080: http
  * 8443: https



### Random portsâ

  * H2 Database (Not used in production environment)

  * ActiveMQ Jmx (Not used in production environment)

  * JMX: (only when started with _startup-debug.sh_ because _-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote_ is being used to launch the JVM)

  * EhCache RMI port: can be configured on _conf/engine/shiro/ehcache.xml_ by editing the cacheManagerPeerListenerFactory element and adding _properties="port=40001"_ , for using port 40001.



    
    
    <cacheManagerPeerListenerFactory>  
      class="net.sf.ehcache.distribution.RMICacheManagerPeerListenerFactory"  
      properties="port=40001"/>  
    

## App Engineâ

### Fixed portsâ

  * 6990: App remote object and RMI registry



### Random portsâ

  * Jmx: configurable with:
        
        # Global setting for all applications  
        pulse.global.appengine.jmxport=9011  
          
        # Configuration for a specific application  
        pulse.app.<app_slug>.appengine.jmxport=9013  
        



  * Other Jmx (because app engine is being started with* -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote* a second random port is being open. This can probably be removed)

  * On AppEngineProcess start, when getting the Pulse Server cluster leader remote reference, a RemoteExporter is being created and this opens a random RMI port as well. (This can potentially be fixed to use the configured RMI Object port. Not sure about the amount of effort because this code path is being used by other components)




## Running processes on Spark (e.g. Data Source Analysis, Rules Snapshot Evaluation)â

  * A random port is opened (didn't have the chance to check where it comes from)



## Conclusionsâ

The table below summarizes the possible causes for TCP connections to random ports that are showing up on customer's logs and what could be a possible fix for each one:

Random port origin| Possible fix  
---|---  
EhCache RMI port| Configure as described above  
App Engine Jmx| Configure as described above  
App Engine Other Jmx| Remove `-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote` from JVM args when launching application engine (if really not needed).  
  
## Typical customizationâ

Typically, the following configurations are added/edited in `pulse.properties` to match the customer's environment.
    
    
    pulse.manager.rmi.localregistryport=1099  
    pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.spark.driver.port=36560  
    pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.spark.blockManager.port=20800  
    pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.spark.port.maxRetries=20  
    pulse.manager.rmi.objectport=1100

Source: https://cam.feedzai.com/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/the-application-life-cycle
Title: The Application Life Cycle | Feedzai Pulse
============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)
  * [Working with Applications](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/)
  * The Application Life Cycle



# The Application Life Cycle

Was this page helpful?Â 

An application can be in one of the following states:

  * **`STOPPED`**  


  


In the `STOPPED` state, the application is completely shut down, without any alive App Engine.

  * **`BOOTSTRAPPED`**  


  


The `BOOTSTRAPPED` state means that the application is in _standby_ state. All its services are started but they only validate the changes being done.

  * **`STARTED`**  


  


An application that is `STARTED` is assumed to have all of its application replicas alive.

  * **`DEGRADED`**  


  


The `DEGRADED` state indicates that an application may have an issue and may not fully provide all the processing guarantees. For example, there might not be any replica handling the events of a given partition. The application transitions to this state when one of the following conditions are met:

    * There are application replicas running distinct versions.
    * Not all of the replicas are started.
    * Some replicas are down.
  * **`CRASHED`**  


  


An application becomes `CRASHED` if there are no application replicas alive that can be considered healthy.

  * **`SELF-HEALING`**  


  


An application starts a self-healing process if it has reached an unhealthy state and Pulse began performing recovery actions in an attempt to restore the application to a healthy state. To learn more about how and when these recovery actions are performed, see [Automatic Application Repair.](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/automatic-application-repair)




Furthermore, there are also four _maintenance_ states, meaning that some state transition is taking place:

  * **`APPLYING CHANGES`**  
When updating the application.
  * **`BOOTSTRAPPING`**  
When the application crashed and is being restarted, or after stopping an application.
  * **`STARTING`**  
When the application changes from `BOOTSTRAPPED` to `STARTED.`
  * **`STOPPING`**  
When the application is being stopped.



An application in a maintenance state should be displayed as follows. Note that the wheel on the top right corner of the image should be spinning.

When the application is in a maintenance state, crashed application replicas will not be recovered. Moreover, no other Application Lifecycle operations (publish, stop, etc.) can be performed in parallel. They will, however, be queued if Pulse is configured to do so.

# Configuration Overview

Setting up component encryption requires configuring encryption between internal Pulse components as well as between external components (e.g. between RabbitMQ brokers, or between Cassandra Nodes). On the Pulse side, this is done by setting a default encryption configuration in the pulse.global properties, which can be overridden for each component that require different configurations.

Configuring encryption between Pulse and an external component requires configurations both in Pulse and in the external component. The configuration of the properties in Pulse are generally the same, regardless of the external component whereas the configuration in external components is specific to the component. The table in the section Configuring external components summarizes the main configuration requirements for each external component. The page [Configuring External Components](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/configuring-external-components) describes the configuration requirements for external components in more detail.

The following sections give you an overview of the security concepts and settings for component encryption.

## Understanding keystores and truststoresâ

Component encryption requires configuration of keystores on the server side and truststores on the client side. This applies regardless of the component; however, the format of the keystore and the truststore may vary between components. The following terminology is used to identify the different formats:

  * **Java Truststore** : contains the public certificate of the CA that signs the server certificates in JKS format (.jks file). Is referred in this article as truststore.jks.
  * **Java Keystore** : contains the server certificate signed by the CA and the server's private key (.jks file). Is referred in this article as keystore.jks.
  * **Certificate Authority** (CA): contains the same as a truststore, but in a PEM format (.pem file). This format is required by Rabbit MQ. Is referred in this article as ca.pem.
  * **Server certificate** : contains the same as a Keystore, but in PEM format (.pem file). Is referred in this article as certificate.pem.
  * **Server certificate private key** : (.pem file). Referred in this article as key.pem.



The files mentioned above are used in the case when all certificates are signed by an internal CA and all components are configured to trust this CA (i.e. approach implemented in Pulse by default). Other scenarios are out of the scope of this page. In Pulse, the configuration files depend whether Pulse acts as a server or as a client. Pulse acts as a client in most cases in which Pulse server/application engine communicate with an external component (e.g. between Cassandra or RabbitMQ. It acts as a server in communications between Pulse internal components (e.g. between the application engine and the Pulse server with RMI).

To help the configuration process, Pulse includes scripts to help creating keystores and truststores. You can visit the page [Creating Certificates](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/creating-certificates) for more information on how to configure these scripts.

## Configuring Pulse propertiesâ

Component encryption is implemented in Pulse using a default configuration specifying the required files in the client and server side for all components. This default configuration can be overridden for any component. For example, if Cassandra needs a different file configuration, the properties can be overridden to create an exception for Casandra. With this approach, the Pulse properties of the components that share the same encryption configuration only need to be defined once.

Configuring custom properties

Some components require separate configuration not fully covered in the global encryption properties (e.g. relational databases). Visit the page [Configuring External Components](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/configuring-external-components) to learn more about this.

In the following example, all the components have default configuration for server authentication except for Cassandra, in which the encryption is disabled:
    
    
    # Default encryption properties  
    pulse.global.encryption.trustLevel=SERVER_AUTH  
    pulse.global.encryption.protocol=TLS  
      
    # Default encryption configuration for client-side components  
    pulse.global.encryption.client.truststore.file=cert/trusted-ca.jks  
    pulse.global.encryption.client.truststore.storepwd=trusted-ca-store-pwd  
      
    # Default encryption configuration for server-side components  
    pulse.global.encryption.server.keystore.file=cert/my-identity.jks  
    pulse.global.encryption.server.keystore.storepwd=my-identity-store-pwd  
    pulse.global.encryption.server.keystore.keypwd=my-identity-key-pwd  
      
    # No encryption on Cassandra  
    pulse.global.cassandra.encryption.trustLevel=ENCRYPTION_NONE  
    

The configuration above specifies the passwords for the truststore on a client side (trusted-ca.jks) and the keystore on the server side (my-identity.jks). Similarly to database connection passwords, store passwords may be encrypted.

### Authenticationâ

The authentication is specified in the trustLevel property as described in the above code block.

Pulse supports the following authentication:

  * **Encryption Only:** Pulse does not validate the certificate presented by the server, and thus, truststores are not required on the Pulse side. A keystore is still required if RMI is to be encrypted since this component acts as a server. The value of the property is ENCRYPTION_ONLY.
  * **Server Authentication:** Pulse validates the server certificate by checking if the certificate is valid and signed by a trusted entity. This requires a truststore on the client configuration and a keystore on the server configuration. The value of the property is SERVER_AUTH.
  * **Client Authentication:** In addition to server authentication, clients present a certificate to the server and the server must to trust it. This requires an additional keystore on the client configuration and a truststore on the server configuration. The value of the property is CLIENT_AUTH.



## Configuring external componentsâ

The following table provides a summary of the files that are required for each external component that communicates with Pulse.

The page [Configuring External Components](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/configuring-external-components) describes the configuration requirements for external components in more detail.

Origin (Client)| Destination (Server)| Client Configuration| Server Configuration  
---|---|---|---  
Pulse server, App Engine| Rabbit MQ| truststore.jks, truststore password| ca.pem, certificate.pem, key.pem  
Rabbit MQ| Rabbit MQ| ca.pem| ca.pem, certificate.pem, key.pem  
Pulse server, App Engine, Spark, any other java client app| Pulse server, App Engine| truststore.jks, truststore password| keystore.jks, server certificate key password, keystore password  
Web Browser| Pulse server| should contain the certificate authority installed| keystore.jks, server certificate key password, keystore password  
Pulse server, App Engine| Cassandra| truststore.jks, truststore password| keystore.jks, keystore password (needs to be the same as the server private key password)  
Cassandra (inter-node communication)| Cassandra| truststore.jks, truststore password| keystore.jks, keystore password (needs to be the same as the server private key password)  
Pulse server, App Engine| Spark| truststore.jks, truststore password| keystore.jks, keystore password  
Pulse server, App Engine| Relational database| truststore.jks, truststore password| On Posgres: keystore.jks, keystore password. Other servers may have distinct requirements.  
  
## Next stepsâ

Now that you have basic knowledge about the default Pulse properties, check the page [Configuring External Components](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/configuring-external-components) for more information about configuring component encryption.

# Configuring Encryption for External Components

This page walks you through the configuration of component encryption, with focus on external components.

## RMI configurationâ

The RMI encryption configuration is inherited from the default one (`pulse.global.encryption.*`) unless it is overridden in `pulse.manager.rmi.encryption.*`. For example, to disable encryption on RMI communications, set this property as follows:
    
    
    pulse.manager.rmi.encryption.trustLevel=ENCRYPTION_NONE  
    

External RMI clients (e.g., custom services) need to be updated if they communicate with a Pulse server with encrypted RMI â see the API documentation for further information.

## Pulse Management Tool configurationâ

The Pulse Management Tool (pulsemgmt.sh) communicates with a running Pulse server using JMX through an RMI connector. If RMI is configured to use encryption, this tool must be invoked with a correspondent client-side encryption configuration.

The Pulse Management Tool is completely standalone (i.e. it only manipulates MBeans), and so it doesn't access the Pulse configuration. To use it with encryption, you must set up (and system protect) a file with the encryption configuration and invoke the tool with the **-encryption** command line option, e.g.:
    
    
    $ pulsemgmt.sh -shutdowncluster -encryption encrypt.properties  
    

The following is an example of an encrypt.properties file:
    
    
    encryption.trustLevel=SERVER_AUTH  
    encryption.client.truststore.file=/opt/pulse/conf/engine/secret/trusted-ca.jks  
    encryption.client.truststore.storepwd=trusted-ca-store-pwd  
    

info

The `encrypt.properties` file must be protected with restricted read permissions. Note that the passwords in this file are not encrypted.

## RabbitMQ configurationâ

Rabbit Version

Use of SSL in Rabbit was verified in version 3.6.14 / Erlang 20.1. Previous versions have known issues with SSL, see <https://www.rabbitmq.com/which-erlang.md>.

Rabbit requires separate configurations for each of the following channels:

  * Connections between the RabbitMQ broker (server) and Pulse (client).
  * Intra-datacenter broker connections, for mirroring.
  * Inter-datacenter broker connections, for federation.



These are documented in the following sections.

### Between broker (RabbitMQ) and Pulseâ

#### Pulse sideâ

The Rabbit encryption configuration is inherited from the default client one (`pulse.global.encryption.client.*`) unless it is overridden in `pulse.manager.cluster.dc..messaging.encryption.*`. Having SSL requires the broker IPs to have the port explicitly configured in `pulse.manager.cluster.dc.messaging.brokers`. This port is defined on the Rabbit-side configuration defined below.

#### Rabbit sideâ

Rabbit requires the CA certificate, server certificate and server private key to be in separate files, in .PEM format. The certificate generation documentation shows how to generate these in a PKCS12 file (keystore.pkcs12). Having this file, the above PEM files can be extracted as follows:
    
    
    $ openssl pkcs12 -in keystore.pkcs12 -passin file:secret/keystore.pwd -nodes -nokeys -cacerts -out cacert.pem  
    $ openssl pkcs12 -in keystore.pkcs12 -passin file:secret/keystore.pwd -nodes -nokeys -clcerts -out cert.pem  
    $ openssl pkcs12 -in keystore.pkcs12 -passin file:secret/keystore.pwd -nocerts -out key.pem  
    

info

The key.pem password is requested interactively by openssl when introducing the third line of the above code block.

These PEM files are then configured on the rabbitmq.config file (see [https://www.rabbitmq.com/ssl.html](https://www.rabbitmq.com/ssl) and <http://erlang.org/doc/man/ssl.html> for detail the `ssl_options` section):
    
    
    [  
        {rabbit, [  
            {loopback_users, []},  
            {ssl_listeners, [5671]},  
            {ssl_options, [  
                {cacertfile, "/path/to/cacert.pem"},  
                {certfile, "/path/to/cert.pem"},  
                {keyfile, "/path/to/key.pem"},  
                {password, "<key.pem password>"},  
                {verify, verify_none},  
                {fail_if_no_peer_cert, false}  
            ]}  
        ]}  
    ].  
    

### Intra-datacenter broker communicationâ

Intra-datacenter communication in RabbitMQ requires the certfile and unencrypted keyfile to be included in a single file:
    
    
    $ cat /path/to/cert.pem > /path/to/chain.pem  
    $ openssl rsa -in /path/to/key.pem -passin pass:<key.pem password> >> /path/to/chain.pem  
    

info

The chain.pem contains the unencrypted key, and the reading access should be restricted.

Since RabbitMQ relies on an underlying implementation of Erlang to establish its connections, some Erlang-level configurations must be provided. These are done via environment variables which are set through the rabbitmq-env.conf, which is automatically loaded when Rabbit MQ server is started.

  1. The following is an implementation of using Erlang:
         
         $ echo `erl -eval 'io:format("~p", [code:lib_dir(ssl, ebin)]),halt().' -noshell`  
         "/path/to/erlang/<ssl-version>/ebin"  
         

info

The output of the command above includes quotes, so it cannot be directly used via a $( ) subshell, or they would be escaped and considered part of the string.

  2. Create the file `rabbitmq-env.conf` in the directory `/etc/rabbitmq`.

  3. Add environment variables to the file created in step 2. Remember to replace the SSL path that you obtained in step 1. A recommended approach is to take value of the output of step 2 and set the environment variable for the Erlang path without the quotes. See an example in the next code block:
         
         ERL_SSL_PATH="/path/to/erlang/<ssl-version>/ebin"  
         RABBITMQ_SERVER_ADDITIONAL_ERL_ARGS="-pa ${ERL_SSL_PATH} -proto_dist inet_tls -ssl_dist_opt server_certfile /path/to/chain.pem -ssl_dist_opt server_secure_renegotiate true client_secure_renegotiate true"  
         RABBITMQ_CTL_ERL_ARGS="-pa ${ERL_SSL_PATH} -proto_dist inet_tls -ssl_dist_opt server_certfile /path/to/chain.pem -ssl_dist_opt server_secure_renegotiate true client_secure_renegotiate true"  
         

See <https://www.rabbitmq.com/clustering-ssl.html> for RabbitMQ's own information.




### Inter-datacenter broker communication (federation)â

Configuring federation with encryption requires the following changes relative to a non-encrypted setup:

  1. The protocol changes from "amqp" to "amqps"
  2. The address now receives the explicit port (:5671)



An example of SSL federation URI with the changes already applied is provided below:
    
    
    # RabbitMQ Cluster 1  
    rabbitmqctl set_parameter federation-upstream my-upstream \  
        '{"uri":["amqps://<user>:<pass>@<server in cluster 2>:5671", "amqps://<user>:<pass>@<server in cluster 2>:5671", ...], "ack-mode":"no-ack"}'  
    rabbitmqctl set_policy --apply-to exchanges federate-me "^global-"\  
        '{"federation-upstream":"my-upstream"}'  
      
    # RabbitMQ Cluster 2  
    rabbitmqctl set_parameter federation-upstream my-upstream \  
        '{"uri":["amqps://<user>:<pass>@<server in cluster 1>:5671", "amqps://<user>:<pass>@<server in cluster 1>:5671", ...], "ack-mode":"no-ack"}'  
    rabbitmqctl set_policy --apply-to exchanges federate-me "^global-" \  
        '{"federation-upstream":"my-upstream"}'  
      
    # Make federation queues replicated so they are also highly available  
    rabbitmqctl set_policy replicate-queues-federation "^federation" '{"ha-mode":"all"}' --apply-to queues  
    

## Kafkaâ

Kafka supports all encryption trust levels defined in Pulse. As a Java-based system, it supports the standard Java certificate formats used in Pulse and other Java-based components.

### Pulse sideâ

The Kafka encryption configuration is inherited from the default client configuration defined by properties with the `pulse.global.encryption.client.*` prefix. However, it can be overridden by configurations defined with the `pulse.manager.cluster.dc.<dc>.messaging.encryption.*` prefix. In addition to the standard Pulse encryption, Kafka also supports server authentication based on the IP address of the certificate. This is not enabled by default. To enable it, set the `ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm` raw property to _https_.

### Broker sideâ

The Kafka broker configuration is very similar to the Pulse/Server configuration. Server authentication requires a keystore in jks format, whereas client authentication requires a truststore for the trusted clients. These are configured in _server.properties_ as shown below (for server authentication only):
    
    
    # Listener protocol must be either SSL or SASL_SSL, depending on SASL authentication being used or not  
    listeners=SASL_SSL://172.17.0.3:9092  
      
    # Key and truststore properties  
    ssl.keystore.location = /path/to/keystore.jks  
    ssl.keystore.password = <the.keystore.password>  
    ssl.key.password = <the.keystore.private.key.password>  
    ssl.truststore.location = /path/to/trustedca.jks  
    ssl.truststore.password = <the.truststore.password>  
      
    # Disable hostname verification  
    ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm=  
      
    # Needed because otherwise kerberos is assumed  
    sasl.enabled.mechanisms=PLAIN  
    sasl.mechanism.inter.broker.protocol=PLAIN  
    

This configuration includes SSL on inter-broker communications.

### Mirror-makerâ

Mirror-maker is used on multi-datacenter setups to achieve topic federation between data centers. Should SSL be used, then the _server.properties_ SSL and SASL properties described earlier in this page must also be specified in the mirror-maker _consumer.properties_ and _producer.properties_ files.

## Relational DB configurationâ

### Postgresâ

#### Server configurationâ

Enabling SSL on a postgres server requires a server certificate and private key with unprotected PEM format. This can be extracted using the same procedure as the one described above for Rabbit.

These files can be installed on the server as described in <https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/static/ssl-tcp.html>.

#### Client (Pulse) configurationâ

The client side is configured at the JDBC connection string level with two available options (see <https://jdbc.postgresql.org/documentation/91/ssl-client.html>):

  * **Without server certificate validations:** Connection URL parameter `ssl=true&sslfactory=org.postgresql.ssl.NonValidatingFactory` needs to be defined. This skips server certificate validations, and thus, does not require a truststore. However, this option is less secure.
  * **With server certificate validations:** Connection URL parameter ssl=true needs to be defined as well as the two system properties `javax.net.ssl.trustStore` and `javax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword`. The last two system properties only need to be defined if the global pulse configuration is not set.



### Oracleâ

#### Client (Pulse) configurationâ

The Oracle JDBC thin driver supports JSSE encryption through its standard `javax.net.ssl.*` properties, which are automatically set on all Pulse components as long as a global encryption configuration is defined. The Pulse side configuration requires the following:

  * JKS keystore and truststore configured in the `pulse.global.encryption.*` properties.
  * _tnsnames_ definition in the connection URL specifying the tcps protocol, as described in <https://docs.oracle.com/cd/B19306_01/java.102/b14355/sslthin.htm#BABHFBJD>.



Both server and client authentication are supported.

## Cassandra configurationâ

The full Datastax documentation can be found [here](https://docs.datastax.com/en/cassandra/3.0/cassandra/configuration/secureSSLIntro.html).

### Client (Pulse) to nodeâ

Cassandra configuration in cassandra.yaml is very similar to the Pulse/Server configuration. Server authentication requires a keystore in jks format whereas client authentication requires a truststore for the trusted clients. These are configured in the cassandra.yaml client_encryption_options as shown below (for server authentication only):
    
    
    # enable or disable client/server encryption.  
    client_encryption_options:  
        enabled: true  
        # If enabled and optional is set to true encrypted and unencrypted connections are handled.  
        optional: false  
        keystore: path/to/keystore.jks  
        keystore_password: <the.keystore.password>  
        # require_client_auth: false  
        # Set trustore and truststore_password if require_client_auth is true  
        # truststore: conf/.truststore  
        # truststore_password: cassandra  
      
        # More advanced defaults below:  
        # protocol: TLS  
        # algorithm: SunX509  
        # store_type: JKS  
        # cipher_suites: [TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA,TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA,TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA,TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA,TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA,TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA]  
    

The keystore file can be the same as in Pulse as long as it is signed with the CA that Pulse trusts. Additional certificates are not required on the Pulse side.

The encryption configuration on the Pulse side can be specified either under `pulse.global.encryption.client.*` (or under `pulse.global.cassandra.encryption.*` if a specific configuration is required for Cassandra).

### Node-to-nodeâ

Node-to-node encryption is configured similarly to the client-to-node encryption. Client-to-node is defined in the client_encryption_option, whereas the node-to-node is defined in the server_encryption_options section.

As with the node-to-node configuration, JKS key and trust stores may be required.

See <https://docs.datastax.com/en/cassandra/3.0/cassandra/configuration/secureSSLNodeToNode.html> for details.

## Jetty server / REST API configurationâ

REST API encryption can be configured with self-signed certificates (without CA) as described [here](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/security-configuration/configuring-an-ssl-certificate). This method can be used in a scenario in which only Jetty SSL is configured. However, the certificates generated by the scripts described in the page [Creating Certificates](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/creating-certificates) could be used instead. The scripts are configured in `$PULSE_HOME/conf/engine/jetty/jetty.xml` as defined [here](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/security-configuration/configuring-an-ssl-certificate).

## Spark configurationâ

Configuring communications security on Spark requires addressing:

  * Communications between Pulse code running on Spark Executors and Pulse.
  * Communications between Pulse code running on Spark Executors and the Spark Cluster (e.g., HDFS access on data source analysis).
  * Communications between Pulse and the spark cluster (e.g., launching jobs, HDFS access on datas source previews).
  * Communications between cluster components. These depend on the containers where spark is deployed.



These are documented in the following sections.

### Securing communications between Pulse executors and Pulseâ

Pulse jobs submitted to Spark need to communicate with Pulse through RMI or access event/profile storage, and so they require truststores (and possibly keystores if client authentication is used). By default, executors inherit the encryption configuration defined in pulse.global and the event/profile storage config, and thus a truststore must be present on the configured location and with the same passwords. This truststore can be the same as the one specified for Spark internal protocols.

### Spark standaloneâ

#### Protocols over SSLâ

##### Pulse sideâ

SSL security configuration passed to Spark when submitting jobs is specified, in Pulse, under the `pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.spark.ssl.*` space.

info

The `spark.*` properties mentioned in this section are set under `pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.*`.

The properties below inherit the settings set in the Pulse global encryption configuration if not set explicitly:

  * spark.ssl.protocol
  * spark.ssl.keyPassword
  * spark.ssl.keyStore
  * spark.ssl.keyStorePassword
  * spark.ssl.trustStore
  * spark.ssl.trustStorePassword



The SSL properties above specify default properties for the following protocols (Spark 1.6.3):

  * fs (for file distribution).
  * akka (essentially job control).



See <https://spark.apache.org/docs/1.6.3/security.html#ssl-configuration> for additional encryption properties and instructions on how to configure each protocol separately.

Since the properties above are automatically set by Pulse, to enable SSL the only setting to be configured is the following:
    
    
    spark.ssl.enabled=true  
    

Note that Spark 1.6.3 does not support at-rest encryption of temporary files such as shuffle files and cached data.

#### Spark sideâ

info

The Spark nodes require `openssl` to be installed in order to be able to create the connection between them, even before Pulse is started.

The following needs to be configured on each Spark node (conf/spark-defaults.conf file) for SSL to be used between nodes:
    
    
    spark.ssl.enabled true  
    spark.ssl.keyPassword <Password>  
    spark.ssl.keyStore /path/to/keystore.jks  
    spark.ssl.keyStorePassword <KeyStorePassword>  
    spark.ssl.protocol TLS  
    spark.ssl.trustStore /path/to/trustedca.jks  
    spark.ssl.trustStorePassword <TrustStorePassword>  
    

### Protocols over TCP with SASLâ

The RCP protocol is implemented over SASL and must be encrypted because store sensitive properties are passed over it. On a setup with no user authentication (i.e., kerberos), a shared secret string must be configured in Pulse and Spark nodes.

#### Pulse sideâ

SASL is enabled with the following Pulse properties:
    
    
    pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.spark.authenticate=true  
    pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.spark.authenticate.secret=<SECRET>  
    pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.spark.authenticate.enableSaslEncryption=true  
    pulse.global.services.modules.datascience.spark.forward.spark.network.sasl.serverAlwaysEncrypt=true  
    

#### Spark sideâ

The following must also be configured in each Spark container machine, by creating/modifying the conf/spark-defaults.conf file in the Spark nodes:
    
    
    spark.authenticate true  
    spark.authenticate.secret <SECRET>  
    spark.authenticate.enableSaslEncryption true  
    spark.network.sasl.serverAlwaysEncrypt true

# Creating Certificates

Pulse includes scripts to help creating keystores and truststores for component encryption.

Both of these files contain certificates that are used for authentication. This guide explains how to use the scripts to configure [Component Encryption with Server Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption#component-encryption-with-server-authentication).

The scripts generate:

  * Server keystores with a private key and a certificate chain with two entries:
    * Server certificate signed by a Certificate Authority (CA).
    * Public certificate issued by the CA (i.e CA certificate).
  * Client truststore with the CA certificate.



The certificates are generated both in JKS which is typically required by Java-based components (e.g. application engine, Pulse server) and PEM formats required by some external components (e.g. Rabbit).

## Selecting server authentication approachâ

This section explains component encryption configured with server authentication. For each Feedzai's customers, the authentication approach is selected on a case-by-case basis, and normally fall under one of these options:

  * **Self-signed certificates**

Requires generating self-signed certificates and configuring all Pulse components to trust them. This approach assumes that the person generating the certificates has also the role of internal CA. As an example, this could be configured by a Feedzai employee from the delivery team (i.e. referred to as Feedzai in this guide). A typical scenario for this approach is to use it in a test environment.

info

Pulse distributions include a bin/create-keystore.sh script to generate self-signed certificates. This could also be used on a configuration where self-signed certificates are used instead of certificate chains. This option is simpler when only one component is secured (i.e. typically jetty).

  * **Certificates signed by an internal CA**

Requires receiving certificates signed by an internal CA and configuring all the Pulse components to trust this CA. In this approach, the internal CA is generally handled by a separate department belonging to a Feedzai's customer.

A typical scenario to use this approach is a production environment. Typically, Feedzai's customers have an internal CA that might be handled by a department of security (i.e. referred to as client security team in this guide).




## Handling the configuration procedureâ

The configuration procedure can be divided in 3 main steps:

  1. Configure a CA that is used to issue a CA certificate as well as to sign the server certificate. Generally, this is only required for the self-signed certificate approach.
  2. Configure a truststore with a CA certificate that can be then placed in Pulse components acting as clients.
  3. Configure a keystore that can then be placed in Pulse components acting as servers. The keystore contains a certificate chain (server certificate signed by the CA with a digital signature, and the CA certificate) and a private key.



The following diagram illustrate the 3 main steps, including the main differences between a testing and a production environment.

## Configuring encryption with server authenticationâ

warning

The scripts below generate working files with sensitive information such as private keys and passwords. The files are stored in a directory named "secret" that is created by the scripts, but are not required by Pulse or any component.

The scripts should not be executed in a running pulse machine. The scripts only require the openssl and keytool tools to be available on the machine that is used to execute them.

The scripts are located in the folder _certificates_ inside the pulse folder.

The scripts can be open using a text editor and they contain configuration instructions. The recommended order to configure the scripts is the following:

  1. Open and execute commands in **create-ca.sh**.

This script must be executed first because it contains the CA Certificate that will be used in commands by the other scripts.

  2. Open and execute commands in **create-truststore.sh**.

Generates a truststore in a JKS file with the CA Certificate (file truststore.jks). The password to access this file is stored in the secret/truststore.pwd file.

  3. Open and execute commands in **create-keystore.sh**.

Generates a keystore with a private key, a certificate signed by the CA, and the CA certificate (file keystore.jks). The keystore password and the private key password are stored in the secret/keystore.pwd and secret/privatekey.pwd files, respectively.




Alternatively, the execution order of 2 and 3 can be switched.

The size and validation of the private keys are set when the scripts are configured. The recommended values are 2048 byte and 10 years, respectively.

### Testing environmentâ

This section guides you through the configuration of the scripts in a typical testing environment scenario. In addition to configure truststores and keystores in Pulse components, the Feedzai team plays the role of CA.

To configure component encryption with server authentication execute the following actions:

#### Run create-ca.sh to generate the CAâ

Do you have CA configured?

If you have already a CA configured, skip this step and jump to the subsection Run create-truststore.sh to generate the truststore.

  1. Navigate to the pulse/certificates folder and open the script create-ca.sh with a text editor.
  2. Follow the instructions described in the script. The main actions are the following:
     1. Create a directory with the name _secret_ (i.e. certificates/secret) to store your CA password. If you have already this directory, you can skip this step and continue to the next step.

     2. Generate a file with a CA password using the following command:
            
            $ apg -n 1 -m 32 > secret/ca.pwd  
            $ CERT_PWD=`cat secret/ca.pwd`  
            

     3. Generate the CA Certificate file and the CA private key by executing the following (file output `rootCA.crt`):
            
            $ openssl req -new -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:$KEY_SIZE -subj /CN=rootCA/OU=Pulse/O=Feedzai/C=PT/ -keyout $CA_KEY_FILE -out $CA_CERT_FILE -days $CERT_DAYS -passin pass:$CERT_PWD  
            

where the variables are replaced by the following (recommended naming):

Variables| Values  
---|---  
`$CA_CERT_FILE`| rootCA.crt  
`$CA_KEY_FILE`| secret/rootCA.key  
`$CERT_NAME`| rootCA  
`$CERT_DAYS`| 3650  
`$KEY_SIZE`| 2048  
`$CERT_PWD`| Defined in step 2(b)  
  
As a verification step you can check the content of the CA Certificate with the following command:
            
            $ openssl x509 -in $CA_CERT_FILE -text -noout  
            




#### Run create-truststore.sh to generate the truststoreâ

  1. Navigate to the pulse/certificates folder and open the script create-truststore.sh with a text editor.
  2. Follow the instructions described in the script. The main actions are the following:
     1. Generate a file with the truststore password by executing the following:
            
            $ apg -n 1 -m 32 > secret/truststore.pwd  
            $ TRUST_STORE_PWD=`cat secret/truststore.pwd`  
            

     2. Generate the truststore file in a JKS format using the CA Certificate that is trusted by all components acting as clients (i.e. certificate `rootCA.crt` generated in the subsection Run create-ca.sh to generate the CA). To do so, execute the following command (file output `trustedca.jks`):
            
            $ keytool -importcert -keystore $TRUST_STORE_FILE -alias rootCa -file $CA_CERT_FILE -noprompt -storepass $TRUST_STORE_PWD  
            

where the variables are replaced by the following (recommended naming):

Variables| Values  
---|---  
`$TRUST_STORE_FILE`| trustedca.jks  
`$CA_CERT_FILE`| rootCA.crt  
`$TRUST_STORE_PWD`| Defined in step 2(a)  
  
The password defined for the variable $TRUST_STORE_PWD is requested when opening the file. This password avoid unapproved file editing, for example, changing the certificates within the file. As a verification step, check the file `trustedca.jks` by executing the following command:
            
            $ keytool -list -keystore $TRUST_STORE_FILE -storepass $TRUST_STORE_PWD  
            




#### Run create-keystore.sh to generate the keystoreâ

  1. Navigate to the `pulse/certificates/` folder and open the script `create-keystore.sh` with a text editor.
  2. Follow the instructions described in the script. The main actions are the following:
     1. Generate a file with the keystore password by executing the following:
            
            $ apg -n 1 -m 32 > secret/keystore.pwd  
            $ SERVER_STORE_PWD=`cat secret/keystore.pwd`  
            

     2. Generate a file with the private key password by executing the following:
            
            $ apg -n 1 -m 32 > secret/privatekey.pwd  
            $ SERVER_KEY_PWD=`cat secret/privatekey.pwd`  
            

     3. Generate a private key with the following command (file output `key.pem`):
            
            $ openssl genrsa -out key.pem $KEY_SIZE  
            

where the variable $KEY_SIZE can be replaced by 2048.

     4. Generate the certificate signing request (csr) with the following command (file output `req.pem`):
            
            $ openssl req -new -key key.pem -out req.pem -outform PEM -subj /CN=pulse/O=server/ -nodes  
            

Then run the following command to visualize the certificate signing request and verify that it has no issuer yet:
            
            $ openssl req -text -in req.pem  
            

     5. Performing the CA role, sign the certificate signing request using the certificate `rootCA.crt` and the root private key with the following command (file output `req.signed.pem`):
            
            $ openssl x509 -req -CA $CA_CERT_FILE -CAkey $CA_KEY_FILE -in req.pem -out req.signed.pem -days $CERT_DAYS -CAcreateserial -passin pass:$CERT_PWD  
            

where the variables are replaced by the following (recommended naming):

Variables| Values  
---|---  
`$CA_CERT_FILE`| rootCA.crt  
`$CA_KEY_FILE`| secret/rootCA.key  
`$CERT_DAYS`| 3650  
`$CERT_PWD`| Choose a password  
  
The password chosen for the variable `$CERT_FWD` is used to generate the digital signature that is added to the certificate.

As a verification step, run the following command and verify that the certificate has already an issuer (i.e. rootCA), in opposition to the verification that was done in Step 2(d).
            
            $ openssl x509 -in req.signed.pem -text -noout  
            

     6. Create a package in a pkcs12 format containing the certificate chain (self-signed certificate and the CA certificate) and the server private key with the following command (file output `server.pkcs12`):
            
            $ openssl pkcs12 -export -out keystore.pkcs12 -in req.signed.pem -inkey key.pem -certfile $CA_CERT_FILE -passout pass:$SERVER_STORE_PWD  
            

where the variables are replaced by the following (recommended naming):

Variables| Values  
---|---  
`$CA_CERT_FILE`| rootCA.crt  
`$SERVER_STORE_PWD`| Defined in Step 2(a)  
  
The password defined for the variable `$SERVER_STORE_PWD` is used in the next step to convert the file to a JKS format.

     7. Convert the pkcs12 file to JKS format using the following command (file output `keystore.jks`):
            
            $ keytool -importkeystore -srckeystore keystore.pkcs12 -srcstoretype PKCS12 -srcstorepass $SERVER_STORE_PWD -destkeystore $SERVER_KEY_STORE_FILE -deststoretype JKS -noprompt --deststorepass $SERVER_STORE_PWD -destkeypass $SERVER_KEY_PWD  
            

where the variables are replaced by the following (recommended naming):

Variables| Values  
---|---  
`$SERVER_STORE_PWD`| The password defined in Step 2(d), i.e. ServerStorePassValue  
`$SERVER_KEY_STORE_FILE`| keystore.jks  
`$SERVER_STORE_PWD`| Defined in Step 2(a)  
`$SERVER_KEY_PWD`| Defined in Step 2(b)  
  
As a verification step run the following command:
            
            $ keytool -list -v -keystore $SERVER_KEY_STORE_FILE -storepass $SERVER_STORE_PWD -keypass $SERVER_KEY_PWD  
            

The output gives you information about:

        * Number of keystores: "Your keystore contains N entry"
        * Self-signed certificate: The first certificate fingerprints
        * CA certificate: The second certificate fingerprints
     8. Clean up temp files with the following command:
            
            $ rm -f key.pem req.pem req.signed.pem  
            




### Production environmentâ

In a typical production environment, Feedzai has the responsibility to configure truststore and keystore files in Pulse components whereas Feedzai's customer manages the CA.

The procedure to configure the scripts in a production environment is similar to the procedure used in testing environments. Therefore, this section only highlights the differences between both environments and you are referred to section Testing environment for more details about the full procedure.

#### Generate a CAâ

In a scenario of production environment, the script `create-ca.sh` is not needed because the CA is managed by Feedzai's customers.

#### Run create-truststore.sh to generate the truststoreâ

In a testing environment, Feedzai creates a truststore using the CA certificate generated by this team using the script `create-ca.sh`. In a Production environment, Feedzai has to:

  1. Contact the client security department that is responsible for managing CA certificates to request a CA certificate file.
  2. Generate a truststore using the CA certificate sent by the CA (see image below).



For more information about creating a truststore, check the subsection Run create-truststore.sh to generate the truststore under the section Testing environment.

#### Run create-keystore.sh to generate the keystoreâ

In a testing environment, Feedzai team signs the certificate signing request by performing the role of internal CA.

In a Production environment, Feedzai has to:

  1. Generate the certificate signing request.

  2. Contact the client security department that is responsible for managing the CA certificates and send the certificate signing request file to be signed by the CA.

  3. Create a keystore containing the certificate chain (certificate signed by the CA and the CA certificate) and the server private key (see the following image).




For more information about creating a keystore, check the subsection Run create-keystore.sh to generate the keystore under the section Testing environment.

## Learn moreâ

Now that you have basic knowledge about the scripts available to generate keystores and truststores, check the page [Configuration Overview](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption/configuration-overview) to learn more details about configuration for each component in a Fraud Prevention solution.

You can also learn more about the concept of [Component Encryption](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption) in Pulse.

# Configuring an SSL Certificate for Pulse

Must change the default certificate

Pulse bundles a self-signed certificate which allows users to connect to it through HTTPS. This can be found in the conf/engine/jetty/ directory, comprising a keystore and a jetty.xml file. This certificate **must not be used in production** environments, as it is insecure.

In this page you can learn how to set up a certificate for SSL in Pulse.

info

This section describes how to create a self-signed certificate and install it in Pulse for use in the Jetty server. See [Component Encryption](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption) for instructions on securing all Pulse communications.

## Creating your self-signed certificateâ

The **openssl** toolkit is used to generate an **RSA Private Key** and **CSR (Certificate Signing Request)**. It can also be used to generate self-signed certificates which can be used for testing purposes or internal usage.

The first step is to create your RSA Private Key. This key is a 1024 bit RSA key which is encrypted using Triple-DES and stored in a PEM format so that it is readable as ASCII text.
    
    
    $ openssl genrsa -des3 -out server.key 1024  
      
    Generating RSA private key, 1024 bit long modulus  
    .........................................................++++++  
    ........++++++  
    e is 65537 (0x10001)  
    Enter PEM pass phrase:  
    Verifying password - Enter PEM pass phrase:  
    

Once the private key is generated a Certificate Signing Request can be generated. The CSR is then used in one of two ways. Ideally, the CSR will be sent to a Certificate Authority, such as Thawte or Verisign who will verify the identity of the requestor and issue a signed certificate. **The second option is to self-sign the CSR, which will be demonstrated in the next section**.

During the generation of the CSR, you will be prompted for several pieces of information. These are the X.509 attributes of the certificate. One of the prompts will be for "Common Name (e.g., YOUR name)". It is important that this field be filled in with the fully qualified domain name of the server to be protected by SSL. If the website to be protected will be [https://acme.org](https://acme.org/), then enter acme.org at this prompt. The command to generate the CSR is as follows:
    
    
    $ openssl req -new -key server.key -out server.csr  
    Country Name (2 letter code) [XX]:US  
    State or Province Name (full name) []:California  
    Locality Name (eg, city) [Default City]:San Francisco  
    Organization Name (eg, company) [Default Company Ltd]:Acme  
    Organizational Unit Name (eg, section) []:IT  
    Common Name (eg, your name or your server's hostname) []:acme.org  
    Email Address []:[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)  
    Please enter the following 'extra' attributes  
    to be sent with your certificate request  
    A challenge password []:  
    An optional company name []:  
    

At this point you will need to generate a self-signed certificate because you either don't plan on having your certificate signed by a CA, or you wish to test your new SSL implementation while the CA is signing your certificate. This temporary certificate will generate an error in the client browser to the effect that the signing certificate authority is unknown and not trusted.

To generate a temporary certificate which is good for 365 days, issue the following command:
    
    
    $ openssl x509 -req -days 365 -in server.csr -signkey server.key -out server.crt  
    Signature ok  
    subject=/C=US/ST=California/L=San Francisco/O=Acme/OU=IT/CN=acme.org/[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection)  
    Getting Private key  
    Enter pass phrase for server.key:  
    

## Add your certificate to Pulseâ

Once you have your certificate generated (self signed, or signed by an authorized CA), you can import your certificate into the embedded Jetty web server of Pulse.

First you need to generate a password to encrypt your keystore:
    
    
    $ apg -n 1 -m 32  
    PhrirrAyfluwawkofNaljamBytbiaken  
    

If you have a key and certificate in separate files, you need to combine them into a PKCS12 format file to load into a new keystore. The certificate can be one you generated yourself or one returned from a CA in response to your CSR.
    
    
    $ openssl pkcs12 -inkey server.key -in server.crt -export -out server.pkcs12  
    Enter pass phrase for server.key: (the password of your certificate)  
    Enter Export Password: (the new password generated to protect the pkcs12 file, i.e. PhrirrAyfluwawkofNaljamBytbiaken)  
    Verifying - Enter Export Password: (the new password generated to protect the pkcs12 file, i.e. PhrirrAyfluwawkofNaljamBytbiaken)  
    

Now lets create the keystore where Pulse will read the certificate:
    
    
    $ $JAVA_HOME/bin/keytool -importkeystore -srckeystore server.pkcs12 -srcstoretype PKCS12 -destkeystore keystore  
    Enter destination keystore password: (the new password generated to protect the pkcs12 file, i.e. PhrirrAyfluwawkofNaljamBytbiaken)  
    Re-enter new password: (the new password generated to protect the pkcs12 file, i.e. PhrirrAyfluwawkofNaljamBytbiaken)  
    Enter source keystore password: (the password of your certificate)  
    Entry for alias 1 successfully imported.  
    Import command completed:  1 entries successfully imported, 0 entries failed or cancelled  
    

Now copy the resulting file **keystore** to `$PULSE_HOME/conf/engine/jetty/keystore`:
    
    
    $ cp keystore $PULSE_HOME/conf/engine/jetty/keystore  
    

Finally edit your `$PULSE_HOME/conf/engine/jetty/jetty.xml`:
    
    
    <New id="sslContextFactory" class="org.eclipse.jetty.http.ssl.SslContextFactory">  
      <Set name="KeyStore">conf/engine/jetty/keystore</Set>  
      <Set name="KeyStorePassword">PhrirrAyfluwawkofNaljamBytbiaken</Set>  
      <Set name="KeyManagerPassword">PhrirrAyfluwawkofNaljamBytbiaken</Set>  
      <Set name="TrustStore">conf/engine/jetty/keystore</Set>  
      <Set name="TrustStorePassword">PhrirrAyfluwawkofNaljamBytbiaken</Set>  
    </New>  
    

## Enforce SSL Configurationâ

Define the following line in the pulse.properties file:
    
    
    pulse.manager.enforcessl=true  
    

## Configure SSL in FIPS modeâ

Running Pulse in a FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) compliant system, and with a keystore certificate that contains aliases, wildcards, or multiple hosts, may result in the following error when starting the server:
    
    
    java.security.KeyManagementException: FIPS mode: only SunJSSE KeyManagers may be used  
    

To configure Pulse to run in FIPS mode, edit the Jetty configuration at `$PULSE_HOME/conf/engine/jetty/jetty.xml`, and change the `sslContextFactory` definition as follows:
    
    
    - <New id="sslContextFactory" class="org.eclipse.jetty.http.ssl.SslContextFactory">  
    + <New id="sslContextFactory" class="com.feedzai.pulse.service.webapps.jetty.FIPSSslContextFactory">  
    

Depending on the used database, a similar error may prevent the connection from Pulse to the database. This as been observed when trying to connect to PostgreSQL using the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver. In such cases, it may be required to explicitly configure the driver to use the appropriate SSL factory.

For PostgreSQL, this can be achieved by configuring the JDBC connection URL to explicitly specify the SSL factory to be used:
    
    
    pulse.global.database.jdbc=jdbc:postgresql://<HOST:PORT>/<DATABASE>?ssl=true&sslfactory=org.postgresql.ssl.DefaultJavaSSLFactory  
    

The above configuration will use the default Java SSL factory provided by the JVM, rather than the PostgreSQL JDBC driver's custom SSL implementation. This ensures that the database connection uses the FIPS-compliant security providers from the Java runtime environment.

warning

This configuration disables the certificate aliases and SNI (Server Name Indication). As of now, there are no alternatives to run Pulse with FIPS and certificate aliases, or SNI.

Title: Configuring Kerberos for Data Science Resources | Feedzai Pulse

# Configuring Kerberos for Data Science Resources

Pulse stores data science resources on the filesystem. To work with those resources in Pulse, users need to have access to the respective files. You can use group properties to grant access.

This page describes how to use groups and group properties to grant a group access to the following data science resources:

  * Data sources (created/used by plan executions, model evaluations, rule evaluations, sandbox evaluations)
  * Statistic file of data source analysis
  * Model binaries from model training and hyperparameter tuning
  * Spark archive file (initialization of a leader app jvm process)
  * Spark-libs (initialization of a leader app jvm process)



## Hierarchical groups and access rightsâ

When Pulse users try to access a data science resource, Pulse needs to access the respective files using Kerberos credentials. These credentials can be defined either in the Group Properties field of a group, or in the _pulse.properties_ file.

Pulse doesn't only consider the groups that are explicitly assigned to the user, but also their parent groups in the group hierarchy.

If none of the user's groups or their parent groups has any Kerberos credentials defined for the given resource, Pulse tries to fall back on credentials defined in the _pulse.properties_ file, if there are any.

## Group propertiesâ

To configure a group to use specific Kerberos credentials, add the following key-value pairs in the **Group Properties** field of the group:

Key| Value  
---|---  
defaultPath| The path to the folder of the tenant on the HDFS.  
kerberos.keytabPath| The path to the keytab file of the tenant.  
kerberos.principal| The principal authentication to be used for Kerberos. Normally, it has the following format: `username/resource@REALM`.  
  
## Using groups to control visibilityâ

The members of the groups that are set up this way can control who can see resources stored in the group's directory.

To set the resource visible only to that specific group, complete the following steps. Note that the steps presume that the user has the membership of the group(s) that they select in step 3.

  1. Open the resource.

  2. Select the  button, and select **Specific Groups**. Select the group from the list of groups.

  3. In the list of permissions, select **Read / Update / Delete** according to your choice. A check mark appears next to them when selected.

  4. **Save** the resource.




If the visibility of a data science resource is public (i.e. not limited to a specific group), then Pulse will use the Kerberos credentials defined in the _pulse.properties_ file, if there are any.

## Exampleâ

Let's consider an example where you want to configure the following Pulse groups to access HDFS directories:

  * _TeamA_ and _TeamB_ are two groups that should have access only to their own respective directories, plus a directory with common resources (containing Spark archives and Spark libs).
  * The members of the _landlords_ group should have access to all directories. They also have a directory for their own resources that should not be accessed by anyone else.



To configure this, the following needs to be set up:

**1\. HDFS directories:**

Directory| Description| Permissions| Owner| Group  
---|---|---|---|---  
/user/pulse_common/| The common directory that stores files common to all teams, for example spark-libs, spark-archive, etc. The user of each team must belong to its group to be able to access this directory.| 770| pulse_common| pulse_common  
/user/pulse_landlord/| This directory is specific to the landlord. It is used to store files with sensitive data of all teams.| 770| pulse_landlord| pulse_landlord  
/user/teamA/| This directory is specific to TeamA. It stores the data science resources of this team.| 770| pulse_teamA| pulse_teamA  
/user/teamB/| This directory is specific to TeamB. It stores the data science resources of this team.| 770| pulse_teamB| pulse_teamB  
  
**2\. HDFS users:**

Each of these users must be configured with Kerberos authentication using a keytab file.

User name| Description| Member of the group(s)| Maps to Pulse group  
---|---|---|---  
pulse_common| The HDFS user through which Pulse users will access common files.| pulse_common| all groups in Pulse  
pulse_landlord| The HDFS user through which the landlords will access landlord-specific files.| pulse_landlord, pulse_common, pulse_teamA, pulse_teamB| landlords  
pulse_teamA| The HDFS user through which members of TeamA will access their own files.| pulse_teamA, pulse_common| TeamA  
pulse_teamB| The HDFS user through which members of TeamB will access their own files.| pulse_teamB, pulse_common| TeamB  
  
**3\. Pulse properties** in the _pulse.properties_ file:

Replace the placeholders (marked with `<...>`) with the respective values. These properties allow Pulse users to access common files.
    
    
    pulse.global.services.modules.distributed.jobs.kerberos.enabled=true  
    pulse.global.services.modules.distributed.jobs.kerberos.principal=<principal_of_pulse_common>  
    pulse.global.services.modules.distributed.jobs.kerberos.keytabPath=<keytab_path_of_pulse_common>  
    pulse.global.services.modules.distributed.jobs.spark.master=yarn-client  
    pulse.global.services.modules.distributed.clusterDirToReceive=hdfs:///user/pulse_common/spark-libs  
    

**4\. Pulse groups and users:**

In Pulse, create three groups:

  * landlords
  * TeamA
  * TeamB



For each of these groups, add the following key-value pairs in the **Group Properties** field:

Key| Value  
---|---  
defaultPath| The path to the respective HDFS directory of the group.  
kerberos.keytabPath| The path to the group's keytab file.  
kerberos.principal| The principal authentication to be used for Kerberos. Normally, it has the following format: username/resource@REALM.  
  
Add the users to their respective group. Landlord users must be added to the teams' groups as well.

After configuring the above, users must set the resources visible only to the group. If the visibility is not restricted to the respective group, Pulse will use the credentials that are defined in the _pulse.properties_ file to access the resource.

# Configuring AD FS

AD FS in one of the available services that can act as an IdP enabling SPs to communicate with it using the SAML 2.0 standard. This service is responsible to provide Single Sign-On (SSO) of existing users as well as to enable user provisioning. For certain actions, the AD FS can be configured in different ways. Full description of the AD FS configuration is beyond the scope of this guide, however, basic configurations that enable SSO in Pulse are described below as examples. These examples include:

  * Obtaining Pulse IdP properties when using AD FS.
  * Configuring Pulse in AD FS as a Relying Party Trust (i.e. SP).
  * Configuring users in AD FS that are mapped to Pulse users.
  * Configuring claim rules in AD FS that will be part of the SAML assertion to communicate user information to Pulse such as language, groups, roles, or tenants.



## Obtaining Pulse IdP propertiesâ

When the IdP used is the AD FS, all the Pulse's IdP related properties (prefix: `pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.idp`) can be obtained from the AD FS federation metadata file. This federation metadata is available using the following URL:

`https://<ADFS_DOMAIN>/FederationMetadata/2007-06/FederationMetadata.xml`

The federation metadata file contains various information about the AD FS instance. To know how to map the information contained on this XML to the Pulse properties, please check: [Configuring SSO using a generic IdP](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/single-sign-on/configuring-sso-using-a).

## Add a relying party trustâ

This section describes how to configure a Pulse instance as a relying party trust (i.e. SP).

The SP can be configured manually or automatically by importing configuration data generated by metadata. The second method is described in this section as an example.

At this point you should have AD FS installed, and the properties that enable SSO configured on Pulse.

AD FS configurations

Note that the SP configuration based on importing configuration data from metadata described in this section is not necessary the preferred method for all the production systems. This method is illustrated in this section as an example. Refer to the [AD FS Documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-fs/operations/create-a-relying-party-trust) for full configuration details.

  1. Open the Pulse URL that provides metadata information for the specific instance, e.g. `https://<BASE_PULSE_ADDRESS>/pulseviews/api/sessions/samlsso/metadata`, and export the file as XML.

  2. Open the **Server Manager AD FS**.

  3. In the Server Manager AD FS, open the **Tools** bar and select the option **AD FS Management**.

  4. In the AD FS window, expand the folder **Trust Relationships**.

  5. Open the folder **Relying Party Trusts**.

  6. In the **Actions** panel, choose the option **Add Relying Party Trust...**.

  7. Click start, and choose the option **Import data about the relying party from a file**.

  8. Open the XML file generated in Step 1 and click **Next** to create the SP. Note that at the end of this step you can open the IdP sign in webpage and check that the new SP is already available.




## Add new usersâ

This section describes how to configure a user in the active directory that will be mapped to a Pulse user with two roles, i.e. _Pulse Admin_ and _Pulse Reader_. These two roles are used in this section as examples and the configuration to map user roles is optional. However, if users are configured to map user roles, the roles have to exist in Pulse.

  1. Open the **Server Manager AD FS**.

  2. Open the **Tools** bar and select the option **Active Directory Users and Computers** , which will open the following window:

  3. In the window **Active Directory Users and Computers** , select the option **Create a new user in the current container** .

  4. Add the **First name** _SsoUserTest_ and the **User logon name** _[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#c794b4a892b4a2b593a2b4b387b7b2abb4a2eab3a2b4b3b4e9a4a8aa)_ and click **Next >**.

  5. Set a password for this user.

  6. Open the **SsoUserTest** user and select the option **Member Of**.

  7. Select the option **Add** to add new groups: _Pulse Admin_ , _Pulse Reader_.




## Create claim rulesâ

This section describes how to configure claim rules to map Pulse user name and two user roles. The AD FS claims rules are sent as attributes within SAML assertions. They are essential for Pulse to perform user provisioning correctly.

The configuration of the AD FS to map user roles is optional along with languages, groups, and tenants. Therefore, the configuration described in this section is only an example of a configuration option.

  1. Open the **Server Manager AD FS**.

  2. Open the **Tools** bar and select the option **AD FS Management**.

  3. In the AD FS window, expand the folder **Trust Relationships**.

  4. Open the folder **Relying Party Trusts**.

  5. Choose an item from the list of relying party trusts that you wish to establish the claims, right click on the item and select **Edit Claim Rules...**.

  6. Select **Add Rule** , and select the claim rule template _Send LDAP Attributes as Claims_.

  7. Provide the following information:

     1. Claim rule name: _Name ID._
     2. Attribute store: _Active Directory._
     3. LDAP Attribute: _User-Principal-Name._
     4. Outgoing Claim Type: _E-Mail Address._
  8. Add another rule and select the claim rule template _Transform an Incoming Claim._

  9. Provide the following information:

     1. Claim rule name: _Email claim_.
     2. Incoming claim type: _E-Mail Address_.
     3. Outgoing claim type: _Name ID_.
     4. Outgoing name ID format: _Email_.
     5. Select the option **Pass through all claim values**.
  10. (Optionally) Add another rule and select the claim rule template _Send Group Membership as a Claim_.

AD FS configurations

Note that the choice of the claim rule template described in this section is not necessary the preferred option for all the production systems. This option is illustrated in this section as an example. Another option is to extract the claims from the LDAP attributes. Refer to the [AD FS Documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-fs/deployment/configuring-claim-rules) for full details about configuring claim rules.

  11. Provide the following optional information:

     1. Claim rule name: e.g. _RoleAdminCheck_.
     2. Outgoing claim type: e.g. _User.roles._ Note that this property is used by Pulse by default to map to a user role. For example, the properties User.language, User.groups and User.tenants would map to languages, groups and tenants.
     3. Outgoing claim value: e.g. _admin_. Note that this value maps to a user role in Pulse, and thus, it has to match the name of the role configured in Pulse. For example, to map to a tenant, the claim value has to match the tenant name configured in Pulse.
  12. (Optionally) Repeat Steps 10 and 11 to add a claim rule to map to the Pulse role _pulseviews_.

  13. Repeat Steps 5 to 12 to create claim rules for other SPs.
