# Configuring Keycloak

This page describes how to integrate Keycloak as the Identity Provider (IdP) into the Pulse environments. The integration is tested for Keycloak version 16.1.1. Take this into consideration when following this guide and the official Keycloak documentation.

Feedzai uses Keycloak to provide single sign-on (SSO) across its products: Pulse, Case-Manager (CM) and SAR Manager (SARM).

In Feedzai deployments, Keycloak is not used for user management, only for session management and the authentication protocol layer. Instead, users are authenticated and fetched from a federated Identity Provider.

The authentication request/response calls follow the standard [SAML](http://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/Post2.0/sstc-saml-tech-overview-2.0-cd-02.html#5.1.Web%20Browser%20SSO%20Profile%7Coutline) (for Pulse and CM) and [OIDC Authorization Code Flow](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#CodeFlowAuth) (for Pulse and SARM).

The following diagram shows how Feedzai products connect to Keycloak and where relevant information for single sign-on is stored.

## Installing Keycloakâ

Refer to the official Keycloak guide for installation instructions. In Feedzai Cloud, Keycloak is configured in Standalone Clustered Mode for high-availability and with frequent database backups for an added layer of data loss protection. Consider these options for on-premise deployments.

After successfully starting Keycloak, create a new realm as described [here](https://www.keycloak.org/docs/16.1/server_admin/#_create-realm), from now on referred to as REALM_NAME.

## Federating an Identity Providerâ

For customers that have an IdP available, Keycloak should be configured to federate user management and authentication to that IdP. Keycloak has out-of-the-box support for configuring federation using Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and OpenID Connect (OIDC). Multiple Social login providers can also be configured. Refer to [chapter 12](https://www.keycloak.org/docs/16.1/server_admin/#_identity_broker) of the Keycloak Server Administration Guide for specific configurations.

Keycloak can be configured to transparently redirect to the federated IdP by setting an Action in the Browser Flow for the Identity Provider Redirector as explained in [this section](https://www.keycloak.org/docs/16.1/server_admin/#default_identity_provider) of the Keycloak documentation.

## Connecting Feedzai products to Keycloakâ

In Feedzai Cloud, products are configured out-of-the-box for a seamless single sign-on experience. For on-premise deployments each product must be individually configured to connect to Keycloak.

info

Note that all URLs mentioned in this document are the ones visible externally to the cluster, not internal ones. These authentication protocols work at the browser level.

The settings below include **`{VARIABLES}`** and **`<manual instructions>`** that need to be **replaced with the actual values**.

### Pulse real-time scoringâ

#### Keycloak Configurationâ

To configure Keycloak to accept Pulse connections, complete the following steps:

  1. Create a new SAML client where the Client ID is the HTTPS URL of the real-time scoring Pulse environment (from now on referred as PULSE_SCORING_URL). Before saving, do the following changes to the default configuration:
     1. Turn on Sign Assertions
     2. Set SAML Signature Key Name to `NONE`
     3. Set Valid Redirect URIs to `{PULSE_SCORING_URL}/*`
     4. Set Base URL to `{PULSE_SCORING_URL}`
     5. Set Logout Service Redirect Binding URL to `{PULSE_SCORING_URL}/pulseviews/api/sessions/samlsso/logout`
  2. Save the client and go to the Mappers tab to configure how the user roles are propagated.
  3. Create a new mapper of type User Attribute:
     1. Set SAML Attribute Name to User.roles.
     2. Set SAML Attribute NameFormat to Basic.
     3. Set User Attribute to roles.
  4. Save the mapper.



#### Pulse propertiesâ

Create the following properties to configure Pulse to connect to Keycloak for SSO.
    
    
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.enabled=true  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.idp.entityId=https://{KEYCLOAK_HOSTNAME}/auth/realms/{REALM_NAME}  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.idp.sso=https://{KEYCLOAK_HOSTNAME}/auth/realms/{REALM_NAME}/protocol/saml  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.idp.slo=https://{KEYCLOAK_HOSTNAME}/auth/realms/{REALM_NAME}/protocol/saml  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.idp.x509cert=<Copy the Keycloak realm certificate from the Realm Settings Keys tab>  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.security.authnRequestsSigned=true  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.security.wantAssertionsSigned=true  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.sp.privateKey=<Follow Appendix A of this page to use the private key from Keycloak client SAML Keys>  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.sp.x509cert=<Copy the certificate from Keycloak client SAML Keys>  
    

If Pulse is behind an SSL termination proxy, also add the following property:
    
    
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.sp.forceHttps=true  
    

The real-time scoring Pulse environment works as a SAML proxy for CM. Create the following properties to configure this proxy behavior. These properties do not apply to the Data Science environment of Pulse.
    
    
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.proxy.samlsso.cm.privateKey=<Follow Appendix A to use the private key from CM Keycloak client SAML Keys>  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.proxy.samlsso.cm.x509cert=<Copy the certificate from CM Keycloak client SAML Keys>  
    

### Data science environmentâ

#### Keycloak configurationâ

Follow the same instructions to create a SAML client as described in the _Pulse Real-time Scoring_ section of this page, adjusting the URL for the Pulse Data Science environment.

#### Pulse propertiesâ

Configure the same properties as described in the _Pulse Real-time Scoring_ section of this page, adjusting the SAML Keys for the Pulse Data Science client created in Keycloak and excluding the CM proxying properties.

### Case Managerâ

#### Keycloak Configurationâ

Follow the same instructions to create a SAML client as described in the _Pulse Real-time Scoring_ section of this page, adjusting the URL for Case Manager.

The property for the Logout Service Redirect Binding URL in CM is different from Pulse, the correct URL to use is `{CASE_MANAGER_URL}/api/session/saml-logout`.

#### Case Manager Configurationâ

The CM configuration is simpler because it uses the real-time scoring Pulse environment as its SAML proxy.

Merge the following JSON settings in `{CASE_MANAGER_INSTALL}/conf/config.json` replacing `CASE_MANAGER_URL` with the correct value:
    
    
    {  
      "cm": {  
        "url": "{CASE_MANAGER_URL}"  
      },  
      "pulse": {  
        "sso_saml_auth": true  
      }  
    }  
    

### SAR Managerâ

#### Keycloak Configurationâ

To configure Keycloak to accept connections from SAR Manager, complete the following steps:

  1. Create a new openid-connect client with Client ID SARM (in this case the name doesn't need to match the SARM URL). Before saving, do the following changes to the default configuration:
     1. Set Access Type to confidential.
     2. Turn on Authorization Enabled.
     3. Set Valid Redirect URIs to `{SARM_URL}/*`
     4. Set Web Origins to `{SARM_URL}`
  2. Save the client and go to the Mappers tab to configure how the user roles are propagated.
  3. Create a new mapper of type User Attribute:
     1. Set User Attribute to roles.
     2. Set Token Claim Name to roles
     3. Turn on Multivalued
  4. Save the mapper.



#### SARM Configurationâ

Merge the following top-level YAML settings in the `{SARM_INSTALL}/config/sarm.yaml`:
    
    
    auth:  
      oidcJwkUrl: {KEYCLOAK_URL}/auth/realms/{REALM_NAME}/protocol/openid-connect/certs  
      oidcDiscoveryUri: {KEYCLOAK_URL}/auth/realms/{REALM_NAME}/.well-known/openid-configuration  
      oidcClientId: sarm  
      oidcClientSecret: {SECRET} // Copy the secret from SARM Keycloak client Credentials tab  
      oidcCallbackUrl: {SARM_URL}/auth/callback  
    

## Testing the integrationâ

Single sign-on should now be working. When a user logs in into one of the Feedzai products and then navigates to another one, no further login should be required.

If it is not working as expected, check the logs for both Keycloak and the affected Feedzai product for troubleshooting error messages.

For single logout to work properly, the Federated Identity Provider must support this feature and must be specifically configured to do so.

## Security hardeningâ

Secrets (such as the OIDC client secret) are shown in clear text in the Keycloak's Admin UI and are also stored in clear text in Keycloak's database. Because of this, it is recommended to restrict access to Keycloak Admin UI as [described here](https://www.keycloak.org/docs/16.1/server_admin/#admin-endpoints-and-console) and make sure that the database is only accessible from Keycloak nodes and access is granted only to authorized accounts. Note that the OIDC client secret is also stored in clear text in SARM configuration so this configuration file should also be protected with appropriate permissions.

## Appendix A - Convert Private Key Formatâ

To use the private key from Keycloak SAML client in Pulse, it needs to be converted to PKCS#8. Copy the private key and save in file pk.rsa and run the following Linux command:
    
    
    paste -d'\n' <(echo "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----") \  
      pk.rsa <(echo "-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----") | \  
      fold -w64 | openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt | \  
      sed '1d;$d' | tr -d '\n'  
    

If Pulse is configured to use a secret to encrypt sensitive configuration properties, the private key must be encrypted before setting the property.

Copy the resulting output and use it to set the private key Pulse property. Delete the `pk.rsa` file because it's no longer necessary.

# Configuring Keycloak in Pulse with OpenID Connect

Was this page helpful?Â 

This page describes how to integrate Keycloak as the Identity Provider (IdP) into the Pulse environments using OpenID Connect. The integration has been tested for Keycloak version 20.0.1. Take this into consideration when following this guide and the official Keycloak documentation.

## Connecting Feedzai products to Keycloakâ

### Pulse real-time scoringâ

#### Keycloak Configurationâ

To configure Keycloak to accept Pulse connections, complete the following steps:

  1. Create a new OpenID Connect client, filling a descriptive Client ID (from now on referred as `CLIENT_ID`), e.g. pulse-oidc, and optionally define Name and Description. Before saving, and referring to the HTTPS URL of the real-time scoring Pulse environment as `PULSE_SCORING_URL`, do the following changes to the default configuration:
     1. Enable Client authentication (sets this client as _confidential_) and Service accounts roles.
     2. Set Root URL to `{PULSE_SCORING_URL}`.
     3. Set Valid Redirect URIs to `{PULSE_SCORING_URL}/*`.
  2. Save the client and go to the Client scopes tab to configure the claims to include in JWTs besides the standard ones.
  3. Create a new OpenID Connect Client scope (or change an existing one) such that the following claims are included: JWT Claim| Mapper| Required?| Where to add  
---|---|---|---  
preferred_username| username (predefined/built-in)| Yes| Access token  
aud| audience resolve (predefined/built-in)| Required if the server validating the tokens requires audience claim  
name| full name (predefined/built-in)| No, but recommended, so that the user's Full Name is available to Pulse  
email| email (predefined/built-in)| Required when using features that send emails to users (e.g. 4eye check); otherwise, recommended  
locale| locale (predefined/built-in)| No, but highly recommended if internationalization is enabled at the IdP and the locale is used in Pulse  
`roles.$CLIENT_ID` is the default in Pulse, but can be configured| client roles (predefined/built-in)| Yes, becuse the users need roles to be able to access the Pulse UI| Userinfo  
`groups` is the default in Pulse, but can be configured| Custom mapper created by configuration with Mapper Type "Group Membership";  
**"Full group path" must be disabled**|  Required only when users are associated with groups and that information is to be propagated to Pulse  
`tenants` is the default in Pulse, but can be configured| Having tenants associeted with users is not a concept of Keycloak; the workaround is to have that information as a user attribute, and then use a custom mapper created by configuration with Mapper Type "User Property", to map the value of that attribute to the "tenants" claim| Required only when users are associated with tenants and that information is to be propagated to Pulse  
  4. Save the Client scope and add it to the client for Pulse, making sure it is set as "Default".
  5. Configure other settings, such as token/session durations, flows, etc.
  6. Save the client.



#### Pulse propertiesâ

Create the following properties to configure Pulse to connect to Keycloak for SSO using OpenID Connect.

The client secret (referred as `CLIENT_SECRET` in the configuration example below) can be retrieved at the Credentials tab of the client in Keycloak. Since this is sensitive information, the corresponding property in Pulse has encryption enabled. Therefore, if Pulse has an encryption key for properties set up, then the value of this property needs to be encrypted  using that key.

The _discoveryURI_ (referred as `DISCOVERY_URI` in the configuration example below) is the URL of the "well known" endpoint of the IdP, and appears at the Realm Settings page of Keycloak as a link to "OpenID Endpoint Configuration".
    
    
    ####################################################  
    #                  OIDC  
    ####################################################  
    pulse.global.oidc.clientId=<CLIENT_ID>  
    pulse.global.oidc.secret=<CLIENT_SECRET>  
    pulse.global.oidc.discoveryURI=<DISCOVERY_URI>  
      
    ####################################################  
    #                  JWT Auth Provider  
    ####################################################  
    # The following property is the id of the configuration, only needed to enable the plugin  
    # if no other property is set  
    pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.provider.jwt.idpConfig.id=feedzai-keycloak  
      
    # Defaults for connection timeouts to the IdP and JWT clock skew  
    #pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.provider.jwt.idpConfig.connectTimeoutMs=500;  
    #pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.provider.jwt.idpConfig.readTimeoutMs=500;  
    #pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.provider.jwt.idpConfig.maxClockSkewSeconds=60;  
      
    # Default values for JWT claim names/paths, for clientID = `CLIENT_ID`  
    #pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.provider.jwt.idpConfig.tenantsPath=/tenants  
    #pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.provider.jwt.idpConfig.groupsPath=/groups  
    #pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.provider.jwt.idpConfig.rolesPath=/roles/<CLIENT_ID>

# Configuring SSO Using a Generic IdP

Single Sign-On (SSO) in Pulse uses SAML 2.0 standard as the protocol to authenticate and authorize users that are provisioned by an external Identity Provider (IdP).

This guide describes the configuration of SSO using a generic IdP. If you are using Microsoft AD FS as the IdP of choice, please visit the page [Configuring AD FS](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/single-sign-on/configuring-ad-fs).

## Pulse SSO propertiesâ

Configuring **SSO** in Pulse requires setting a number of properties. Pulse needs to:

  * Know what is the IdP that it will connect.
  * Have a private key for signing Pulse requests and a corresponding X509 certificate.
  * Have a private key for signing On-Behalf Proxy requests and a corresponding X509 certificate.



Contact Feedzai to set up these properties for your environment.

### Identity provider propertiesâ

The IdP properties have the `pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.idp` prefix and the easiest way to know what to include in them is to obtain the **IdP XML metadata**. This XML contains configuration and integration details for SAML 2.0 and is usually made available on a URL. Alternatively, it can be exported as a file on the IdP configuration interface.

The following code block shows the relevant portion of this XML that contains the information that Pulse needs to communicate with the IdP and to which properties the information should be copied.
    
    
    <EntityDescriptor xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:metadata" ID="..." entityID="{{idp.entityId}}">  
        ...  
        <IDPSSODescriptor protocolSupportEnumeration="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol">  
            ...  
            <KeyDescriptor use="signing">  
                <KeyInfo xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#">  
                    <X509Data>  
                        <X509Certificate>  
                            {{idp.x509cert}}  
                        </X509Certificate>  
                    </X509Data>  
                </KeyInfo>  
            </KeyDescriptor>  
            ...  
            <SingleLogoutService Binding="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:bindings:HTTP-Redirect" Location="{{idp.slo}}"/>  
            ...  
            <SingleSignOnService Binding="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:bindings:HTTP-Redirect" Location="{{idp.sso}}"/>  
            ...  
        </IDPSSODescriptor>  
    </EntityDescriptor>  
    

### Service Provider Propertiesâ

The SAML 2.0 standard requires the sign out requests to be signed by the two parties (i.e. Pulse and the IdP). This requires Pulse to have a private key and a X509 public certificate. Optionally, Pulse and IdP can also be configured to sign the Sign in requests.

The following code block exemplifies how to generate the private key and the respective self-signed x509 certificate.

info

Please check if you can use self-signed certificates for **SSO** in your deployment.
    
    
    # Generate a new Private Key and respective self-signed Certificate, valid for $CERT_DAYS days  
    openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:$KEY_SIZE -keyout $PK_TEMP_FILE -out $CERT_FILE -days $CERT_DAYS -subj "/C=PT/O=Feedzai/OU=Pulse/CN=feedzai.com"  
      
    # Convert the Private Key to PKCS#8 format  
    openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform pem -nocrypt -in $PK_TEMP_FILE -outform pem -out $PK_FILE  
    

where the variables are replaced by the following:

Variable| Value| Notes  
---|---|---  
`$KEY_SIZE`| 1024| 1024 is the minimum key size required by some IdPs  
`$CERT_DAYS`| 3650|   
`$PK_TEMP_FILE`| pkTempFile.pem|   
`$PK_FILE`| pkey.pem| The PKCS#8 private key file.  
`$CERT_FILE`| cert.pem| The X509 certificate file.  
  
The contents of `$PK_FILE` and `$CERT_FILE` must be copied to the corresponding properties in Pulse, respectively:

  * `pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.sp.privateKey`
  * `pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.filter.samlsso.sp.x509cert`



### On-behalf service provider propertiesâ

Pulse is also able to act as a non-standard on-behalf service provider proxy (e.g. Case Manager uses this option).

For each proxy service provider that will use Pulse to handle SAML messages on its behalf, you have to repeat the process of obtaining a private key and respective certificate, but copy the contents of `$PK_FILE` and `$CERT_FILE` to the following Pulse properties instead:

  * pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.proxy.samlsso.<spKey>.privateKey
  * pulse.manager.services.core.security.authplugin.proxy.samlsso.<spKey>.x509cert



info

For Case Manager, replace `<spKey>` with `cm`.

## Configure IdP to communicate with Pulseâ

After configuring Pulse to communicate with the IdP and trust its information, the IdP also needs to be configured to work with Pulse. The SAML 2.0 standard also defines a standard metadata XML for service providers to make their configuration and make their integration details available (e.g. identification, login and logout endpoints, public certificate).

After configuring Pulse for SSO, the XML metadata can be obtained by accessing the following address:
    
    
    https://<BASE_PULSE_URL>/pulseviews/api/sessions/samlsso/metadata  
    

If Pulse is configured to act as an on-behalf service provider (e.g. Case Manager), you can obtain the metadata for the referred service provider by using the following curl request:
    
    
    curl -X POST \  
      https://<BASE_PULSE_URL>/pulseviews/api/samlproxy/metadata \  
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \  
      -H 'Cookie: SSOcookie=<A_VALID_PULSE_COOKIE>' \  
      -d '{  
      "spKey": "<spKey>",  
      "baseUrl": "<BASE_HTTPS_URL>",  
      "loginEndpoint": "<SAML_LOGIN_ENDPOINT>",  
      "logoutEndpoint": "<SAML_LOGOUT_ENDPOINT>"  
    }'  
    

Most IdPs have a method to import these XML metadata files. Even if they don't, this metadata contains all the information that you might need to add Pulse as a trusted service provider on the IdP.

## Configure user provisioningâ

note

This step is not required if authorization is configured to be performed in Pulse.

Now that Pulse and the IdP trust and know how to communicate with each other, you can configure user provisioning.  Besides the authentication info, Pulse and Case Manager also need to receive authorization information along with users authentication. This information is essential to perform user provisioning (i.e. creating a Pulse user on the fly).

The user provisioning configuration must be set on the IdP configuration interface. Since this configuration is different according to the used IdP, this section focuses on explaining what needs to be configured, as opposed to how to configure it. If Microsoft AD FS is the IdP of choice in your deployment, please visit the page [Create claim rules on AD FS](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/single-sign-on/configuring-ad-fs#create-claim-rules).

Pulse performs user provisioning based on the values of SAML attributes within an authentication response. SAML attributes are sent inside the AttributeStatement XML element. Each of these attributes has a name and one or more values.

The following code shows a sample SAML authentication response sent by the IdP to Pulse:
    
    
    <samlp:Response ID="..." Version="2.0" IssueInstant="..." Destination="https://pulse-local-signed:8443/pulseviews/api/sessions/samlsso" Consent="..."  
        xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol">  
        <Issuer xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion">{{idp.entityId}}</Issuer>  
        <samlp:Status>...</samlp:Status>  
        <Assertion ID="..." IssueInstant="..." Version="2.0" xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion">  
            <Issuer>{{idp.entityId}}</Issuer>  
            <Signature xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#">...</Signature>  
            <Subject>  
                <NameID Format="...">{{user.username}}</NameID>  
                <SubjectConfirmation Method="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:cm:bearer">...</SubjectConfirmation>  
            </Subject>  
            <Conditions NotBefore="..." NotOnOrAfter="...">...</Conditions>  
            <AttributeStatement>  
                ...  
                <Attribute Name="User.roles">  
                    <AttributeValue>UserRole1</AttributeValue>  
                    <AttributeValue>UserRole2</AttributeValue>  
                </Attribute>  
                <Attribute Name="User.groups">  
                    <AttributeValue>UserGroup1</AttributeValue>  
                    <AttributeValue>UserGroup2</AttributeValue>  
                </Attribute>  
                <Attribute Name="User.tenants">  
                    <AttributeValue>UserTenant</AttributeValue>  
                </Attribute>  
                <Attribute Name="User.language">  
                    <AttributeValue>en-US</AttributeValue>  
                </Attribute>  
                <Attribute Name="User.fullname">  
                    <AttributeValue>User Full Name</AttributeValue>  
                </Attribute>  
                ...  
            </AttributeStatement>  
            <AuthnStatement AuthnInstant="..." SessionIndex="...">...</AuthnStatement>  
        </Assertion>  
    </samlp:Response>  
    

After receiving the message above, besides the user name Pulse will extract the following information for the authenticated user:

  * **Roles:** UserRole1, UserRole2
  * **Groups:** UserGroup1, UserGroup2
  * **Tenant** : UserTenant
  * **Language:** en-US
  * **Full Name:** User Full Name



When working with these settings, consider the following:

  * Roles, groups and tenants are matched by name. They have to previously exist in Pulse, otherwise the authorization will fail. Exception messages to search for:
    * `Group <name> does not exist`
    * `Role <name> does not exist`
  * All SSO-Users must have at least one group or role associated with them. Exception message to search for:
    * `User <username> has no group/role`
  * The name of SAML attributes presented above may be changed. 
  * Besides being created when a user signs into Pulse for the first time, the user information is updated every time the user signs in.
  * The content of exchanged SAML messages may be logged. Package: com.onelogin.saml2, Level: debug.

# Configure Jetty to Log HTTP Requests

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse uses Jetty **9.4.X** as the back-end engine for the web server. It is possible to configure the engine to automatically log every HTTP request into a log file (which will appear in the `log/` folder). To do so, itâs necessary to add a new logger entry to the file `conf/engine/jetty/jetty.xml` in Pulse:
    
    
      <Configure id="Server" class="org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server">  
        <Arg name="threadpool"><New id="threadpool" class="org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool"/></Arg>  
        ...  
        <Set name="RequestLog">  
          <New id="RequestLog" class="org.eclipse.jetty.server.CustomRequestLog">  
            <!-- Writer -->  
            <Arg>  
              <New class="org.eclipse.jetty.server.AsyncRequestLogWriter">  
                <!-- Make http request log rotate by day. -->  
                <Arg><Property name="solr.log.dir" default="log"/>/yyyy_mm_dd.request.log</Arg>  
                <Set name="filenameDateFormat">yyyy_MM_dd</Set>  
                <!-- Only delete rotated files after a week.  -->  
                <Set name="retainDays">  
                  <Property name="solr.log.requestlog.retaindays" default="7"/>  
                </Set>  
                <Set name="append">true</Set>  
                <Set name="timeZone">UTC</Set>  
              </New>  
            </Arg>  
            <!-- Default format String: -->  
            <!-- Arg><Get class="org.eclipse.jetty.server.CustomRequestLog" name="EXTENDED_NCSA_FORMAT"/></Arg -->  
            <!-- Custom format String: https://javadoc.io/doc/org.eclipse.jetty/jetty-server/9.4.51.v20230217/org/eclipse/jetty/server/CustomRequestLog.html -->  
            <Arg>{{date: %{YYYY-MM-dd:hh:mm:ss:SSSZ}t},{response status:%s},{hostname: %{client}a}, {response time: %{ms}Tms}, {hostname: %{Host}i}, {user: %u}, {Connection status: %X}, {response status: %s}, {first line: %r}, {address client: %{client}a}, {address server: %{server}a}, {MAC: %{local}a}}</Arg>  
          </New>  
        </Set>  
      ...  
    

The API of`CustomRequestLog` for **Jetty v9.4.51.v20230217** (used by **Pulse 25.0.15+**) is described at [the jetty-server documentation](https://javadoc.io/doc/org.eclipse.jetty/jetty-server/9.4.51.v20230217/org/eclipse/jetty/server/CustomRequestLog.html).

By using this `CustomRequestLog` itâs possible to satisfy the following requirements from [CR707 PCR4293 Fraud Event Logging Components_Requirements](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1-sx4FN8fwfxIAzGY1YAu2sTHoVttuP5lwqJtv_P-Ef4/edit?usp=sharing):

Requirement| Loggable| RequestLog Argument (string format)  
---|---|---  
Properly formatted and accurate timestamp|   
Must be in a format supported by `Jetty DateCache.`| 
    
    
    {date: %{YYYY-MM-dd:hh:mm:ss:SSSZ}t}  
  
Status code for the event type request was successful or not|   
Itâs possible to know via the HTTP response code.| 
    
    
    {response status:%s}  
  
Device identifier (MAC address or other unique identifier)|   
Likely not possible since printing physical address is the same as printing the IP of the client or server in our tests.| 
    
    
    {MAC: %{local}a}

  
It prints the IP as physical address.  
Session / Transaction ID|   
Likely not possible since API doesnât provide a way to get an unique identifier for the request.|   
Autonomous System Number (hostname)|   
Possible. Could be necessary to print the host header for it.| 
    
    
    {hostname: %{Host}i}

  
Might be possible for client to send wrong information.  
Source IP (IPv4)| | 
    
    
    {address client: %{client}a}  
  
Source IP (IPv6)|   
Likely possible since IPv4 works, but untested.| 
    
    
    {address client: %{client}a}

  
It should also print IPv6 if used. **Not tested.**  
Status Code| | 
    
    
    {response status: %s}  
  
Response Time| | 
    
    
    {response time: %{ms}Tms}  
  
Additional headers (i.e., HTTP headers)| | 
    
    
    {Header_Name: %{Header_Name}i}  
  
Where appropriate, the username and/or userID shall be included|   
Likely not possible since API doesnât provide a way to get an unique identifier for the request.|   
Where appropriate, the command executed shall be included| | 
    
    
    {first HTTP line: %r}  
  
Where possible, all data shall be formatted as key-value-pairs allowing for easy extraction| | E.g.:  

    
    
    {{date: %{YYYY-MM-dd:hh:mm:ss:SSSZ}t},{response status:%s},{hostname: %{client}a}, {response time: %{ms}Tms}, {hostname: %{Host}i}, {user: %u}, {Connection status: %X}, {response status: %s}, {first line: %r}, {address client: %{client}a}, {address server: %{server}a}, {MAC: %{local}a}}  
  
Where possible, a unique event identifier shall be included for event correlation; a unique event identifier shall be defined per event type6|   
Likely not possible since API doesnât provide a way to get an unique identifier for the request.|   
  
The third column of the table above shows examples of possible values for the argument `formatString` that needs to be passed to the constructor of `org.eclipse.jetty.server.CustomRequestLog#CustomRequestLog( org.eclipse.jetty.server.RequestLog.Writer, java.lang.String )` in order to print the requirements of the first column.

# Event Storage Dump Logging

## Event Storage Dump Loggingâ

In case of a major failure, the Smart Event Storage Dump will log the event that failed to be persisted in the file. This event can contain confidential information, therefore, these logs should only be logged to the [Confidential Logger](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/monitoring/logging/logging-confidential-data). In order to do that the following configurations must be added to the `logger.xml`:

To the "common" logger:

Main Log Appender
    
    
    <logger name="com.feedzai.dump.storage.impl.files.FileDumpWriter" level="off"/>  
    

To the confidential logger:

Confidential Log Appender
    
    
    <!-- In trace level it will log the events that failed to be persisted into disk -->  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.dump.storage.impl.files.FileDumpWriter" level="off" additivity="false">  
        <appender-ref ref="CONFIDENTIAL-ASYNC"/>  
    </logger>

# Log Confidential Data

Was this page helpful?Â 

Confidential or Personal Identifiable Information (PII) must **NEVER** be logged. However, in some cases, it might be necessary to access confidential data in logs to investigate production issues. In such cases, Pulse can expose logs with confidential data to a set of files that is separate from the normal application logs. Confidential logging should be activated only when it is absolutely necessary, for the time of an investigation.

This page explains how to configure the confidential logger.

warning

The confidential log files **MUST NEVER** be sent to uncontrolled environments (e.g., cloud services such as Amazon CloudWatch) and they **MUST** be deleted immediately after the investigations.

## Introductionâ

Pulse uses the Logback framework to create confidential logs. Confidential logging uses two main concepts of Logback:

  * **loggers** : they receive the log messages from Pulse, and pass them to the right appender.
  * **appenders** : they store the log messages in their final destination.



In Pulse, every process (i.e. Pulse server, or app engine) can send messages to more than one logger. Each logger can be connected to one or more appenders. Each appender sends the messages to a different file or to the network/terminal. This way, you can log each process' data to a separate file, and you can turn confidential logging on or off separately for each process.

For example, confidential logs of the Pulse server process will be written to `CONFIDENTIAL-pulse.log`, while a confidential log of an app engine named _my-app_ will be written to `CONFIDENTIAL-app-my-app.log`. This helps you minimize the amount of PII that is logged.

You can configure confidential logging by editing the file `PULSE_HOME/conf/loggers/logger-confidential.xml` of the server(s) that you want to log data from. This file uses Logback's log configuration syntax.

To ensure that confidential logs aren't appended to the normal log files, such as `pulse.log` and `app-<APP-NAME>;.log`, you must have well-configured confidential loggers and confidential appenders in the `logger.xml` file.

Avoid exposing confidential information

You must ensure that your logger.xml file has the correct confidential logging setup. Otherwise, you may be exposing confidential logs in the normal log files.

## Enabling confidential loggingâ

To enable confidential logging, perform the following steps in the file `PULSE_HOME/conf/loggers/logger-confidential.xml` using [Logback's syntax](https://logback.qos.ch/manual/) in the `logger.xml` file:

  1. Create a confidential log appender. See an example in the following sections.
  2. Create a confidential logger. Configure that logger so that it uses the appender created in step 1. See an example in the following sections.
  3. To kick off logging, set the _level_ property of the logger to the desired level (e.g., "info", "trace", ...). Any confidential log written by Pulse with a logging level above or equal to the configured level will appear in the respective `CONFIDENTIAL-*.log` files.



### Example: creating confidential log appendersâ

The following example creates two confidential log appenders, the "CONFIDENTIAL-ASYNC" appender is the one that receives the log messages, and passes them to the "CONFIDENTIAL" appender, which sends them to the defined output. Since it uses the _pulse.logcontext_ variable, it creates a separate file for each process.

Confidential log appenders
    
    
    <appender name="CONFIDENTIAL" class="ch.qos.logback.core.FileAppender">  
      
        <filter class="ch.qos.logback.classic.filter.ThresholdFilter">  
            <level>TRACE</level>  
        </filter>  
      
        <file>log/CONFIDENTIAL-${pulse.logcontext}.log</file>  
      
        <encoder>  
            <pattern>%-5level %d{ISO8601} }%-65(%P{slug} %P{appId} %P{member}) %P{isLeader}] %-40(}%thread]) %-65(%logger{0}.%M:%line) %msg%n%xEx{full}</pattern>  
        </encoder>  
    </appender>  
    <appender name="CONFIDENTIAL-ASYNC" class="ch.qos.logback.classic.AsyncAppender">  
        <appender-ref ref="CONFIDENTIAL"/>  
        <queueSize>2048</queueSize>  
        <discardingThreshold>0</discardingThreshold>  
        <includeCallerData>true</includeCallerData>  
        <neverBlock>true</neverBlock>  
    </appender>  
    

### Example: configuring the confidential loggerâ

To ensure that confidential logs written by Pulse are never exposed in the normal log files and are always appended to the `CONFIDENTIAL-*.log` files, you MUST ensure that the following logger is configured in the `PULSE_HOME/conf/loggers/logger-confidential.xml file` file.

Confidential Logger
    
    
    <!--  
        WARNING:  
            - This logger MUST NEVER be commented. Otherwise, confidential logs will end up in the normal log files.  
            - This logger MUST NEVER be set to a level different than 'off', UNLESS it is strictly necessary to perform investigations that requires the visualization of confidential logs.  
            - This logger MUST NEVER be set to a level different than 'off' if the logs written by the configured appender will end up on insecure environments (e.g., Amazon CloudWatch).  
            - If this logger is set to a level different than 'off' to perform strictly necessary investigations, it MUST be set to 'off' again immediately after ending the investigations and all the produced log files must be immediately deleted without being sent to any untrusted/insecure medium.  
    -->  
    <logger name="confidential" level="off" additivity="false">  
            <appender-ref ref="CONFIDENTIAL-ASYNC"/>  
    </logger>  
    

This logger MUST NEVER be commented. Otherwise, confidential logs written in Pulse will end up in the normal log files.

It is possible to configure more granular confidential log levels, by setting the level at class/package scope. To do this, configure loggers with classes/package names prefixed with `confidential.`, as shown in the following example:

Examples of more granular confidential logging
    
    
    <logger name="confidential.com.feedzai.pulse.libs.lists.UpdatableInMemoryList" level="error"/>  
    <logger name="confidential.com.feedzai.pulse.libs.lists.ImmutableListsRuntimeLoader" level="info"/>  
    

# Turning off confidential logging

To turn off confidential logging completely, set the logger's level to "off" and ensure that the logger has the following property set: `additivity="false"` .

Reset confidential loggers level to OFF

Make sure that the level of the confidential logger is set to "off" after ending any investigation. Otherwise, confidential logs continue to be written to the `CONFIDENTIAL-*.log` files.

Never comment or change any property besides the level in the main confidential logger.

# Log Partitioning Information on Plan Operator

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse can be configured to log information about the way Pulse partitions work when calculating the values in the plan operator.

The logger property `com.feedzai.pulse.datascience.plan.operators.impl` allows to configure which details should be logged. The following logging levels are available:

Level| What is logged  
---|---  
info| A set of partitioning fields with corresponding metrics.   
Computed metrics partitioning schemas of multiple _Group By_ fields.

**Example**

# Logging Reference for Security Audits

Was this page helpful?Â 

Feedzai Pulse contains three distinct logs that can be tailored to obtain the exact needs of a security audit, e.g. a PCI-DSS security audit. This section documents the relevant logging configurations in Feedzai Pulse and how to perform them, including examples and recommendations. The main goal is to allow engineers to perform specific actions more easily, such as editing the logging configuration during audits.

tip

There are three main logging approaches that may be helpful in audits:

  * **Security audit:** contains information usually very relevant for security audit, i.e. for PCI-DSS compliance;
  * **Tracing interceptor:** includes logging at the HTTP request level;
  * **Auditing:** log calls made to resource managers.



## Loggingâ

All operations executed internally by Pulse are accordingly logged to several levels of detail in log files located in the **PULSE_HOME/log** directory. In some specific cases, logs can also be logged into databases.

Find more information about logging and the respective configuration in the [Logging](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/monitoring/logging) page.

The logging configuration file located in **PULSE_HOME/conf/logger/logger-legacy-audit.xml** allows the configuration of **security audit** and **tracing interceptor** logs. For **auditing** , it is also necessary to edit the Pulse properties file in **PULSE_HOME/conf/pulse.properties**.

warning

It is the user's own responsibility to change the logging configuration. Changes may result in the loss of valuable information for investigating problems. If the default configuration is changed, support teams may not be able to help, therefore, the user should be extremely careful when editing this file.

## Security audit loggingâ

To enable the security audit file, the user must change the configuration file that is located in **PULSE_HOME/conf/logger/logger-legacy-audit.xml**.

The appenders section define where the logging messages will end up. Find more information about the different available appenders in the **Appenders** section in the [Logging](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/monitoring/logging) page.

By default, this is the code block where the security logging is disabled:
    
    
    <!--  
          Start of security audit logging.  
    -->  
    <!-- SECURITY-AUDIT LOGGING TAG  
    <appender name="SECURITY-AUDIT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">  
      <file>log/${pulse.logcontext}-security-audit.log</file>  
      <filter class="ch.qos.logback.core.filter.EvaluatorFilter">  
        <evaluator class="ch.qos.logback.classic.boolex.OnMarkerEvaluator">  
          <marker>SECURITY_AUDIT</marker>  
        </evaluator>  
        <onMismatch>DENY</onMismatch>  
        <onMatch>NEUTRAL</onMatch>  
      </filter>  
      <filter class="ch.qos.logback.classic.filter.ThresholdFilter">  
        <level>TRACE</level>  
      </filter>  
      <encoder>  
        <pattern>[%-65(%P{slug} %P{appId} %P{member}) %P{isLeader}] %msg%n</pattern>  
      </encoder>  
      <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.TimeBasedRollingPolicy">  
        <fileNamePattern>log/${pulse.logcontext}-security-audit.%d{yyyy-MM}-week-%d{WW}.log.gz</fileNamePattern>  
        <maxHistory>16</maxHistory>  
      </rollingPolicy>  
    </appender>  
      
    <logger name="com.feedzai.pulse.service.security.SecurityLogging" level="trace" additivity="false">  
      <appender-ref ref="SECURITY-AUDIT"/>  
    </logger>  
    SECURITY-AUDIT LOGGING TAG -->  
    <!-- End of security audit logging. -->  
    

To enable it, comment in both "Security-audit logging tag" strings as shown below:
    
    
    <!--  
          Start of security audit logging.  
    -->  
    <!-- SECURITY-AUDIT LOGGING TAG -->  
    <appender name="SECURITY-AUDIT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">  
      <file>log/${pulse.logcontext}-security-audit.log</file>  
      <filter class="ch.qos.logback.core.filter.EvaluatorFilter">  
        <evaluator class="ch.qos.logback.classic.boolex.OnMarkerEvaluator">  
          <marker>SECURITY_AUDIT</marker>  
        </evaluator>  
        <onMismatch>DENY</onMismatch>  
        <onMatch>NEUTRAL</onMatch>  
      </filter>  
      <filter class="ch.qos.logback.classic.filter.ThresholdFilter">  
        <level>TRACE</level>  
      </filter>  
      <encoder>  
        <pattern>[%-65(%P{slug} %P{appId} %P{member}) %P{isLeader}] %msg%n</pattern>  
      </encoder>  
      <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.TimeBasedRollingPolicy">  
        <fileNamePattern>log/${pulse.logcontext}-security-audit.%d{yyyy-MM}-week-%d{WW}.log.gz</fileNamePattern>  
        <maxHistory>16</maxHistory>  
      </rollingPolicy>  
    </appender>  
      
    <logger name="com.feedzai.pulse.service.security.SecurityLogging" level="trace" additivity="false">  
      <appender-ref ref="SECURITY-AUDIT"/>  
    </logger>  
    <!-- SECURITY-AUDIT LOGGING TAG -->  
    <!-- End of security audit logging. -->  
    

All output will be generated in the file located in **PULSE_HOME/log/your-pulse-log-context.security-audit.log.xml.** In the above configuration, it is possible to change this file's name and location as well as other parameters, such as the logging level and compressed name file.

## Events logged in the security auditâ

**User:**

  * USER_CREATED,
  * USER_UPDATED,
  * USER_DELETED,
  * USER_LOGIN,
  * USER_LOGIN_FAILED,
  * USER_PASSWORD_CHANGE,
  * USER_PASSWORD_CHANGE_FAILED,
  * USER_PASSWORD_EXPIRED,
  * USER_PASSWORD_MANUALLY_EXPIRED,
  * USER_DISABLE_BY_INACTIVITY,
  * USER_MANUALLY_DISABLED,
  * USER_MANUALLY_ENABLED,
  * USER_DISABLED_BY_TOO_MANY_WRONG_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS,
  * USER_TWO_FACTOR_CONFIG_DELETED,



**Roles:**

  * ROLE_CREATED,
  * ROLE_UPDATED,
  * ROLE_DELETED,



**Tenants:**

  * TENANT_CREATED,
  * TENANT_UPDATED,
  * TENANT_DELETED



**Tenant Groups:**

  * TENANT_GROUP_CREATED,
  * TENANT_GROUP_UPDATED,
  * TENANT_GROUP_DELETED



**Groups:**

  * GROUP_CREATED,
  * GROUP_UPDATED,
  * GROUP_DELETED



## Tracing interceptor loggingâ

caution

Note that the tracing interceptor logging is very wordy and the log files will grow at a very fast rate. Enable this logging only if strictly necessary.

By using the tracing interceptor, you enable the logging of events at the level of HTTP requests.

It is possible to enable the logging of events by adding the following line to the **PULSE_HOME/conf/logger/logger-project.xml** configuration file:

`<logger name="com.feedzai.pulse.web.api.commons.exceptions.TracingInterceptor" level="trace"/>`

## Auditing loggingâ

caution

Note that the **auditing logging** is very wordy and the log files will grow at a very fast rate. Enable this logging only if strictly necessary.

The purpose of auditing is to keep a log of calls that are made to resource managers. To enable it, follow the instructions in the Auditing page.

The configuration below represents a specific security audit whose purpose is to enable logging to a file. To do so, perform the following changes displayed in  **pulse.properties** , as well as in the **PULSE_HOME/conf/logger/logger-legacy-audit.xml** file.

pulse.properties
    
    
    pulse.manager.auditing.logger.name=auditing  
    pulse.manager.auditing.logger.level=trace  
    

logger.xml
    
    
    <!-- Start of auditing logging. -->  
    <appender name="AUDITING" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">  
        <file>log/${pulse.logcontext}-auditing.log</file>  
        <encoder>  
            <pattern>%msg</pattern>  
        </encoder>  
        <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.TimeBasedRollingPolicy">  
            <!-- Daily rollover with gzip compression for the archives, keeping up to 30 -->  
            <fileNamePattern>log/${pulse.logcontext}-auditing.%d.log.gz</fileNamePattern>  
            <maxHistory>30</maxHistory>  
        </rollingPolicy>  
        <encoder>  
            <pattern>%-5level %d{ISO8601} [%-65(%P{slug} %P{appId} %P{member}) %P{isLeader}] %-40([%thread]) %-65(%logger{0}.%M:%line) %msg%n%xEx{full}</pattern>  
        </encoder>  
    </appender>  
    <appender name="AUDITING-ASYNC" class="ch.qos.logback.classic.AsyncAppender">  
        <appender-ref ref="AUDITING" />  
        <queueSize>8192</queueSize>  
        <discardingThreshold>0</discardingThreshold>  
        <includeCallerData>false</includeCallerData>  
    </appender>  
    <logger name="auditing" level="trace" additivity="false">  
        <appender-ref ref="AUDITING-ASYNC"/>  
    </logger>  
    <!-- End of auditing logging. -->

# Set Up Microsoft LightGBM Logging

Was this page helpful?Â 

To log information about what happens when training a model with the LightGBM provider, you can configure the logging levels from the most basic "INFO", up to the most extreme level "TRACE".

## Logging levelsâ

The LightGBM provider has several modules, each with different responsibilities. You can control the logging level per module.

Module name| Description| Logging level description  
---|---|---  
**LightGBMBinary ClassificationModel**| Implements the OpenML class responsible for loading a model and scoring instances.   
It is also called when saving the model to disk.| ERROR: Report that saving model to disk failed.  
**LightGBMBinary ClassificationModelTrainer**| Responsible for training a LightGBM model.   
  
At the end of the train it saves an intermediate representation to disk that is then passed to LightGBMBinaryClassificationModel for the final model save to disk.| 

  * INFO: Information messages reporting the stage at which the training is.
  * ERROR: For errors during train.
  * DEBUG: Report #train-instances, training parameters and features, more details on the sub-stages of training, progress in number of train iterations.

  
**LightGBMModelCreator**|  Starts all load/fit operations and validations prior to starting the aforementioned model load/fit process.| 

  * INFO: Message with filepath from which the model is being loaded.
  * ERROR: Errors when training the model or the validations for a model fit/load fail and where it is it trying to read from.

  
**LightGBMSWIG**|  Low-level implementation for model scoring.| 

  * INFO: Saving model to disk calls.
  * ERROR: Errors saving model to disk.
  * DEBUG: Saving model to disk calls with file paths.
  * TRACE: Show prediction score per instance. Note that this level is **very verbose!**

  
**LightGBMUtils**|  Loads the LightGBM libraries.| 

  * INFO: When the libraries are loaded.
  * DEBUG: Names of the libraries being loaded.

  
**SWIGResources**|  Lowest-level implementation level for resources handling during model scoring.| 

  * DEBUG: In-memory instantiation of model.
  * TRACE: Resource release calls.

  
**SWIGTrainResources**|  Lowest-level implementation level for resources handling during model fitting.| DEBUG: Details for train memory allocation.  
  
## How to set up loggingâ

To configure such log levels, edit the file `conf/logger.xml`. Also, for Spark Standalone `spark-libs/logback-executors.xml` should also have such log levels.

### Example configurationâ

An example of configuring for maximum log level follows. Feel free to copy-paste, but beware of having too much logging enabled (see table above):

conf/logger.xml & spark-libs/logback-executors.xml
    
    
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMBinaryClassificationModel" level="trace"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMBinaryClassificationModelTrainer" level="trace"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMModelCreator" level="trace"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMSWIG" level="trace"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMUtils" level="trace"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.SWIGResources" level="trace"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.SWIGTrainResources" level="trace"/>

# Monitoring Cassandra Driver Sessions

Was this page helpful?Â 

Multiple Pulse components can be configured to work with a Cassandra database, such as the Profile Store and the Event Storage. The `/metrics` API exposes several metrics that allow Pulse operators to monitor the Cassandra drivers that these different components use to communicate with the Cassandra cluster(s).

This page describes how to configure the monitoring of these drivers, as well as the available metrics.

## Cassandra drivers and their configuration propertiesâ

Within a Pulse App Engine, several Cassandra drivers can be created depending on the defined configurations. If a Cassandra connection configuration is provided at the global level, a Cassandra driver may be created at the App Engine level, which can then be used by the multiple components within the App Engine, as long as the Cassandra connection configuration of these components is either not provided (defaults to global) or equal to the one defined at the global scope. Otherwise, the component itself will create its own Cassandra driver.

The prefix of the Cassandra driver metric names, as well as the metric tags, changes depending on whether the driver is created by the App Engine or by a specific component within the App Engine:

Metric Name Prefix | Description | Tags  
---|---|---  
      
    
    pulse.cassandra.driver.stats

| For the Cassandra driver that can be created by the App Engine. | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType_  
      
    
    pulse.workflow.cassandra.driver.stats

| For the Cassandra driver that can be created within the scope of a given workflow component. | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType  
workflowId  
workflowDesc  
elementId  
elementDesc  
context_  
  
## Available metricsâ

The following table lists all the metrics that are exposed for each Cassandra driver:

Name | Description | Unit  
---|---|---  
Counters  
      
    
    <prefix>.blocking-executor-queue-depth

| The total number of queued-up tasks in the Cassandra driver's blocking executor. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.connect-to

| The total number of Cassandra hosts the driver is currently connected to. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.executor-queue-depth

| The total number of queued-up tasks in the Cassandra driver's main internal executor. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.inflight-requests

| The total number of inflight requests to Cassandra hosts. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.known-hosts

| The total number of Cassandra hosts currently known by the driver, regardless of whether the hosts are up or down. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.open-connections

| The total number of currently open connections to Cassandra hosts. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.reconnection-scheduler-task-count

| The total number of queued up tasks in the Cassandra driver's reconnection executor. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.request-queue-depth

| The total number of enqueued requests on all Cassandra hosts. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.task-scheduler-task-count

| The total number of queued-up tasks in the Cassandra driver's scheduled tasks executor. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.trashed-connections

| The total number of currently trashed connections to Cassandra hosts. | #  
Gauges  
      
    
    <prefix>.authentication-errors

| The number of authentication errors while connecting to Cassandra nodes. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.client-timeouts

| The number of requests that timed out before the driver received a response. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.connection-errors

| The number of errors while connecting to Cassandra nodes. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.ignores

| The number of times a request was ignored due to the retry policy, for instance, due to timeouts or unavailability. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.ignores-on-client-timeout

| The number of times a request was ignored due to the retry policy after a client timeout. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.ignores-on-connection-error

| The number of times a request was ignored due to the retry policy after a connection error. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.ignores-on-other-errors

| The number of times a request was ignored due to the retry policy after an unexpected error. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.ignores-on-read-timeout

| The number of times a request was ignored due to the retry policy after a read timed out. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.ignores-on-unavailable

| The number of times a request was ignored due to the retry policy after an unavailable exception. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.ignores-on-write-timeout

| The number of times a request was ignored due to the retry policy after a write timed out. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.other-errors

| The number of requests that returned errors not accounted for by another metric. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.read-timeouts

| The number of read requests that returned a timeout (independently of the final decision taken by the retry policy). | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.retries

| The number of times a request was retried due to the retry policy. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.retries-on-client-timeout

| The number of times a request was retried due to the retry policy after a client timeout. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.retries-on-connection-error

| The number of times a request was retried due to the retry policy after a connection error. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.retries-on-other-errors

| The number of times a request was retried due to the retry policy after an unexpected error. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.retries-on-read-timeout

| The number of times a request was retried due to the retry policy after a read timed out. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.retries-on-unavailable

| The number of times a request was retried due to the retry policy after an unavailable exception. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.retries-on-write-timeout

| The number of times a request was retried due to the retry policy after a write timed out. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.speculative-executions

| The number of times a speculative execution was started because a previous execution did not complete within the delay specified by speculative execution policy. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.unavailables

| The number of requests that returned an unavailable exception (independently of the final decision taken by the retry policy). | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.write-timeouts

| Returns the number of write requests that returned a timeout (independently of the final decision taken by the retry policy). | #  
Meters  
      
    
    <prefix>.bytes-received

| The number of bytes received by the Cassandra driver so far. | #  
      
    
    <prefix>.bytes-sent

| The number of bytes sent by the Cassandra driver so far. | #  
Timers  
Metrics regarding the number of user requests performed on the Cassandra cluster: 

  * The total number of requests.
  * The requests rate (in requests per second), including 1, 5 and 15-minute rates.
  * The mean, min and max latencies, as well as latency at a given percentile.

On this page

# Monitoring Event Storage Dumps in Pulse

Was this page helpful?Â 

This page describes how to monitor the dumping of events when they fail to be written to the Event Storage in Pulse using the `/metrics` endpoint.

## Introductionâ

In Pulse, each Workflow has it own Event Storage. When events reach the end of the workflow they are persisted in the Event Storage. If the Event Storage isn't avaliable (e.g.: Database is offline) the events are dumped to disk and are reprocessed later on by the Event Storage Dump component.

It is essential to know if this component is operating within reasonable limits. By taking monitoring metrics from the Event Storage Dump, Pulse operators can have access to different information related to event dumps operations via the `/metrics` endpoint.

info

To enable the component that reports this metrics, reach out to the Feedzai Customer Success (CS) team.

## Metricsâ

The metrics are associated with an application, identifiable via an `appSlug` tag, where the service is running.

The `appType` and `metricType` tags, that are also associated with these monitoring metrics, are common to other metrics exposed in Pulse and App Engines. They inform where the metrics were collected (Pulse Server or App Engine) and what type of metric it is being reported (e.g. APPLICATION), respectively.

Name | Description | Unit | Possible Values | Tags  
---|---|---|---|---  
Gauges  
      
    
    pulse.dump.storage.retry.queue.size

| The total number of events that are present in the in-memory queue to be written to the dump file in the retry folder. | # | >= 0 | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType  
workflowID  
workflowDesc_  
      
    
    pulse.dump.storage.failed.queue.size

| The total number of events that are present in the in-memory queue to be written to the dump file in the failed folder. | # | >= 0 | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType  
workflowID  
workflowDesc_  
      
    
    pulse.dump.storag.recovery.job

| Whether the auto recovery job that reprocesses events dumped into the retry folder, is running or not. | Boolean | `true` \- Job is running  
`false` \- Job is not running | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType  
workflowID  
workflowDesc_  
Counters  
      
    
    pulse.dump.storage.dump.entries.retry.counter

| The total number of events that are currently stored in the disk to be retried by the auto recovery job. | # | >= 0 | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType  
workflowID  
workflowDesc_  
      
    
    pulse.dump.storage.dump.entries.failed.counter

| The total number of events that are currently stored in the disk but that already reached the maximum amounts of retry, therefore are no longer reprocessed and need to be recovered manually. | # | >= 0 | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType  
workflowID  
workflowDesc_

            "pulse.dump.storage.retry.queue.size,appSlug=,metricType=APPLICATION,workflowDesc=,appType=PULSE_APPLICATION,workflowID=": {
                  "value": 0
            },
            "pulse.dump.storage.failed.queue.size,appSlug=,metricType=APPLICATION,workflowDesc=,appType=PULSE_APPLICATION,workflowID=": {
                  "value": 0

# Monitoring Processing of Feedback Records in Pulse

This page describes how to monitor the processing of feedback records in Pulse using the `/metrics` endpoint.

## Introductionâ

Feedback records are a core concept of Pulse that allow users to provide feedback about past decisions from the system, e.g. when a transaction was previously marked as not fraudulent, but was actually fraudulent. This mechanism allows:

  * Data Scientists to re-iterate over the metrics, rules and Machine Learning models used by the workflow, and use the feedback to iteratively improve the performance of the system.
  * Users to evaluate the performance of the system by comparing the decisions of Pulse with the received feedback.



The Feedback Storage Service is the service responsible to manage all the CRUD operations related with feedback records.

It is essential to know if this service is operating within reasonable limits. By taking monitoring metrics from the Feedback Storage Service, Pulse operators can have access to different information related to feedback operations via the `/metrics` endpoint.

## Metricsâ

The metrics are associated with an application, identifiable via an `appSlug` tag, where the service is running.

The `appType` and `metricType` tags, that are also associated with these monitoring metrics, are common to other metrics exposed in Pulse and App Engines. They inform where the metrics were collected (Pulse Server or App Engine) and what type of metric it is being reported (e.g. APPLICATION), respectively.

Name | Description | Unit | Possible Values | Tags  
---|---|---|---|---  
Gauges  
      
    
    pulse.feedbackstorage.status

|  The current status of the Feedback Storage Service. This state is computed by looking at the current state of the internal components of the service. This means that: 

  * If **all components are UNAVAILABLE** , then the **service is UNAVAILABLE**.
  * If **all components are AVAILABLE** , then the **service is AVAILABLE**.
  * If the **components have different states** then the **service is DEGRADED**.

The DEGRADED state can happen, when for example feedback messages are dropped to the deadletter because of an issue in either the Event Storage or the Messaging Broker.  | # | 0 - UNAVAILABLE  
1 - AVAILABLE  
2 - DEGRADED | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType_  
      
    
    pulse.feedbackstorage.feedbacks.queue.size

| The total number of entries that are present in the feedback messaging queue to be processed by the service. | # | >= 0 | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType_  
      
    
    pulse.feedbackstorage.event-storage-worker-app-{appId}-wf-{workflowId}.queue.size

| The total number of operations pending in the executor of a given event storage. There is 1 executor per AppID-WorkflowID, the name of the metric will depend on that. | # | >= 0 | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType_  
      
    
    pulse.feedbackstorage.available.publishers

| The total number of available publishers (that publish to the feedback queue on a REST/RMI request) at a given point in time. | # | > 0 | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType_  
Counters  
      
    
    pulse.feedbackstorage.deadletters.event-storage.counter

| The total number of events that are currently stored in a deadletter, for the event-storage inserts. | # | >= 0 | _appSlug  
metricType  
appType_  
      
    
    pulse.feedbackstorage.deadletters.messaging.counter

metricType  
appType_  
Timers  
Timers contain the following metrics: 

  * **count:** Number of events;
  * **max:** Max Latency;
  * **mean:** Mean Latency;
  * **min:** Minimum Latency;
  * **p50:** Latencies in the percentile 50;
  * **p75:** Latencies in the percentile 75;
  * **p95:** Latencies in the percentile 95;
  * **p98:** Latencies in the percentile 98;
  * **p99:** Latencies in the percentile 99;
  * **p999:** Latencies in the percentile 99.9;
  * **stddev:** Standard deviation of the latencies;
  * **m15_rate:** Rate in the last 15 minutes;
  * **m1_rate:** Rate in the last 1 minute;
  * **m5_rate:** Rate in the last 5 minutes;
  * **mean_rate:** Mean rate;
  * **duration_units:** Seconds;
  * **rate_units:** Calls/Second;

  
      
    
    pulse.feedbackstorage.feedbacks.consumption

| The latency associated with consumption of feedback messages. | seconds | >= 0 | _appSlug

# Monitoring Processing of Profiles in PKernel

Was this page helpful?Â 

PKernel is used to calculate real-time metrics to enrich events.

Having in mind that the majority of projects create real-time metrics, it is essential to know if PKernel is operating within reasonable limits. By taking monitoring metrics inside PKernel, we let Pulse operators to have access to different information related to PKernel via the /metrics endpoint.

These metrics are associated with:

  * a given PKernel, which is identifiable via a pkernelID tag;
  * a plan workflow element, which is identifiable via the workflowElementID tag;
  * a workflow, identifiable via the workflowID tag;
  * an application, identifiable via an appSlug tag.



Besides using the abovementioned tags to identify the PKernel monitoring metrics in the scope of an application, in certain cases, it is also necessary to identify the metrics in relation to PKernel components where these are being collected. This is possible through the following tags:

  * `queryName` \- Used when metrics are being registered inside a PQL query. The value that is assigned to this tag is the name of the query on the PQL plan code.
  * `stateType` \- Used when the metrics are related to operations performed on a given type of state object. The values associated with this tag can be deque or map. Deques are windows that contain the events processed within a certain time-frame; maps are dictionaries that contain the aggregations (e.g., avg, max) grouped by the values present in certain fields of an event.



The `appType` and `metricType` tags, that are also associated with these monitoring metrics, are common to other metrics exposed in Pulse and App Engines. They inform where the metrics were collected (Pulse Server or App Engine) and what type of metric it is being reported (e.g., APPLICATION, BUSINESS), respectively.

# PKernel Probes

Was this page helpful?Â 

PKernel probes, like the Pulse ones, provide a means to expose PKernel internal instrumentation data, allowing it to be stored in a central location for subsequent analysis.

## Existing Probesâ

The following probes are built-in in the PKernel 2.0 (with RocksDB):

Description| Probe Name| Schema| Notes  
---|---|---|---  
The time that an Event took to be processed inside of PKernel.| pkernel_post_event| timestamp : Long| Current timestamp in milliseconds.  
latency_ns : Long| Latency measured in nanoseconds.  
The time that an Event took to be processed inside of PKernel after acquiring the lock.  
This allows to understand the true time spent inside PKernel, ignoring possible queue effects of the lock.  
(Available from PKernel 2.1.0+)| pkernel_post_event_inside_lock| timestamp : Long| Current timestamp in milliseconds.  
latency_ns : Long| Latency measured in nanoseconds.  
The time that an Array of Events took to be processed inside of PKernel.| pkernel_post_events| timestamp : Long| Current timestamp in milliseconds.  
latency_ns : Long| Latency measured in nanoseconds.

Title: Data Source Analysis | Feedzai Pulse
============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)
  * [Core Concepts](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts)
  * [Data Sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources)

On this page

# Data Source Analysis

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse lets you extract simple metrics from your data so that you can easily perform high-level analyses and start uncovering some patterns in your data.

Depending on the data type, Pulse calculates different metrics for each data field. The following matrix shows which are the metrics available for each field type:

| Histogram| Mean| Std. Dev| Min| Max| Count| Distinct| Missing Values Count  
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---  
Numeric| Yes| Yes| Yes| Yes| Yes| Yes| No| Yes  
Categorical| Yes| No| No| No| No| Yes| Yes| Yes  
String| No| No| No| No| No| Yes| No| Yes  
  
This may help you uncover, for example, data quality issues where your dataset includes negative values in transaction amounts.

info

With Pulse, there is no need for you to load your data into a distributed database and manually run queries to analyze the data.

Statistics generation is distributed in Spark. This means that even for very large sets of data, with several TB in size, Pulse is very fast to compute metrics and to simplify your data validation and understanding stage.

## Breakdownsâ

When you run an analysis, in addition to generating overall metrics, Pulse also calculates them over field combinations. This allows you to break them down by another categorical field and its values, usually the one that labels transactions, for example, as fraud or not fraud.

info

When you analyze a data source, you must always select for which breakdown fields and values you want Pulse to calculate statistics.

If Pulse allowed you to skip this action, and simply calculate broken-down statistics for all possible combination of fields and values, it would rapidly cause performance degradation due to lack of computational resources.

The following images display the analysis on the _TransactionAmount_ field broken down by fraud and non-fraud transactions. A pattern emerges indicating that, in this dataset, fraud is more prevalent in lower value transactions.

Note that Pulse will not consider any invalid instance in your dataset for calculating these metrics. For example, rows with an incorrect date format or a value not specified for a categorical field are always skipped.

In histograms, the number of instances displayed for each bin is always an approximate value.
