On this page

# Data Types

Was this page helpful?Â 

Each field of a [data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) is characterized by a type that indicates its purpose in a data science context. Data sources are specified by their schema, and by the mapping between field types for data science and an underlying native data type. Possible field types are the following:

## Simple fieldsâ

Type | Description | Configuration and native type | Example  
---|---|---|---  
Categorical |  Fields that represent a finite amount of values of a discrete variable, that are useful in a Machine Learning setting.  In Pulse you can use categorical fields to group specific business terms, or contract/domain specifications.  As a heuristic, it is recommended that whenever the number of possible values exceeds ~10, you set the field type as String. In these cases, the number of possible values is too large for both a human and a machine learning algorithm to analyze and extract valuable insight.  However, you can use Plans to transform (categorical or string) fields with too many categories into useful features. For example, using a UDF to categorize Merchant Category Code (MCC) values into Merchant Category Groups (MCG).  |  Each discrete value to be considered as valid for the field. All possible values of the field must have the same native type. Possible native types are: 

  * String
  * Integer
  * Long
  * Boolean

| CountryCode: 484, 124, 136, 840  
Numeric |  Fields that represent a continuous value. Pulse is able to generate arithmetic-based calculations and charts to analyze numeric fields such as distribution histograms, maximum, minimum, count, mean and standard deviation.  You cannot perform Group By aggregations using Numeric fields as group by fields. |  Possible native types are: 

  * Integer
  * Float
  * Double

| TransactionAmount  
String |  Text-based fields that in their raw format, usually, have no meaning in a data science context, when training a model.  Although strings are not valuable in their raw format, they can be used for data science after some kind of processing or transformation with plans. For example, checking if an address starts with numbers or is in all caps.  However, they may be useful in rules, for example to check if a value is in a list and may or may not be a categorical.  Additionally, strings are also useful as support information for scored instances when visualizing model and rule evaluations, for example the client id, or even to analyse the performance of your models and rules broken down by these string fields.  |  Possible native types are:

  * String
  * Utf-8 String

| CardholderAddress  
Date Time |  Fields that represent a date. Information like a timestamp is also numeric, however, looking at a timestamp and not considering its temporal properties would render it useless. Thus, Pulse processes data representations separately.  Time-based information is useful for Pulse to validate data sequence and also very important to allow and facilitate time-aware operations. For example, helping the user selecting fields that represent time for time window-based aggregations.  |  Timestamp: A [UNIX timestamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time), in seconds or miliseconds.  Date Time: A moment specified in a given format, for example dd/MM/yyyy.  |  Timestamp: 1350776834512 Date Time: 30/06/2016  
  
## Complex fieldsâ

Complex fields are used to describe structured data. When a complex field is defined it will represent a data structure like a list, map, tuple or set.

Type | Description | Configuration | Example  
---|---|---|---  
Map |  Consider a transaction processing system with multiple POS. Each POS might have a lot of characteristics (e.g., battery usage, exterior temperature, etc), which might vary from one manufacturer to another. This information is difficult to maintain in a fixed data schema. Thus, you can define a map for POS properties (the information stored in the map must all have the same data type).  Pulse only supports maps with primitive types as keys, and whose values are either primitive types or tuples.  | Types of key-value mapping. For example, Map of Integer - String | 
    
    
    test  
    {  
      1: "Alaska",  
      2: "Minnesota"  
    }  
              
      
  
List |  Consider a transaction that has two processing codes. While the data schema might have two different fields for each of the processing codes, it might be more convenient to include a list or a set type field containing both.  Keep in mind that the difference between sets and lists is that Sets don't allow duplicate values.  Pulse only supports lists and sets whose elements are either primitive types or tuples.  | Type of all items in the list. For example, List of Integers. | 
    
    
      
    [1, 2, 44, 1]  
              
      
  
Set | Type of all items in the set. For example, Set of Strings. | 
    
    
      
    ["Alaska", "Arizona"]  
            
      
  
Tuple |  Aggregate several items which can be of any simple type. Use tuples for the fields that might contain different known attributes.  Pulse only supports tuples whose elements are primitive types.  | Types of each element of the tuple. For example, Tuple of 3 items. | 
    
    
      
    {  
      amount: 2,  
      country: "New York",  
      timestamp: 123456  
    }  
            
      
  
## Importing complex fields in CSV filesâ

Internally in the [Event Storage](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/event-storage), Pulse uses system types directly. When importing data from a CSV file, fields with complex data must be represented as JSON strings.

The syntax rules for complex data fields in CSV files are the following:

  * Complex fields need to be represented as strings.
  * Each complex field needs to be enclosed between quotation marks.
  * If a complex field contains strings, the quotation marks around the strings must be escaped with a second quotation mark.
  * Keys of complex fields must be strings. If in the schema they are defined as numeric type, they will be converted to the numeric type automatically, after reading the value from the string form in the CSV file.
  * If you have stand-alone quotation marks within a string, it becomes \"".



As an example, let's take the following data row (displayed as a column for better readability):

Timestamp | 
    
    
      
    1350776834512  
            
      
  
---|---  
Date | 
    
    
      
    30/06/2016  
            
      
  
Country Code | 
    
    
      
    124  
            
      
  
Transaction Amount | 
    
    
      
    124.99  
            
      
  
Cardholder Address (string) | 
    
    
      
    "221b Baker St, London NW1 6XE"  
            
      
  
POSProperties (tuple) | 
    
    
      
    {  
      1: "Alaska",  
      2: "Minnesota"  
    }  
            
      
  
ProcessingIDs (set of Integers) | 
    
    
      
    [1, 2, 44, 1]  
            
      
  
ProcessingNames (list of strings) | 
    
    
      
    ["Alaska", "Arizona"]  
            
      
  
Items (list of tuples) | 
    
    
      
    [  
      {  
        AmountUSD: 2.00,  
        Product: "Awesome Shirt"  
      },  
      {  
        AmountUSD: 242.00,  
        Product: "LED television 42" smartTV"  
      }  
    ]  
            
      
  
To import this row, the CSV file must look the following way:
    
    
    Timestamp,Date,CountryCode,TransactionAmount,CardholderAddress,POSProperties,ProcessingIDs,ProcessingNames,Items  
    1350776834512,30/06/2016,124,124.99,"221b Baker St, London NW1 6XE","{""1"": ""Alaska"", ""2"": ""Minnesota""}","[1, 2, 44, 1]","[""Alaska"", ""Arizona""]","[{""AmountUSD"": 2.00, ""Product"": ""Awesome Shirt""}, {""AmountUSD"": 242.00, ""Product"": ""LED television 42\"" smartTV""}]"  
    

## Mapping of data types from Parquet filesâ

Parquet files encode the type of each field, in addition to the values. When Parquet files are [imported into Pulse](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/importing-your-dataset-into-pulse), those types are automatically converted into the data types supported by Pulse, listed in the tables above. The mapping between Parquet data types and Pulse data types is as follows:

Parquet type| Pulse type| Configuration  
---|---|---  
`INT32`| Numeric| Integer  
`INT64`| Numeric| Long  
`INT64` with `TIMESTAMP` logical type annotation| Date Time| Timestamp in milliseconds (Long)  
`INT96`  
(Deprecated in Parquet, but used in Spark for timestamps)| Date Time| Timestamp in milliseconds (Long)  
`FLOAT`| Numeric| Float  
`DOUBLE`| Numeric| Double  
`BINARY` with `STRING` logical type annotation| String| String  
`BINARY` with `ENUM` logical type annotation| String| String  
`BINARY` with `JSON` logical type annotation| String| String  
`BINARY` with `NULL` logical type annotation| String| String  
`BOOLEAN`| Categorical| Boolean  
`MAP`| Complex Field| Map  
`MAP_KEY_VALUE`| Complex Field| Map  
`LIST`| Complex Field| List  
Nested Object| Complex Field| Tuple  
  
caution

Not all data types supported by the Parquet format can be imported into Pulse. Fields whose types are not mapped to a Pulse data type as described in the table above will be ignored.

## Impact of data types on memory consumptionâ

Adjusting the data types can significantly reduce the memory footprint of individual records. This can be extremely important in an application that handles thousands of events per second. The application will probably define multiple time windows that store events in memory.

You must be aware about the size occupied by your events, to be sure that there is enough memory for the events in the time windows you eventually define.

As an example, consider an application that processes 300 events per second and whose schema has 10 string fields that store 8 characters each. Defining a 24 hours window will result in the following memory consumption:

**24** hours Ã **60** minutes Ã **60** seconds Ã **300** events Ã **10** fields Ã **88** bytes each = _**21 GB**_

If you replace all string types with integers you will end up with:

**24** hours Ã **60** minutes Ã **60** seconds Ã **300** events Ã **10** fields Ã **16** bytes = _**4 GB**_

This alternative is much lighter than 21 GB, in fact it is about **5 times** smaller.

Try to choose the appropriate field types whenever possible to help reduce the memory used.

info

Since Strings use quite a lot of memory, only use them to save text that can't be categorized. Otherwise, there are other field types that suit data better.

The following table contains the size of each available data type:

Type | Example | Size (64bits JVM)  
---|---|---

# AutoML

Was this page helpful?Â 

AutoML automates feature engineering, model training and hyperparameter tuning. The following topic describes in more detail what AutoML does.

## Why use AutoML?â

Finding the right features and models for a data set is a cumbersome task: creating features, training models, tuning their parameters and testing the changes are all repetitive tasks. AutoML automates these tasks, using the fraud detection experience of Feedzai. Data Scientists can kick-off new fraud fighting projects with AutoML, or can use it to find interesting features for existing models.

Feedzai IQ

Further time savings can be achieved with [Feedzai IQ](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/about-pulse#feedzai-iq), which provides ready-to-adopt risk assessment solutions that don't require extensive data science work, thanks to federated financial risk intelligence aggregated from the Feedzai global network.

## Prerequisitesâ

To be able to run AutoML against a data source, you need to prepare the data first.

  * Date and datetime fields need to be converted to Unix timestamp format.
  * The data cannot contain NULL values. Instead, you need to add a default value:
    * Strings coalesced to empty string ('').
    * Categoricals should be coalesced to an existing value or to a new categorical value representing the NULL, typically a value called "other".
    * Numericals should be coalesced to a meaningful number, for example -999, -1 or 0, depending on their valid range.
    * Dates and datetimes should be coalesced to a default value, for example-2208988800, which corresponds to 01-01-1900 in Unix timestamp format.
  * The input data source can't use empty string ('') as NULL.



## Feature engineeringâ

Feature engineering is the process of applying domain knowledge to derive new characteristics from existing data. These new characteristics, the **features** might help to build better machine learning models for a specific purpose.

In Pulse, features are represented by [Maps and Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) in a [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans). When executing a Plan, Pulse processes the input data and creates a new data source that contains new fields. The value of those fields is defined by the Map and Metric operators of the Plan.

AutoML has a list of data field transformations that can be useful according to Feedzai's experience in the fraud fighting domain. Those transformations are based on the semantics of the data fields, combining fields with specific meaning into features. For example, if a data source has two location data fields, it might be useful to calculate the distance between the two. So, AutoML has a transformation that computes the distance between two location fields.

To allow AutoML to apply those transformations, when [defining an AutoML run](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/creating-features-and-models-automatically) you need to provide a [semantic file](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/automl/semantic-file) that maps the input data fields to semantic tags. For example, the _Name_ field can be tagged with the _name_ tag. This way AutoML knows the meaning of this input field, and it can compute the number of words in the name, which can be useful to fight fraud.

In summary, AutoML follows these steps to create features:

  1. Looks at the semantic file and maps the data fields to their meaning.
  2. Based on the data fields' meaning and on the list of transformations, AutoML creates a plan containing Map and Metric operators.
  3. Executes the plan on the input data source, and saves the result in a **features data source** that contains the data enriched with the new data fields.



## Dataset splitâ

When you create the AutoML run, you define which parts of the input data source will be used for training and for validation. Optionally you can also choose to have a test data set to simulate a blind evaluation of the best model found.

You define these data sets by selecting the time range for each task: training, validation, and optionally test. That means for example that data records that have a timestamp falling into the training time range will be used for training the models.

AutoML creates the training, validation and optionally the test data source based on the defined time ranges.

Planning training, validation and test data sources

To avoid under- or overfitting, plan the time ranges carefully. Ensure that the resulting data sets contain enough data for their purpose. A typical ratio is 50% for the training, 30% for the validation, and 20% for the evaluation data set.

Note that if you don't define a test data set, AutoML uses the validation data set for the final evaluation of the best model found. Since the validation data set was used for finding the best model, it is not an optimal solution to use it to test the data. Hence it's recommended to use a test data set.

## Filtersâ

If the input data source contains different types of events, and you don't want AutoML to consider all of them when creating metrics or training models, you can apply filters.

AutoML allows you to define the definition of two kinds of filters:

  * If you define a **profile filter** , AutoML will create metrics that consider events filtered by the defined expression. Example: you might want to filter for only transaction submissions and payment updates -`event_type = "transaction_submission" OR event_type = "transaction_payment_status_update"`
  * If you define a **scorable filter** , AutoML will train the models based on events that satisfy the expression of this filter. Example: you might want to filter for only transaction submissions -`event_type = "transaction_submission"`



The scorable filter will create a new filter operator in the plan that splits the data source.

## Feature selectionâ

In this step, AutoML first trains an H2OGradient Boosted Trees model on a sample of the training dataset. GBT models are quick to be trained, and provide a feature importance ranking out of the box.

Then Pulse reduces the features to the subset that has the highest feature importance according to the GBT model. This way, Pulse keeps only a subset of the features for the model training step of AutoML. The features that AutoML keeps contribute with 90% of the importance rating.

Note that Pulse has another [feature importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance) calculation method as well, which you can use later on, after you evaluated a trained model. That feature importance calculation method is different from the process that AutoML uses.

## Reduced features planâ

The AutoML Pipeline combines the plan generated in the **Feature Engineering** step with the subset of features from the **Feature Selection** step, and reduces the plan. It does so by removing the least important features discovered in the Feature Selection step. This prevents data scientists from manually removing the operators that will produce useless features.

## Model training and evaluationâ

After selecting the most important features, AutoML creates a Hyperparameter Tuning job to train and evaluate models. Hyperparameter Tuning jobs distribute the model training and evaluation in the Spark cluster.

Finally, AutoML compares the models based on the metric that you selected to be optimized, and recommends the best model.

## Learn moreâ

  * [Creating an AutoML run](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/creating-features-and-models-automatically)
  * [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans)
  * [Maps and Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference)
  * [Semantic file](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/automl/semantic-file)
  * [Hyperparameter Tuning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/hyperparameter-tuning)

# Feature Importance

Machine learning models rely on many features to learn how to predict patterns. To develop a model with high performance in the field of fraud prevention, data scientists might need to select hundreds of features to train the model. The process of selecting features is complex, and there is a risk of including features that have none or even negative contribution to the model.

**Feature importance** is a functionality that can be used to determine the impact of each feature on a machine learning model.

Data scientists can use this functionality to identify the subset of variables that contribute the most and the least to the model predictions. With this information, data scientists have more visibility on how the model is using the features to score transactions. Additionally, data scientists can remove features that have low contribution to the model without decreasing model performance (i.e. declining evaluation metrics). This allows reducing model complexity and computation time.

Ultimately, with the help of the feature importance, data scientists can develop models that fight fraud more efficiently and that are easy to interpret.

In Pulse, feature importance is calculated after training a model, during the evaluation stage. Check the [Evaluating a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model) page to learn how to use this functionality in Pulse.

## How Pulse calculates feature importanceâ

In Pulse, the importance of a feature is calculated by replacing the feature with noise and measuring the impact on model performance.

Pulse completes the following steps to compute feature importance:

  1. Randomly samples the dataset using the _Sample Percentage_ and _Random Seed_ values defined by the user as input parameters.
  2. Computes _Transaction Recall_ (and _Cost Recall_ , if an additional cost field is selected) at the closest False Positive Rate (FPR) value to the value defined by the user for the model with the original features.
  3. For each feature used to train the model:
     1. Randomly shuffles values of the feature between the different instances.

     2. Computes _Transaction Recall_ (and _Cost Recall_ in case an additional cost field is selected) at the closest FPR value to the value defined by the user for the model with the feature shuffled.

     3. Subtracts the _Transaction Recall_ (and _Cost Recall_ , if an additional cost field is selected) computed in Step 3.b. to the value computed in Step 2. This yields the absolute importance of each feature:

_AbsoluteImportance i = Recall_baseline - Recall_shuffledi_

where _Recall_baseline_ is the recall of the original evaluation, _Recall_shuffled i_ is the recall of the evaluation with featurei shuffled. As an example, considering the calculation of absolute importance for the feature Transaction Amount, the expression becomes:

_AbsoluteImportance TransactionAmount = Recall_baseline - Recall_shuffledTransactionAmount_

     4. For each feature, relative importance is calculated as follows:

where N is the total number of features. As an example, considering the calculation of relative importance for the feature Transaction Amount, using an evaluation that has 100 features including MCC Code, the expression becomes:




### Using Recall to calculate absolute importanceâ

As presented in the step-by-step description of the algorithm, FPR (i.e. percentage of genuine transactions incorrectly classified as fraudulent) and Recall (i.e. percentage of fraudulent transactions correctly classified as fraud) are both used to calculate absolute importance in Pulse.

This metric is calculated as the difference between Recall before and after shuffling the values of the feature between different instances at a selected FPR.

Recall can be plotted against FPR, which is the so-called **ROC Curve** (see figure below).

As shown in the figure, Recall after shuffling can be equal, higher or lower than the Recall before shuffling.

This yields to an absolute importance approximately equal to zero, negative or positive, respectively. Therefore, the outcomes are the following:

  * **Absolute importance approximately equal to zero** : for features that have no significant contribution to the model predictions.
  * **Negative absolute importance** : for features that have a negative contribution to the model predictions.
  * **Positive absolute importance** : for features that are important to the model predictions.



There are different parameters that can be selected to compute feature importance which are described in the next subsection.

## Parametersâ

Feature importance is computed using the following parameters selected by the user:

  * **Sample Percentage** : percentage of randomly sampled instances in the data. When selecting this parameter the user should take into account the trade-off between having a representative set of data to compute feature importance and runtime. Additionally, the user should take into account that all data is loaded into memory to compute feature importance, and thus, high sample percentage values may lead Pulse to run out of memory in the case of extremely large datasets. The default value of the sample percentage is 30%.

  * **FPR** : value at which the Recall is calculated. The default value of FPR is 1.00%.

  * **Random Seed** : value that affects both of these operations: the order to which the instances of the features are shuffled and the instances that are sampled to compute feature importance. Note that the percentage is defined by sample percentage. This value can be used by data scientists to check the stability of the results using different seeds and keeping all the other conditions the same.

Check stability with random seeds

If the results are similar using different random seeds it means that the user is likely using enough data to compute feature importance.




The following parameter can be also optionally selected when computing feature importance:

  * **Additional Cost Field** : a field that is used as a weight for the metrics of the evaluations (of both models and rules). In a typical fraud detection scenario, the selected feature for this field is the transaction amount. By adding an additional cost field, Recall is calculated based on the feature specified in this field (i.e. Cost Recall) in addition to be calculated based on the number of transactions (Transaction Recall).



## Feature importance resultsâ

A typical report with results of feature importance is illustrated in the following image.

The features are ranked according to the level of importance. In this example, is easy to identify that the first four features impact the model whereas the remaining features have low impact on the outcome decisions of the model.

Extra functionalities that data scientists can use to analyze the results of feature importance, including comparing results of two model evaluations, are described in the [evaluating a model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model#analyzing-the-model-evaluation) page.

# Hyperparameter Tuning

Was this page helpful?Â 

**Hyperparameter tuning** is the process of fine-tuning parameters to obtain the optimal set of parameters for a specific use case. When fine-tuning parameters without automating this process, it is time-consuming to define a different set of parameters and run the model training in each iteration. Hyperparameter tuning helps the user to determine the optimum parameters for a given machine learning context in an automated way.

## Introduction to hyperparameter tuningâ

Depending on the use case, a certain set of parameters will work better than others, so the goal of data scientists is to try as many sets as possible to know which one allows to achieve an optimized solution for that specific use case. Hyperparameter tuning relies on experimental results, allowing data scientists to train and evaluate multiple models with a diverse set of parameters by algorithm simultaneously.

Pulse generates the performance statistics for all the selected algorithms with all the parameter combinations. This saves time and keeps the models organized. Data scientists can iterate faster to determine the algorithm and set of parameters that optimize model performance. They are, thus, able to spend more time searching for insights in the data, which could improve the performance even more. Given the massive quantity of model evaluations that a hyperparameter tuning can originate, the exploration mode functionality facilitates how the user can explore and compare those evaluations obtained. As such, it helps users to make a decision in a more informed manner.

## Grid search (parameter sweep)â

The **grid search** (aka. parameter sweep) is considered the standard way of performing a hyperparameter tuning. The grid search consists on an exhaustive search, or sweep, of an exponentially large grid of possible hyperparameter combinations for a learning algorithm. Some key points of this process to consider are:

  * You manually specify a set of values for each hyperparameter.
  * Pulse creates a model for every combination of values. Take a very simple example (as in the image below): if you have 3 hyperparameters and you specify 2 values for one and 3 values for another, after performing the sweep, the grid will return (2*3) = 6 models.
  * Once the sweeping is finished, you can make queries and sort the models by performance metrics (such as _FPR_) by using the exploration mode.



## Hyperparameter tuning evaluation methodsâ

Hyperparameter tuning will behave different according to the selected evaluation method.

When selecting either cross or split validation the several models will be all trained and evaluated within the same distributed job. This will cause the model evaluation to run on a single partition which will lead to evaluations time much larger than the single evaluation jobs. The evaluation results will only be available after all the models finish training.

For the validation data source method, the models will be trained within the same distributed job, but a single evaluation job will be triggered as soon as each model finishes its training. Once the models are evaluated, the results will be available at the hyperparameter tuning page, without being necessary to wait for the remaining trainings and evaluations to finish.

### Exploration modeâ

Once the creation step of a hyperparameter tuning is finished, the exploration one follows. The **exploration mode** is a view where you explore and analyze results to learn which evaluations perform better for a certain business target. There are two exploration mode views available in Pulse: a global view in your model project, where you can combine single model evaluations with hyperparameter tuning evaluations, and another view specific to each hyperparameter tuning.

The key points of the exploration mode are:

  * Possibility to add targets and metrics
  * Search filter that supports a flexible listing:
    * Selecting model and hyperparameter tuning evaluations
    * Selecting by algorithm and data source
  * Possibility to select evaluations and add them to the results comparison table
  * Possibility to clear applied evaluations from a target



## Single model evaluation vs. hyperparameter tuningâ

Hyperparameter tuning brings important advantages when compared to creating and evaluating models one by one. The following table sums up the most significant of them:

Single model| Hyperparameter tuning  
---|---  
  
  * Trains and evaluates models one at a time.

| 

  * Tuning evaluation combinations:
    * launches and combines the possible combinations of the selected parameters
    * tries more than one algorithm and for each one of them specifies multiple parameters simultaneously

  
  
  * The model is trained and evaluated in a distributed way. Typically performs better than hyperparameter tuning.

| 

  * Spark distributes the training so that several models are trained and evaluated simultaneously according to the selected validation method.

  
  
  * Instances are partitioned across many tasks and collected in a final logical block resulting in an aggregation of scored instances.

| 

  * No output scored instances since the model binary is not saved.

  
  
## Learn moreâ

Check the following pages in the User Guide to learn how the hyperparameter tuning functionality fits in a model life cycle and how it works in Pulse:

  * [Tuning Model Parameters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters)
  * [Exploring Hyperparameter Tuning Results](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters/exploring-hyperparameter-tuning-results)

# Model Evaluation

Was this page helpful?Â 

Evaluating your model against a dataset means analyzing how it is performing, and how close you are to reaching the objectives of your data science project.

The performance of models can be analyzed in **model evaluations**. A model evaluation first runs the model to score the possible values of the target variable in a specific data source.

Then Pulse compares the scores with the actual labels of the target field. It calculates relevant model performance metrics, and displays them in an informative layout.

Model evaluations can be created in two ways:

  * Automatically, in the Validation step of the [model training process](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model).
  * Manually, by creating a new model evaluation for any existing model.



## The evaluation data sourceâ

The evaluation can be run against the data source of the model training, using cross-validation or split percentage strategies. Alternatively, when evaluating a model that has already been trained on a given data source, Pulse will execute the evaluation against a user-specified data source. Thus, no validation method is applicable as the entire dataset is used for testing. It's the user's responsibility to ensure that the data source provided for evaluation is not the same that was used during training.

Compatible data sources

You can evaluate the same model with any different data sources, as long as they contain all the fields that the model requires. This means that you must always evaluate a given model with [compatible data sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#compatible-data-sources).

## The evaluation target variableâ

The evaluation can use the same target variable as the model, if it has any. Alternatively you can select another field as target variable for the evaluation. The format (type and possible values) of the evaluation target variable must match the format of the target variable used in the model training, if there was any.

Also, the position of the specified target variable must correspond to the position of the target used for training. Learn more about [compatible data sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#compatible-data-sources).

## Model performance metricsâ

When the model evaluation is finished, Pulse displays **model performance metrics** such as ROC curve, confusion matrix, cost-based metrics, etc.

### ROC curveâ

Most importantly, the **ROC curve** is a simple and visual way to assess a model's performance. ROC curve plots the Recall (Y axis) over the False Positive Rate (X axis).

The best possible prediction method would yield a point in the upper left corner ('A' in the picture) or coordinate (0,100) of the ROC space, representing 100% Detection with 0% False Positives. The (0,100) point is also called a perfect classification. A completely random guess would give a point along the diagonal line 'C' (the so-called line of no-discrimination).

Keep in mind that when the model's performance is sufficiently good, the difference between the curves might become unnoticeable. Analyze the computed metrics for more precise results.

### Comparing modelsâ

Model evaluations are useful in your data science project to perform easy comparisons over earlier versions of the model, with a different parameter configuration, different features, etc.

Pulse allows you to compare the metrics of two different models, to evaluate their performance. For that, their target variables must have the same data type and possible values.

### Breakdownsâ

When you generate a model evaluation, in addition to generating overall performance metrics Pulse also calculates them over field combinations. This allows you to break them down by another categorical field and its values, and evaluate your model performance for each of those possible fields and value combinations. For example, checking the performance of your model segmented by each suspicious country.

### Score distributionâ

To analyze the model results, another useful information is the **score distribution**. The score distribution graph shows the distribution of scores predicted by the model for each value of the target variable.

It allows to visually inspect the separation power of the evaluated model. In a good model, the values of the target variable are separated into different areas of the graph. In the following example, setting the Threshold between 50 and 100 will separate _False_ from _True_.

## Learn moreâ

To fully understand model evaluations, make sure you also go through the following concepts:

  * [Cost Fields](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/cost-fields)
  * [Custom Evaluation Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/custom-evaluation-metrics)
  * [Business Targets](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/business-targets)



Check the following pages to learn how to put model evaluations into practice:

  * [Evaluating a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model)
  * [Tuning Model Parameters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters)
  * [Comparing Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models)

# Model Training

Was this page helpful?Â 

**Training a model** means running historical data through a machine learning algorithm to produce a model. You use the trained model in workflows to predict the value of a specified **target variable** in live data.

As part of the [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop), it is common to try different model training algorithms or keep making adjustments to model parameters and [feature plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans), and repeat training until you reach a satisfactory performance.

The following sections give you more details on how models are trained in Pulse.

## The event's journey during the model trainingâ

Naming conventions

When a transaction is flowing in the workflow, it is called an **event**. When an event is enriched with features, it is known as an **instance**. The instance does not traverse the workflow; it is computed using the event data and then used for training (offline data science) or scoring (runtime).

When Pulse loads a training event, it can be filtered before reaching a feature plan. If it reaches the feature plan, an instance with the computed real-time and scheduled metrics is generated. It also includes data transformations and enriched data, in addition to some of the raw features from the event. The instance can then be filtered again before generating the final data source, which Pulse will use to train the model.

Wasted computation?

It might seem odd to compute metrics for events that can later be dropped, but it actually has a simple use case. For instance, when training a model for fraud prevention in card-not-present transactions, it might be important to consider the number of card-present transactions. In this case, you could drop the card-present transactions using a [filter operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) before generating the plan output and after computing the count metric.

## Omnichannel modelsâ

Note that in some cases you might want to train models using data from several data sources for [channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/channels). For example, you might be scoring debit card transactions (main data source) and leveraging information about internet banking events (secondary data source). This can be achieved by executing an [omnichannel plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#deployable-omnichannel-plans)) on the input data sources. The output of that plan can then be used for model training.

## Supervised and unsupervised machine learningâ

Pulse allows two different machine learning approaches:

  * Training a model through **supervised machine learning** , where the purpose of the model is to predict the label of a target variable. To train a classification model, the data used for the training needs to be labeled.
  * Training a model with **unsupervised machine learning**. In this case, a target variable is not used for training.



## Target variableâ

The purpose of a classification model is to predict the label of the target variable. Although Pulse's main use case is fraud detection, you can run your [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) and train your models to predict the value for any [categorical](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) target variable, not just fraud/not-fraud. This way you can solve the following classifications problems, during both the data science stage and in Production:

  * Binary classification, for example fraud/not fraud.
  * Multiclass classification for target variables with more than two categories.



As mentioned before, unsupervised machine learning models don't require a target variable for training.

## External modelsâ

Instead of creating and training your model in Pulse, you can [import a model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model/importing-an-external-model) that you trained in an external system (using DataRobot, H2O, scikit-learn, the caret package in R, or custom code written in Python or R).

Known limitation - DataRobot

DataRobot allows training models based on string fields, but Pulse doesn't support that. To achieve the same in Pulse, convert the fields that have string type to categorical fields, before training a model based on that data.

## Validation methodâ

When training a classification model, it is important to validate the model performance with an independent set of data that was not used to train the model. Pulse automates the task of validation and allows you to select from the following options:

  * Validation using the split percentage method for a given ratio
  * Cross validation up to 20 folds
  * Validation against a second data source
  * No validation



Memory consumption of training models

Pulse executes model training jobs as a distributed job. It's recommended to monitor and optimize the memory

allocated to distributed jobs, to ensure that they have the necessary resources to run successfully. In case the distributed job encounters memory issues, consider the following:

  * During model training, the training data set is fully in memory.
  * For the split percentage and cross validation methods, the evaluation data set is also fully in memory.
  * Validation against a second data source executes as a separate job. Therefore, it does not impact the memory of the training.



### Split percentageâ

**Split percentage** of an _X%_ ratio just uses that amount of data for training and the remaining _(100 - X)%_ for validation.

The model that is stored, however, is trained with 100% of the data. This validation method is simple and fast.

Although the split is done deterministically, the obtained performance metrics is just a single data point, hence this validation method is not reliable for time-aware datasets. In addition, because we don't know the natural order of the instances of the dataset, if the specific problem being tackled is time-based (e.g. fraud detection), then we want to guarantee that the transactions are ordered in time before doing the split. Otherwise, we may be training the model with "future" patterns and testing with past ones.

On the other hand, if all hard-to-classify instances are placed in the training dataset, the results will be inflated since it will only need to validate against easier instances. These are all important considerations to take in any type of evaluation in addition to the split percentage.

A default value of 70% ratio is a common practice.

When to use split percentage

You should opt for the split percentage method for quick iterations, especially if your dataset is very large, and for non-time-aware problems.

What makes an instance easy for a binary classifier?

Models attempt to extract patterns from the observed data. With more unique instances, the model is able to better understand what the target concept is, and how to define it (Is this transaction fraudulent? Yes, because ...).

Intuitively, this reasoning only has significance inside the domain of observed data. When scoring an instance that _looks like_ fraudulent transactions that were previously observed by the classifier, it can easily tag the instance as fraud.

However, when there are no transactions that look like the one requested, or there are a few but they have mixed classes, this decision becomes harder.

### Cross validationâ

**Cross validation** is a method that attempts to minimize the variability observed with split percentage. It splits the data into _N_ equally-sized blocks, and uses _N-1_ blocks for training and _1_ for validation. The training/validation process is repeated by shifting the blocks until all _N_ blocks have been used for validation. Choosing _N=10_ would yield the following sequence of training and validation runs:

The results are then equally averaged creating a final rundown. The averaging process inherently minimizes the variability of the result. However, the greatest advantage over split percentage is that each instance appears both in the training and in the test dataset (in different runs) thus ensuring that each instance influences the final result.

Nonetheless, cross-validation requires training _N-1_ models, which might be unwieldy for large datasets.

When to use cross validation

You should opt for this method in the final iterations of your [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) when micro-optimizing the model definition, or if the training operation is fast enough that doesn't break your work cycle.

You shouldn't use it for time-aware problems.

### Validation against a second data sourceâ

This validation method allows you to validate the model against a data source of Pulse, other than the training data source.

The data fields selected for the validation must match the fields of the training data set.

## Sampling strategyâ

Sampling strategies are techniques that artificially modify the class distribution of the dataset. This can be used for biasing the model creator into believing that the class distribution is different from the one observed in the dataset. The class distribution is heavily biased in the real world (such is the case with fraud). Class imbalance is a widely known problem that affects many machine learning models. The problem arises when the number of instances from one class is so low that they become mostly irrelevant for training purposes. This generates classifiers that do not have enough sensitivity for the uncommon class (failing to detect fraudulent transactions and instead opting to score every transaction as valid; this has better accuracy compared to misclassifying a few instances of both classes).

When defining the sampling strategy, you can specify the _X%_ that you would like the dominant class to have. The strategy will transform the dataset in a way that ensures this ratio.

Imagine that your training dataset consists of 99.5% non-fraud transactions and 0.5% fraud transactions, and you wish to train the model with 95% and 5% respectively.

You can achieve the desired ratio with either an undersampling or an oversampling filter both with 95% ratio (because non-fraud is the prevalent class).

  * **Oversampling**

Produces more data of the minority class (by copying) to achieve the desired ratio. The instances of the dominant class are kept intact and the dataset grows in size.

  * **Undersampling**

Deletes instances from the majority class to meet the ratio. Instances of the minority class are kept intact and the dataset shrinks in size.




Depending on your dataset, you should use a different sampling strategy. On the one hand, oversampling introduces more instances but the information contained in them is the same. This makes the dataset bigger (but not better) and therefore the training process is slower. On the other hand, undersampling loses information that was present in the deleted instances.

## Improving modelsâ

A model is defined by a set of parameters: some are defined by the user, whereas others are selected based on the training data when applying the algorithm to the data.

The performance of the model can be improved by:

  * Optimising the hyperparameters (parameters that can be selected by the user). This process is named hyperparameter tuning.
  * Comparing different machine learning algorithms. For example, XGBoost vs Random Forest vs Deep Learning.
  * Changing the training dataset. For example, to a more recent dataset.



Adjust the feature set that is being used to train the model. Some patterns might not being captured by the current feature set. Bear in mind that for a fair and insightful comparison you should be assessing the performance in the same data set.

## Configuring white-box explanationsâ

During model training, users can configure the **white-box explanations** , which consists in the calculation of the features that led to a transaction's score. This calculation occurs in runtime after adding the **trained model** to the workflow.

note

Although white-box explanations are configured in the Pulse UI, their output is only visible in Case Manager.

For more information on the parameters that must be configured in this field, visit the [Training a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model) page.

For more information on this subject, read the [White-Box Explanations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/white-box-explanations) page.

## Immutabilityâ

Since a model is immutable by definition, once you train it with a specific dataset and machine learning parameterization, it will always yield the same results for a given test dataset. If you change the parameters or the training dataset, you are effectively generating a different model.

In alignment with this, when you create a model in Pulse, the configuration you used to train it cannot be changed afterward. Once you configure algorithm parameters and the input data source when [training a model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model), these are permanently part of what distinguishes a model iteration from the previous one in your project.

So if you change any model dependency such as the data source, which is also immutable, you are creating a new iteration in your [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop). In addition, immutability allows Pulse to isolate the model during the data science phase from the same model when deployed to Production. This way you can safely correct and improve your models without affecting your Production workflow.

Deploying improved models

If you need to deploy corrections and improvements to your current model, you can simply run the training procedure and generate a new model. Then configure the scoring service in your workflow with the new model.

Nevertheless, Pulse still allows you to effectively manage your model project and the performance of multiple model iterations. [Model evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation) are what exposes results and not the model itself. A model evaluation always produces the same results over a given model, reinforcing the need for different models for each iteration in your project.

## Learn moreâ

Check the following pages in the User Guide to learn how to put models into practice:

  * [Training a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model)
  * [Importing an External Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model/importing-an-external-model)
  * [Model Evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation)

# White-Box Explanations

Was this page helpful?Â 

White-box explanations (WBE) is a tool that aims at providing explanations for predictions of machine learning models in Case Manager (CM). It reduces the amount of time data scientists spend setting up rules that will generate explanations in CM (i.e. less than 2 hours) and allows analysts in CM to understand why a transaction received a certain score, including a breakdown of the contributions to that score.

As a result of providing explanations for each transaction score in CM, WBE supports analysts in two main aspects:

  * Guidance on how to proceed when they need to understand the reason behind a transaction alert.
  * Insight on why the model is delivering high scores to certain transactions.



## Introduction to WBEâ

WBE lists the most important features that influence a transaction's score in CM, allowing analysts to understand the reason behind that score.

The flow of WBE starts in the model, where you can configure explanations. During this configuration, data scientists can add explanation messages. After that, the model is put into Production (i.e. workflow), where it will score and create explanations for transactions. Finally, analysts using CM will be able to see the explanation messages previously generated by Pulse at the end of the workflow.

Explanations in model evaluation

Currently it is not possible to generate explanations in the model evaluation.

## WBE algorithmâ

Depending on the algorithm you use to train the model, the following algorithms can be used for the explanations:

  * **Feedzai Feature Contribution** : an algorithm based on the fraud ratio gain, for models trained with the [Feedzai Random Forest](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training/feedzai-random-forest) algorithm.
  * **TreeSHAP Feature Contribution** : an algorithm based on [Shapley values](https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/generated/shap.explainers.Tree.html), for models trained with Microsoft LightGBM or Feedzai FairGBM.



Note

Explanations provided through Shapley values, which are our Feature Contribution (FC) weights, are computed based on the prevalence ratio of the dataset (e.g., the rate of fraudulent transactions) â the base value. Each FC weight demonstrates how much that feature contributed to the difference between the prediction score and that base value. Therefore, if the prediction score is higher than the base value, the sum of the normalized FC weights must be 100% of the prediction score. However, if the prediction score is lower than the base value, the sum of the normalized FC weights will be -100%. This is a rare event in financial crime use cases, given the low rate of financial crime when compared to the whole set of transactions.

## Learn moreâ

Check the following pages in the User Guide to learn how to put WBE into practice:

  * To set up WBE, go to the [Training a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model) page and read the Training Parameters section.
  * To check how WBE are produced in runtime, read the [Adding Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models) page.

# Data Partitioning for the Metrics Operator

Was this page helpful?Â 

Data partitioning is a key step for processing distributed jobs in a Spark cluster spawned by [plan executions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) to enable Pulse to handle large volumes of data efficiently.

When you add [metrics operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#metrics) to a [plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans), Spark needs to re-organize the data before calculating the metrics defined in each metrics operator. During this data re-organization, all the rows (e.g., in fraud applications each row corresponds to a transaction) that share the same value in the fields that are configured as _Group By_ in the metrics operator are placed within the same Spark partition.

Pulse allows you to configure data partitioning using flexible UI options to ensure that Spark performs data re-organization as homogenous and well distributed as possible.

## How does it work?â

To get the best out of the data partitioning options available in the UI, it is important that you understand the logic behind this concept.

When you complete the configurations of your plan with all the required operators, you can generate the output data source by running a plan execution. The plan execution spawns distributed Spark jobs that are responsible for handling the heavy work so that Pulse can process large volumes of data (i.e. often hundreds or even thousands of TBs).

Spark streams data through its graph of operators, which maps reasonably well to the graph of operators that you configure in the plan's workspace that is available in the Pulse UI. This means that, in general, every row of the input data (e.g. in fraud applications each row corresponds to a transaction) is fully processed from the source to the sink.

If you have a plan with metrics operators, **the following data partitioning logic is applied** when you run the plan execution:

  1. Spark streams all the data and process upstream operators (i.e. processes all the data that flows through the operators that precede the metrics operator).

  2. The data that arrives at the metric operator is re-organized according to each set of _Group By_ fields (e.g. Set 1: _card_number_ \+ _merchant, S_ et 2: _city)_ defined in this operator. This process also is known as shuffling in the Spark terminology. For each set of _Group By_ fields, all the rows that share the same value in the fields as defined in the _Group By_ are placed within the same Spark partition.

For example, consider that you define a set of _Group By_ with the fields _card_number_ \+ _merchant_.

All the transactions that share the same Card Number AND the same Merchant are placed within a single Spark partition. The example shown below uses only the _Merchant_ as the _Group By_ field to provide a simple visualization of this process. Note that one Spark partition can (and will likely) contain data from various sets of _Group By_ fields.

  3. Pulse takes each partition and feeds it in streaming to PKernel, which is the Feedzai's stream processor for profile calculation. In this step, PKernel is responsible for calculating the metric defined in the metrics operator using data organized by _Group By_ as explained in the previous step.

  4. Steps 2 and 3 are repeated for each set of _Group By_ fields so that all metrics are covered with a shuffle. For instance, if you have two metrics, the step sequence 2-3 is repeated twice as shown in the example below:

     * Iteration #1 (e.g. Metric 1: _card_number_ \+ _merchant_): Spark re-organizes all the data by _Card Number_ AND _Merchants,_ and then PKernel performs the profile calculations.
     * Iteration #2 (e.g. Metric 2: _city_): Spark re-organizes all the data by _City_ , and then PKernel performs the profile calculations.



### The challenge of unbalanced dataâ

A typical data partitioning method is to hash the values of each row and then send the rows that share the same hashed values to the same partition. However, when dealing with unbalanced data this method might introduce some inefficiency.

For example, imagine that you configure a metrics operator with a metric that has the _Group By_ field _Merchant_. Now assume that you have two large merchants (Retailer 1, Retailer 2) each of which represents 1/3 of the total data, and then the remaining 1/3 of the data is a long-tail of very small merchants (Merchant 1, Merchant 2, ... , Merchant N). If you use the hash approach to partitioning data, there is nothing from preventing the most popular values from falling in the same partition:

This unbalanced data distribution is oblivious to the population and would require extra memory in the Spark workers to compute the data that is shown in Partition 1.

Continuing with the example above, an efficient way of dividing the data into different partitions would be the following one:

The data-aware optimizer available in Pulse allows you to set a plan execution that spawns an efficient data partitioning to maximize the memory allocated to the Spark workers. This option is specially advantageous when you are dealing with unbalanced data because it takes into account the popularity of each set of values for _Group By_ fields.

## Data partitioning optionsâ

Pulse has the following data partitioning options available:

  * hash-based partitioning
  * manual partitioning
  * data-aware optimizer



The data-aware optimizer is the default option for data partitioning, but you can configure a different partitioning method to be used by default in the main configuration file `$PULSE_HOME/conf/pulse.properties`, under the property `pulse.global.ui.plans.datapartitioning.method`.

The available values for this key are `data-aware`, `hash-based` and `manual`.

### Hash-basedâ

The **hash-based** option does not take into account the popularity of each set of _Group By_ fields when performing the data re-distribution into different partitions.

Additionally, this method does not optimize the number of partitions used by the shuffle. In fact, the hash-based method sets the same number of partitions used in the plan input. This number is obtained by reading chunks of 128MB from the input and making each chunk a partition.

On the plus side, this method is less computationally expensive than the popularity aware method explained below. This option might be beneficial when you are computing metrics that have _Group By_ fields that are expected to lead to a balanced data distribution.

Check the pages [Creating a stratified sample](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/creating-a-stratified-sample) and [Creating metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics) to learn how to choose the hash-based option.

### Manual Partitioningâ

The **manual partitioning** option allows you to specify the number of partitions to which the values of your dataset are distributed. Manual partitioning uses the hash-based approach to distribute the rows with the same values to the same partition according to each set of _Group By_ fields.

Check the pages [Creating a stratified sample](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/creating-a-stratified-sample) and [Creating metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics) to learn how to choose the manual partitioning option.

Configuration of manual partitioning

When selecting the `manual` partitioning option, you can manually set the number of partitions to a custom value in the Pulse UI. The default number of partitions is 100.

If you regularly need to specify a different number of partitions, you can set a custom number of partitions via configuration.

For example, to use manual partitioning with 20 000 partitions, you can set the following properties in the main configuration file `$PULSE_HOME/conf/pulse.properties`:
    
    
    pulse.global.ui.plans.datapartitioning.method=manual  
    pulse.global.ui.plans.datapartitioning.partitions=20000  
    

### Data-aware optimizerâ

The **data-aware optimizer** option takes into account the popularity of the values according to each set of _Group By_ field.

The number of partitions used by the shuffle are dynamically computed, and they adapt to the actual data. The data-aware optimizer uses the minimum number of partitions that allows for a homogeneous distribution of the data that respects the set of _Group By_ values.

The data-aware optimizer provides the following configurable options:

  * **Most important K cut-off** : The number of the most popular entities (i.e. a set of equal values) that are tracked for collecting statistics and re-organizing data into different partitions. You can choose a large _K cut-off_ value (e.g. 50 000).
    * Consider the example in which you configure a metrics operator with a metric that has the _Group By_ field _Merchant_. Assume again that you have two large merchants (Retailer 1, Retailer 2) each of which represents 1/3 of the total data, and the remaining 1/3 of the data is a long-tail of very small merchants (Merchant 1, Merchant 2, ... , Merchant N). If you choose the k cut-off value equal to 2: the data associated with Retailer 1 and 2 will be re-organized using then data-aware optimizer option, whereas the remaining rows are re-organized with the hash-based approach.
  * **Maximum rows per partition** : The number of maximum rows that fit on each partition. For example, if you know that each row in your dataset averages to 1KB, and that your Spark executors have 4 GB of heap for data (because they have 12 GB available for the executor, e.g.), then it is acceptable to configure 4 million rows per partition.



Check the pages [Creating a stratified sample](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/creating-a-stratified-sample) and [Creating metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics) to learn how to choose the data-aware optimizer option.

#### Computing statisticsâ

Pulse logs statistics into the logging files of the job when you run a plan execution with the data-aware optimizer option. This helps data scientists to know how the data is being partitioned and, in case of failing to compute a plan, it might also help them to understand the reason behind the failure.

For each set of _Group By_ fields that is shuffled (e.g. set1: "card-number"+"merchant"; set2: "device-id"), the following data is computed:

  * Median
  * Average
  * Top 10 most predominant set of _Group By_ field values and the corresponding cardinality.



This statistics can be accessed in the log folder, using the logging level DEBUG.

# Operator Reference

Was this page helpful?Â 

When designing a [plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) to [process your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data), the following operators are available:

## Operators in deployable plansâ

### Sourceâ

Defines an original data source the plan takes as input. Uses the schema of the data source to define the input format for the plan.

A [non-deployable plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#non-deployable-plans) can take several sources, for example, coming from different files.

### Mapâ

Performs major data transformations on your datasets. Lets you add new fields to the current data schema, remove existing ones, and update expressions that define how the value of a field is calculated. You can also reorder the fields on the "Add Fields" tab of a map operator in a manner that better suits your work.

Use the map to manipulate your data, [clean up your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/cleaning-up-the-data), transform your data, perform calculations on existing fields to [derive features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-derived-features), etc.

You can configure field additions and updates with advanced expressions implemented in [UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions).

### Filterâ

Applies an expression to the data and narrows down its scope.

Use the filter to, for example, obtain only transactions from a specific merchant that require different processing.

You can apply filters with expressions implemented in [UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions).

### Listâ

Accesses the content of a list and stores it to a new field which gets added to the events that traverse the list operator.

### Metricsâ

Generates measurable information, aggregates results and gives you valuable insight on your data, for the [time windows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#window) you define.

Calculates all selected aggregations for all possible combinations of selected time windows and grouping fields.

Available aggregations are **avg** , **count** , **max** , **min** , **sum** , as well as advanced expressions implemented in [UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions).

Use metrics, for example, when in a [features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering) plan you want to calculate the total amount (**sum**) spent by each card (**Group By**), in a single day (**Window**).

### Sampleâ

Reduces the current data to a configurable percentage of the original size. Sampled values are randomly selected using the sampling percentage as the selection probability.

Sampling a dataset multiple times, with the same percentage, will always return the same resulting data.

Use the sample, for example, when implementing a [Stratified Sample](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/creating-a-stratified-sample) to reduce the number of non-fraud transactions in your dataset.

### Sinkâ

Terminates the logical flow of the plan.

When you run the plan, the sink outputs the result of the plan to a new data source and to a file in your filesystem.

Non-deterministic functions

When you apply UDFs in Map, Filter or Metrics operators, the usage of non-deterministic functions can result in non-deterministic results. For example, when you include any randomness factor into your expressions.

Source and sink operators

Pulse automatically adds a source and a sink operator to deployable plans. You need only to configure them when executing the plan.

Clipboard

You can use the clipboard  in order to copy-paste operators in plans. This helps you save time by allowing you to create plans more efficiently without the need of specifying all their fields each time you create a new plan, letting you use the operators you have already configured.

## Operators in non-deployable plansâ

Some operators only make sense at a design and exploration stage in your data science project. When processing a data stream in real-time to classify instances as `true` or `false` (let's take the fraud detection use case as an example), these activities are not repeatable nor applicable, for instance when joining data from separate sources.

As such, the following operators are only available for [non-deployable plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#non-deployable-plans), and perform typical data manipulation activities you might do in a database:

### Group Byâ

Groups data on a combination of fields, calculates aggregated metrics for each grouping, and outputs the result to a new field in the resulting dataset. Available aggregations are **avg** , **count** , **max** , **min** , **sum**.

For example, group by _card_number_ and use the _max(amount)_ aggregation over a one-month window to obtain the highest transaction amount for each card in the last month.

### Lookup Byâ

Availability of Lookup Metrics

The `Lookup By` operator is only available when using the [Railgun engine](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine), and when explicitly enabled via configuration. To activate this functionality, reach out to the Feedzai Customer Success (CS) team.

Extends the capabilities of the `Group By` operator by providing a way to select which group to return the aggregated value of. (By default, `Group By` always returns the aggregation that matches the value of the grouping fields in the current row.)

The `Lookup By` operator allows specifying a retrieval field (or set of fields) that is different from the grouping field(s), thus overriding the default behavior of the `Group By` operator.

For example, group the data by _recipient_ID_ and use the _sum(amount)_ aggregation over a one-week window, and then use _sender_ID_ as the lookup field to obtain the total amount received in the last week by the account that is sending money in a transaction.

### Joinâ

Combines rows from two workflow data paths that match on the specified fields.

Allows for **Left** , **Inner** , **Right** and **Full** join.

### Unionâ

Combines the resulting data from two workflow data paths.

Both datasets must have the exact same fields with the same types, which can be specified in a different order. The output schema can be chosen when configuring the union.

# Cost Fields in Rules

A **cost field** is a field of the instances that is used as a weight for the metrics of the evaluations (of both models and rules), typically the transaction amount in a fraud detection scenario.

Using cost fields in model evaluations or rule evaluations allows you to transform any metric (which by default is count-based, e.g. Recall, Precision, etc.) into a cost-based metric (e.g. Money Recall, if the field chosen is a form of cost of the instance).

The following image displays cost fields included in a rule evaluation. This example depicts an evaluation of a block of rules where the plot shows the cost performance and the _Results_ table displays the cost FPR and Recall.

# Custom Evaluation Metrics in Rules

Was this page helpful?Â 

An evaluation metric is a function that can be applied to the data obtained during a machine learning model/rule validation.

In a data science project, an evaluation metric allows you to inject business logic into an objective model/rule evaluation. This allows you to evaluate trained models/rules based on the business value they deliver.

You can add an evaluation metric to your project by defining a function that receives:

  * The number of True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP) and False Negatives (FN), and outputs a number in an open domain.
  * The cost-TP, -TN, -FP and -FN. The cost field variants are based on the weight a data field in the Instance, typically the transaction amount in a fraud detection scenario, rather than using a count-based approach.



The following image depicts where you can create a new evaluation metric. Check the User Guide to see how you can [define evaluation metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model#using-custom-evaluation-metrics), for example, in a model evaluation.

You can apply a custom evaluation metric, written by you and adjusted to your use case, to any existing model evaluation or rule evaluation.

Availability

The values of cost-based evaluation metrics are available to model evaluations or rule evaluations only if you define a cost field for the evaluation.

If you do not define a cost field for an evaluation, then Pulse will not be able to compute your custom evaluation metrics and you will not have access to them.

Was this page helpful?Â 

# How Rules Work

Rules can have lasting effects on both the workflow and the event itself.

Workflow-halting rules

A single rule can stop an entire workflow. You must be careful when configuring the control flow of a rule.

If a rule is enabled and the [condition of a rule](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules/rules-components) is _true_ , then Pulse executes the following actions:

  1. An entry is added to score tracking.
  2. One or more actions are triggered immediately.
  3. The target variable of the event is set with a value as specified in the rule. For example, setting the _fraud_ field as _true_.
  4. The execution of the workflow proceeds as specified in the rule.



Changes to "event" are not visible to other rules

Note that any changes made to score results, target variable or outcome are not visible to other rules in the same rule service element. This enforces that rules evaluate independently of their order.

## Execution orderâ

There are several key aspects of how a rule is executed. For a rule to be executed or have any effect at all it needs to be enabled. This, however, doesn't guarantee that the rule is executed. You must consider both how the control flow works and the order of the rules, as defined in your project.

Each rule service has its own set of rules defined in a rules project. These rules are unique to the service instance and have a specific order by which they are executed. This is important because triggering one rule can cause others to be skipped.

Another key aspect of the rules is that they are executed independently from each other and in an ordered fashion.

If you need to reuse variables in several rules, check [this section about environments](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules/rules-components/#integration-with-environment-metrics-and-variables).

## Triggering actionsâ

Rules can have a great impact on the whole workflow. One of the things they can do when fired is to trigger [actions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/actions-and-action-listeners), which will be caught and processed by action handlers.

Actions can have parameters whose value is defined in the rules. For example, a "sendEmail" action can have the parameters "to" and "subject" with values "[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#d9b4b8b0b599bca1b8b4a9b5bcf7bab6b4)" and "Rule Alert".

For details on how to define which parameters should be available in each action check the [Actions and Action Listeners](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/actions-and-action-listeners) page.

## Controlling the workflow executionâ

Each rule can define what should happen to the workflow when the rule is fired.

This is especially useful when you want to ignore the evaluation of further rules, or even abort the rest of the workflow, as soon as one rule is triggered. Available options are as follows:

  * **Continue**

The execution continues to the next rule or, if there is none, to the next workflow element.

  * **Stop Workflow**

The workflow execution stops. Actions resulting from the current rule will be triggered for the current event.

  * **Next Workflow Element**

No more rules are executed in this rule service instance and the execution continues to the next workflow element.

Title: Rule Components | Feedzai Pulse
============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)

  * [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules)
