On this page

# Time, schedules and timezones

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Timestamps: moments in timeâ

Every event that Pulse receives must carry a timestamp â a specification of _when_ the event happened. This is necessary so that Pulse can compute metrics such as ânumber of events in the last 24 hoursâ (among other things), since this requires knowing which events happened when.

Timestamps can take several forms. The following are the two most common formats:

  * UNIX timestamp, i.e. number of milliseconds (or seconds) since January 1, 1970 00:00 UTC. For example,1620037816000.
  * ISO 8601 timestamp, i.e. a string with date, time and timezone. For example, 2021-05-03T09:49:48+00:00.



## Timezonesâ

The same timestamp will correspond to different local time (and sometimes date) depending on the timezone:

Timestamp| Time in UTC (Iceland)| Time in UTC-12 (Baker Island)| Time in UTC+8:45 (Eucla)  
---|---|---|---  
1620037816000| Monday, 3 May 2021 10:30:16| **Sunday, 2 May** 2021 22:30:16| Monday, 3 May 2021 19:**15** :16  
2021-05-03T10:30:16+03:00| Monday, 3 May 2021 07:30:16| **Sunday, 2 May** 2021 19:30:16| Monday, 3 May 2021 16:**15** :16  
  
As you will see below, some Pulse operations are timezone-dependent. For example, to ârun a job at midnightâ, Pulse needs to know: which midnight? Midnight in Iceland? Midnight in Eucla? Events that Pulse receives may happen in any timezone anywhere in the world. To schedule jobs and perform other operations consistently, Pulse needs to pick one reference timezone and stick with it. This timezone, which we will call the internal timezone, defaults to the local timezone of the machine where Pulse is running. It can be explicitly configured to a different one via the _pulse.global.timezone_ configuration property.

This is similar to dealing with different units of measurement. For example, if you are comparing distances to a threshold of 100 meters, you will convert all measurements to meters â it does not matter if they were originally in miles or in yards. In fact, a timestamp does not necessarily convey _where_ the event happened anyway. Just because a timestamp is in UTC does not mean the event happened in UTC â it might have been converted by some intermediate system. Similarly, if a distance is expressed in nautical miles, it does not necessary mean it was measured at sea.

Changing the default value of the internal timezone can be advantageous. For example, consider a deployment for an Australian client where the system architect wants the jobs to run at midnight local time, when the system is under the lowest load. If the machines are not in Australia, the default timezone might be UTC â in this case the job execution time needs to be set to 10 PM. It is much more intuitive though to configure the internal timezone to UTC+10 and set the job execution time to 0 AM.

A word of caution: some timezones, such as âEurope/Lisbonâ (as opposed to âWESTâ or âUTC+1â), automatically incorporate daylight saving time. In these timezones, the time of 1:30 AM, for example, might be observed twice on the same day (in October) or not at all (in March). For this reason it is not recommended to use such timezones as the internal timezone. This is another reason to explicitly set the internal timezone instead of relying on the default.

## Workflow clockâ

Pulse performs many time-based operations, for example:

  * Compute a real-time metric (see [Plans in workflows - Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#metrics)) such as ânumber of events since the start of the dayâ.
  * Run a scheduled metrics job (see [Scheduled Metrics Jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/scheduled-metrics-jobs)) at midnight.
  * Enable a list item (see [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists)) on 2021-05-03 at 15:00.



From the section above, you already know that this time is relative to the reference timezone. But is it _the time_ as we know it? Not quite.

Unlike in the outside world, **time in Pulse only moves when Pulse receives events**. For example, if Pulse needs to enable a list item at 15:00, it will not do so until it receives an event that happened after 15:00 (even if it has to wait for days). This allows Pulse to correctly process events if they are consistently late. For example, a bank might only send information about transfers made during the weekend on Monday morning. In this case, when processing each transfer, Pulse âpretendsâ that it _is_ still the weekend.

Itâs also important that (under normal circumstances) **time in Pulse only moves forward**. While Pulse is designed to handle consistently delayed events correctly (per above), it does not retroactively process late events if more recent events have arrived in the meantime.

Instead, Pulse processes these âout of orderâ events as if they were recent. This is a limitation of how Pulse computes real-time metrics, but it affects the logic for the entire workflow.

Here is how this works in practice. The current time in Pulse is stored in the **workflow clock**.

  * When there are no events, the clock does not change.
  * Each new event, if itâs more recent than the workflow clock, will advance the clock. For example, if the clock is at 1620037816000 (10:30 UTC) and there is a new event with a timestamp of 09:40 UTC-1 (i.e. 10:40 UTC), the clock will advance to 1620038416000 (10:40 UTC).
  * If a new event is older than the clock, Pulse will override its timestamp to equal the clock. The clock itself remains the same.



## How workflow clock and internal timezone affect Pulse functionalityâ

In this section you will see how Pulse clock and the internal timezone affect different functionality of Pulse.

### Listsâ

Pulse [Lists](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) use the workflow clock to enable and disable items. For example, if an item needs to be enabled on 2021-05-03 at 10:30 UTC, it will happen when the workflow clock reaches that moment in time (i.e. when Pulse receives an event with a timestamp higher or equal to 2021-05-03 10:30 UTC).

### Real-time metricsâ

Real-time metrics (see [Plans in workflows - Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows)) use the workflow clock to compute aggregations over time periods. For example, in a metric like âtotal amount transacted by customer in the last 24 hoursâ, 24 hours are counted backwards from the workflow clock, i.e. the latest event received by Pulse.

Real-time metrics may also rely on the internal timezone. For example, a metric with a window expression _reset (_: day)_ , which means the metric is reset every day at midnight, will depend on Pulseâs notion of midnight. If Pulse timezone is set to UTC, then the metric will reset at midnight UTC. (Remember, the timezone of where the events actually happened is irrelevant.)

### Scheduled metrics jobsâ

[Scheduled Metrics Jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/scheduled-metrics-jobs) can be triggered in two ways:

  * Automatically, based on their schedule (e.g. ârun every midnightâ).
  * Manually, using a button in the Pulse UI.



In both cases, Pulse uses the workflow clock, but the behavior is different. There are two main questions:

  * When does the job start?
  * What time period does the job consider?



Here is a quick summary, assuming the job computes metrics with windows of 2 days.

Job triggered...| Job starts...| Time period  
---|---|---  
Automatically on schedule (âevery midnightâ)| When **workflow clock** reaches âmidnightâ in **internal timezone**.| Events with timestamps within 2 days of âmidnightâ in **internal timezone**.  
Manually (through the UI)| Immediately| Events with timestamps within 2 days of the **current workflow clock**.  
  
Below are a few important considerations based on this behavior.

#### Automatically triggered jobsâ

Keep in mind when thinking about when the job starts:

  * The job is triggered based on the workflow clock, not real-world clock. If itâs 1 AM in the real world, but the last event received has a timestamp of 23:59, **the job will not trigger until a more recent event is received**.
  * **If Pulse does not receive events on a given day, the job for that day will never trigger.** If Pulse only receives events on April 30 and then only on May 3, the first event of April 30 will trigger the job for that day, and the first event of May 3 will trigger the job for that day. No jobs will run for May 1 or May 2.
  * In case of Omnichannel scheduled metrics (see [Plans in workflows - Omnichannel metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#omnichannel-metrics)), there are multiple workflows involved: the main workflow and one or more secondary workflows. In this case Pulse uses the **clock of the main workflow**. The same considerations as above apply. For example, **if there are no events on the main channel, the job will not trigger** , no matter how many events are received on the secondary channels.



Keep in mind when thinking about the time period considered by job:

  * The time period for the job is calculated as follows: time when the job is supposed to trigger â biggest metric window size. Note again that the time period is not counted from current value of the workflow clock, but from the time the job is scheduled to run (e.g. midnight).
  * The âtime the job is scheduled to runâ (e.g. midnight) is interpreted according to the internal timezone.
  * In case of Omnichannel scheduled metrics (see [Plans in workflows - Omnichannel metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#omnichannel-metrics)), **the same time period is used consistently across all channels**. If the main workflow clock is on May 3, the job will correspond to midnight of May 3 and the time period will be counted from that moment in all channels. It does not matter if some of the secondary workflows, for example, have not received events since May 2 or, to the contrary, have already received events from May 4.



Example:

Workflow clock| Job schedule| Window size| Time period  
---|---|---|---  
May 3, 01:30 AM| midnight (**0 AM**)| 2 days| May 1, **0 AM** â May 3, **0 AM**  
  
#### Manually triggered jobsâ

  * The time period is until the timestamp of last event received. If you trigger a job on Monday but the last received event was on Friday, the time period will be until Friday, not Monday.
  * In Omnichannel scheduled metrics, the time period is until the timestamp of the last event received on the main channel. Like with automatic jobs, the same time period is applied consistently across all channels.



Example:

Workflow clock| Job schedule| Window size| Time period  
---|---|---|---  
May 3, **10:30 AM**|  midnight (0 AM)| 2 days| May 1, **10:30 AM** â May 3, **10:30 AM**

Title: Best Practices for AutoML's Feature Engineering Stage | Feedzai Pulse

Was this page helpful?Â 

# Best Practices for AutoML's Feature Engineering Stage

At the start of a project, the schema is usually already defined. In addition, fraud or money laundering patterns should also be characterized and understood so that you know which fields to use in the transformations. The transformations already encode Feedzai's knowledge into what is the best strategy to build features to tackle financial crime. This is all that is needed for AutoML basics: you can now create a semantic file with such knowledge in your hand.

Schema definition

Sometimes it's hard to have schemas completely defined at the beginning of a project. The same applies to the definition of scorable events, and other important aspects of the underlying data generation process that we do not control.

Take this opportunity to reflect on what's the minimum reliable information you have about the data. With it, consider building the semantic file with the least assumptions possible. Start by selecting only one grouping entity and tagging the most important fields, e.g., event timestamp, and transaction amount.

Semantic files let you map schema fields to common entities that are useful for feature engineering. Doing this allows you to speed up the initial task of creating a feature engineering plan from nothing. So, in case you don't have any data yet, you can still use AutoML to create a plan with features that leverage domain knowledge, therefore expected to be useful.

[Learn which tags are supported by semantic files](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/automl/semantic-file#list-of-input-tags).

When you want to have aggregations with more than one grouping entity, you need to create a _composite field_. This is useful for the case when you want to track behavior over an entity with low cardinality. For example, when processing money transfers, you will most likely want to track how many transactions a person does for a given country. **To do this, you need to define a composite field that combines the originator account and the destination country.**

entity vs grouping-entity tags

Entity tags will only be used for _countDistinct_ aggregations. When defining a field as an entity, AutoML will not use it for counts, sums, or any other aggregation that is not a distinct aggregation.

Imagine this scenario for a payment processor's data set: define `customer_id` as grouping-entity and `merchant_country` as an entity. This combination will only create the following subset of profiles. For the sake of simplicity, we're omitting other aggregations based on timestamp (e.g. velocities), or numeric fields (e.g. avg amount).

  * `group by customer_id count()`
  * `group by customer_id countDistinct(merchant_country)`



If you also want to track the counts per customer and merchant country, you need to define a composite grouping entity:
    
    
    {  
      "@type": "composite",  
      "fields": [  
        "customer_id",  
        "merchant_country"  
      ],  
      "tags": [ "grouping-entity" ],  
      "fieldDesc": "customer_id_merchant_country"  
    }  
    

Keep in mind that grouping entities with very low cardinality (<10) or highly skewed, can compromise your job execution. Check the Don'ts section below for more context.

Remember that grouping entities will not just create the aggregations/profiles. These metrics will also be used to compute ratios and other derived transformations.

The following is an example of a semantic file.

**semantic-file.json**
    
    
    [  
      {  
        "@type": "simple",  
        "tags": [  
          "amount"  
        ],  
        "fieldDesc": "amount"  
      },  
      {  
        "@type": "simple",  
        "tags": [  
          "entity"  
        ],  
        "fieldDesc": "acceptor_id"  
      },  
      {  
        "@type": "simple",  
        "tags": [  
          "entity",  
          "country",  
          "location"  
        ],  
        "fieldDesc": "acceptor_country_code"  
      },  
      {  
        "@type": "simple",  
        "tags": [  
          "timestamp",  
          "datetime"  
        ],  
        "fieldDesc": "event_occurred_at"  
      },  
      {  
        "@type": "simple",  
        "tags": [  
          "grouping-entity"  
        ],  
        "fieldDesc": "card_pan"  
      },  
      {  
        "@type": "simple",  
        "tags": [  
          "amount"  
        ],  
        "fieldDesc": "account_available_credit"  
      },  
      {  
        "@type": "simple",  
        "tags": [  
          "datetime"  
        ],  
        "fieldDesc": "account_open_date"  
      },  
      {  
        "@type": "simple",  
        "tags": [  
          "grouping-entity"  
        ],  
        "fieldDesc": "customer_id"  
      }  
    ]  
    

Based on the semantic file, AutoML will create a **deployable plan** where it will expand as many features as it can.

Before submitting your AutoML run, be sure to create job profiles with appropriate Spark configurations considering your data volume and complexity. AutoML will use the default job profile of Pulse for each type of job it launches. The only exception is the job profile for feature selection, for which AutoML will use the profile configured in `pulse.properties`. If your AutoML run fails during the feature engineering phase, it's probably due to memory issues. Use job profiles to tune memory usage.

A crucial consideration that affects the feature engineering process is the existence of **partitioning in runtime**. Briefly, runtime partitioning is essential when processing very high throughputs, e.g. 1000 TPS at peak. Having your data partitioned across different machines means that machine 1 will not see **in real time** the data of machine 2. Because of this, you will need to decide what is your main grouping entity and make sure it is the same as the partitioning key. This is usually the customer/card/account field. If you don't match the partitioning keys in the grouping, then AutoML will generate real-time metrics that might not be possible to compute during runtime.

## Dosâ

  * Verify which timestamp field of your schema is the one that will be used to represent the time in which the event occurred. This field will need to be provided in the first page of the AutoML wizard. **This is the timestamp used to compute the metrics.**

  * **Choose one main grouping entity only.** Even if your data is not partitioned in runtime now, consider the likelihood of having partitioning in the future. Remember that when your data is partitioned you won't be able to leverage entities that can be seen across multiple runtime partitions. On the other hand, more grouping entities lead to a more thorough exploration of feature combinations.

Putting the runtime partitioning issue aside, also consider the pros/cons of having potential marginal gains on model performance versus strain on processing pipeline. Think about what behavior mostly describes your fraud or money laundering patterns. Typical grouping entities are: customer/account, or card (in a card channel).

  * Create a job profile that is reasonable for your feature engineering plan.

  * If you expect very large data volumes (1M events per day or more), tweak window sizes under the advanced options. As a general rule, avoid real-time windows greater than 1 day: real-time windows are kept in memory, and thus impact memory performance as well as recovery. Read more about this under the [Metrics best practices](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics) pages.

  * When starting from a Solution (e. g. Transaction Fraud for Retail Banking Cards or Transaction Fraud for Retail Banking Transfers and Instant Transfers), always check first its template semantic file.




## Don'tsâ

  * **Avoid grouping entities with very low cardinality** (i.e. low number of different values). This will depend on the project so be aware of this when reusing semantic files. For example, if you're looking at data mostly from 1 or 2 countries, using the country code as a grouping entity can be problematic. All your data will be split per these categories, and your pipeline will run in a very large chunk of data. This in turn will cause out-of-memory errors. However, if you're expecting your data to be well distributed across many countries **and you don't have partitioning in runtime** , this could be a reasonable **grouping** entity.

  * Be mindful of your âentityâ tags. Entities are used for distinct counts (e.g. distinct beneficiaries per customer). Too many distinct aggregations on long windows in large data sets is known to have a high memory footprint in the Data Science environment. In addition, these aggregations are very computation-intensive in runtime. As a rule of thumb, try to keep the entities to the minimum needed for the project you are doing.




## Data split stageâ

The data source splitting stage is a sub-stage in the feature engineering stage. At the data split stage, Pulse will split your data set into two or three subsets: training, validation, and optionally testing. Although this intermediate stage is rarely a point of failure, it still deserves some considerations.

As a general Machine Learning guideline, these splits are 80/20/20, i.e., 80% of your data for training, 20% for validation, and 20% for testing (hold-out data set). Here, we enforce that the split be defined timewise, because our transformations are time sensitive.

Splitting is done through a filter, which can generate data with empty partitions (or blocks) for the validation and testing splits. This doesn't impact the model results. However, Data Scientists might want to use these validation and test sets for other operations. In this case, they will experience degraded computational performance compared to the same data with these empty blocks removed. In the long run, having empty data partitions will cause HDFS/S3 degradation related to having many empty files/blocks.

To solve this, manually partition your data through JupyterLab by coalescing the data source. As a rule of thumb, if the data source is 20% of the initial data, it should have 20% the number of partitions (see the snippet below).
    
    
    >>> # Load the validation set through the ds-api  
    >>> df_valid = feedzai.pulse_to_pyspark(  
    ...     spark_session, app_name, datasource_name  
    ... )  
    >>> # The number of partitions will be the same as in the feature eng data source  
    >>> df_valid.rdd.getNumPartitions()  
    1000  
    >>> feedzai.pyspark_to_pulse(  
    ...     spark_session,  
    ...     # Save a new data source coalesced to have only 200 partitions  
    ...     df_valid.coalesce(200),  
    ...     app_name,  
    ...     datasource_name + "_coalesced",  
    ...     "/path/for/this/new/datasource",  
    ... )

# Best Practices for AutoML's Feature Selection Stage

The main concept behind AutoML's feature engineering approach is expansion-reduction. The goal is to explore as many possible features as it is computationally feasible. Then, only the most relevant features should be chosen.

In the reduction step, AutoML trains a Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT) model on a sample of your development data. The GBT model is used as a surrogate to get its model feature importance. By default this step selects the top-K features so that their relative importance is 90% of the total.

On the advanced options of the AutoML wizard you can select the sample size that will be used for the GBT model.

Feature importance

This methodology is different than the one used by Pulse for individual model importance. Speed is paramount for AutoML. Thus, it's preferable to use GBT on a sample of the training data. This enables faster iterations.

Pulse's feature importance is done by computing the difference in Recall after shuffling each feature individually, for a given FP-Rate. This makes this algorithm model agnostic. However, it also makes it computationally heavy when the number of features is large and/or you have a very unbalanced data set (and thus need a larger sample).

AutoML's feature importance for feature selection is a simpler algorithm that trains a GBT model and gets its feature importance. Only one model is trained, and thus it only goes through the randomly sampled data once.

If your target rate is very low on your features data (e. g. 1 basis point), bear in mind you should tune your feature importance job to use approximately 1M instances.

At the end of the feature selection stage, Pulse will create a new features plan with **only the selected features and their dependencies**.

# Best Practices for AutoML's Hyperparameter Tuning Stage

The last stage of AutoML is hyperparameter tuning (HPT). Here, AutoML will train a range of models through OpenML, tuning their hyperparameters in one go. There are some important considerations during this stage:

  1. This will use the **model training** logic: 1 big Spark task per model.
  2. Trained models are kept on the machine where they are trained, and then discarded. This happens because the goal of HPT is getting the best model configuration and not all the model binaries. At the end of the run the best model will be retrained and kept within Pulse.
  3. Evaluations will **not be distributed**. They run with as much parallelism as the model training, i.e., 1 Spark task.
  4. If 1 model fails to train, then the HPT stage also fails. This happens because HPT considered a single job as part of the AutoML pipeline. If you want to re-run HPT under a different job configuration, you can do so by using an empty semantic file, and selecting the appropriate data source as input, i.e., the one with features already computed.
  5. It will use **Random Search**.



That being said, most best practices here rely on configuration. Check the [model training documentation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training) that explains how to create a job profile for model training. From there you will see that you should:

  * Size the executor for the biggest machines in the cluster.
  * Allocate all the cores of the machine for the single task with `spark.task.cpus`.
  * Allocate all the cores and memory of the machine with `spark.executor.cores` and `spark.executor.memory`. Leave only a little overhead with `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` to account for serialization/deserialization overheads.
  * No need for any meaningful YARN memory overhead since there are no shuffles.
  * Reduce `spark.memory.fraction` significantly, e.g., to 0.05; since there is no shuffling or caching, it is all user memory for the training.



Remember that one of the possible sources of failure is that the data must fit in memory during training. Because of this you should tune your model training jobs to use the largest machines. The plural here is important. Be aware that if you tune your job to fit only a few machines (say, 1 or 2), you will only be able to run that same number of models in parallel. In addition, to speed up this job, try leveraging the CPU cores the machines have available. Donât forget that the job will not be distributed. It will run 1 task per model.

This approach contrasts with the typical Model evaluations. In this case your evaluation will be done streaming your validation data in one very long task. That being said, **if your data set is large, use a small time period for the evaluations in HPT**.

## Hyperparameter tuning algorithmâ

The algorithm used in AutoML is different from the one used on a regular HPT job.

The manual HPT job uses grid search, i.e., the user specifies which parameters will be used. AutoML uses Random Search instead. For random search, Pulse will draw the possible parameters from the following probability functions:

### Feedzai Random Forestâ

Parameter | Default | xmin | xmax | p(x)  
---|---|---|---|---  
Depth | 20 | 5 | 100 | x  
Trees | 100 | 50 | 500 | x  
In-bag factor | 0.65 | 0.2 | 1 | x  
N. Features | 0.3 x k | -4 | -0.5 | k x 2x,  
where k is the number of features.  
Split method | one-vs-others | one-vs-others  
all-vs-all |  | Discrete.  
Min. instances per split | 2 | 0 | 1/3 | nx,  
where n is the number of samples.  
Prior | Parent |  |  | No search.  
  
### Generalized Linear Model (GLM)â

The lambda search is deferred to H2O to perform it internally.

---|---|---|---|---

# Aggregations

The core aspect of [metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric) is the ability to perform aggregations over time on a grouping entity (or a set of grouping entities). The general rule when creating the actual metrics is always to keep it as simple as possible. This applies also to the window definition and to the actual aggregation expression. Let's break down each one of these:

## Windowsâ

The rule of thumb is to have two main sets of windows: 1 for real time (e.g. 24 hours), and another for scheduled metrics (e.g. 1 month). However, note that with very large payloads in runtime, the size of the real time windows might need to be adjusted. Real time windows, albeit faster to compute, imply that data that goes inside the window (c.f. [filters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics)) must be kept in memory. Also, during recovery, the data pertaining to the largest real-time window must be reinjected into the workflow before operations can resume.

## Group-byâ

When using the [`Group By` operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#group-by) to group by multiple fields, always have the high-cardinality ones first since they will dictate [how the data is partitioned in the Spark shuffle](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/data-partitioning-for-the-metrics-operator) (if you want to group by `card_pan` and `merchant_id`, and there are 1M cards but just 100 merchants, you will want to select `card_pan` first to avoid having 100 very large tasks that might run out of memory).

tip

This manual optimization is not necessary when using [Railgun](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/).

## Aggregationâ

The "aggregation" input lets you define what type of aggregation is to be done. Note that the `countDistinct` aggregation is more performant in runtime than in the Data Science Platform. This means that having a lot of `countDistinct`s will make your Data Science job slower. In addition, these are memory intensive aggregations, as the whole state is needed to be able to expire elements as the clock moves forward.

Some advanced aggregation examples:

### Velocity of transactionsâ
    
    
    (  
        let first_timestamp = first().event_occurred_at ?? 0 in  
        let last_timestamp  = last().event_occurred_at  ?? 0 in  
        let time_span       = (1 + last_timestamp - first_timestamp ) / ( 60*60*1000.0 ) in  
        let count           = count() in  
      
        ( if ( count <= 1 ) then 0 else count / time_span )  
    )  
    

### The time since the previous event within this aggregationâ
    
    
    // (in milliseconds)  
    (  
        ( last().event_occurred_at ?? 1 ) - ( prev().event_occurred_at ?? 1 )  
    )  
    

## Dosâ

  * Use "simple" aggregations (from the UI).
  * Use Approximate count distincts if you expect the counts to be large.
  * Create an "aggregation repository" with the expressions that are commonly used. This will help you avoid bugs.



## Don'tsâ

  * Avoid writing too many advanced aggregations.
  * Avoid count distincts with long windows. Distinct aggregations are the most costly, because all the events must be kept inside the window at all times. (c.f. Approximate aggregations). This cost mostly affects the Data Science Platform and not necessarily Runtime (see [Scheduled Metrics Jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics/scheduled-metrics-jobs)).
  * Don't use real-time metrics with long windows unless you have direct support from Feedzai's product team. The experimental nature of the feature means that it is not recommended for general usage.



## Advanced optimization techniquesâ

  * Salting null values/large entities that can be ignored. SMJs already ignore null values.
  * Metrics are very sensitive to data skew and suboptimal data partitioning. Make sure your data sources are well partitioned by checking that each uncompressed CSV part takes about 128 MB in HDFS or closer to 512 MB in S3. That being said, as a rule of thumb, as long as each part is about 100 MB in size, it should be good enough. If you have too many partitions, you can coalesce them manually. Check the Spark documentation for more information on coalescing.
  * Fields that are not necessary in a feature engineering plan should be dropped at the beginning, or in a preprocessing plan or JupyterLab script. This is due to Spark that sends data across machines during execution. By removing columns that are unused, Spark will send less data between machines. This will allow you to use less memory per executor, thus providing more parallelism. **Rule of thumb** : start by looking at large complex fields and constant fields.
  * Filters inside metrics do provide _some_ improvements in memory usage. They are not as impactful as removing unnecessary fields. Generally speaking, if you are measuring something that can be tracked only in specific event types, try to have as specific a filter as possible. Even though this won't reduce the bulk memory consumption by Spark, it will reduce memory being consumed during the aggregation.

# Constraints

Although Pulse uses the same feature definition offline (Data Science Platform) and online (Runtime Environment), there are important distinctions between them.

This distinction means that as a best practice, runtime environment constraints should be known upfront before creating metrics manually.

In the following sections you can find the most common constraints when developing metrics.

## Runtime Environmentâ

When processing high throughputs in runtime (e.g. 1000 TPS at peak), it is advisable to have **runtime partitioning**. This means that events will be processed by different machines, according to a partitioning strategy. The most common strategies are to partition by card/account. This way it is guaranteed that all events from cards are processed in **real time** by the same machine.

So when designing **real time metrics** you must be aware if partitioning is active in your runtime environment. If it is, and the metric does not contain said key as the root grouping entity, there will be a discrepancy in the calculations between the Data Science and Runtime environments. Note that **this does not affect scheduled metric jobs (SMJs)**. Because SMJs are applied to events fetched from the Event Storage, they will always see all the events that are processed, independently of the partitioning key. For more details on SMJs best practices, go to the [Scheduled Metrics Jobs (SMJs)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics/scheduled-metrics-jobs) page.

The following table summarizes the points to keep in mind when working with metrics:

| Context| Implication  
---|---|---  
Runtime Partitioning| When data is partitioned in runtime, each node will only see a subset (partition) in real time.Partitioning is needed to process large volumes (rule of thumb: >500 events per second).| Real-time metrics must use:

  1. The same field as the partitioning key as the root grouping entity.
  2. Or, an entity with its domain within the partitioning key.

  
Scheduled Metrics Jobs (SMJs)| Metrics with long windows run in batch jobs in runtime. These batches are scheduled to run at specific times to not overload the system.| Re-running the plan with the same data in the Data Science environment will lead to small errors (up to 1% mismatch in value) in a few samples of data (approx. 1% of samples, depending on job configuration and cluster capacity).  
Optimizations in SMJs| Because SMJs are special jobs that fetch data from storage and write the results as a key-value pair, there are a few optimizations done that are not possible in the Data Science Platform.| Null values in grouping entities are excluded from the SMJ. This helps reduce failure risk due to skewness.Distinct aggregations are one-shot, meaning that the memory consumption is much less than in runtime.  
  
## Data Science Platformâ

Within the data science platform (offline) there are different considerations to take into account. The next table highlights scalability concerns that are relevant when executing plans. In these plans an input data source is processed, metrics are computed on top of it, and the resulting data source is persisted.

| Context| Implication  
---|---|---  
Spark Jobs & data volume| Metrics done in the Data Science Platform make use of Spark to distribute the workload across an Hadoop cluster.Distributing metrics through a Spark job implies data will be moved around in the cluster in large quantities. Due to the nature of profiles, each value of an entity (e.g. each card or account) will be processed in the same Spark machine (or executor).| Even though a metric might only need 2 or 3 fields to compute, Spark will still move the records with all their columns to the executors.  
Spark Jobs & skewness| Very high skews in grouping entities (e.g. 10% of entities represent 90% of the total records), can make Spark Tuning more complex.| Avoid including highly skewed grouping entities in your metrics.If they cannot be avoided, there are two main avenues to solve it:

  * Randomize special entities (eg. govt, gmail, ...)
  * Salt the largest entities: added cost of then joining the features

  
Window sizes| In the Data Science Platform, all windows are processed through Spark. Even though the SMJs effect is simulated, a large window will still be computed "in-memory" inside the Spark executors.| Very large windows might be feasible in runtime, but not in Data Science Platform.  
  
Learn more about the implications of distributed Spark jobs within the Data Science Platform on the [data partitioning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/data-partitioning-for-the-metrics-operator) page.

Learn more about the implementation of [SMJs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/scheduled-metrics-jobs).

### Dosâ

  * Use data-aware optimized partitioning.
  * Only use **real-time** metrics with grouping entities that are guaranteed to be complete in runtime. (c.f. Runtime partitioning). Example: partitioning key = country, then if users are segregated by country, they can still be used as grouping entities. Partition key = CustomerID, then only customers or other entities that are not shared across customers can be used as grouping entities in real-time metrics.



### Don'tsâ

Railgun supports long time windows

These restrictions do not apply when using the [Railgun engine](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/).

  * Avoid creating metrics with very long time windows to mimic "write-once streaming" features (e.g. "Time since the first time this customer used this device").
  * Don't use very large windows. For very large volumes, the rule of thumb is to use 1 month as the maximum window size.

# Best Practices for Metrics in Railgun

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Usage of `min()` and `max()` aggregationsâ

As explained in the [Metrics in Railgun](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#max--min) page, using `min()` and `max()` aggregations with field values that are **monotonically increasing** or **decreasing** (respectively) should be avoided, due to performance issues.

This constraint only applies to windowed metrics ([sliding](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#sliding-windows) or [landmark windows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#landmark-windows)). [Non-windowed metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#non-windowed-metrics) do not have this limitation, as they don't maintain a deque of expiring values.

If you need to compute `min` or `max` over monotonically changing values (such as timestamps), consider the following alternatives:

  1. **Use[non-windowed metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#non-windowed-metrics)**: If you need to track the minimum or maximum value over the entire lifetime of an entity, non-windowed metrics are the recommended approach. However, since non-windowed metrics, by definition, include all events from the beginning of recorded data, this may not be suitable if you only need to compute aggregations over shorter periods (e.g., days rather than years).

  2. **Reduce timestamp cardinality** : If you need to use windowed metrics with timestamps, reduce the cardinality of possible timestamp values by rounding them to a coarser granularity. For example, round timestamps to the nearest second, minute, 10 minutes, hour, or day. This approach has proven effective in practice, as it limits the number of distinct values that need to be tracked in the deque while still maintaining useful temporal precision.

Determining the appropriate cardinality

Depending on the use case, it may be possible to overshoot or undershoot the optimal granularity for timestamp values.

If the right temporal resolution is not immediately obvious based on your needs, reach out to the Feedzai Customer Service for guidance on how to determine the cardinality values for optimal performance.




## Number of Metric operatorsâ

Similar to PKernel, Railgun's performance improves when the workflow includes fewer metric operators.

## Backfill performanceâ

### Impact of cascading metrics in backfillsâ

If a workflow has **cascading metrics** (i.e. metrics that are computed based on other metrics), then it is recommended that the upstream metrics (that are used downstream by other metrics) are all grouped in the **same metrics operator**. Additionally, this metrics operator should only contain those upstream metrics.

One important expectation is that the downstream metrics operators will only have a few upstream metrics (e.g. **5â10 upstream metrics**). That is because of how metrics backfill works and the optimizations that are applied to it:

  1. A backfill is the process by which the state of newly created (or updated) metrics is "filled up" using past events that were originally processed before the metric was created.
  2. To do so, events are replayed from the Event Storage, passed through a simplified version of the workflow, and sent to Railgun.
  3. If there are no cascading metrics, there's an optimization that's applied on the Railgun side that consists in processing these events in **batches**. This means that, instead of updating the metrics being backfilled one event at a time, they are updated (for example) 500 events at a time. Because the processing is done in batch, it's not possible to output the updated value of the metrics for each event while the backfill is running. This is not a problem because, in this case, since there aren't any cascading metrics, the value of the metrics for each event is not needed during the backfill.
  4. If cascading metrics are added (say, metrics M1 â M2, where M2 is calculated based on the values from M1), M1 cannot be backfilled with this batch optimization; the value of M1 needs to be updated for each event, in order to backfill M2 as well. In other words, there is a performance hit when cascading metrics are used: M1 now has to be updated one event at a time, even though M2 can still be updated in batches of multiple events. The performance of updating M1 one event at a time depends on how many other metrics are defined in the same Metrics Operator as M1. The more metrics there are in the operator, the lower the potential throughput; e.g., if there are **5 metrics** in the same operator, it may be possible to backfill M1 at around **5000 events/sec** , but if there are **200 metrics** the throughput may drop to around **200 events/sec**. Therefore, using fewer upstream metrics allows improved backfill performance.



### Maintaining metric values during automatic backfillsâ

Metrics backfills that are triggered manually will [continue to output values based on the original metric definition](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/backfills#backfills-triggered-manually-via-the-ui) (if that version was already available in Railgun when the backfill was initiated) until the backfill is complete.

However, when a backfill is automatically triggered by a metric definition change, the default behavior is for the metric to return the fallback value until the backfill is complete. Still, it is possible to employ a workaround to ensure that metrics in automatically triggered backfills continue outputting the values based on the original definition during the backfill process.

To do so, follow these steps:

  1. **Clone the metric** :  
Create a duplicate of the metric that requires changes.
  2. **Apply changes to the clone** :  
Implement the necessary modifications on the cloned metric.
  3. **Publish the cloned metric** :  
Publish the cloned metric with the applied changes.
  4. **Wait for backfill completion** :  
Allow the backfill process to complete for the cloned metric.
  5. **Delete the old metric** :  
Once the backfill is finished, delete the original metric. Do not yet publish this change; proceed directly to the next step.
  6. **Rename the new metric** :  
Rename the cloned metric to match the name of the original metric, and publish the app. This ensures continuity and avoids the need to update downstream dependencies that were using the original metric name.



These guidelines allow for a smoother transition during backfills, by maintaining the integrity of metrics during the backfill process.

### Managing the queue of backfill jobsâ

#### Ordering backfill jobs by sizeâ

Because backfill jobs are added to an ordered queue as soon as changes to metrics are published, and get picked up from the queue according to their publish order (except where [automatic optimization](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/backfills#backfill-optimization) is possible), it is important to manage this queue to ensure that long-running backfills do not block more urgent ones.

Therefore, when there are changes to be done in multiple metrics using different window sizes, it is recommended to first change the small-window metrics, and publish the application, thus triggering the corresponding backfills. Only then the metrics with large windows should be changed and published. This ensures that the smaller metrics can be executed quickly, without having to wait for the longer backfills to finish first.

Another technique that can be used to manage the backfill queue is to [manually trigger backfill jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/managing-metrics-backfills#triggering-a-new-backfill-job), since such jobs are prioritized over automatically triggered ones.

#### Handling duplicate metric backfillsâ

[Pulse automatically optimizes backfill queues](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/backfills#backfill-optimization) by consolidating the backfill jobs in the queue whenever possible, and skipping backfills for metrics that have already been backfilled, to avoid redundant work that would impact the performance and responsiveness of the application.

However, these optimizations do not apply to metrics that are updated while a backfill for their older version is already running. Therefore, as additional steps to reduce the amount of duplicated work performed in backfills, it is recommended to:

  * Avoid making rapid and frequent changes to metrics;
  * Manually [cancel backfills](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/managing-metrics-backfills#canceling-a-backfill-job) whose metrics have been updated in the meantime, and therefore have triggered a new backfill job.

# Reproducibility Notes

Even though the feature definition from Data Science is exported to Runtime as-is, there are a few reproducibility caveats. These are mostly due to the natural difference between processing historical data versus real time streaming.

When comparing feature values from both environments, be aware of:

  * **Repeated timestamps**. If the timestamp precision is seconds, then with 100,000 events per day, you're guaranteed to have different events occurring at "the same time". With a millisecond precision, note that, while unlikely, it's also possible to have events with the same timestamp during peaks (think about >500 TPS). The consequence of this is that some of these simultaneous events might have their features computed in a different order in DS vs Runtime.
  * **SMJs running time**. SMJs are "simulated" in Data Science by computing the metrics with the same schedule (CRON expression). However, at runtime the result of the SMJ will only be available **after the metrics are computed**. In the meantime, some events were already processed through the workflow and were using the result from the previous SMJ. In Data Science, because we are batching these jobs, the metrics are available to all events happening after the schedule.

# Scheduled Metrics Jobs

When writing metrics in the Data Science Platform, one must always be aware how these impact computation in runtime. As mentioned before, metrics with long windows should be defined as scheduled. This scheduling will make the aggregation update in a tumbling fashion (i.e., "every X time"), instead of sliding (i.e., "every event").

While in the Data Science Platform the implications of using SMJs are relatively easy to manage, there are important considerations to take into account for **runtime** :

  * SMJs are optimized expressions that run as one-shot, i.e., only the minimum needed data is fetched from past events and the result is stored as a map between grouping entities and respective values. These data are stored in the so-called **profile storage**.
  * There will be 1 Spark Shuffle per metrics operator inside a Plan. Remember this is the heaviest computation, as it reorganizes data per grouping entity.
  * There are a few automatic plan optimizations specific to SMJs in the workflow:
    * operators removed if they don't impact SMJs;
    * operators merged if they have no inter-dependency (also in DS);
    * unused fields are not read from the event storage (remember SMJs in runtime read events pulled from Event Storage, i.e., events that already went through the Workflow).
  * Null values in grouping entities are automatically filtered out. This leads to less data being used to compute the SMJ _and_ it usually reduces skewness of grouping entities.
  * There is an option to automatically select which grouping entities are used for the shuffle. Having this option enabled will reduce the number of shuffles, thus reducing the running time of SMJs. However, it does not take into account the grouping entity cardinality. If you are using low-cardinality entities in many aggregations (independently of being the first, second, or third grouping entity of the aggregation), disable this option.
  * If you have SMJs that are dependent on one another (i.e. two subsequent Metrics blocks inside a Plan), **you must enable cascading scheduled metrics** in the workflow. If you don't, due to the one-shot nature of SMJs, the downstream SMJ won't be able to fetch the output of the upstream SMJ.

# Cleaning up the data

Was this page helpful?Â 

You'll often receive raw data with problems, limitations, inconsistencies and all-around quality issues. Once you have matched the raw data to your internal schema, you must make sure that you only work with relevant and high-quality data.

To clean up your data, and address data quality issues, you need to design and create a [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans). This generates a new and clean [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources).

While this task is very similar in nature to the previous task in this guide â[Validating the schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/validating-the-data-schema)â its purpose is not the same. This task handles data quality from the perspective of the value and correctness of information contained in the dataset, while the previous one rather focuses on fixing the structure and formatting of your dataset.

## How toâ

For example, to clean up your data and remove negative values from numerical fields, such as the _TransactionAmount_ , execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab , add  a new Plan.

  2. Set the Plan as [Non-Deployable](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans).

  3. Design your data cleansing Plan as displayed in the following image.




Configure the elements as follows:

  1. Edit  the Source element and specify the Data Source. For example, _Transactions_.

  2. Edit  the Map element to correct the negative values, as follows:

Clipboard

You can also copy  Operators to the clipboard in order to paste them in other Plans. This helps you save time by allowing you to create plans more efficiently without the need of specifying all their fields each time you create a new plan, letting you use the operators you have already configured.

     1. Select the **Fields to Update** tab and specify which is the field to be cleaned. For example, _TransactionAmount_.

     2. Write the update expression for the field. For example:
            
            if (TransactionAmount < 0) then 0 else TransactionAmount  
            

     3. Add the field to the list of fields to be updated.




Finally:

  1. the plan to execute all actions on the original Data Source and generate an improved one.

     1. Define the **Data Source with ID 1** as the original, lower quality, Data Source. For example, _Transactions_.

     2. Configure the **Data Sink with ID 3** as the new and clean Data Source. For example, _Cleaned Transactions_.

Job Profiles

You can select a Job Profile by expanding the  menu. This is helpful because Plans are executed by Spark Jobs, and by using this option you can select a profile with a set of Spark properties that best fulfil the needs of the task that you want to execute. Learn more about [Job Profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/jobs-and-job-profiles#job-profiles) in Pulse, how to [create](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/creating-a-job-profile), [select](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles), and [edit their properties on-demand](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/editing-properties-on-demand).

     3. Execute the Plan to generate a new Data Source, in Pulse, named _Cleaned Transactions_. Pulse also saves an output file with the transformed data to your filesystem.

  2. [Analyze](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis) the _Cleaned Transactions_ Data Source to confirm that there are no negative values for the _TransactionAmount_ field.




## Next Stepsâ

Once you have a clean and valid dataset, you are ready to [design advanced Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data), [analyze your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data) and [generate features for your models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering).

# Importing your dataset into Pulse

Was this page helpful?Â 

This article describes how to make data that is stored in a CSV or Parquet file available in Pulse as a [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources).

info

Alternatively, you can perform this action from the JupyterLab  user interface. Standard notebooks are available within [JupyterLab](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/interacting-with-pulse-via-jupyterlab) â in particular the Data Loading Standard Notebook, which demonstrates how to successfully load data into Pulse through Feedzai's Data Science API.

## How toâ

To import a dataset into your Pulse application and create a [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources), execute the following steps:

  1. Ensure that the data file contains valid values of the [Pulse data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types).

  2. In the Data Science  tab, add  a new Data Source.

  3. Select the **URL Path** from where to import the data. The data file can either be stored locally, or in a Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS). Examples for the URL Path: `/opt/datasets/transactions.csv`, or `file:///opt/datasets/transactions.parquet`.

  4. In the **Advanced Options** , you can configure who has access to the Data Source.

  5. Check the **Data Source Preview** to see how your data will be imported.

CSV-only

For CSV files, you can adjust the **Includes Header** , **Delimiter** , **Quotes** , **Line Separator** and [**Missing Values**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#missing-values) fields to define how Pulse should interpret and import the raw data from your file.

The Parquet format is more strictly defined, so these manual adjustments are not required.

  6. Advance to the **Data Source Characterization** step, where you can review the **Type** and **Configuration** that Pulse assigned to the fields of the data source.

CSV-only

For CSV files, you can adjust the inferred characterization for the data fields. See the Inferred types and values for CSV files section for details.

Parquet files contain explicit type specifications, which are [mapped directly to Pulse types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types#mapping-of-data-types-from-parquet-files) and are not modifiable.

  7. Select **Create Data Source** to make your dataset available in Pulse.




### Inferred types and values for CSV filesâ

CSV files don't support indicating the type of each field, which is required information for the Pulse data science loop.

To accelerate the Data Source creation process, Pulse automatically looks at the first few thousand rows of your dataset file and infers what is the data type and possible values for each field.

For example, Pulse can suggest that:

  * A _Timestamp_ field should be of type _Timestamp_ , in milliseconds.
  * A _code_ field is _Categorical_ and the possible categories are A, B, and C.



caution

Pulse infers the values for _Categorical_ fields based on the observed occurrences in the first few thousand rows of your dataset. However, those rows might not contain all possible values. If there are other possible values, you must add them manually.

When importing a CSV file, you can verify the and change the data types for the fields, and configure  their possible values:

Learn more about [data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types).

## Fixing invalid instancesâ

When importing a certain dataset for the first time, usually there are records that can not be imported. These failed records or data rows are also called **[invalid instances](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources#invalid-instances)**. The Pulse UI shows the number of invalid instances only after you run a [Data Source analysis](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis), using the  button.

To get information about the invalid instances during this import, use the invalid instances button  to display the list of fields that had values which couldn't be imported.

Hover over the  icon to get more information about what is wrong with the data field values.

To fix invalid instances, after investigating their cause in the UI, you can combine the following two approaches:

  * Change the data: preprocess the dataset externally (e.g. using Python), to transform invalid values into valid ones. This approach helps when in the same data field, in different records there are different types or formats.
  * Change the schema: duplicate the data source, and change the data type, or the configuration of the data type. This can help if there is only a categorical value missing, or if you picked the wrong setting when defining a data type.



## Duplicating a Data Sourceâ

Since data schemas in Data Sources are [immutable](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources), if you need to make changes to a Data Source, you must create a new one. However, if you need to fix or adjust it without having to restart from scratch, you can duplicate an existing Data Source as follows:

  1. In the Data Science  tab, Duplicate and Change  an existing Data Source.
  2. Specify the path from where to import the data. The data file can either be stored locally, for example, `/opt/datascience/transactions.csv` or in HDFS.
  3. Preview how your data will be imported. The Delimiter, Quotes, Line Separator and Missing Values will be exactly the same as the original Data Source.
  4. Change the Data Source Characterization, namely editing the [**Type** and **Configuration**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) of any field.
  5. Create a new Data Source.



## Next stepsâ

Once you have your raw data configured in Pulse, follow up by making sure that your original dataset is correctly [converted into a valid data schema](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/validating-the-data-schema).

Once you have a Data Source, you can then start analyzing and transforming your data with [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) and building [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules).

# Validating the data schema

Was this page helpful?Â 

Your project's data schema often does not match the data schema you receive from the client. Pulse lets you convert each field in the raw data and define how it should be converted to match your project's data schema.

You must look into the data schema of the [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) containing your raw data, and define how to convert each field to a Data Source that makes sense in your Data Science project.

This task represents solving a common data quality issue, focusing on fixing the structure and formatting of your dataset. Similarly, the next task in this guide â[Cleaning up the data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/cleaning-up-the-data)â handles data quality from the perspective of the value and correctness of information contained in the dataset.

## How toâ

To convert the original dataset into the internal schema of your Data Science project, compose a [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) as follows. For example, to perform a direct conversion from a raw data field to an identical field with a different name:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab , add  a new Plan.
  2. Set the Plan to [Non-Deployable](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#non-deployable-plans).
  3. Design your schema validation Plan as displayed in the following image:
  4. Configure the elements as follows:
     1. Edit  the **Source** element and specify the **Origin Schema**. For example, select the _Transactions_ Data Source to copy and use its data schema in the Plan.
     2. Edit  the **Map** element to:
        1. Add a field and set the **Output Field Name** as the target name for the field in your project, for example, _TransactionAmount_. Set the name and type from the original raw data field as the **Expression** (for example, _trAmnt_) and **Type**. Confirm that you added the new field.
        2. Remove the original raw data field from the Data Source.
     3. Repeat step 4. b. to convert each data field, using the appropriate **Expression** and **Type** according to your schema validation requirements.
  5. Run the plan to execute all actions on the original Data Source and generate an improved one.
     1. Define the **Data Source with ID 1** as the original Data Source. For example, _Transactions_.

     2. Configure the **Data Sink with ID 3** as the new and validated Data Source. For example, _Validated Schema_.

     3. Use the  button to run the Plan and to generate a new Data Source in Pulse, named _Validated Schema_. Pulse also saves an output file with the transformed data to your filesystem.

  6. [Analyze](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data) the Validated Schema Data Source to confirm that the raw data was converted to the target schema for your Data Science project.



No mapping

When there is no mapping from the raw data to your target schema, you can use the Map operator in a Plan to add a new output field with an empty Expression. Run the Plan to fill in this field with the Missing Value you configured for the Sink.

## Next stepsâ

Once you have mapped the raw data to your project's schema, you may need to address quality issues and [clean up your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/cleaning-up-the-data).

# Analyzing and sampling your data

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse provides a toolset to help you in uncovering interesting data insights, which you can explore as features in your models. It also helps you in balancing your data to make it easier to manipulate and understand.

With Pulse you can perform the following operations over your data in your Data Science project:

  1. [Identifying patterns](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/identifying-patterns)  
Run statistical analyses on your data to reveal patterns and gain some initial insight on both the contents and quality of your dataset, without writing any code. Pulse generates histograms, minimum, maximum, median, count and percentiles over each specific data field of the dataset and allows you to further explore these analytics by breaking them down by other fields of the dataset.
  2. [Creating a stratified sample](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/creating-a-stratified-sample)  
Learn how to design a [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) to generate a stratified sample out of the original data and start your [Feature Engineering](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering) work from a stable and more balanced dataset.

On this page

# Creating a Sandbox Evaluation

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

By creating a Sandbox Evaluation, you will be able to test your Rule and Model projects as in a production environment. After setting up the rules and models you have specified, you will be able to test their performance over your [Data Sources](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) as if they were in Production, before deploying them.

You can evaluate your rules and models, therefore being able to identify potential problems before deploying them and predict the performance of your system.

## How toâ

To create a Sandbox Evaluation, execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Data Science** tab, â add a Sandbox Evaluation.

  2. Specify the **Data Source** , i.e. the data that will be tested in your Sandbox Evaluation. By choosing the **Partitioning Fields** , the Sandbox evaluates the performance of rules and models as it would do in workflows, once the solution is deployed. For example, select **Card** as a partition field: When the Sandbox Evaluation is created, all transactions from that card will have been processed together. Therefore, the node in charge of processing it will not have visibility of the transactions not associated to that card.

  3. If the resources you are configuring require time-based metrics, specify the field of the **Data Source** that is to be used as the timestamp field.

  4. Select the **Outcome Variable** , i.e. the ground truth: the value against which the evaluation will process its results.

  5. Choose the **Resources** and [Outcome Combinator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/outcome-combinator). You can select as resources the **Models** and **Rules projects** you have created, the **Resource Parent** being such project.

Reordering

Bear in mind that you can reorder the resources so that your sandbox evaluations simulate a workflow as close as possible to the one that will be later deployed in production. By reordering the resources, the Sandbox Evaluation will simulate exactly the order in which events are processed.

  6. Choose your **Reporting** configuration and create the evaluation. In this step, you will choose how the results of the evaluation will be presented. By selecting no **Additional Cost** and no **Breakdowns** , you will see all metrics in general. If you add an additional cost field, the system will collect all those metrics that are also weighed by a data source field (e.g. making rows with higher values of the field impact the metrics more).

  7. You can also choose **Breakdowns** to analyze metrics according to the possible values of a categorical field in the data source. Breakdowns allow users to understand the impact of Rules and Models as segmented by the particular values of the breakdown fields that are selected, similarly to rules and models evaluations.




## Next Stepsâ

After creating your Sandbox Evaluation, you will be able to [Evaluate your Sandbox Results](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/testing-your-work-in-a-sandbox-environment/evaluating-your-sandbox-results). When the evaluation of the results is satisfactory, you will be able to move on to the [deployment of your work into Production](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production).

Check also [how Pulse projects work](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/how-pulse-projects-work) for some background to understand what is involved at this stage.

On this page

# Evaluating your Sandbox Results

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

Evaluating your Sandbox results against a test dataset is crucial in understanding how it is performing, and how close you are to reaching the objectives of your Data Science project.

Now that you have learned how to [create a Sandbox Evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/testing-your-work-in-a-sandbox-environment/creating-a-sandbox-evaluation), you will need to generate a Sandbox Evaluation over a trained set of [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) and [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and analyze the evaluation results.

## How toâ

To analyze the **Sandbox Evaluation** results, execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Data Science tab** , select a **Sandbox Evaluation** from the **Sandbox Evaluations list.**

  2. Select an existing **Sandbox Evaluation**.




## Results by Scoreâ

The **Results by Score** focus on the field of the **Outcome Score** and the real final label. Based on that particular field, this allows you to understand the performance of your **Sandbox Evaluation**.

Therefore, you can understand how the system behaves independently of the outcome decision that was specified on the outcome decision field. For example, it will help you decide whether to change the score threshold for the final decision.

In the **Results by Score** tab, you can perform the following actions:

  1. Analyze the **ROC Curve** for the selected evaluation.

Exact values

Hover the mouse pointer over the plot line to inspect the exact values for the **Recall** and **FPR** metrics and the respective **Threshold**.

Cost-based Metrics

If you define a **Cost Field** , then the **ROC Curve** will also plot the values for _Cost-Recall_ vs. _Cost-FPR_.

  2. Configure the **X/Y Plot** to display a curve for any **X-Axis** and **Y-Axis**.

Exact values

Hover the mouse pointer over the plot line to inspect the exact values for the **X-Axis** and **Y-Axis** metrics and the respective **Threshold**.

  3. During the creation of a **Sandbox Evaluation,** you can select the breakdown for the metrics. Therefore, here you can see all the values for the metrics of the segmentation and its combinations. You can also change the threshold.

  4. Use the **View ROC curve** option to see which of the breakdown metrics can be seen in the ROC curve.

  5. You can also see the metrics per service for all the resources the **Sandbox Evaluation** has. This is useful for understanding the performance computation times of the resources analyzed in the sandbox. It helps you to grasp the performance gains or losses you will experience in your live Workflow and evaluate the tradeoffs. For instance, you can identify whether a Rules project takes too long (in the **Ind. Avg.**) whilst not adding much to the performance (by analyzing **Recall** and **FPR** metrics), therefore allowing you to consider whether to keep it.

  6. Export the results to a CSV file, if desired.




## Results by Outcomeâ

By analyzing the **Results by Outcome** , you can understand how the system behaves regarding the outcome decision that was specified on the outcome decision field. It works similarly to the **Results by Score** , but it does not provide a movable threshold. You can learn more about the performance of your Sandbox evaluation by analyzing these results:

  1. Select the outcome values to be shown either if `True` or `False`.
  2. You can export the results to a CSV, both **Per Breakdown** and **Per Services**



### Configurationâ

In the **Configuration tab,** you can see all the information regarding the **Sandbox Evaluation** you are seeing.

It contains all the information chosen in the creation of the Evaluation:

  * Data Source
  * Segments
  * Resources to Analyze
  * [Outcome Combinator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/outcome-combinator)
  * Additional Cost Field
  * Output Result Name and Directory Path
  * Time when the last update was made and who made it



## Learn Moreâ

You can learn more about the different concepts related to Sandbox Evaluations in the following pages:

  * [Outcome Combinators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/outcome-combinator): Learn more about what they are and what purposes do they serve.
  * [Sandbox Evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/sandbox-evaluations): Have a complete grasp on how Sandbox Evaluations are useful and all the details they comprise.
  * [Evaluating a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model): Learn more about different ways of testing your system by evaluating models.

# Creating a Job Profile

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse allows you to create [job profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles) that can be used to apply a set of property configurations when running jobs. This page describes how to create a job profile.

## How toâ

To create a new job profile, access your application and execute the following actions:

  1. Select the Jobs  tab to have access to the **Job Configuration Profiles** list.

tip

By default, the **Jobs** tab is collapsed under the **Advanced Tabs**. Use the  button to extend this section.

  2. Select the  button to configure a new job profile.

New Job Configuration Profile wizard

When you create a new job profile, the Spark properties that are displayed in the default profile (Pulse Properties Profile or PPP) are automatically copied to this new profile as a base configuration. You can edit these properties and add new ones. However, you cannot delete base properties using the Pulse UI. I f you want to eliminate base properties, you must delete them directly from the pre-configured source (_e.g._ the _pulse.properties_ file). By doing so, the changes are propagated to all the job profiles.

  3. Add a **Name** for the new job profile.

  4. To add new Spark properties:

     1. Insert the name of the Spark property in the **Key** column.

     2. Insert the **value** or encrypted value of the Spark property.

     3. Select the  button.

  5. To edit the value of a property:

     1. Locate the Spark property that you want to change.

     2. Press the current value of the property.

     3. Add a new value or encrypted value and select the  button to save the changes.

Editing spark properties

The values of the base properties are shown in light grey text. The value of new properties and the ones that were edited are shown in black text. You can revert  the edited value of a base property to the one that is defined in the PPP. You can delete  a non-base property from the list.

caution

The gray properties displayed in the job profile table are default properties used for data science jobs. Therefore do not use these properties as a reference for Scheduled Metric Jobs.




## Next stepsâ

Now that you know how to create job profiles, learn how to [select profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles) to be used in the data science tasks that are executed by Spark jobs.
