# Editing properties on demand

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse allows you to configure Spark properties on demand, while setting up a Data Science resource (e.g. Model Execution, Hyperparameter Tuning) that is executed in a distributed way. This gives you full control over the configuration of the [Spark job](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/jobs-and-job-profiles) that performs the calculations for that specific resource.

Valid only for a single Job Execution

The properties that you define on demand are valid only for this single Job Execution. In other words, Pulse does not save the changed values to any Job Profile.

To configure properties on demand, perform the following actions:

  1. While setting up a Data Science resource, in the **Advanced Options** select the **Job Profile** that you want to start with. Check [Selecting a profile on demand](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles#selecting-or-editing-a-profile-on-demand) to learn more about this action.

  2. Use the  button to load the properties of the selected profile for editing. As an example, the image below shows the editing menu for the task [Data Source Analysis](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis):

  3. To add new Spark properties:

     1. Insert the name of the Spark property in the column Key.
     2. Insert the value or encrypted value of the Spark property.
     3. Select the button .
  4. To edit the value of a property:

     1. Locate the Spark property that you want to change.
     2. Select the current value of the property.
     3. Type a new value or encrypted value and  **Save the Changes**.
  5. Finish creating the resource that you are configuring. In the previous example, select the **Analyse** button to save the Data Source Analysis. It starts the Spark job that executes the necessary computational tasks using the settings you selected in the previous steps.




## Next stepsâ

Now that you have configured all aspects related to Job Profiles, you can start [processing your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data) efficiently by taking advantage of the optimized profiles that you have created.

# Selecting profiles

Was this page helpful?Â 

Pulse allows you to choose the profile that is more suitable for the Spark job that you want to run using the options below:

  * **Setting the default profile for the application** : allows you to set a profile that is used by default every time that you create any Data Science resource. You can look at this option as a global setting for the whole application.
  * Setting a default profile for a Job type: allows you to associate a profile to a Pulse resource (e.g. [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance)). This option prevails over the application default.
  * **Selecting a profile/editing properties on demand, for a specific job** : allows you to choose a profile or edit properties directly when creating a specific Pulse resource. This option prevails over the other two, but only for the current resource that you are creating.



## Setting a profile as default for the Appâ

To set a profile as default for the whole application, perform the following steps:

  1. Select the **Jobs** tab to have access to the **Job Configuration Profile** list:

tip

By default, the **Jobs** tab is collapsed under the **Advanced Tabs** , and you need to use the  button to reach it.

  2. Locate the target profile that you want to choose as default, and select the **Star** button.




## Setting a profile as default for a Job typeâ

Preference over by default option

The option defining a profile by **Job type** prevails over the option Defining a profile by default.

To associate a profile to a **Job type,** access your application and execute the following actions:

  1. Select the **Jobs** tab to have access to the **Job Configuration Profile** table.

  2. Select the  button to have access to a list of **Resource Type** and **Job Profiles**.

  3. For each **Resource Type** choose a target **Job Profile**.

  4. Use the  button to save your configurations.




## Selecting or editing a profile on demandâ

Editing properties on demand

In addition to the selection on demand you can **edit the properties** on a selected profile for this Job Execution. Check the page [Editing properties on demand](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/editing-properties-on-demand) to learn more about this option.

To choose a profile, access your application and execute the following actions:

  1. In the task that you are setting up expand the Advanced Options using the  button. As an example, the following image shows the **Advanced Options** menu when you create a Data Source Analysis:

  2. Select the Job Profile that you want to use to execute this task.

tip

You can open the profiles in separate windows to take a look at the properties by using the  button. This option also allows you to edit the properties in the **Job Profiles** , except for the "Pulse Properties Profile" (PPP), which is profile read-only.




## Next stepsâ

Check the page [Editing properties on demand](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/editing-properties-on-demand) to learn how to edit the properties in a **Job Profile** while setting up a Data Science task.

On this page

# Adding custom services

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

**Custom Services** implement custom logic which you can add to your runtime [Workflows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows). Other than Input Adapters you can use other **Custom Services** that react to messages as they are processed in the **Workflow**. For example, **Action Listeners** , merging decisions from different [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models), implementing caching, processing events to be displayed in dashboards, etc.

Depending on what the **Custom Service** is designed for, it may be connected in the data flow together with out-of-the-box services such as **Plan** , **Scoring** , and **Rules** , or just as a disconnected element that adds extra logic without affecting the flow of events.

## How Toâ

To add and configure a **Custom Workflow Element** to your **Workflow** , for example, to process events immediately before reaching the end of the **Workflow** :

  1. In the  **Workflows** tab, select an existing **Workflow**.

  2. Drag a new **Custom Workflow Element** to the **Diagram** canvas.

  3. â Edit the **Custom Workflow Element**.

  4. In the **Main** tab:

     1. Select the **Custom Service** you want to apply in your **Workflow**.
     2. If the **Custom Service** has been developed to contribute to a [Workflow Outcome](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes), select an **Outcome**. After being processed at a **Custom Workflow Element** , the _< outcome_name>_ and _<outcome_name>_score_ fields in the event schema will reflect the processing.
  5. In the **Schemas** **tab,** if the **Custom Service** operates over the data itself:

     1. Confirm that the **Service Input** and **Service Output** are consistent with the data you expect for the **Custom Service**.
     2. Make sure the **Service Input** and **Service Output** are correctly mapped from the **Event Schema** , for each real-time event moving along the **Workflow**.
  6. In the **Properties** tab, set the values for each property to define the service configuration in your **Workflow**. Properties and default values depend on how the **Custom Service** is developed.

  7. â **Connect** the previous service in the **Workflow** to the **Custom Workflow Element** , if it is part of the data flow. For example, if you implement an **Action Listener** in a **Custom Service** , you just need to add it to the **Diagram** canvas, without having to  **Connect** it.




### Solving schema conflictsâ

If Pulse invalidates your [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#conflicts) due to schema mapping conflicts in a Workflow Service, you must solve them as follows:

  1. â Edit the **Service**.
  2. Select the **Schemas** tab.
  3. Look for a count of **Input Conflicts** and **Output Conflicts** above 0.
  4. Select each **Conflict** filter to see which fields could not be mapped. Alternatively, select the **Service** filter and locate the conflict fields in the **Event Schema**. These are marked as _Missing Input_ or _Missing Output_.
  5. If the **Event Schema** contains a field that you can map to the **Service Input** or **Output** , manually enter the name of that field.



The following images display schema conflicts during resolution:

Conflicts count

Note that Pulse will still display the original conflicts count even after you have solved them.

Removed fields

If a **Plan** you configured for a **Plan Service** removes fields from the workflow schema, then you must ensure that subsequent services in the **Workflow** do not require those fields. Otherwise, Pulse will generate schema conflicts, invalidate your **Workflow** , and you will have no available fields to map from.

In these cases, you should redesign your **Plan** , articulate it with the remaining Data Science work to be used in runtime, and redeploy it to your **Workflow**.

## Next Stepsâ

Proceed with the designing of your Workflow by adding, configuring and connecting other services. Check the following pages:

  * [Adding input adapters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-input-adapters)
  * [Adding plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-plans)
  * [Adding models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models)
  * [Adding rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules)

On this page

# Adding input adapters

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

**Input adapters** are the [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows) element that allow your application to know how to consume data from an external source.

Your **Workflow** can consume data from different sources, such as CSV files, REST APIs, sockets reading ISO8583-formatted messages, etc. Thus, for each data input in your project, your **Workflow** needs a different **Input adapter**.

Adding **Input adapters** is the first step in designing your **Workflow**.

## How toâ

To add and configure an Input adapter to your [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows), execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Workflows** tab, select an existing **Workflow**.

  2. Drag a new **Input Adapter Service** to the **Diagram** canvas.

  3. â **Edit** the **Input Adapter Service**.

  4. In the **Main tab** , select which [Custom Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#custom-services) implements the functionality for your **Input Adapter**. Pulse includes an embedded **Synthetic Generator** that acts as a test input Custom Service, and periodically injects dummy data into your **Workflow,** according to its **Schema**.

  5. In the **Schemas tab** , confirm that the **Service Output** is consistent with the data you expect for your project.

Extra fields

Note that the **Service Output** contains more fields that the **Schema** you specified for the **Workflow**. Pulse automatically adds a _timestamp_ and UUID fields to the event schema.

Additionally, for each [configured Outcome](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) Pulse adds the boolean _< outcome_name>_ and _<outcome_name>_score_ fields.

  6. In the **Properties** tab, set the values for each property to define the service configuration in your **Workflow**. Properties and default values are defined at the **Custom Service** that implements your **Input Adapter**.




## Next Stepsâ

Proceed with the designing of your Workflow by adding, configuring and connecting other services. Check the following pages:

# Adding models

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

Similarly to [Workflow Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-plans), Pulse lets you take the **Model** definition that yielded the best results during the Data Science stage directly into Production without significant effort.

Once you obtain a [Model Evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) that shows that your **Model** configuration has reached or surpassed business objectives, you can simply apply it in runtime.

The **Scoring Service** in a **Workflow** runs events through the Machine Learning algorithm, by default Feedzai Random Forest (FZRF), with the exact same parameter configuration as tested during the Data Science stage.

## How toâ

To add and configure a [Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) to score events in your **Workflow** , execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Workflows** tab, select an existing **Workflow**.
  2. Drag a new **Scoring Service** to the **Diagram** canvas.
  3. â **Edit** the **Scoring Service**.
  4. In the **Main** tab:
     1. Define to which of the [Workflow Outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) the **Model** will contribute. After being processed by a **Scoring Service** , the _< outcome_name>_ and _<outcome_name>_score_ fields in the event schema will reflect the **Model** decision.

     2. Select the **Model** you want to apply in your runtime processing.

     3. Optionally, define a **Filter** to narrow down events that are scored in your **Workflow**. Filter conditions are written in PulseQL.

Fields used in Filter

You can only use fields in the **Filter** which were present in the [data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) you used to train the **Model**.

     4. Define how much **Weight** the **Model** results will have in the final decision, when the event arrives at the end of the **Workflow**. For example, you can have real-time events flowing through different **Scoring Services** and [Rules Services](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules). These scores need to be combined to produce a final score for the event.

     5. White-Box Explanations that were added with the new model in a first instance (see section **Training parameters** in [Training a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model) ) are then visible in the **Scoring Service** and automatically used.

Migrating old White-Box Explanations

After upgrading your Pulse version to **Pulse 20.1** ,

you may need to reconfigure the old WBE. This is in case you enabled the old **Feedzai Random Forest Feature Contribution** , which only generated contribution numbers and could not work with natural language sentences. To do so, **Edit** the **Scoring Service** and follow the instructions in the UI.

Furthermore, if you were using the old **Feature Contribution** for **Model Explanations** , then you were most likely using a Custom extended **Alert Storage Service**. In that case, please check **Case Manager 8.1** release notes for more information as you no longer need to do that.

Explanations on critical path

**True** â Explanations are calculated in the **Scoring element** and put in the event.

**False** â Explanations are only calculated in the **Dead Letter** (i.e. at the end of the workflow).

  5. In the **Schemas tab** :
     1. Confirm that the **Service Input** and **Service Output** are consistent with the data you expect for the **Model**.
     2. Make sure the **Service Input** and **Service Output** are correctly mapped from the **Event Schema** , for each real-time event moving along the **Workflow**.
  6. â **Connect** the previous service in the **Workflow** to the Scoring Service.



### Solving schema conflictsâ

If Pulse invalidates your [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#conflicts) due to schema mapping conflicts in a Workflow Service, you must solve them as follows:

  1. â Edit the **Service**.
  2. Select the **Schemas** tab.
  3. Look for a count of **Input Conflicts** and **Output Conflicts** above 0.
  4. Select each **Conflict** filter to see which fields could not be mapped. Alternatively, select the **Service** filter and locate the conflict fields in the **Event Schema**. These are marked as _Missing Input_ or _Missing Output_.
  5. If the **Event Schema** contains a field that you can map to the **Service Input** or **Output** , manually enter the name of that field.



The following images display schema conflicts during resolution:

Conflicts count

Note that Pulse will still display the original conflicts count even after you have solved them.

Removed fields

If a **Plan** you configured for a **Plan Service** removes fields from the workflow schema, then you must ensure that subsequent services in the **Workflow** do not require those fields. Otherwise, Pulse will generate schema conflicts, invalidate your **Workflow** , and you will have no available fields to map from.

In these cases, you should redesign your **Plan** , articulate it with the remaining Data Science work to be used in runtime, and redeploy it to your **Workflow**.

# Adding plans

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

One of the great advantages of Pulse is to make the deployment of Data Science work into runtime seamless and without any significant effort. **Workflow Plans** are the direct translation of deployable [Data Science Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) as runtime services.

**Workflow Plans** thus allow you to process live data and generate features exactly the same way as during the Data Science stage of the project.

Once a deployable **Data Science Plan** , for example, a features plan, is tested and ready to deploy to Production, Pulse creates an execution. A **Plan Execution** represents a snapshot of the **Plan** and all of its configurations at the time it ran, making it available for runtime.

## How toâ

To add and configure a **Plan** to your **Workflow** , for example, to calculate features on live data, execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Workflows** tab, select an existing **Workflow**.
  2. Drag a new **Plan Service** to the **Diagram** canvas.
  3. â Edit the **Plan**.
  4. In the **Main** tab:
     1. Select the [Data Science Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) you want to apply in your runtime processing. Only **Deployable Plans** are available.
     2. Select the **Plan Execution** to carry the input and output schemas of the **Plan** , as defined during Data Science stage, into your workflow.
  5. In the **Schemas** tab:
     1. Confirm that the **Service Input** and **Service Output** are consistent with the data you expect for the **Plan**.
     2. Make sure the **Service Input** and **Service Output** are correctly mapped from the **Event Schema** , for each real-time event moving along the **Workflow**.
  6. In the **Properties** tab, set the values for each property to define the service configuration in your **Workflow**. Properties and default values are defined by Pulse.
  7. â **Connect** the previous service in the **Workflow** to the **Plan**.



### Solving schema conflictsâ

If Pulse invalidates your [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#conflicts) due to schema mapping conflicts in a Workflow Service, you must solve them as follows:

  1. â Edit the **Service**.
  2. Select the **Schemas** tab.
  3. Look for a count of **Input Conflicts** and **Output Conflicts** above 0.
  4. Select each **Conflict** filter to see which fields could not be mapped. Alternatively, select the **Service** filter and locate the conflict fields in the **Event Schema**. These are marked as _Missing Input_ or _Missing Output_.
  5. If the **Event Schema** contains a field that you can map to the **Service Input** or **Output** , manually enter the name of that field.



The following images display schema conflicts during resolution:

Conflicts count

Note that Pulse will still display the original conflicts count even after you have solved them.

Removed fields

If a **Plan** you configured for a **Plan Service** removes fields from the workflow schema, then you must ensure that subsequent services in the **Workflow** do not require those fields. Otherwise, Pulse will generate schema conflicts, invalidate your **Workflow** , and you will have no available fields to map from.

In these cases, you should redesign your **Plan** , articulate it with the remaining Data Science work to be used in runtime, and redeploy it to your **Workflow**.

### Addressing errors in plan definitionâ

When defining the components of a **Plan** , you may encounter errors that would result in failures during the [plan execution](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#plan-execution).

Some of those errors are detectable when defining the Plan, and Pulse will show warnings to allow them to be fixed before deploying the plan to production.

One such error is defining [fields](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#field) based on a [PQL expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features) (e.g. within a [`Metrics` or `Map` operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference)). Operators that require null coalescing (i.e. [default fallback values](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#fallback-value)) will produce a warning in the UI if the coalescing operator (`??`) and value are missing:

To fix this situation, provide a fallback value in the PQL expression input field, e.g. `?? 0` or `?? ""`.

A similar warning will be shown if built-in functions are used in collections (like `List`s, `Set`s or `Map`s). For example, an expression like
    
    
    ["test", "test1", "test2"].contains("testing")  
    

will fail because the `contains` function is not supported in collections used in the PQL fields of Map Operators or Metric Operators.

Attempting to use such functions in that context will result in a warning in the UI:

The alternative is to use [UDFs (User Defined Functions)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions), e.g.:
    
    
    com.feedzai.pulse.pkernel.runtime.CollectionUDF.contains(["test", "test1", "test2"], "testing")  
    

Besides these preventive warnings, Pulse will also allow recovering from execution errors that are not detectable at design time. Refer to [Automatic Application Repair](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/automatic-application-repair) and [Workflow recovery](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#workflow-recovery) for more information on how to recover from execution errors.

# Adding rules

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

**Rules** add an extra layer of scoring and decision-making to your project in runtime. Just like [Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models), **Rules** contribute to the classification of events moving along the **Workflow** and to the final [Workflow outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes).

Once you reach a [Rules Evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/evaluating-rules-using-a-snapshot) that shows that your **Rules** block has reached or surpassed business objectives, you can simply configure the same block of Rules to run within a service in runtime.

You can deploy blocks of [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) in a runtime **Workflow** by adding **Rules Services**. Typically, you can deploy different **Rules Services** both for detection, for example, blacklisting users, and for a decision, for example weighing in on the final score.

## How toâ

To add and configure a block of [Rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) to score events in your **Workflow** , execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Workflows** tab, select an existing **Workflow**.

  2. Drag a new **Rules Service** to the **Diagram** canvas.

Rules Services

When selecting Rules Services in workflows, a snapshot is automatically generated and selected in the configuration dialog. You cannot select any other snapshot than the automatically-generated one.

  3. â **Edit** the **Rules Service**.

  4. In the **Main** tab:

     1. Define to which of the [Workflow Outcomes](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/configuring-outcomes) the **Rules** will contribute. After being processed by a **Rules Service** , the _< outcome_name>_ and _< outcome_name>_score_ fields in the event schema will reflect the **Rules** decision.

     2. Select the **Rules Project** that contains the block of **Rules** you want to apply in your runtime processing. The **Rules Project** also defines the input schema for the **Rules Service** as defined at the Data Science stage.

Self-Service Rules

All usage of self-services interface is performed through a Rules Workflow Element.

When adding a [Self-Service Rules project](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-a-self-service-rules-project), a snapshot is automatically created and assigned. The latest snapshot is built adding changes on top of the one published before it (as reflected in the Publishing section). Older snapshots are kept and can be changed via API to allow a more sophisticated and greater control over the system. This allows you to easily look up the history of the published rules and roll back, if needed.

Self-Service Rules in a Multi-Tenancy scenario

In order to have a workflow ready for Self-Service Rules in a Multi-Tenanted scenario, you should add two rule elements:

        * One pointing to a Global Simple rules projects
        * One pointing to a By-tenant Simple rules project.

     3. Select the **Rules Snapshot** to specify which **Rules** to execute in the **Rules Service**. The **Rules Snapshot** carries the **Rules** , their order of execution and individual contribution to outcomes and scores, as defined and evaluated during the Data Science stage.

Multi-Tenancy Solution

If the Workflow is being configured with a [Rules Project](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-or-updating-the-rules-project) of the type Multi-Tenancy,  the **Rules Snapshot** has information related to the **Rules** that are going to be applied to each Tenant.

     4. Configure whether **Workflow** generates **Explanations** as to why the **Rules** triggered.

Explanations on critical path

If you choose to compute **Explanations** on the **Critical Path** , they will immediately be accessible to be processed in **Custom Service,** once they are generated.

  5. In the **Schemas** **tab** :

     1. Confirm that the **Service Input** and **Service Output** are consistent with the data you expect for the **Rules**.
     2. Make sure the **Service Input** and **Service Output** are correctly mapped from the **Event Schema** , for each real-time event moving along the **Workflow**.
  6. In the **Properties** tab, set the values for each property to define the service configuration in your **Workflow**. Properties and default values are defined by Pulse.

  7. â Connect the previous service in the Workflow to the Rules Service. You can also learn [to organize your work with blocks](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/operations-guide/app-collaboration-loop/how-to-organize-your) in order to do this in a most efficient way.




### Solving schema conflictsâ

If Pulse invalidates your [Workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#conflicts) due to schema mapping conflicts in a Workflow Service, you must solve them as follows:

  1. â Edit the **Service**.
  2. Select the **Schemas** tab.
  3. Look for a count of **Input Conflicts** and **Output Conflicts** above 0.
  4. Select each **Conflict** filter to see which fields could not be mapped. Alternatively, select the **Service** filter and locate the conflict fields in the **Event Schema**. These are marked as _Missing Input_ or _Missing Output_.
  5. If the **Event Schema** contains a field that you can map to the **Service Input** or **Output** , manually enter the name of that field.

Conflicts count

Otherwise, Pulse will generate schema conflicts, invalidate your **Workflow** , and you will have no available fields to map from.

# Advanced workflow configurations

Was this page helpful?Â 

The following section explains the various configurations that you can set in the Advanced tab of a specific workflow (as seen in the following image):

## Action parametersâ

Each action can have its own parameters. Parameters allow passing event specific information when an action is triggered.

One example would be for a "sendEmail" action to have the parameters "to" and "title" with values "[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#4429252d2804213c25293428216a272b29)" and "Rule Alert".

In the **Workflow** **Advanced** **tab** , it is possible to define which parameters each action has (by default has none) in the configure action dialog (accessible by clicking the config button on the action).

When defining parameters it is possible to choose their name, type and if its value is required or optional.

Parameters can have simple types like _String_ or _Number_ or more complex ones like:

  * **Dimension** , restrict the set of possible values of the parameter to a Dimension's items.
  * **List** , the value of the parameter will be a list (not a list item). This can be useful to reference, for example, card blacklists.
  * **RDL Variable** , when configuring the value of the parameter it will be possible to choose from the list of RDL variables available within the rule. When the action is triggered the parameter will have the value of that variable.



Currently, actions can only be triggered directly by [rules](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/rules) where it is possible to specify the value that each action parameter will have when the action is triggered. This can be done by clicking the config button available on the action that has more than one parameter.

## Action listenersâ

When configuring action listeners, the list of available listeners is populated from the existing services. For a service to be listed either:

  * The service is a part of a workflow
  * The service is part of the overall application environment and implements a `com.feedzai.pulse.api.apps.model.rte.workflow.action.WorkflowActionHandler` interface from the _com.feedzai.pulse :pulse-api_ module



## Event Storage configurationâ

This option allows to define whether an Event Storage is created for the workflow. The recommendation is to enable this as it is a requirement for most workflows (it is necessary for Workflow recovery, Scheduled Metrics Jobs as well as feedback updates).

## Workflow recovery configurationâ

This allows to define whether Workflow recovery is enabled. Most workflows should enable it and define the recovery period to be the same as the largest real-time metric (typically 24h or less).

When recovery is enabled, you must also provide the recovery time configuration in the _Interval_ field, which will correspond to the time frame we would like to replay events from. Currently, two functions can be used to determine the interval of the data that is going to be recovered: **sinceLast** and **last**.

The** sinceLast** function will recover all events since the specified last point in time. The **last** function will recover all events from the specified past point in time to the last timestamp in the event storage.

The syntax for these functions is the following:

  * `sinceLast-HHhMMm`

    * HH - The hours in 24-hour mode (0-23). This field is **optional**.
    * MM - The minutes (0-59). This field is **mandatory**.
  * `last-HHhMMm`

    * HH - The hours. We are not restricted by the values 0-23. This field is **optional**.
    * MM - The minutes. We are not restricted by the values 0-59. This field is **mandatory**.



Below are some examples of recovery configurations:

  * **last-30m** \- With this configuration, if the last event in the event storage is at 16h30, it will recover events from 16h00. If the last event is at 00h10, it will recover events since 23h40 from the previous day. In order words, it always recovers the last 30 minutes counting back from the time of the last event in the event storage.
  * **last-48h0m** \- Recovers the last two days of events.
  * **sinceLast-23h30m** \- Using this configuration, if the last event is at 23h31, it will recover events from 23h30 in the present day (in this case 1 minute). If the last event is at 22h00, then it will recover events since 23h30 from the previous day, i.e. the last 22 hours and 30 minutes.



The default value is _last-30m_.

### Advanced properties: Checkpoint-based workflow recoveryâ

In a production environment, Pulse can be configured to store the necessary events for real-time metrics calculation on disk. In this case, Pulse creates **checkpoints** , i.e. regular snapshots about the events and the state of the metrics. After a server failure, Pulse can reload the last checkpoint and recover the metrics status starting from there. This saves time when the server needs to be restarted. However, it takes toll on the metrics calculation speed, as Pulse puts metrics calculation on hold while creating a checkpoint. Hence, this setting needs to be carefully tested.

Limitations

Note that this feature is in continuous development, and as of now it does not provide full feature parity to the previous, RAM-based version.

Additionally, if this feature is enabled, do not edit or remove existing metrics. Edited metrics are not recoverable after a server failure, meaning that those metrics will only take new events into consideration after any server restart.

## Partition Keysâ

Allows to configure the partitioning keys for scaling horizontally the workflow processing across Pulse replicas.

## Other propertiesâ

We also allow to add arbitrary key/value properties to the workflow advanced configuration. The possible properties that are considered here are the ones under the _advanced_ portion in Workflow Manager Service Configuration.

info

We recommend using Pulse properties

to manage those rather than defining them in the workflow, as doing so makes the properties bound to the application metadata when most of those properties are environment-specific (i.e., they can change from production to development).

### Workflow slugâ

The only property that must be configured in the workflow advanced properties is the workflow slug. This allows to then define different Workflow Manager Service Configuration  properties for different workflows (with various slugs) across the same application scoped prefix pulse property.

You can do so by setting the key to _workflowSlug_ and the value to the intended slug. Then use that slug where mentioned in the Workflow Manager page.

# Configuring outcomes

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

Before modeling your **Workflow** you must define what decisions it will produce as output. Outcomes represent those decisions, for example fraud/not fraud.

Pulse adds each outcome decision field (e.g _fraud_) and outcome score field (e.g. _fraud_score)_ to the schema of events moving along the workflow. As you add elements such as [Scoring Services](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-models) and [Rules Services](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-rules), you must also configure how they affect these fields, i.e. how they contribute to each of the final decisions and scores of the **Workflow**.

## How toâ

To define the outcomes of your workflow execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Workflows** tab, select an existing **Workflow**.

  2. the workflow's outcomes. Add a new outcome, and select if it is the outcome of a multi-classification problem or a binary classification.

Multiple outcomes

In the same **Workflow** you can have multiple outcomes to fine-grain the decision and perform classification in complex cases. Adding a second outcome, for example _fraud_type,_ would allow you to harvest more information in case the transaction is fraudulent.

  3. In case of a multi-classification problem, type the possible values separated by a comma.

  4. Select the default value for the outcome.

  5. Add another outcome, or **Save** the workflow outcome definition.




## Next Stepsâ

You have now finished performing the initial configurations required for your workflow. Proceed by adding elements to design the workflow. Check the following pages:

  * [Adding input adapters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/deploying-a-project-into-production/designing-a-workflow/adding-input-adapters)

# Workflow services properties

Was this page helpful?Â 

It is possible to specify the configuration properties of any [Workflow Service](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#workflow-elements) (**Input Adapter** , **Plan** , **Scoring** , **Rules** and **Custom**) in several ways. Any configuration property has the following components:

  * **Identifier** : All **Workflow Services** have this property (which is `empty` by default). You can assign the same properties to a group of **Workflow Services** that share the same **Identifier** value.
  * **Property Base** : All **Workflow Services** have this immutable attribute that defines which is the type of service. For example, a **Plan Workflow Service** has a property base of `services.rte.workflow` whereas **Input Adapters** and **Custom Workflow Elements** have a different **Property Base** depending on how the underlying Custom Service was configured:
    * **Synthetic Generator:** Has the property base `services.rte.workflow.syntheticgenerator`.
    * **Custom Services:** Specified using the `@PropertyBase("services.modules.mycustomservice")` annotation in your service's `Configurator` class.

# Using Cross-channel Metrics

Was this page helpful?Â 

caution

Cross-channel metrics are only supported when using the [Railgun Engine](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine).

Pulse supports [Cross-channel metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#cross-channel-metrics), when using [Railgun](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine), and the following section explains how to create these type of metrics, in which only one Pulse application workflow calculates the metric and another workflow can fetch and use the metric value without contributing to it.

If your Risk Strategy needs to use some of these metrics, follow the guidelines below to know how to create them in Pulse.

Assuming that the **secondary workflow** already exists, then, to create some **Cross-channel** metrics via Pulse UI, it's necessary to do the following:

  * Create a **schema** for the **Primary workflow** :

    * Since this is the main schema, it doesn't need to have any fields that the **Cross-channel** metric might use.
  * Create an **Omnichannel plan** :

    * Since **Cross-channel** metrics is just a subset of **Omnichannel** metrics, the type of the plan should be set as **Omnichannel**.

Make sure to tick the **Omnichannel** as enabled, and configure both schemas properly.

  * Create a **Cross-channel** metric:

    * Now, when adding a new metric to this **Omnichannel** plan, it will ask to configure both channels.

Note that the fields used by the metric will only be the ones in the secondary channel.

  * Then, when saving the **Cross-channel** metric:

    * The metric called `mainfielda_avg_1h` is a **Cross-channel** metric, meaning that only events from the **secondary workflow** (that use the `secondary_schema` schema) can contribute to the metric, and the saved plan can also use it's value.
  * Now, save the **plan** and create a **snapshot**.

  * Finally, you can create/edit the **primary workflow** to use the **Omnichannel plan** with the **Cross-channel** metric.

# Using Lookup Metrics

Was this page helpful?Â 

Availability of Lookup Metrics

The `Lookup By` operator is only available when using the [Railgun engine](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine), and when explicitly enabled via configuration. To activate this functionality, reach out to the Feedzai Customer Success (CS) team.

[Lookup By metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#lookup-by) provide a powerful extension to standard Group By metrics, by allowing users to choose which group's aggregation to retrieve for an event, based on fields other than the groupBy fields.

This page describes how to create a Lookup By metric in Pulse, and provides a practical example of how to combine it with standard Group By metrics to calculate new [derived fields](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#features).

## Creating Lookup By Metricsâ

To create a Lookup By metric in Pulse, follow these steps:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open the features plan.

  2. Drag a  operator to the plan if there is none yet.

  3. Edit  the Metrics operator:

  4. Select the  button to add a new metric to the Metrics operator.

  5. Select the **Group By** fields over which to calculate aggregated metrics. For example, _receiver_ID_ :

  6. Select the  button to activate the **Lookup By** input field.

  7. Select the appropriate look-up fields from the available options. For example, _sender_ID_ :

warning

The lookup fields must be in the same number and of the same data type as the group by fields, and arranged in the same order.

  8. Define the remaining sections (Window, Aggregation, Description) as needed, according to the regular process for [Creating Metric](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics).

  9. Save the Metrics operator with look-up configuration.

  10. Save the Plan with new metrics.




## Combining Lookup By with Group By Metricsâ

Lookup By metrics are often useful when combined with standard Group By metrics. To do so, add both types of metrics to the same Metrics operator, and combine them with a [Map operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#map).

The following example demonstrates how to set up such a combination of metrics for the use case of calculating an accountâs recent running balance at each transaction. It assumes that the input data stream contains at least the fields `sender_ID`, `receiver_ID`, and `amount` (in addition to the obligatory [timestamp](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#timestamp)).

  1. Create (if necessary) a **Metrics** operator as described above, and  edit it.

  2. Select the  button and add the first metric to the Metrics operator. This will be a regular **Group By** metric, to get the total amount sent by the transaction's sender.

     1. In the **Group By** section, select the _sender_ID_ field.
     2. In the **Window** section, set the window to _7 days_.
     3. In the **Aggregation** section, select the _sum_ function over the _amount_ field.
     4. Set the **Name** of the metric to _total_sent_1w_.
  3. Select the  button and add the second metric to the Metrics operator. This will be a **Lookup By** metric, to get the total amount received by the transaction's sender.

     1. In the **Group By** section, select the _receiver_ID_ field; activate the Lookup By input area as described above, and add the _sender_ID_ field to it.
     2. In the **Window** section, set the window to _7 days_.
     3. In the **Aggregation** section, select the _sum_ function over the _amount_ field.
     4. Set the **Name** of the metric to _total_received_1w_.
  4. Review the **Metrics** operator with the two metrics. Confirm that the grouping and lookup fields are correctly set for each metric by hovering over the ð paperclip icon next to each field in the **Group By** column.

Then,  the Metrics operator.

  5. Add a **Map** operator to the plan by dragging the  button to the plan's diagram, after the Metrics operator.

  6. Edit  the Map operator. In the **Fields To Add** tab, create a new field as follows:

     1. Set the **Output Field Name** to _balance_1w_ ,
     2. Set the **Expression** to `total_received_1w` \- `total_sent_1w`.
     3. Leave the **Type** as the default _Numeric_.

Finally,  the Map operator.




By completing these steps, the plan will now add the _balance_1w_ field to each event, representing the account's running balance over the past week at the time of the transaction.

# Conditional Expressions in PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

Conditional expressions of PQL return a value based on a condition.

Syntax:
    
    
    if <condition> then <then-case-expression> else <else-case-expression>  
    

Where:

  * `<condition>` is a boolean expression.

  * `<then-case-expression>` and `<else-case-expression>` are obligatory values.

If the condition is true, the conditional expression returns the value of the then-case-expression, otherwise the value of the else-case-expression.




Example:
    
    
    if( POSEntryMode == 'Swiped' or POSEntryMode == 'Keyed' or POSEntryMode == 'Chip' )  
      then 'Card Present'  
      else POSEntryMode

# Function Calls in PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

Function calls allow you to execute predefined functions on current values. There are two types of functions that can be called:

  * Built-in functions of Pulse
  * User-Defined Functions (UDFs) â a set of additional functions bundled with Pulse



This topic gives an overview of the possible function calls, and points you to the right topics to learn more.

## Built-in functionsâ

### Checking NULLsâ

Return type| Method| Description  
---|---|---  
`bool`| `isNull(int? a)`| Checks if an integer value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(long? a)`| Checks if a long value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(double? a)`| Checks if a double value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(float? a)`| Checks if a float value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(bool? a)`| Checks if a boolean value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(string? a)`| Checks if a string value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(tuple? a)`| Checks if a tuple value is null.  
  
### Math functionsâ

All methods of the [java.lang.Math](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/Math.html) package are available in PQL. Besides those methods, you can use the following math functions:

Return type| Method| Description  
---|---|---  
`int`| `max(list_of_int)`| Returns the maximum value of a list of numbers.  
`long`| `max(list_of_long)`| Returns the maximum value of a list of numbers.  
`double`| `max(list_of_double)`| Returns the maximum value of a list of numbers.  
`float`| `max(list_of_float)`| Returns the maximum value of a list of numbers.  
`int`| `min(list_of_int)`| Returns the minimum value of a list of numbers.  
`long`| `min(list_of_long)`| Returns the minimum value of a list of numbers.  
`double`| `min(list_of_double)`| Returns the minimum value of a list of numbers.  
`float`| `min(list_of_float)`| Returns the minimum value of a list of numbers.  
`boolean`| `between(int val, int left, int right)`| Returns true if the value is greater or equal to the left boundary and lower or equal to the right boundary.  
`boolean`| `between(long val, long left, long right)`| Returns true if the value is greater or equal to the left boundary and lower or equal to the right boundary.  
`boolean`| `between(double val, double left, double right)`| Returns true if the value is greater or equal to the left boundary and lower or equal to the right boundary.  
`boolean`| `between(float val, float left, float right)`| Returns true if the value is greater or equal to the left boundary and lower or equal to the right boundary.  
  
### Stringsâ

Return type| Method| Description  
---|---|---  
`string`| `str(int a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(long a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(double a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(float a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(bool a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(string a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`int`| `indexOf(string s, string c)`| Returns the index within string `s` of the first occurrence of the string `c`.  
`string`| `substring(string s, int begin)`| Returns a new string that is a substring of string `s`.  
`string`| `substring(string s, int begin, int end)`| Returns a new string that is a substring of string `s`.  
`bool`| `contains(string s, string c)`| Returns `true` if string `c` is a substring of string `s`, or `false` otherwise.  
`bool`| `startsWith(string s, string c)`| Returns `true` if string `c` is a prefix of string `s`, or `false` otherwise.  
`bool`| `endsWith(string s, string c)`| Returns `true` if string `c` is a suffix of string `s`, or `false` otherwise.  
  
Container functions in `Map` and `Metrics` operators

Functions that operate on collections (like `List`s, `Set`s or `Map`s) are not supported in the PQL fields of [Map Operators or Metric Operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference).

For example, using `contains` or `indexOf` on collections in PQL fields of such operators will result in an error.

The recommended alternative is to use UDFs (User Defined Functions) instead of these built-in functions.

## UDF callsâ

Pulse comes with a set of [User-Defined Functions (UDFs)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions) that can be used in addition to the built-in functions.

UDFs in Metrics

When using UDFs in metric filters and aggregations, UDFs receive fields from a single event and not from a collection of events.

You can use the following syntax to call a UDF:
    
    
    <class_name>.<function_name> ( <arguments> )  
    

For example, to concatenate two strings:
    
    
    Strings.strcat("One", "Two") // Returns "OneTwo"  
    

java regex syntax

Pulse uses the Java regex flavor for UDFs, which means that all regular expressions must conform to the syntax and rules of Java's `java.util.regex.Pattern` class.

According to the usual regex syntax, when you need to match a literal special character that has meaning in regex (e.g. `*`, `+`, `?`, `.`), you must escape it using a backslash (`\`) within the regex pattern (e.g. `\*`, `\+`, and so on).

However, because the regex pattern itself is often passed as a Java String literal, the backslash (`\`) used for escaping the regex special character must itself be escaped according to Java String rules.

Therefore, to include an escaped character like `\*` (match literal asterisk) in a regular expression defined as a Java string, you must write it as `\\*`.

# Handling NULL Values with PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

NULL is a special value that represents the absence of a valid value. Any operation that acts on it as if it was a valid value fails with a NullPointerException. Untreated datasets might contain NULL values, and so they are potentially unsafe for any activity within Pulse. This topic describes how to make datasets more robust by handling NULL values using PQL expressions.

## Replacing NULL valuesâ

One of the common ways to handle NULLs is to replace them with a value that fits into the data field's type. It's common to pick the substitute value so that it doesn't represent a meaningful value for that data field. For instance, a NULL in the transaction amount field could be replaced by 0. To accomplish this replacement, you can use the **coalesce operator** (`??`) in a map operator or metric operator.

Usage of the ?? operator:
    
    
    <good-case-value> ?? <null-case-value>  
    

This expression returns `<good-case-value>`, unless `<good-case-value>` is NULL. If `<good-case-value>` is NULL, the expression returns `<null-case-value>`.

Example:

### Coalescing aggregations to a value other than 0â

Aggregations return 0 instead of a NULL when there are no values to count the aggregation on. For example, when the maximum amount is queried over a time window using a filter that filters out all the records.

In some cases you might want to return something different from 0.

The following example shows how to return -1 in case an aggregation of a metric is called on an empty subset of data:

### Nullable typesâ

Untreated input fields can contain NULL values. Hence, PQL treats every input field as a nullable type, meaning a type that can contain NULL values in addition to an original data type.

This fact is marked with a ? in the data type name.

For example, the _Amount_ field is not of _double_ type, but of _double?_ , meaning a type that contains all double values plus the NULL.

When using both nullable and non-nullable types in an [arithmetic operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/operators-in-pql) or in a [function](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql) that returns a numeric value, the resulting data type is nullable.

# Operators in PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

This topic gives you an overview of the arithmetic and boolean operators that you can use in PQL expressions, and the precedence of all operators.

## Arithmetic operatorsâ

PQL uses the following arithmetic operators:

Operator | Meaning  
---|---  
`+` | addition  
`-` | subtraction  
`*` | multiplication  
`/` | division  
`%` | integer remainder  
`^` | exponentiation  
  
Example: `Balance - Amount`

Type promotion when using arithmetic operators

The arithmetic operators obey the following type promotion rules:

  1. If at least one of the arguments is a double, the result is a double.
  2. If at least one of the arguments is a float, the result is a float, unless the result is a double because of the first rule.
  3. If at least one of the arguments is a long, the result is a long, unless the result is a double or float because of the first two rules.



## Boolean operatorsâ

Boolean operators are operators that return a boolean value. They include:

  * `<` , `<=`, `==`, `!=`, `>=`, `>`

info

Only numeric values can be compared with the <, <=, >=, and > operators.

  * `and` , `or` , `!` (not)




Example:
    
    
    POSEntryMode == 'Swiped' or POSEntryMode == 'Keyed' or POSEntryMode == 'Chip'  
    

## Operator precedenceâ

The following table lists PQL operators according to their precedence order. Operators at the top of the table have higher precedence.

Operator type | Operator(s)  
---|---  
grouping | `(expr)`  
unary | `+expr`, `-expr`, `!`  
arithmetic - exponential | `^`  
cast | `exp:type`  
arithmetic â multiplicative | `*`, `/`, `%`  
arithmetic â additive | `+`, `-`  
coalesce | `??`Note that this operator has a different precedence in RDL.  
comparison | `<`, `<=`, `==`, `>=`, `>`, `!=`  
logical â AND | `and`  
logical â OR | `or`  
assignment | `=`  
  
Cast operator precedence

Notice that the _cast_ operator precedence lies between arithmetic operators. If an expression needs to be cast before an exponentiation, it needs to be enclosed in parentheses (_grouping_ operator).

The following rules apply:

  * operators with higher precedence than other operators are evaluated before them;
  * operators on the same line have the same precedence: 
    * all binary operators except for the assignment operator are evaluated from left to right;
    * assignment operator is evaluated right to left.



### Examplesâ

Arithmetic and boolean operators of PQL follow the common rules of mathematics regarding functionality and precedence.

Arithmetic and boolean operators have higher precedence than the [`??` (coalesce) operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/handling-null-values-with-pql), meaning that the `??` operator gets evaluated after arithmetic and boolean operators.

Example: `a + b ?? c + d` is equivalent to `(a+b) ?? (c+d)`.

# PQL Data Types And Conversions

Was this page helpful?Â 

This topic gives you an overview of data types in PQL, and how to convert data from one data type to another.

PQL uses the following **primitive data types**.

Data type| Examples  
---|---  
int| 
    
    
    -289
    
    0
    
    42  
  
long| 
    
    
    123456789
    
    1l
    
    -2L  
  
float| 
    
    
    0.99
    
    -1.23e-100f
    
    3.14F  
  
double| 
    
    
    1234567.89012
    
    1.23456e300d
    
    1.23456e-300d
    
    1e1D  
  
bool| 
    
    
    true
    false  
  
string| 
    
    
    "John Doe"
    'John Doe'  
  
These data types are equivalent to the Java primitive data types. To see the exact definition or range for each, check the [Java documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html).

The **non-primitive data types** of PQL are:

  * Tuples
  * Collections:
    * Lists
    * Sets
    * Maps



Do not confuse these types with lists and map operators that you can create in the Pulse UI. They belong to two different levels of implementation. The non-primitive PQL data types are used only in PQL queries, when computing features. When the PQL computation is finished, Pulse stores the data of these non-primitive types as _Complex_ fields in the output data source.

## Data type mapping between Pulse and PQLâ

The following table shows to which PQL data type each [Pulse data type](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) is mapped when using input data fields:

Pulse field type (input)| PQL type  
---|---  
Categorical| string  
Complex| the same non-primitive type of PQL  
Date Time| long (UNIX timestamp format)  
Numeric| int, long, float, double  
String| string  
  
The following table shows which PQL data type can be passed as output to which type of output fields. The output field is the data field that the map or metric operator is creating/updating, and its type is one of the [Pulse data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types).

PQL type| Pulse field type (output)  
---|---  
any data type| Categorical  
int, long, float, double| Numeric  
long, int (UNIX timestamp format)| Date Time  
any non-primitive type| Complex  
string| String  
  
## Converting dataâ

In PQL, each data field, constant, variable, or aggregation result is of a primitive data type. To convert from one data type to another, you can use the following options:

  * Cast operator, to cast a value of a numeric type into another numeric type. Learn more about this operator in the next section of this page.
  * The `str()` [built-in function](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql#built-in-functions) to convert a numeric value to a string.
  * [User-defined functions (UDFs)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql#udf-calls). There are [built-in UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions) that can be used after creating an alias for them. Example: to convert the merchant category code to integer, you can use the `DataConversionTools.stringToInt()` function.



### Cast operatorâ

The cast operator allows you to cast values from a numeric type (int, long, float or double) to another numeric type. There is no built-in cast operator between numeric types and booleans or strings.

To cast a value, use the following syntax: `<value to convert>:<target type>`

Example: `Amount:int` is the value of the Amount field cast to integer.

# PQL in Derived Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

Derived features are new data fields that were calculated based on the original data set.

To create derived features, there are two different cases:

  * Computing data based on a single event (not on aggregated data), using a map operator.
  * Calculating a value based on an aggregation of events, often combining map and metrics operators.



This topic describes how to use PQL in both cases.

## Derived fields without aggregationâ

To calculate new values based on input fields, you can use **map operators** in plans. For that, add a map operator to the plan that processes the input data, and add the PQL expression in the _Expression_ field.

You can use any of the [building blocks of PQL](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features#pql-expressions), except for the aggregations.

### Exampleâ

The following example adds a field called _CountryMatch_ that shows if the merchant country is the same as the country where the card was created.

## Derived field based on aggregationsâ

To aggregate data, use a **metrics operator** in the plan. The UI of the metrics operator allows you to use a shorter list of aggregations: Avg, Min, Max, Count, Count Distinct, Sum and Standard deviation. Other calculations need PQL statements.

PQL allows you to use the following **aggregations** in the _Expression_ field of an aggregation when editing a metrics operator:

Aggregation| Description| Usage example  
---|---|---  
**avg**(field_name)| Returns the average value of the selected numeric field from the aggregated data set.| `avg(Amount)`  
**count**()| Returns the number of rows in the aggregated data set.| `count()`  
**max**(field_name)| Returns the maximum value of the selected numeric field from the aggregated data set.| `max(Amount)`  
**maxBy**(field_name)| Returns the event containing the maximum value in the given numeric field.| `maxBy(Amount).MerchantId`  
**min**(field_name)| Returns the minimum value of the selected numeric field from the aggregated data set.| `min(Amount)`  
**minBy**(field_name)| Returns the event containing the minimum value in the given numeric field.| `minBy(Amount).MerchantId`  
**stddev**(field_name)| Returns the standard deviation of the selected numeric field's values within the aggregated data set.| `stddev(Amount)`  
**sum**(field_name)| Returns the sum of the selected numeric field values in the aggregated data set.| `sum(Amount)`  
  
### Navigate on an aggregated data setâ

The first(), last(), and prev() methods allow to access the first, last, and previous row of the aggregated data set.

  * The current record is the last row of the current dataset if it entered the window, depending on the filters.
  * **first()** is the first transaction in the current window.
  * **last()** is the last transaction in the current window.
  * **prev()** is the transaction before last() that entered the window.



#### Examplesâ

To calculate the geographical distance traveled between two transactions, you can create the following aggregation in a metrics operator:
    
    
    DistanceUtils.haversine(latitude, longitude, prev().latitude, prev().longitude)  
    

To calculate the time span between the first and last transaction within a given window per merchant, you can create the following aggregation in a metrics operator:
    
    
      
    ( let first_timestamp = first().Timestamp ?? 0 in  
      let last_timestamp = last().Timestamp ?? 0 in  
      ( last_timestamp - first_timestamp ) / 60*60*1000.0  
    )

# Reserved Keywords in PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

Some keywords and symbols cannot be used outside of their original purpose. That means that within a PQL expression, they cannot be used as name of variables, fields or UDFs.

Besides the reserved keywords and symbols, there is a third list of words that cannot be used in PQL expressions due to limitations related to Java.

## Reserved keywordsâ

Keyword| Purpose  
---|---  
and| Comparison operator  
as| Import aliasing  
asc| Order criteria (ascending)  
bool| Boolean type  
by| Field descriptor (i.e. group by, order by)  
desc| Order criteria (descending)  
double| Double type  
else| Conditional branching  
float| Float type  
from| Select descriptor (i.e. select from)  
group| Grouping operator  
if| Conditional branching  
import| Import statement for UDFs  
in| Variable binding (i.e. let a = 1 in)  
int| Integer type  
into| Select target (i.e. group by price into ev)  
join| Join operator  
let| Variable binding (i.e. let a = 1 in)  
limit| Limit operator (i.e. limit 1, 10)  
long| Long type  
on| Join operator  
or| Comparison operator  
order| Order operator  
select| Select operator  
Stream| Stream declaration  
string| String type  
then| Conditional branching  
unit| Unit type  
where| Select discriminator  
  
## Reserved symbolsâ

Symbol| Purpose  
---|---  
.| Field accessor  
+| Addition  
-| Subtraction  
*| Multiplication  
/| Division  
%| Division remainder (mod)  
^| Exponentiation  
<| Less than  
<=| Less than or Equal to  
=| Assignment  
==| Equal  
!=| Different  
>=| Greater than or Equal to  
>| Greater than  
{| Block separation  
}| Block separation  
:| Casting, selection, etc.  
;| Statement separation  
@| Annotation  
??| Coalesce operator

# Handling Feature Importance errors

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

When the computation of Feature Importance is not successfully executed, Pulse returns an error message. This can occur, for example, when the sample percentage is not low enough in a large dataset.

To compute Feature Importance all data is loaded in memory, and thus, high Sample Percentage values may lead Pulse to run out of memory in the case of extremely large datasets.

## How toâ

When the computation of Feature Importance fails a label in the **Model Evaluation** list shows the status "FI:Error" as shown in the figure below:

To solve the error execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Model Project** window, select the **Model Evaluation** where you want to solve the error.

  2. Select  to access the following view:

  3. Use the button  to compute Feature Importance. Alternatively, you can  the computation of Feature Importance.

     1. **Try again:** Set the [input parameters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance#parameters) (i.e. False Positive Rate, Sample Percentage and Random Seed) to compute Feature Importance. By default these parameters are the same as chosen in the previous trial. One recommended approach is to choose a lower **Sample Percentage** to reduce the amount of data that is loaded in memory.
     2. **Dismiss** : Remove the error label "FI:Error" displayed in the **Model Evaluation** list.



## Learn Moreâ

Once you learn how to handle Feature Importance errors, you can return to [evaluating a model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model).

Ãou can also visit the page [Feature Importance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/feature-importance) for more information about this functionality in Pulse.

# Importing an external model

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

Pulse can integrate with tools that you normally use and are familiar with. You can import models that you created and trained in third party systems. After importing a Model, you can evaluate it and use it in Workflows as any other Model in Pulse.

## How toâ

To import an externally trained model, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab , select a Model Project from the Model Projects list.

  2. Add  a new model.




Duplicating an existing Model

When fine-tuning model parameters, instead of importing a Model again, you can duplicate an existing imported Model. For that, use the **Duplicate and Change** option on that model. This option loads a copy of it, with all the properties and values that were selected when the Model was originally imported.

  3. Select **External Model**.

  4. Select the **Algorithm** you used to train the model. Use the link button  at the end of the line to learn more about each algorithm. If you don't find the algorithm you need in the list, contact your administrator to discuss the integration possibilities.

  5. Type the **Model Path** , which is the path to the physical location of the model folder. For the requirements regarding the content of the model folder, see the table in the next section.

  6. If the Model Path has a model.json file that defines the data schema, Pulse automatically loads the schema in the **Fields to Select** area. Otherwise, select **Use Pulse Schema** , and select a data source that is compatible with the data that was used for training the external model.

danger

If models are imported via App Collaboration to a clustered environment, the model binary is only propagated to all nodes if the `modelStorageDirectory` property is configured to use a distributed filesystem such as HDFS.

  7. Select the **Target Variable** and the necessary fields for the data schema in the **Fields to Select** area.

In the case of an unsupervised machine learning algorithm (e. g. Isolation Forest), remove the field that you plan to use as target variable. This will avoid label leakage, since a realistic anomaly detection model does not have access to the label.




## Requirementsâ

The Model import assumes the following about the imported model:

Provider| Requirements  
---|---  
Feedzai| `*.model.gz` (a serialized FZRForest object, compacted)  
H2O| A folder called _model_ , containing either a `*.zip` (MOJO) or `*.jar` (POJO)  
DataRobot| A folder called _model_ , containing a `*.jar` file. The model has to be trained in DataRobot version 4.4.1 or above.  
  
## Next Stepsâ

Now that your model is trained, you can [evaluate its performance](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model), or [compare it with other models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models).

# Exploring hyperparameter tuning results

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

After performing a hyperparameter tuning, you want to analyze and explore the evaluations that were generated to learn and choose which parameter combination you will want to use to train your model.

Since the dimension of all the variables to consider can be significantly long, the exploration mode view within hyperparameter tuning is available to help you perform this task. The exploration mode view displays the information in a way that makes it easier for you to compare the performance of the different evaluations and, thus, make a more informed decision on what set of parameters to choose.

## How toâ

To start exploring the results of the hyperparameter tuning, go through the following steps:

  1. Open the hyperparameter tuning from the corresponding list box in your **Model Project**.

  2. Switch to the **Exploration Mode** tab.

  3. Select  and [Configure Targets for evaluation](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model#exploring-evaluation-results). As an example, consider you want to have a _Recall_ at approximately 1%. Configure the target as follows:

     1. Name the metric that the target will reflect, is this case _Recall_ @ 1%.

     2. Configure the new target by selecting the target metric, _#Recall_ , and the preferred strategy to reach the target, Approximation 1 %.

     3. Choose which are the **Metrics** to Show. Besides _#Recall_ you may want to add more metrics to be able to compare more information.

Adding targets

You can add more targets with other metrics to the exploration mode view.

  4. [Analyze the results for each target](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model#analyzing-the-model-evaluation) and compare them among all selected **Model Evaluations**.

Changing values

By hovering over a result and selecting the available button, you are able to change that value back and forth. This enables you to experiment if another value changes that metric or any other metric, making it easier to compare of how values do or do not interfere with each other.

As you proceed with your analysis, you may want to mark an evaluation in the **Evaluations** list as reference , making it easier to make comparisons between that specific evaluation and any other.

  5. Filter the results by algorithm and data source in **Evaluations**.

  6. Open one specific evaluation to view it in more detail, namely the **ROC Curve**. You can add another evaluation in this area and, thus, have a detailed view of two evaluations at the same time.




Global Exploration Mode

Consult the [global Exploration Mode view](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model#exploring-evaluation-results) to learn about how it can also help you decide on the best evaluation for your model.

## Exporting to a modelâ

Once you have decided on the parameters set that has performed the best, you may want to export it to a model. For that proceed as follows:

  1. Open the **Hyperparameter Tuning** from the corresponding list box in your **Model Project**.
  2. Open the **Evaluations** tab.
  3. Select the [Export to model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters#exporting-to-a-model) button of the corresponding hyperparameter tuning.



Notice that the new model will display all fields already filled in with the parameters used in the evaluation you chose.

## Next Stepsâ

Once you have learned how to use the exploration mode, learn about the Export to Model process in the [Tuning model parameters](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/tuning-model-parameters) page and train your new model.
