# Best Practices for Plans

Was this page helpful?Â 

Within a map or metric operator, you cannot refer to a field that has been added inside that same operator. In case of such dependencies, you have to use more than one operator to calculate the final field. Also, performance considerations need to be taken into consideration when organizing your maps and metrics into plans.

The following sections describe best practices regarding maps, metrics and plans.

## A simple planâ

Due to performance reasons, it is recommended to organize map and metrics operators in a single plan, containing all feature engineering logic.

In a simplified example, the plan could have the following operators:

  1. A map operator to calculate simple features.
  2. A metrics operator to calculate time-based aggregations.
  3. Typically another map operator to calculate features based on the metrics.



## Large number of metricsâ

It can happen that the plan has to calculate hundreds of metrics.

Due to limitations of Java, when a metrics operator contains around 200 metrics, the plan might crash. This number depends on the length of the metrics' PQL code. The solution for this is to separate the metrics into two or more operators.

When separating the metrics into two or more different metrics operators, it's a good practice to keep metrics in the same operator if they have the same field in the first place in the _Group By_ field. For example, if you have some metrics that group events by _Card_ , and some other metrics that group events by _Card_ and _ShippingAddress_ , then you can keep these metrics in the same operator to speed up the computation.

This way, Spark has to do only one shuffle for those metrics, which is usually the most time-consuming part of Spark computations. However, this technique has the cost of higher memory usage.

## Scheduled metricsâ

When you have scheduled metrics in a plan, Pulse has to recompute everything up to that point in the plan. If you have a lot of computations before the scheduled metrics operator, it might create a big overhead in computation time. This is usually a non-issue since scheduled metrics are normally computed during the night and are not subject to the real-time constraints. Nevertheless be aware of this in case you think your computations will be taking longer than a night in production.

As an exception to the one plan rule, having two plans in this situation can be a trade-off between storage space and computational times.

## Addressing errors in plan definitionâ

When defining the components of a **Plan** , you may encounter errors that would result in failures during the [plan execution](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#plan-execution).

Some of those errors are detectable when defining the Plan, and Pulse will show warnings to allow them to be fixed before deploying the plan to production.

One such error is defining [fields](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#field) based on a [PQL expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features) (e.g. within a [`Metrics` or `Map` operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference)). Operators that require null coalescing (i.e. [default fallback values](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#fallback-value)) will produce a warning in the UI if the coalescing operator (`??`) and value are missing:

To fix this situation, provide a fallback value in the PQL expression input field, e.g. `?? 0` or `?? ""`.

A similar warning will be shown if built-in functions are used in collections (like `List`s, `Set`s or `Map`s). For example, an expression like
    
    
    ["test", "test1", "test2"].contains("testing")  
    

will fail because the `contains` function is not supported in collections used in the PQL fields of Map Operators or Metric Operators.

Attempting to use such functions in that context will result in a warning in the UI:

The alternative is to use [UDFs (User Defined Functions)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions), e.g.:
    
    
    com.feedzai.pulse.pkernel.runtime.CollectionUDF.contains(["test", "test1", "test2"], "testing")  
    

Besides these preventive warnings, Pulse will also allow recovering from execution errors that are not detectable at design time. Refer to [Automatic Application Repair](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/working-with-applications/automatic-application-repair) and [Workflow recovery](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#workflow-recovery) for more information on how to recover from execution errors.

# Creating a Plan for Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

In Pulse, a plan entity defines a transformation flow of one data source into another data source. In a plan it is possible to add, update and remove fields, or calculate metrics on the data.

To create a plan, execute the following steps.

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, add  a plan.

  2. Add a **Name** for the plan.

  3. Select the **Deployable** option. This option ensures that you can deploy your plan to another environment (e.g. QA or Production) later on.

  4. In the **Schema** field, specify the data schema that the plan is built on. You can select an existing schema, or an existing data source.

For example, if you select the* Data with Features for Models* data source, then the plan will be based on a copy of the current schema of that data source.

  5. Use the **Confirm** button to acknowledge that future changes in the origin schema won't change the schema of the plan.

  6. In the **Timestamp Field** , select the schema field that represents the timestamp of the events. When Pulse aggregates the data over a time period, it will consider this field as the timestamp of the event.

Only fields of [timestamp](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) type can be selected.

info

If you don't select a timestamp field for the plan, you won't be able to create metrics in the plan later on.

  7. If you want to use data from more than one channel, select the **Omnichannel** option, and configure the channels as follows:

     1. Add a **Name** for the **Main Channel**. This channel contains the events that you want to process, and uses the schema selected in step 4.

     2. **Secondary channels** provide additional information that you can use to process the events of the main channel. You can use the **Add Channel** button to add secondary channels.

For each secondary channel, add a **Name** , a **Schema** and the **Timestamp Field** that that channel will use.

There should be at least some fields that can be cross-referenced between the channels. For example, both schemas might include a customer identifier, even though it might be actually called differently in each schema.

  8. **Save** the plan settings.

On this page

# Creating Derived Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

This page describes how to edit and run an existing plan that creates a new data source with new features.

In the example shown, you can see how to add a new field that is calculated based on a single transaction. If you want to create a feature that is based on many aggregated transactions, you must use [metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric), i.e. historical profiles â refer to the page on [creating metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/creating-metrics).

## Adding the featuresâ

To add new features, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open the features plan.

  2. Drag a **Map** operator to the plan if there is none yet.

Clipboard

To save time, you can use the clipboard  to copy-paste operators in plans. This allows you to add operators without the need of specifying all their fields each time you create a new plan.

  3. Edit  the map as follows:

     1. Select the **Fields to Add** tab.

     2. In the **Output Field Name** column, specify the name of the new feature.

     3. In the **Expression** column, write the [Pulse Query Language expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features) that calculates the output value. For example, the following expression calculates whether the credit card was present at the transaction:
            
            if (POSEntryMode == 'Swiped' or POSEntryMode == 'Keyed' or POSEntryMode == 'Chip') then 'true' else 'false'  
            

     4. Define the **Type** of the output field. In the example of calculating whether the credit card was present at the transaction, the type of the output field is _Categorical_ , with two possible values: _true_ and _false_.

     5. Confirm that you want to add the field to the output schema, using the  button.

     6. Add all the features to the map operator by following the previous steps.

     7. **Save** the map operator.




## Creating the data source with the featuresâ

  1. To create a new data source which includes the new field(s), execute the following actions:
     1. With the plan still open, use the  button to execute the plan.
        1. In the **Data Source** tab, select the data source that will be the input for the plan. For example _Cleaned Transactions_ , or _Model Features v1_. If the plan has more than one channel, select the input data source for each channel.
        2. In the **Data Sinks** tab, configure the output of the plan:
           * **Name** for the output data source. For example, _Rule Features v1_. **Type** : _Parquet_ (default) or _CSV_ , depending on what type of output file you want to generate.

Parquet format is recommended

Using the Parquet file format for data files is highly recommended. Besides allowing a direct encoding of data types (which automates the mapping of field types when importing datasets), it also improves performance and disk usage: compared to CSV, Parquet files occupy less space and take less time to load.

           * **Directory Path** : the path and file name where Pulse will store the output file, containing the data of the new data source. Example: `file:///datasets/rule-features-v1.parquet`. Note that the format varies according to the operating system.
        3. Use the  button to execute the plan. It generates a new data source in Pulse, named _Rule Features v1_. Pulse also saves an output file with the transformed data to your filesystem.
     2. Check the new data source to confirm that its schema includes new fields.





================================================================================

============================================================

  * [](/pulse/latest/)
  * [Rule Guide](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/)
  * [Creating Features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/)
  * Creating Metrics



# Creating Metrics

Was this page helpful?Â 

You can create new fields to augment a [data source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) based on an aggregation of events over a period of time. These kind of features are called [**metrics**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric), or **historical profiles**.

Metrics describe typical behavior. For example: this customer typically uses two devices, and makes one transfer per month to pay the rent. Certain behavior patterns, or changes in the behavior, may help you detect financial crime.

Metrics operator limits

For performance reasons, there are limits to the number of Metrics operators that can be added to a Plan. For more information about this, see [Limits](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/limits).

To add new metrics, execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open the features plan.

  2. Drag a **Metrics** operator to the plan if there is none yet.

Adding metrics operators

To save time, you can use the clipboard  to copy-paste operators in plans. This allows you to add operators without specifying all their fields each time you create a new plan.

  3. Edit  the metrics operator as follows:

     1. Add an **Operator Name** for the metrics operator.

     2. Add  a new metric to the operator. Later, when you run the plan, Pulse will add this metric to the output data source as a new field.

     3. Set the **Group By** fields over which to calculate aggregated metrics. For example:

        1. _AccountID_ , to aggregate metrics for each card number.
        2. _MerchantID_ , to aggregate metrics for each merchant.
        3. _AccountID_ , _MerchantID_ , to aggregate metrics for the profile of each card number in each merchant.
     4. If relevant, set the **Lookup By** fields (matching the count and types of the **Group By** fields) to define which group to retrieve.

tip

For more detailed information on setting up Lookup By metrics, refer to the [Using Lookup Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics/using-lookup-metrics) guide.

     5. In the **Window** section, configure the time window over which to calculate the metric.

        1. In the **Expression** field, add the time interval that you want to include. For example, _1 hour_ or _7 days_.

This means that you want to calculate a metric based on the events of the last hour, or of the last seven days.

For details on the syntax supported in window expressions, please refer to the [Time window](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#time-window) section of the documentation on Plans in Workflows.

        2. If you use the **Delay** field, recent events will not be immediately accounted for. For example, a 3-hour window with 1-hour delay means that out of the last 3+1=4 hours of events, the last 1 hour will not be considered. This is useful if you are computing a historical baseline profile and donât want it to be influenced by recent behavior.

        3. **Is tumbling** : tumbling windows expire all events at once, once they reach their predetermined size. Afterwards, they start filling again and the cycle repeats itself.

        4. You can define a **Filter** for the time window. Only events that fulfill the filter condition will be taken into account when calculating the metric. Use [Pulse Query Language (PQL) expressions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features) returning a boolean value to define the filter.

     6. In the **Edit Update Period** section, choose if the metric should be updated in real time, or periodically on a schedule.

        1. **Real Time** : ideal for metrics with a small window (e.g. less than one day), to ensure that rapid attacks are detected.

Under Real Time, select the _Update on every event_ option. The _Update every_ option is available for legacy reasons and should not be selected. This option is currently not accepted for omnichannel plans. It will be supported in future versions of Pulse.

        2. **Scheduled** : ideal for metrics with a large window (e.g. 1 month). Since there is less fluctuation in the long-term behavior, the metric can be updated less frequently. To specify when the metric should be updated, you can either set _Start of_ or _Scheduled_.

In the latter, you must type a [Cron expression](https://www.quartz-scheduler.net/documentation/quartz-2.x/tutorial/crontriggers.html), e.g. `0 0 12 * * ?` (i.e. _At noon every day_).

     7. In the **Aggregation** section, select the **Function** you want to use to calculate the metric. If the function needs a parameter, select the **Field** that provides that parameter.

Limitations when storing the state of real-time metrics on disk

Note that storing the state of metric on disk is in continuous development, and it does not provide full feature parity to the previous, RAM-based version.

Examples of functions:

        * To calculate the sum of the _TransactionAmount_ field over each time window, for each _group by_ field: the function is _Sum_ , and the parameter field is _TransactionAmount._
        * To calculate the number of the transactions over each time window, for each _group by_ field: the function is _Count_ , and it has no parameters.
     8. Optionally, in the **Advanced** tab of the Aggregation section, you can define a [Pulse Query Language (PQL) expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features). This tab allows you to compute more complex values. When calculating metrics in a plan that is based on more than one channel, the Advanced tab is not available.

     9. **If your plan has more than one channel** , do the following:

        1. Toggle off all secondary channels that are not relevant for the metric using the toggle next to the channel's name in the Group By section.
        2. You can decide not to include main channel data in the aggregation. To do so, select the **Do not include main channel data in the aggregation** option. Select this option when the main channel has no data relevant for the aggregation. For example, when processing debit card transactions, it might be useful to know how many devices the customer has used. This information can be aggregated from the online banking channel. But unlike online banking, the main channel (debit cards) will not contain any information about devices.
        3. After selecting the _group by_ field(s) for the main channel, select the matching field(s) for each active secondary channel. If there is more than one _group by_ field, the order of the fields **must** match across the different channels.
        4. If you selected an aggregation function that has parameters, select the parameter fields for each channel.
        5. Note that only scheduled metrics can use data from secondary channels. If you create a real-time metric with data from secondary channels, you will receive an error message when saving the metric.
     10. In the **Details** section, add a description for the metric.

  4. Use the **Save** button to add the metric to the operator.

  5. The metrics get a default name. You can hover over a metric and use the  button to rename it.

# Creating the Data Source with the Features

When you create a plan, you create a recipe of how to transform the input data source into the output data source. To actually create the output data source, you need to run the plan.

Testing in data science environment

If you create a plan execution in data science environment, the metrics are calculated immediately. However, in a real-time scoring environment, scheduled metrics (SMJs) may take considerably longer. This may lead to differences when you run a plan execution in a data science environment vs. when you use the same plan to score the same events in a real-time scoring environment.

To simulate the behavior of SMJs, you can use the `context.plan.delay.*` Pulse property. It delays the update of scheduled metrics in the data science environment. For each plan, set it to the time that it takes for the SMJs to finish. Get in touch with Feedzai if you want to use this setting.

## How toâ

To create a new data source which includes the new field(s), execute the following actions:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open the features plan.
  2. Use the  button to execute the plan.
     1. In the Data Source tab, select the input data source for the plan execution. For example, _Cleaned Transactions_.

If the plan has more than one channel, select the input data source for each channel.

     2. In the **Data Sinks** tab, configure the output of the plan:

        * **Name** for the output data source. For example, _Rule Features v1_.
        * **Type** : the file format of the output data â _Parquet_ (default) or _CSV_.

Parquet format is recommended

Using the Parquet file format for data files is highly recommended. Besides allowing a direct encoding of data types (which automates the mapping of field types when importing datasets), it also improves performance and disk usage: compared to CSV, Parquet files occupy less space and take less time to load.

        * **Directory Path** : The path and file name where Pulse will store the output file, containing the data of the new data source. Example: `<file:///datasets/rule-features-v1.parquet>`. Note that the format varies according to the operating system.
     3. Use the  button to have access to additional configurations:

        1. **Job Profile** : Allows you to choose a profile to optimize CPU cores and memory assigned to the Spark job that will run the plan.

        2. [Data Partitioning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/data-partitioning-for-the-metrics-operator): If you have metrics operators in your plan, this functionality allows to choose the **Data Partitioning** option that enables Spark to reorganize the data into different partitions as homogenously and well distributed as possible. Pulse allows you to choose one of the following options: **Data-Aware Optimizer** , **Hash-Based** , and **Manual Partition**. These options are described in detail in the [Data Partitioning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/data-partitioning-for-the-metrics-operator) page.

Metrics operators

The data partitioning option takes effect only if you have metrics operators in your plan. Otherwise, this option does not affect the performance of the plan execution.

     4. Use the  button again to execute the plan. It generates a new data source in Pulse, with the name you selected for the data sink. Pulse also saves an output file with the transformed data to your file system.

  3. When the plan execution is finished, check the new data source to confirm that its schema includes new fields.

On this page

# Using Lists in Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

To access a field of a list item in a plan, you need to add the field to the plan. This can be useful when you have reference data stored in lists, like risk levels, or country-related information. This topic describes how to add fields of lists to a plan, and how to access them in a feature.

Features cannot use multi-tenant lists

Multi-tenant lists are not supported in plans. More specifically, the user cannot select multi-tenant lists in a list operator.

If in a plan you want to use list values to compute features, you need to add the list field to the plan. This is the objective of the list operator. For each event that traverses the list operator, this field will be populated with the corresponding list item value from the list.

List items can have an **expiration date**. This expiration date applies to the list operator as well, meaning that if the corresponding list item is not valid at the time of the timestamp of the event, the field in the event will have a null value. You can set the timestamp field in the following places:

  * for a deployable plan under the Configure Plan Schema option.
  * in a non-deployable plan: for each operator, you can select the timestamp field individually, in the Timestamp Field option.



If there is no timestamp field defined, the list items that have expiration date are ignored.

## How toâ

To add a field of a list to a plan, perform the following steps:

  1. In the **Data Science** tab, open the plan you want to edit.
  2. Drag a **List** operator to the plan.
  3. Type a **Name** for the list operator.
  4. For each list field that you want to add to the plan, perform the following steps:
     1. In the **Output Field Name** column, type a name for the new field. This is the name by which you will be able to find the list value when using it in the plan.
     2. In the **List** column, select the list that you want to use in the plan.
     3. In the **Operation** column, select what you want to do with the list. The available operations are:
        1. **Get** : returns the value of the field specified in the List Field column, corresponding to the list item identified by the Item Value Expression. Applies only to complex lists.
        2. **Contains** : returns true if the list contains an item identified by the Item Value Expression.
     4. In the **Item Value Expression** column, type an expression that defines the key for which the list operator will retrieve the value. This expression is the connection between the event and the list. It is a [PQL expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features), meaning that you can use anything you can normally use in a map operator, for example:
        * event fields
        * constants
        * boolean and arithmetic operators
        * UDFs
        * coalesce operator
     5. In the **List Field** column, select the field of the list that you want to use in the plan. This field is available only if you selected a complex list in the List column.
     6. Use the  button to add the field to the list operator.
  5. **Save** the list operator.



As a result, in the features (map and metric operators) of the plan you can access the list value associated to the current event, by typing the name you gave in the _Output Field Name_ column. The value that this field contains is the value that belongs to the key you defined in the _Item Value Expression_.

## Exampleâ

You may have a positive/negative list about known merchants. A merchant may be risky, hence transactions with that certain merchant might need to be declined. Transactions with other merchants might need to be approved, or might need a review. A positive/negative list accumulates all this knowledge in one place.

In this case, the list is defined in the following way:

The list items have the _Merchant Id_ as key, and either 'decline', 'approve' or 'review' in the _Action_ field. Example:

Merchant Id| Action  
---|---  
898776| 'approve'  
556949| 'decline'  
132214| 'review'  
  
Now, you may want to use the knowledge accumulated in this list in the plan. For instance, when processing a transaction, you might want to calculate the number of transactions initiated by the same card with risky merchants.

To allow that, add the _Action_ field of the _Merchant PosNeg list_ to the plan. The key that will connect the event with the list is the _MerchantId_. The new field of the event will be called _MerchantAction_.

Now you can use the _MerchantAction_ field in the metric, as any other event field. It contains the action ('decline', 'approve' or 'review') according to the merchant of the event.

# Using PQL in Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

**Pulse Query Language** (**PQL**) is Pulse's query language that allows users to compute complex values based on input data fields.

This topic introduces the basic concepts of PQL.

To learn how to use PQL in some specific scenarios, read the following user guides:

  * [Handling NULL values with PQL](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/handling-null-values-with-pql)
  * [PQL in derived features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/pql-in-derived-features)
  * [Calling UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql#udf-calls)



## Usageâ

The following image shows an example of how PQL is used in a map operator to create a derived field in a plan.

This map operator adds a categorical field called _Card Present Flag_ , representing whether there was a bank card present in the transaction. The PQL expression is in the _Expression_ column.

## PQL expressionsâ

In the Pulse UI, users can combine the following building blocks (values, operators, functions, subclauses) into PQL expressions:

Building block / subclause| Purpose, observation| Example(s)  
---|---|---  
Constants of [primitive data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/pql-data-types-and-type-conversions)| Use a fixed value| 
    
    
    1.999
    'true'
    'Swiped'  
  
Input data fields| Use values of the input data.After typing the name of the data field, resolve the typed name to an existing data field name from the list that the UI offers.| 
    
    
    Amount  
  
`:` (i.e. the [cast operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/pql-data-types-and-type-conversions#cast-operator))| Convert data into another data type| 
    
    
    Amount:int  
  
[Arithmetic operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/operators-in-pql#arithmetic-operators)| Calculate a new value from two values of int, long, float or double type| 
    
    
    Balance - Amount  
  
[Boolean operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/operators-in-pql#boolean-operators)| Calculate a new true/false value| 
    
    
    and
    or
    !
    ==  
  
[Function calls](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql)| You can call two types of functions: built-in functions, and custom functions (aka. UDFs)| The following example calls the _between()_ built-in function:
    
    
    between(Amount, 0, 200)  
  
[Conditional expressions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/conditional-expressions-in-pql)| Return a value based on a condition| 
    
    
    if Amount > 1000 then 'HighAmount' else 'LowAmount'  
  
Variable declarations| Declare auxiliary variables that help you calculating other values| The following example shows how you define two variables (first_timestamp and last_timestamp) in order to calculate a third value (last_timestamp - first_timestamp ) / 60*60*1000.0)
    
    
    ( let first_timestamp = first().Timstamp ?? 0 in
    let last_timestamp = last().Timestamp ?? 0 in
    ( last_timestamp - first_timestamp ) / 60 _60_ 1000.0 )  
  
Collections, tuples| Work on tuples, lists, sets, and maps of data instead of a single data field| In the following example, OrderItems is a list of orders. Each item of the list is a tuple with the following fields: ItemId, Quantity, Price
    
    
    OrderItems.get(0).Quantity  
  
[Aggregations, and functions over aggregated datasets](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/creating-metrics)| Aggregate data to calculate minimum, maximum, average, or alternatively to access specific records of the aggregated dataset| 
    
    
    avg(Amount) - prev().Amount  
  
`??`(i.e. the [coalesce operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/handling-null-values-with-pql))| Handle NULL values| 
    
    
    Amount ?? 0  
  
Reserved keywords

Some keywords and symbols cannot be used outside of their original purpose. See the list of [reserved keywords](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/reserved-keywords-in-pql) for more information.

### `CollectionUDFs` classâ

Package: `com.feedzai.pulse.pkernel.runtime`

As the CollectionUDFs class is included in the runtime package of Pulse, you don't need to define an alias to use the functions of this class.

Lists vs Maps

The collection called Map of Pulse Query Language (PQL) and Rule Definition Language (RDL) is the equivalent of a Pulse list created under **Lists** . The following table refers to them as **Maps**.

Modifier and Type| Function| Description  
---|---|---  
Integer| count(Object collection)| Returns the number of entries in aÂ collectionFails with _UnsupportedOperationException_ Â if _collection_ is neither a Map nor a Collection.
    
    
    // Returns 2
    CollectionUDF.count(map("a": 1, "b": 2))

# Data Types in Rules

RDL uses its own data types. When using a field or a list, the values get automatically converted to these data types. This topic describes the data types that RDL uses.

## Primitive data typesâ

The following table shows the **primitive data types** of RDL. These data types are equivalent to the Java primitive data types. To see the exact definition or range for each, check the [Java documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html).

Data type| Examples  
---|---  
int| 
    
    
    -289
    
    0
    
    42  
  
long| 
    
    
    123456789
    
    1l
    
    -2L  
  
float| 
    
    
    0.99
    
    -1.23e-100f
    
    3.14F  
  
double| 
    
    
    1234567.89012
    
    1.23456e300d
    
    1.23456e-300d
    
    1e1D  
  
bool| 
    
    
    true
    false  
  
string| 
    
    
    "John Doe"
    'John Doe'  
  
## Collectionsâ

RDL uses the following collections: lists, sets, maps, and tuples. They are the equivalent of the [complex data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types#complex-fields) that you can use in the schema of a data source.

In RDL, the collection called map is the equivalent of a [list](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) created under **Lists** . Hence all collection operators can be used on them.

Best practice

Although it is possible to define collections directly in the rule using RDL, **the recommended method is to create a[list](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/lists) outside of the rule, under Lists** . This way you can maintain the rules more easily, since a change in the list items does not imply the change and deployment of the whole rule.

Explicitly iterating over lists is not recommended

It is not recommended to iterate explicitly over Pulse lists (e.g., using filter, all, etc), as this is highly inefficient. Pulse lists are optimized for contains/lookup operations.

# Operators in Rules

Was this page helpful?Â 

The Rule Definition Language (RDL) is designed for defining variables and conditions for Rules in Pulse. RDL queries event data, and transforms it using operators and function calls.

This topic gives you a list of operators that you can use when writing rules.

## Operatorsâ

The following table explains the meaning of each supported operator.

Rules failing with null values

Rules fail to be evaluated if an RDL expression in the condition or in the variables returns a null error, i. e. if the last evaluated operator in the expression's tree returns a null error. In that case Pulse skips that rule and continues the workflow with the next rule or the next workflow element.

Check the **Input parameters** column in the following table to see whether the respective operator returns a null exception when receiving a null value in the input value.

In the case of operations over collections, check the **Description** column of the table to see which ones return a null exception when the collection is `null`.

### Comparison operatorsâ

`**==** , **!=**`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Checks if the two operands are equal or not.| Any [primitive data type](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/data-types-in-rules). The two operands must be of the same type.| 
    
    
    card_present_flag == true
    
    merchant_country == 'EU'  
  
`**<** , **>** , **< =**, **> =**`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Compares two values of an ordered domain.| Numeric data types: `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`| 
    
    
    amount > average_amount_per_card_in_1_month * 1.5  
  
### Arithmetic operatorsâ

`**+** , **-** , ***** , **/** , **%**`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
The arithmetic operators obey the following type promotion rules:

  1. If at least one of the arguments is a double, the result is a double.
  2. If at least one of the arguments is a float, the result is a float, unless the result is a double because of the first rule.
  3. If at least one of the arguments is a long, the result is a long, unless the result is a double or float because of the first two rules.

| Numeric types: `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`The arithmetic operators throw a null exception if any of the input parameters is `null`.| 
    
    
    5%2

Returns the integer remainder of the division 5/2.  
  
### Boolean operatorsâ

`**and**`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Returns `true` if both received arguments are true.| BooleanThe and operator throws a null exception in the following cases:

  * `nullExpression` and `true`
  * `nullExpression` and `false`
  * `true` and `nullExpression`

| 
    
    
    card_present_flag == false and merchant_country == 'RU'  
  
`**or**`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Returns `true` if at least one of the received arguments is true.| Boolean| 
    
    
    CardWatchList.contains( tokenized_card_PAN ) or RiskyCountries.contains( card_country )  
  
`**!**`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Inverts the value of a boolean expression.| BooleanThe `!` operator throws a null exception if the input parameter is `null`.| 
    
    
    ! CardWatchList.contains( tokenized_card_PAN )  
  
### Functions on RDL Maps, and Pulse Listsâ

Lists created in Pulse under **Lists** are represented in RDL as RDL Maps.

`_MyList_ **[** _my_key_ **]**`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Returns the value stored in the List under the referred key.| my_key: the same type as the key of the list| 
    
    
    transactionContinent = Countries[ country_code ].continent_code;

Fetches the continent code for the current _country_code_ from the _Countries_ list.  
  
`_MyList_.**contains**( _my_key_ );`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Checks if the List contains a value for a specific key.| my_key: the same type as the key of the list| 
    
    
    isInBlackList = blackList.contains( tokenized_card_PAN );  
  
### RDL Lists and RDL Setsâ

Note that RDL Lists are not the same as Lists created in Pulse under **Lists** .

`_MyCollection_ **[** `condition` **]**`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Creates a window of the collection according to the condition.If the condition defines a single element of a collection, the `[ ]` can be used to access the data in that single element. Example: `_countryList_[ _country_code_ ]._continent_code_`|  condition: see examples on the right| 

  * Create a new list with the countries where the current card (_card_number_) is whitelisted:
        
        myWhiteListCountries = WhiteList[ card_number ] .country_code;

  * Create a new list (aka. window) with the last 5 events that have the same card number as the current event:
        
        lastEvents = event [ 5 tuples by card_number ];

  * Access the second event in the lastEvents window:
        
        secondEvent = lastEvents[2];

  * Create a new list with the last five events where the terminal type was X or Y:
        
        lastEventsWithTerminalTypeXZ = event [ 5 tuples where terminal_type == "X" or  terminal_type == "Y" ];

  * Create a new list (aka. window) with the last 3 events of the last 24 hours that have the same card number as the current event:
        
        lastEvents24Hours = event [ 3 tuples by card_number for 24h ];


  
  
`_MyCollection_.**contains**( `expression` )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Checks if the collection contains a specific element.| expression: must match the data type of the collection elements| 
    
    
    cardWatchList.contains( tokenized_card_PAN )  
  
`_MyCollection_.**filter**( _my_field_ => `condition` )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Filters the elements of a collection based on a condition.The operator throws a null exception if the collection is `null`.| 

  * _my_field:_ a field of the collection
  * condition: boolean expression

| 
    
    
    lastEvents.filter( amount => amount > 200 )

Returns only the events where the amount is over 200.  
  
##### Explicitly iterating over Lists is not recommended

It is not recommended to iterate explicitly over Pulse Lists (e.g., using filter, all, etc), as this is highly inefficient. Pulse Lists are optimized for contains/lookup operations.

`_MyCollection_.**any**( _my_field_ => `condition` )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Returns `true` if at least one element of the collection fulfills the given condition.The operator throws a null exception if the collection is `null`.Use it carefully on large collections, as the rule will have to do a check on all incoming transactions, against all list elements.| 

  * _my_field:_ a field of the collection
  * condition: boolean expression

| 
    
    
    myWhiteListCountries.any( country => Countries[ country ].continent_code == transaction_continent )

Returns `true` if the _myWhiteListCountries_ list contains any country that is on the same continent as the current event.  
  
##### Explicitly iterating over Lists is not recommended

It is not recommended to iterate explicitly over Pulse Lists (e.g., using filter, all, etc), as this is highly inefficient. Pulse Lists are optimized for contains/lookup operations.

`_MyCollection_.**all**( _my_field_ => `condition` )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Returns `true` if all elements of the collection fulfill the condition.Use it carefully on large collections, as the rule will have to do a check on all incoming transactions, against all collection elements.The operator throws a null exception if the collection is `null`.| 

  * _my_field:_ a field of the collection
  * condition: boolean expression

| 
    
    
    customerDevices.all( device -> device.score < 500 )  
  
##### Explicitly iterating over Lists is not recommended

It is not recommended to iterate explicitly over Pulse Lists (e.g., using filter, all, etc), as this is highly inefficient. Pulse Lists are optimized for contains/lookup operations.

`_MyCollection_.**sum**( _my_field_ )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Sums all the numeric values in the collection.The operator throws a null exception if the collection is `null`.| _my_field:_ a field of the collection| 
    
    
    lastEvents.sum( amount )  
  
`_MyCollection_.**count**()`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Counts the elements in the collection.The operator throws a null exception if the collection is `null`.| N/A| 
    
    
    lastEvents.count()  
  
`_MyCollection_.**min**( _my_field_ )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Returns the lowest element in the collection.The operator throws a null exception if the collection is `null`.| _my_field:_ a field of the collection| 
    
    
    lastEvents.min( amount )  
  
`_MyCollection_.**max**( _my_field_ )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Returns the highest element in the collection.The operator throws a null exception if the collection is `null`.| _my_field:_ a field of the collection| 
    
    
    lastEvents.max( amount )  
  
`_MyCollection_.**avg**( _my_field_ )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Returns the average of the elements in the collection.The operator throws a null exception if the collection is `null`.| _my_field:_ a field of the collection| 
    
    
    lastEvents.avg( amount )  
  
### RDL Listsâ

Note that RDL Lists are **not** the same as Lists created in Pulse under **Lists** . See the previous section.

`_MyRDLList_.**at**( _my_index_ )`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Applies only to RDL Lists.Returns the value stored in the RDL List under the referred index.The at operator throws a null exception if the input parameter is `null`.| _my_index:_ integer| 
    
    
    lastEvents.at(2)

Returns the second event of the _lastEvents_ list.  
  
### Selecting a value dynamicallyâ

`_outputVariable_ = **match** if `condition` then `expression1`; else `expression2`; end end`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
Implements an if-then-else block.If the condition is true, the output variable receives the value of expression1. Otherwise the output variable receives the value of expression2.| 

  * _outputVariable:_ any type.
  * condition: boolean expression.
  * expression1 and expression2: the same data type as the _outputVariable_.

| 
    
    
    events = event [ 3 tuples by card_number for 24h ];
    
    prevEvent = match
    
      if events.count() > 2 then
    
        return events.at(2);
    
    Â Â elseÂ ifÂ events.count()Â >Â 1Â then
    
        return events.at(1);
    
      else
    
        return null;
    
      end
    
    end

Returns the last event from the _events_ list.  
  
### Othersâ

``expression1` **??** `expression2``

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
The coalesce (`??`) operator returns expression1, unless expression1 is `null`, in which case it returns expression2.In RDL, the coalesce operator has the highest precedence when used in conjunction with arithmetic or boolean operators, meaning that it gets evaluated before the other operators.| Any| 

  * Return -1 if _MyList_ is empty, otherwise return the amount average of the list:
        
        MyList.avg( amount ) ?? -1 

  * Example to illustrate the precedence in relation to other operators:
        
        1 + null ?? 3 + 4

This expression is equivalent to
        
        1 + (null ?? 3) + 4

...and returns 8 as the result.

  
  
`UDF (User-defined function) calls`

Description| Input parameters| Examples  
---|---|---  
You can call [User-Defined Functions](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-rules/built-in-udfs) to perform specific computations.| | 

  * Find the location of the substring "775" in the _card_acceptor_id:_
        
        matchLocation = StringUtils.indexOf( card_acceptor_id , "775" );

  * Fetch the first letter 3 positions after the match location found with the above query:
        
        letterAfterMatch = StringUtils.substring( card_acceptor_id );

  * Check if the email_domain field matches the defined [Java pattern](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/util/   regex/Pattern.html):
        
        isNumericDomain = StringTools.regexMatches( "[0-9]+.com", email_domain );

  * From the complex field called _countries_map,_ retrieves the string value associated to the "USA" key:
        
        CollectionUDFs.getString( countries_map, "USA" )

  * From the complex field called _countries_map,_ retrieves the integer value associated to the "USA" key:
        
        CollectionUDFs.getInt( call_code_map, "USA" )


  
  
## Operator precedenceâ

The following table lists RDL operators according to their precedence order. Operators at the top of the table have higher precedence.

Operator| Precedence  
---|---  
grouping| `(expr)`  
unary| `+expr` `-expr` `!`  
cast| `(type) expr`  
coalesce| `??`   
Note that this operator has a different precedence in PQL.  
arithmetic â multiplicative| `*` `/` `%`  
arithmetic â additive| `+` `-`  
comparison| `>` `>=` `==` `<=` `<` `!=`  
logical â OR| `or`  
logical â AND| `and`  
assignment| `=`  
  
warning

Unlike other languages, in RDL the operator `or` takes precedence over the `and` operator.

The following rules apply:

  * Operators with higher precedence are evaluated before the ones with lower precedence.
  * Operators in the same line have the same precedence:
    * All binary operators except for the assignment operator are evaluated from left to right.
    * Assignment operator is evaluated right to left.

# Signing in as Pulse Administrator

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

With Single Sign on (SSO) enabled on Pulse, regular users can only sign in via  SP-initiated. However, Pulse Administrators can still sign in using a static URL:
    
    
    http://<BASE_PULSE_ADDRESS>/pulseviews/login/  
    

The main driver for this option is to allow Pulse Administrators to create new users using this URL, which otherwise would only be possible with user provisioning. Note that this option should be only used in special situations since the suggested method to create a user is through user provisioning.

## How Toâ

To sign in as Pulse administrator and create a new user execute the following actions:

  1. Access the static URL provided for Pulse Administrators: `http://<BASE_PULSE_ADDRESS>/pulseviews/login/`

  2. Enter your Administrator's credentials.

  3. Select **Administration** in the toolbar.

  4. Open the **Security** tab and add  a new user.

  5. Fill in the user information and select **Save**. On most SSO setups, user authorization is performed on the IDP. In this case the user creation form is the following:

Note that in the case of SSO, the fields are **read-only**. If SSO is configured with authorization in Pulse,

you have to specify if the user is an SSO user or not, and set its authorization properties.




## Next Stepsâ

Learn more about sign in scenarios with SSO:

  * [Signing in via SP-initiated](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-single-sign-on/signing-in-via-sp-initiated)

## How Toâ

## How Toâ

  * For this example, two pulse instances have been [configured in the IdP as SPs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/single-sign-on/configuring-ad-fs#add-a-relying-party-trust):

# Configuring Two-Factor Authentication

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

To sign in with Two-Factor Authentication (**2FA**), first you need to configure **2FA** on your mobile device to be able to generate a code that can be then entered in the sign in form.

In Pulse, 2FA uses Time-Based One Time Password (TOTP) to generate a temporary code. Learn more about [TOTP in Pulse](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor).

## How toâ

To configure **2FA** , execute the following steps:

  1. Access a Pulse URL. If you are not signed in yet you are redirected to the main Pulse Sign in form.

  2. In this form, insert your Username and Password and use the  **Sign in** button to continue to the next step.

  3. Your are prompted with an interface showing an alert that **2FA** has not been configured yet. Use the  **Configure** button to continue this process.

  4. To configure **2FA** on your device you have two options:

     1. Automatically, by reading the QR code using the code generator application on you device.

     2. Manually, by selecting the option _You can view the code and add it manually_ and typing on your mobile device the Account Key provided in the configuration interface.

  5. Insert the PIN code generated by the mobile application that you are using and finish this configuration by selecting the  **Register Application** button. If the PIN Code is valid, a new interface is displayed as shown in the figure below. The interface provides a reset code to reset the 2FA configuration. Learn more about [resetting **2FA**](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/resetting-two-factor-authentication).

  6. Use the  **Go to Application** button to access Pulse.




## Learn Moreâ

Learn more about [Resetting Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/resetting-two-factor-authentication).

# Resetting Two-Factor Authentication

Was this page helpful?Â 

## Whyâ

If you want to add Two-Factor authentication (2FA) to one or more devices or if you lost your mobile device in which 2FA was configured, you can reset the 2FA configuration. To reset 2FA you have to follow one of these scenarios:

  * Resetting 2FA of a signed in user: if you want to add more devices
  * Resetting 2FA of a user signed out with the reset key: if you lost your mobile device but you still have the reset key
  * Resetting 2FA of a user signed out without the reset key: if you lost your mobile device and you do not have the reset key.



The steps to reset 2FA for each of these scenarios are described below.

## How toâ

To reset 2FA execute the following steps according to the scenario that suits you.

### Resetting 2FA of a signed in userâ

  1. Navigate to the  Settings tool on Pulse UI to open the Settings menu

  2. Use the  **Reset Authentication** button to proceed to the reset the 2FA configuration.

  3. You are redirected to the sign in form. Enter you PIN code and use the  **Verify Code** button to finish the last step of reset your 2FA configuration.

  4. Your are redirected to the sign in form that requires configuration of 2FA on your mobile device. To learn how to configure 2FA on a mobile device check the page [Configuring Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/configuring-two-factor-authentication).




### Resetting 2FA of a user signed out with the reset keyâ

  1. Access any Pulse URL to be redirected to the main Pulse sign in form.
  2. In this form, insert your Username and Password use the  **Sign in** button to continue to the next step.
  3. You are prompted with the sign in form associated with the second validation step to access Pulse. Insert the reset code, instead of using the PIN Code generated by your mobile device, and Reset Two-Factor Authentication.



You are prompted with an interface to configure 2FA on your mobile. For a full description on how to configure 2FA on your device check the Section [Configuring Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/configuring-two-factor-authentication).

### Resetting 2FA of a user signed out without the reset keyâ

In this scenario, you have to request your Administrator to execute the reset of your 2FA configuration. The Administrator has an endpoint that allows disabling 2FA to a specific user. The following steps show how an Administrator can disable your 2FA configuration so that you can re-configure it again.

  1. The administrator navigates to the  Administration tool.

  2. The administrator open the  Security view.

  3. The administrator selects your user account to edit. The User form is opened with information regarding the **Status** of 2FA.

  4. in the User form, the administrator selects the  **Disable Authentication** button to reset your 2FA configurations on your mobile device(s).

  5. The Administrator is prompted with a warning window with the option  **Disable** to proceed with the reset.




Next time you sign in to Pulse you are requested to configure 2FA on your mobile device. To learn how to configure 2FA on a mobile device check the page [Configuring Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/configuring-two-factor-authentication).

## Learn Moreâ

Learn more about [Configuring Two-Factor Authentication](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/signing-in-to-pulse/signing-in-with-two-factor/configuring-two-factor-authentication).

# Bundle structure

Was this page helpful?Â 

The bundle generated by the Export Resource option contains JSON files that are organized in separate folders according to resource type allowing easy management by different end-users. The content of the files is structured in a human readable format. This allows you to:

  * Quickly inspect the content of each file.
  * Add or delete any item of your resource list (e.g. add a **Rules Project** to the bundle).
  * Peer-review your resources.



## Folder structureâ

The **Export Resource** generates a resource bundle that is compressed in the zip format.

When you unzip the file you will notice that the content is organized in different folders with the following structure:

    â   â   âââ example_model_1.model.gz # This is the binary of the example_model_1.json  
    â   âââ model_project_name_2  
    â       âââ example_model_3.json

Each folder contains a JSON file for each element added to the resource bundle.

Export Lists

**Lists** are always exported by default, and thus, the folder will contain a JSON file for each List that you have on your Pulse Application. However, you can choose to include the **List** items of each **List**.

## File structureâ

You can open JSON files using a standard editor to inspect the content. The table below provides the main key information that you can find inside in each file for each resource folder.

Folder| Description  
---|---  
lists| **Lists** are automatically exported. This folder contains a JSON file for each **List** that you have configured on your **Pulse App**.  
models| This folder contains a JSON file for each **Model** included in the resource bundle organized in separate folders for each **Model Project**.Note that you can include the binary of each **Model** when exporting the resources. In this case, the **Model Project** folder will contain the binary of each **Model.**  
plans| This folder contains a JSON file for each **Plan** included in the resource bundle.Note that you can include the execution of each **Plan** when exporting the resources. The metadata of the execution is stored within the file JSON file of the Plan.  
rulesProjects| This folder contains a JSON file for each **Rules Project** included in the resource bundle.Note that you can include a list of snapshots for each **Rules Project** when exporting the resources. The metadata of the snapshots is stored within the file JSON file of the Rules Project.  
tenantGroups| This folder contains metadata of the **Tenant Groups** that you have in your **Pulse app**.  
tenants| This folder contains metadata of the **Tenant** that you have in your **Pulse app**.

# Troubleshooting Tips

Configuring custom properties can be challenging due to the number of different configurations that are required to fully set up [component encryption](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/administrators-guide/securing-an-environment/component-encryption).

Here are some tips if you run into issues:

  1. Ensure you're using the right software versions, as the most common source of errors is the usage of incorrect software versions. Ensure the following minimum versions are in use:

     * **Java** : 8u141
     * **Rabbit** : 3.6.14 / Erlang 20.1
  2. Check for errors in the Pulse logs. The most common configuration errors which are easily identified in the logs are:

     * The client side is configured without encryption and the server side is configured with encryption (or vice-versa).
     * The public key of the certificate in the client truststore does not match the private key of the server keystore.
     * The truststore does not include the certificate of the CA that signs it.
  3. Check if the server is configured with SSL by using `openssl s_client -connect <server:port>` and verify if the certificates are displayed in the command output.

  4. Set the encryption lib log level to trace by adding `<logger name="com.feedzai.ssl" level="trace"/>` to logger.xml. If the logs are significantly longer than expected, it might be a sign that too many SSL connections are being established.

info

Establishing too many SSL connections might have an impact on performance.

  5. Under extreme circumstances, run the following command: `set -Djavax.net.debug=all`. This should be used with caution because it produces a long log. Check the following page to understand the generated logs: [https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/ReadDebug.html](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/ReadDebug).

On this page

# Semantic file

Was this page helpful?Â 

To give meaning to input data fields in an AutoML run, you need to provide a semantic file that tags the data fields to their meaning. The following sections describe how to create the semantic file, and give a list of tags you can use for input fields.

## Why tagging?â

When [defining an AutoML run](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/creating-features-and-models-automatically), you provide a semantic file that maps the input data fields to semantic tags. The semantic tags translate the meaning of the fields, providing the only portion of human knowledge that is required to power AutoML.

If AutoML knows the meaning of the input fields, it can combine them into features using [map and metric operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference). For example, the _Name_ field can be tagged with the _name_ tag. This way AutoML knows the meaning of this input field, and it can compute the number of words in the name, which can be useful to fight fraud.

Without tagging the input data fields, AutoML cannot generate features. The quality of the models generated by AutoML relies heavily on the quality of tagging.

## Creating the semantic fileâ

The semantic file is a JSON file, in which each data field is an object with the following information:

  * **@type** : A string containing the type of the tag, which can be _"simple"_ or _"composite"_. Use the **composite tagging** to compose one or more tagged input fields into a single tag. By default, the _address_ and _coordinate_ tags are composite. See their description in the list of tags.
  * **tags** : A vector of strings with the tag(s). See their description in the list of tags.
  * **fieldDesc** : A string with the visible name of the field. In _composite_ tags it is optional. If you provide a fieldDesc, it will be used as the name of the new field. Otherwise AutoML generates a field name by concatenating the tags you provided.



The following is a simple semantic file, for a data source with four data fields. The last tag creates a composite tag over two fields.
    
    
    [  
        {  
            "@type": "simple",  
            "tags": ["name"],  
            "fieldDesc": "Name"  
        },  
        {  
            "@type": "simple",  
            "tags": ["amount"],  
            "fieldDesc": "TransactionAmount"  
        },  
        {  
            "@type": "simple",  
            "tags": ["longitude"],  
            "fieldDesc": "TransactionLongitude"  
        },  
        {  
            "@type": "simple",  
            "tags": ["latitude"],  
            "fieldDesc": "TransactionLatitude"  
        },  
        {  
            "@type": "composite",  
            "fields": ["TransactionLatitude","TransactionLongitude"],  
            "tags": ["coordinate"],  
            "fieldDesc": "TransactionCoordinates"  
        }  
    ]  
    

**To create the semantic file** for your data source, you can download a template from Pulse. To do so, start [creating a new AutoML run](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/creating-features-and-models-automatically), select the data source, and use the **Download template file** option in the Semantic File field. Then simply add the tags to the fields.

The following are the **rules of tagging** :

  * At least one field must be tagged in the semantic file.
  * Each field can appear only once.
  * Each field must exist in the schema of the data source. However, [complex data fields](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types#complex-fields) shouldn't be tagged, as they won't be used by AutoML.
  * A composite tag must refer to fields that are tagged in the same file. For example, if you add the _coordinate_ tag, in the same file there must be a field tagged with _longitude_ , and one tagged with _latitude_ , and the name of these fields must be listed in the _coordinate_ tag, under _fields_.
  * A contextual tag should be accompanied by the corresponding _grouping-entity_ or _amount_ tags.



## List of input tagsâ

The following table lists the built-in tags of Pulse that can be used by Data Scientists in the semantic file when creating a new AutoML run, to tag the fields of the input data source.

Note that Pulse doesn't set the tags on its own. If the semantic file doesn't provide a tag for a field, Pulse cannot create features based on it.

In addition, the below file can be extended by developers with custom tags used by custom transformations.

Contextual tags

Contextual tags are tags that don't trigger any transformation _per se_. Theyare intended to be used by their companion tag.

For example, the Data Scientist might want to tag the field "card_id" as a _grouping-entity_. Additionally adding the contextual tag _card_ will make AutoML only trigger transformations that make sense for cards.

You can find existing contextual tags in the table below.

Usage example:
    
    
    {  
      "@type": "simple",  
      "tags": [  
        "grouping-entity"  
        "card"  
      ],  
      "fieldDesc": "card_id"  
    },  
    

Type | Observation  
---|---  
address |  A composite tag that combines fields with line1, line2, zip, city, region and country tags. Example for tagging:
    
    
      
    {  
      "@type": "composite",  
      "fields": [  
        "CustomerAddressLine1",  
        "CustomerAddressLine2",  
        "CustomerAddressZipCode",  
        "CustomerAddressCity",  
        "CustomerAddressRegion",  
        "CustomerAddressCountry"  
      ],  
      "tags": ["address"],  
      "fieldDesc": "CustomerAddress"  
    }  
              
    

To tag an address at least two components of the address must be present, so a minimal example would be:
    
    
      
    {  
      "@type": "composite",  
      "fields": [  
        "CustomerAddressLine1",  
        "CustomerAddressZipCode",  
      ],  
      "tags": ["address"],  
      "fieldDesc": "CustomerAddress"  
    }

line2 | The second line of an address  
zip |

region |

    {

      "fields": [  
        "TransactionLongitude",  
        "TransactionLatitude"  
      ],  
      "tags": [ "coordinate" ],  
      "fieldDesc": "TransactionCoordinates"  
    }

latitude | A double, representing the latitude of a location  
location | This tag can be attributed to either countries or cities. Fields that have this tag will be compared. For example, if a data source has two fields that have the city and location tag, Pulse will generate a feature that checks if they match.  
datetime | Tag for a field containing date and time in milliseconds, in Unix timestamp format  
expiration-datetime | Tag for expiration dates, e. g. card expiration date.  
yymm-datetime | Tag for fields of datetime with format yyMM.

Typically a subset of the fields tagged with the entity tag. For example, imagine that we set the grouping-entity tag for card_id and client_id, and set the entity tag for card_id, client_id, user_phone and user_email. All the aggregations (averages, counts, sums, etc) will be performed by card, and also by client. Additionally, AutoML has features that count the number of distinct clients, emails and phones by card and distinct cards, emails and phones by client. Example for a composite field as grouping entity:
    
    
      
    {

        "mcc"  
      ],

      "fieldDesc": "customer_id_mcc"  
    },  
          
    

A composite grouping entity can work independently. If we want a composite grouping-entity with A, B, no need for A and B need to be tagged independently, which would create profiles for A, B and A+B.  
acquirer, card, country, customer, ip, merchant, account |  Contextual tags that make grouping-entities only trigger transformations that make sense according to that semantic. Usage example:
    
    
      
    {  
      "@type": "simple",  
      "tags": [  
        "grouping-entity"  
        "card"  
      ],  
      "fieldDesc": "card_id"  
    },  
            
      
  
timestamp | A field of date and time value based on which the data can be aggregated for the metrics. Expected format: Unix timestamp.

# Business Targets

Pulse includes an exploration mode that lets you analyze your [model evaluations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models) and [hyperparameter tuning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/hyperparameter-tuning) results from a business perspective. This provides an extra layer of depth to data science model evaluations by letting you fine-tune them with extra business-related performance metrics.

In a fraud detection scenario, it is common that your [data science loop](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-science-loop) is targeted at maximizing fraud detection without violating business goals. For example, if the business goal is to not exceed 1% FPR, the data science loop should just try to optimize your model performance at that fixed FPR. You'll probably reach a point where you have a large number of model evaluation with small differences in configuration and performance.

**Business targets** in Pulse are very useful to display comparative analyses of all these model evaluations at once, under different criteria, and help you navigate results. For example, determine, for each model evaluation, which one performs the best, i.e. captures the most fraud money, when you set the FPR as approximately 1%.

For each business target and model evaluation, Pulse displays the classification threshold and selected metrics for which the configured criteria reach their best performance in each evaluation.

The following image displays Pulse's exploration mode with different business targets configured.

Analyzing evaluations

Note that you can combine and add to your targets both single model evaluations and evaluations resulting from a hyperparameter tuning.

So, with business targets, you have an improved ability to:

  * Check the performance of your model evaluation at different score thresholds.
  * Assess how close model evaluations are to your success/acceptance criteria, without breaking SLAs.
  * Detect possible cost-efficiencies when you make very small adjustments. For example, understanding how much your model's Recall improves when you slightly decrease your classification threshold.



## Learn moreâ

Check the following pages to learn how to put model evaluations into practice:

  * [Evaluating a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model)

  * [Comparing Models](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/comparing-models)

# Cost Fields

A **cost field** is a field of the instances that is used as a weight for the metrics of the evaluations (of both models and rules), typically the transaction amount in a fraud detection scenario.

Using cost fields in model evaluations or rule evaluations allows you to transform any metric (which by default is count based, e.g. Recall, Precision, etc.) into a cost-based metric (e.g. Money Recall, if the field chosen is a form of cost of the instance).

Non-cost metrics weigh each transaction equally, with cost 1. Using a cost field gives it a weight that is proportional to the value of the field. e.g., money value.

The following image displays cost fields included in a model evaluation. This example depicts a comparison between two evaluations both on count-based and cost metrics, and displays the cost FPR and Recall in the metrics table.

# Custom Evaluation Metrics

An **evaluation metric** is a function that can be applied to the data obtained during a model validation or rule validation.

In a data science project, an evaluation metric allows you to inject business logic into an objective model or rule evaluation. This allows you to evaluate trained models and rules based on the business value they deliver.

You can add an evaluation metric to your project by defining a function that receives:

  * The number of True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP) and False Negatives (FN), and outputs a number in an open domain.
  * The cost-TP, -TN, -FP and -FN. The cost fields variants are based on the weight a data field in the instance, typically the transaction amount in a fraud detection scenario, rather than using a count-based approach.



The following image depicts where you can create a new evaluation metric. Check the User Guide to see how you can [define evaluation metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/evaluating-a-model#using-custom-evaluation-metrics), for example, in a model evaluation.

You can apply a custom evaluation metric, written by you and adjusted to your use case, to any existing model or rule evaluation.

Availability

Since custom evaluation metrics can be built from both count and cost based way, they are available to model evaluations or rule evaluations only if you define a [cost field](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-evaluation/cost-fields) for the evaluation.

If you do not define a cost field for an evaluation, then Pulse will not be able to compute your custom evaluation metrics and you will not have access to them.

The following image shows how you can add a custom evaluation metric to a model evaluation.

# FAQ on Gradient Boosting Frameworks

Was this page helpful?Â 

This section contains answers to common questions when configuring a gradient boosting framework in Pulse.

## What is string indexing?â

String indexing goes by many other names as well, such as label encoding and integer encoding. For an overview of this technique, you can read [this article](https://towardsdatascience.com/categorical-encoding-using-label-encoding-and-one-hot-encoder-911ef77fb5bd).

## What is considered too many categories?â

According to Microsoft LightGBM's recommendations, you should not have too many categories in a categorical feature. This could mean hundreds or thousands, as it depends on the model. For performance, categorical values should not be limited to <1% of the training instances.

If there are too many categories, the recommendation is to index them and declare that feature as numerical. However, LightGBM / FairGBM will then assume such values **are** sorted. This means the mapping you choose matters. We recommend using frequency-based or risk-based indexing.

This choice implies that you must do the string indexing yourself, by adding a step to the features plan. In this step, take a mapping (through a list operator or user-defined function that loads the mapping from disk) and apply it to the input feature to generate the numerical feature to be used by the LightGBM / FairGBM model.

Remember that this indexing must work reliably and in the same manner in any environment, be it data science phase, or QA, or Production, to avoid compromising the model features and behavior.

There are cases with performance improvements where up to 10,000 categories were indexed through frequency for a categorical feature. Declaring that feature as numerical decreased performance around 1% recall.

As with all data science tasks, you should experiment and figure out how many categories give you the best results for your project.

## Does Pulse's categorical features indexing algorithm impact my model?â

This particular way of categorical ordering by Pulse (lexicographic order) does not affect your model results because LightGBM / FairGBM assumes the categorical features have no order, and sorts the different categories prior to splitting by the objective function.

The essential part is that the indexing is the same during training and scoring (which Pulse does).

## How are missing/null values handled?â

LightGBM and FairGBM handle nulls properly. In Pulse this is done by mapping any null / missing value to a NaN value in the backend, which is then interpreted as missing (you cannot disable this level of missing value handling in Pulse by design).

It is possible to consider 0 values as missing by enabling "Use zeroes as missing".

LightGBM and FairGBM handle splits and missing values in scoring using the following rules:

  * For categorical features: 
    * Categorical splits are performed in "one" vs "others" approach, with the split category of interest going to the left of the split, and the remaining categories go to the "others" side, on the right side of the split.
    * A missing value in a categorical feature split allots the instance to the right side of the split. This is the "other" categories side.
  * For numerical features: 
    * A numerical split places numbers smaller than the split point to the left, and larger ones to the right of it.
    * _If there were no missing values during model training_ , the missing value in scoring is replaced by 0 and the splits are followed accordingly.
    * _If there were missing values during model training for that split_ : missing values are allocated to the side of the split that reduces training loss the most (during prediction that side is chosen as well).



See [this thread](https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM/issues/2921) in the LightGBM forum for more details.

info

FairGBM does not handle missing sensitive attribute values.

## What are the training speeds for the different boosting types?â

There aren't any benchmarks available online. However, by [modifying the benchmarks](https://github.com/guolinke/boosting_tree_benchmarks) and testing for the HIGGS dataset, it is possible to get an idea of the speed difference on a large dataset.

Feedzai has conducted tests for LightGBM. See the test results below.

info

Note that, for FairGBM, extra computations make it slower than LightGBM during train. For this reason, such results do not apply to FairGBM.

#### Training time for the Higgs datasetâ

The Higgs dataset is a dataset with 28 features and 11M rows, of which 10.5M rows are used for the model training. The tests were conducted on a Dell laptop with 4 cores (x2 because of hyper-threading) and 32G RAM.

##### boosting_type=GBDTâ

Measurement| Measurement value  
---|---  
Real| 10m 12s  
User| 51m 57s  
System| 1m 8s  
  
##### boosting_type=GOSSâ

Measurement| Measurement value  
---|---  
Real| 8m 17s  
User| 42m 59s  
System| 1m 1s  
  
##### boosting_type=DARTâ

Measurement| Measurement value  
---|---  
Real| 60m 9s  
User| 363m 31s  
System| 2m 8s  
  
#### Conclusionsâ

As it is a single dataset and machine under comparison, these results serve only to give an idea of the different boosting model training speeds.

This comparison in particular shows roughly a **20% reduction** in training time whilst using **GOSS** boosting type instead of **GBDT**.

The biggest difference comes from using `boosting_type=DART`, which is roughly **6x slower** than **GBDT** in this case.
