# Feedzai FairGBM

Was this page helpful?Â 

Fair Gradient Boosting Machine or FairGBM (FGBM) is a constrained optimization (CO) framework developed by Feedzai on top of Microsoft LightGBM.

FairGBM enables training LightGBM models with fairness constraints (e.g., equality among different ethnicities, genders, age-groups, or any other sensitive attribute). This requires defining a sensitive column that details the protected subgroup each training instance belongs to (note that this column must be in categorical format). FairGBM reduces FPR or FNR disparities between the different subgroups of the population, according to your choice for the parameter `(Fairness) Constraint type`:

  * `FPR` reduces FPR disparities (useful for punitive contexts, such as fraud detection).
  * `FNR` reduces FNR disparities (useful for assistive contexts, such as granting loans).
  * `FPR,FNR` reduces both FPR and FNR disparities.



In this topic you can learn about the parameters and the usage in Pulse of the Feedzai FairGBM in Pulse.

## Feedzai FairGBMâ

The biggest advantage of Feedzai FairGBM is that it improves group fairness (e.g., by age, ethnicity, gender), on top of LightGBMâs existing advantages (low memory usage and good performance).

One of its limitations is that training is slightly slower than LightGBM in order to provide fairness.

You can choose from several boosting types:

  * **Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT)**
  * **Gradient Based One Side Sampling (GOSS)** : faster than the one above but may yield slightly lower predictive performance.
  * **Dropouts meet Multiple Additive Regression Trees (DART)** : can be much slower but might yield higher predictive performance as dropout can yield less over-fitting.



## FairGBM in Pulseâ

Pulse can train FairGBM models and even import external ones. Only numerical and categorical features are supported. String fields are not used in the FairGBM models.

Numerical features are passed along to the model without transformation, whilst categorical features go through an automatic string-indexing algorithm.

To train a model, FairGBM requires a sensitive column to be selected during train. That column must be categorical. This allows FairGBM to train a fairer model regarding the different population groups available in that column.

### Categorical features handling in Pulse for FairGBM modelsâ

Since FairGBM can only take in numerical values, categorical features are fully supported by running a simple **string-indexing algorithm at both training and scoring time** , by transforming the category string value into the _nth_ index in the lexicographically-sorted list of categories of a categorical variable.

See the example for the string indexing applied to a categorical feature value:

Property| Value  
---|---  
Input value| `"adam"`  
Categorical feature categories| `[ "John" , "42", "Adam", "zoe", "adam", "Jane" ]`  
Categories in lexicographic order| `[ "42", "Adam", "Jane", "John", "adam", "zoe" ]`  
Output value| `4`  
  
Notice that indexes start from 0 and for ASCII character codes, numbers come before letters, and uppercase letters come before lowercase ones.

This arbitrary choice does not affect analytical performance as FairGBM does not consider any order for categorical features.

## Training a model in Pulseâ

To train a model in Pulse, start a new model training just like any other model type. If you need more details, see the [Training a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model) page.

All categorical features in the training (and scoring) schema are automatically mapped using the algorithm explained in the section above before being sent to FairGBM. The same mapping is automatically used during scoring.

Numerical features are not transformed.

## Importing a model to Pulseâ

You can import a FairGBM model trained outside Pulse as well.

### Model import pathâ

To import a model there are two options available:

  1. Import the model from a model file path:
     1. The path needs to point to a valid FairGBM model file that FairGBM exports in .txt format.
     2. Since you are not providing the schema, you must define the schema inside the Pulse UI.
  2. Import the FairGBM model from a folder path:
     1. The folder pointed to must contain at least the following files:
        1. `FairGBM_model.txt` (mandatory) - the model file as in 1.a.
        2. `model.json` (optional) - a JSON designating the model schema
     2. Since `model.json`is optional:
        1. If not present in the folder, you have to define the schema inside the Pulse UI, as in 1.b.
        2. If present, it will be used for the model schema, unless you override it as in 1.b.



info

Regarding section _2.a.ii_ , see this [example JSON file](/pulse/latest/schema_categoricals.json) for binary classification with both numerical and categorical features.

### Importing models with categoricalsâ

If an imported model had categoricals in training, you had to index them, and thus that same indexing must now be performed during scoring, in whichever environment is used.

If indexing during training and scoring does not match, the model scores will be affected.

You have several options and must ensure consistency of those transformations:

  1. If you declare, in the Pulse model schema, a variable to be categorical, lexicographic order will automatically be used by Pulse for string indexing during scoring:
     * The only way to have correct scores is to train externally in the first place with the same indexing algorithm, otherwise the model's categorical features in training and scoring differ from each other.
  2. If you declare, in the Pulse schema, a variable to be numerical (and at the input it is a string that you had to string-index), you're going to have to do the same exact string-indexing transformation for scoring yourself:
     * Make sure you use the same indexing during training and scoring, but that in scoring, such transformations are reliable across environments, with tolerable latencies and memory usage for your use case.



## Parametersâ

Check the configuration parameters for FairGBM below:

Parameter| Description| Default value  
---|---|---  
`(Fairness) Sensitive group column`| Fairness constraints are enforced over this column.| (must be provided)  
`(Fairness) Constraint type`| Enforces group-wise parity on the given target metric for the selected group column.| `FPR`  
`(Fairness) Global constraint type`| Type of global constraint to enforce during training of fairness constraints.| `FPR,FNR`  
`(Fairness) Global target FPR`| This is an inequality constraint: inactive when FPR is lower than the target.| `0.05`  
`(Fairness) Global target FNR`| This is an inequality constraint: inactive when FNR is lower than the target.| `0.5`  
`(Fairness) Objective function`| For FairGBM you must use a constrained optimization function.| `constrained_cross_entropy`  
`(Fairness) FPR tolerance for fairness`| The tolerance when fulfilling fairness FPR constraints.| `0.0`  
`(Fairness) FNR tolerance for fairness`| The tolerance when fulfilling fairness FNR constraints.| `0.0`  
`(Fairness) Multipliers' learning rate`| The Lagrangian multipliers control how strict the constraint enforcement is. **Note that you should use higher values for larger datasets.**| `10000`  
`(Fairness) Initial multipliers`| The Lagrangian multipliers control how strict the constraint enforcement is.| `0`  
`(Fairness) Stepwise proxy for fairness constraints`| The type of proxy function to use for the fairness constraint.| `cross_entropy`  
`(Fairness) Stepwise proxy for global constraints`| The proxy function to use for the objective function.| `cross_entropy`  
`Boosting type`| The type of boosting model.| `gbdt`  
  
In Pulse, all parameters follow the above specifications, including default values. Handling missing values is always enabled.

Note that there are some parameters that only apply to GOSS and DART boosting modes. Such parameters always have respectively GOSS or DART in their names.

MULTIPLIER TUNING

The Lagrangian multipliers are essential to ensure fairness, and may not be trivial to tune. To tune the multipliers' learning rate, start with the default value (i.e. `10000`), and bear in mind that it roughly increases with the biggest group size. A crude rule of thumb is that the multipliers' learning rate should be between `0.01*n_rows` to `0.1*n_rows`, where `n_rows` is the number of training instances.

CAVEAT

Usually, you choose a decision threshold after training according to one or more of the following metrics: FPR, alert rate, recall, precision, sensitivity, money recall. However, when it comes to FairGBM, this target metric should be provided as a training hyperparameter via `(Fairness) Global target FPR` and/or `(Fairness) Global target FNR`, depending on the optimization goal(s) set in `(Fairness) Global constraint type`. For example, if you want to deploy a fair model at 5% FPR, you must set `"(Fairness) Global target FPR"=0.05` before training. This ensures that your target metric is fulfilled near a threshold of 0.5 (or 500). You can later fine-tune the final threshold after training, but the results should be around 0.5 (or 500).

## Logging configurationâ

If you want to know in more detail the progress of the process, you can check the [LightGBM Logging Configuration](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training/lightgbm-logging-configuration) page to configure logging to suit your needs.

# Feedzai Random Forest

Was this page helpful?Â 

Feedzai Random Forest (FZRF) is a machine learning algorithm developed by Feedzai. It is an enhanced variation of the [original Random Forest algorithm](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf).

Random forests use labeled data to learn its patterns. A random forest consists of a typically large number of decision trees, where each decision tree is a model. Each decision tree model is created by feeding each tree a random subset of the data (i.e. bagging).

In this topic you can learn about the parameters and the usage of Feedzai Random Forest.

## Parametersâ

You can learn more about each parameter of FZRF in the following table:

Parameters| Description| Default values| Possible values| Notes  
---|---|---|---|---  
**In-bag factor**|  This parameter tells you which percentage of instances are used to train a particular tree, while the rest is used to calculate the out-of-bag error.| 0.65| Double between 0 and 1.| See FAQ's question number 2 to learn more about how the bagging is performed.  
**Maximum depth of trees**|  The number of nodes in the longest path from the root of the tree to a leaf. The higher the number, the larger the model will be.Large models mean more splits, meaning they capture more information about the data. However, as mentioned, they result in large sized models that can reach GBs. Also, a high number of maximum depth of trees is likely to lead to overfitting.| 20| Positive integer.| This can be a number from 1 to the number of instances in the training set.In practice, splits don't separate just one transaction from the others, so depending on the rate of the target class and features being used to train, you won't see a considerable difference in model performance (i.e., if you change the maximum depth from 100 to 200). However, the size of the model may change considerably so a small number is advisable.  
**Number of trees**|  The number of decision trees in the forest.| 100| Positive integer.| There are diminishing returns, and training time increases linearly with the number of trees. Typically this parameter is set between 500 or 1000, but only if the dataset isn't particularly big.  
**Feature selection function**|  The metric that defines how to pick the feature for the next split.| Information gain| Information gain: The next split will be the one that maximizes the information gain, i.e., that splits the two classes better. This means these feature selection functions give you a concrete number on how well you separated your two classes (e.g. fraud vs non-fraud) after a split. Your goal is to be able to separate the two classes as best as possible.|   
**Minimum instances for split**|  For a split, the selected node has to have at least this number of instances in its subtree.| 2| Positive integer.| The typical value is 10 or 20. If you select a number equal or bigger than the number of transactions, then you never do any split.  
**Number of candidate features**|  The number of features to be used in each node as candidates for the next split.| 0| Positive integer, between 0 and the total number of features in the dataset.| The default value (i.e., 0, zero), means that the square-root of the total number of features will be used.  
**Prior function**|  This parameter is used only when estimating the distribution of a node that has no transactions.| Empty| Empty: Assigns an equal probability for each class. If it's a fraud vs non-fraud scenario, 50% for each.Random: assigns a random probability for each class.Parent: uses the probability distribution of the parent node.| The estimation happens when scoring an event that has null values in a feature that is used to split nodes in the trees.  
**Split method**|  The way the algorithm splits categorical nodes into new branches.| One vs Others| One vs others: the split is done into two new branches: one category branch vs an "others" branch. This one results in longer training time.All vs all: the split is done into as many branches as the number of categories. Typically, you will not obtain better results from this value, as it's prone to overfit if there are a lot of categories and it also requires larger disk space, which potentially means trouble.|   
  
## FAQâ

### What is the condition for the nodes to be split?â

**What is the condition for the nodes to be split, is it ' <' goes left and '>=' goes right or '<=' goes left?**

It shouldn't make any difference if you are trying every split.

### Is bagging with or without repetition?â

Without repetition for each tree. With repetition "across trees", as shown in the figure below.

This means that a tree will never look at the same instance twice, but multiple trees in the same "forest" will most likely see overlapping instances.

### How do null values impact the computation of information gain, especially with categoricals?â

If you are trying to split on a categorical and an instance has a null in that field, you must count the instance for the total. Yet you shouldn't count it for the specific subset when calculating the information gain.

A few more notes regarding FZRF and null values:

  * FZRF will ignore any instance where the class label is missing. This means that the whole instance is dropped during training.
  * FZRF will use instances where the features have missing values up to the first split using that feature (i.e. for each tree/branch).



The consequence of the last point is that when a feature with very high number of missing values is being tested for splitting, it may **have very high information gain**. This will lead the model to select the feature, hence dropping most of the instances in the training data.

### Is the data replicated into memory for each tree due to bagging?â

Yes, because trees are trained in parallel and each in-bag dataset is a partition of the initial data.

# LightGBM Locale Issues

Was this page helpful?Â 

When using versions older than LightGBM v3.2.0 or Pulse 22.0, there may be wrong scores during prediction due to locale mismatches between train and prediction environments.

caution

This caveat applies to versions **older** than Pulse 22.0, that includes a patched version of LightGBM, so that there are no locale issues

The fix is also present in all of the following Pulse hotfix versions:

  * >= 19.1.41
  * >= 20.1.18
  * >= 20.3.20
  * >= 21.1.3



When importing models that were trained with the help of Java in some way, follow this rule:

  * When training LightGBM models outside Pulse using Java tools, enforce locale **LC_ALL=C** during model training to avoid broken scores.



This is true whether using a Java LightGBM provider such as MMLSpark, or any LightGBM provider such as Python's, together with Java tools like JEP.

note

This rule can only be ignored if you know your LightGBM provider uses the core LightGBM library release v3.2.0 or later.

### Explanationâ

If Java is not using the default **C** locale, it will break LightGBM's, producing a LightGBM model file that will be read back incorrectly.

Although LightGBM in Pulse uses Java as well, it no longer suffers from this issue since we patched LightGBM and are using that patch, that will come out in the LightGBM v3.2.0 release.

### How to control the locale?â

Depending on where the job is running, there are several ways to override a locale. If running a local process prepend `LC_ALL=C` to your command or do `export LC_ALL=C` before using your command. If you are using Spark, pass the Spark property `spark.executorEnv.LC_ALL=C`.

# LightGBM Logging Configuration

Was this page helpful?Â 

The LightGBM provider of Pulse can be configured to log information. You can configure the logging levels, from the most basic INFO, up to the most extreme level TRACE on the several modules of the LightGBM provider.

This topic describes the logging levels, and how to set up logging.

## Logging levelsâ

There are several modules available, each with different responsibilities. To fill out the logging configurations you must use the fully qualified name of the module (as in the examples on the bottom of the page), by adding the prefix "com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm." to the module name. You can control the logging level per module.

Module name| Description of the module| Description of the logging levels  
---|---|---  
**LightGBMBinaryClassificationModel**|  Implements the OpenML class responsible for loading a model and scoring instances. It is also called when saving the model to disk.| ERROR: Report that saving model to disk failed.  
**LightGBMBinaryClassificationModelTrainer**|  Responsible for training a LightGBM model. At the end of the train it saves an intermediate representation to disk that is then passed to LightGBMBinaryClassificationModel for the final model save to disk.| INFO: Information messages reporting the stage at which the training is  
ERROR: For errors during train  
DEBUG: Report #train-instances, training parameters and features, more details on the sub-stages of training, progress in number of train iterations  
**LightGBMModelCreator**|  Starts all load/fit operations and validations prior to starting the aforementioned model load/fit process.| INFO: Message with file path from which the model is being loaded  
ERROR: Errors when training the model or the validations for a model fit/load fail and where it is it trying to read from.  
**LightGBMSWIG**|  Low-level implementation for model scoring.| INFO: Saving model to disk calls.  
ERROR: Errors saving model to disk.  
DEBUG: Saving model to disk calls with filepaths.  
TRACE: Show prediction score per instance (**might be too much logging!**)  
**LightGBMUtils**|  Loads the LightGBM libraries.| INFO: When the libraries are loaded.  
DEBUG: Names of the libraries being loaded.  
**SWIGResources**|  Lowest-level implementation level for resources handling during model scoring.| DEBUG: In-memory instantiation of model.  
TRACE: Resource release calls.  
**SWIGTrainResources**|  Lowest-level implementation level for resources handling during model fitting.| DEBUG: Details for train memory allocation.  
  
## How to set up loggingâ

To configure such log levels, edit the file `conf/logger.xml`. Also, for Spark Standalone `spark-libs/logback-executors.xml` should also have such log levels.

### Example configurationâ

The following snippet is an example of configuring the logging level for all modules of LightGBM. Debug is a good default level.

In files `conf/logger.xml` and `spark-libs/logback-executors.xml`:
    
    
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm" level="debug"/>  
    

Alternatively, the debug level can be chosen/overriden individually for each component. The snippet below is equivalent to the snippet above, all components use the debug level:

In files `conf/logger.xml` and `spark-libs/logback-executors.xml`:
    
    
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMBinaryClassificationModel" level="debug"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMBinaryClassificationModelTrainer" level="debug"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMModelCreator" level="debug"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMSWIG" level="debug"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.LightGBMUtils" level="debug"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.SWIGResources" level="debug"/>  
    <logger name="com.feedzai.openml.provider.lightgbm.SWIGTrainResources" level="debug"/>

# Microsoft LightGBM Provider

Was this page helpful?Â 

Light Gradient Boosting Machine or LightGBM is a gradient boosting framework for several types of tree-based learning algorithms.

In this topic you can learn about the parameters and the usage of the Microsoft LightGBM Provider in Pulse.

## Microsoft LightGBMâ

The biggest advantage of Microsoft LightGBM is that training can be very fast with low memory usage and good performance. Whilst Microsoft LightGBM models support ranking, classification and regression tasks in a distributed manner, Pulse's LightGBM machine learning provider only supports binary classification tasks.

One of its limitations is that LightGBM only receives numerical data (even for categorical features). This means that strings must undergo a process called _String Indexing_ , where a mapping of 1:1 from a string to a numerical value is performed. Of course, this mapping must be maintained consistent at all times (training and scoring).

You can choose from several boosting types:

  * **Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT)**
  * **Gradient Based One Side Sampling (GOSS)** : faster than the one above but may yield slightly lower predictive performance.
  * **Dropouts meet Multiple Additive Regression Trees (DART)** : can be much slower but might yield higher predictive performance as dropout can yield less over-fitting.
  * **Random Forest (RF)** : not recommended as it is not a true Random Forest but uses boosting as well - use our FZRF instead.



## LightGBM in Pulseâ

Pulse can train LightGBM models and even import external ones using this provider. Only numerical and categorical features are supported, string fields are not used in the LightGBM models.

Numerical features are passed along to the model without transformation, whilst categorical features go through an automatic string-indexing algorithm.

### Categorical features handling in Pulse for LightGBM modelsâ

Since LightGBM can only take in numerical values, categorical features are fully supported by running a simple **string-indexing algorithm at both training and scoring time** , by transforming the category string value into the _nth_ index in the lexicographically-sorted list of categories of a categorical variable.

See the example for the string indexing applied to a categorical feature value:

Property| Value  
---|---  
Input value| `"adam"`  
Categorical feature categories| `[ "John" , "42", "Adam", "zoe", "adam", "Jane" ]`  
Categories in lexicographic order| `[ "42", "Adam", "Jane", "John", "adam", "zoe" ]`  
Output value| `4`  
  
Notice that indexes start from 0 and for ASCII character codes, numbers come before letters, and uppercase letters come before lowercase ones.

This arbitrary choice does not affect analytical performance as LightGBM does not consider any order for categorical features.

## Training a model in Pulseâ

To train a model in Pulse, start a new model training just like any other model type. If you need more details, see the [Training a Model](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/model-guide/training-a-model) page for a refresher.

All categorical features in the training (and scoring) schema are automatically mapped using the algorithm explained in the section above before being sent to LightGBM. The same mapping is automatically used during scoring.

Numerical features are not transformed.

## Importing a model to Pulseâ

You can import a LightGBM model trained outside Pulse as well.

### Model import pathâ

To import a model there are two options available:

  1. Import the model from a model file path:
     1. The path needs to point to a valid LightGBM model file that LightGBM exports in .txt format.
     2. Since you are not providing the schema, you must define the schema inside the Pulse UI.
  2. Import the LightGBM model from a folder path:
     1. The folder pointed to must contain at least the following files:
        1. `LightGBM_model.txt` (mandatory) - the model file as in 1.a.
        2. `model.json` (optional) - a JSON designating the model schema
     2. Since `model.json`is optional:
        1. If not present in the folder, you have to define the schema inside the Pulse UI, as in 1.b.
        2. If present, it will be used for the model schema, unless you override it as in 1.b.



info

Regarding section _2.a.ii_ , see this [example JSON file](/pulse/latest/schema_categoricals.json) for binary classification with both numerical and categorical features.

### Importing models with categoricalsâ

If an imported model had categoricals in training, you had to index them, and thus that same indexing must now be performed during scoring, in whichever environment is used.

If indexing during training and scoring does not match, the model scores will be affected.

You have several options and must ensure consistency of those transformations:

  1. If you declare, in the Pulse model schema, a variable to be categorical, lexicographic order will automatically be used by Pulse for string indexing during scoring:
     * The only way to have correct scores is to train externally in the first place with the same indexing algorithm, otherwise the model's categorical features in training and scoring differ from each other.
  2. If you declare, in the Pulse schema, a variable to be numerical (and at the input it is a string that you had to string-index), you're going to have to do the same exact string-indexing transformation for scoring yourself:
     * Make sure you use the same indexing during training and scoring, but that in scoring, such transformations are reliable across environments, with tolerable latencies and memory usage for your use case.



## Parametersâ

Check the configuration parameters in the [official documentation of LightGBM](https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io/en/v3.3.3/Parameters.html). In Pulse, all parameters follow those specifications, including default values. Handling missing values is always enabled.

Note that there are some parameters that only apply to GOSS and DART boosting modes. Such parameters always have respectively GOSS or DART in their names.

## Logging configurationâ

If you want to know in more detail the progress of the process, you can check the [LightGBM Logging Configuration](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training/lightgbm-logging-configuration) page to configure logging to suit your needs.

## Learn moreâ

  * [Microsoft LightGBM official documentation](https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io/en/v3.3.3/index.html)
  * [Microsoft LightGBM code on Github](https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM)
  * [FAQ on Gradient Boosting Frameworks](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/models/model-training/faq-gradient-boosting-frameworks)

# Backfills

Was this page helpful?Â 

Due to Railgun's streaming nature, when a new metric is defined (or an existing one is updated), its value will initially only account for the events which are processed from that point forward. For accurate results, older data corresponding to the period covered by the metric's time window needs to be collected retroactively, in a process called a **backfill**. Backfills are triggered automatically for any new or updated metrics, forming an ordered queue.

Depending on the size of the profile's windows, and frequency of events, backfilling historical data can take some time due to the potentially high volume of data to be processed. Therefore, all backfills are executed asynchronously, so they won't interfere with application updates.

A UI is available to [manage the queue of backfill jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/managing-metrics-backfills), so that long-running backfills can be canceled to allow for quicker or more urgent ones to proceed, and restarted later.

## How backfills are triggeredâ

There are two main ways that backfills can be triggered: automatically due to the app publishes that create or modify metrics, or manually via the UI.

Backfills failing due to encrypted database password

If triggering a backfill results in a Pulse error stating that the Pulse property `pulse.app.database.password` could not be decrypted, then you need to update Pulse to a more recent version.

### Backfills triggered via app publishesâ

Whenever an app publish action includes the creation or modification of metrics, Pulse will automatically trigger a backfill for the affected metrics. The exception is when only the name or [fallback value](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/metrics#fallback-value) of a metric is changed.

When a backfill is initiated through a publish action, new metrics or existing metrics with modifications will return the fallback value until the backfill is complete. Metrics that have not been changed remain unaffected.

Preserving metrics values during backfills

Refer to the [Best practices for metrics in Railgun](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics/railgun#maintaining-metric-values-during-automatic-backfills) page to learn how to preserve metrics' values when making changes that trigger automatic backfills.

See the table below for more details on the kinds of changes that trigger automatic backfills, and what is the impact of each change.

### Backfills triggered manually via the UIâ

[Manual backfill initiation via the UI](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/managing-metrics-backfills#triggering-a-new-backfill-job) is primarily intended for maintenance and support purposes.

When a backfill is manually triggered, the behavior of the affected metrics will depend on whether they had already been backfilled automatically or not:

  * Metrics that had already been backfilled automatically and were outputting values computed from real-time data, will continue to output real-time computed values (based on the old definition) during the manual backfill process.
  * Metrics that had not yet been automatically backfilled and therefore were not yet outputting values computed from real-time data (i.e. were returning their fallback values), will continue to output the fallback value during the manual backfill process.



In both cases, like with automatically triggered backfills, the affected metrics will start outputting values based on the new definition once the manual backfill is complete.

## Backfill optimizationâ

Railgun backfill queues are automatically managed to avoid redundant work and ensure that each metric is only backfilled once.

For example, when an app is published with new or updated metrics, a new backfill job is added to the queue. This job backfills those new metrics, as well as any existing, unmodified ones that aren't yet fully backfilled. However, if a new backfill job is picked up and by then the previously existing metrics are already backfilled by earlier publish jobs, the system automatically skips those metrics in the new job.

Similarly, when multiple backfills are scheduled (not yet running) for the same app and workflow, the system will automatically merge them by skipping the original backfills and creating a new backfill job containing all metrics that need to be backfilled.

info

Backfills that are manually triggered via the UI are not affected by this optimization, and will always backfill their selected metrics, even if they have already been backfilled.

This behavior allows for maintenance operations where re-backfilling specific metrics is necessary.

This optimization does not apply to metrics that are updated while a backfill for their older version is still running, nor does it reorder backfill jobs in the queue to prioritize smaller or more urgent ones. For recommendations on how to handle these cases, refer to the [best practices for managing the queue of backfill jobs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics/railgun#managing-the-queue-of-backfill-jobs).

## Backfill triggers and their effectsâ

The following table details the different actions that can cause a metric backfill.

#| Location| Change| Impact  
---|---|---|---  
1| [Metrics Operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#metrics)| A new metric is created.| 

  * The new metric will be backfilled. It will only start to output values once the backfill finishes.
  * No impact on the remaining metrics.

  
2| [Metrics Operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#metrics)| The definition of a metric is changed, e.g. window definition, group by fields, or aggregation â with the following exceptions:

  * Changing the name of the metric.
  * Changing the fallback value.

| 

  * The modified metric will stop outputting values. It will only restart outputting values once the backfill finishes.
  * There's no impact on the remaining metrics.

  
3| [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/navigating-pulse#plans)| Metrics are moved from one Metrics Operator to another (existing or new one).| Same impact as #1, since this will require new metrics to be created in one of the operators, and deleted from the other.  
4| [Plans](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/navigating-pulse#plans)| The type of a field is changed, either on the Plan Schema or in a field that is created inside the plan (e.g. by a map operator in the plan), without renaming the field, and the affected field is used in a metric.Note that if the field is renamed, then the metric definition will change and scenario #2 will apply.| Same impact as #2, since metric definition changes.  
5| [Workflows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/navigating-pulse#workflows-tab)| A Plan Service with metrics is deleted and a new one with the same name is created, including plan and plan execution.| All metrics in the Plan Service will be backfilled (because the internal identifier that is generated for the service changes).  
6| [Backfills tab menu](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/navigating-pulse#backfills-tab)| A backfill is [manually triggered](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/managing-metrics-backfills#triggering-a-new-backfill-job).| 

  * You can choose the **Metrics** within the **Metric Operators** of the **Workflow Plan Services** that should be backfilled.
  * Note that the metrics that are going to be backfilled will not have their values set to null / fallback value during the backfill process, which means that, until the backfill is complete, they will return the old values from before executing the backfill.

# Metrics in Railgun

Was this page helpful?Â 

A [metric](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#metric) is the smallest unit of work in Railgun. It is defined by a time window, a set of `group by` fields (optionally coupled with a matching set of `lookup by` fields), an aggregation function, and an optional filter.

As an example, the metric _"total amount spent by each card over the last month"_ defines a window (_last month_), a `group by` field (_card_) and an aggregation (_total amount_).

## Metric componentsâ

### Windowsâ

The time window that is defined for a metric determines the set of events that are used to compute the metric value. The events that are within the window can change over time â as new events arrive to Railgun, some may be added to the window, while others, that were already in the window, may leave/expire from the window. Railgun ensures that the metric values are kept up to date as events enter and leave the window.

In stream processing, there are many types of windows that can be defined. Below, we list the window types that are supported by Railgun.

#### Sliding Windowsâ

To define a sliding window we just need to specify its size (as a time interval). The window will hold all the events received within this time interval. For example, a sliding window with a 10 minutes size will contain only the events received during the past 10 minutes.

The metric value is updated as soon as new events enter the time interval defined by the window, and/or old events are no longer within this time interval â i.e. as the logical time in Railgun advances. Do note that, as Railgun processes events and the logical time in Railgun advances, it could happen that the window becomes empty (without events) if indeed there are no events for the time frame that is defined by the window.

In Railgun, the lower bound of the window (older events) is exclusive, while the upper bound (more recent events) is inclusive.

#### Landmark Windowsâ

Unlike sliding windows, landmark windows expire all events in the window at once at well-defined moments in time. These instants are defined by a reset expression using the `reset(unit:_)` syntax.

New events are added to the window until the time reaches the trigger instant defined by the reset expression. At that moment, the window resets and starts to refill as new events arrive.

For instance, using `reset(day:_)` means the window resets every day at 00:00.

Landmark windows have some limitations in Railgun that are important to point out:

  1. The reset instant depends on both the expression and the system time zone. Railgun can be configured with a specific time zone for all windows.

  2. The expression must define a **fixed interval** at which the window resets. Non-constant frequencies (such as specific weekdays or day-of-month ranges) are not supported, since they are also used by Railgun to configure time intervals for backfills and data retention, which require a predictable, constant repeating frequency.

The following table lists the supported expressions for landmark resets:

Expression| Reset frequency  
---|---  
`reset(day:_)`| Daily at 00:00  
`reset(hour:_)`| Every hour at the start of the hour  
`reset(min:_)`| Every minute at the `:00` second mark  
  
Default values

When a unit is omitted from the expression, Railgun assumes the value is `0` for smaller units and `_` (every) for larger units. For example, `reset(day: _)` automatically assumes `hour: 0`, `min: 0`, and `sec: 0`.

  3. The lower bound of the window (older events) is inclusive, while the upper bound (more recent events) is exclusive.

  4. Currently, Railgun does not support using landmark windows together with:

     * Count Distinct aggregations being used in a metric inside those windows;
     * Output Every;
     * Snapshot Metrics;
     * Delays specified for those windows.



No support for tumbling windows

[Tumbling windows](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/concepts-glossary#tumbling-windows) are similar to landmark windows. The difference is that tumbling windows are only defined by their size, and they tumble/reset every time they reach that size. Railgun only supports landmark windows because tumbling windows don't provide a practical advantage over them.

Additionally, tumbling windows may not yield the result that users are expecting. For instance, the tumbling of the windows starts counting at the origin of the Unix time. It is a common misunderstanding that a tumbling windows of 1 day would reset every day at 00:00, but this does not happen due to adjustments such as leap seconds.

#### Adding Delays to Windowsâ

In addition to the window types that are listed above, it is possible to add a delay to a window. For instance, Railgun allows to define a sliding window of one day with a delay of one day, as a way to compute the metric based on the events only from the previous day.

#### Non-windowed Metricsâ

Railgun makes it possible to define metrics that are not bound to a specific time window. These metrics include all events available in the system, and are updated as new events arrive. Such windowless metrics are useful for computing aggregations over the lifetime of the associated entities; for example, the total amount spent by a customer since the beginning of recorded data, or the first time a customer executed a certain type of transaction.

info

Non-windowed metrics can only use a limited set of aggregations. Whereas metrics with sliding time windows can use all aggregations, non-windowed metrics are limited to the `Max` and `Min` aggregations.

When first creating a non-windowed metric, the resulting [backfill](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/railgun-engine/backfills) will process all events from the earliest available records until the current time. The value of the metric will then be continually updated as new events arrive, while keeping into account the values previously calculated, even when these values result from events that later expire from the maximum data lookup period due to the application of our data retention policies.

For example, a metric that computes the total amount transacted by a customer towards a specific beneficiary will seamlessly accumulate the value as new transactions are processed; older transactions that are no longer available in the system will not decrease the value of the metric, since Railgun preserves an internal state for metric values as part of its operation.

warning

If the definition of a non-windowed metric is updated, the metric will be backfilled again, but the new value will not take into account events that are no longer available due to the data retention policy.

### Group Byâ

Similar to SQL, we can define a (non-empty) set of fields in the events to partition windows into groups and compute aggregations individually over these groups. As an example, we can group by the country field to do a count of transactions per country.

The metric then returns the aggregated value (count of transactions) of the group whose key matches the grouping field (country) of the current event.

### Lookup Byâ

Optionally, it is possible to specify a set of alternative lookup fields, compatible with the grouping fields, so that the metric will return the aggregation for the group matching the `Lookup By` fields of each event, instead of the group matching the `Group By` fields.

This overrides the default behavior of the `Group By` operator, and allows the retrieval of the aggregation for any of the partitions, as long as the schema of the data stream contains additional fields that can hold the same values as those of the grouping fields (e.g. a _sender_id_ and a _recipient_id_ , or a _origin_country_ and a _destination_country_ , etc.) and can therefore be specified in group-by/lookup-by pairs.

This expands the range of insights the metric can provide, such as determining the total amount received by the account that is sending money in a transaction.

A specific example where such lookup metrics might be useful is to calculate an accountâs recent running balance (net flow of money) within a rolling period of time, such as the past week prior to each transaction. To do so, one might set up the following structure:

  * A regular group-by metric to get the total sent by the transaction's sender:  
`{ groupBy: [$sender], aggregation: sum($amount), window: 7 days }`
  * A lookup metric to get the total _received_ by the transaction's sender:  
`{ groupBy: [$receiver], lookupBy: [$sender], aggregation: sum($amount), window: 7 days }`
  * A [map operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference#map) that subtracts the former from the latter (`total_received_7d - total_sent_7d`), thus combining the two metrics into a third [derived field](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#features) providing the sender's current balance.



The [Using Lookup Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics/using-lookup-metrics) page describes how to implement this example in detail.

Compatibility of the lookup and grouping fields

For the lookup to work, the lookup fields must be compatible both in number and [data type](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) with the grouping fields.

Refer to the [Using Lookup Metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics/using-lookup-metrics) page to learn how to create lookup metrics in Pulse.

warning

Lookup By fields are not supported in cross-channel metrics.

### Aggregationsâ

Aggregations allow performing computations over the multiple events that are in the metric window at a given point in time.

#### Countâ

Returns the count of events.

  * **Initial value:** 0
  * **Return type:** long



#### Sumâ

Returns the sum of values of a given field in the events.

  * **Supported operand types:** integer, long, float and double
  * **Initial value:** null
  * **Return type:** long (if operand is an integer or long) or double (if operand is a float or double)



info

The sum is computed as a plain Java sum. Railgun does not use algorithms such as [Kahan's summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahan_summation_algorithm) to reduce numerical errors when summing float or double values.

#### Averageâ

Returns the average value of a given field in the events.

  * **Supported operand types:** integer, long, float and double
  * **Initial value:** 0
  * **Return type:** double



#### Standard Deviationâ

Returns the standard deviation of the values of a given field in the events. The standard deviation is computed in an incremental way by using the [Knuth-Welford's online algorithm](https://www.johndcook.com/blog/standard_deviation/).

  * **Supported operand types:** integer, long, float and double
  * **Initial value:** 0
  * **Return type:** double



#### Max / Minâ

Returns the maximum or minimum value that was observed for a given field in the events. For sliding windows, Railgun computes this aggregation by using the [sliding window minimum/maximum algorithm](https://www.nayuki.io/page/sliding-window-minimum-maximum-algorithm).

  * **Supported operand types:** integer, long, float and double
  * **Initial value:** null
  * **Return type:** same type as the operand



Performance guideline(s)

The algorithm that is used is designed to be as computationally efficient as possible, taking into account that the state is persisted on disk. The algorithm keeps a sorted deque of values that will eventually become the current maximum/minimum values as events expire from the window.

However, if the values of the operand that is used in the aggregation are monotonically increasing (for `min`), such as a timestamp, or monotonically decreasing (for `max`), the underlying deque that is used will keep increasing in size because all values will eventually become the current maximum/minimum. As a consequence, latencies will increase as this deque grows (due to the cost of serializing/deserializing the deque) and may eventually hit a system limitation.

For reccommendations on how to handle these kinds of metrics, refer to the [Usage of min() and max() aggregations](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/best-practices/metrics/railgun#usage-of-min-and-max-aggregations) section in the "Best Practices for Metrics in Railgun" page.

#### Prevâ

Returns the previous value that was observed for a given field.

  * **Supported operand types:** boolean, string, integer, long, float and double
  * **Initial value:** null
  * **Return type:** same type as the operand



#### Lastâ

Returns the last value that was observed for a given field. The use of this aggregation is **only useful when the metric uses a filter** where only a subset of events can update the aggregation (in this case it would return the value of the field for the last event that matched the filter). Otherwise, the value returned by this aggregation is the value of the field in the event that is currently being processed, which makes the metric useless.

  * **Supported operand types:** boolean, string, integer, long, float and double
  * **Initial value:** null
  * **Return type:** same type as the operand



#### Count Distinctâ

Returns the **exact** count of distinct values of a set of fields (one or more fields) in the events.

As an example, if we observe the following values for the fields `(country,amount)`:

Event| Country| Amount  
---|---|---  
1| Portugal| 100  
2| Spain| 200  
3| Spain| 300  
4| Portugal| 100  
  
...then, a distinct count with the fields `(country,amount)` would return 3; a distinct count with field `(country)` would return 2; and a distinct count with field `(amount)` would return 3.

  * **Supported operand types:** boolean, string, integer, long, float and double
  * **Initial value:** 0
  * **Return type:** long



Performance Guideline(s)

Even though there isn't a strict limit to the amount of operands that can be used in the aggregation, a maximum of 2 is recommended. The size/space of the values of the operand fields may also have an impact on the overall performance. Larger values imply larger keys in RocksDB, which reduces the amount of data that the system can cache in memory.

The cardinality of distinct values may also have a performance impact. More distinct values increases the likelihood of having to read values from disk (instead of reading them from memory), which has a performance impact.

### Filtersâ

A filter is a boolean expression against which events are evaluated to decide whether a given event should (if evaluates to true) or not contribute to the metric value. The filter expression **is optional** and is defined as a [PQL expression](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/using-pql-in-features#pql-expressions).

#### Functions available in filtersâ

In the PQL expression that defines the filter, there are some utility functions that are available and can be used. As an example, the `StringUtils.upperCase` function can be used in a filter: `StringUtils.upperCase(country) == "PORTUGAL"`.

Railgun doesn't allow for clients to plug in their own functions. Instead, it supports the following commonly used functions:

Name| Fully Qualified Name  
---|---  
StringTools| com.feedzai.commons.udfs.StringTools  
StringUtils| org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils  
Collections| com.feedzai.pulse.fraud.udf.Collections  
Country| com.feedzai.pulse.fraud.udf.Country  
Crypto| com.feedzai.pulse.fraud.udf.Crypto  
Location| com.feedzai.pulse.fraud.udf.Location  
Maths| com.feedzai.pulse.fraud.udf.Maths  
Strings| com.feedzai.pulse.fraud.udf.Strings  
Time| com.feedzai.pulse.fraud.udf.Time  
Zip| com.feedzai.pulse.fraud.udf.Zip  
CollectionUDF| com.feedzai.pulse.pkernel.runtime.CollectionUDFs  
  
More functions can be added to this list but must be first evaluated by the Railgun maintainers.

danger

This feature is maintained to facilitate Railgun adoption. It will eventually be deprecated, and as such it has limited support.

info

This limitation only applies to the usage of functions in metrics' filters. **It does not apply** to the usage of functions (UDFs) in Pulse map operators.

## Fallback Valueâ

When defining a metric in Pulse, users may choose to define a **fallback value** for the metric. When this fallback value is defined, Pulse will automatically coalesce `null` metric values to the value that the user defines.

There are two occasions where metrics calculated by Railgun can return a `null` value:

  1. **When the metrics' aggregation can output a null value**. As an example, a "Last" aggregation can return `null` if there is no last value (i.e. no event is contributing to the metric), or if the last value exists but is null. But a "Count" will never output a `null` as it will return 0 if no event is within the metric window. See the default values for each specific aggregation that Railgun supports.

  2. **While the metrics is being backfilled**. For example, when a metric was just created, or its definition was updated, it will output a `null` value until its backfill successfully completes.




This means that any downstream logic in Pulse workflows must take into account that the metrics' values can be `null`. The possibility to define a fallback value for these cases makes the workflow's behavior more user-friendly and less error-prone.

**By default** , the fallback value is enabled with a predetermined value that is automatically derived from the metric output type:

  * If the output type is a **String** , null values will be coalesced to an **empty string** ("").
  * If the output type is an **Integer or floating point** , null values will be coalesced to **0**.
  * If the output type is a **Boolean** , null values will not be coalesced, remaining as **null**.



The fallback value can also be **set to a custom value** , by entering the desired value in the input box next to the "Enable" checkbox:

Custom fallback values

Custom fallback values must be appropriate for the metrics' data type; otherwise the validations will fail. If the input box is left empty, then a null or empty string (for String data types) will be used for the coalesced value.

It is also possible to **disable the fallback value** (by unmarking the "Enabled" checkbox). In this case, no coalescing wil be applied. If the metric value is null, then it will be forwarded as null to the remainder of the workflow.

## Output Every (Scheduled Metrics equivalent)â

This is a feature that can be optionally enabled and that causes the metric value to only be updated/refreshed at a given frequency, defined by a reset expression. It is as if Railgun periodically takes a snapshot of the metric value at a given moment in time, and outputs that value until the next snapshot is taken.

The update frequency is defined by a reset expression (see Landmark Windows for supported units).

Rationale for `output every`

This feature was added so that users can have metrics that semantically are equivalent to [scheduled metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/scheduled-metrics-jobs), i.e. metrics that only refresh/update with a given frequency, and that are computed by running Spark jobs against the Event Storage.

Performance-wise, the metric continues to be updated in real time â its internal state continues to be updated one event at a time.

No support for the `first` aggregation

The `first` aggregation is not supported due to performance reasons. To compute the first aggregation Railgun would need to keep a queue of all event field values that can potentially become the output of the aggregation. This means that the queue would grow linearly with the number of events in the window.

For the same reason, it is not a good idea to use the minimum aggregation over a timestamp.

## Snapshot Metricsâ

This feature is similar to Output Every metrics, with the caveat that instead of storing a single snapshot that is then replaced by a more recent one, Railgun allows a pre-defined number of snapshots to be stored and read.

As with Output Every, the frequency of the snapshots is defined by a reset expression; the difference is that Snapshot metrics also require the user to define a snapshot retention. For example, using `reset(day:_)` with a retention of 4 snapshots allows the user to read data from the past 4 days.

info

Snapshot metrics can be used as a replacement for the Output Every metrics by configuring a Snapshot metric with a retention value of 1.

However, keep in mind that Output Every metrics are more space conservative and will have better performance.

Since we store multiple snapshots we must be able to query these snapshots. To achieve this, users can inject an event with a timestamp in the past and Railgun will look up the closest previous snapshot available.

The example below shows how injecting events in a certain day will return the snapshot stored in the previous day. If a snapshot is no longer available due to being expired, Railgun will return a 'null' value in response.

## Cross-channel metricsâ

A **cross-channel** metric is a specific case of an [omnichannel metric](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#omnichannel-metrics) that only has **2[channels](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows#channels)**, in which:

  * Only one **Secondary** channel can contribute to the cross-channel metric.
  * Only one **Main** channel will fetch the metric value, created and updated on the **Secondary** channel.
    * The **Main** channel **cannot contribute** to the cross-channel metric.



Note that each channel has its own detection strategy, and it's implemented in a Pulse application [workflow](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows).

See the [Using cross-channel metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering/creating-metrics/using-cross-channel-metrics) page to know how to create Cross-channel metrics in Pulse.

caution

Do not confuse these metrics with [omnichannel metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/workflows/plans-in-workflows#omnichannel-metrics), which are a superset of metrics that can be used in multiple channels, and can have **more than one** channel contribute to them. Also note that Railgun doesn't support omnichannel at the moment.

# Creating a Stratified Sample

Was this page helpful?Â 

Generating a stratified sample is very common in fraud detection scenarios and represents the basis for [Feature Engineering](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering).

Pulse enables you to design a [Plan](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans) and generate a stratified sample from terabytes of historical data, with little need for manual actions, technical proficiency in external tools and access to cluster infrastructure.

info

Alternatively, you can perform these actions from the JupyterLab  user interface. Standard notebooks are available within [JupyterLab](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/interacting-with-pulse-via-jupyterlab) â in particular the Sampling Notebook, which demonstrates how to apply efficient sampling strategies over large datasets using Feedzai's sampling library.

## How toâ

The following instructions exemplify a way to generate a stratified sample for a card fraud scenario. This plan extracts some cards that never had fraud, and all fraudulent cards, out of the original data, and obtains all transactions for those cards.

To design a plan and generate a stratified sample for the _Transactions_ data source, execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Data Science tab** ,  **Add** a new plan.

  2. Set the plan as [Non-Deployable](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans#non-deployable-plans).

  3. Design your Stratified Sample plan as displayed in the following image:




Configure the elements as follows:

  1. Edit the **Source** element and specify the date source. For example, _Cleaned Transactions_.

  2. Edit the **Map** element to add a new field to the date source, as follows:

Clipboard

You can also  copy Operators to the clipboard in order to paste them in other Plans.

     1. Select the **Fields to Add** tab and name the new field as _isFraud_.

     2. Write the following expression for the field value:
            
            if (Fraud == 'True') then 1 else 0  
            

     3. Add the field to the list of fields to be added to the date source.

  3. Edit the **Group By** element to specify grouping by _AccountID_ (represents the card number in this case) and calculate the _Sum_ aggregation of the _isFraud_ field.

Checkpoint

At this stage you have the number of fraud occurrences for each card number, calculated into the _sumFraud_ field. The plan workflow will branch to segment fraudulent cards from cards that never observed fraud.

  4. Edit the **Filter** element with the following expression to obtain only the card numbers **with** fraudulent transactions.
         
         sumFraud > 0  
         

  5. Edit the **Filter** element with the following expression to obtain only the card numbers **without** fraudulent transactions.
         
         sumFraud == 0  
         

  6. Edit the **Sample** element to extract only 5% of all cards **without** fraudulent transactions.

Checkpoint

At this stage you have all fraudulent card numbers separate from a smaller subset of all cards that never had fraud. The plan workflow will recover the complete transactions for all cards in both branches and re-merge them together as a single dataset.

  7. Edit the **Join** element to perform a join operation, by _AccountID_ , with the original data and recover the original transactions for those cards. You now have all transactions for cards where fraud **occurred**.

  8. Edit the **Join** element to perform a join operation, by _AccountID_ , with the original data and recover the original transactions for those cards. You now have all transactions for cards where fraud **never occurred**.

  9. Execute a **Union** of both **Join** elements.

  10. Save the results of your plan to a data **Sink**. For example, a new date source named _Stratified Sample_.




Finally:

  1. the plan to execute all actions on the original date source and generate an improved one.

     1. Define the **Data Source with ID source** as the original date source. For example, _Cleaned Transactions._

     2. Expand the  to have access to additional configurations:

        1. [Job Profile](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles): Allows you to choose a profile containing properties that best fit the **Spark Job** that you want to run. Check the page [Selecting Profiles](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/tuning-job-executions-with-job-profiles/selecting-profiles) to learn more about this functionality.

        2. [Data Partitioning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/data-partitioning-for-the-metrics-operator): If you have [Metrics Operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference) in your plan, this functionality allows to choose the **Data Partitioning** option that enables **Spark** to re-organize the data into different partitions as homogenous and well distributed as possible. Pulse allows you to choose the options: **Data-Aware Optimizer** , **Hash-Based** , and **Manual Partition**. These options are described in detail in the **[Data Partitioning](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/data-partitioning-for-the-metrics-operator)** page.

Metrics Operators

The **Data Partitioning** option takes effect only if you have metrics operators in your plan. Otherwise, this option does not affect the performance of the plan execution.

     3. Configure the **Data Sink with ID sink** as the new and clean data source. For example, _Stratified Sample._

     4. **Run** the plan to generate a new data source, in Pulse, named _Stratified Sample._ Pulse also saves an output file with the transformed data to your filesystem.

  2. [Analyze](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data) the _Stratified Sample_ data source to check the distribution of fraud and non-fraud transactions.




## Next Stepsâ

When you have sampled and understood your data, you are ready to move on to [designing features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering) for your model.

# Identifying Patterns

Was this page helpful?Â 

Before you generate metrics and design features you must first understand your data, and what are the clues that might indicate how each record should be classified in the end. For example, clues that point to fraudulent and non-fraudulent transactions.

To start gaining some initial insight into your dataset and uncover patterns, you must run a preliminary analysis on a [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources). Pulse lets you visualize statistics for each data field and break them down, for example, by fraud or not-fraud.

info

Alternatively, you can perform these actions from the JupyterLab  user interface. Standard notebooks are available within [JupyterLab](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/interacting-with-pulse-via-jupyterlab) â in particular the Data Exploration Standard Notebook, which demonstrates how to perform efficient data exploration using Feedzai's exploration library.

## How toâ

To perform an analysis on your [Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources) and, as an example, start identifying some fraud patterns, execute the following actions:

  1. In the  **Data Science** tab, select your **Data Source** from the **Data Sources list**.
  2. Use the  option to generate statistics for the **Data Source**. Select which are the breakdown fields and values to slice the results into. For example, **Fraud**.
  3. Use the  **View Statistics** option to go in depth into the generated insight for each field. When looking into the analysis details to understand the data, you can:
     1. **Analyze statistics**  
For example, look for negative values in _Numerical_ fields such as _TransactionAmount_. This may suggest that there is work to do, namely [cleaning up your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/cleaning-up-the-data).

     2. **Breakdown the statistics** , for example by **Fraud**  
This lets you observe your data and start to identify patterns, such as different distributions when you look at the _CardholderPresent_ field in fraudulent and non-fraudulent instances separately. This may hint at some correlation between the _TransactionAmount_ and _Fraud_ fields that you should further explore when [processing your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data).




Generated statistics

Depending on the data types you defined for each field when [importing your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/cleaning-and-loading-your-data/importing-your-dataset-into-pulse), Pulse [generates different metrics](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis).

For _Numerical_ fields, Pulse generates arithmetic metrics such as mean, minimum and maximum, while for _Categorical_ data, Pulse only generates the total count and distinct values.

Breakdowns

When you [analyze a Data Source](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-source-analysis), you must always select for which breakdown fields and values you want Pulse to calculate statistics.

Skipping this action and simply calculating broken-down metrics for all possible combination of fields and values could rapidly cause performance degradation due to lack of computational resources.

## Next Stepsâ

You are now able to perform a high-level analysis on your historical data and have raised some insights, e.g. how the cardholder being present at the transaction or how the transaction country correlates with fraud.

You are ready to [sample your data](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/creating-a-data-science-project/processing-your-data/analyzing-and-sampling-your-data/creating-a-stratified-sample) and start [designing features](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/feature-engineering) for your model.

# Conditional Expressions in PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

Conditional expressions of PQL return a value based on a condition.

Syntax:
    
    
    if <condition> then <then-case-expression> else <else-case-expression>  
    

Where:

  * `<condition>` is a boolean expression.

  * `<then-case-expression>` and `<else-case-expression>` are obligatory values.

If the condition is true, the conditional expression returns the value of the then-case-expression, otherwise the value of the else-case-expression.




Example:
    
    
    if( POSEntryMode == 'Swiped' or POSEntryMode == 'Keyed' or POSEntryMode == 'Chip' )  
      then 'Card Present'  
      else POSEntryMode

# Function Calls in PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

Function calls allow you to execute predefined functions on current values. There are two types of functions that can be called:

  * Built-in functions of Pulse
  * User-Defined Functions (UDFs) â a set of additional functions bundled with Pulse



This topic gives an overview of the possible function calls, and points you to the right topics to learn more.

## Built-in functionsâ

### Checking NULLsâ

Return type| Method| Description  
---|---|---  
`bool`| `isNull(int? a)`| Checks if an integer value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(long? a)`| Checks if a long value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(double? a)`| Checks if a double value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(float? a)`| Checks if a float value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(bool? a)`| Checks if a boolean value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(string? a)`| Checks if a string value is null.  
`bool`| `isNull(tuple? a)`| Checks if a tuple value is null.  
  
### Math functionsâ

All methods of the [java.lang.Math](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/Math.html) package are available in PQL. Besides those methods, you can use the following math functions:

Return type| Method| Description  
---|---|---  
`int`| `max(list_of_int)`| Returns the maximum value of a list of numbers.  
`long`| `max(list_of_long)`| Returns the maximum value of a list of numbers.  
`double`| `max(list_of_double)`| Returns the maximum value of a list of numbers.  
`float`| `max(list_of_float)`| Returns the maximum value of a list of numbers.  
`int`| `min(list_of_int)`| Returns the minimum value of a list of numbers.  
`long`| `min(list_of_long)`| Returns the minimum value of a list of numbers.  
`double`| `min(list_of_double)`| Returns the minimum value of a list of numbers.  
`float`| `min(list_of_float)`| Returns the minimum value of a list of numbers.  
`boolean`| `between(int val, int left, int right)`| Returns true if the value is greater or equal to the left boundary and lower or equal to the right boundary.  
`boolean`| `between(long val, long left, long right)`| Returns true if the value is greater or equal to the left boundary and lower or equal to the right boundary.  
`boolean`| `between(double val, double left, double right)`| Returns true if the value is greater or equal to the left boundary and lower or equal to the right boundary.  
`boolean`| `between(float val, float left, float right)`| Returns true if the value is greater or equal to the left boundary and lower or equal to the right boundary.  
  
### Stringsâ

Return type| Method| Description  
---|---|---  
`string`| `str(int a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(long a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(double a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(float a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(bool a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`string`| `str(string a)`| Returns a new string that is the textual representation of `a`.  
`int`| `indexOf(string s, string c)`| Returns the index within string `s` of the first occurrence of the string `c`.  
`string`| `substring(string s, int begin)`| Returns a new string that is a substring of string `s`.  
`string`| `substring(string s, int begin, int end)`| Returns a new string that is a substring of string `s`.  
`bool`| `contains(string s, string c)`| Returns `true` if string `c` is a substring of string `s`, or `false` otherwise.  
`bool`| `startsWith(string s, string c)`| Returns `true` if string `c` is a prefix of string `s`, or `false` otherwise.  
`bool`| `endsWith(string s, string c)`| Returns `true` if string `c` is a suffix of string `s`, or `false` otherwise.  
  
Container functions in `Map` and `Metrics` operators

Functions that operate on collections (like `List`s, `Set`s or `Map`s) are not supported in the PQL fields of [Map Operators or Metric Operators](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/plans/operators-reference).

For example, using `contains` or `indexOf` on collections in PQL fields of such operators will result in an error.

The recommended alternative is to use UDFs (User Defined Functions) instead of these built-in functions.

## UDF callsâ

Pulse comes with a set of [User-Defined Functions (UDFs)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions) that can be used in addition to the built-in functions.

UDFs in Metrics

When using UDFs in metric filters and aggregations, UDFs receive fields from a single event and not from a collection of events.

You can use the following syntax to call a UDF:
    
    
    <class_name>.<function_name> ( <arguments> )  
    

For example, to concatenate two strings:
    
    
    Strings.strcat("One", "Two") // Returns "OneTwo"  
    

java regex syntax

Pulse uses the Java regex flavor for UDFs, which means that all regular expressions must conform to the syntax and rules of Java's `java.util.regex.Pattern` class.

According to the usual regex syntax, when you need to match a literal special character that has meaning in regex (e.g. `*`, `+`, `?`, `.`), you must escape it using a backslash (`\`) within the regex pattern (e.g. `\*`, `\+`, and so on).

However, because the regex pattern itself is often passed as a Java String literal, the backslash (`\`) used for escaping the regex special character must itself be escaped according to Java String rules.

Therefore, to include an escaped character like `\*` (match literal asterisk) in a regular expression defined as a Java string, you must write it as `\\*`.

# Handling NULL Values with PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

NULL is a special value that represents the absence of a valid value. Any operation that acts on it as if it was a valid value fails with a NullPointerException. Untreated datasets might contain NULL values, and so they are potentially unsafe for any activity within Pulse. This topic describes how to make datasets more robust by handling NULL values using PQL expressions.

## Replacing NULL valuesâ

One of the common ways to handle NULLs is to replace them with a value that fits into the data field's type. It's common to pick the substitute value so that it doesn't represent a meaningful value for that data field. For instance, a NULL in the transaction amount field could be replaced by 0. To accomplish this replacement, you can use the **coalesce operator** (`??`) in a map operator or metric operator.

Usage of the ?? operator:
    
    
    <good-case-value> ?? <null-case-value>  
    

This expression returns `<good-case-value>`, unless `<good-case-value>` is NULL. If `<good-case-value>` is NULL, the expression returns `<null-case-value>`.

Example:

### Coalescing aggregations to a value other than 0â

Aggregations return 0 instead of a NULL when there are no values to count the aggregation on. For example, when the maximum amount is queried over a time window using a filter that filters out all the records.

In some cases you might want to return something different from 0.

The following example shows how to return -1 in case an aggregation of a metric is called on an empty subset of data:

### Nullable typesâ

Untreated input fields can contain NULL values. Hence, PQL treats every input field as a nullable type, meaning a type that can contain NULL values in addition to an original data type.

This fact is marked with a ? in the data type name.

For example, the _Amount_ field is not of _double_ type, but of _double?_ , meaning a type that contains all double values plus the NULL.

When using both nullable and non-nullable types in an [arithmetic operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/operators-in-pql) or in a [function](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql) that returns a numeric value, the resulting data type is nullable.
