# Operators in PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

This topic gives you an overview of the arithmetic and boolean operators that you can use in PQL expressions, and the precedence of all operators.

## Arithmetic operatorsâ

PQL uses the following arithmetic operators:

Operator | Meaning  
---|---  
`+` | addition  
`-` | subtraction  
`*` | multiplication  
`/` | division  
`%` | integer remainder  
`^` | exponentiation  
  
Example: `Balance - Amount`

Type promotion when using arithmetic operators

The arithmetic operators obey the following type promotion rules:

  1. If at least one of the arguments is a double, the result is a double.
  2. If at least one of the arguments is a float, the result is a float, unless the result is a double because of the first rule.
  3. If at least one of the arguments is a long, the result is a long, unless the result is a double or float because of the first two rules.



## Boolean operatorsâ

Boolean operators are operators that return a boolean value. They include:

  * `<` , `<=`, `==`, `!=`, `>=`, `>`

info

Only numeric values can be compared with the <, <=, >=, and > operators.

  * `and` , `or` , `!` (not)




Example:
    
    
    POSEntryMode == 'Swiped' or POSEntryMode == 'Keyed' or POSEntryMode == 'Chip'  
    

## Operator precedenceâ

The following table lists PQL operators according to their precedence order. Operators at the top of the table have higher precedence.

Operator type | Operator(s)  
---|---  
grouping | `(expr)`  
unary | `+expr`, `-expr`, `!`  
arithmetic - exponential | `^`  
cast | `exp:type`  
arithmetic â multiplicative | `*`, `/`, `%`  
arithmetic â additive | `+`, `-`  
coalesce | `??`Note that this operator has a different precedence in RDL.  
comparison | `<`, `<=`, `==`, `>=`, `>`, `!=`  
logical â AND | `and`  
logical â OR | `or`  
assignment | `=`  
  
Cast operator precedence

Notice that the _cast_ operator precedence lies between arithmetic operators. If an expression needs to be cast before an exponentiation, it needs to be enclosed in parentheses (_grouping_ operator).

The following rules apply:

  * operators with higher precedence than other operators are evaluated before them;
  * operators on the same line have the same precedence: 
    * all binary operators except for the assignment operator are evaluated from left to right;
    * assignment operator is evaluated right to left.



### Examplesâ

Arithmetic and boolean operators of PQL follow the common rules of mathematics regarding functionality and precedence.

Arithmetic and boolean operators have higher precedence than the [`??` (coalesce) operator](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/handling-null-values-with-pql), meaning that the `??` operator gets evaluated after arithmetic and boolean operators.

Example: `a + b ?? c + d` is equivalent to `(a+b) ?? (c+d)`.

# PQL Data Types and Type Conversions

Was this page helpful?Â 

This topic gives you an overview of data types in PQL, and how to convert data from one data type to another.

PQL uses the following **primitive data types**.

Data type| Examples  
---|---  
int| 
    
    
    -289
    
    0
    
    42  
  
long| 
    
    
    123456789
    
    1l
    
    -2L  
  
float| 
    
    
    0.99
    
    -1.23e-100f
    
    3.14F  
  
double| 
    
    
    1234567.89012
    
    1.23456e300d
    
    1.23456e-300d
    
    1e1D  
  
bool| 
    
    
    true
    false  
  
string| 
    
    
    "John Doe"
    'John Doe'  
  
These data types are equivalent to the Java primitive data types. To see the exact definition or range for each, check the [Java documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html).

The **non-primitive data types** of PQL are:

  * Tuples
  * Collections:
    * Lists
    * Sets
    * Maps



Do not confuse these types with lists and map operators that you can create in the Pulse UI. They belong to two different levels of implementation. The non-primitive PQL data types are used only in PQL queries, when computing features. When the PQL computation is finished, Pulse stores the data of these non-primitive types as _Complex_ fields in the output data source.

## Data type mapping between Pulse and PQLâ

The following table shows to which PQL data type each [Pulse data type](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types) is mapped when using input data fields:

Pulse field type (input)| PQL type  
---|---  
Categorical| string  
Complex| the same non-primitive type of PQL  
Date Time| long (UNIX timestamp format)  
Numeric| int, long, float, double  
String| string  
  
The following table shows which PQL data type can be passed as output to which type of output fields. The output field is the data field that the map or metric operator is creating/updating, and its type is one of the [Pulse data types](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/data-sources/data-types).

PQL type| Pulse field type (output)  
---|---  
any data type| Categorical  
int, long, float, double| Numeric  
long, int (UNIX timestamp format)| Date Time  
any non-primitive type| Complex  
string| String  
  
## Converting dataâ

In PQL, each data field, constant, variable, or aggregation result is of a primitive data type. To convert from one data type to another, you can use the following options:

  * Cast operator, to cast a value of a numeric type into another numeric type. Learn more about this operator in the next section of this page.
  * The `str()` [built-in function](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql#built-in-functions) to convert a numeric value to a string.
  * [User-defined functions (UDFs)](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features/function-calls-in-pql#udf-calls). There are [built-in UDFs](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/understanding-pulse/core-concepts/user-defined-functions) that can be used after creating an alias for them. Example: to convert the merchant category code to integer, you can use the `DataConversionTools.stringToInt()` function.



### Cast operatorâ

The cast operator allows you to cast values from a numeric type (int, long, float or double) to another numeric type. There is no built-in cast operator between numeric types and booleans or strings.

To cast a value, use the following syntax: `<value to convert>:<target type>`

Example: `Amount:int` is the value of the Amount field cast to integer.

# PQL in Derived Features

Was this page helpful?Â 

Derived features are new data fields that were calculated based on the original data set.

To create derived features, there are two different cases:

  * Computing data based on a single event (not on aggregated data), using a map operator.
  * Calculating a value based on an aggregation of events, often combining map and metrics operators.



This topic describes how to use PQL in both cases.

## Derived fields without aggregationâ

To calculate new values based on input fields, you can use **map operators** in plans. For that, add a map operator to the plan that processes the input data, and add the PQL expression in the _Expression_ field.

You can use any of the [building blocks of PQL](/pulse/latest/docs/common/pulse/users-guide/rule-guide/creating-features/using-pql-in-features#pql-expressions), except for the aggregations.

### Exampleâ

The following example adds a field called _CountryMatch_ that shows if the merchant country is the same as the country where the card was created.

## Derived field based on aggregationsâ

To aggregate data, use a **metrics operator** in the plan. The UI of the metrics operator allows you to use a shorter list of aggregations: Avg, Min, Max, Count, Count Distinct, Sum and Standard deviation. Other calculations need PQL statements.

PQL allows you to use the following **aggregations** in the _Expression_ field of an aggregation when editing a metrics operator:

Aggregation| Description| Usage example  
---|---|---  
**avg**(field_name)| Returns the average value of the selected numeric field from the aggregated data set.| `avg(Amount)`  
**count**()| Returns the number of rows in the aggregated data set.| `count()`  
**max**(field_name)| Returns the maximum value of the selected numeric field from the aggregated data set.| `max(Amount)`  
**maxBy**(field_name)| Returns the event containing the maximum value in the given numeric field.| `maxBy(Amount).MerchantId`  
**min**(field_name)| Returns the minimum value of the selected numeric field from the aggregated data set.| `min(Amount)`  
**minBy**(field_name)| Returns the event containing the minimum value in the given numeric field.| `minBy(Amount).MerchantId`  
**stddev**(field_name)| Returns the standard deviation of the selected numeric field's values within the aggregated data set.| `stddev(Amount)`  
**sum**(field_name)| Returns the sum of the selected numeric field values in the aggregated data set.| `sum(Amount)`  
  
### Navigate on an aggregated data setâ

The first(), last(), and prev() methods allow to access the first, last, and previous row of the aggregated data set.

  * The current record is the last row of the current dataset if it entered the window, depending on the filters.
  * **first()** is the first transaction in the current window.
  * **last()** is the last transaction in the current window.
  * **prev()** is the transaction before last() that entered the window.



#### Examplesâ

To calculate the geographical distance traveled between two transactions, you can create the following aggregation in a metrics operator:
    
    
    DistanceUtils.haversine(latitude, longitude, prev().latitude, prev().longitude)  
    

To calculate the time span between the first and last transaction within a given window per merchant, you can create the following aggregation in a metrics operator:
    
    
      
    ( let first_timestamp = first().Timestamp ?? 0 in  
      let last_timestamp = last().Timestamp ?? 0 in  
      ( last_timestamp - first_timestamp ) / 60*60*1000.0  
    )

# Reserved Keywords in PQL

Was this page helpful?Â 

Some keywords and symbols cannot be used outside of their original purpose. That means that within a PQL expression, they cannot be used as name of variables, fields or UDFs.

Besides the reserved keywords and symbols, there is a third list of words that cannot be used in PQL expressions due to limitations related to Java.

## Reserved keywordsâ

Keyword| Purpose  
---|---  
and| Comparison operator  
as| Import aliasing  
asc| Order criteria (ascending)  
bool| Boolean type  
by| Field descriptor (i.e. group by, order by)  
desc| Order criteria (descending)  
double| Double type  
else| Conditional branching  
float| Float type  
from| Select descriptor (i.e. select from)  
group| Grouping operator  
if| Conditional branching  
import| Import statement for UDFs  
in| Variable binding (i.e. let a = 1 in)  
int| Integer type  
into| Select target (i.e. group by price into ev)  
join| Join operator  
let| Variable binding (i.e. let a = 1 in)  
limit| Limit operator (i.e. limit 1, 10)  
long| Long type  
on| Join operator  
or| Comparison operator  
order| Order operator  
select| Select operator  
Stream| Stream declaration  
string| String type  
then| Conditional branching  
unit| Unit type  
where| Select discriminator  
  
## Reserved symbolsâ

Symbol| Purpose  
---|---  
.| Field accessor  
+| Addition  
-| Subtraction  
*| Multiplication  
/| Division  
%| Division remainder (mod)  
^| Exponentiation  
<| Less than  
<=| Less than or Equal to  
=| Assignment  
==| Equal  
!=| Different  
>=| Greater than or Equal to  
>| Greater than  
{| Block separation  
}| Block separation  
:| Casting, selection, etc.  
;| Statement separation  
@| Annotation  
??| Coalesce operator  
  
## Java keywordsâ

For internal compatibility reasons, the following Java keywords are not allowed:
    
    
    abstract  
    assert  
    break  
    byte  
    case  
    catch  
    char  
    class  
    const  
    continue  
    default  
    do  
    enum  
    extends  
    final  
    finally  
    for  
    goto  
    implements  
    instanceof  
    interface  
    native  
    new  
    package  
    private  
    protected  
    public  
    return  
    static  
    strictfp  
    super  
    switch  
    synchronized  
    this  
    throw  
    throws
